All in all, I wish I could give this more than one "yes." A truly rare gem in the wilds of indie games (and the wasteland of EA).
Think Firefly wild west scifi meets Prison Architect base building.
In general, I avoid EA games as they often fail to deliver anything but hollow promises and shallow games. RimWorld is one of the rare exceptions (Factorio being another). It is a complete game that is well polished, intuitive, and highly extensible. It's only in EA because the developer is still releasing and tweaking things.
Pros:
- Highly customizable. From the various options to the crazy different scenarios to a bazillion workshop mods. You can make it almost as stupid easy or impossibly hard as your heart desires.
- Survival done right (Don't Starve comes to mind here). Yes you die and fail a lot, but you nearly always know why and how to do better next time. It's usually your fault, not the game's. Improving yourself on the next run is natural and a lot of fun.
- Highly intuitive. Uses WASD for scrolling, mouse for selection and orders. Lots of menus and statistics.
- Highly engaging storylines. You start to become attached to your little guys and gals. I cry inside everytime one of them dies (which is unfortunately often).
- You can force orders on almost anyone at almost anytime. This gives the player a lot of control to fix problems they see before everything falls apart. This game would super suck without this.
- Still getting better and deeper with each new release.
Cons:
- The time dialation could use some work. There's only 1x, 2x, and 3x. I permanently set mine on 3x and wouldn't mind even faster options. Also, the game forces to 1x in crucial situations like raids. While that's great to let you assess the situation, I often want to set it back to 3x when I'm ready but can't for too long IMO.
- This is both a pro and a con, but there are some frustrating AI things like villagers not effeciently stacking objects. It's a pro because there are mods to address most any problem in the game (including the stack issue). It's a con because these things aren't in the base game but should be (and we shouldn't have to search for mods to fix basic functionality). It is still an EA though, so there's hope.

Runaway: A Twist of Fate, is the third and final (as of right now) entry into the Runaway game trilogy. The story, while leaping ahead a bit in time from the cliffhanger ending of Runaway: Dream of the Turtle, can be considered a direct sequel since it wraps up the events from that game.
If you have played either of the other two games, which is recommended if you want to know the full story, then you will be familiar with the control scheme. This is a point and click adventure, with the left and right mouse buttons used to explore and pick up items. In your inventory you can examine and combine items, and select them to use in the environment. The puzzles are on the same level of difficulty as the first two games. There are no ways to fail, so if you are having trouble just keep exploring and combining items until you find the solution. A nice addition is a button to press that will show you all the hotspots in an area. That definitely helps make some of the pixel hunting go a lot faster.
The graphics have seen a nice upgrade from the previous game. My biggest complaint, the character models, have been improved, and while still not the best, are more than serviceable. The backgrounds are as nice as they have been in the Runaway series.
The voice acting and sound continues to be done well. There are some new original songs in Runaway: A Twist of Fate. Plenty of effort has been put into making the sound top quality.
One of my biggest complaints of the series has been the underwhelming involvement of Gina. Although saving her is a main plot point of the first two games, she is never really present for much of the games. You have no chance to form any sort of attachment to her. That is addressed in this game, where you will be able to control Gina for large parts of the game. She almost feels like a new character, because you did not have much interaction with her in the previous games. Brian is clearly a different character than when he began the first game, but it makes sense after the adventures you have been on together.
Runaway: A Twist of Fate felt like the shortest game in the series. However, what is there is very enjoyable, and I would much rather play a shorter game that is filled with quality content than a longer game that wears out its welcome.
I fully recommend Runaway: A Twist of Fate. I felt like the previous game, Dream of the Turtle, was a drop in quality in the series, but the trilogy ends on a high note. An additional adventure in the saga of Brian and Gina would be welcome.
Grade: B+

The game itself is mediocre but playable, although some puzzles are counter-intuitive and are difficult to comprehend without a guide.
The hint system isn't that good either. It works sometimes, but usually it points to something you already interacted with and can't do anything else (but it doesn't hint that you need to get an extra item from somewhere else), thus the hint is wasted and it's gonna take ~2 minutes or so to recharge...
What was really annoying is poorly implemented clicking system. Sometimes when you click on an object, it doesn't register or does the wrong thing (for example when you need to throw a powder into the portal, instead the game teleports you as if you pressed the portal with your regular cursor (not the powder one).
This is especially painful during the jigsaw minigame. You have 60 seconds and 35 puzzle pieces. Simple math hints us that you have 1.7 seconds per piece... Even if you memorize all the spots where the pieces go, it's stil impossible due to:
a) you need time to rotate the pieces (which adds at least 1 second or more especially if you need to rotate it several times)
b) there is only 5 pieces visible (which means you can't start with corners, unless you get lucky, because what pieces you get is randomly generated)
c) the precision on the placement must be spot on. Even if you know where to place a piece, sometimes it would cancel anyway and get thrown into the box on the right, thus wasting the precious time.So it's kind of pixel hunting at this point...1.7 seconds to find the correct pixel. GOOD LUCK!
As a result we get an achievement that is impossible to complete for a human being, and i highly doubt even a perfectly scripted bot would be able to (see reason c).
This negative review is staying, unless the achievement gets fixed.

It's a very exciting and fun mode which give lots of opporunity for a losing team to get back into the match and stage a come back and win. If you've played conquest in Battlefield this should be very familiar.  Unlike comparable tank games like Warthunder and World of Tanks, Armored Warfare’s economy is generous and doesn’t needlessly punish you. You don’t lose money playing the highest tier tanks. You don’t lose credits if you don't do well in a match. RNG is not the god of this universe. And you don’t even need to spend a single dime in order to do well. Premium vehicles are largely reskins of existing progression tanks and the unique premiums are not more powerful than comparable progression tanks tier for tier.

The great features of this game include hilarious dialogue from human enemies, non-enemies, and clap-trap robots, as well as a seemingly endless combination of weaponry with different abilities.  Your characters are more-or-less customizable to your game-play style (provided you pick the right character) and with the DLC's there are hours upon hours of play time to be had.  Also, unlike many other games where if you die you have to go back to the last savepoint, in this game you have a chance to save yourself.  Should you be downed by enemies, simply kill one during the "fight for your life" event and you get back up and can continue.  Should you actually die, you simply respawn after paying a sum of money at a NEW-U station and continue the fight!
The not so great features are that the game gets REALLY repetitive as far as enemies and quests go.  After 2-3 hours of gameplay, I find myself having to do something else due to the mind-numbing repetitiveness of the game.  Also, the only way to get anywhere is to do it quickly, so those who prefer to sneak around and kill slowly and methodically are going to have a problem.  The enemies respawn rather quickly, so even if you go quickly through the quest areas you will be fighting enemies both on your way there and on your way back out.  Lastly, the vehicles are not balanced once you enter the second play-through.  This means that while you usually are at a level that can easily handle everything you come accross for quite some time, they can easily destroy your vehicle and consequently put you into an instant "fight for your life" event.
Overall I still enjoy this game after the countless hours I have spent playing it.  I would reccommend this game for anyone who enjoys a good old-fashioned FPS game with an RPG twist.

A rhythm game this is not. You have to block arrows that fly at you by moving around a shield using the directional buttons, but as you can move the shield around whenever you want the only rhythmic aspect is the beat the arrows make impact with the center at. Kind of. The syncopation is *far* from perfect, and the off-beat ticking noise made with each blocked arrow is distracting enough that it makes keeping the beat actively more difficult. Furthermore, because you have to maneuver the shield in front of any given arrow *before* it arrives, if you fall into a groove and start pressing buttons on the beat, you will die immediately.
But it's free, yeah, so if you really, really liked Super Hexagon, and that one boss battle in Undertale then give it a try, but if you're expecting a rhythm-based skill game, this isn't it.

Review:
A promise of something, that could be a fantastic game, a survival against the cold, harsh alien world.
We definitely need games like that, incorporating resource management, skill progression and turn based combat.
Unfortunately this game isn't it.
I will skip graphics and audio part. Graphics is 800x600 and attempts to switch to full screen will make this game unplayable. Audio is stock, but doesn't annoy.
The real problem with this game is gameplay.
Apparently, this game was not play-tested, or if it was, it was playtested by someone with a wciked sense of cruelty.
You see, this title is one, total RNG bull♥♥♥♥.
There is no difficulty setting - each and every game will see you fukked right up in the back end of your gastric system.
Of course, challenging games can be fun, but in 'Link' this isn't even challenging.
Let me show you what I mean.
The rescue mission, lowest difficulty. Survivor starts at the exact opposite end of the map. Your guys rush to them, only to run out of stamina (it regenerates 1 point of stamina per turn, so if you have 5 max, you need 5 turns to regenerate it to max).
You move your survivor towards rescue party.
What happens? Lowest mob moves towards your survivor and kills it with two hits.
Amazing. Or perhaps survivor spawned with a sniper rifle, in which case it may be the only character to survive, whereas your rescue crew will be ganbanged by 3 spiders.
Seriously, there is no difficulty progression. Base attacks, the very first one, will pitch your tiny group of soldiers against a horde of 8-12 aliens, many of which will be top tier units capable of killing your soldier with ONE hit.
Honestly? What was supposed to be a challenging fun, was revealed to be frustrating RNG hell.
What else? Generic loot, limited skill choice and upgrades (for example you can only research one of four techs per branch, characters are limited to like 5 skills).
Constantly growing threat level, even if all you do is just farming for food.
Constantly dropping heat and stamina levels, heat drops even when a soldier sleeps (wtf?).
This crap is really not worth playing. I say this with a heavy heart because I had expectations for this title.
Unfortunately, this one is not a game to be lightly tossed aside. It is a game to be thrown away with great force - and with regret.

I'm pleasantly reminded of FTL, among others, and the game mechanics are fantastic.  TLDR, Buy it.
Main differences between Link and FTL:
- Space combat -> squad combat,
- Dialogue-tree missions with narrative text -> Squad combat missions, trying not to die of exposure or raiders
- Journeying through space -> Protecting your base, and gathering resources from nearby
- Brave Spaceman Seeking Danger On An Adventure -> Tired Spacemen Trying Not To Freeze Or Starve Or Get Murdered By Snow Jawas And Their Stompy Robot Spiders
- New game : Choose what ship to play each game with -> New Game : Choose team-members and victory conditions
- Unlock new team members instead of new ship types
You start with three people in your base / crashed ship.  You build different rooms in the space available, which can passively gather resources, or perform useful tasks when you have a person spend their turn there.  Your team members can level up and gain abilities from a skill tree, and if they have the right ones they're better at using some buildings than others, or have bonuses in combat.   There's a surprising amount of deep and well-balanced resource-balancing strategy here, only some of which I've uncovered.
Your main resources are fuel, food, tools, and knowledge.  You also have characters, which spend stamina and heat to perform tasks, health and heat on away missions, and can die if mismanaged, or be rescued and added to your team on some missions.  Food is used when characters rest to regenerate stamina, tools and knowledge are used to make buildings and equippable items, fuel is used to heat the furnace room (or the entire base, if you upgrade that room enough).  You can upgrade rooms to higher tiers, and some of the higher tiers require access to power, which requires building a power generator next to them and keeping it running via having someone spend their time there every turn.
Away missions seem to fall into three groups -- 1) scavenging for items without freezing to death or getting mauled by bandits, 2) hunting various tiers of badguys to make them less likely to storm your base, 3) trying to escort characters from the wrong side of a map over to the exit zone, so they can join your team.  Available missions change slightly over time, so it's worth checking every once in a while.  The stamina system takes getting used to, though.  Every combat turn, you regenerate as much stamina as you had left at the end of last turn -- so sure, you can technically do four things in a turn if you want, but if you do you'll be limited to doing one a turn until you take a few turns to sit still and breathe and let your stamina regenerate.  Meanwhile, everyone who paced themselves is doing two things a turn all fight, because they paced themselves...  ...but sometimes, if an enemy has just one hit left, it's worth it to spend the extra stamina just to kill them before they can attack you again.  Or is it?  Combat also involves an armor stat, melee and ranged attacks, weapons and armor and trinkets that you have to figure out how to craft all by yourself, and of course various special abilities you can spend XP on when characters level up.
And then there's the laboratory building, where you can research all kind of things that give you special benefits to any of the above systems -- like having your heat meters all go down half as fast, or having all buildings produce twice as much of their resource type.
What I'm trying to say is that they did a very good job of keeping the core number of variables simple (food, fuel, tools, knowledge, buildings, and characters that can do stuff at buildings), and then adding all kinds of very reasonable upgrades and complications for people who know how to make it work.  The only thing in between me and the very difficult victory conditions is my own lack of knowledge of the game -- but I'm learning and improving every time, and every loss I've had is because of a choice I made, and not bad luck.  The unlockables provide a nice goal to reach too -- someday, I'll have unlocked every character, and done every victory condition at least once.

This game was a pleasent surprise for me. The game was alot more nuanced than alot of the people give it credit for. Now, I paid about a buck for this game, and it was very worth it. Is it worth $5? Eeh.... maybe?
This game plays as a series of short campaigns. You build, you manage resources and you send characters on tactical missions, but before long you either succeed or fail the campaign. If you succeed you get points to unlock new characters for the next campaign. It's unforgiving, but if you lose, you aren't losing much because the games are short. Either way, you notice things you could improve in your next game.
The tactical element is not immediately intuitive but is interesting. The stamina system lets you overexert your characters at the cost of future actions, and does it very smoothly. Mistakes here can get characters killed in a hurry. The system is complex without being cumbersome.
The base-building is surprisingly nuanced as well. You start off with practically nothing and there's a very sharp growth curve that you have to keep up with, or you get overwhelmed.
Rogue-likes this unforgiving are usually too stressful to be fun for me, but since the length is short it's much less frustrating than losing a run of, say, ToME or Don't Starve. It feels like a fun challenge, rather than a game that makes you scared to take risks. I think Desktop Dungeons is the only other game to really pull that off.
Not a huge amount of content, but definately worth a couple bucks. No bells and whistles on the presentation, but if you can see past the graphics the game itself is solid.

After getting the complete version of TM2 during the Steam Winter Fail 2016 (Most of the discounts weren't my cup of tea), I have one thing to say about this game compared to the only other TM game I have played, TM Sunrise.
This game will TEST YOU. It will test you to no end on your precision and how well you can powerslide without sending your car careening into a lampost. One you get it down, you can get that adrenaline rush that the whole of Sonic The Hedgehog wishes it could give you. Getting medals is also a challenge, even with the lower difficulty tracks. I just go for silver medals in single player, because the golds are basically MLG pro (At least they don't quickscope you the moment you get in the lead). The only problem I see with single player is currently, I don't think you can have multiple opponents to race against. Solo is 1v1 the whole way through (As far as I can tell). The physics are still what you'd expect from trackmania: go fast and you'll win, but you might wind up launching yourself off the track at that bump in the road or fly off at the next dip in the road and put yourself into a roll that costs you your silver medal.
Complimenting the challenge is the great aesthetics and performance. My computer runs this game at near perfect frames, and the vibrant color palette (DAT SKYBOX BE DOUBLE-D SEXY) makes the game pop.
This review is just based on my completion of all the white-flag challenges, so my experience can't say the same other players.
In the end, I say that this is a good installment in the Trackmania franchise, and worth my 20 bucks. I recommend you  do what I did, and grab it before the Steam Winter Fail ends, or wait for the next discount on the franchise. Fans won't be disappointed (Maybe).

I Must have missed something along the way, because when this game came along I was all psyched for the continuation of the series. A point and click adventure puzzle game series with a nice complex plot that felt like someone's imagination had runaway with them (with a nice sci/fi twist that kept you guessing.)  Then came this game.
Essentially, this game says: Nope! Sorry.  We made up the other two.  They were interpretive fantasies of the main character.  Nothing actually happened the way you spent hours figuring out and playing through.  It was a terrible let down. Some of the puzzles were a bit obscure in the others, however they (their stories) were entertaining enough to keep my interest and make me into a hopeful for this game. With the onset of A Twist of Fate, I've personally decided not to buy another game from Pendulo Studios.
The voice cast is completely different for starters, as it sort of grinds at your ears after getting to know the other characters in the other two games in the series.  Not enough to be game breaking, but enough that you notice.. repeatedly.  I'm not saying they're not a good cast, they did do a good job, but you can't get by without noticing within the first 5-10 mins.   The artwork is nicely done, and very enjoyable.  The color tones of the various areas help set the mood of each chapter splendidly.
All in all, taken as an individual game it is enjoyable.  The puzzles are difficult without being impossible and usually very intuitive.  (I did run into a few places where descriptions or items were referenced without having previously been seen, something that I did not run into in the other games in the series.)  In particular, A Twist of Fate seems somewhat easier than the other two Runaway games - something I wouldn't mention if it wasn't very noticable.  Sadly, it seemed almost dumbed down and changed around for the masses, appealing to a wider audience by compromising story plot and introducing a larger number of cutscenes.
I'm certain someone out there will point out some major flaws in my review for whatever reason, but in summation: I don't like or recommend the game.  The game by itself is nice, well thought out, and the plot is interesting- bringing an entertaining conclusion to the series... (that being said, -again in summation- in relation to the rest of the series, the game sucks.)

Annoncé en 2014 comme se voulant être une révolution dans les simulations pompier / police, EmergeNYC nous montre ici une première "démo technique" bien prometteuse. Alors oui en effet pour l'instant, il n'y a pas grand chose. La ville n'est pas modélisée, les bugs sont nombreux, l'optimisation hasardeuse ( de 50 fps à 5 fps selon les endroits avec ma config ) et j'en passe. Mais pour ce qui est présent dans le jeu, à savoir quelques véhicules de pompier que l'on peut conduire librement, ça laisse présager un
dans le futur.
Ici on est clairement sur de la simulation pure et soignée, les sirènes et les gyrophares des véhicules sont contrôlables manuellement ( d'ailleurs ils ont chacun des sirènes personnalisées ) qui ont un réel effet sur le trafic ( même si pour l'instant il est un peu hasardeux ). En ce qui concerne la conduite, elle est lourde et réaliste mais facile à prendre en main ( assez similaire à celle de GTA IV appréciée par les amateurs du genre ).
Faute de pouvoir en dire trop pour l'instant à cause de son contenu limité, il fait nul doute que le jeu va s'améliorer au fil des mises à jour, avec nottament la police et les ambulances, ainsi qu'un mode multijoueur. Si vous voulez soutenir des développeurs indépendants dans l'ambition de réaliser un jeu de simulation complet et abouti proche d'un AAA, foncez et achetez EmergeNYC !

Oxenfree is a short but amazing experience, completed in less than 4 hours.
Like a lot of other story-driven games, what you do is basically just walk, chose between different lines of dialogue, and go through little puzzles.
This game is in a lot of ways like "FireWatch" (which is a good thing if you like it), it has a very good design, a captivating story, a nicely built atmosphere thanks to the soundtrack, and a spoonful of mystery.
Now of course this also comes with the same cons : backtracking, which you will have to do quite a bit, especially if you try to go ahead without any indications and end up going the wrong way.
An other con for this game could be the price, it wasn't for me since i bought the game while it was on sale, but i can understand why people wouldn't want to pay 20$ for a 4 hour game.
Of course you would be missing something, because Oxenfree really is a game worth playing, so if you are reading this while the game is on sale, don't even hesitate.
There isn't a lot I can say to keep the review spoiler free, however, if you liked FireWatch, Night In the Woods, What Remains of Edith Finch, and other such games, you will absolutely enjoy this game without a doubt.

There are many good ideas in this game, but sadly when a technical issue makes your multiplayer game unplayable in multiplayer, it invalidates everything you've done.

Unless that unlikely improvement happens, avoid this game. It's kinda worse than the game just being bad on all levels, because it feels like we're missing on a pretty fine experience here...

What we have here is a fairly decent start to a roguelike that quickly gets consumed by its own weaknesses. You start every game at the beginning: great. You can upgrade your character through progression: super. Your upgrades stay with you when you restart: just what I wanted.
After that though, we encounter the two biggest design flaws for the game. First, the ratio of player power to enemy power doesn't follow appropriately and you soon find yourself in a situation where the enemies are far too powerful. Second, the fact that you can only fire in four directions means you are severely limited in what you can hit at any given time; plus, enemies have no such restriction, making the design choice questionable at best. The combination of these two things means there is a definite "correct build" that you must go through to get very far into the game, which for this type of game reduces player agency in their progression.
The graphics are very well done, with high-quality pixel art and a great palette. There's never any confusion because of graphics as to what's going on, with the slight exception that it can be difficult to see your character or other enemies when they're behind something, like a tree, even with the fade out of the object. Not sure what the fix is to this, but it's only just "okay" as it is.
The sound feels powerful and the music is good, but not terribly memorable. All in all, the game starts off letting you feel like you're doing very well but quickly descends into an exercise in futility. After a point, you never really feel very powerful any more and you just see the progression as a chore. That's unfortunate because there's a lot of potential here.
All in all I don't think I can recommend the game, not because it isn't fun for a while, but more because it should be fun for a lot longer and isn't. The difficulty curve doesn't track in a way that pushes you to keep coming back, but instead punishes you for doing well early on, punishes you for minor mistakes, punishes you for not being able to see behind objects, and punishes you if you've made the wrong build along the way.
If there were a "maybe" button, I'd select that. Since I can't, I'd say skip this and go for any number of other games like it that are better.

I tried to stick with it and give it another chance every couple updates, maybe try multiplayer. To this day, i havn't been able to get a successful multiplayer game started and the game feels more and more RNG luck based. Chars have been nerfed into uselessness, and most of the whole game has been "rebalanced" to a degree that i would consider it a different game entirely. I've decided to retire the game indefinately and remember the fun it used to be.

Game crashes, a fair bit more than one would expect for a simple X-COM knockoff.  I don't get where they think there is anything rogue-like about this, this is just ♥♥♥♥♥♥ X-COM.  It is actually why I had it on my wishlist, I like X-COM.
But I don't like this.  Where X-COM ramps upward in difficulty Link kicks you in the balls and laughs about how it has stacked the deck against you before sitting down and dealing you a hand.  Any cockups with your resource management will kill you, the margin for error is so stupidly small you will regularly be ruined by no true fault of your own.
Inexplicably the game's icon is of a red dragon head, I don't get that, probably a relic of a previous game they were using the engine for and just forgot to provide their own for the new game.

very good game, with two seperate types of gameplay.  The neat thing is though, at the start of each playthrough you get to set your own objectives from a list.  The game ends when you meet the objectives, so you can design your own level of difficulty.
In the base-building section you construct buildings.  You have to worry about production, adjacency bonuses, and the balance between teching up and using what you have to produce items useful in the short term.  Fun and interesting system with a couple little quirks, what gives it replayability is that you pick a crew of 3 people from a list of 20ish, and each has a special bonus.  a number of the bonuses give a different room type which changes up optimal layouts, and presents interesting new design choices.
In the exploration/combat portion of the game you move around and fight hostile aliens.  The system uses action points.  Moving a square, attacking, and using a skill all simply cost 1 AP (although one or two skills cost 2 AP).  The interesting wrinkle here is that you regenerate AP equal to your leftover AP from last turn (minimum 1)  For example a starting character has a standard 5 AP.  He can use two, and then refill to full.  if he has to do something important he can use 3 (down to 2), and then refill back to 4.  from there it is easy for him to just take one the next turn, or keep using 2 a turn at 4 instead of 5, so that first extra was just kinda borrowing.  if something really bad happens and you need to use all 5, then you end up spending 3 turns recovering before you can do anything.  Lord help you if something else attacks you while you recover.
The tutorial doesn't cover enough (you level up by clicking the character's empty skill slot), the game sometimes crashes when loading a mission, I ran out of objectives to complete before I unlocked all the characters, and there are still a couple little typos, but overall I highly recomend this game

This is the game where Pendulo really started to find their feet in making a good adventure game. Most of the parts of the game that are weak are actually from trying to support things from Runaway 1 and 2. Gina and Brian co-star in this game that begins with Brian's funeral with flashbacks discovering just how our hero ended up where he did.
With a doubleclick speed-walk system and a hint system that's actually fun to use (and yes, I did use it a couple of times), Pendulo have learned from their past flaws and worked up to a new high. The game is beautiful, the characters are entertaining and the puzzles are almsot exclusively clever.
It's hard to recommend this game to people who have not played Runaway 1 and 2 (it ties in fairly closely), but at the same time, it's a great adventure game. The Next BIG Thing is funnier... Yesterday has a couple of neater tweaks, but this is the best overall.

So this is not a polished, deeply involved game. The dialogue in the tutorial is rough. The resolution isn't good. (Though the Alt-Enter trick to make it full screen helps considerably). The graphics are serviceable.
It's a fun little survival roguelike, however. You pick three characters to start and pick three goals from among a list of easy and difficult tasks that comprise your winning condition. You then give your characters tasks each day to build up your base, gather resources, sleep, explore, etc. Win or lose, you get some points that you can use to unlock new characters to choose from in your next play through.
There is quite a lot of variety in characters, skill upgrades, and equipment. Combat is straightforward and brutally fair. There's a real risk of dying all of the time, which keeps you engaged.
Would I have wanted to pay $25 for this? No. Was it worth my five bucks? Definitely.

Graphics generally are not that important to me, but this looks like something that should be played on an Amiga 500 in 1994 with the old Philips Monitor, not a modern PC, where 1080p monitors are the norm...but perhaps the dev is actually coding this on an Amiga 500 with the old Philips monitor in 1994!
In any case, the premise of the game is cool and I was digging the base building bit, which is reminiscent of the original UFO: Enemy Unknown base building mechanic: You build improvements in each square to provide resources for your guys etc...
The tactical part of it is pretty ropey with zero difficulty curve. Perhaps I need to send all my guys out on the first mission? Generally, I just send one as it's the first mission, simply a scavenging hunt and that should be a breeze, right? Wrong. My soldier dude is no match for two little spiders, he can't kill a frickin' baby deer and he gets cold, weak and downright lazy after about 2 turns. Also, there seems to be no escape except to fight once an enemy is on the same square as your little dude. Not very tactical, is it?
I want to like this game as I think there are some interesting ideas but it just comes off as too amateurish to warrant any more attention from me.

Before I describe what makes Oxenfree good. I just wanna rant about the game mechanics for one quick moment. WHAT is with people and QTE!? WHY does EVERY action in this game have a time limit like we're late for work and have to rush through shower, breakfast, driving, and everything else!? Now if that seriously bothers you then Oxenfree isn't the game for you. If not then we'll get into the creme de la creme, the frosting on the cake, the reason that makes Oxenfree Oxenfree. The story telling.
You're exploring an island when spooky things happened and you're trying to survive. Story wise I wouldn't call this innovative or oscar winning material, but it's really down to earth because the main focuses of the story is the character interaction. It's like Supernatural, even though they're supposed to be fighting demons, vampires, or freaking cthulhu at this point if I have to take a guess, but almost always they'll end up ♥♥♥♥♥ing about family friends or whatever while the bad guys just patiently wait in the background for them to finish bickering. Which brings me to my next point, art.
While most of the developers nowadays chooses to insert cutscene into their game. Oxenfree does the opposite of that. The game never throws a screen in front of you and expects you to quietly sets for a minute or two while the game do it's thing. Which creates a very smooth and immersive experience. i.e: even though I'm not wearing a VR headset I feel like I'm experiencing the story from the protagonist's perspective and I want to root for them. Which is essential in a point and click game.
All in all I'd say even though I wish Oxenfree could give us more time with the QTE (some choices literally only have seconds before the dialogue disappers), and it wouldn't hurt to at least add some basic setting like gamma adjustment and maybe volume setting. I'd still recommend this game if it's around 50% off or more.

There are various reasons I enjoy this especially for multiplayer. It's  a free non-FPS game anyone can jump into, and plenty silly. Most interesting to me is that it splits the difference on a pair of bifurcation points that oft divide gamers:
. (The DM mode pits 3 heroes against the dungeon master)
. (your wins get you cash to buy options, but never a raise in raw power)
I know that I tend to prefer games with some sort of progress, but in most RPG-style games it means noobs and vets can't play together. And I usually prefer co-op games, but I know some folks prefer competitive games. I like that Dungeonland offers all of these at once. So sure, there are some annoying bugs, as you'd expect from a Paradox game. But there's a lot of fun to be had, and at free the price is certainly right to try it with a few friends. Don't grab it expecting a Diablo-clone to enjoy on your own; most single-player diablo-clones out there are better. This is a game to play with friends in DungeonMaster mode, with voice chat on, and plenty of taunting.

I tried to stick with it and give it another chance every couple updates, maybe try multiplayer. I've decided to retire the game indefinately and remember the fun it used to be.

I'm going to throw you a bone here and give this a thumbs up, because I believe this game could truly start to become a great thing with a few more months of work..
But believe me when I say that I'm going to be brutally honest in what follows:
Open ended Advancement; build your own unique class as you go, point by point, skill by skill. This is amazing and there are too few games doing this sort of system these days.
PvP to the nth power. if you're not in town, you're fair game. But death is not horribly penalized, so its okay.
The Developers are thus far, actively fixing the issues listed below, the review will be regularly updated as is appropriate.

Huzzah! I'm being told that this is not so bad as it was previously and that there is potential for big finds and that the general rate of earning has been evened out!
Crafting items requires materials (Makes sense, right?) but what you scavenge in the wastes are not the materials you need to craft items.. No, you scavenge the materials you need to make the materials you need to make items. This would be fine if I didnt need to make dozens of individual parts, each taking up at minimum a minute and a half of my time EACH. No.
You get the pellet gun pretty early on after doing a few quests, unfortunately, it's completely worthless since the starter shotgun has the ability to do dozens of points more damage and is, for some reason, just as accurate. In fact, all weapons seem to have roughly the exact same accuracy. No.
The english translations are misleading and faulty, telling you lies that ultimately end up wasting your time.
The game would be better WITHOUT the voice acting. I would rather read the text than hear these people speak. It is HILARIOUSLY awful. No, really, The voice acting in this game makes the voiceovers from Oblivion sound like a choir of angels. No. ♥♥♥♥ no.
Your inventory is limited by your strength, this makes sense, sure. But seeing as I literally cannot hold enough materials to craft a large majority of the items, this is pretty much game breaking. This issue is alleviated slightly by being able to place things in storage and just craft from there

Huzzah again! The Developers have added bulk storage. This also somewhat helps to alleviate the rigors of point 6 and makes it not such a glaring issue.
The game is only vaguely playable, but there is already a premium shop.
There is more to be said about this game, almost all of it negative. The concept behind everything would be amazing, in fact it would be a blast if any other part of it had been executed in any reasonable fashion.
I understand that this is an Alpha, but this game is not in an Alpha state.. All of these flaws should have been uncovered by a few hours of internal play testing by the developers.
I was excited about this title, but I can now say without doubt that you've made a genuinely terrible mistake in releasing this game in its current state. Chances are, any hope you had of generating a good early buzz around it are now completely gone and you've forced yourself into a long, grueling, uphill battle if you choose to persevere.
Good luck and I hope you have an ace up your sleeve. You're going to need it.

First off, Borderlands is one of the best FPS games ever released.  There have been literally hundreds of thousands of words written about Borderlands since it was first released, it's that kind of game.  Without question it made a huge impact on the gaming landscape, not just when it was released but for years to come.
So why is this game so great?  Simply put, it combines several popular game mechanics, many not seen in FPS form before, into one fun, easy-to-learn-but-hard-to-master package.  While the concepts themselves may not be truly original - alien wasteland setting, tongue-in-cheek humor, part-based randomized loot, multiple player classes with a level-based skill tree, 4-player co-operative gameplay - they'd never been combined together in one FPS.  Atop that, 4-player co-op during the main campaign was something that hadn't been seen in an FPS since the days of Duke Nukem 3D, back in the era of dial-up when such things were rather complicated to arrange.  Borderlands not only reminded people about 4-player co-op, it reminded them that it could be really, really good in an FPS.
Beyond that, Borderlands takes some of the core concepts of hack-and-slash games like Diablo and shows that those same concepts work great for FPSes.  +1 Sword of Smiting?  Why not an x4 SMG of Why Bother Aiming Its Basically A Shotgun?  Magic spells?  Call them action skills, and maybe add some explosions.  Elemental attacks?  Eh, who hasn't thought guns would be cooler with fire added?  Sure, instead of hack-and-slash it's shoot-and-loot, but at the core its the same thing: fun, in a randomized way.
There are of course a few little missteps here and there, things that Gearbox didn't nail down quite as perfectly as the rest of the game.  The somewhat lax scaling of enemies, the sparseness of fast travel stations in some areas, the utter uselessness of many weapons if given the wrong parts, how easily co-op partners can completely miss the plot if rushed.  All comparatively minor, but they're there (and, impressively, fixed in the sequel).  That said, it's a drop in the bucket, detracting in only the smallest of ways from an overall excellent game.
Borderlands is another milestone in gaming, the prototype for a new formula of FPS that looks to continue on for years to come.  To say it is a good game would be an understatement.

Even though I never played a Telltale game before, I am familiar with the concept as I followed the Radbrad on youtube on his journey through the first Walking Dead series. I am glad I did this as I am actually too squeamish to have played it myself and probably would have stopped at some point like I almost stopped with Resident Evil Revelations 2 and actually have stopped playing Alien Isolation.
Yeah, you can laugh.
I am also glad I did it because I am interested in the concept  of storytelling. The telltale concept offers a  way for players to interact with the storyline. I use this term interact in a rather broad sense as a game is, by its very nature, a means to interact with a storyline, even if a game has only got a very shallow storyline.  In this it differs from a book or a movie in which the story is fixed and the reader/watcher is passive.
So I am glad that I found the Tales of the Borderlands, because it is game I find interesting to explore even though I have no specific love for the Borderlands settings. I recall Borderlands as a rather boring shooter that had nothing remarkable to offer to me but its cell-shaded look. I understand it has acquired a dedicated following nevertheless.
Tales of the Borderlands is in many ways the opposite of Borderlands in that it has a lot of story and background, but lacks the freedom that Borderlands offers (in a fashion) and which is offered by open world games such as Skyrim or Dragon Age III.
In this the Telltale game is a total different game and has nothing to do with the shooter.
However, as an interactive storyline the game actually is a bit of disappointment.
But I am getting ahead of myself.
Tales is no doubt a fun game. The characters are engaging and the storyline is both funny and fun. The story is way over the top in many ways, but this seems something that is part of the Borderlands mood and it is well captured.  People are double crossing eachother, selling each other out, lying, cheating and prepared to kill each other in various ways but there is also love, loyalty and dedication. I like the bond between Fiona and Sasha, the two sisters. But there is also a 'bro' bond between Rhys and Vaughn, although that between the two sisters seems the stronger.
The bickering between Fiona and Rhys is amusing and is part of what keeps the whole going. You might after a while wonder why they put up with each other at all, but reason isn't important here. It is just sheer fun and I hope they won't go cliche all the way and have them fall in love.  Telltale: please don't.
The game doesn't slack and keepsthrowing one scene after the other at you and some are pretty hilarious. In fact I was surprised that I only played the game for about five hours, because it felt much longer to me.
However there also some clouds on the horizon.
For one it has become obvious to me that the choices in dialog are mostly superficial. While you are often given three options, the game plays out the same way and even regardless of what you said.  One example of this is when a bounty hunter is chasing Fiona and Sasha into a garage, they are confronted by girlfriend of the bounty hunter. The bounty hunter then becomes friendly because she has promised her friend to stop with that line of work. As Fiona you can react in three ways, one of which is pretending that nothing has happened, which is the line I selected. Then after a few sentences the girlfriend suddenly asks you why you say that the bounty hunter was chasing you, while this was exactly not what I had Fiona say.
This occurs at various moments and after a while I realized that overal what you said hardly mattered, although there are moments that the game notifies you that this or that person will remember this or that. We are told that these decisions will be used as input for the next episodes.  That sounds nice, but the danger is that when you find yourself often in the minority, you can expect to see a tale develop that is not to your liking. And it is even a question whether a popularity vote will result in a good story.
In addition I foresee some serious issues with the story. There is a marvelous article about Mass Effect that tries to explain why Mass Effect 3 ended in the way it did. The gist of this article is that because Mass Effect 1 and 2 left a lot of loose ends the options left were so bewildering that only by killing a lot of the people or solving them the options could be reduced to manageable proportions. People thus found themselves cheated.
This is exactly the situation this game is facing.
After two episodes it has a lot of loose unfinished business to take care of and instead of doing that, the trailer for episode three suggests we might see more.  If it keeps adding more and more it might end up disappointing people as much as Mass Effect 3 did. Kill your darlings!
As a last issue I want to mention that the game offers little in the way of challenging puzzles and situations. Most interaction, besides dialogs, consist of nothing more than looking at something, picking things up or pushing button or throwing switches.  The few more complex puzzles have such obvious solutions that they offer no challenge.
This then leaves one to wonder at what point the game stops being a game. If interaction doesn't matter than one could just watch the Radbrad youtube walkthrough instead.
Verdict
The game is no doubt fun and funny but it is actually more an interactive movie than a game..Your choices seem hardly to matter and complex puzzles and situations are far and in between and offer no challenge.  If you do not mind this then you can enjoy the ride by just following the story, but do not expect much more.  I personally found the characters, setting, dialogue and background interesting enough to look forward to the next episode.

A taste of things to come, this tech demo allows one to drive a vehicle around a segment of the fictionalized Manhattan where the game's to be set. As a start, it's a simple one but a good one.
Pros:
+ Driving Physics: The game handles well behind the wheel, which is important, as thus far all you can do is drive.
+ Graphics: What we have that isn't simple whiteboxes is pretty....Well, pretty. Plenty of options to futz with as necessary, too.
+ An Emergency Services Simulator: Something many gamers have been pining for (lookin' at you, ArmA/GTA-(City)PDFR folks), the game will, once fully released, be a fully fleshed-out simulator of the big three: Fire, Medical, Police.
+ Controls: You can play with the sirens however you want, there's three-stage emergency lighting. There's controls already in play for ladders and most of the vehicle functions you could want.
Cons:
- Whiteboxes: Pretty much every building except two or three of the firehouses are at this point whiteboxes. Obviously, this is a demo-exclusive con.
- Traffic: The AI traffic is...Rather jumpy. Even when you don't have a siren blaring or lights flashing, they're pretty quick to jump out of your way. This will be fixed in a November patch, however.
- FPS Camera Position: Each vehicle I jump into, it seems the camera is set too far forward. This is particularly noticable in the battalion. ADDED: I have been informed this is as it is because the vehicle interiors are still under development, which I wholly understand.
- Options Consistency: It seems changes made in launcher are somewhat independent of changes made in the in-engine options menu. I'll set the game to full screen at my default resolution, and each time the game loads, it windows at about half my standard resolution, and needs to be set again.
The cons at this point outnumber the pros from where I stand. But this IS a tech demo. And it will be expanded. I wholeheartedly recommend this as a project that will come into something amazing. If you're looking for a full product now, you're not going to get what your after. But if you want to show support for the development, and fiddle around with a number of fire department vehicles (as well as ambulances and police vehicles fairly soon), then buy in. If you appreciate emergency services, you'll be glad you did.

This is a very simple, yet fun, space exploration game. You chose one of three space ships, then configure the galaxy, and you're off. You have so many years to explore the galaxy, collect booty, meet people, experience the weirdness, and then to race home before your time limit runs out. The rules become very clear and you see the limits you have to work within, but everything is shrouded in mystery until you discover all the details by experimenting. The space battles have a tactical component, but it's often better to avoid combat until you've found a lot of allies and better equipment. This is a psuedo-turn-based game. You select a star system and travel, at that system you are given a choice of engaging a race, collecting booty, or experiencing an event. When you engage in combat it becomes an rts; guide your ships to where you'd like to position them, select your targets, and use your abilities.
There's something compelling about the gameplay, especially with how quick the game is, perhaps it has to do with how easy it to die when you know you made such an obvious mistake. You can play this game without actually engaging in combat, which I find refreshing. This isn't a game you can play for hours. After you've really gotten it down it's fun for a game here and there, and when you've burned out on it, leave it hiding in your library to be rediscovered. I recommend it for those who have 15 minutes on their lunch break. This will apeal to those who like casual to light strategy rogue-like games.

is a strategy roguelike game developed by Brainwashing Games that has just come out of a relatively short period of Early Access. It combines a great roguelike combat system and interesting base management gameplay where resource management is vital to ensure the survival of your crew.
The story starts off with your ship having malfunctioned and crashlanded to a snow-clad and hostile planet. Help is on it's way but with no nearby ship to evacuate the crew, the survivors will have to survive the hostile environment and the aggressive Xenos until help finally arrives.
The gameplay consists of basically two main parts, one is the base building and resource management phase and the other revolves around exploration and doing missions outside. First I will talk about the base building component. I just have to say that it's a good surprise to have this in a roguelike game as it changes how you would normally thrive in the other games in the same genre. The mechanic is a la the XCOM series where you build different components on each room at the cost of valuable resources. These rooms can be further upgraded to increase it's functionality, provided that you've amassed enough of the required resources. There is also a "Doomsday" meter (not sure what it's called exactly) that fills up slowly as each day passes by. Once it reaches 100, the local Xenos will initiate base invasion (I got a Game Over because of this since there's no chance for me to survive when I'm down to two crew member).
The resources I've mentioned consists of Food (for obvious reasons), Knowledge (required to build and craft advance components), Fuel (To heat up) and Tools (for building and crafting), Resources are scarce and vital for both maintenance of the crew and to build rooms.
The other part of the game consists of doing exploratory missions out of your crashed space ship either to salvage, to rescue other survivors (added to your crew if you're successful) or bounty hunting to lower the threat meter. The combat revolves around careful management of Stamina. In battle you can either choose to spend all of it to rush and kill the enemy in one swoop at the cost of slow regeneration afterwards, or take it slow and steady and ensure your crew have ample amount of stamina in case things go south. Of course, this is an arctic planet so the longer you're outside, the faster you'll lose your heat. Once it gets down to zero and your men will go down one by one. The best course of action is to get out, get what you need, get back ASAP.
Now that's all covered, I'm gonna mentioned the pros and cons of this game and hopefully it'll explain why I gave Link a thumbs down.
They say first impressions are a powerful thing and unfortunately, this game doesn't leave a good one for me.
I have high hopes for the game, and the devs seem committed too. I'm gonna wait until a few more updates and patches to roll in and I'll gladly jump into the game again and adjust my review accordingly. I'm confident that once the rough edges are smoothed out, Link will definitely be a contender for a hidden gem title. For now, I simply cannot recommend this unless roguelike and strategy games are your cup of tea, then by all means, go for it. For $5 you can't go wrong.

Conditionally, I recommend this game. If all you're looking for is a murderfest with guns blazing, Wolfenstein: The New Order is great for that. Whether it's dual wielding assault rifles or shotguns (or sniper rifles or handguns, I guess), or just rolling up on Nazis with a death laser, it's a pretty good stomp and romp with plenty of flash.
That said, the writing is not... great. While the plot is solid and walks through the numbers, the extreme violence of the game isn't contextualized whatsoever. BJ has some kind of "oh god all the killing" going on throughout the game, but it feels less like what it should be (an exploration of what killing, even justified killing, does to a human mind) and more just "god there's so many Nazis to kill, I'm so tired."
Which would be fine, really, if they didn't try to make it seem deep while being so shallow. Even a character like Brock Sampson got tired of killing eventually, and became something more. BJ is just... kind of soulless, in comparison. I always felt like I wanted more from BJ, but there just was nothing to see.
The other characters aren't very well explored. I might have missed something because while BJ calls the old woman an old friend, I had never seen her before. Her character is entirely forgotten past her introduction. Anya has virtually no characterization, and in fact most of her voice lines are narrating her *cousin's* story rather than speaking on her own story. I didn't get to see Wyatt's characterization, but Fergus's was almost too expected. I think the only character with any bite was the crazy lady.
Overall a good shooter but a kind of lukewarm story. Which is a shame, really, because the setting could truly be used for some interesting things.

This is an interesting little title. Link plays very much like a board game that varies based on 3 victory rules that you choose before starting a new game. Victory rules might include:
-Killing a ringleader
-Surving 15 rounds
-Caching 20 units of fuel
etc.
This adds a lot of variability to the game once you understand the core mechanics as your strategy to achieving all of the three victory rules (and ensure rescue) will determine your strategy.
Every game is a race against the clock. With each passing round your survivors will lose energy and heat and the increase threat of a base attack means that will have to be proactive with your strategy from the get-go. Do you hunker down, reasearch weapon tech and arm your survivors for a full on base attack? Or do you brave the surface of the alien planet to hunt down the native inhabitants in order to put off the inevitabilty of an invasion for a few more rounds?
This is an early access game and as such still has many bugs and glitches that crop up from time to time. For the most part it has not been too devastating or game breaking. Further, this game is very very difficult for the first five or ten rounds until you start to become more efficient with your round managament. In about 15 games I may win 4 or 5, depending on victory rules of course.
Further, won games grant you requistion points used to buy heros that have their own special abilities that bring a further layer of variability to your initial strategy. Heros may be robotics experts, commandos, leaders, rangers or mechanics- all with a unqiue skill set to offer.
There are many other features included like rescue missions, resource scavenging, reasearch and technology etc- more than I am willing to list for the sake of this mere thumbs up.
All in all I reccomend Link. It is a relaxing, albeit challenging little game with lots of replayability for the price.

I started my adventure with Borderlands 2, when friends convinced me to get it on sale, despite my hesitation. Since I generally dislike shooters and I'm not that good I didn't expect to like it. Eventually, though, I got to play way too much, and definitely the game is on my favorites list. Then I wanted to know more about the NPCs - the playable characters in the first game. I heard a lot about how Borderlands 1 is a great game, and that some of my friend were tired of playing Borderlands 2 because it's all the same. I also heard Borderlands is better on a PC than on a console. So I had my expectations high. But I only ended up disappointed...
Technically, it's probably not good to compare older game against newer. However, with bunch of franchises people say they prefered the older games in the series. I've always wondered to what extent it's actually nostalgia speaking.
In case of Borderlands it seems pretty simple. Both games are funny, certainly, but I'd say Borderlands 2 wins in this regard a bit. However, the first games had more interesting and meaningful characters. (On the other hand Maya's ability seem more practical than Lilith's).
I've played a lot of Borderlands 2 and I got used to mechanisms in that game, I was surprised they weren't there in Borderlands 1. For example the inventory in Borderlands 1 is much more confusing, comparing is not as simple and clear. However, the absolutely BIGGEST problem with the first game is loot, and loot levels. My character is now level 25, I'm doing story missions and side quests appropriate for my level, and I get level 13 drops... What's wrong? It seems like loot levels are totally random. My weapons are extremely weak, because they are at least 5 levels below my character's level, there's nothing good for purchase in the machines. The only place that has any chance of giving something more appropriate are the big treasure chests. They usually give loot for too high level though. It's just terribly poorly-balanced...
Another problem I found is the map. The game says it has partial controller support, but the controller seems to work basically everywhere, except for the map. But even with the mouse, viewing the map is extremely awkward, having to zoom out every time you need to find your objective, and the movement is just quite unnatural to me.
And then one more thing is that, in comparison to Borderlands 2, you have to pick up money and ammo drops manually, instead of just running into them. It never really bothered me much, though, so I don't find it particularly problematic. And it's also something that I can totally forgive an older game for not implementing.
The rest of the things are on the same level in both games, and that is really good level. Borderlands is still vey very enjoyable game, totally worth recommending. But if, like me, you started with Borderlands 2 and go down to Borderlands 1 expect fall damage, also as it is in the game itself.

Ok, I have to admit: it is hard to judge a free to play game which has an achievement obtained by 2 players over 10 (which is an insanely high percentage) that literally requires you to "finish the game in less than 17 minutes".
And yeah, you can finish it actually within twenty minutes.
But it's also free, this is always a plus.
Anyways, we have a platformer here with horrendous graphics (but since I think a developer alone did all the work it's ok), and with not-so-fast to understand controls and mechanics. It took me some time to get into the game.
The graphics aspect though is quite heavy in a bigger evaluation, since its really poor value affects also the menu and all the other parts of the game.
For what concerns controls, they too aren't that polished. You'll often need to repeat a single level part without ragequitting. It supports gamepads, but no remapping so no WASD/other configurations, and this sucks for a PC game.
Power-ups and bonuses don't add that much, they have little value and they can be easily missed. Your character won't "upgrade" that much".
On a sidenote, you can't even save.
And for the "exploration" hashtag the game offers in the menu, well, there's nothing great to explore. The story wouldn't be that bad, but really to me it wasn't developed at all. It's like a draft.
I don't know, I have read many positive reviews but to me the combination of awful graphics and poor (often very poor and frustrating) controls, especially when jumping and slipping on the floors, kinda forces me to review negatively this game even if it's free. I wouldn't replay it.

As of writing this, I've only played the first episode, but wow, I was blown away...
It has the same witty humour as the rest of the Borderlands franchise, with some hilarious throwbacks to the previous games that will make any long-time fans of the series chuckle. But even people new to the franchise can find solitude in the well written story, meaningful choices and frankly a setting like no other.
This is the first of the TellTale games I've played, and I found it to be a truly unique experience that works really well with the Borderlands universe. There's still plenty of action and psycho-slaughtering, but the quick time events feel rather natural and they keep you on your toes! Don't get caught laying back and taking your hands off the keyboard because you never know when some random dude will attempt to kill you! It's Pandora after all.
However, the main issue I have with the game is its episodic format. There are only two episodes out at the moment (third one coming soon), but the game has been out for a pretty extensive period of time at this point and the episodes seem to come out really slowly… I’m concerned that when I catch to the most recent episode, I may have to wait months for the next one, and in that time I’d have forgotten all the meaningful decisions and events that had occurred up until that point.  I’m hoping that TellTale will be able to power through these last few episodes and get them released in a timely manner. This is only an issue because the game is just so damn good! Keep it coming TellTale, you’re onto a real winner with this game here!

From playing the Tutorial and one playthrough:
Link is a fairly challenging turn-based strategy game. Balancing risk and reward, the game keeps you on a knife's edge. Do you send your tired survivors out to look for food, or rest them up, but risk starvation? Do you spend time sitting in the library gathering research points, or spend precious materials to build a pistol? Do you try for that last cache of supplies on the map, risking frostbite?
Each character in your crew can be used for one action a day. These vary from building new rooms or clearing away supplies, to crafting new tools or exploring outside of the ruined ship. Exploration outside moves you to a combat map were you explore for supplies and either evade or confront the native people who are intent on overwhelming your party. Characters gain experience and learn new skills, so losing a crew member is always a fearful possibility.
The game graphics are mainly static backgrounds and tokens that you drag across the screen. It plays much like a boardgame, and has some depth too the decisions you make. Fairly enjoyable experience for the cost, and the replayability is decent: successfully accomplishing your objectives (which you get to pick at the start of the game), gives you requisition points to unlock new crew members to start new games with.

I like a lot this turn-based strategy game. Each turn, you choose an action for each crew member, you can: create a room in the base or craft something (weapon, armor), or help a character with low stats  to stay alive, giving him (her) food, heat or health in the appropriate room, or pick a mission and send one or more characters outside to find resources (there are also other types of missions). During a mission, the characters explore a map and fight enemies in turn-based combat. It's cold, so they can't stay outside for too long.
You have to manage the characters and the scarce resources, with the lurking menace of a base invasion that will happen in a determined number of turns. There are various strategies to try and things to learn, with rooms that can be upgraded and the characters who gain useful skills with experience. I like the retro pixel graphics. The interface reminds in some aspects a board game:  in the base, to do an action, you slide a character token on a room and then make a choice in a menu. I appreciate this style and all works well so far. The tutorial teaches well the basics. In normal mode, you pick three goals (with various difficulty levels) and you succeed when you reach them. A successful run gives points to unlock more characters. So far, I played a few runs and I reached the easier goals. I will play more.

I feel like I should preface this review by saying that A) Bane of the Cosmic Forge is the first first-person dungeon crawling crpg that I've ever played to completion, and B) I did this with the express purpose of importing a party into Crusaders of the Dark Savant. Also, this was within the last year, I wasn't alive when these games came out originally.
Bane of the Cosmic Forge is something pretty unlike any other cRPG I've ever played. Sure, it looks uglier than sin and the character design has aged like♥♥♥♥♥♥and the story is complete nonsense BUT! The dungeon design, while really brutal in the early-going, consistently surprised me. Essentially the whole game takes place in a single mega-dungeon type area with several different subsections. The design of these individual subsections and the way they wove together at times was clearly the work of a group of designers who knew what they were doing. Once you've got a handle on the mechanics of this game, exploring these areas becomes so much fun. Some of the puzzles were pretty obtuse if you werent drawing a map (or unless, like me, you cheated and used the automap mod) but this is the age of information and if google's at hand you'll be fine, there's tons of resources for this game.
The character creation in this game is pretty cute, you have to roll high in specific stats to qualify for individual classes, like so many cRPGs from this time. The thing is, as you level up your stats will advance and you can actually switch to these classes at level 1 later on, while keeping all of your skills, which is a neat feature.
Honestly though, having played through a good chunk of this game's frankly incredible sequel, Wizardry 7, I can't say that this one is too worth playing. There's one tileset, the sound sucks (I just muted it and listened to podcasts while I played), and after a while the tedium does start to set in. Still, coming out the other end of it is pretty rewarding (even if the final boss that I experienced was kinda lackluster).
Basically, it's pretty good, pick it up if you already have any interest in DOS cRPGs, and the ability to import your characters into Wizardry 7 with some of the neater equipment from this game is fun. If you get bored of this one though, it's packaged with its sequel which just takes all of its ideas and improves on them, with several more tileset and beautiful VGA pixel art. Plus it's dirt cheap so if you don't like it or it takes you a while and a few tries to even play the damn thing, like me, you're not losing too much.

Oxenfree is a fantastic paranormal story driven game with impressive graphics and tonnes of replayabitily. The main game itself keeps you on egde for the entire playthrough of around 6-8 hours. Oxenfree heavily focuses on the topic of time and parallel universerses to make its story diverse from anything I have ever played.

Graphics are gorgeous and the visual style of the game is breathtaking.
The story and lore of Oxenfree is very strong and with multiple endings no two playthroughs feel the same at all.
Atmosphere in Oxenfree is gripping. I experienced no bugs and was fully imserved for the entire story.
Cons:
Movement can feel sightly slow and getting a new objective to someplace across the entire playarea can feel slow.
Some response actions can feel unrealistic to say, as in, you could play the whole game being a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to everyone but I guess thats an option for the user going for every ending.
Some things to note:
Oxenfree does include mild jumpscares, but nothing thats going to leap you out of your chair.
I feel the game is most enjoyable playing through in one sitting, just for the atmosphere and to keep you on edge.
The second playthrough builds on top of the base game and is very exciting to go back to.

I started my adventure with Borderlands 2, when friends convinced me to get it on sale, despite my hesitation. Since I generally dislike shooters and I'm not that good I didn't expect to like it. Eventually, though, I got to play way too much, and definitely the game is on my favorites list. Then I wanted to know more about the NPCs - the playable characters in the first game. I heard a lot about how Borderlands 1 is a great game, and that some of my friend were tired of playing Borderlands 2 because it's all the same. I also heard Borderlands is better on a PC than on a console. So I had my expectations high. But I only ended up disappointed...
Technically, it's probably not good to compare older game against newer. However, with bunch of franchises people say they prefered the older games in the series. I've always wondered to what extent it's actually nostalgia speaking.
In case of Borderlands it seems pretty simple. Both games are funny, certainly, but I'd say Borderlands 2 wins in this regard a bit. However, the first games had more interesting and meaningful characters. (On the other hand Maya's ability seem more practical than Lilith's).
I've played a lot of Borderlands 2 and I got used to mechanisms in that game, I was surprised they weren't there in Borderlands 1. For example the inventory in Borderlands 1 is much more confusing, comparing is not as simple and clear. However, the absolutely BIGGEST problem with the first game is loot, and loot levels. My character is now level 25, I'm doing story missions and side quests appropriate for my level, and I get level 13 drops... What's wrong? It seems like loot levels are totally random. My weapons are extremely weak, because they are at least 5 levels below my character's level, there's nothing good for purchase in the machines. The only place that has any chance of giving something more appropriate are the big treasure chests. They usually give loot for too high level though. It's just terribly poorly-balanced...
Another problem I found is the map. The game says it has partial controller support, but the controller seems to work basically everywhere, except for the map. But even with the mouse, viewing the map is extremely awkward, having to zoom out every time you need to find your objective, and the movement is just quite unnatural to me.
And then one more thing is that, in comparison to Borderlands 2, you have to pick up money and ammo drops manually, instead of just running into them. It never really bothered me much, though, so I don't find it particularly problematic. And it's also something that I can totally forgive an older game for not implementing.
The rest of the things are on the same level in both games, and that is really good level. Borderlands is still vey very enjoyable game, totally worth recommending. But if, like me, you started with Borderlands 2 and go down to Borderlands 1 expect fall damage, also as it is in the game itself.

My Rimworld Story: One sunny day, in my medium sized colony, my colonists were in the middle of a good summer harvest. Suddenly, sirens sound, the screen flashes red, and at the bottom right corner a small box with the words "Raid (boss)" appear. What does that mean? It means that the supreme leader of the planetwide pirate band has joined in on a raid on my peaceful colony. Raiders pop out of drop pods, assault rifles, snipers, and the boss, weilding a rocket launcher. I send my colonists to their positions, my colonists survive, but we still have casualties: two adult alpacas, and a newborn alpaca, less than a season old. The raiders are all either dead or too hurt to move. Among the barely living is the pirate boss. For the crime of killing my alpacas, death is too light a punishment. I learn that my colonists would gain a mood boost for killing the leader, but it isn't worth it. I capture the leader, I put him in a nice cell, I tend his wounds using the best medicine, feed him the best of food, he is going to need it. Once his wounds are healed, tended by my nurse, I bring in my doctor, who also has the psychopath trait. My prisoner falls asleep, and my doctor goes to work. When the pirate boss wakes up, he isn't sure that he is awake, everything is still black, "Am I dead?" he may have thought. "No, I can still feel the pain." He cannot see. His eyes have been replaced with golden orbs (thanks btw modders for that) his legs have been replaced with logs for him to waddle on. He touches his own body, franticly, trying to find waht else has been ripped from his body. He is horrified, and his horror is intensified as he hears somebody enter the room. He kicks and screams as he is grabbed forcefully, and led out of his luxorious room. He is sure he is going to die now. He hears a knife being drawn, but they cut nothing but the bindings from his hands. He is sent away. To wander blindly through a hostile planet. He probably got mauled by wild animals or even killed by the pirate gang he once commanded, but I dont like that ending. I imagine that he is drifting around, begging for scraps, aimless. I like to imaging that he occasionally grabs a random passerby, and just tells his story, not unlike the old sailor from Coleridge's "Rime of the Ancient Mariner"

Oh my god. Rimworld.
I bought this game a long, long time ago. I originally owned it long before it was on Steam, so I'd guess I have 200+ hours on this masterpiece. Rimworld is such a creative take on such an overused idea. People stranded away, and now they've gotta survive.
Basebuilding:
Although the customization♥♥♥♥♥♥doesn't have much variety, I'm sure there's more stuff I haven't seen, as I still haven't research any of the cosmetic techs, ever. The basebuilding is fun as hell, and I always feel like my buildings are gonna mean something. Abandon a project mid construction? Maybe you can use it as cover to hide from the bandit's sniper, who never seems to miss a shot.
Traits/Skills:
These are the bread and butter of your Rimworld experience. One of the largest parts of Rimworld, what your colonists can do, and what goes on in there head. The relationships that form between them, are what helps you bond with them. I've never been so attached to little digital characters. Not even in the Sims.
Combat:
This is what makes Rimworld hard. No deaths on your side? You'd assume the fight went well. But when your only doctor lost a leg, who's gonna help him? What about when that simple bullet wound turns into an infection? Are you gonna amputate it? The limbs of all these people are almost as important as them themselves, and even if you just survived a raid aganist all odds, the missing bodyparts can make you feel so helpless. The way the cover in this game works, combined with the skill, and the heart pounding moment when you just pray that your doctor is knocked into shock and not killed, is part of what makes Rimworld, Rimworld.
Conculsion:
Every little thing in this game comes together creating a masterpiece, that is unrivaled by any game I've ever played in its genere. Feels like a game I can always fall back on, and just hop on and play. The developers clearly care about and love this game, and I don't know why its considered an early access with all the♥♥♥♥♥♥it has.
TL:DR This game is ♥♥♥♥ing amazing. Buy it.
