Hey, so what is Rimworld? Rimeworld is a gem in what seems to be a forgotton genre mix of strategy and role playing games.
Rimworld throws you into a world with a bunch of survivors, who each have their own skill sets and useful traits like cooking, hunting, building etc. YOU as "pretty much their god" will decide what they do, what they eat, where they can and cannot go. You are pretty much their savior as well as their doom, depending on how good you are at micro managing, resource control, building, creating working structures and defenses.
It definitely is not easy, you will have your colony killed a lot by pirates, wild animal hordes and acid rain. You will have you colonists go crazy, run around naked until they die or kill other colonists, you will have your colonists starve, resort to cannibalism, which in the end makes them crazy, and die again...
You might discover hidden structures, unearth them, only to find out there was an ancient killing machine hidden within, which will ultimately kill your entire colony and make you lose, yet again...  XD
But what caught me in this game, are the endless possibilites, the 100000 different ways you will miserably fail in this game, and the billions of different ways you will succeed and build a florishing colony of battle hardened survivors!
You can build ACs, gun turrets, traps, kitchens, crafting rooms, rec rooms with TVs and couches, train animals of all kinds to fight with you or serve as your resource carrying donkeys, raid pirates, defend yoruselves against intrudors, IMPRISON them, execute them and/or recruit them, trade with travelling caravans of far away factions, create your own trade caravans, build a space shuttle and leave the planet... The possibilites are completely endless...
Now, was this game worth my money? Yes! Absolutely yes! I personally can't wait where this game is going, but you will definitely get your money's worth in return.

It's still a good game, it's just significantly more difficult and more frustrating than Trackmania Stadium.

Runs beautifully on a 1060, but the gameplay itself isn't very enjoyable (for me). Running and gunning is utterly discouraged on anything but the two lowest difficulties, and AI will either spot you from the other side of the map behind  a crate or let you run up to them without waking up. The flow of action is constantly broken up by breaking boxes to find a health kits.
The game also suffers from attempting to cram many modern game systems in, such as cover and (awful) stealth. There are sections that you'll be forced to play like any other shooter, peeking out and taking shots rather than actually enjoying yourself. If you want old Id gameplay, just play DOOM.

Let me start by saying the game is great, overall. Its nothing too amazing, but a great game none the less. Its gameplay is randomly generating thus giving the plaer an indefinite replay value, so it can be easy to get your moneys worth out of this game if its your thing. But speaking of the price, its 10$ and thats pretty on edge of how much its worth through my experience. I got it for free in a giveaway myself, and its a great game, but I'd say its more around worth 5$, if its on sale buy thing game, if its not: invest into taking some more ime to see if its your cup of tea.
On to the gameplay, theres alot to say and to keep it short I'll say this:
The gameplay is a solid 8.5/10, its a randomly generated fun adventure full of things to explore. The mechanic of having to return after 30 years in-game is a unique and brilliant touch to a game of this genre. It gives you an almost arcade like feel of constantly trying to get a new highscore, its simply addicting and fun so see what you can get. Playing this game blind will make your experience ALOT better too, playing it blind will make the game so intresting to discover things, I know from experience there will be many occasions you thought youve seen everything, but suddenly a brand new ship, race, battle, etc. comes up. If these thigns sound appealing to you, look into this game more, its a really great relaxing time waster. (and I almost forgot to mention: its got quite the FTL like feel to it, but with a wide range of completely new, different mechanics.)
TL;DR: The games pretty good. Is it worth 10$? That depends on your likings because 10$ is the maximum price the game could be worth, if the game is on sale you should totally buy it. It's a well-made, rouge, never ending, suprising, random, curious, almost FTL-like experience that will leave you addicted to getting a higher score or explore more each time.

** Recommended, but with stipulations.  :)
Back in 1984 I played the original Wizardry game and fell in love with PC gaming forever.  I played the entire series and enjoyed them all to a point, but 6-8 were masterful RPGs with a connected storyline that spanned the trilogy (you could port your characters from one to the next).  The character depth and NPC interaction was amazing at the time (NPCs remember how you treat and interact with them and it matters throughout the games).  The puzzles and critical thinking you needed to utilize to figure things out were challenging.  It was difficult, no doubt, but after you learned the ins and outs it gave a great gaming experience.
THAT SAID, the only way that a younger current generation could ever enjoy this game is to understand a few things:
You can't be hung up on graphics, because these are pitiful by today's standards.  You can't expect all the user bells and whistles of today's games like auto-mapping, quest journals, etc.   None of that is there, and you either have to map and journal by hand or you can use the "Wizardry 6 - Cluebook" that comes with the Steam purchase and is located in the "C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam\steamapps\common\Wizardry6\Bonus Content" (default) directory.  If you want to experience the golden age of RPG gaming, I'd recommend you do it with this companion guide and/or a walk-through from the internet (there are many and these games have a cult following).  This way you get to experience the great parts of the game, while mitigating the frustrating parts.  You absolutely should research the internet for assistance with the character generation, as it can be daunting, but it quite enjoyable once you understand it.
Definitely pick it up during a Steam sale for under $2 and that way if you don't enjoy it, you didn't lose much.
** - Just an FYI if you purchase this, you can hit "Enter" at the copy protection scheme, as it isn't necessary with the Steam version.

So I’ve decided to change up my format style to make the reviews a little less convoluted and address what game creators classify as the features of their game. With that said I got Oxenfree on sale expecting it to be a game right up my alley and I wasn’t wrong. I’m still young enough to enjoy the teen drama without it being overly obnoxious as well as being a huge sucker for mystery. From there I can address the first point and what most would call the gameplay: Dialogue and Conversation.
So from the start we’re introduced to Alex, Jonas and Ren then once on the island we meet Clarissa and Nona. From the start we can tell the relationships of the characters as if they’re all loudly shouting who they are so you can easily categorize them. You’ve got the edgy jaded teen, the well liked but awkward one, the disliked but awkward one, queen ♥♥♥♥♥ and the quiet but pretty one who no one dislikes because she lacks a personality to dislike. Now while what I’m saying does sound quite harsh this is only how I felt at the start, as the characters progressed and I got to know them. I understood their reasoning even if some of the reasons were bad. I did feel like some of the text bubbles didn’t give me enough time to answer and some lingered too long but they did managed to nail how a conversation flows. Conversation is never one person to the next person, it’s a mess of people trying to get their ideas out before they forget them and it’s shown here fantastically. While the specifics of what they say don’t bring me back to a fond state of nostalgia of being a teen it still does remind me of how much it sucked. Which may be good or bad depending from person to person.
One of their listed features is the radio mechanic which I felt was a small part but it did aid the mystery. I’m a pretty jumpy person so the first time the radio went off I won’t lie I screamed. It adds a fun little mechanic to what otherwise would just be a walking and talking game. The radio also aids with the stellar voice acting. I enjoyed them character voice actors and didn’t just feel like it was a bunch of adults pretending to be kids. I say that but I still love teen wolf. Either way I think the mechanic worked well enough but I feel if there was something slightly more engaging I would enjoy it more.
Now the Art was fantastic. The character design is great especially with how hateable of a face Ren had. Besides that slight joke the art was really charming but still lets you fall into the mystery of it. The art is reminiscent of this cartoon series called Detentionaire and I think both are quite similar yet still different enough. Speaking of the mystery, the music really pulled you in. Every time I was playing this game I completely tuned out the world around me and was involved in the story. I feel the music really helps with this as well as a solid mystery. It says within the story it has an inspiration from World War II and I can see that but I feel like it’s forgotten. The teens being written like teens don’t care about the connection and it feels like you shouldn’t either. I don’t think they thought about it too much. I feel like they should of maybe focused a bit more on the character drama between Alex her group of friends
If they focused on that instead of sprinkling hints of something bigger it might have been slightly more interesting or if they made the cast older by a few years. I think both would have aided me being interested in the WW2 connection but I felt a disconnect between me following the character and me following the story.
Despite what some would say is harsh criticism, I found myself really enjoying this game. I really loved the main character and when she was angry, I was angry. I think the creators really loved making this game and it shows. They portrayed the character emotions well and the story flowed well. I felt like it climaxed fantastically and there was never a point where I was bored or lost. The whole world of the game dragged me in and I loved it. The only point I could add would that the story would probably fit a graphic novel better then a game but regardless of that I still rate it highly.

Two steps forward and three steps backwards for the latest in the Sherlock Holmes series.
Rating 5/10
The first thing I should say is that I've yet to play Sherlock Holmes: Crimes & Punishments, the previous game in the series, so I can only relate to the changes and my experience in comparison to The Testament of Sherlock Holmes and previous Sherlock games.
One of the biggest changes and most noticeable is that of both Holmes and Watson. It's the first thing you'll notice, they both look much younger and both characters have new voice actors. It's not only appearances that have changed but also their behaviour. It's almost as though these are entirely different characters. There's very little of the old Sherlock Holmes in this new take on the character, he's overly emotional and more driven to action than the previous incarnations in the series. Then comes Watson, previously he was helpful, offering polite advice and motherly concern, whereas in Devil's Daughter he stands around doing very little whilst looking like Jude Law.
Mentioning Jude Law is important because I believe the inspiration for The Devil's Daughter comes from the recent Sherlock Holmes films. As you play through the game you'll see various intentional, or unintentional, nods, such as the music in the tavern brawl, the unfinished Tower bridge and the hunt through the woods to name a few. However it's the action more than anything that reminds you that this is a new direction for the series. Instead of logic puzzles we now have extended Quick Time Events, mini-games and environmental puzzles. Some of these are utterly terrible, such as the swamp chase, and really feel like a misstep as not only do they go on for too long but feel out of place. Perhaps these events have been included to pad out the game's length, although even with them the game is criminally short.
However there are some positives, it looks fantastic in places and there's a real feel of Victorian London. Some of the cases are interesting and the new deduction mechanism works well. No longer are you bound to a deduction board but now you are figuring out connections in Holmes' head. Each strand of thought can be connected until you feel you've figured out who the guilty party is. Which leads us to the best part of the game, the final conclusion of each case. You have a choice to make and the game won't hold your hand as you make it. You may very well be condemning an innocent man but you have to trust your deductions and the evidence provided.
The series has clearly moved in a new direction, instead of being a traditional adventure game like previous games in the series it is more reminiscent L.A Noire, which is far superior in every way. I just hope for the next game they'll remember who Holmes and Watson are meant to be.

Dear Developers,
If you’ll read this...
The game is great, and I don’t think it’s worse than your previous game - Sins and Punishments, as many of the reviews here on Steam seem to suggest. I think it’s in the same league as that game - some of the aspects are better, I think, and some are worse.
The decisions you made concerning the characters – their new look and personas, and overall change of the tone of the game, I can take them or leave them, but in general the changes didn’t bother me much.
As an experiment it’s ok. But I think the timelessness of the classic Sherlock Holmes character and the tone of classic stories are a better setting for your games than this emotionally-driven approach you took this time.
The main gripe I have with the game is the lack of logic and hard evidence when the player is given the task to condemn/absolve the suspects at the end of some of the cases (namely, Infamy and Chain Reaction).
In my opinion in these cases the player has to guess who is the culprit based on hunch, rather than on evidence and logic.
The whole Infamy case suffers from this, as 2 of 3 suspects are not developed as characters at all, and the third one is over-developed.
In Chain Reaction the motivation of the culprit is not clear at all (did he really need that much money that he needed to kill his accomplices, and have all the money from the whole Bank of England vault all to himself. Also, his character and motivation, in my opinion, contradicts to the type of crime he committed... etc. For example if developers could just put some kind of paper in the game that would explain how much money he needed, and how much was stolen from the Bank, that would make investigation more logical and clear...)
Also, the main villain could have used a bit of character development during the course of the game, and not only have a hysterical outbreak at the end of the game. To me, the ending was not rewarding because the motivation and character of the antagonist weren’t clear.
Also, for upcoming games, please do not hesitate to make the difficulty a bit harder. :)
But overall, a great game, thank you!

All in all, I wish I could give this more than one "yes." A truly rare gem in the wilds of indie games (and the wasteland of EA).
Think Firefly wild west scifi meets Prison Architect base building.
In general, I avoid EA games as they often fail to deliver anything but hollow promises and shallow games. RimWorld is one of the rare exceptions (Factorio being another). It is a complete game that is well polished, intuitive, and highly extensible. It's only in EA because the developer is still releasing and tweaking things.
Pros:
- Highly customizable. From the various options to the crazy different scenarios to a bazillion workshop mods. You can make it almost as stupid easy or impossibly hard as your heart desires.
- Survival done right (Don't Starve comes to mind here). Yes you die and fail a lot, but you nearly always know why and how to do better next time. It's usually your fault, not the game's. Improving yourself on the next run is natural and a lot of fun.
- Highly intuitive. Uses WASD for scrolling, mouse for selection and orders. Lots of menus and statistics.
- Highly engaging storylines. You start to become attached to your little guys and gals. I cry inside everytime one of them dies (which is unfortunately often).
- You can force orders on almost anyone at almost anytime. This gives the player a lot of control to fix problems they see before everything falls apart. This game would super suck without this.
- Still getting better and deeper with each new release.
Cons:
- The time dialation could use some work. There's only 1x, 2x, and 3x. I permanently set mine on 3x and wouldn't mind even faster options. Also, the game forces to 1x in crucial situations like raids. While that's great to let you assess the situation, I often want to set it back to 3x when I'm ready but can't for too long IMO.
- This is both a pro and a con, but there are some frustrating AI things like villagers not effeciently stacking objects. It's a pro because there are mods to address most any problem in the game (including the stack issue). It's a con because these things aren't in the base game but should be (and we shouldn't have to search for mods to fix basic functionality). It is still an EA though, so there's hope.

Trackmania Canyon is probably the most satisying game of the TrackMania² lot.  The stadium approach of endless boring technical fullspeed maps where all speed gains come from just holding down one button or key for the entire map while sticking to a single ideal race line, both the stock and popular genres of custom made maps in Canyon demand precision drifting through impossibly thin margins at blistering speeds.
Nothing comes close to matching the sense of speed and visceral satisfaction this game offers at knocking fractions of a second off of your personal bests.  Or watching your car fly into space after getting intimately familiar with a canyon wall or lamppost.  The time attack format and typical bite sized map length of 30-60 seconds allow for experiences that are challenging without becoming too frustrating, either from the perspective of the new player who's still bouncing off walls or the ladder points nerd trying to get that one perfect run.
You should definitely buy this game if you have any interest in going fast.

Ok, I love this game but I understand that it's not for everyone. A few of the main issues that people seem to have:
- Teamwork is essential, without it the match is just a stomp fest from the opposing teamwork.
- You rely heavily on your team mates, this is great when it works, but can be super frustrating when people just do their own thing.
- Somebody needs to do the boring jobs. Defending and logistics can be boring, but if nobody does it it's basically an instant loss.
- Some SL's are bad, some are good. Anyone can be an SL.
- You need to communicate and you need to listen. Your main source of info on where the enemy are is your teams communication. You really really need a mic for this and you need to be willing to talk to strangers.
- You also need to be willing to take orders from strangers.
- Vehicles are used sparingly. No personal taxis.
- Tactics and positioning win fights, not being a good shot or having fast reflexes, though it helps.
- There is no kill feedback or kill count until the match is over.
- Game is not yet optimized. Unless you have a current gen nvidia gpu and a decent cpu, you may need to sacrafice some graphics to get high frame rates.
- Respawn time, and time to actually get into the fight, can sometimes be long. This is especially true with no teamwork. Spawn points are set up by your team mates and your squad leader which requires multiple people working together, if there is no teamwork then there are no spawn points. In these cases the only spawn available to you might be literally miles away from the actual fighting.

It’s hard to believe that the Dark Savant trilogy began 26 years ago in 1990 with Bane of the Cosmic Forge. Resisting these games, I see gameplay elements that were new at the time, but now mark the RPG genre forever. I can’t begin to explain how much this series of Wizardry 6, 7, and 8 ushered in the whole RPG genre. Unfortunately, there are plenty of other articles about how great Wizardry is, and I’m not going to be another re-write. The real question is whether or not Wizardry 6 and 7 are still relevant today and worth playing.
Over a period of two weeks in Wales (lovely place for a holiday), with absolutely no internet, I brought out the paper and pencils and painstakingly mapped each tile in my epic adventure. It became apparent quickly that this is the largest drawback of the Wizardry series, especially 6 and 7. While in newer cRPGs it is easier to figure out the map without a physical drawing, the darkness and confusion of 6 and 7 make this incredibly difficult. Every dungeon has many twists and turns painted in the same theme. Essentially, it’s the same wall staring at you over and over again. In Wizardry 6, I spent a good 2 hours trying to figure out how to open a door in the first dungeon, only to find a button on a wall that I hadn’t mapped. Of course, I could never see that button unless I was in the perfect spot. All in all, this makes a very very frustrating experience.
What amazed me, however, was the incredible depth of character. There are a variety of classes in Wizardry, each working in a completely different way to the others. The customization of loot and character RNG is far beyond even contemporary titles. I spent 4 hours in character creation alone.
But even with amazing character design, the game is brutally difficult. I won’t lie, in true 90s fashion both games are incredibly unbalanced. Some dungeons are a breeze, others one-shot your best characters. I can’t tell you how many times I had to load a save just because I walked into the wrong room and got accosted by pixelated robbers. Please nerf.
NPC actions are a breath of fresh air. Instead of boring chat options, you can talk unlimited to NPCs and cultivate rapport. You can even attack them (although that’s ill advised, they hold important parts of the lore and items you NEED to complete the game).
Speaking of lore, even with very limited ‘story’ the game still manages to keep a whole universe cultivated. Multiple endings (which were novel in 1990) and multiple beginnings allowed for huge variety in playthroughs, and honestly even the sparsely told story is much better than many RPGs today.
I promised to evaluate the state of Wizardry in today’s world, and I hope I’ve made it clear that for all its glory, Wizardry 6 and 7 (which are practically the same game, you can even carry your party over from 6 to 7) is no longer relevant in this age. I simply can’t recommend spending time in a frustrating mess unless you are a true RPG connoisseur. Even then, there are plenty of better games to play. It’s a new dawn, and Wizardry doesn’t have a place in the gaming world anymore. Rest in peace.
Final Scoring:
Story - 7
Gameplay - 7
Relevancy - 0
Graphics - 3 (unless you're 'that guy')

So I have had about 12 hours in this game now and it is starting to get somewhere for me. ;-) Imho the game is a little overwhelming at first. I am used to games like Battlefield and the likes, but no realism shooters. This one is not really realistic, but a lot closer to it that most AAA titles.
So what is this game really and what do you need to do to enjoy it?
1) This game does not take you hand and gives you one of those boring tutorials. You should watch a few video tutorials first though, because there is some important info you should have before jumping into the battlefield. And even then, some stuff might not be obvious. For me this is fine. The game just has a learning curve like that. This leads really well into my next point:
2) Use a headset!!!!!!!!!! You HAVE TO communicate. Especially at the beginning, most people are really trying to help you out if there is anything you don't understand right away. You also HAVE TO coordinate your attacks. Some of the time you will actually see your enemy, some of the time you have a scop and that might help you acquiring a target, but a lot of times your squad leader will just use binoculars and just tell you roughly where to shoot. It is amazing when you have a 50cal shooting at you and your squad leader is good enough to get 5 people to shoot at the position of that gun and suddenly he tells that the enemy is down. He can see, you just shoot. ......so yeah, this is just one example, but communication is key at all times. The developers really thought about that as well. You can either chat with you squad or surrounding people or as a squad leader you can individually talk to other squad leaders.
3) Be a mate. ;-) Most people here try to help everyone else. As soon as somebody decides to just charge in or shoot before being told to, you die. Squad leader wants to circle around an enemy and you don't wanna be seen.....suddenly one person in the squad decides to shoot: everybody dead, because we were heard and then seen because of it. Do what your leader tells you to do.
4) Don't get frustrated by the shooting right away. it is VERY different from what I am used to, and not being able to zoom at all on most guns feels weird, but that is realistic. You enemy has the same problem. And when you get shot at, try too find out roughly where it is comiung from and just tell your squad to rain hell on that position. Most of the time, that works. ;-) Also, this game is not ONLY about shooting. A lot of it is tactics.
So overall, if you have time enough to sit through a game that might take an hour, enjoy to talk to team mates (most people do), like to coordinate or support, want a real challenge, like big battles: buy it!
Well, I personally will play this a lot when I find the time. ;-)

Wizardry... A legendary name for a legendary game franchise, created by two U.S.A. college students in their spare time, one can’t help but wonder if they thought or even knew that their game, along with the Ultima franchise, would shape RPGs as we know them today. Probably not. But they did, and whether they knew of the greatness they would achieve is no longer questionable, but one thing is certain: a particular video game publisher out there wants us to remember the fun times we had playing Wizardry (at least from Wizardry VI, the subject of this review, onwards) because we can now purchase them and play them legally from websites such as
and Steam.
Wizardry VI: Bane of the Cosmic Forge came to make our Dungeons & Dragons senses tingle way back in 1990 for the Amiga and DOS platforms. And for a game that’s as advanced as this one is, which is by the standards set in 1990, by the way, this game had a lot of cool features. A complex character creation system, skills that increased the more you used them, there’s more,
I’m sure, but I can’t exactly remember them.
Gameplay-wise, the game feels like a turn-based version of the RPG known as 'Eye of the Beholder’. When starting out, you must create a party of between 2-6 members, and you can choose their race, gender, class, what skills they specialize in, etc. Now, I’m fully well-aware that in this day and age, most people prefer to play with characters who are based into the story, but for me, at least, this is a welcome change. After creating the characters that will be in your party, you then venture into the castle, where the Cosmic Forge is said to rest. Your party has to fight and build up their skills and experience by fighting life-or-death battles with rats, bats, rogues, and for whatever reason, moving vines. At times, you must use their skills to solve puzzles. It isn’t much, again, by today’s standards, but back then, things like this in video games were unheard of. Using skills, such as Search to find hidden things within the game’s world, could make the game easier or harder, depending on the skills you invested points into.
If you came here to see what music you can rock out to while playing the game, you... are totally S.O.L., my friend! The only “music” you can hear in this game is what sounds like the flapping of wings and something banging around on walls. And even then, you only hear it when you’re standing still. Now, when you hit enemies while you’re in battle, you’ll hear what sounds like a weapon of some sort hitting something else that’s metal, but it plays no matter what enemy you hit, regardless of whether or not they wear armor. Again, that’s just a small nitpick of mine, it’s not a make-or-break deal. At least, for me it isn’t.
Graphics are actually very-well developed. You can tell what monsters (with a few exceptions) are of what type and in the inventory, you can tell (usually) what type of weapon is what, based on the name and item icon. And while the tilesets in the game are good-looking as well, be prepared to see them A LOT.
Unfortunately, I can only in good conscience recommend this game to Hardcore Dungeons & Dragons fans. Or, to someone who has the patience of a saint for all of the grinding you’ll be doing throughout the game, and believe, you WILL do quite a bit of grinding if you want to get even remotely close to the end of the game.

I'm probably less than halfway through this game, so what have I done with my 34 hours of play time?
Rolling characters takes a long time. There is no easy reroll button. Create a character, sigh at his or her crummy stats, delete the character, repeat. I try to play with the first characters I roll, but I die a lot in the opening castle, so I spend a few hours creating a party of 6 elite adventurers, and then die a lot with them.
Without the option of rolling even higher stats, I resort to saving and loading the game constantly. Early enemy encounters can be fair or unfair; unfair encounters lead me to restarting dosbox and loading my last save, fair encounters lead me to a phyrric victory, followed by saving, resting, saving, resting, saving, resting, being surprised by an enemy, quitting, loading, resting saving, moving on. Locked doors can be successfully picked and opened, or jammed and forever closed. It takes an average of ten reloads to successfuly pick a lock-- all of the doors are locked; some locks must be left alone until later.
The grind doesn't end, but the feeling of helplessness does. After the first few hours of play, i experience a battle that takes all of my strategy, cunning, and items to beat. This victory is not phyrric. This victory is glorious. I am a thirty year old man who stands up and pumps his fist.
With a new confidence, I begin to explore in earnest. The levels are all mazes. They are all connected, so the world feels vast. The world is a maze. The world is a vast and beautiful maze that connects many smaller mazes. The vast maze sprawls like the tentacles of a giant octopus. The small mazes stack level upon level, doubling in on themselves and zig-zagging vertically. Navigating the staircases that crowd each level takes hours. On the screen, the world is endless identical gray, stone corridors. In my mind, it's a dark and forbidding world whose respect I am earning.
Some very close boss battles later, each of which took many reloads and ended with a satisfied sigh of relief, I reach the Pyramid. Gone are the Pirates and Lizardmen and Jelly Clouds that populated the castle, and the mountain, and the mine, replaced by a Shamaness and her many subclasses. Native, Priestess, etc. They wear grass skirts and bare breasts. Each encounter makes me wish I could just complete this dungeon and forget that it ever existed, but even with a completed map, navigating the pyramid takes hours. Every time i encounter an enemy, I feel a little bit of my enthusiasm die. I have all the requisite pieces to continue now, but despite the nostalgia and child-like engagement ellicited by this game, I feel that perhaps the spell has been broken.

If you're reading this, you already know the basic gameplay: it's a shmup with RPG elements. One thing that you can't tell from the videos and screen shots is how confusing it can be when you start. You're thrust into the game world with very little explanation, and you have to figure stuff out as you fight and die and die and die. Some people will find this fun (including me, which surprised me) and some people will find this frustrating and quit. It's up to you to guess which category you'll fall into.
I haven't experienced any bugs, but I have run into some.. unusual balance decisions. Enemy melee attacks seem to be much weaker than their projectiles, which in turn are much weaker than the projectiles spawned when they die, so you have to be more afraid of enemies when they die than when they chase you. Like I said, kind of odd, but once you notice that pattern and get used to it, it's no less fun.
Skills don't look very balanced to me, either, but respeccing is cheap so that's not necessarily a big deal.
Graphics and sound are pretty subjective, and you can check them for yourself in the above video, but FWIW I really like them. The one exception is the voice acting, which I didn't think was the 'so bad it's good' type. I thought it was the 'so bad it's really terrible' type.

Oxenfree is a narrative game about some insufferable ♥♥♥♥ing teenagers getting stuck on a haunted island. Well, that's not entirely fair—of the five, on is actually kinda nice, one can be made nice if you keep chipping away at her, and one is you, the protagonist, whom you can make into actually quite a nice character through dialogue options. I made my Alex into someone I quite liked; confident, easygoing, funny, intelligent, and viewing all this supernatural stuff as just some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t she had to shoulder through.
Gameplay-wise, Oxenfree (a title that, as I recall, doesn't actually have anything to do with the game) is a visual novel with more walking, and occasionally winding a crank or finding the right radio signal. A thing I really liked is that you're allowed to just not pick anything and stay silent during dialogue options, a feature I used fairly often when every option would've made me sound like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
For some reason, the characters don't swear. They drink, smoke, do drugs, and make♥♥♥♥♥♥jokes, but I think one "hell" and one &quot♥♥♥♥♥quot; are all you can get out of 'em. They actively go out of their way to avoid saying &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; or "♥♥♥♥," which just confused me. Also, they cotton on to the idea of supernatural stuff kinda unrealistically quickly, but that's less jarring.
The character models are kinda janky. A lot of times, it's clear that they're not interacting at all with the 2D backdrop.
The game also loses something when it gets to the last 40% or so and moves from "let's try to find each other and figure out what the ♥♥♥♥'s going on" to "let's
." It's still good, but a little of the magic's gone.
But whatever the game's flaws, it really grabbed me in a way that I completely didn't expect. I was genuinely interested in seeing what would happen next, to the point that I went to bed thinking "Oh boy, tomorrow I can play more Oxenfree!" which doesn't happen very often. Even if the game has some design decisions that bemused me, it's really engaging and involving, and I recommend it for that.
Also, it's apparently got multiple endings and♥♥♥♥♥♥ but I feel like replaying the game to get all of them would diminish the effect of the story somewhat. I did the story I did, made the decisions I made, and got the ending that fit that best, and that's all there is to it.

I would like to recommend this, but honestly I can't. Even for its "low" price. Even if it's an indie game, assuming that indie games have lower budget and they can be imperfect. This game is far from perfect.
I initially bought this game because of my friend who also bought it. There was a nice discount so I was like "well, whatever". I like rogue-like/rpg games (even when it comes to modern games of that genre). What's the worst that could happen, this game was cheaper than a pack of cigarettes.
When I first played the game it was a really nice experience. There is a few classes to choose from (like 10), each with different skill/perk set and stats, look etc. It's nice to have this kind of diversity. So I started playing the game.
This game is pretty simple and kinda reminds me of Binding of Isaac (it's not a carbon copy though, but you can see the inspiration). The difference is you don't get rooms with enemies, they come in waves, also you get levels. But still you get temporary boosts (potions) and 1-run boosts (relics). In addition you can also have a minion and a "charm" which is a stat item.
it's repetitive but a game can have replayability of sorts. You get few different bosses and enemies, they get tougher, some get affixes (special abilities), you develop your hero, get new relics and such. But there isn't really much fun about it. It's a shame, but I'll talk about a few things in detail in a second.
Mostly consisting of areas and difficulty levels. The latter seems obvious, as for the first: often I feel like the areas are almost the same but with ground colored in white/green/yellow, even some statues/models are reused, and I really didn't expect that. You also get relics which are fun but some seem overpowered for the moment and often you feel like there's little control over them. Also I've never felt like "gee I would like to get X now to make this run better/more fun". Isn't that exactly the opposite of what SHOULD be happening?
You get levels and new skills abilities but the descriptions are really confusing and it often feels like some of the perks are underwhelming which shouldn't ever happen in such a game. Again, I didn't feel any urge to level up in any other way than "this will maybe improve my fighting capabilities by 0.05% yay". I get that some of the perks are better, some are worse, some will only work with enough attack speed/damage, but still...
Ok I thought the game was simple enough to never touch this subject,  but... Controls in the game are really sketchy, honestly. One of the things is that you get to use the mouse in game, you see the cursor while playing, but still you control and attack with WASD and arrows. Kinda strange, but ok, let's say that's the way this game is made, it's not bad, just a bit confusing at start. On the other hand you can go to the right and attack to the left, which is cool for kiting with ranged heroes (and melee as well).
Sometimes you can't tell if there's a wall on your way, or you're gonna pass right through.
The voice acting is terrible and I feel it would be way better if they didn't even bother recording the voice lines. There's a few of them and you hear the same line over and over again. Most of the responses are super edgy even though it doesn't fit the design (that's the way I feel about it). Other than that the audible part of the game is OK, nothing to complain about.
It's ok, pseudo-retro-ish style like in many indie games released in past 3-4 years. But still, as mentioned before they could've made the areas a bit more interesting and varied. I didn't mention some of the projectiles are really tricky to see/recognize, but I'm not sure if that's how it was supposed to be. My humble opinion: they should be easy to spot, but hard to dodge/avoid.
This is where it gets really though... Due to lack of replayability factor (other than mindless grinding, which ends quickly because you have only 9 abilities per hero to discover) I wanted to ask myself what content is there waiting for me, but there isn't really much about the game. I was really so bored after playing for 1.5 hour (I felt like I've seen everything) I wanted some confirmation about this, and my friends actually confirmed there's not much more to this game than what I've already seen. Co-op would be fun, but you can either play local co-op or you have to... PAY FOR THE DLC. I mean jesus, the 2 DLCs this game has cost more than the game itself and one of them is pretty much a MUST HAVE if you want to play with your friends over the internet. This really sucks.
: It's not really that bad, it has a lot of flaws, but it's somewhat playable, just really boring after a short session, unless you LOVE doing the same thing over and over again, but you could be playing any other game of the genre and most probably have more fun. It's really repetitive, there isn't much of a reward for playing. There's a lot of stuff unlocked with the DLCs (like multiplayer) so consider the price for the game + dlcs as a full product price. I personally felt like the game I bought was just the demo and a way to "hype" me into buying the additional content. I didn't get hyped at all. Game sucks.

So Sherlock holmes Devil's daughter: On the one hand it has a great idea with deduction and clues, calling suspects out in their lies like in L.A. noire and making deduction from evidence to solve the cases. On the other hand, all the "puzzles and QTE sequenses arn't really entertaining for the most part and drag on for far too long. The primary example of this is the temple sequens which has a ton of these puzzles, 3 floor puzzles a turn puzzle and a button puzzle before its over. I ended up skipping most of the puzzles because I was more excited about the story and solving the cases. The puzzles work only when they are ment to help us solve the mystery like solving a sequens of events to create a narrative while puzzles that just try to prolong the time we spend untill the next section of gameplay feel unesssary. Why do we have to solve 3 different versions of a lockpick puzzle that just keep us from the story by prolonging the run time with needless button pressing(The interface in these puzzle sections could use some work too.)and if its so essential why do you give the option to skip it at all. Tell a story though these tasks, advance the plot, don't just try to gate us from the next objective. This game is at its best when its giving cases with a moral dimention. showing actions and consequenses that are not all black and white. The cases however are fairly easy to solve once you realise that the game is develobed in such a way that if you stick with it and go though all the locations on every case you will often find that the last solution you can come up with is the correct one. In summery: Far too few cases of actual importance, far to many QTE and puzzle  sinqueses that are simply there to stop us from progessing. Stick to what you do best, which are the great cases and mysteries and make those sequenses longer instead of packing the game with far too many unesssary action sequenses.

I am enjoying the "you-know-what" out of DvDrum! As a former drummer, I can say that, although I haven't a clue about the technical stuff in this simulator, I am having an absolute BLAST playing along with my favorite songs. The drum sounds awesome and I have adjusted cymbals, toms, bass drum and, yes..even the COWBELL to my liking, haha. Man, I gotta say to all the drummers out there, "Have you ever told your GF, BF, Husband, Wife or your friends that you used to be in a band and they kinda shrugged and just looked at you with hint of, 'Oh, sure you did' ?" Well, I can say that transitioning from hands and feet to using your fingers on your keyboard requires practice...the end result is well worth it. Not only are people believers now, but I am just plain having a blast playing the songs from our band's set list. The sounds are adjustable and this simulator has a whole bunch of options that I really don't understand, yet. I feel I have only scratched the surface of what can be done with this program. It has MIDI input, btw, but I pound my mechanical kb mercilessly and it is still holding on with no breaks or keys falling off. I have also purchased a cheap membrane-type keyboard and it works fine, as well. I will say that when it comes to playing exactly like a drum set, I have not worked up to keeping time on the hi-hat and cymbals 100% of the time with my fingers...but I see progress with practice. There's all kinds of programmable stuff for the professional...again, which I don't "get". I'll have to read about that stuff, sometime.
I would recommend this to my family and friends...I would even recommend DvDrum to a band whose drummer couldn't make it to the gig!   9.7/10
EDIT: Dec 19, 217- With practice, I am able to keep time on my hi-hat key(s) while playing with drumless tracks and the sound comes through better than the original song because "I" control the drum volume and I jack up the crispness of the cymbals for a really clean, personalized version of my favorite songs. To recap, using just my fingers and my keyboard, I now play the kick bass, tom toms, snare, cymbals and hi-hat as I hear in most songs. When I initially began using DvDrum, I was hitting only the snare and kick bass as I played along with music. Proves to me that, with practice, you'll "get it" and will surely blow your expectations away.

Bought this game last week while it was 50% off. Whether you enjoy the game or not really depends alot on the squad itself, especially the squad leader.
A good squad leader doesn't necessarily mean a pro who is leading the team to victory, there's more aspects to that. At least to me, a win or loss doesn't matter as long as I had fun. Squad isn't a fast-paced shooting game like CSGO, hop/bam/shoot. The map is huge, with the limited stamina, like others said: Squad can be the Walking Stimulator, so with that being said, the gameplay can be long. Therefore getting good teammates, people who have the right amount of patience, squad members laughing at their own fails, a teeny tiny bit of fooling around - all of these makes a great game.
Personally for me, I feel so blessed to have the best of luck meeting the best squad leaders and members.
There was only that one time when a squad leader ask me to stop wasting time and get to the vehicle when the capacity is already full since it's not a humvee or those big vehicles. Left me stranded, pushes the blame when I didn't make it in time when I had to walk all the way to the location.
Whether to buy the game or not: Yes, please. You should really consider getting it, the community so far has been great :) There's no need to own whatever loot crates or dlcs to get top of the game, the name "Squad" says it all, you and the members. Together & united XD

Squad had to be one of the worst FPS war simulators I have played from any video game within the genre ever. While the sounds of the game are amazing and the community is friendly, this is the most minimalist first person shooter I have ever played. The only thing that is complex is the 40 keys that can be pressed for different kinds of communication between squad and individual player. It is like someone took battlefield 1 and stripped away everything fun about it including intense action, fun guns, realistic building demolition, and complex weaponry. 90% of the buildings are pointless, empty rooms with nothing inside and they even have staircases that lead to blocked off roofs (aka super lazy developers and map designers). The developers are too lazy to even add a ♥♥♥♥ing lampstand in these empty, boring "buildings." People talk about realisim, and yet every building you enter is completely ♥♥♥♥ing empty; no furniture, no wallpaper, no originality in the slightest. Most of the time you will die from people you never see, and half the time you are getting shot at your screen goes borderline black as if you are having a ♥♥♥♥ing stroke every time a bullet whizzes over your head. At least make it simple for you to find your surrounding team, even if you can't see where the enemy are camping from. After a pointeless two hour game you will realize you could have been playing a game where "realistic shooter" doesn't mean minimalist, lazy development. If only this game was optimized, cheap, and had decent graphics compared to every other shooter, the game could be placed with a simple rating of okay. Do yourself a favor and don't fall into the group that calls this game realistic instead of what it really is, lazy development. This game is so realistic you can't even climb over a 3 foot wall or climb through a window.

In addition to the other comments, some tips, which are also generally applicable to Wiz 7 (I haven't done 8 yet):
1. Spend the extra time rolling characters. Spread it out in 20-30m bursts over days if you want. I like to have the following:
Lord, maxing strength if possible. (No switch intended. Late-game ebony, mantis, etc will ensure super low AC)
Ninja, with enough extra points to assign stats for a guaranteed profession switch to Samurai when needed. Allows maxed Kirijitsu by late game. (One game I made this a super-ranger who went ninja at level 8).
Samuri or Monk, with enough extra points to assign stats for a guaranteed profession switch to Ninja. Allows maxed Kirijitsu by late game. Have one Samuri by or after Hall of the Dead, so you can equpi Murusama Blade. Second-best weapon in game (to Excalibur, which pretty much never drops).
Rawulf priest with stats to change to bishop at first profession change. Rawulfs can always switch back to priest because they start with 12 PIE.
Mage with stats to switch to bishop at first profession change. (I like elf because 10 INT, 10 PIE, making priest-mage switching very easy)
Mage with stats to switch to bishop at first profession change. (I like elf because 10 INT, 10 PIE)
One mage should pick Knock-knock at earliest opportunity to address lack of thief.

Absolutely wonderful kart/plane/boat-racing game.
Pros:
Lost's of variety in characters and levels.
Some of the most gorgeous and breath-taking level design in any game. As for it being a racing game, easily the best I've played. The way that each lap transforms into something new making the whole race feel like one coherent whole is just fantastic.
Each "kart" mode feels different and unique in how they handle and with lot's of mods to cater to your specific taste in feel. Car mode handles as responsive as any other kart racer I've played. Boat racing has some extremely well thought out physics that make it really feel like you're driving in water. Flying is probably the most bland but also the most intriguing to look at since the levels do such interesting things while you're in the air. Overall they do the job and feel quite fulfilling.
4 player local coop=awesome. Lot's of different modes to play with each other including battles and special race types.
Online multiplayer for those who'd rather play with larger groups of "real" people.
Cons:
Settings are set outside of the game from a launcher which makes for some nasty alternating between executables to get things just right rather than having them in game and changed on the fly for more direct contrast.
You have to play through the whole campaign mode to unlock all the different characters, levels, and mods. I suppose this is per the norm these days to entice you to play through the campaign but honestly, the campaign itself should be enticement enough to get you to play it rather than teasing you with a treat in front of your nose so that you continue chasing after the treat rather than actually caring about where it's taking you. Seriously, just let me play as Shadow from the get go, I'll be much happier.
No easy handicapping built in to balance out skill levels between players. Makes for a poor party game in which you wish to bring a lot of new players and veteran players together to scream and laugh together.
Overall:
Not much to complain about here, the game is solid for what it is. It wanted to be an awesome hybrid of racing, boating, and flying and they did a killer job at it. From a personal perspective in which I hunt for awesome party games, it could have been a bit better like not making me go through all of the campaign so that my friends can play with whatever character they want. At least they allowed the players to play together in the campaign which is a nice breath of fresh air.
Tons of fun, had me giggling with nerdy delight at the amount of love poured into this game. I highly recommend you give it a go if you're at all into kart racing games.

The (16 colors only) graphics don't lie; This isn't a modern game with modern sensibilities masquerading in retro clothing.  This is a genuine NES-generation RPG built to essentially replicate D&D on PCs not even powerful enough to run Windows 3.x...
I'll be up-front with it: In this game, you start by building a party by rerolling virtual dice, sometimes for hours, until you get stats you can accept in your pre-planned growth strategy that will last the whole game before you even set foot in the dungeon.  If mashing a reroll button (which is made even less convenient by not letting you cancel out - you have to finish making a character before you can try again) to get the stats you want doesn't appeal to you, turn around, now.
Even if you get attributes you like, you can still be screwed by randomly having only 3 hit points on a melee character in a game where a mere rat hits for 5 hp, you have full death on 0 hp, revive items and spells are extremely rare outside the late game, and even if you did, you PERMANENTLY lose 1 Vitality (on characters with an average of 10), which drops future HP growth.  Basically, if you take one unlucky hit, you have to reload.  (And there's no soft reset, you have to finish the combat or alt-tab and force-close the program...)
To stop this, you can try to use a sleep spell, and insta-kill the rats, right?  HAHA! NOPE! Enjoy missing against an unconscious enemy about 60% of the time, and then having about a 50% chance that your sword won't penetrate the "armor" of the rat.
Then, you have the locked doors.  Highly random, and failure frequently JAMS the door, making it impossible to open except by magic or single-use keys that are rare drops.  At least reloading is faster, here.
Unlike other D&D clones, however, skills are train-through-use, not unlike Elder Scrolls.  This makes many skills, like weapon skills, easily trained by merely hitting the target (not that such an event is at all common) while only a few require actually spending skill points on them.  In some ways, this is great, as it means you can power-grind characters all you want.  On the other hand, this means that the game basically just flat-out expects you to power-grind every skill to max fairly early on, and 100 points in a skill isn't necessarily going to mean you succeed.
That said, unlike Wizardry 8, there's extremely large room for multiclassing abuse.  This is a game that is more free-form about its character creation specs, and if you gained a single level as a bard, you can continue to train bard music then turn into a mage, take up some spellcasting, then go samurai to continue training as a singing, spell-casting, warrior.
This is also a game old enough that having all the women topless wasn't a major concern, the manual is written as if it assumes you're 8 years old, and rolling a female character means you take a -2 to strength, but, "That's OK, because women have a +1 to personality and karma!"  (Note: they're both basically useless. That said, the gender-restricted valkyrie class is generally worth it, anyway, and the caster classes don't need strength... unless you multi-class to a hybrid class.)
If the idea of ridiculous power-grinding appeals to you, and you don't mind savescumming 'till your fingers bleed, then maybe, just maybe, you'll be the sort of person that loves this sort of game.  I can't even explain why, it's just a COMPULSION.  You'll beat that lock next time! You are so close to making that spectacular ninja-valkyrie or psionist-monk!

My girlfriend bought me this game today as a surprise gift through Humble store. After checking its Steam store page, I was a bit confused as to what she actually paid for, since the game was listed as free to play. Turns out the game is free with a sliver of content and then you have to pay for the rest.
The game is very colourful and pretty, but also poorly optimized. My (admittedly aging, but still very able) notebook couldn't hold the fps consistently up. I could live with that, if the gameplay wasn't so bad.
The game feels really simple, but not in a good way. The maps in the mission I chose to play were all flat pieces of land with some enemies and several mob-spawning towers. Fighting felt sluggish, imprecise and pointless. I played the game with two bots and would sometimes let them kill the monsters in my stead, because to do it myself was just a painful experience.
During the 33 minutes of gameplay I found two bugs. One was an invisible boss that spawned after I killed the actual boss. The invisible boss was constantly roaring and attacking the ground, probably mad about the game quality and his lack of visibility. The other was a graphical glitch, that showed huge white tile under another boss monster. Neither of these bugs were game-breaking, I managed to finish the three stage mission fine. Then again, they were annoying.
There are only three characters. They have one skill each (there might be more to unlock through coins, but I never got that far). They apparently can do skill combos together, but this just didn't happen for me and the bots. It wasn't badly needed though, as the combat was not enjoyable anyway.
Even though the Evil Genius's sidekick encourages you to "Enjoy the looting", there is no actual loot apart from coins.
You are encouraged to use physics to throw objects and animals (!) around to hit your enemies, but most of the time this just doesn't work. Sheep are for some reason thrown in a big arc, over the heads of enemies you were aiming at. Even with careful positioning, I was not able to hit anyone with sheep. <- This sentence now looks ridiculous.
The developers stated that this game is supposed to be enjoyed as a coop game with three other players, but I don't see how I would persuade anyone to buy this. And now, according to other reviewers, the support of multiplayer has been dropped (I haven't tested it though), so their selling point is... gone.
In short, the game is really simple and doesn't stand up to the competition of Torchlight, Diablo and others.
I understand this is the maker's first game, I've read about all the troubles they had while developing this (one dev even had to sell his car) and I wish them good luck in the future. Still, I can't recommend this game.

My Rimworld Story: One sunny day, in my medium sized colony, my colonists were in the middle of a good summer harvest. Suddenly, sirens sound, the screen flashes red, and at the bottom right corner a small box with the words "Raid (boss)" appear. What does that mean? It means that the supreme leader of the planetwide pirate band has joined in on a raid on my peaceful colony. Raiders pop out of drop pods, assault rifles, snipers, and the boss, weilding a rocket launcher. I send my colonists to their positions, my colonists survive, but we still have casualties: two adult alpacas, and a newborn alpaca, less than a season old. The raiders are all either dead or too hurt to move. Among the barely living is the pirate boss. For the crime of killing my alpacas, death is too light a punishment. I learn that my colonists would gain a mood boost for killing the leader, but it isn't worth it. I capture the leader, I put him in a nice cell, I tend his wounds using the best medicine, feed him the best of food, he is going to need it. Once his wounds are healed, tended by my nurse, I bring in my doctor, who also has the psychopath trait. My prisoner falls asleep, and my doctor goes to work. When the pirate boss wakes up, he isn't sure that he is awake, everything is still black, "Am I dead?" he may have thought. "No, I can still feel the pain." He cannot see. Oh my god. Rimworld.
I bought this game a long, long time ago. I originally owned it long before it was on Steam, so I'd guess I have 200+ hours on this masterpiece. Rimworld is such a creative take on such an overused idea. People stranded away, and now they've gotta survive.
Basebuilding:
Although the customization♥♥♥♥♥♥doesn't have much variety, I'm sure there's more stuff I haven't seen, as I still haven't research any of the cosmetic techs, ever. The basebuilding is fun as hell, and I always feel like my buildings are gonna mean something. Abandon a project mid construction? Maybe you can use it as cover to hide from the bandit's sniper, who never seems to miss a shot.
Traits/Skills:
These are the bread and butter of your Rimworld experience. One of the largest parts of Rimworld, what your colonists can do, and what goes on in there head. The relationships that form between them, are what helps you bond with them. I've never been so attached to little digital characters. Not even in the Sims.
Combat:
This is what makes Rimworld hard. No deaths on your side? You'd assume the fight went well. But when your only doctor lost a leg, who's gonna help him? What about when that simple bullet wound turns into an infection? Are you gonna amputate it? The limbs of all these people are almost as important as them themselves, and even if you just survived a raid aganist all odds, the missing bodyparts can make you feel so helpless. The way the cover in this game works, combined with the skill, and the heart pounding moment when you just pray that your doctor is knocked into shock and not killed, is part of what makes Rimworld, Rimworld.
Conculsion:
Every little thing in this game comes together creating a masterpiece, that is unrivaled by any game I've ever played in its genere. Feels like a game I can always fall back on, and just hop on and play. The developers clearly care about and love this game, and I don't know why its considered an early access with all the♥♥♥♥♥♥it has.
TL:DR This game is ♥♥♥♥ing amazing. Buy it.

Hey, so what is Rimworld? Rimeworld is a gem in what seems to be a forgotton genre mix of strategy and role playing games.
Rimworld throws you into a world with a bunch of survivors, who each have their own skill sets and useful traits like cooking, hunting, building etc. YOU as "pretty much their god" will decide what they do, what they eat, where they can and cannot go. You are pretty much their savior as well as their doom, depending on how good you are at micro managing, resource control, building, creating working structures and defenses.
It definitely is not easy, you will have your colony killed a lot by pirates, wild animal hordes and acid rain. You will have you colonists go crazy, run around naked until they die or kill other colonists, you will have your colonists starve, resort to cannibalism, which in the end makes them crazy, and die again...
You might discover hidden structures, unearth them, only to find out there was an ancient killing machine hidden within, which will ultimately kill your entire colony and make you lose, yet again...  XD
But what caught me in this game, are the endless possibilites, the 100000 different ways you will miserably fail in this game, and the billions of different ways you will succeed and build a florishing colony of battle hardened survivors!
You can build ACs, gun turrets, traps, kitchens, crafting rooms, rec rooms with TVs and couches, train animals of all kinds to fight with you or serve as your resource carrying donkeys, raid pirates, defend yoruselves against intrudors, IMPRISON them, execute them and/or recruit them, trade with travelling caravans of far away factions, create your own trade caravans, build a space shuttle and leave the planet... The possibilites are completely endless...
Now, was this game worth my money? Yes! Absolutely yes! I personally can't wait where this game is going, but you will definitely get your money's worth in return.

So I have had about 12 hours in this game now and it is starting to get somewhere for me. ;-) Imho the game is a little overwhelming at first. I am used to games like Battlefield and the likes, but no realism shooters. This one is not really realistic, but a lot closer to it that most AAA titles.
So what is this game really and what do you need to do to enjoy it?
1) This game does not take you hand and gives you one of those boring tutorials. You should watch a few video tutorials first though, because there is some important info you should have before jumping into the battlefield. And even then, some stuff might not be obvious. For me this is fine. The game just has a learning curve like that. This leads really well into my next point:
2) Use a headset!!!!!!!!!! You HAVE TO communicate. Especially at the beginning, most people are really trying to help you out if there is anything you don't understand right away. You also HAVE TO coordinate your attacks. Some of the time you will actually see your enemy, some of the time you have a scop and that might help you acquiring a target, but a lot of times your squad leader will just use binoculars and just tell you roughly where to shoot. It is amazing when you have a 50cal shooting at you and your squad leader is good enough to get 5 people to shoot at the position of that gun and suddenly he tells that the enemy is down. He can see, you just shoot. ......so yeah, this is just one example, but communication is key at all times. The developers really thought about that as well. You can either chat with you squad or surrounding people or as a squad leader you can individually talk to other squad leaders.
3) Be a mate. ;-) Most people here try to help everyone else. As soon as somebody decides to just charge in or shoot before being told to, you die. Squad leader wants to circle around an enemy and you don't wanna be seen.....suddenly one person in the squad decides to shoot: everybody dead, because we were heard and then seen because of it. Do what your leader tells you to do.
4) Don't get frustrated by the shooting right away. it is VERY different from what I am used to, and not being able to zoom at all on most guns feels weird, but that is realistic. You enemy has the same problem. And when you get shot at, try too find out roughly where it is comiung from and just tell your squad to rain hell on that position. Most of the time, that works. ;-) Also, this game is not ONLY about shooting. A lot of it is tactics.
So overall, if you have time enough to sit through a game that might take an hour, enjoy to talk to team mates (most people do), like to coordinate or support, want a real challenge, like big battles: buy it!
Well, I personally will play this a lot when I find the time. ;-)

2. The game can be a little buggy at times, but almost never anything that impedes gameplay enough to cause any bad problems. Also, updates are constantly being released to improve gameplay.
3. People complain about dying many times but as long as you don't spend all your character points on attacking skills you will survive
4. There is more than enough content in this game. There are 3 worlds with 30 waves each and 3 difficulties. An overall of 270 waves without one death. This game can last you as long as you want
5. The graphics may not be 3d or the prettiest, but they are fun and retro
6. The relics and items in this game are funny and creative, such as the threatening "candy hammer"
7. This game does require pacience and determination, but once you get some good relics and are strong enough, the levels all become fun and exciting
Lastly, and THE MOST IMPORTANT POINT is that this is a $6 indie game made by 2 developers and for those standards it is an outstanding game. It is a awesome game anyways, one that I pick up and play all the time, but many complaints about this game are fit for a game by a major franchise with a whole team of developers. For example, the multiplayer was developed by someone who had never used that kind of online code before.
Overall, if you are looking for a great, fun game to last you as much time as you want to put into it with an everchanging emvironment to adapt to, this is your game.

Ah, Wizardry 6. Or, as I like to call it, Locked Doors: The Game. Maybe it's just me, but the doors in this game seem a little hard to open. Having to save before every door is a given; having to reload a save because every door is made of titanium shouldn't be. When you finally pry the door open, you'll be treated to old school monsters like bats and rats that will dodge your every blow as they lay in gentle slumber. No worries, however, for if things get too hairy for you in the depths of this 1990s castle, your characters have the option to run away; which was the default operation of graybeard D&D players who cut their teeth on the 1st edition of the pen-and-paper game. Unbeknownst to you, however, is while you spent thirty rounds swinging in futility at sleeping enemies before they awoke to tear your hide apart, you were set upon by other enemies who ambush you as you run away. Whatevs, you think, I'll just run from them also. Well, when these monsters come to gangbang a party of inadequately-statted paper tigers, they come in droves.
Then, inevitably, Death and his SoundBlaster call, as he stands over your tombstone. Yes, a single tombstone, because in the 8-bit era, your horde of characters are buried in the same hole, piled one upon another like firewood, except firewood is useful and characters in the game of Wizardry are not. But, you, my friend, are a true old school RPG fan, and you never give up. You spend hours rolling another party and head down into the depths, uneasy at the strange feeling that you are not playing a clone of Dungeons & Dragons but of the RPG Paranoia, where the Dungeon is not your friend and the assembly line of heroes who engage in suicide-by-bushwhacker is moving faster than that conveyor belt in I Love Lucy.
You will never give up, not until you beat this damned game. Because it CAN be beaten—can it? Or is this game like the module Tomb of Horrors, an exercise by game developers to assume the role of a merciless and antagonistic god, presiding over a world whose populace is comprised solely of doomed heroes fresh from the womb that see the gates of a hungry dungeon and shudder at their fate.
Addendum: Apparently, there is a tool to boost your ability scores during character creation, which will save you the tedium of hours rerolling your team like I did. It isn't necessary, but welcome, especially on a subsequent playthrough.

It's been a while since this review's been up and originally I'd given this a negative review. I had people commenting and messaging me telling me the game's been changed quite a bit and I should check it out. And I did. This is what I've discovered.
The difficulty has evened out quite a bit. My main gripe wasn't so much the difficulty itself as much as it was it's erratic curve. I made a new guy, a necromancer, and decided to play as far as I could, noting how far I've gotten each time I died. First time I died was to the first boss which is understandable. I was playing a squishy character and I'll admit the death was my fault. Second time I died I'd just killed the first boss and didn't notice all the skeleton archers. Third time I died was at the second boss. Each time I died I learned from my mistake, got stronger and got farther every time. It's tough but it's my kinda tough. I like it. Good job fixing that up fellas.
I also enjoy how easy it is to get right back into the game and breeze through the easy waves. You can skip a bunch of waves at one time and take on all the monsters at once to quickly get to the boss. This is perfect for a game this difficult.
I still have a bit of a problem with the voice acting. I've said this before but if you can't get great voice acting then don't get voice acting at all. Sound effects or just simple grunts and yells would do just fine. I do however love the sound design. In a game where you're killing things ad nauseam it's really important to make it feel good when you defeat an enemy. They make good gorey sounds and explode in a huge mess. The music doesn't get repetative either but it sure as hell gets stuck in my head. So yeah. Great sound design, bad voice acting.
All in all it's a good game. I was completely on the fence about it before but the changes they've made had me changing my mind. I promised I'd update my review and here it is. Don't wanna leave a bad review on a good game. Especially one that doesn't deserve it. I'll keep my old review here up for posterity.

I remember that I had this game and it's predecessors on both Amiga and PC back then. This game is one of the dated RPGs, just a dungeon crawl, a lot like some other classics back then (Bards Tale, Tunnels & Trolls etc.). This game was a real chalenge at that time, you needed to draw your own maps. You had to do searches on a regular basis, because some of the treasures were "invisible" or "well hidden". Of course there was no great and interactive PC/NPC interaction back then - but it already started to show some promise in that direction.
In that time it was a great game, but it really shows it's age now. Of course this shouldn't keep you away from a great game, that takes you back in time a real long way. It still can be a lot of fun to play old school CRPG - I loved the memories it evoked as I played it this time.
One good advice, Save your progress as often as you can. Sometimes the game has a tendency to hang up, and sometimes you'll be overwhelmed by a random encounter. You also need some time to make yourself familiar with character generation and learning what skills really are important, which race or class has which skills, attributes and perks. Also keep some boxed paper beside you, you'll might have to draw maps - some of them, or loose your bearings and sometimes your life because you ran into an already once triggered deathtrap. Oh, and save often.

Prior to this, the only experience I had with sonic driving games was the driving stages in sonic adventure on Dreamcast, so I wasn't too optimistic about what this would be like, but I'm very happy with it.
Graphics - The graphics are gorgeous. There are some bells and whistles that we see in many AAA games that are missing, such as ambient occlusion and reflections, but it's not too much of a problem. There is plenty of detail in the level and character design, and the anti-aliasing is very smooth. I keep a very stable 60fps on a gtx750. Some of the levels are extremely creative, and sometimes I wish I could stop and look at the scenery more. I particularly like the latin themed levels with 'dancing' buildings.
Gameplay - The physics is typical kart racing style, and is well implemented. The drifting is slightly different to mario kart, but close enough that it's easy to pick up. The racing is fast paced and very competitive. I find that the items don't suit the game as much as having items in mario kart does. Mario kart is a much slower, easier game, and the items are a big part of what makes it fun. In SASRT, the races are actually very difficult, and because of the fast pace, the items seem more like a distraction/annoyance than anything. On "high" difficult, the difficulty really IS...well...high. I would have preferred that I can improve by focussing solely on my driving skills, but even when you're driving really well, you're likely to get hit by something towards the end of the last lap that will completely kill your chances of winning. This makes the gameplay seem a little unbalanced.
Design - Typical of most sonic games in recent years. Did not work out of the box with my ps2 controller (needed to use x360ce). Looks like a typical sonic game of the last ten years in terms of the menus. The voices and music are really cheesy; reminds me of many Sega games, going back to Sega rally 2 at least.
Overall - Looks great and plays really well, although I would probably enjoy it more without the items. Difficulty is really high. The thing that any sonic racing game has going against it is that mario kart is so iconic that a sonic racing game, no matter how good, is always going to come across as a bit of a 'clone'. The fact that this game can impress in spite of this, speaks volumes about the quality.

I genuinly like the games created by Frogware studios. An adaptation from the novels of Arthur Conan Dyle and with the appearance in game representing the two main protagonists from the 1984 tv-series "The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes", with Jeremy Brett and David burke.
The games are difficult, true puzzle games. The characters are true to their core and doesn't devoid from how they are represented in the books. Eight games, some better and some worse but the majority of the games were good.
Then came this game. The devil's daughter. So much has changed from the extremely good game "Crimes and Punishment" that I am led to believe that this is a lunge at mainstream appeal.
*Cons*
By the gods where do I start. They changed the appearance of both Watson and Holmes to appear both physically and fashionably as two hipsters from a 2015's men's fashion magazine. Somehow they also seemed 15 years younger. And now, Holmes has a daughter.
Here Sherlock Holmes is not focused on what he is famous for, a cool calculating mind with superb deduction skills, with disciplined attention and efficiency. Where his emotions previously fit a tea spoon - it is now the size of a large lake. An unstable emotional wreck. half of the time (and at all time when interacting with his daughter) it is focused on emotions and  seems more of a cliché family drama show than a criminal investigation as the world's most famous Detective.
The game is littered with plot holes and contradictions and I dare say it is so easy that even of highest difficulty my mind would have more of a challange by building lego or piecing together a furniture from ikea. There is a heavier focus on "action" than deduction in this game. Inconsistent, at that.
For example, we have to do an eavesdrop mission from assassin's creed where all the covers fill up a quarter of the screen in its glaring text to let you know that indeed a barrel or a large crate can offer cover.
Rubbish.
*pros*
I had the option to slap a very annoying, manipulating wench. (side con, I don't picture Holmes acting out in sudden fits of rage)
I also heard a Skyrim refference - My Cousin's out fighting robbers and stealing antiques and what do I get? Guard Duty.
