Oh my god. Rimworld.
I bought this game a long, long time ago. I originally owned it long before it was on Steam, so I'd guess I have 200+ hours on this masterpiece. Rimworld is such a creative take on such an overused idea. People stranded away, and now they've gotta survive.
Basebuilding:
Although the customization♥♥♥♥♥♥doesn't have much variety, I'm sure there's more stuff I haven't seen, as I still haven't research any of the cosmetic techs, ever. The basebuilding is fun as hell, and I always feel like my buildings are gonna mean something. Abandon a project mid construction? Maybe you can use it as cover to hide from the bandit's sniper, who never seems to miss a shot.
Traits/Skills:
These are the bread and butter of your Rimworld experience. One of the largest parts of Rimworld, what your colonists can do, and what goes on in there head. The relationships that form between them, are what helps you bond with them. I've never been so attached to little digital characters. Not even in the Sims.
Combat:
This is what makes Rimworld hard. No deaths on your side? You'd assume the fight went well. But when your only doctor lost a leg, who's gonna help him? What about when that simple bullet wound turns into an infection? Are you gonna amputate it? The limbs of all these people are almost as important as them themselves, and even if you just survived a raid aganist all odds, the missing bodyparts can make you feel so helpless. The way the cover in this game works, combined with the skill, and the heart pounding moment when you just pray that your doctor is knocked into shock and not killed, is part of what makes Rimworld, Rimworld.
Conculsion:
Every little thing in this game comes together creating a masterpiece, that is unrivaled by any game I've ever played in its genere. Feels like a game I can always fall back on, and just hop on and play. The developers clearly care about and love this game, and I don't know why its considered an early access with all the♥♥♥♥♥♥it has.
TL:DR This game is ♥♥♥♥ing amazing. Buy it.

Meaningless mini-games with confusing controls are constantly distracting the action. The game only progresses after every obscure "clue" is found in an environment, despite how trivial. Many actions require you to make otherwise meaningless trips to locations to check a fact or run some kind of “analysis.” This basically means gameplay boils down to a few minutes of clicking on things interrupted by cutscenes and load screens. Some of the only opportunities to actually deduce come during suspect observations where you are offered choices to select from with little or no evidence. Like so many point-and-click games most of the challenge/frustration comes from fighting with the interface or the constant rage-quit moments, “I know what I have to do; what the hell do I need to click on to let me do it!” Usually proceeded by Holmes saying a variation of “I don’t want to do that now.” This was acceptable in games released in 2007, but a decade later Frogwares really needs to work on interface and gameplay if they continue to ask AAA prices for their games.

Hey, so what is Rimworld? Rimeworld is a gem in what seems to be a forgotton genre mix of strategy and role playing games.
Rimworld throws you into a world with a bunch of survivors, who each have their own skill sets and useful traits like cooking, hunting, building etc. YOU as "pretty much their god" will decide what they do, what they eat, where they can and cannot go. You are pretty much their savior as well as their doom, depending on how good you are at micro managing, resource control, building, creating working structures and defenses.
It definitely is not easy, you will have your colony killed a lot by pirates, wild animal hordes and acid rain. You will have you colonists go crazy, run around naked until they die or kill other colonists, you will have your colonists starve, resort to cannibalism, which in the end makes them crazy, and die again...
You might discover hidden structures, unearth them, only to find out there was an ancient killing machine hidden within, which will ultimately kill your entire colony and make you lose, yet again...  XD
But what caught me in this game, are the endless possibilites, the 100000 different ways you will miserably fail in this game, and the billions of different ways you will succeed and build a florishing colony of battle hardened survivors!
You can build ACs, gun turrets, traps, kitchens, crafting rooms, rec rooms with TVs and couches, train animals of all kinds to fight with you or serve as your resource carrying donkeys, raid pirates, defend yoruselves against intrudors, IMPRISON them, execute them and/or recruit them, trade with travelling caravans of far away factions, create your own trade caravans, build a space shuttle and leave the planet... The possibilites are completely endless...
Now, was this game worth my money? Yes! Absolutely yes! I personally can't wait where this game is going, but you will definitely get your money's worth in return.

.

Utterly useless.
To play along to "drumless songs" the program opens your web browser and navigates to their site where you can play audio files by clicking on them. Also, given the fame of the bands they are using I can't imagine they actually have permission to use these tracks: Blur, Dylan, Sabbath, Beastie Boys etc. There's just no way they are doing this legally.
Similarly, the recording features are not in the program itself: instead you can set the program to launch an external exe to record video or sound.
Then we have the quality of the program itself, which is also, surprise, suprise, bad. You can select different samples for each drum but once you have selected one, that's it: you will get the exact same sample played at the exact same volume every time you trigger it.
You can play the drums with your computer keyboard or by clicking on them with your mouse. The mouse clicking is massively inaccurate: there are tons of places you can click on the drum and nothing happens. As far as I can tell you can't use a midi keyboard or other device like launchpad, maschine etc.
The mixer has terribly unintuitive controls: instead of clicking and dragging to set the on-screen pots you have to left click on the pot to select it and then use the scroll wheel to set it, then click left again to exit!
This program is utter garbage. It does next to nothing and what it does do, it doesn't do right.

SUMMARY: A cute "auto-adventure" game that's sort of a "casual min-maxer" (trust me).  The usual price may be a bit high unless you really want to delve into different play modes and achievements, but the easy-yet-challenging rules, clever streamlined presentation, and fun soundtrack make it worth keeping an eye on.
Magic Potion Explorer's plot is simple - a young alchemist complains about her need to find ingredients, and a mysterious woman provides her a dungeon below her potion shop.  Armed with an alchemic squirtgun, our heroine Pastel, wanders into the dungeon.  There she harvests resources, battles monsters, and brews potions on her way to figure out what's up, and who's butt she has to kick to get this abomination removed from beneath her store.
The gameplay itself is simple . . .  kind of.
Magic Potion Explorer's adventuring is completely automated.  Pastel goes through the dungeon, find resources, and battles monsters.  Your goal as the player is to choose which potions she brews to affect her abilities.  That's where it gets a bit complex.
Magic Potion Explorer is essentially a casual game for min/maxers who love to tweak abilities.  Some abilities add, some multiply, some affect capacity, some healing.  There's an entire screen just of the math behind the character.  Having to choose which potion to brew - or if to wait to gather enough resources to unlock others - is a core part of the game.
Depending on difficulty, if Pastel is defeated she returns to her shop or she returns without any potions and starts over except for some bonus resources.  Fortunately the deeper you get the more the game accelerates easier levels, so you can keep delving in less and less time.
The game is also accompanied by a great, dynamic soundtrack; the frenetic auto-adventuring and the fast-paced music played during the game really set the mood, the incidental music for calmer moments is a nice contrast.  I'd say the soundtrack is a major strength of Magic Potion Explorer.
Is this game worth it?  The game's two different play modes and multiple achievements will provide some challenge if you're up for them, though the deliberately limited and focused gameplay may not be for everyone.  At $9.99 it's something to think over - if it was cheaper I'd be a little freer to reccomend it.
I bought it and had a ball.  It was a nice casual/intense mix that I was looking for at the time, and I always like to see games experiment.
So who should get Magic Potion Explorer.
* Someone who wants a kind of casual/stats-raising mix.  It's a good evening game for someone so inclined.
* Someone into streamlined games and games that play with modes.  As a study in creating an effective minimalist game, it's quite good.
* If you're not sure and the game is on sale enough to make you sure.

Having a mic is not just for fun - it's a matter of life and death. For now, if the developers won't abandon the game (which I hope is not going to happen) I consider buying it on final release, at least to see if Squad has to offer something to change my mind.

I ignored this game for a while thinking I wouldn't have the time to get into it. Now that I have, I've become addicted. It's tons of fun building vehicles with the various types of movement parts you can use to make all kinds of combinations including ones that are downright moronic. You're allowed a decent degree of freedom through the game's edit mode which is fairly simple and easy to use and which includes the ability to test your vehicle on a small map to work out any kinks. A build cap keeps things reasonable, but within that, you can make pretty huge vehicles or extremely small ones with a variety of weapons including one that heals your team mates or which specializes in taking down airborne targets. You will be challenged to create something practical and effective on the field within the game's limits, but the game does a good job at giving you enough leeway to be creative and clever.
Most impressive is that with the incredibly diverse ways you can build your vehicle, any number of them will show up online. You can buy other people's designs off of a store, but most people will probably be using ones they've made themselves, meaning you won't know what to expect until the game starts. In a 5v5, all ten machines could be totally different, fitted for various specific roles or built to adapt to a number of them. Once you're in the game, you can pilot your vehicle and pit them competition in different game modes while picking your enemy's vehicles apart piece by piece. The game runs smooth despite the number of completely unique and sometimes large contraptions riding and flying around whole or missing various components. As long as you have health left, you can continue to operate your craft, but it may be missing some or all of its functioning parts, and part of the fun is targeting those parts on your opponent to disable them. Anyone who can avoid damage for 10 seconds or so however will begin to automatically repair any damage all the way back to a full recovery, so even if you're a motionless lump of blocks on the ground with 1% health, your team could rush in and protect you long enough to get back into the fight at full capacity,
The game is FTP, and you start off with a few stock robots you can canibalize for parts to make some pretty good starting designs, so there's no commitment if you don't like it. It's tons of fun, and I recommend it to anyone who enjoys designing, building, and being competitive.

Im a level 82 veteran. I recently picked up this game to get back into it after years of uninstalling it. I came from a time when tech trees were still a thing and plasma weapons could oneshot feeble enemies. prepare to hear a lot of rambling.
Robocraft was a fun game and I could see others still enjoy it but its not quite the same with all its new updates and features. As I previously mentioned about the tech tree, I liked that idea more becuase it was separating high level equipment from lesser advanced battles. There was a need to level up becuase this tree locked every new block or equipment behind a level quota. My level is the fruit of wanting to finish the tech tree. I did not complete the tree becuase I already put the game down.
Combat in robocraft is slightly different now. Before all weapons just relied on reload time and not a power bar that depletes when you use them. Once upon a time people used plasma weapons to deal some seriously fatal damage. The splash damage cripples enemies and enemies stayed that way instead of regenerating after about 10 seconds. I don't know if scouting is necessary anymore as there used to be radars and jammers that took a role in sneaking around. Dying is weird to me since before you had to defend a pilot in the middle of your creation. The pilot was key to the game becuase if the pilot died so did the craft of any damage. Snipers usually aim for the most likely places a pilot would be and instant kill them. The pilot was also the core of the creation as any part that are damage could potentialy destroy entire sections of the creation. Now the Pilot is gone and we only have to rely on shooting random bits of the creation until its health is gone.
I remember many things like when there was a test vehicle mode where bots progressivly get tougher the more you kill so that you can see how adequate the creation really is. I also remember when only a single weapon type could be attached at any given time. Thus there used to be roles, categorizing players as things such as plasma tank or lazer scout or sniper satelite. Satelites were basically the best at spotting but the easiest to target. I think they have become obsolete as I havent seen them in recent game modes. I remember when you had to repair your bot with the currency you get from the match if damaged or destroyed. This was the only hinderence for grinders wanting to stock up on various blocks. I also remember that there was a block or part limit for every level obtained. I start with lets say a one hundred part limit and then level up can now use a hundred and twenty five. I also remember the slur of free premium account opportunities. I remember when there was only team deathmatch to play in and at the beginning they give you three free tech designs to start out with. One was a lazer platform, second was a hovering lazer tech, and the last was a plasma launcher tech. I also remember that if you had multiple plasma launcher type weapons the all fire at once dealing fatal damage. I used this once and shot towards the enemy base killing a flyer type creation in one hit. Now it doesn't matter as it fires just like the lazer weapons, one by one. I do remember the building room being much smaller. I guess this is becuase they needed more room for those megabots type of creations. There was also block tier meaning each tier of block is tougher than before and and was made distinct by colors. White was the starting tier block and I believe that black or red was the final tier block. weapons and systems had a similar system only instead of changing color it was changing the model getting progressivley bigger and deadlier each tier.
Robocraft is by far a fun game but after returning i feel disappointed at it with all its changes and grindy ideas its not so great anymore. Its become more grindy with its loot box nonsense with rng rewards. It also doesn't have quite as fast progression as it used to. It takes way too long for me to scale up after about five matches It was so much quicker and less grindy with the fixed amount of currency you earn in battle than random rewards in a box.
I guess this isn't for me anymore. I tried inviting friends and they have the same thoughts. Its too grindy and pay to win for the likes of us now. maybe back then it would still be appreciable, but im rather sad ill never feel as amazed at this then when it first released. I don't really want to admit that such a good game became such a cash absorbing piece of nonsense but it has become that. I don't recommend this game to any of its old school users but it may still surprise newcomers. I guess im just lost in its old ways. I know that this game isn't quite finished but if it stays as is its not for me anymore.

HELL IS A CLOSED DOOR
First, your puny bunch of adventurers are mowed down by seemingly unconquerable groups of enemies starting right from the first encounter. Then you face a ton of locked doors that get jammed by just looking at them and block the access to the rooms behind them forever. On top of that, this 'gameplay' is embedded in mechanics that are anything but obvious to a common modern player. However you don't give up and after spending hours reading through manuals and guides to create a party that has a chance to survive the first fights and repeated savescumming to open the doors the game throws at you, you spend the rest of the game staring at only one tile-set. It doesn't matter if you are in the castle, on a mountain, in the jungle or on a river you will see cobblestone floors and walls everywhere.
Now what is the appeal to play a game like that ? The beauty of this game is in its sophisticated turn-based fighting system (still unequalled by many “modern” games) beautifully designed monsters (considering the graphical limitations) and interesting, engaging story (It is rather cryptic though and you are mainly left to fill in the gaps with your own fantasy).
So if the downsides don't discourage you and creating your own story that liberates itself from being contained in your computer may tickle your interest, grab a pencil and graphing paper, print out the manual and experience a highlight of RPG gaming.

EDIT: After a year hiatus, I decided to give this game another shot, seeing they are still frequently updating it. I must say, the developers have made massive improvements. Not just to local coop, but the game itself.
First off all, I quickly realized all previous characters are pretty much rendered usless with the new changes, irritating players who have put some serious hours into this game. I understand that frusteration. But with that said, the game feels like a much more enjoyable and polished experience. Most of the bugs I encountered have been squashed. There are still some issues with local coop, but they are manageable.
Secondly, the drop rate and quality of gear is now appropriate for the given difficulty. Since leveling attributes is still painfully slow, good equipment is your best bet. This is something the game severally lacked when I originally played, and made the slow paced leveling system frustrating. Now that gear appears to be better and rewarded more frequently, I am okay with level added attributes points being somewhat meaningless. You also get an enormous amount of gold, but I haven't found much use for it yet.
Difficulty of bosses, crypts, and dungeons has been adjusted and scale more appropriately for the given difficulty. I love the randomness of this game, but no longer do I have to fear a boss is going to spawn and immediately one-hit my whole team. The optional instances are still dangerous and serve as a gambling mechanism for the game, but are no longer completely off limits. I can go into dungeons and crypts and actually feel like I have a chance now.
Overall, this game has come a long way from the last time I played it. It is much more enjoyable, great coop, and reminds me of a more fast paced D3 with cute graphics. If you like dungeon crawlers & rouge-likes with some persistent elements (like Rouge Legacy or Vertical Drop Heroes) I would recommend this game.
==Initial Review==
First off, this review is purely for local coop. I bought the game due to my love for rougelikes and local coop games. I cannot speak for the multiplayer features as of yet. If you are thinking of purchasing this game because it has local coop, heed my warning:
As I've heard many people say, this game has great potential, but for a game that has been out for nearly a year (and has DLC), there are too many inexcusable bugs and problems.
The Bugs:
Local coop is riddled with issues. So much so, I can't recommend this game for coop play. Multiplayer may be a different story. Here are the bugs I ran into in my short 4 hours of local play time:
- Player 2 does not retain charms, but Player 1 does. Charms are the only retained items in the game. This leaves you severally crippled later on in the game as the charms (especially the rarer ones) help you immensely. We were too afraid to switch the character in the player 1 slot to the player 2 slot in fear the character would lose their charm, so we have always kept one character charmless.
- Players will have their stats and/or attributes reset and randomly rolled! After about an hour of consistent game time, I loaded up another round and I suddenly realized my characters stats and skill points were redistributed. Every time this happened I had to spend 30 gems to reset. As far as I can tell, you only get these gems when you get achievements, meaning they are a limited resource and eventually I won't have a solution to this bug!
- Players can get other players stuck in dungeon/crypt puzzles, causing you to have to reset the game. Careful where you stand when figuring out the puzzles, if another player hits the reset button, you could find yourself stuck in a pillar. (stay out of dungeons)
- Dead teammates are your worse enemy. Players can die in too many inconvenient spots. Since you can't walk over dead teammates, you are assured the same fate (i.e. a flame wheel kills your teammate in front of you, you can't move past it and you can't go back because the flame is already on its way back. Any last words?). This happens more often than you would think. (stay out of dungeons)
That was what I found in ~4 hours of local coop. If these bugs were resolved, the game would be much more enjoyable and I would absolutely recommend it. However, I can't recommend it in terms of local coop. There are also several general game play issues I'll lay out below.
General Gameplay thoughts:
The first thing you'll notice playing Hero Seige, is you die way too often without even knowing what hit you. The maps are fairly detailed. Couple that with the bit graphics and it can be quite the challenge to see a tiny red ball one-hit kill you. Some may enjoy this challenge. As an avid fan of rougelikes, it is always a good day to die. But I found it somewhat aggravating suddenly realizing you are dead, with no explanation. If the kill screen didn't tell you what killed you, most of the time you'd have no idea. These instantaneous deaths come quick and often, especially with bosses (which spawn every 6th wave).
Speaking of bosses, their difficulty is incredibly random and unpredictable. It has charm and replay-ability, but it can often crush what seemed like a good run, leaving you somewhat discouraged. Once in coop, we were having a great run, when suddenly a boss spawned and immediately killed my friend and I using his laser ability (pretty sure that was a bug as boss skills visibly charge up). The same goes for the randomly generated dungeons and crypts. Deaths happen so quickly without explanation. I don't recommend venturing forth into the unknown without leveling up a bit.
The character progression is ungodly slow. This is somewhat understandable considering there is no max level. But without the addition of charms and relics you won't notice a difference between character levels.
Despite all those complaints, the rest of the gameplay is exciting and entertaining enough that it is probably worth the $5 if you want to play singleplayer. It plays well on a controller, though It would make more sense that each of the four skills is a button, rather than the  trigger scrolling. The variety of enemies, obstacles, and traps keeps the replay value high.
For now, the game is too buggy to recommend for cooperative play. If the devs up their game, I'll reconsider my review.

Ah, what can I say about this RPG classic? The graphics are terrible, even by the standards of the time, their crude 16 colour EGA awfulness being quickly surpassed by the 256 colour majesty of Westwood's Eye of the Beholder, which followed but a year later.
Moreover, in defiance of even the most slender of expectations, variation in tileset is extremely limited - expect to see castles, dungeons, jungles and mines rendered in the same undulating grey brick, with faded tapestries, rooms filled with rotting furniture and the stygian underworld described in bright yellow text rather than sprites. While far more attention was lavished on the animations of your enemies you should be prepared to see the same yellowish-greyish-pinkish tones portray a multitude of demons, rats, amazons, dwarves and dragons.
The sound too is also terrible, with no music to speak of and only a limited selection of digital samples to relay the clash of steel on steel, ancient enchantments and the death of your foes. Lest that sound too exciting, be warned this is a game where your enemies die with a bang, literally expiring like popped balloons. Indeed, this was a game where the sound was quickly disabled and the mouse driver not loaded, cursor keys and imagination being far better accompaniments.
The plot is borderline nonsense, but expansive and remarkably mature, if such a thing can be said about story involving adultery, murder, madness, a pen that can re-write reality and a half naked she-devil.
And the game itself is unrelentingly punishing - this is the only game I can think of where your ability to access some of the more advanced classes, so temptingly described in the manual, at the beginning of the game rests entirely on a combination of luck and pig headedness.  It is also one of the few games I've come across where a party of six stalwart heroes can be bested within seconds of starting their adventures by bats, rats and weeds, where they can fail to pick a lock and find that door locked for good. It is a game where if one of your characters dies of poison then you better hope you have some means of curing them in addition to resurrecting them, because if you don’t they’ll only die again.
However, if you've read this far and you consider yourself to be one of the few 'hardcore' CRPG gamers left out there, then you owe it to yourself to download this game and persevere. Nearly 25 years after its release, it stills holds the same dark attraction of stats and skills and spells and equipment and deep, turn-based, party-focused combat that for a few years in the mid-1990s seemed to represent the high point of aspirations for RPGs on the PC.
Once you’ve beaten the rats and bats and zombies and Zulus and taken on hell itself and battled through a climatic series of encounters against bosses that feel more like something from Streets of Rage 2. And once you’ve ditched the sticks and rags and found the Avenger and Maenad’s Lance and you’ve got a mage able to launch a tier six nuclear blast capable of incinerating waves of enemies at a time.
Then you’ll have found yourself neck deep in that borderline nonsense plot, playing a game that never fails to keep you on your toes, that rewards intelligence and strategy and speaks to the same desire for challenge and depth that until recently games had somehow managed to neglect. You’ll be hooked and you’ll want to take that band of misfits you’ve so carefully tended for the last 40 hours onward to Wizardry 7 and 8 and the fact that you’ll have to spend more than 100 hours to find out there’s no Wizardry 9 will be a bitter-sweet pill to swallow, but probably one you’ll swallow all the same.

It's Dwarf Fortress for those of us who were always interested in its concept, but couldn't get through the ASCII wall and the learning curve, in a space setting that's heavily inspired by Firefly (so there are a multitude of worlds with varying degrees of technology advancement, and you're going to see people from all sorts of backgrounds). You're in charge of guiding a group of colonists through their trials and tribulations in one of the titular Rim Worlds; distant, isolated planets lacking in strong central government and low in population density, and your job is to get them to stay alive long enough to... do whatever you want, really. There is a clear "end game" goal here (build / access a ship and escape the planet), but the real fun of the game comes from developing your base in whatever way you want, for as long as you can, while surviving the ever-escalating threats that the AI will throw at you.
Both in art style and construction-oriented gameplay, the game is immediately reminiscent of Prison Architect, but Rimworld is much more than that, as it's also packing a surprisingly deep combat system that demands careful planning, both while building and during combat itself, if you want your colonists to live to see another day. The AI "storytellers", a concept not unlike L4D's "director", ensures that you meet a level of challenge that, at the very least, will give you a memorable tale to share after your colonists' demise.
And when the time comes and your colonists die, you WILL feel it. There are many, many easy / dumb ways to die in this game, and learning about them is part of the experience; you'll just HAVE to tell your friends about the one animal handler who died in combat, only to have one of his pets go mad from grief and butcher one of your colonists, or the colonist that sacrificed his life so you could learn about cave-ins the hard way, or the dangers of running a drug operation in a colony full of stressed people fearing for their lives...
If there's one negative aspect about it, it's the fact that its tutorial is simply not good enough. Many important mechanics are barely mentioned or not even touched upon (setting work priorities manually is one such glaring omission); losing colonists because of mistakes you're aware of or gambles gone wrong is fine, but having them die because you didn't understand a part of the UI is frustrating, and there may be a lot of that if you don't go looking for tips before diving in too deep.
Overall though, it's an amazing game. It's in Early Access not because of it being a buggy mess, unplayable or imbalanced; it's simply there to let buyers know that there's still more content being added to it, and the end of early access will mean the end of development for the game. I can't recommend this game enough, it's absolutely worth it at full price!

Judged by story and mystery aspect, and its presentation of late Victorian London, this game is worth an 8+ rating.
Unfortunately, rather cumbersome mechanical elements cannot be so easily overlooked. Nor do I feel the price of nearly $50 on Steam to be properly justified. Still, for those looking for a few hours of fun with a game that doesn't try to pretend to be more than it is, it is worth marking on Steam or Humblebundle and waiting until it's on sale.
The mysteries and stories presented in Sherlock Holmes and the Devil's Daughter take me back to the short stories of Doyle, not so much in theme but in presentation. Each mystery is self-contained, with a straightforward presentation, and doesn't try to pretend to be otherwise. Until Sherlock makes a final decision, you can continue to collect evidence (if you missed something) and refine your deductions. The puzzle sequences themselves are straightforward (I hesitate to say 'elementary'), but do require a player to take a step back, look around, and actually think rather than dive right into pressing buttons. At the same time, the developers avoided making the puzzles as difficult as they could be, and added a pair of gimmicks (one an enhanced spotting feature, the other allowing the player to plot out a future sequence of events or reconstruct a past sequence of events), which allows Holmes to do things no other character can without thrusting the responsibility for that level of acquimen entirely upon the player. It is a balance that, for this game, is just about perfect.
Another joy is the highly detailed environment that delightfully (or not so delightfully) reconstructs elements of Victorian London with all of its mingled elegance and horror. From exclusive Clubs, to hospitals, to the working environment of a chimney sweep, this game doesn't hold back.
Also a high point of this game are the characters. Successful gameplay will require not only stepping into Holmes’ deerstalker cap, but also the shoes of Dr. Watson, and street urchin coat of Wiggins. Watson in particular is worthy of note. While occasionally playing up his traditional role of foil to Holmes, he is also a well-represented example of Holmes making use of others with highly specialized knowledge that he himself does not possess (something that many portrayals of Watson outright ignore if not spit contemptuously upon). Indeed, Watson is presented as the highly skilled medical professional Doyle first made him, and neither he nor Holmes hesitate to make full use of it. For another throwback to the original short stories, Watson's revolver makes an appearance; something often left out in later portrayals.
Players are left free to come to erroneous conclusions, which is a pleasant change from the one-stop-answer common to the genre. And at the end the Player is always free to decide whether to condemn the accused or to justify absolution in some form. While this goes somewhat against more traditional portrayals of Holmes, the presented choices fit quite nicely with the mores of the times and location (let's face it, a late nineteenth century mental institution is preferable only to a late nineteenth century prison). Also interesting is that the developers did not feel compelled to force Holmes into a strictly logic-and-reason role, allowing him the play up the beliefs of others and make an emotional appeal to one character that would otherwise feel extremely out of place.
The flipside to all this greatness is a game interface that is little short of execrable. 'Character profiles' that can be developed by observing important people in each mystery are locked once completed, preventing further detail (or future revision, even after it became clear your original impression was wrong). The AI for the stealth portions is highly simplistic, various 'aim and throw' mechanics are tired and unwieldy, eavesdropping is laughable, the disguises almost utterly unnecessary and (if not removed) fails to draw notice of any other character (though I suppose Lestrade and Watson are well used to Holmes by now). In particular, a mechanic employed when a character needs to 'balance' is worthy of more derision than I can properly apply.  Possibly the best part of all this is that some puzzles offer the option of skipping through them, and you are free to flip between the two difficulty settings at any time without adversely affecting gameplay.
Mechanics aside, there are some story/game elements that are less than compelling. The 'consulting the archives' is at least straightforward, but at the same time left wanting, and various 'chemical analysis' portions are a hand-holding linear a-b-c-d sequence that lacks any immersive qualities that might engage the mind by deciding what types of analysis is appropriate. Some elements (spike walls, rolling boulders) are classics of their genre and not out of place, but are overused, one particular deep-dive into Holmes' imagination is distinctly improbably at best, and another sequence is...highly unlikely given the time (and other) constraints of the setting.
Judged by story and mystery aspect, and its presentation of late Victorian London, this game is worth an 8+ rating.
Unfortunately, those rather cumbersome mechanical elements cannot be so easily overlooked. Nor do I feel the price of nearly $50 on Steam to be properly justified. Still, for those looking for a few hours of fun with a game that doesn't try to pretend to be more than it is, it is worth marking on Steam or Humblebundle and waiting until it's on sale.

Crimes and Punishments is great. With it Frogwares have created not just the best game they ever made, not just the best Sherlock Holmes game, but one of the best examples of adventure games in recent history, if not of all time. For some reason, 2 years later they followed up with The Devil's Daughter, which isn't the worst game in their Sherlock Holmes series, but is very close to being one.
Using the same overall structure ideas and a lot of mechanics, Sherlock Holmes: The Devil's Daughter could be an improvement, an evolution, or a really interesting experiment of change. The team clearly aimed at the latter, but failed spectacularly. They changed the looks and personalities of Holmes and Watson, this time basing them on the Guy Ritchie movies - Watson looks almost exactly like Jude Law, while Holmes doesn't resemble Robert Downey Jr. visually as much, but is animated to look like he's being played by the named actor. The story attempts to be more "personal" and continues from the horribly stupid plot point of the ending of The Testament of Sherlock Holmes, which I was hoping, would be forgotten, but no - Holmes has a daughter now (who's actually Moriarty's daughter), and is emotionally highly unstable when it comes to the topic. And the overall tone and speed of cases is meant to be much more action heavy. And none of that works. Well, okay, 1 thing works - Watson feels less stupid than he sometimes appears to be in books and previous games, but even there - you don't really spend a lot of time with him in this game.

In fact, it's hard to say with whom and with what you spend most of the time. Very first case, for example, spends couple dozen minutes on a stealth section as Wiggins (one of the homeless helpers for Holmes). Then case ends on an escape scene which more or less resolves itself, without you doing much deducting. Next case opens with an extremely boring sports minigame and then spends half an hour in an imaginary Mayan temple, bad puzzles and Indiana Jones references. And those goddamn minigames... Even though I got a bit bored of lock-picking in Crimes and Punishments by the end, it never felt like it was pushing it, never felt like it was out of place. On the contrary, most of the content of The Devil's Daughter is based around these mostly pointless mostly skippable minigames and QTE-like sequences that just do not work. There's a sequence that tries to use the Holmes' intelligence in a fight scene, again emulating Ritchie's movies, but it's all bad guesswork and poorly conveyed controls that work at random in the very same scene. And don't even get me started on the "push the heavy object" puzzles, where even if you figured out what to do, you still have to wait through the agonizing minutes of pushing stuff.

There are attempts of expanding and improving on Crimes and Punishments, but those do not work either. You have more choice in analyzing people, but it's either an obvious choice, or a pure guess on player's part, which improves nothing. Visuals have been refined, but actually make some of the same locations between both games look less memorable and more blurry. Moral choices, which didn't really play a big story part in the previous game and were there to fit Holmes' character and give players more agency, are tied to the ending somewhat. But given that this whole thing is based around the horribly written and executed "Holmes has a daughter he cares about a lot for some reason", it's a moot addition. There are a few good puzzles that expand on the ideas of the previous games, but they are so few and sometimes poorly implemented as well, that it doesn't save the game.
I fully support the idea of experimenting with Sherlock Holmes, especially after reaching such a high point as Crimes and Punishments was. In fact, as I've said many years ago, I'd love to see a modern take on Sherlock from Frogwares (Though the example I used last time, BBC's Sherlock, has since went to crap). But Sherlock Holmes: The Devil's Daughter is a poor execution of a bad idea and a failed experiment. It lost almost everything that made the series Sherlock Holmes and is extremely not fun to play. Whenever the studio returns to the character, I hope they do something else with it.

This was actually a lot better than I had anticipated. I just thought this was gonna be an over-the-top nazi-shooting game. What I got was an actual plot, unique characters, development in both plot and characters, and a sliver of investment into the story.
The world is beautiful, and a lot of thought went into it. I love alternate history, and this is the perfect example. From hearing "House of the Rising Sun" or "Abby Road", but in this universe just adds to the rich illustration of a world where Germany won WWII. Seeing the massive buildings and advanced technology fills you with wonder, and seeing the ghettos of ruined countries that dared oppose Germany fills you with dread. Even just listening in on the conversations of people, you can see the mentality of the people in this world.
That's not to say this game is completely serious. It is still over-the-top, but less than games like Duke Nukem or Saints Row. It's a little crazy and extravagant at times, but nothing typical suspension of disbelief won't cure.
Only negative: The ending seems rushed. Like they had planed for more, but had to release the game before they were ready. But even still, it's good overall.
I suggest it, and I'm looking forward to the sequel.

Im a level 82 veteran. I recently picked up this game to get back into it after years of uninstalling it. I came from a time when tech trees were still a thing and plasma weapons could oneshot feeble enemies. prepare to hear a lot of rambling.
Robocraft was a fun game and I could see others still enjoy it but its not quite the same with all its new updates and features. As I previously mentioned about the tech tree, I liked that idea more becuase it was separating high level equipment from lesser advanced battles. There was a need to level up becuase this tree locked every new block or equipment behind a level quota. My level is the fruit of wanting to finish the tech tree. I did not complete the tree becuase I already put the game down.
Combat in robocraft is slightly different now. Before all weapons just relied on reload time and not a power bar that depletes when you use them. Once upon a time people used plasma weapons to deal some seriously fatal damage. The splash damage cripples enemies and enemies stayed that way instead of regenerating after about 10 seconds. I don't know if scouting is necessary anymore as there used to be radars and jammers that took a role in sneaking around. Dying is weird to me since before you had to defend a pilot in the middle of your creation. The pilot was key to the game becuase if the pilot died so did the craft of any damage. Snipers usually aim for the most likely places a pilot would be and instant kill them. The pilot was also the core of the creation as any part that are damage could potentialy destroy entire sections of the creation. Now the Pilot is gone and we only have to rely on shooting random bits of the creation until its health is gone.
I remember many things like when there was a test vehicle mode where bots progressivly get tougher the more you kill so that you can see how adequate the creation really is. I also remember when only a single weapon type could be attached at any given time. Thus there used to be roles, categorizing players as things such as plasma tank or lazer scout or sniper satelite. Satelites were basically the best at spotting but the easiest to target. I think they have become obsolete as I havent seen them in recent game modes. I remember when you had to repair your bot with the currency you get from the match if damaged or destroyed. This was the only hinderence for grinders wanting to stock up on various blocks. I also remember that there was a block or part limit for every level obtained. I start with lets say a one hundred part limit and then level up can now use a hundred and twenty five. I also remember the slur of free premium account opportunities. I remember when there was only team deathmatch to play in and at the beginning they give you three free tech designs to start out with. One was a lazer platform, second was a hovering lazer tech, and the last was a plasma launcher tech. I also remember that if you had multiple plasma launcher type weapons the all fire at once dealing fatal damage. I used this once and shot towards the enemy base killing a flyer type creation in one hit. Now it doesn't matter as it fires just like the lazer weapons, one by one. I do remember the building room being much smaller. I guess this is becuase they needed more room for those megabots type of creations. There was also block tier meaning each tier of block is tougher than before and and was made distinct by colors. White was the starting tier block and I believe that black or red was the final tier block. weapons and systems had a similar system only instead of changing color it was changing the model getting progressivley bigger and deadlier each tier.
Robocraft is by far a fun game but after returning i feel disappointed at it with all its changes and grindy ideas its not so great anymore. Its become more grindy with its loot box nonsense with rng rewards. It also doesn't have quite as fast progression as it used to. It takes way too long for me to scale up after about five matches It was so much quicker and less grindy with the fixed amount of currency you earn in battle than random rewards in a box.
I guess this isn't for me anymore. I tried inviting friends and they have the same thoughts. Its too grindy and pay to win for the likes of us now. maybe back then it would still be appreciable, but im rather sad ill never feel as amazed at this then when it first released. I don't really want to admit that such a good game became such a cash absorbing piece of nonsense but it has become that. I don't recommend this game to any of its old school users but it may still surprise newcomers. I guess im just lost in its old ways. I know that this game isn't quite finished but if it stays as is its not for me anymore.

Maybe grind and pay to win is too strong of a description for this game and i can say I was very biased when I was making this review. I really dislike the loot box nonsense. I know even after losing a match we'll get one but in my opinion I don't need it.I still loved the old versions more than the current.

Okay now, played a bit during free weekend, and I tell you what:
Graphics: not bad, most models need polishing though
Physics: okay and works most of time but overall needs some tweaking
Levels: mostly good, yet some design decisions are quite arguable
Sound: not the best I've experienced but still quite impressive

Having a mic is not just for fun - it's a matter of life and death. And quite literally, 'cause if you don't have a mic you'll not be able to transfer vital information to your teammates fast enough or issue/accept orders, and it's most likely that your whole squad will be wiped out while you type in the chat.
The game is playable in it's current state (and mostly enjoyable). Sure, there are several game design moments that really need developers' attention (like basebuilding, level design, vehicles or the ability to have two medics per squad) but that's mostly just some criticism for the developers and not to be posted here, and I believe things are subject to change during Alpha. However, very few issues can be defined as 'game-breaking'. I hope one day Squad will become a solid tactical shooter.
Now, you're going to ask why, despite this review is so positive, it's 'not recommended'? The answer is simple... ArmA. Yes, I know that ArmA 2/3 is costly with all DLCs (and barely enjoyable without them), that on release day ArmA games usually contained more game-breaking bugs and missing/broken features than Squad has now (I've been there, and people spent more time on bug tracker than ingame). But it's still much better in many terms. For now, if the developers won't abandon the game (which I hope is not going to happen) I consider buying it on final release, at least to see if Squad has to offer something to change my mind.
So, IMO when Squad hits final release and its price will stay the same it'll be a decent (and cheaper) alternative for ArmA 2/3 with all the DLCs. And if you love tactical shooters then you'll probably find it to be a lot of fun even now.

EDIT: After a year hiatus, I decided to give this game another shot, seeing they are still frequently updating it. I must say, the developers have made massive improvements. Not just to local coop, but the game itself.
First off all, I quickly realized all previous characters are pretty much rendered usless with the new changes, irritating players who have put some serious hours into this game. I understand that frusteration. But with that said, the game feels like a much more enjoyable and polished experience. Most of the bugs I encountered have been squashed. There are still some issues with local coop, but they are manageable.
Secondly, the drop rate and quality of gear is now appropriate for the given difficulty. Since leveling attributes is still painfully slow, good equipment is your best bet. This is something the game severally lacked when I originally played, and made the slow paced leveling system frustrating. Now that gear appears to be better and rewarded more frequently, I am okay with level added attributes points being somewhat meaningless. You also get an enormous amount of gold, but I haven't found much use for it yet.
Difficulty of bosses, crypts, and dungeons has been adjusted and scale more appropriately for the given difficulty. I love the randomness of this game, but no longer do I have to fear a boss is going to spawn and immediately one-hit my whole team. The optional instances are still dangerous and serve as a gambling mechanism for the game, but are no longer completely off limits. I can go into dungeons and crypts and actually feel like I have a chance now.
Overall, this game has come a long way from the last time I played it. It is much more enjoyable, great coop, and reminds me of a more fast paced D3 with cute graphics. If you like dungeon crawlers & rouge-likes with some persistent elements (like Rouge Legacy or Vertical Drop Heroes) I would recommend this game.
==Initial Review==
First off, this review is purely for local coop. I bought the game due to my love for rougelikes and local coop games. I cannot speak for the multiplayer features as of yet. If you are thinking of purchasing this game because it has local coop, heed my warning:
As I've heard many people say, this game has great potential, but for a game that has been out for nearly a year (and has DLC), there are too many inexcusable bugs and problems.
The Bugs:
Local coop is riddled with issues. So much so, I can't recommend this game for coop play. Multiplayer may be a different story. Here are the bugs I ran into in my short 4 hours of local play time:
- Player 2 does not retain charms, but Player 1 does. Charms are the only retained items in the game. This leaves you severally crippled later on in the game as the charms (especially the rarer ones) help you immensely. We were too afraid to switch the character in the player 1 slot to the player 2 slot in fear the character would lose their charm, so we have always kept one character charmless.
- Players will have their stats and/or attributes reset and randomly rolled! After about an hour of consistent game time, I loaded up another round and I suddenly realized my characters stats and skill points were redistributed. Every time this happened I had to spend 30 gems to reset. As far as I can tell, you only get these gems when you get achievements, meaning they are a limited resource and eventually I won't have a solution to this bug!
- Players can get other players stuck in dungeon/crypt puzzles, causing you to have to reset the game. Careful where you stand when figuring out the puzzles, if another player hits the reset button, you could find yourself stuck in a pillar. (stay out of dungeons)
- Dead teammates are your worse enemy. Players can die in too many inconvenient spots. Since you can't walk over dead teammates, you are assured the same fate (i.e. a flame wheel kills your teammate in front of you, you can't move past it and you can't go back because the flame is already on its way back. Any last words?). This happens more often than you would think. (stay out of dungeons)
That was what I found in ~4 hours of local coop. If these bugs were resolved, the game would be much more enjoyable and I would absolutely recommend it. However, I can't recommend it in terms of local coop. There are also several general game play issues I'll lay out below.
General Gameplay thoughts:
The first thing you'll notice playing Hero Seige, is you die way too often without even knowing what hit you. The maps are fairly detailed. Couple that with the bit graphics and it can be quite the challenge to see a tiny red ball one-hit kill you. Some may enjoy this challenge. As an avid fan of rougelikes, it is always a good day to die. But I found it somewhat aggravating suddenly realizing you are dead, with no explanation. If the kill screen didn't tell you what killed you, most of the time you'd have no idea. These instantaneous deaths come quick and often, especially with bosses (which spawn every 6th wave).
Speaking of bosses, their difficulty is incredibly random and unpredictable. It has charm and replay-ability, but it can often crush what seemed like a good run, leaving you somewhat discouraged. Once in coop, we were having a great run, when suddenly a boss spawned and immediately killed my friend and I using his laser ability (pretty sure that was a bug as boss skills visibly charge up). The same goes for the randomly generated dungeons and crypts. Deaths happen so quickly without explanation. I don't recommend venturing forth into the unknown without leveling up a bit.
The character progression is ungodly slow. This is somewhat understandable considering there is no max level. But without the addition of charms and relics you won't notice a difference between character levels.
Despite all those complaints, the rest of the gameplay is exciting and entertaining enough that it is probably worth the $5 if you want to play singleplayer. It plays well on a controller, though It would make more sense that each of the four skills is a button, rather than the  trigger scrolling. The variety of enemies, obstacles, and traps keeps the replay value high.
For now, the game is too buggy to recommend for cooperative play. If the devs up their game, I'll reconsider my review.

Hero Siege is a twin stick shooter inspired by diablo, so you get things like healing wells, dangerous magic on death etc.the levels are set up as arena hold out stages where you are supposed to fend off waves of enemies.
Here's the short version. There's a real review bellow.
Pros
Cool level design.
Cool Character design.
minidungeons.
Cons.
bad hitboxes.
VERY grindy.
slow progression.
boring items.
boring abilities.
You level up and get 2 stat points and one ability point. there are 4 stats to choose from; strength, attack speed, armor, health, and putting one point into any of the first three stats will increase it by a fraction. this is fairly useless when enemies have health values in the hundreds, and attack values high enough to be unaffected by a 0.40 increase in your armor. The ability point is really the only thing you will care about when you level up. you can spend the point in a branching ability tree. the first tier of the tree has two options, an active, and a passive, the passives increase chances, or whatever the ability is supposed to affect, by 1 measely percent, so the obvious choice is to choose the active ability, which is pretty interesting to be fair. the downside is that this active ability is all you're going to get until you are level five. this makes the game progress very very slowly.
one of the stranger things about the game considering its inspirations, is that there are very few items to collect. loot comes along once in a great while, and your first item is likely to be uninteresting. upon beating the first boss an item spawned on a pedestal in front of the portal, it was a green double crescent blade and ot gave me a SLIGHT increase to  my crit chance. the boss itself dropped a token for me that gave me a stat tradeoff attack +4 armor -2. both of these were terribly dissapointing. I killed a drake type boss, and as such i expected an item to reflect that, perhaps an item that had to do with shooting a fireball or having enemies burn the ground on death, but all i got was a change to my numbers.
probably the hardest part of the game to swallow was the awful hitbox detection. i spent a long time getting used to simply hitting enemies. everything is a 2d sprite in sort of an isometric view, which makes it inherently more difficult to judge differences between distances. This can be a nightmare when fighting spiders, which have a large sprite, but a tiny hitbox. and certain classes are particularly bad at hitting enemies, in this case namely the pirate has a hard time because her pistol shots alternate between her left and right hand, which occupy different planes which makes it more than likely you will miss half of your shots unless you're very very used to her. Melee characters are also terrible because their attack animations extend beyond their hitboxes. Compare this with the binding of isaac, it has the same 2d models and the same view, but its fairly clear where you're firing and all that good stuff.
In conclusion, play either diablo or play binding of isaac. This game wants to be both, but it doesn't do either very well. If you see the game on sale, go ahead and buy it, just know that it isnt a tight and clean experience.

It may quite possibly be nostalgia talking but I played this to death in my youth. It is a deep and wonderful RPG in many ways and although it is dated the basic story and the wealth of items and choices is still enjoyable. This is the pedigree from which games like Legend of Grimrock stem and while it isn't as pretty as modern incarnations it is still very atmospheric.
The RPG "simulation" is substantially more complex than what is common in modern games and that makes it necessity to read through the manual at least in part. Everything from attacks to spells have modifiers and classes have a diverse set of mechanics. This in turn means that some classes are weak and brittle until relatively late in the game when they blossom into excellent additions.
There is no hand holding and the assumptions you make when exploring will influence what ending you will get. The feature to bring the party forward to subsequent games is laudable and it was a novel experience when the game was fresh.
I am far less enamoured of the next installment probably because the port to my chosen platform was hideously broken, sluggish and failed to include the party import but the "Bane" was installed for years on my PowerBook 165c, infact that old hunk of plastic still runs and this is still one of the games installed.
In summary at the current Winter Sale price it is well worth adding to your library just for the hell of it and just while playing enough to be allowed to review it I once again got stuck rolling characters to get that perfect race / profession combination. I find it especially heart warming that the copy protection is still in there even if it has been disabled, while I did own the game the tiny irksome nature of looking up codes lent me to learn some basic 68k assembly.
It is highly recommended that you set it to keyboard control only to save on some fiddly clicking as using the arrow keys is substantially faster,.

This review is for Ubuntu Linux. I am on the fence about recommending or not, but the tipping point is the mis-timings that happen during dialogue. Since I am not seeing a lot of complaints in the forum, then I think it must be somewhat specific to my gaming rig here. Even with that, if there was more that I liked about the game, then I would be able to overlook even that serious bug.
So this is a point-and-click game, except you walk to the hot point. This is a dialogue game, but you don't have to say anything. This is a choices matter game, but it is not usually clear what effect your choices had.
This game has two interesting mechanics. As mentioned, the dialogue choices can be avoided, effectively making a fourth dialogue choice, but as mentioned, there were times when the options came up and disappeared before they were applicable. Since some of the puzzles are based on dialogue options, this was real a deal breaker.
The other mechanic was tuning the radio for additional information and for interacting with in-game objects. This is certainly very clever, but not always tons of fun. I did like the additional information, for what it was worth. It was not made clear how a tunable FM radio was also transmitting radio signals, though. I wish they had taken the opportunity to explore some actual electromagnetic science here.
Lastly, the walking back and forth to do things was quite annoying. Yes, the art was very nice, and yes there were often events that happened along the way, but having to serpentine down winding trails and press action buttons to begin slowly climbing rock faces (for what reason?) lost it's fun after the first time through. There are times when you have a loading screen for about 15 seconds, about 5 seconds of moving across the screen, then another loading screen for 15 seconds. When you have to do this over and over, checking a map to make sure you are going the right way, it feels like a chore. And when there is something happening, it is okay, but I walked with Ren from the Comm Tower to the town center and there was no dialogue and no events for the entire trip. It was just fifteen minues of boredom, slowly climbing walls, getting lost down the wrong path in the woods, and that was after tons of dialogue about how it was so important that he would come with me. Why couldn't I have just clicked on the map and arrived immediately? I really grew to hate the transportation, and I would have explored much more of the island, otherwise.
All these complaints said, the characters and the dialogue that exist here are superb. I hope this writer goes on to do many other works. I wish I had seen much more of the characters, and I regretted every time that I felt compelled to interrupt the character conversation, because I wanted to learn more about them. The writer did a good job hinting at interesting backstories, that made me wanting to learn more. Wish I heard more about Nona. Also, the character animations did a lot to give them character depth, too.
But would I play the game again to see a different ending? No chance. Wish someone had gone through with some polish at the end, because it was very close to being a much better experience.

I've never been a huge RTS buff. I certainly enjoy a lot of games in the genre; my childhood was filled with the Jurassic Park RTS "Chaos Island". While I may not be particularly skilled in the genre and I might not pay attention to every new release, without a doubt I consider Age of Empires II one of my favorite games of all time and one of the greatest games ever created.
It's a fairly straight forward RTS. You have 4 resources that you gather, 4 ages to advance through, and all of the civilizations have fairly similar units. However, there's a staggering amount of variety in ways you can approach the game, and it seems like every time I play the game I learn a new trick to better my performance. Perhaps my admiration for the games mechanics is just because I'm not an expert in the genre, but even I can see the mechanics stand head and shoulders above games like mediocre Empire Earth and, I would argue, even the excellent Warcraft III.
I think most can agree that the visuals and sound design in the game is fantastic. There may only be a few songs in the whole game, but man are they some of the catchiest tracks in gaming. I also appreciate how while all the civilizations are similar enough to be able to pick up a new one and not be completely lost, they all have a lot of subtle differences that make it so everyone can have some favorites. Visually I love the Teutons, and their defensive capabilities are great.
It should be noted that this HD upgrade doesn't necessarily boost the visuals in any outstanding way, but it does make it run well on modern PCs without the hassle of trying to get everyone's machine to run the game. The additional civilizations fit in nicely, and I appreciate the boost to the max population size and better online capabilities.
To make a long story short, this game is amazing, and definitely one of the gaming experiences that has stayed inside my rotation of games I play. If you are looking for a stepping stone into the RTS genre, a old AoE fan who has fond memories of the game back in '99, or an RTS buff that hasn't dipped their foot into the AoE pool yet, I can safely (and will vehemently) recommend this game.
(For the record, my hours on record aren't reflective of my time with this game. I probably put a couple hundred into the original release and the Conquerors expansion)

I actually enjoyed it, but that took about a solid 45 minutes of fumbling around with the atrocious controls (which aren't remappable) and figuring out a way to basically ignore most of the level. Difficulty in a game should come from level design, not from you being unable to move properly due to the controls.
Tross is a game that tries to capture the feeling of the Death Star level in Star Wars Rogue Squadron and the ship escape level in Saints Row 4. This is a great idea imo and I gotta admit it's not a terrible game. It'd be a pretty damn good game if the person who chose the control scheme wasn't mad.
First-off the movement groups make no sense. Pitching up and down is paired with rotating your ship and speeding up and down is paired with turning, this applies to both controller and mouse&keyboard. This makes flying an absurdly awkward thing to do, it makes no sense that you would be able to move up and down with the mouse/right joystick but simultaneously not be able to turn with it, instead when you try to turn the ship your entire ship rolls. A sane person (i.e. the people who did Freelancer, War Thunder, or any other flying game) would have paired turning the ship up and down and side to side the mouse/right joystick and put rolling the ship alongside the speed on A&D/Left Joystick. This cannot be remapped.
Secondly, the things that CAN be adjusted start off at very weird settings. Inversion is on by default which makes zero sense because the controller is disabled by default. Inversion only really works well ON joysticks.
Now I say "the controller is disabled by default" loosely, hilariously when the controller is disabled it still works. I would have never even known the controller was disabled if I didn't dig through the settings, I really thought controller support was just plain broken. Why? Because despite the controller being disabled you can still FLY with it. You can fly but you can't shoot, start the level without using the keyboard, or open the menu (granted you can't open the menu even if you have the controller enabled). What switching controllers on does is let you shoot, change the text at the start at levels to press up on controller to start level (W on keyboard still works funnily enough despite the gamepad not being able to start levels when on mouse and keyboard mode) and shoot.
Mouse sensitivity is horrible, the default sensitivity was so low I had to make huuuge swipes across my desk to turn or roll the ship. Now keep in mind I have my mouse set at 8000dpi. I had to double the sensitivity in the game in order to make moving seem even feasible. Doubling is the maximum, this makes me question whether this game is even playable for anyone with a lower sensitivity mouse.
The level designs: they're not bad admittedly, there are some annoyances but honestly if the game controlled properly I would probably enjoy them much more. They've got some nice things to fly around and little tunnels and crevices like one would expect from this type of game. The few problems I have though are more related to the fact that some parts of the levels seem more designed to be unfair than challenging. For instance, the first level has the target rotating, you can only shoot the yellow bit that is moving. Fair enough, the issue with this level is that for a solid 2/3rds of it you can't even get to a place where you can shoot it because the sphere it is on is backed right up against a wall. Most of the time limit will be spent doing fly-bys and waiting for the sphere to hopefully rotate the bit to face you right when you are flying towards it and spam your guns at a pre-aimed spot where it will rotate into. This would be a lot easier if not for the awkward control scheme. With the control scheme, adjusting your craft to shoot at a moving object is more often than not possible, which is presumably why all the levels that I played after do not feature a moving target at all.
The next level is actually feels somewhat well designed. You fly through a bunch of tight vertical pillars into an area where the targets will send out two large horizontal walls to crush you. This is straightforward enough and makes sense. The part that doesn't make sense is the "debris" which gets sent flying at you during this attack. There are cubes all over the floor that supposedly get tossed around by the impact of the walls, the issue is half these cubes manage to magically clip right through those two solid walls trying to crush you. They then start bouncing everywhere, somehow now unable to clip through the walls, creating a cluster♥♥♥♥ in the tiny space between the upper wall attack and the actual ceiling of the level. I'm perfectly fine with the idea of debris flying everywhere as an obstacle but not if the stuff magically appears out of nowhere and start flying at you from unknown angles. At that point it's not a matter of avoiding the cubes but hoping to hell the physics engine doesn't bounce one at you from behind the camera where you can't see it.
There are other issues which I will get into in the actual video review (this is a lot of text as is).
I can't recommend this game in the current state. The level design is actually not horrible, I would recommend this game if it weren't for the dreadful control scheme. Either fix the damn controls, or give the players the option to change the controls themselves. It should go without saying that a game that relies on precise moving should have controls that function well. Nobody wants to play Freelancer with qwop controls. The only way I have managed to progress in the game is basically by flying up to the top of the levels where there are minimal obstacles and flying the plane sideways for the rest of the game. If this game controlled well it'd probably be a pretty damn good game.

Robocraft, a game of building a bot and doing PvP battles with it. Sound simple, right? Well, strap in... First and formost, this game is still being developed so many of the issues I see with it may be changed, I am not expecting it though. Firstly, crates. Now, while the idea is nice and all, it is very limiting to your creativity as you cannot easily choose a block to get. They started giving robits as a reward, but it is too little too late. Also, the resale value w/o premium is laughably low, which compounds this issue. The robot shop is cool and all, but allows for people who should not be using a certain bot to use it, as well as being just an easy way to not have to build anything. I think it should be a place to share pics of robots, and nothing else. Next, the removal of the tech tree. The teech tree, as well as CPU being tied to rank, game a sense of accomplishment to the game, that is not here. The tech tree gave you a goal, and a means to reach it. The tiers also did the same thing. When you finally unlocked the part you have been wanting forever or you reach T10 it feels amazing. When they made it so you did not have to work to get your mega SMG or T-X1 armor, it was an utter punch in the gut to those who spent hours grinding for those. The balance issues are also worth noting. Rails, well, they are almost useless, SMG beats them out when you time your shots, chain shredders are just complete killing machines that will, when used right, kill everyone on the enemy team and come back for more, flak is making flyers less viable, and missiles make this game lose the close quarters feel when everyone is hiding from some missile flyer. And to cap this all off, megabots... They removed megas... I'll leave it at that.
TLDR: This game is still in EA, and these can change, but the direction shift of this game makes it a hard sell. Some aspects are fun, yes, but many others are lacking and bring this game down severely.
