A rather unique and nice FPS shooter with Parkour, that is important but not invasive like in most games I played, Time To Kill high enough to make even "weakest" weapons kill well enough with some degree of aim, and low enough to allow retaliation, make fights slightly longer and more spectacular, as well as make tactical thinking, flanking etc. matter even for running away.
What is worth mentioning here is: this game is about objectives. Kills are always important, but there is pretty much one game mode, which consist of one team attacking and doing specific things that vary from map to map, and defenders, who have to stop them for up to 15 minutes. There is also stopwatch mode that simply adds another round, where teams swaps, and depending on how the first round attackers performed, the ones in the second one have to either do the same in set time for a draw, or do more (or all) before the time goes off for a win.
Gunplay here is very smooth and well made - almost all weapons feel good and different from each other, even in particular "categories" - which means most people will find weapons they like and hate. Not to mention most weapons have very little difference in On Paper Damage Per Second - so even pistols can kill well enough, and the most different thing about them is simply how they feel - but as far as killing power goes, most weapons are well balanced.
What is also nice about this game is that you don't need to Aim Down Sights to have good accuracy - jumping, etc. will increase spread - but even then, you can shoot well enough from the hip. It is especially rewarding when you learn more about parkour and overall get some experience in game.
Another thing - different mercenaries. There are 5 main categories of mercs, each giving access to specific things, like medics having healing and the ability to revive people who are downed but not yet finished, fire supports who can give ammo and have some tactical skills like airstrikes or rocket launcher that can deal a lot of damage to objectives. Overall - each mercenary is very different, with different stats and speed, each one of them have a specific "skill", but all of them are as good at killing as others. More health might seem like a huge advantage, but weapon damage is high enough that once you get used to the game and score headshots more or less consistently - you will also get kills everyone cares so much about even as low health medic.
Loadouts - cream and butter of the game - there are a few tiers of loadouts for each mercenary you will get from cases you either get from a match, buy for credits earned ingame, or from "elite cases" bought for real money - yer normal microtransactions. Tiers are: no tier, lead, iron, bronze, silver, gold, cobalt, special edition, obsidian.
Each loadout can have up to 3 auguments, like 15% less damage from own explosives, faster reload, reload when running - overall, you can do well even without them, but they are noticeable. Also - each loadout has different set of weapons, and each mercenary has pretty much access to 3 primary weapons, 3 side weapons and 3 meele weapons, at least for now - there is planned a new generation of loadouts where each mercenary will receive one additional primary, secondary and meele.
No tier (default loadout if you have none) has 0 auguments, lead has 1, iron 2 and starting from bronze - 3. So nothing above bronze, which might not be as common as iron or lead - will be stronger. The only difference is how they look, with everything being only a different skin except for Obsidian - these are special real money loadouts with different models (not much in most cases, but you will notice them right away) - but they are not stronger. Bronze is common enough that even newer players will find a lot of them.
Gaphics are good - I don't know what to say about them - characters, while not exactly ♥♥♥♥♥iful to me, I cannot say they are ugly either. Maps are well designed and looks nice overall - weapons looks and sound nice. There are "potatoe setting" guides for people who might have some issues with performance and game, while looking somehow less appealing - still looks good enough to play.
Overall, I recommend this game since the devs do put some work into it - they learn - and they started lately to add more content. I do have issues with this game, but nothing big enough to stop me from playing it every now and then for longer periods of time.
So if you are looking for CoD or CS:GO - this is not it, but if you are looking for a shooter that is fast, movement is fast and you can parkour around for even more faster movement and fights are also not "tanks, healers, DPS" - this is a game for you. Everything can kill, everything hurts - both for you, and for the enemy. Skill matters - aim matters - thinking matters, and each can contribute to a win, even if you're lacking in something. The playerbase is not big - a lot of players seems to leave as they are very likely to meet veterans who just like the game and have much more experience - but it's not hard to get better at this game, even without basic FPS skills like aim.
TL;DR
Pros:
- Smooth gunplay with low TTK, but high enough to not make you die right away
- Diverse mercenaries, where even "low hp medic" can kill very efficiently
- Well designed map with different objectives, a lot of side areas for tactical flanking
- A lot of different weapons that feel different but kill well enough - so whichever you prefer will do as well as another weapon in hands of someone else
Cons:
- Grind - or at least - special edition grind, as there are often events that require a lot of playing if you do not spend real cash. But, if you like the game and enjoy it - it's not that much of an issue.
- No proper training room - there is an assault course, but targets are stationary and does not provide real training aside from good starting point for learning parkour.
- Low player base - you will easily find servers to play on, but you will often meet "veterans" who will probably obliterate you. There is a fairly new Casual Match Making system, but since it's new and player base changes constantly - you might not get best experience out of it.
- NaCl - but same for every online shooter - it could be in pros if it was low enough to be a mere diet supplement

This is a nice casual past-time, looks like a top-down shooter, but you are confined to a single area and have to fight waves of enemies in order to progress. The game has easy controls that can be mapped, with seperate keys for movement, and another set for shooting (in all directions) so you can for example walk to the left but shoot to the right or downwards. You also can use a couple of specials which are unique per character. These are unlocked as you progress character level. When you die, you keep the character level. This works like in Rogue Legacy and other similar games.
The downside of this system is, that for a long while you have to be grinding without making any significant progress. I had to level up my character to around level 18 before I could get past the second boss, ie. wave 12. But after that things went a bit faster. The enemy damage scales with your character level, but the enemies do not. So you can steamroll a couple of levels later on, as long as you avoind being hit.
I can recommend the game for a quick in-between, but the grind can be a bit frustrating at times. :6.5/10:

Hero Siege is probably the best value I've gotten for my money in a long time.  It is a simple enough game, a rogue-like with a number of interesting classes to choose from each with their own skill tree for you to customize them with.  Each level is a large (several screens worth) rectangular arena filled with randomly positioned traps and decorations.  After the player spawns the monsters begin to spawn in waves entering from the four doors at the center of each edge.  There is a short delay between waves which can be cut short with a button press.  After defeating enough waves you get to fight a boss.  During the waves other things can spawn such as chests or one level (and extremely lethal) side dungeons.  Keep going until you die.
Once dead you can restart from the beginning retaining your level.  The draw comes from being able to get just a little further each time and seeing what relics you uncover to power up your character and the radical ways they can change how you play.  The simple nature of the gameplay and the reasonably attractive graphics make it wasy to loose track of time while playing.

If you are a fan of FPS combined with RPG elements, then this game is a must buy.

Sherlock Holmes: The Devi's Daughter is a 3D, first (or third, if you prefer) person adventure game where you assume the role of the worlds greatest detective. Use your skills of observation and deduction to find the guilty party.
Pros:
Graphics are decent
Good mix of puzzles from easy to challenging
Good voice acting
Well optimized
The game flows well from case to case
Several hours of game play
No hand holding when it comes to naming the guilty party
Plot twist
Cons:
The stealth parts are very predicable
Most if not all of the clues are in a very small area
The downstairs neighbor is (main story) is a bit transparent
In this game, you don't play as just Sherlock Holmes. At times, you can play as Watson, or Wiggins. It depends on the case, but the most part, you are Sherlock Holmes.
Most of the puzzles are logical and well thought out, (as Holmes would have wanted it). When it comes to deducing the crime, you can go inside the mind of Holmes and see all of the possibilities based of the clues you found. Using the clues and the suspect profiles, you can conclude the likelihood that one suspect is guilty while the others are innocent. However, beware that you can name the wrong person for the crime and an innocent person can go to jail... that is if you choose to condemn them. You always have the option to absolve the suspect of the crime even if you know for certain that you have the right one.
“Why would I let a thief/murderer go if I'm sure I have the right one?”
It's not as simple as finding the bad guy and sending them to jail. A couple of cases involve ethical dilemmas as well. Do you choose the ethical thing or the right thing?*
There are a couple of minor design issues I had with this game. There are two occasions where you have to be stealthy. The first time isn't to bad. The second time, though... Simply observe the AI's behavior patterns for a minute... literally a minute. Much to easy. The other issue is that most of the clues are easy to find because they're in a very small area, so if you missed something, you weren't paying much attention to it. It's hard to miss a clue.
At the time of this review, Sherlock Holmes: The devil's daughter, was selling for $49.99.  I logged in about 21 hours of game, including obtaining all of the achievements. That's a bit pricey in my opinion so if you want to get this game, do what I did and wait for a sale.
*(This has nothing to do with the game but it will give you an idea of the ethical or right choice you may have to make)
A police officer arrests a suspect and begins to read him his rights when, suddenly, the suspect slips off this cuffs and tries to get away. By the time he's caught, he's put into a squad car a carted off to jail before his rights are read to him. Two months later, the officer is on the stand and the suspects lawyer asks him point blank, “Did you read him his rights”? The officer knows that the suspect was a lifelong criminal and had been in and out of jail entire life. Besides, the suspect was caught red handed committing the crime be was on trial for, BUT if the officer says no, this guy walks. So the officer says, “Yes, I did. I read them in full”.
That may have been an unethical thing to do, but it's almost certainly the right thing to do.

Hero Siege is probably the best value I've gotten for my money in a long time.  It is a simple enough game, a rogue-like with a number of interesting classes to choose from each with their own skill tree for you to customize them with.  Each level is a large (several screens worth) rectangular arena filled with randomly positioned traps and decorations.  After the player spawns the monsters begin to spawn in waves entering from the four doors at the center of each edge.  There is a short delay between waves which can be cut short with a button press.  After defeating enough waves you get to fight a boss.  During the waves other things can spawn such as chests or one level (and extremely lethal) side dungeons.  Keep going until you die.
Once dead you can restart from the beginning retaining your level.  The draw comes from being able to get just a little further each time and seeing what relics you uncover to power up your character and the radical ways they can change how you play.  The simple nature of the gameplay and the reasonably attractive graphics make it wasy to loose track of time while playing.

This is a coffee break game in the old-school sense of the phrase. It's a turn-based "board game", with play sessions lasting from ten to thirty minutes, depending on whether you die early or play to the end.
Basically, you pick a "class", which determines your starting gear and the value of given items (Military players will want to collect weapons and tech, Scientists will want samples of alien lifeforms with a secondary emphasis on tech, and Pirates will focus on "treasures", mostly consisting of otherwise useless sulptures and shiny things).
The endgame score is equal parts skill and luck. You'll need to figure out what does what, and you'll need to be lucky enough to find things to do the things that do things. (Hint: Smash the Timeless Bauble and type "Nova Cannon" or "Hyperdrive", depending on which you don't have yet.)
Every so often, the game board will spawn with one of three "Major" random events. To beat these, you'll need to either look up a game guide, or try your hand at trial and error.
By the time you've got things figured out, you'll really only be playing this game to try to beat your last score. This is the primary charm of the game. "Oh neat! I found this really valuable thing really early on in the game! I sure do feel lucky!". The parts of the game that require skill are equally emotionally-rewarding. "Wow! I can't believe I vapourised an entire Urluquai armada!"
For $10, you really can't go wrong for something that'll always be in your library whenever you need to kill ten minutes. Time is money, especially in this game.

The game made me really exhausted.
My purchase was made based on the "overwhelmingly positive" reviews, plus I loved the beautifully painted backgrounds, building up the atmosphere of the island the friends landed on. Esthetically, this game is a gem.
But after the first hour spent with the characters I realized that nothing really was going to happen and that the story is not the "keep-me-at-the-edge-of-the-seat" type. This game is about talking and walking, period. And while the first one might be bearable (well, the characters are teenagers, so they are talking about some meaningless stuff without any emotional engagement, like robots reading verses from a chicken soup recipe), the second one is becoming more and more painful and irritating with every step you have to make on the endlessly winding paths on the island. This reminded me of The Neverhood game, where in one place, in order to obtain a single disk to fill a gap in the story, you had to walk 38 screens to the right, pick up the disk, and then 38 screens to the left - if you remember this, you'll get the point.
While you walk and talk, things happen. But don't expect to see "overnight party gone horribly wrong", "poltergeist", "freaks and geeks", "terrifying ghost story", "interactive horror flick", "creeps" or anything like it. The game didn't manage to build anything from the list shown in trailers. It's a loose set of points on a timeline, without any climax or twists. You just fix them on the go, then come back to walking and talking.
When I finished the game (8.5 hrs) I thought like maybe I should try another scenario, another path, a different set of replies to reveal some hidden stories, to find more letters, to make more friends, to see different reactions... But then, with all the characters back again on the ferry, I realized I didn't want to go through the pain of 38 screens to the right, 38 screens to the left just to see different statistics at the end - it's not worth it.
The art in the game is superb. The music is perfectly tuned to the art (loved it!). They both are not enough, though, when you lack an emotionally binding story and a good pacing.

I will not go into detail, as it may spoil the luster of the game.
To start, the concept is unique and engaging. Who wouldn't want to watch a base grow and blossom, survive onslaught, or be overcome by an indominable force? Community mods help extend gameplay, and the community itself is overwhelmingly positive. It is due to the concept and community that makes me very tempted to give RimWorld a green light, especially understanding the current Alpha development. Unfortunately, I cannot recommend this game as it stands now in Alpha 16.
A game should have one difinitive element: a goal, a storyline, and/or a series of objectives; the separation of goal and set of objectives it to signify the difference between an "endgame condition" and "perpetual play" mode, respectively. RimWorld has none of these elements. I am hopeful this is due to the early stage of developement, and hope to be proved wrong. (**Spoiler Alert!** To date, the endgame is to launch a resource-intensive ship with some or all of your colonists into space, and game over.). Fundamentally lacking in a hook to engaage the player leaves me no choice but to downvote.
Bones to pick:
In "Vanilla edition (i.e. without mods), resources are relatively scarce for the cost of construction, colonists are almost always outnumbered during raids, extremely rare events (solar flares strong enough to disable electronic devices on the below the ionosphere and eclipses, plagues, etc.) happen quite frequently. I understand the frequency of events can be manually set, but the concept of these events occuring multiple times a year by default is quite ludicrous. The leveling system cuases colonists to rapidly lose experience and levels the moment an activity stops; in actuality, repetition reduces the effect of forgetting. Interation with visistors is strictly outside of player's control. In general, control over colonists are limited to "do this activity" and setting priority levels. That is to say, players can't directly encourage communication between colonists and anybody who is not a prisoner. Lastly, if the player wishes to eliminate a faction, the likelyhood that the player and target are balanced in either manpower or firepower is slim at best and always sides in favor of factions. Overwhelmingly, numbers trump technology and gear. Lastly, the UI is clunky in vanilla mode and potentially horrid when a number of excellent community mods are implemented.
What I would like to see in this game:
A stroyline, plot, a goal, or objectives
Conquest - take out the enemy
Diplomacy outside of paying for relations and requesting support, such as alliances, sending aid to allies, coordinated  attacks, timed caravan trades between both factions,
Expansion - take over another colony
Vehicles (researchable or not, armed/armored and not) to traverse the rough and tough RimWorld.
Vanilla resource generation or more resources or mines or some way to not run out of precious machine parts and   metals of all sorts. Otherwise, this game quickly becomes a farming simulation.
Overall, some of these issues have been handled skillfully and brilliantly by the mod community, making aspects of this game excellent. Due to the most vital element of a game not being present, I am unable to recommend this game in its current stage of development. Hopeful for the future, as this game has a lot of potential yet to be implemented. Noting my gameplay is 116 hours, a substantial portion of that was allowing the game to play in high speed until an imminant danger event occurred, and throoughly vetting the wonderful community mods (there are many, many, many mods that I hope will be incorporated into the vanilla game, such as permaent worlds).

I've never been a huge RTS buff. I certainly enjoy a lot of games in the genre; my childhood was filled with the Jurassic Park RTS "Chaos Island". While I may not be particularly skilled in the genre and I might not pay attention to every new release, without a doubt I consider Age of Empires II one of my favorite games of all time and one of the greatest games ever created.
It's a fairly straight forward RTS. You have 4 resources that you gather, 4 ages to advance through, and all of the civilizations have fairly similar units. However, there's a staggering amount of variety in ways you can approach the game, and it seems like every time I play the game I learn a new trick to better my performance. Perhaps my admiration for the games mechanics is just because I'm not an expert in the genre, but even I can see the mechanics stand head and shoulders above games like mediocre Empire Earth and, I would argue, even the excellent Warcraft III.
I think most can agree that the visuals and sound design in the game is fantastic. There may only be a few songs in the whole game, but man are they some of the catchiest tracks in gaming. I also appreciate how while all the civilizations are similar enough to be able to pick up a new one and not be completely lost, they all have a lot of subtle differences that make it so everyone can have some favorites. Visually I love the Teutons, and their defensive capabilities are great.
It should be noted that this HD upgrade doesn't necessarily boost the visuals in any outstanding way, but it does make it run well on modern PCs without the hassle of trying to get everyone's machine to run the game. The additional civilizations fit in nicely, and I appreciate the boost to the max population size and better online capabilities.
To make a long story short, this game is amazing, and definitely one of the gaming experiences that has stayed inside my rotation of games I play. If you are looking for a stepping stone into the RTS genre, a old AoE fan who has fond memories of the game back in '99, or an RTS buff that hasn't dipped their foot into the AoE pool yet, I can safely (and will vehemently) recommend this game.
(For the record, my hours on record aren't reflective of my time with this game. I probably put a couple hundred into the original release and the Conquerors expansion)

Let me explain something about this game. This game has a multiplayer that is NOT for the casual gamer. It is quite competitive, and it likes to display this competitiveness all up in yo' face. You WILL see that one dude (or multiple, I mean, they're everywhere) that can finish the track in half the time it takes you to finish it. I see this every other time I go onto this game.
The game has a steep learning curve that requires at least an hour or more in order to learn the basic physics of the game. After that, there are tricks that, once learned, can help you set better times in the multiplayer. (i.e. Left-CTRL braking & using a controller.) The tracks in this game play a major role in shaping your skills, as they are user-created. They can go from being pretty basic to being some of the hardest tracks you'll encounter on your time here.
I know very well that time makes all the difference in the multiplayer. In fact, it MEANS the difference. Times are what determine your position in a round, and the time is calculated in thousandths of a second, making photo finishes seem like nothing. You can set a record time in a single round, only for someone to beat you by .002. It really can be that close. There IS the odd tie, but it doesn't happen that often.
Now, you should go into this game knowing that you're not gonna win your first race by a long shot. Practice makes perfect. It blends in the arcade-style driving physics and fantasy environment with a competitve multiplayer that stands with some of the best. I've never been so involved in a racing game that isn't a sim. Trackmania 2 also has its own ladder system, which determines how well you do amongst other players worldwide. And we're not only talking worldwide, either. It can track official progress to as close as your own state (if you live in the US, that is). You have a number for everything, from server rankings, to single player rankings, to country rankings. The better you do, the more the number goes down, and the more accomplished you feel.
I recommend this game, because it makes the $20 you'll dump on this game worth the cost. Now, do mind, this was a game that was made BEFORE the UPlay era, so it doesn't require the UPlay launcher. Instead, it has its own launcher for launching titles, although it still is in need of serious revision.

Hero Siege, as you can tell by my small amount of time playing it, is not nessecarily fun. Its an OKAY time-killer at best, using simplistic mechanics. Hero Siege is a game heavily inspired by Diablo and others. You play as one of many classes and beat waves after waves of Enemies until you finish the game. There are relics which increase some of your powers, various temporary items which are lost upon death which give stats or skills, statues that increase your stats permanently and potions with temporary buffs/debuffs. The game tends to be fun, however it takes time to get used to controls and the chaos going on. It depends a lot on luck and lucky generation of items, or else you're going to die for sure and restart all over again. Once you get a hang of it, it becomes fun but a bit boring as you're so strong it's no longer a challenge. Be wary after finishing a game on one difficulty you restart with no items on the next diff.
>I'd give it a 8.5/10
>Pros: Fun, lots of randomization, lots of items, good if you're a fan of rogue-likes and Diablo clones, graphics are neat. I previously stated bugs and imbalances as negative sides, however most of them are now fixed and they keep being fixed as reports come in.
>Cons: Campaign acts which will come out in the future are all PAID DLC, also dislike the concept of not only having a DLC but an even more expensive "Collector's Edition". (DLC with acts and rest of the game should be free, collector's edition should be the purchase to support the developer rather than having it all paid for)

I've played a lot of Age of Empires II. The original was one of the first games I remember playing, besides the original Warcraft. I played it when it first came out in 1999, and I still plally it occasionally to this day. As far as RTSs go, AoE II may not have been revolutionary as Warcraft or Starcraft or Command and Conquer, but it's still a great entry in the genre.
Now that we've established Age of Empires is a good game (which you probably already knew if you're interested in this), let's talk about the HD rerelease. A lot of games are getting the "HD treatment" these days and some of them *cough* Might and Magic III *cough* are abysmal and even inferior to the original versions that are available elsewhere. So how is the AoE II port?
Well...it's fine. Most of the graphics are exactly the same as the original with a few noteable exceptions such as farms and fire effects and the resource tooltips (for whatever reason). To be honest, I don't care for these changes. In my opinion, if you're going to do an HD remaster, either upgrade ALL the sprites or just leave the classic style. Fortunately, if you don't like the new sprites, you can download the original art assets from the Steam Workshop.
Yes that's right, the HD remaster of Age of Empires II has Steam Workshop support. This means (as it usually does) that if you ever get bored with the games many campaigns, you can always download more. Or new unit sprites. Or different HD texture packs. Or new music. Basically whatever you want.
The other big elephant in the room (literally, two of the new races get elephants) are the new "expansions" (let's be real here, it's DLC). There are three of them, and each one adds four (or in one case, five) new civilizations and everything that that comes with, including new campaigns. This is EXCELLENT. The fact that the devs care enough about this almost 20 year old game to breathe new life into it on a regular basis is incredibly appreciated. And the expansions are good. The races are (mostly) balanced as far as I can tell. The  campaigns are interesting if you're into that sort of thing. And of course there's multiplayer if you get bored of beating up the AI in the large amounts of new maps.
Overally, there's no better way to play this game. The remaster is as good as the original on its own, but with the added expansions (that often go on sale with the game) and the addition of the Steam Workshop, this edition easily surpasses the original and is a wonderful experience even today in 2017.

To preface my thoughts: I did not play Battle Knights alone. I experienced only half of what makes the game what it is. But I think that was the best part about it. My friends and I started with the multiplayer versus mode. After an hour of winning, losing, joining into teams and trading memebers of my team, we switched the bonus dungeon mode.

Little thing about the dungeon - you have to play it in all one go. My friends and I spent about another hour playing it, only to get to the third stage and die from exhaustion. The next day we booted it up, and found out that we had to redo it. So we did it again, and it was still just as challenging and just as fun. For those of you who do not like rage games, then this is not for you. For everyone who does, grab a friend who hates them and force them to play it with you. We never finished it (not yet, anyway), but you can finish it with the proper amount of skill and timing.
So Pros:
Forces you to think
Challenging
Multiplayer
Little to no bugs (The developers do a very good job staying in contact with the audience and keeping them informed on what is going on.)
Can be played for a short or long amount of time.
Cons:
Challenging (No, it is REALLY challenging and may make you doubt your skills as a gamer.)
Multiplayer is the best way of playing it. (If you have no friends, then you're out of luck with this game)
Has to be played in one go. (The campaign does not. Let me restate this: the campaign can be played in multiple goes. The dungeon run, however, can not be.)
So all in all, it's a pretty good game. The feel of it reminds me a lot of shovel knight, with how the art style looks and such. If you're looking for a party game to play with friends , this would be a good suggestion.

Its retro presentation indicative of the design philosophy driving it all, Battle Knights seeks to deliver an intensely challenging platforming experience. Level design and enemy placement reward memorization, dexterous platforming and careful melee. Best played with a gamepad!
There's a ton of game here. On top of a single-player / co-op campaign spanning 6 unique zones complete with boss battles and optional challenge stages, the devs have packed in an impressive amount of bonus content by way of additional game modes, 3 of which wait to be unlocked.
Getting into the habit of blocking is paramount for survival as the 3 hits you're afforded can vanish in a blink. Bringing up that SSB-ish shield, however, saves you from suffering any non-spike damage for as long as it's active. While your attack range feels Wonderboy wimpy, there are random power-up drops that offer a Castlevania Adventure-like projectile to accompany each slash, although these are limited use.
Dungeon Run mode is my personal favourite of what's available in Battle Knights, taking the classic "pushy level" and making it into a self-contained, multi-stage adventure. Like the rest of Battle Knights, it's punishingly difficult and the forced scrolling can get frustratingly speedy but there's real satisfaction to be had learning a Dungeon Run level and executing it perfectly.
I'm looking forward to trying the multiplayer modes out with a buddy! :)

Great game greatly recommended.
Your small group of colonists AKA pawns will go through both pleasant and catastrophic events in a story told by "AI storyteler", registered member of The Sadists union. Your choice of storyteler will strongly influence the story you'll live - from almost peacefull base building to complete mayhem. You'll have to adapt to cold, heat, sickness, hunger, attacks by animals, humans and mechanoids.... Don't let the cartoony graphics fool you. Each colonists' (and animals') psychical and physical health is simulated in great detail including social interactions between people. Temperature can and will wipe your colony just as likely as a firestorm or raid of angry tribals.
Your job is to act as a Godlike architect, define where to build buildings, plant a field, where store specific items, what to manufacture etc. Your main tool is the system of job priorities for all colonists so that the colony will mostly run unattended without much micromanagement under normal circumstances. When a crisis strikes (which will be pretty often) you're always able to manually force a pawn to do certain job. In combat you'll take complete control of one or several pawns in Xcom-like pausable realtime manner.
Game still in early access but currently (Alpha 16) pretty far in development, very stable and I believe that majority of game systems are in place. There is a huge base of useful mods on Workshop ranging from utility/quality of life improvements to significant overhauls including Cthulhu cult worshipping madness :)

I got this as part of a Humble Monthly Bundle. I personally would not pay $50 for it.
Pretty stunning. I do like how when doing character analysis, things are (usually) detailed enough to notice the parts you have to click on without giving up and running your mouse over the whole character for the place it wants you to find.
Not perfect, but believable and good.
Usually work really well or are enjoyable to use. I love the deductions screen, filling it out it really satisfying. Working at the analysis table was also great, for the most part. You may be corrected for trying to open a bottle before using a tool with it, but it's usually pretty intuitive.
Exploring the streets was interesting, though many of them ended up being really pointless. I was really sure for a while that I was hearing someone screaming out in pain in one area (when I was looking for a missing person!) and nope, no way to find that person, just a random sound effect. The game could and should take more advantage of these open areas, give us something to do in them.
In so many places in the game I am left wildly guessing what to do next. For example:
1. In at least two places while hunting for clues, you cannot progress unless you make a certain assumption in the deduction screen first.
2. You often have to travel back to previously investigated locations just to talk to someone again or look at something again. This isn't always marked in your objectives, and won't always be obvious otherwise.
3. In at least one part, Sherlock says he needs to talk to someone about something, so I figured it was the next step - however, you are never actually able to talk to the person about that, even though it could be useful to the investigation.
4. Many, many times you will be able to click on a clue from across the room, but another clue's clickable indicator won't show up unless you move your mouse precisely over where it wants you to at the exact distance away. This becomes a major headache when you can't progress because, despite hovering over everything, the clickable icon didn't show up unless you chose one specific spot of the clue. Additionally, some items can be looked at for multiple clues on the item, and unless you find all of them, you can't progress. Sometimes the clickable icon lights up green after looking at something, but sometimes it doesn't, so I wasn't always sure if I was done with an object or not.
5. Sometimes you will notice clues but you can't click on them until you've noticed other clues first. For example, in one scene you can't look at a weapon until you've looked at everything else in the area. In another scene, you can't look at the source of an issue before trying to figure out what happened as a result of the issue. I don't see why you can't look at everything available to you all at once, and piece together the logic afterwards.
6. While you can figure out the goal of a puzzle based on environmental clues in some areas (markings on the wall giving hints, or statues' expressions guiding you), in other sections it falls into the "punishing without giving any hints" territory. For example, there's such a room with tiles that fall into a spike pit, with no logic for where you're supposed to go beyond trying over and over. You're left wildly guessing, because there are no hints.
7. Despite Sherlock's impressive imagination, he can't predict or say aloud any thoughts to help you out on your 30th try of something. This becomes doubly annoying when, for example, he'll give hints about which tools to use in which order at the analysis table, but has no ideas whatsoever about how to prevent his hand from being stabbed through in a Mayan temple puzzle.
8. Some puzzles just don't seem to work properly. For example, in one room in the Mayan temple you're supposed to turn the room in intervals of 180, 90, and 45 degrees. Somehow my room ended up about 5 degrees off of a place I needed it to be, no matter how I turned the room it was still off. Despite Sherlock being able to jump in other areas, he couldn't walk or jump from the slightly-off platform to the switch.
9. Additionally, despite being able to climb walls, rocks, and tree vines in other areas, Sherlock can't do this in all areas. For example, he can't climb a stack of crates or a rock wall in another area, or jump across a gap. Instead, you have to solve a tedious puzzle solely for the purpose of giving him something to climb or walk across more easily. After seeing his ability to jump or run across gaps in one area, you may not realize that the game now expects you to roll out a perfectly flat surface with no gaps for him to use. On the flip side, you may then expect a tedious puzzle in another area, but find he can now suddenly jump across.
More save spots would be really useful for the skippable sections, such as running through the swamp or dying in the Mayan temple's poison puzzles. If it could save just before you died instead of before even starting the sequence, it would be much more forgiving to players who are just trying to figure out what the heck they're supposed to be doing.
I got frustrated to the point where it was no longer enjoyable so many times. You're left feeling like an idiot because you didn't hover over another object in just the right way, or you didn't guess that a person was lying before trying to look around a room for clues.
Many of the quick time events can be skipped, but not all of them. In the discussion boards, devs will help with save games if you're unable to pass an un-skippable section.
Some puzzles can be skipped, but others cannot. The mechanics of the puzzles are not always friendly to limited controller usage.
Subtitles available for all dialogue. Dialogue can be read again in the case notes.
Most of the game can be passed with point and click, however, you do need to also move around the environment and operate a 3rd person camera. You can switch to a first person view which I find easier.
Worth a bit of tinkering with if you get it in a bundle or on sale. Definitely not total garbage, but will almost definitely frustrate you in many areas. You will probably use a guide at least once.

Trackmania 2 Canyon has a lot of pro's and con's and is only really just getting a thumb's up from me. This is also purely my opinion.
Pros:
- Good Graphics
- Good Car Physics (i.e. good/fun drfiting and handling)
- Variety of single player maps
- Good multiplayer
- I haven't tried Map Making, but I've heard from friends and reading reviews that it's good.
- Leaderboards for lap times is excellent, and adds some competitiveness in both single player and multiplayer.
Cons:
- The only real game mode is time attack, which has no collision with other cars, and is purely just you driving and seeing the 'ghost' of other cars. This makes the game repetitive after a while. There needs to be other game modes like Race or Elimination, with collision. This would add heaps more fun and diversity, and reduce the repetitiveness.
- You only get one type of car. This isn't a major problem, but having a few different looking cars just adds more diversity which is good.
- As it is TrackMania 2 CANYON, theres only 1 type of environment. Yes this is expcted when buying the game, but once again, this makes the game repetitive, and for $20 you'd expect a little more.
- Car customization is very basic, and is still hard to do.  And you're customized skins can't be seen (Unless they download the skin youve made manually) by other players on multiplayer, so you're basically showing off your nice skin to bots on single player.
- There's no real atmosphere. Your purely just driving through a track. There's no birds flying around, or planes flying over or anything to add some atmosphere to the game. It's just your car and the track.
- This isn't really a con, but, when your car falls into water, theres no splash at all. It just goes into the water and NOTHING happens, you just sink or float.
So overall, you're paying $20 to drive 1 car around various tracks, doing the same game mode over and over again. Yes, this is still fun, especially with friends, but the game lacks any real change in pace, and gets repetitive after a while. Overall I would say buy it when it's on special, as it is definitely not worth $20.

Weird Worlds: Return to Infinite Space falls somewhere between Civ 5 and FTL, incorporating diplomacy aspects and space battles. For the majority of the game, you will be flying to different star systems, picking up valuable items, specimens, ship parts, or ambassadors to bring back to your homeworld in the Glory system. The combat can be pretty interesting when you manage to get good upgrades and recruit multiple pilots for your flotilla, but it's usually best to avoid confrontation in the beginning of the game.
Unfortunately, all of the events and alien races can be seen in about 20 playthroughs on the "long" setting, and the long setting itself seems too short. This game would be far better if it had much more content and even longer playtimes, and I can't help but feel it would be more fun to continue upgrading your ships and battling for much longer instead of having to return back to your planet.
If you like games that have some depth yet allow you to sit back and relax while playing, Weird Worlds might be right up your alley.

I've played through Old Blood, and am currently replaying it to get the achievements. That said, I think New Order is the better of the two, and I haven't even finished the first level at the time of me writing this. I'm not saying Old Blood is bad, just that at the moment, New Order seems more promising. Off the bat, New Order feels like it has more content and is more interesting.
The perk system is more satisfying and visually appealing in NO than OB.
NO starts you off in a futuristic D-Day style attack on a huge Nazi compound, while OB starts with you sneaking into Castle Wolfenstein (also a huge Nazi compound).
Already on the first level, NO is showing signs of allowing multiple paths toward your objective (being able to breach a bunker in two different locations. OB only allows you to make one decision throughout the whole story (granted, it is a major one, but I would rather be able to make more smaller decisions)
I am aware that OB was originally supposed to be a DLC for NO, but was later fleshed out into a stand-alone game. Since this is the case, it makes sense that OB feels to be lacking in content compared to what I have seen so far in NO.

When you died in the game, you can resume the game on the same wave with reduced HP. The key to clear this game is collecting the relics. The relics greatly boost your stats or give unique special effects, thus it's very important to get these relics. Relics can be obtained from chest (crystal chest has the higest chance to drop relics), clearing a stage, dungeon drop or from shop (usually obtainable for 1000 coins). Each time you level up, you get 2 stats point and a skill point. The objective of this game is to pass until the final wave. On the end of a stage (each 6 waves) you will face special bosses. Boss has special skills that will conduct after a specific time. Beating a boss is pretty easy if you have some relics with you.

(-) No Audio Settings, as a streamer I had to turn down the entire desktop audio to effectively get the stream to a nice sound again. I'd usually like to just turn down the music and adjust effects/dialogues slightly

It's Dwarf Fortress for those of us who were always interested in its concept, but couldn't get through the ASCII wall and the learning curve, in a space setting that's heavily inspired by Firefly (so there are a multitude of worlds with varying degrees of technology advancement, and you're going to see people from all sorts of backgrounds). You're in charge of guiding a group of colonists through their trials and tribulations in one of the titular Rim Worlds; distant, isolated planets lacking in strong central government and low in population density, and your job is to get them to stay alive long enough to... do whatever you want, really. There is a clear "end game" goal here (build / access a ship and escape the planet), but the real fun of the game comes from developing your base in whatever way you want, for as long as you can, while surviving the ever-escalating threats that the AI will throw at you.
Both in art style and construction-oriented gameplay, the game is immediately reminiscent of Prison Architect, but Rimworld is much more than that, as it's also packing a surprisingly deep combat system that demands careful planning, both while building and during combat itself, if you want your colonists to live to see another day. The AI "storytellers", a concept not unlike L4D's "director", ensures that you meet a level of challenge that, at the very least, will give you a memorable tale to share after your colonists' demise.
And when the time comes and your colonists die, you WILL feel it. There are many, many easy / dumb ways to die in this game, and learning about them is part of the experience; you'll just HAVE to tell your friends about the one animal handler who died in combat, only to have one of his pets go mad from grief and butcher one of your colonists, or the colonist that sacrificed his life so you could learn about cave-ins the hard way, or the dangers of running a drug operation in a colony full of stressed people fearing for their lives...
If there's one negative aspect about it, it's the fact that its tutorial is simply not good enough. Many important mechanics are barely mentioned or not even touched upon (setting work priorities manually is one such glaring omission); losing colonists because of mistakes you're aware of or gambles gone wrong is fine, but having them die because you didn't understand a part of the UI is frustrating, and there may be a lot of that if you don't go looking for tips before diving in too deep.
Overall though, it's an amazing game. It's in Early Access not because of it being a buggy mess, unplayable or imbalanced; it's simply there to let buyers know that there's still more content being added to it, and the end of early access will mean the end of development for the game. I can't recommend this game enough, it's absolutely worth it at full price!

My first negative review but I felt I had to write it. This game is the definition of tedious for me. I only played half an hour and I was already sick of it. There is no investigating there is a lot of handheld highlighted stuff you "analize" and tedious, tedious, tedious minigames. They are not hard, they are not interesting you just have to do the same low-skill dexterity "puzzle" keep the mouse in a circle keep the other circle in a circle with WASD.
Before I go into minor spoiler field I will talk about performance.  It's poor. Frequent drops into the 20's framerate  when it has no reason to be under 60, Frameskipping galore and an unpleasant experience altogether, Yes the enviroment looks nice, UE4 has the tools to render some beatiful scenes, but if the developer can't do both beatiful graphics and steady performance, I prefer worse graphics anyday. And no, turning down the settings doesn't help the drops, the GPU usage just goes down without any bottleneck from the CPU, RAM or Storage.
The settings menu is functional at best, not a lot of fiddleling around to improve performance (AA can't be turned completely OFF for example).
Even locked to 30fps with RivaTunerServer doesn't stop the framepacing issue. Turn around to quickly and you've got a head-ache on your hands.
Minor Spoiler
During the first mission you have to follow a bloke on the streets of White Chappel and the whole affair is a scripted, "cinematic", borderline QTE (without the Q and the E really) affair. If you played Assassin's Creed (any of them) and remember those "Follow X-characther" missions where you had to duck under one of the 2-3 covers every 30 seconds when the X-character turned to check his 6 you know what this mini-game is all about. It's boring, plain and simple and it does nothing but pad the contet needlesly and keeps you from what you are here for, solve some misteries!
I don't like these mini-games, I don't like how they ask nothing of me but to waste my time before I get to the "mistery solving". I don't like having to eat a plate of♥♥♥♥♥♥for the few nuts hidden inside, nuts that are rotten.
And after all that you get to the puzzles which are mediocre at best. There is hand-holding all the way. You have everything highlighted, you can't go forward until you have found all the clues, you are funneled into a corridor that directs you to the solution. You feel like you are not necesary to the proccess beyond clicking the mouse because how you click it and why is not up to you.
So yeah. Stay away from this game if you like creative puzzle solving and hate tedious "skill" mini-games that test nothing but your patience.
But if you are not bothered by the performance issues, by the mini-games, or even derive pleasure from them, and want a not so demanding puzzle-solving experience give this game a try.

The gameplay is creative when compared to most sherlock holmes I played. It basiclaly includes making deductions, building character portraits by observing clues, some well crafted puzzles but most of them are easy (but the thing is if you have both the hard and easy puzzles it makes the game enjoyable).
It also includes some pressing keys in timed cutscenes and etc, but what I really enjoyed was making deductions and um changing clothes. Yes- so going to the Scotland Yard wearing a bath gown is possible. Sherlock Holmes can dress in his casual suit or disguise himself to be a pastor or a sailor boy if he prefers along with changing hats and facial hair.
Holmes possess  various techniques that is useful for finding clues : the imagination technique which makes him visualize the past using the present clues and also the "T" technique which he uses to find clues which normal people can't see.
What I primarly noticed when playing the game was  the accessable streets and how big and distant they are. When compared to the previous games, the streets were merely partially acessible and not many people were around. However in this game version- you could talk to most people and even choose a cab to travel. Oh yes and you have the ability to buy newspapers and even check the headlines from a paper boy.
Multiple characters could be selected such as Toby the cute doggie, Wiggins and Dr. Watson. The game has many enjoyable events which are scary and other times entertaining such as the "Exorcism" xD
The story was the most interesting aspect of this game. On one side you see him tackling family problems, a witch and on the other side arresting psychopaths and saving innocent people. Your deductions would eventually lead you to a conclusion on which you should choose to determine the guilty criminal's fate. On that aspect the game can make you a bit emotional. There are 4/5 different story settings which is refreshing and the certain choices you make in the game while talking to people could change the story's direction.
Some of the story settings are
1. Mayan Pyramids
2.Sewers
3.Cemetery
4.Gambling houses etc
The graphics are good but some cutscenes seems very laggy but nevertheless in terms of quallity graphic art the game surely made it's mark. I loved the carefully detailed graphics especially.
The game soundtracks are exceptional. I personally enjoyed the music that played during the credits and the one that played when you are walking in baker street and outside the scotland yard premises.
The achievements are very easy to get except winning that lawn bowling match, took me a few tries lol
Replay value is medium and I would still play some cases if Im bored.
It would be nice to have some more DLC content other than the clothes, maybe one or two cases? The lagginess of the game should be fixed. Other than that, the game is pretty entertaining and had some epic jaw dropping moments.

I've played a lot of Age of Empires II. The original was one of the first games I remember playing, besides the original Warcraft. I played it when it first came out in 1999, and I still plally it occasionally to this day. As far as RTSs go, AoE II may not have been revolutionary as Warcraft or Starcraft or Command and Conquer, but it's still a great entry in the genre.
Now that we've established Age of Empires is a good game (which you probably already knew if you're interested in this), let's talk about the HD rerelease. A lot of games are getting the "HD treatment" these days and some of them *cough* Might and Magic III *cough* are abysmal and even inferior to the original versions that are available elsewhere. So how is the AoE II port?
Well...it's fine. Most of the graphics are exactly the same as the original with a few noteable exceptions such as farms and fire effects and the resource tooltips (for whatever reason). To be honest, I don't care for these changes. In my opinion, if you're going to do an HD remaster, either upgrade ALL the sprites or just leave the classic style. Fortunately, if you don't like the new sprites, you can download the original art assets from the Steam Workshop.
Yes that's right, the HD remaster of Age of Empires II has Steam Workshop support. This means (as it usually does) that if you ever get bored with the games many campaigns, you can always download more. Or new unit sprites. Or different HD texture packs. Or new music. Basically whatever you want.
The other big elephant in the room (literally, two of the new races get elephants) are the new "expansions" (let's be real here, it's DLC). There are three of them, and each one adds four (or in one case, five) new civilizations and everything that that comes with, including new campaigns. This is EXCELLENT. The fact that the devs care enough about this almost 20 year old game to breathe new life into it on a regular basis is incredibly appreciated. And the expansions are good. The races are (mostly) balanced as far as I can tell. The  campaigns are interesting if you're into that sort of thing. And of course there's multiplayer if you get bored of beating up the AI in the large amounts of new maps.
Overally, there's no better way to play this game. The remaster is as good as the original on its own, but with the added expansions (that often go on sale with the game) and the addition of the Steam Workshop, this edition easily surpasses the original and is a wonderful experience even today in 2017.

TICK'S TALES – UP ALL KNIGHT
PUBLISHER – Phoenix Online
DEVELOPER – Digital Bounce House
GENRE – Point & click adventure
THE BASICS:
Remember King's Quest? Tick's Tales is basically a spoof of that, only shorter. Good entry point for people who have never tried a “Sierra style” adventure game.
THE FLOW AND THE STORY:
You are...er, AHEM...you play as a hapless loser who wants to pull the town's legendary sword out of its stone in order to impress the girl of his dreams. In order to do that, he needs to fulfill the requisite quests to prove his strength, wisdom, and courage (where have I seen those before?...). Naturally, doing so will require that he do everything from scarfing down some incredibly hot mints, to helping an owl with his vision problem, to saving the townspeople from their dire fate – an eternity of being forced to play Bingo and sing karaoke. The horror! The horror!
CONTROLS:
Mouse-driven everything – movement, inventory, and dialogue. Simple, straightforward, and effective.
GRAPHICS:
8/16-bit visual style, intended to remind you of the old Sierra games. The graphics suit the game, and are more detailed than you might expect for such a thing. Even the very, very few “hunt the pixel” situations are set up so that the pixel you want to click is incredibly obvious.
SOUND:
Chiptunes. Either you love 'em or you hate 'em. Decent ones in here. Only one sound FX is a bit annoying (the “dream” sound when Tick imagines his crush talking to him); it's a bit ear-piercing. Aside from that, the music/sounds are varied and reasonable, and they do their job.
OVERALL:
A good game, and a pleasant way to kill a couple of hours. If you're new to the point-n-click genre, this could be a good entry point. The characters do a good job of nudging you on your way, generally without explicitly telling you do do X.

S&ART's levels come in many different shapes and sizes, and all of them provide a rich, detailed and fun experience for the players. From challenging levels make Rainbow Road look easy to wonderfuly crafted thematic levels such as  Dream Valley, S&ART has a level for every skill level.
Every vehicle and level in S&ART has it's unique style and feel and style. From General Winter's Tank to Shogun's wooden... Chariot, The level of character diversity in S&ART easily surpasses the majority of arcade racing games on the market.
The addition of boats and planes has opened up many unique opportunies for fun and often whacky levels. However, this is no
or
. The boats often feel slow and clunky, and the feeling of being in water is only kept there by the predictable wave effects. The planes are meant to be the fastest and most agile of the vehicles, and yet they feel very bloated and dance through the sky instead of cutting through the air. Drifting is also a very gimicked function on these two modes, and serves as a tie-in feature to keep the feel of the game consistent.
From 'Capture the Chao' to 'Battle Arena', secondary modes serve as mostly a distraction (albeit an intresting and somewhat fun one) from the core of the game. The fun that one may have is generally very inconsistent as these modes generally rely on utilising one feature of the game over and over again.
Graphical customisation cannot be done in game, it must be instead configured through an external menu. The placement of the menu items in game are also have a 'console port' feel, with clunky selection menus and awkwardly placed buttons.

Being new to MOBA's, I may not be the most qualified to review this game but I want to take a shot at it.
For someone like me (who is new to MOBA) this is the game to get into them on. The tutorial is great. (I'll never understand why people complain about having to do a tutorial, especially when the number one complaint is that your team-mate doesn't know how to play) . It's also obvious to see that the developers tried to create a positive (and non-toxic) atmosphere for the community.
They dev's created what seems to be a TRULY F2P and "NOT" P2W game. Any actual money you shell out is either for character customization or permanent boost to XP, both of which can be purchased by earning gems in-game.
I found the tutorial helpful and information from the other sources on how to play to be plentiful and easy to find. There are quite a few people and groups dedicated to Strife (though I fear their numbers are shrinking) including a Discord group. That said, I guess I am too new to understand why this game did not get off the ground. Even in it's current (and seemingly abandoned state-more on this later) state, it is playable and thoroughly enjoyable. Due too the limited number of people still playing, I found myself playing mostly 'VS. BOT' matches.
While playing, I ran into what almost seemed to be some kind of hack/bot attack, that would force my character to return to home AND 'STAY' there. All other aspects of the game were accessible and functional, I just couldn't move my player. This occurred several times, each time resulting in my being labeled as AFK and receiving a ban (each one longer than the previous) and being tagged as a 'leaver' in-game.
When I tried to talk about it with other players, my chats vanished from the chat window or were met with rather odd and  sarcastic responses. Which leaves me to believe that the game has fallen under control of one or more players with a unique skill-set. I filled out a ticket but, was assured that that was a waste of time, as no ticket has been answered in almost 2 years (and the dev's had gone silent on any and all aspects of the game for about the same period of time). (Which I found confusing when looking at a patch from December 6, 2017 that seems to have surprised most of the players.)
If the current state of the game is that it is abandoned (DON'T buy any of the DLC or purchase any of the in-game currency) and there are as I suspect (and hope to be wrong about) hacks loose in-game, it's more than sad. Looking around as much as I did for info on the best MOBA to get into, Strife had some of the nest reviews of ANY MOBA active or not, right now. With virtually zero comments on a negative or toxic community, a majority of reviews make reference to the notion that Strife was what they had hoped LoL would be, or Strife, Or Hon, or other MOBA's. I was hard pressed to find ANY negative reviews of the game outside of the few posted here.
I even came across a few reviewers who expressed a desire to see Strife try to reboot itself, revive itself, etc. With the vast majority of companies focusing on MOBA's for mobile platforms now (only 3 come to mind for non-mobile platforms that may make an appearance in the next year or so) I think it would be a shame to scrap Strife completely WITHOUT ONE LAST DITCH EFFORT.
There is a need for MOBA with a different approach and eye on resolving the issue of toxic communities in the genre. Strife could have (and still could) filled that void. Maybe pushing the game hard from that angle with true commitment would be the fresh breath of life it (and the players) need.

As for the game's creamy center, it is very tactics heavy with an emphasis on flanking. What's new, right? Well... nothing really except that unit spamming absolutely will not work. To achieve victory you have to use the proper tactics for the situation at hand.
Something I like about the game is the cinematic mode that allows you to pause the game, plan your strategy, give the appropriate movement orders, unpause and watch it all unfold. The mode does have it's shortcomings though. Mainly, the camera cuts from unit to unit showing both your troops and the enemies. It looks cool but it doesn't allow you to get any kind of idea of just how well your strategy is working out. Luckily, you can cut in and out of cinematic mode to periodically assess, rethink and reposition. Even the greatest Armchair General is going to have to do this regularly. You might want to stay away from this entirely unless or until you have an earned confidence in your ability to react quickly and plan and execute the level of tactics that this game calls for. It doesn't take long at all for a German Panzer division, even when outnumbered or outclassed, to roll right over a bad strategy.

I have heard this game (favouribly) being compared broadly as a kind of 'space solitaire' game. But it doesn't look or even at first blush play like solitaire, so I want to explain why the analogy works for me:
In solitaire, you have the same 52 cards, arranged in such a way that their order is different, so sometimes you might get snuffed out early by an unlucky deal, and sometimes you might fly through for victory - you don't really mind which, because games don't take long so the stakes never feel so high that you'll never play it again.
Weird Worlds shares some of this in common. The star system is filled with mostly the same items and hazards, but the order you encounter them switches out, so in one play through you might have exactly the item you need to best deal with an encounter, and another time you might not.
This means that a lot of it is luck based, but half the fun is replaying the game and seeing where luck will take your exploration of the galaxy this time.
That's not to say it's all luck - fitting out your ships with the best gear takes a bit of decision making, and it's possible to learn the function of special objects to understand whether they're worthless and tradable, or could come in handy. Plus the real time combat segments are basic, but reward people who avoid combat before becoming sufficiently tooled up.
Occasionally, too, the game likes to switch things up by layering a 'meta' plot, usually difficult to resolve, above the usual exploration. Some sort of crisis which the player must solve in order to score a 'win.' These are rare, but always welcome.
Like Solitaire, this is an ideal game to kill a short space of time with, but better than solitaire, it rewards repeat play with just a modicum of depth to be discovered beneath the surface.

Two years ago I’ve played Sherlock Holmes: Crimes & Punishments the previous title in this series and i though very well of that game. In fact there were so many things right with it. For starters it was a good game, it had a good selection of 6 cases in a relatively new format (for a game), which was, many short stories instead of one long one (which in this case worked excellent) It had a real good depiction of sherlock and watson, the game focused heavily on story as much as gameplay (not ancient genre conventions) and because of that, it presented freely many kinds of gameplay styles , ranging from classic interrogation with a suspect to contextual actions. This was achieved doing different things across the game, from placing and object in a certain place, to smelling  a tobacco pouch to identify its brand, to throwing an harpoon on a pig (long story) to know more about a killer. All this was just the starting point, then you had your detective sense, which enabled you to find hidden prints of missing objects, and then you had your clues screen in which you associated different facts, like it was part of your brain,  and ideas about the case flowed along until you reach one of many deductions to find the resolution.
You had even your notebook, in which you had pictures about the different characters you meet, another page with tasks to do, and then you have your map with places to go, and finally your inventory which is not only objects but also questions and facts.
It was really something.
You had lots of things to take in (many of which, were optional) but amazingly enough, there was nothing out of place, everything was balanced and there was not too much of anything. More important, none of these different styles of gaming (action, puzzles, visual clues) felt wrong or out of place. This was the best strength for Crimes & Punishments: this game was an adventure for the new century. And it dared to be what an adventure can be, an interactive experience to tell stories and make you feel part of it, regardless of what style of game it chooses.
Crimes  & Punishments accomplished that, and you felt like solving a mystery like sherlock holmes (and if you read the novels, it was much more close to it, than, for example, the guy ritchie movies....)
The Devil's daughter has many of those things, but...it fails in other things. First, the story: this time there are 4 cases, the fifth is the resolution of the story between cases, which is not a bad thing in itself, but it makes this game considerably shorter. The story for the cases are... almost good at best... and pretty bad at worst. One of the great things about the previous game was that you could choose different solutions to a case, only one of them being the good one, but the good one was not so evident. You could make the wrong choice. In this game, one of the cases has a very obvious deduction, then another one its not so obvious and it is a good mystery, but, it incorporates a very long and completely unnecessary and out of place sequence of deathtraps in a mayan temple (with sherlock playing as lara croft) which of course doesn't go well (Even if you like tomb raider) In this game, many of the action minigames felt too much and out of place. The problem is not having an action game, but having too much of them (unbalanced) or just one that doesn’t make too much sense.
Then, the next case, has a solution that feels very contrived, even checking the facts, even checking the forums online and researching about it after the fact, it just doesn't make too much sense (there's a recurring subject online about the resolution of one particular case being a little off) some characters that are presented into the case out of nowhere, others that have red herrings that are badly placed. Finally, the last story which is the story with sherlock's daughter feels to much forced, and without much meaning besides the intense moments.
The voice acting in this game comes very mixed. There are good voices of course, most of the supporting characters in fact like lestrade, wiggins, and many other ones on different cases, but then for some of the main game characters, like kate (sherlock's daughter) the voice acting is bad (at least in english).

Then the choice to change considerably the looks and voice of both sherlock and watson didn't do well for me.
It went too far away from the novels (which was one of the strengths of the previous games) in fact one of the great things about the previous game was that it resembled so much the original characters from the novels and it looked NOTHING like the ones from that guy ritchie movie.... and in this game.... frankly, watson looks a lot like jude law...
On the technical side the game uses an improved version of the unreal engine, UE4 (previously it was version 3) so technically, the game is better, but it kind of looks less detail sometimes, like for example making a character portrait. But at other times, the weather effects and scene details are really good. Too bad the characters doesn't look that good. Probably it is a matter of making better use of the new tool.
It’s sad that after making not only the best adventure from 2014 but also making adventure games relevant again, they falled so short on this one, but I’m sure there's a very talented group of people there working at Frogwares and they're next game will be much better, especially because they are departing from the Sherlock Holmes territory and into HP Lovecraft .

A very conflicted experience, but overall a good time.
Pros:
- Good variation of activities
- Campy but cozy storytelling
- Some legitimately good detective moments
Cons:
- Few solutions are clear cut, a lot of it feels like guesswork
- A few puzzles and segments are designed in a very linear fashion that only seems to make good sense to the developers.
After getting used to the controls and mechanics of the game, I was hooked even though certain parts of the game made me incredibly frustrated. If there's anything I'd suggest it is to polish the games more, and do more QA.
A lot of the times I wasn't sure if I'd come to the right conclusions, because there was never really concrete evidence as to who did it. And I'd like to see more freedom in gameplay, instead of walking around crossing off a checklist in a sort of linear design.
In the end, I really enjoyed the game despite the flaws - and I'm excited to go back and play previous titles, as well as looking forward to potential future ones.

First, the positives. This game was surprisingly great fun. It feels a bit like a Telltale Game with a little more walking around. The detection elements really make you think. Even though I ended up making the right choices most of the time, I really had to think about them, and the moral choices really add another layer to your decisions. On the negative side, I completed this game in 8 hours, without rushing it. I have 100% of the achievements too. Since you basically know what's going on after one playthrough, there's not really any replay value. I can't see a lot of point to replaying on the harder difficulty, since I know the correct choices for everything, and there isn't enough content that I'd forget.
So to sum up, this is a great game, but definitely not worth the £30 it's selling for on Steam as of the date of this review. I got this as part of a Humble Bundle. If I'd paid for it, I'd have felt a bit stiffed. Get it on sale for sure, at a price you think is worth the eight hours of admittedly fantastic entertainment.

Magical Eyes - Red is for Anguish is a great mystery visual novel about supernatural events and people with super powers. It's also a nice introduction to what seems to be an episodic series. The game contains a prologue that sets up the world and main character and the first chapter of the game. Chapter 1 focuses on one big mystery about a doll that has been spiriting people away. One of the things I like about the game is that it keeps changing perspectives - the game focuses on the main character Yuu Amakawa most of the time but for certain scenes it will switch to one of the other characters that you meet.
The game has a nice structure to it - each day you find out more about the case and at the end of it there's a section called reasoning mode where you have to answer 3-4 questions about what you have found out. If you answer these correctly you can get extra scenes that will reveal some extra information. This is a good reason to pay attention during the game, but if you get it wrong you can just load a save.
The presentation is really good. I noticed that there are a lot of backgrounds in the game which make the action scenes more exciting. The music fits each area well, the character art is good and there's even a great opening animation that really impressed me. I wouldn't mind seeing an anime of this when all the chapters are complete. I'm usually not a fan of these episodic games but Magical Eyes has really good pacing. It doesn't even end on a cliffhanger - it just has a small hint of what could be in the next one. Can't wait for chapter 2!

I've played a lot of Age of Empires II. The original was one of the first games I remember playing, besides the original Warcraft. I played it when it first came out in 1999, and I still plally it occasionally to this day. As far as RTSs go, AoE II may not have been revolutionary as Warcraft or Starcraft or Command and Conquer, but it's still a great entry in the genre.
Now that we've established Age of Empires is a good game (which you probably already knew if you're interested in this), let's talk about the HD rerelease. A lot of games are getting the "HD treatment" these days and some of them *cough* Might and Magic III *cough* are abysmal and even inferior to the original versions that are available elsewhere. So how is the AoE II port?
Well...it's fine. Most of the graphics are exactly the same as the original with a few noteable exceptions such as farms and fire effects and the resource tooltips (for whatever reason). To be honest, I don't care for these changes. In my opinion, if you're going to do an HD remaster, either upgrade ALL the sprites or just leave the classic style. Fortunately, if you don't like the new sprites, you can download the original art assets from the Steam Workshop.
Yes that's right, the HD remaster of Age of Empires II has Steam Workshop support. This means (as it usually does) that if you ever get bored with the games many campaigns, you can always download more. Or new unit sprites. Or different HD texture packs. Or new music. Basically whatever you want.
The other big elephant in the room (literally, two of the new races get elephants) are the new "expansions" (let's be real here, it's DLC). There are three of them, and each one adds four (or in one case, five) new civilizations and everything that that comes with, including new campaigns. This is EXCELLENT. The fact that the devs care enough about this almost 20 year old game to breathe new life into it on a regular basis is incredibly appreciated. And the expansions are good. The races are (mostly) balanced as far as I can tell. The  campaigns are interesting if you're into that sort of thing. And of course there's multiplayer if you get bored of beating up the AI in the large amounts of new maps.
Overally, there's no better way to play this game. The remaster is as good as the original on its own, but with the added expansions (that often go on sale with the game) and the addition of the Steam Workshop, this edition easily surpasses the original and is a wonderful experience even today in 2017.

Get it if you like low-powered urban fantasy. (Supernatural stuff exists, but is relatively infrequent and not known to the greater public.)
