This game is great for everyone, whether you're a veteran of previous Borderlands games, someone looking to learn about the great world of Pandora, or a
casual who wants a game to play.
As you all know, TellTale has made an engine they very much love, and that is the interactive story games. Tales from the Borderlands feels a bit like The Wolf Among Us, where you can actually enjoy playing the game, and your choices really do matter, rather than TWD2, where until the end, all roads lead to the same destination.
Personally I have never been able to get through Borderlands 2, I just lose interest after five minutes of killing large creatures with insane guns, however, this game makes me excited to retry the previous Borderlands games, and maybe even buy the newer one.
Each episode is roughly two-three hours long, this game has a total of 6 episodes to be released. Value wise you're getting 12-18hrs worth of gameplay for $20-30, depending on where you buy it from. If you like to think of these games more as interactive stories, then imagine paying around $20 for a 12-18hr long movie. It's worth every penny.
My only gripe with this game is how slowly the episodes are being released, they're more focused on the TellTale Game of Thrones game, rather than this one. As three episodes have been released in the GoT series, whilst only two were released in the same amount of time in the Borderlands game.
Overall this game gets a 9/10 from me, and is definitely on the same level as The Wolf Among Us, story wise. Comparing the gameplay between those two games, they have definitely innovated since last year, and created more interactive elements to their game.

-Combat odds heavily stacked against you even on lowest enemy threat level settings

I recommend FTL instead if you are looking for a quick-play space game, though you may have fun with this for an hour or two.

A great game and a great revival or the Wolfenstein IP. Changing my review to "not reccomended" for the reasons below because I can no longer reccomend anybody purchase a product developed or published by Bethesda.
Edit 12/06/2017: Bethesda now has the stones to try and charge for mods again. This constant piecemealing of content for cash and outright exploitation of console users with no other choice is unacceptable. I won't be buying a Bethesda game again.
Edit 14/06/2017:
I've been getting a lot of comments so I've decided to write a quick FAQ of them:
1) This plan is good because modders can make money - You are completely correct that modders should have a right to make money but a better way to do this would be to have built-in donate buttons on the workshop and on
. There is absolutely no reason Bethesda needs to take a slice of the profits for someone elses original work.
2) Bethesda has a right to monetise mods that use Bethesda assets - Bethesda already profits from the sale of these assets in the first instance, a profit that is increased because people know about and expect the modding community to make stuff better. Nobody is using these assets outside of the product that was already purchased.
3) It wont effect the games with mods already - So they say. They also have a big section in the games EULA that mods can only be free. Regardless of whether or not the older games are directly influenced, you've got to look fowards.
Fallout 4 released without the very convenient Steam Workshop. It also had the standard Bethesda mod checkbox ui on the splashscreen disabled. The developers literally went out of their way to try and force people to use
mods.
Assuming Bethesda is a gigantic video games company that cares about profits this will only get worse in future release. They will begin to release games that are even less finished, have more small DLC and try and control it all through a proprietary system. When there is backlash against this they may even change the licensing on their editing software so that mods HAVE to be released through their systems or say that non-creator club mods are no longer allowed.
They would not be the first company to do something like this. Remember that this kind of thing tends to creep in over time.
4) It's good for consoles - The idea of modding for consoles is a point of discussion anyway but I don't see how having yet another storefront that uses yet another made-up currency is anything other than further exploitation of console users. If console users really want modding thats both censorship and cost free (how modding has been for years) they should also resist this new system.
5) Why put a negative review on a game that won't be affected - When you give money to a company you give a company a little bit more power. To buy something good (like Skyrim) and ignore all the bad things the company will do with your money is simply unethical. To a greater or lesser degree we are all complicit with a lot of large companies doing a lot of very bad things, but gaming is something I truly love and I won't stand by and watch one of my favourite companies do this to it's fanbase in the name of squeezing a few more dollars out of each of them.

A couple of reviews claim that you can have experienced all the game has to offer in just a handful of playthroughs... Not true. It only takes 10-40 minutes to play through once though, so it's easy to pick up and play "just one game". But people,
You can -think- you've seen it all, but there are several story branches that simply don't always unlock. There are multiple endings, and gameplay is a bit different each time around thanks to random galaxies, and 3 settings each with 3 options that decide what your starting ship is, the size of the map (and approx game length), and the density of the nebula in the universe (Which greatly dictates where you can and can't travel at the start of the game.) You can download the game's precursor, Strange Adventures in Infinite Space, from the publisher's website,
if you want to get an idea of what this is all about.
I'm not saying you won't tire of this game after playing it a dozen or so times, you will see repeats of items, but this is part of the charm and fun of this game--once you learn what items are out there to be found, how species will interact, you can hone a strategy that will allow you to actually 'beat' the game, by which I mean unlock and win one of the 'hidden' storylines. You can bet that most of the people giving this a thumbs-down after <10 or so hours never got this far.

I owned Weird Worlds on my iPad and played it for hours before I found it on Steam, and bought it here too. I find it to be a great diversion, a light space RPG that I can blast through without any real time commitment. It doesn't have a huge variety of content - you'll see most of what there is to see on the first few plays, but there are subtle random elements which will lead to little surprises for a while after that. Exploration is by far the highlight, finding treasures and technology and using them to upgrade your ship. Combat is probably the weak point - it's quite basic and rather difficult in early game, best avoided until you have no other options. The variety of weapon effects is nice though.
Weird Worlds isn't a difficult game particularly, but as with any Roguelike there will be times when you just can't get a break. This is necessary to maintain a little sense of achievement when you do win, but for me the draw that keeps me coming back is to beat my high score and the two 'boss' events that occasionally happen.

Great game greatly recommended.
Your small group of colonists AKA pawns will go through both pleasant and catastrophic events in a story told by "AI storyteler", registered member of The Sadists union. Your choice of storyteler will strongly influence the story you'll live - from almost peacefull base building to complete mayhem. You'll have to adapt to cold, heat, sickness, hunger, attacks by animals, humans and mechanoids.... Don't let the cartoony graphics fool you. Each colonists' (and animals') psychical and physical health is simulated in great detail including social interactions between people. Temperature can and will wipe your colony just as likely as a firestorm or raid of angry tribals.
Your job is to act as a Godlike architect, define where to build buildings, plant a field, where store specific items, what to manufacture etc. Your main tool is the system of job priorities for all colonists so that the colony will mostly run unattended without much micromanagement under normal circumstances. When a crisis strikes (which will be pretty often) you're always able to manually force a pawn to do certain job. In combat you'll take complete control of one or several pawns in Xcom-like pausable realtime manner.
Game still in early access but currently (Alpha 16) pretty far in development, very stable and I believe that majority of game systems are in place. There is a huge base of useful mods on Workshop ranging from utility/quality of life improvements to significant overhauls including Cthulhu cult worshipping madness :)

This is an ok game, has some nice touches in it with a lot of unit variety. It's basically as another reviewer said Company of Heroes but a big scale (for example your tank units come with 5 in each section) so you feel like a real General rather than a company commander. It's also in my opinion more realistic in some ways - infantry get slaughtered, tanks get knocked out pretty quickly vs the right defences like anti tank guns or tank destroyers and artillery really does play havoc when it lands accurately. You can play as either the Americans invading Normandy or the Germans fighting on the Eastern front in the campaign. In Skirmish mode you can play as America, Germany and the USSR (Russia) which gives nice unit look variety.
However there is still a lot to be desired - the gameplay does become easily boring as it's pretty much the same. You call in reinforcements using credits you earn from capture points (no base building) and can win every map just by dominating in artillery if you plan it right. In some maps I only needed one tank unit and the rest was anti tank guns and artillery destroying everything that moved. Units like infantry are basically obsolete and they will be wiped out the second anything fires so it doesn't allow many tactics apart from tank rushing in my opinion. The units are pretty much identical however for all nations - I've not noticed any special tactics or way of playing myself.
Overall if it's on sale (around half the asking price now) it is certainly worth a buy and you'll get a good few hours out of it.
I also have read that the multiplayer has gone offline - while this doesn't bother me personally that would be a downside for most. The option still is in the menu though so I'm not sure what is going on with that.

If I could have stuck this Review as Informational, I would have. I found myself warming up to the game, but it is -not- everyone's cup of tea.
When it comes to this game, I'm not entirely sure what to say, as it has it's ups and downs. At a glance, you'd find yourself presented with a graphically pretty adventure game with a lovely soundtrack and some good voice acting, however- the game doesn't seem satisfied to 'merely' present itself as such. Thus, while there is a fairly enjoyable system put into place for finding clues, and making deductions (in the vein of what I had -wished- was in Soul Suspect), and the whole adventure game-y puzzle solutions- the game also decides to fill itself with a number of sometimes peculiar mini games, and QTE's. Some are obnoxious, others less so, even fun (But screw Lawn bowling).
Content wise, there's a number of 'Cases' in the games, serving as the games chapters (some long, and some short), with each one providing their own particular flavour. Whilst they all bear unique scenarios and characters, they build an overarching storyline for the game, which was one of the game's stronger points (It was quite akin to playing a novella of Sherlock Stories, in a more adventure game sense). Well, except for the fact that there's a bit of a 'choose your own adventure' aspect to each Case, given that they have multiple endings based on whether you correctly deduce who and what happened- and even then, you can still make a 'moral' choice based on that outcome. (I gave less tosses about the moral choices, since they mostly seemed like a more pet the dog type outcome).
In any event, I know that despite myself, I ended up ultimately enjoying the game, but I still felt grateful that I acquired it as part of a humble bundle, as the price is altogether steep, and there were technical quirks to the game that I felt did more harm than good at times.
Still, if you're looking for a sherlock holmes flavoured adventure/puzzle game that is a bit more along the lines of the Robert Downey Jr movies, as opposed to Old school sherlock here ya go.

If you liked Portal for the story, you won't like this. While it has an awesome story, The Talos Principle suffers from grindy, boring puzzles that are dissociated from the game's narrative. The story is delivered via computer terminals and the occasional audio log, all of which you can easily have read/listened to before completing even a third of the game's puzzles, which means that you'll exhaust the game's exposition until you can get past a MASSIVE grind wall of puzzles. This frustrated the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of me and made me watch the game's ending on Youtube, since I couldn't bear having to tough out ten more hours of increasingly difficult puzzles before getting on with the game's story. This problem wouldn't have occured had the game wisely parceled out bits of exposition after each puzzle, like Portal did. It makes this game feel like two discrete experiences: The first is a compelling Sci-Fi thriller novel; the second is a gigantic treadmill of challenging-but-not-at-all-compelling spatial logic puzzles.
It's a shame, because had those two experiences been properly intertwined, then The Talos Principle would be something I'd consider to be on par with Myst, Riven, and Portal. It's got a great presentation, excellent ambiance, wonderful music, and a great story. It just doesn't come together that well into a cohesive whole because of how the puzzles and story are kept quarantined from one another.

Fighting Game: The Game.
Divekick is a love-letter to the tropes and conventions of our favorite method of beating up our best friends oh these many years of video game history. If you find yourself with a competitive itch or an urge to smack-down the people close to you, Divekick provides a means to do that. There are oodles of characters, gems, and even special moves in what purports to be a game of two-button simplicity. It will become apparent over play there's more going on than just diving and kicking, but it's up to you as a player to find out how to integrate these different elements.
What started out as a half-parody, half-serious demonstration of rock-paper-scissors at its highest virtual level has turned into a bit of an overdone parody as it plays on--the sheer volume of special moves, character movements, and accessories on top of "hit the other guy" can make or break the experience. If you want the stripped down version of classic rochambeau, there's that too, but you'll be learning special moves and selecting gems while you do it.
Recommended for fighting game enthusiasts and newbies with a good sense of humour. The fun is within you--the kick becomes the dive. Don't give up yr training~

I had an amazing experience playing Squad, and were generally welcomed by the friendly and helpful community.
Unfortunately, I am unable to recommend this game at its current "Early Access" state, as it suffers from performance issues. I encountered frequent mouse lags (delays) when firing my weapon. This issue became a dreadful nuisance during large firefights; when your teammates depend on you for protection or support. Having a weapon that slightly stutters and fire after a 2 second delay is a big “NOPE, NO BUY” for me.
The vehicle lock to squad leaders exclusively, is also a stupid anti-griefing mechanism that needs to be removed in my opinion. We were pinned down by heavy enemy fire. Half of our squad was killed (including our SL) and the other half were injured. Once friendly reinforcement arrived from another Squad. “Squad 2” members were unable to drive our vehicles to safety or used as cover to shield us from the incoming bullets, since the vehicle was locked. The rescue attempt was in all vain because another player from another squad couldn’t commandeer our vehicle.
Another negative experience for me is the dreaded night maps. Despite cranking up all the settings to the brightest, I couldn’t see anything in front of me; even from half meter away. Running into walls or buildings became a huge displeasure, yet alone getting mistakenly shot by my teammate on the other side of the road.
It is likely Squad will improve in the near future but the time being I'm not ready to put my faith any EA games now, as the gameplay is subjected to change...I won't be making the same mistake as I did for Insurgency and Red Orchestra 2, when the devs added stats and ranking/leveling-Perk systems.

Weird Worlds: Return to Infinite Space is a rogue like space exploration game. This is the game from which FTL was inspired.
The game is charming in the way that only older PC titles can be, an emphasis has been placed on the writing making each run an interesting experience as you come across all manners of weird and wonderful random events as you complete your mission.
The game offers some customisation allowing you to determine the size of the galaxy, your starting ship and a few other variables, these will effect the length of your game as well as the difficulty. An average run on a normal galaxy should take roughly 15 - 20 mins.
Weird Worlds holds a special game and definitely worth a look if you enjoyed FTL and are looking for more, or are a fan of the 4x space genre or the roguelike genre, while it is neither it does blend the 2 nicely and creates something special.

First of all, let me state that this is my first interview on Steam, and that I rarely give interviews because while every game has a silver lining as well as a fault, I believe that most people should try for themselves rather than rely on the viewpoint of others when it comes to video games.
That being said.
This.
Game.
Is.
Perfect.
I don't mean in terms of polished, finished, or completed. I mean that Hero Siege sounded and proved itself to be a game that I had been craving for years. As a a Diablo II junkie, the nostalgia I feel from the game's font is overwhelming. I enjoy all of the memories that flood into my mind as the game freezes for a tad when a player's ports aren't forwarded, much like Diablo II would. This game pays a wonderful homage to Diablo II, and I love it. I love everything about it. For a long time I said to myself "Matyas, you know what game you want to play? You want to play Diablo II mystery dungeon executed in the same manner of a Bullet Hell roguelike, such as Realm of the Mad God."  Well hot damn, here it is.
Not only does Hero Siege have obvious influences from games that I adore, but Hero Siege in itself is a game that begs to be played. The classes are robust and each has a different strategy for success, the soundtrack is wonderful, the controls are easy and yet have an obvious learning curve, and with a little effort and a bit more time, anyone should be able to complete act 1 and be on their way to success. Local Co-Op means that you can team up with your best friend to slay wave after wave of monstrosity as it, in turn, tries to destroy you. Online Multiplayer, while still in early alpha, is wonderful.
Customization, while a bit lacking, is still available in the forms of different hats you can use to identify yourself. A skull, a mohawk, Master Chief's helm, and Naruto are just several options you have - But you have to work for them. Earning achievements and killing bossess for crystals is the only way you can show others how much of a special snowflake you are.
This game is a godsend in my opinion, early stages or not, and I love it. I fully recommend it.

This is an incredibly hard game to review, mainly because it's pros and cons even out each other too damn much.
Hero Siege showcases a very fun, frenetic and addicting gameplay: some of its mechanics remind a lot of other games (the Diablo Series, the classic roguelike games, even some bullet-hell action games sometimes) and it's actually even more engaging while playing in two. The random buffs/debuffs/relics/runes/whatever that you can pick up make the game sessions something different every time you play, and that adds up a lot to the replayability. And even though, from start to finish, the mechanics do not evolve throughout the game, for some reason they never bore me, and I keep coming back at it.
And...that's it! Because the other faces of this game have pretty much a lot of flaws. Classes are enough balanced as far as skills go, but making a build around the 4 stats you are given is pretty much useless...the only way I see to make some effective characters is building up either a lot of HP or Swiftness and letting the other stats increase using potions, relics (which are the only way to balance out the uselessness of the stat system) and statues. Also, skill descriptions are sometimes partially incorrect, missing some information or just wrong.
The Boss mechanics are interesting and I like the fact that those are random too. However, some boss design is just plain unbalanced in comparison to some classes' possibilities (getting the Laser-Eye on wave 6 on a newly made character is 90% a brutal OHKO. This goes for other bosses like Champion Nautilus, which are ok on advanced stages or for higher-level characters...and those are without mentioning the blue laser drop that can randomly spawn on your head and cripple your health bar, which are incredibly hard to dodge since the laser just shoots randomly and then starts to spin)...I am not complaining about the game being hard, because I like challenging games; however this design makes it just frustrating.
However, my main issue with this game is how it is programmed. Coding in this game is literally trash, every character has its own glitchy issue with some of the skills. The Dash attack with the Samurai can throw you out of the map bounds, the Marksman can sometimes spawn unlimited turrets, and so on... Oh, and not only classes are bugged: sometimes pressing CTRL makes you drop some Runes randomly, while playing on co-op with a controller and a keyboard makes the game get a fatal crash with random actions from the second player (the one with the keyboard).
This game represents the trend that has condemned most of the game industry lately: the possibility to distribute in a digital fashion games and patch them whenever they need/want made the developers lazy. A game should be published almost FLAWLESS, and it should be patched to IMPROVE it and to fix minor bugs, not to get a different fatal error every time we get an upgrade...(this also happened on older console games, but to an incredibly lesser extent).
To sum it up, do I recommend this game? If you can get it + dlc at max 4€ or 4.50$, definitely, YES, because its gameplay is actually addicting and fun and it can appeal to a lot of people due to its mix of different elements from differents genres, and seeing the major overhaul from the first version (where you could access shops every time you needed and gold dropped like apples from everywhere) I only hope that most of its flaws will be improved (mostly skill descriptions, skill glitches and fatal errors with the keyboard). However, as it stands now, 9€ to get the game + dlc is too much for what you get, which is a good game with too much bugs. Maybe, if sometime every major glitch is fixed, that price would be good, but definitely not now.

Hero Siege is a game that stands somewhere between a
(most notably, The Binding of Isaac) and a
(like Zelda, or Diablo).
It certainly takes many aspects of those games, but turns them into something of its own.
I've only finished the game twice on normal mode, with a melee and a ranged class. I did try 2 others classes, but didn't beat the game with those, just wanted to try them out.
It's a weird game to review, actually. I don't consider it a good game. At all. However, if you manage to overcome all of its faults, it becomes a very fun game where you feel like a God and everything explodes around you. It's not well designed, but it surely is a lot of fun,
!
There's quite a bit to mention about the game, so I'll try to write a brief overview of the game's systems, and then give an extended opinion about certain design concepts.

, it has a 16bit style, very similar to how JRPGs look, only on a bigger scale. I liked it. Take into account though, that there is A LOT of things on the screen all at once, between enemies, destructable terrain, or permanent objects like trees. These often obstruct your vision of traps and enemy bullets, which makes it a bit too hard to dodge, early in the game. As I said, late in the game, you're God, so you will not worry about such petty matters.
I didn't pay much attention to the
. Not that it was bad, but I play these games while zoning out with my own music, or podcasts. From what I've heard, it wasn't bad, but didn't really add to the experience.
The
were actually pretty satisfying. Perhaps not on their own, but controller vibration was very well used to make you feel like you're actually exploding everything around you. The combination of these 2 was very good!
However! There's a problem inherent to this: when you're very aware that you're doing damage, you're not aware that you're taking it... The game doesn't give you much feedback when you're close to dying, and early on, it can mean your death. And prepare to die a lot, as the game is very unbalanced. More on that later.
Now, I'll try to just explain what the game actually is,
.
You go from map to map, fighting waves of enemies. At the end of each map (6 waves), there's a random Boss fight, with a random item reward. Every 3 (or 5) Bosses, there will be a fixed Boss, marking the end of an Act. There are 4 Acts in the main game, with an additional 5th on the DLC (which I don't own).
While it is very similar to TBoI, it's much longer, and less structured. On each map, here's what you aim for:
-
- you have 1 slot. You press a button to use it. It can go from healing you, droping a bomb, a barrage of missiles, giving you a potion, etc.
-
- these are far more important. They often give you very powerful attributes, or perhaps a passive ability (like a chance of doing a long range attack along with you basic attacks, etc), or defensive/offensive orbital companions. This is where the meat of your progression is, aside from upgrading your skills.
-
- there are 3 chests. Some are common, and require no key. They contain keys, potions, or coins inside. There are Golden chests, that require a normal key (with a generally higher pay rate), and also Crystal Chests, that require a crystal key (and generally reward you with an item).
-
- these are mini-dungeons, without a boss. Sometimes, they'll appear on the map. You'll usually find lots of traps and/or a puzzle inside. If you overcome it, you'll get a free item.
-
- these are similar to crypts, but they have a bigger focus on combat. More enemies, and also a Boss fight. It will also reward your with an item.
-
- these will have one item, one potion, and 4 stat upgrades, for different prices. It's hard to make use of them early on, but they're useful when you get enough money.
-
- these function like pills in TBoI. Their effect is unknown to you, until you try it. After that, you can use its color to recognize its effect (which is different in every run). These can grant you upgrades and downgrades, but they're essential to your success, since there will be a lot of them. It's your biggest source of attribute upgrades, aside from items, despite carrying a risk.
-
can include crates, pots, or just vegetation. All of these drop something of potential use.
While there seem to be many options, the game has a very hard difficulty wall. Once you pass it, however, you'll snowball out of control, and reach the end of the game so overpowered that you don't need to dodge anything and you won't lose more than 5% of your HP, even walking over every trap and enemy.
The other important aspect of this game is your
.
There are a bunch of different classes (maybe 9? didn't count), some melee, some ranged. You gain XP by killing enemies, and are able to spend 2 attribute points, and 1 skill point. The attributes are the same for all classes (Damage, Attack Speed, Damage Reduction, and Health). The skills vary from class to class, but there are a few common features.
Every character you create has permanent progression (leveling is permanent). However, as I said, items and potions are the most important part of progression, and those are contained in the run itself. Each character is also level up individually.
The
is more old-school than I was expecting, which I'm not sure it fits into what it's going for in terms of structure. But more on that later.
Most of it is passive abilities. Each character has 4 active skills, but they have a cooldown associated with, and while useful, they don't make as much of an impact as the passive ones. A lot of your skill tree is having a %chance of doing *action* when you attack. I actually liked that aspect of the game, but it also makes gameplay closer between classes.
With all of this, I can see people milking this game for hundreds of hours, between classes and different difficulties. However, it doesn't seem to be as replayable as, say, TBoI, due to its length. Each run may take 3 hours, and is long enough for you to get most of the items.
The game has many flaws (which I failed to mention), but it can be a fun game, if you overcome its difficulty. It's not expensive, so sure, give it a try!

At first I was a bit skeptical about this game, decided to give it a chance during the free weekend after a friend suggested to try it.
Tried a few things in the shooting range and was not amused at all. The game looked weird to me, mainly due to the fact that at the back of my head I was comparing it with Arma3 and it was actually quite obvious that the game was still in alpha.
Despite all of that, decided to join a EU/UK server. First experience was quite OK, took some time to get used to certain things like changing classes and squads, found some try hard SLs, but what I really liked was the sound and the effects.
After a few hours in the server, really got immersed but was still struggling to understand a few things.
Next day joined a polish server (it was the only server that was not full and had a decent ping for me and my buddy), which was filled with♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and other funny polish words, did not understand♥♥♥♥♥♥what the SL wanted even after mentioning a few times to use at least a couple of English words (understood only my call name and certain locations in the area). Surprisingly we still managed to coop and win, mainly due to the fact that all of the SLs seemed to be coordinated on our side.
Later joined a EU/UK server, since the polish one was not the best place for us due to obvious reasons. We joined a squad, I was kicked out a few minutes later to make room for the SLs friend, which I'm OK with but would've appreciated a warning of some sort, since I did get my kit changed to the basic (loan wolf), which is♥♥♥♥♥♥ especially if you're in the middle of a battle. Joined another squad, after a few minutes the SL left without telling anyone and a random guy became the SL. He immediately switched duties and made me the SL (I did not ask for this). As a new comer without proper experience, I struggled quite heavily being the SL, but once I figured out the basics at least for communication and other minor things, it was tolerable and thanks to the guys we did quite OK (the squad finished second/overall stats). While the map was changing, me and my buddy decided to make a squad for new comers and just see what will happen. At first I was just simply lost, had no idea where to begin and where should we go. I was more focused communicating with the squad and forgot to ask the other SLs about their plans, so at the beginning there was zero communication between the SLs, but for some unexplainable reason everyone went to different locations and we successfully took over 3 objectives at once. The guys at my squad were good fellas but some of them were very impatient and were constantly flooding the comms with questions what to do next when the objective at the time was quite clear, which was to take up positions at a specific location and defend until we establish properly in the area. I had a few guys leaving the squad, but new guys joined immediately. At certain times I was a bit♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off with all the obvious questions I had to answer (while in Arma3 it's quite obvious what certain people have to do without the SL explaining it to them, since most of the time the squad is made out of people that you have already been together). So the impatience of a couple of people was a bit frustrating and was causing an unnecessary chaos in the comms while at the same time I was discussing with other SLs on our further actions to make sure we dominate further and win. To be honest despite the frustration, I actually liked the situation I was put in as we were constantly under fire and pinned down, the comms were flooded with information and questions from the squad and other SLs. Somehow we managed to hold our ground and were able to progress further to the next objectives. The squad finished first with the best stats, but I was not happy with the overall performance especially from my side as I was struggling with basic things like understanding how to place an FOB, ammo resupply and etc, while at the same time being constantly under fire, under pressure from the squad and other SLs.
Either way, this game is getting a huge thumbs up from me and I'm really looking forward to what the developers have to offer more. This game does offer certain things like movie sound effects, team play, basic tactics and etc, in a way Arma3 lacks. When the action kicks in, you get really immersed in it and sometimes just want to hide from all of it. I really hope they are going to improve the logistics (maybe more spawn points or something relevant) and add more things (like air support, artillery and etc). I enjoyed the weekend, therefore I decided to purchase the game to support the developers and continue with improving myself at it.

Divekick remind me ALOT of One Finger Death Punch - game loads in a window instead of fullscreen, game has average quality Flash artstyle, some Asian Martial Arts influence (in some of the music/announcer), and two button gameplay. There's not alot for me to ramble about in DiveKick - two players attempt to win a Best of 10 (win 5 rounds) 2D fight with the act of jumping (Dive) and dive kicking (kick) You have a Dive button and kick button - Diving makes you jump (and probably double jump or do other motions for some characters) and the Kick button makes you kick towards the opponent when in the air, or jump back when you are on the ground.  There is a Kick meter that powers up as you perform attacks and allow you to perform either an aerial or ground based special move if you press Dive and Kick simultaneously. And that it. Every character have different jump heighs and kicking angles, and some might be able to do a second kick downward or upwards, or even teleport or swing on a grappling belt, or fly. Learn you character's movement and try to react to the enemy or bait them into an opening.
I picked Dr. Shoals for some reason and she worked out for me with her wide angle dive and her ability to kick a second time at a sharper angle. I lost the first fight, but afterwards, I understood the game and completed it within 30 minutes without loosing a fight (but I certainly lost some rounds).
Divekick is pretty fun, though, you will only get the best value out of this game if you have friends or an online community to play this with. You can also play the story mode with each character if you want to see how they play or have any interest in the silly story - the game has a meme-ish and online gaming referencial sense of humor, so some people will find Divekick passé.

Coming from a Project Reality player, I am not disappointed with this game at all.
This game is not at all like ARMA in terms of a complete in-depth military sim. Neither is it like a tactical fast-paced FPS like Insurgency. I'd say it's if ARMA and Battlefield had a baby. Realistic, yet not at all hard to learn even if you're trying to learn how to be a squad leader.
Right off the bat, if you're a random and don't have friends to play with, you will still have a great time playing this game because squading up with random players that have mics actually leads to better synergy if you work together as a unit.
Just know that this game has a HUGE emphasis on team-play, a one man army will definitely not cut it and if that is what you're looking to do this game is not for you.
PROS:
- Promising early access content
- Awesome teamplay
- So far, graphics are looking great
- Communication in squads are a blast
- Very accessible, easy to jump in if you pay attention
- You don't need to jump into a clan and have friends to have effective teamwork
CONS:
- Early access, so optimization might not be the best. Definitely improving.
- Joining a game with full squads and not being able to get in one with communicating players is boring
- Poorly optimized with AMD CPU's... huge turnoff imo.

So, i'd like to kick this off by pronouncing my love to Weird Worlds: Return to Infinite Space. The concept is simple, but is very addictive as you scour the galaxy with your ragtag fleet of ships, destroying all in your way! Or, picking up a 4th dimensional piece of space-art to sell at the space-market.
So, the game boils down to this: You're given a set amount of in-game months to explor the universe, returning to the earth-equivelant to get a score. The score is based on the events you've seen, planets visited, people, cargo, battles, and ships. These are all tracked against your playthroughs. This creates a very compelling environment, seeing as one playthrough can be completed in the time it would take to eat a sandwich and chips.
The bulk of the game is spent exploring the galaxy, divided into segments that are color coded. Each planet can have one of a few things. As you travel from planet to planet, in-game months will pass. The exploration is fun, due to the game's sense of humor and cartoon art style, and it's a joy etting high tier items.
The combat isn't the game's strong point. Depending on the planet you visit, you may choose to engage in battle. Your ships and their equipment are displayed against the enemy forces. You have to individually turn ships to make their weapons point the right direction, and command your ships to more or halt or escort. It's not horrible, but it's certainly annoying having a ship destroyed just because you didn't turn it correctly.
Overall, i'd really reccomend this game. It's an underated classic that is well worth the price of admission, if you can stand the occasional annoyance.

Hero Siege is a game that stands somewhere between a
(most notably, The Binding of Isaac) and a
(like Zelda, or Diablo).
It certainly takes many aspects of those games, but turns them into something of its own.
I've only finished the game twice on normal mode, with a melee and a ranged class. I did try 2 others classes, but didn't beat the game with those, just wanted to try them out.
It's a weird game to review, actually. I don't consider it a good game. At all. However, if you manage to overcome all of its faults, it becomes a very fun game where you feel like a God and everything explodes around you. It's not well designed, but it surely is a lot of fun,
!
There's quite a bit to mention about the game, so I'll try to write a brief overview of the game's systems, and then give an extended opinion about certain design concepts.

, it has a 16bit style, very similar to how JRPGs look, only on a bigger scale. I liked it. Take into account though, that there is A LOT of things on the screen all at once, between enemies, destructable terrain, or permanent objects like trees. These often obstruct your vision of traps and enemy bullets, which makes it a bit too hard to dodge, early in the game. As I said, late in the game, you're God, so you will not worry about such petty matters.
I didn't pay much attention to the
. Not that it was bad, but I play these games while zoning out with my own music, or podcasts. From what I've heard, it wasn't bad, but didn't really add to the experience.
The
were actually pretty satisfying. Perhaps not on their own, but controller vibration was very well used to make you feel like you're actually exploding everything around you. The combination of these 2 was very good!
However! There's a problem inherent to this: when you're very aware that you're doing damage, you're not aware that you're taking it... The game doesn't give you much feedback when you're close to dying, and early on, it can mean your death. And prepare to die a lot, as the game is very unbalanced. More on that later.
Now, I'll try to just explain what the game actually is,
.
You go from map to map, fighting waves of enemies. At the end of each map (6 waves), there's a random Boss fight, with a random item reward. Every 3 (or 5) Bosses, there will be a fixed Boss, marking the end of an Act. There are 4 Acts in the main game, with an additional 5th on the DLC (which I don't own).
While it is very similar to TBoI, it's much longer, and less structured. On each map, here's what you aim for:
-
- you have 1 slot. You press a button to use it. It can go from healing you, droping a bomb, a barrage of missiles, giving you a potion, etc.
-
- these are far more important. They often give you very powerful attributes, or perhaps a passive ability (like a chance of doing a long range attack along with you basic attacks, etc), or defensive/offensive orbital companions. This is where the meat of your progression is, aside from upgrading your skills.
-
- there are 3 chests. Some are common, and require no key. They contain keys, potions, or coins inside. There are Golden chests, that require a normal key (with a generally higher pay rate), and also Crystal Chests, that require a crystal key (and generally reward you with an item).
-
- these are mini-dungeons, without a boss. Sometimes, they'll appear on the map. You'll usually find lots of traps and/or a puzzle inside. If you overcome it, you'll get a free item.
-
- these are similar to crypts, but they have a bigger focus on combat. More enemies, and also a Boss fight. It will also reward your with an item.
-
- these will have one item, one potion, and 4 stat upgrades, for different prices. It's hard to make use of them early on, but they're useful when you get enough money.
-
- these function like pills in TBoI. Their effect is unknown to you, until you try it. After that, you can use its color to recognize its effect (which is different in every run). These can grant you upgrades and downgrades, but they're essential to your success, since there will be a lot of them. It's your biggest source of attribute upgrades, aside from items, despite carrying a risk.
-
can include crates, pots, or just vegetation. All of these drop something of potential use.
While there seem to be many options, the game has a very hard difficulty wall. Once you pass it, however, you'll snowball out of control, and reach the end of the game so overpowered that you don't need to dodge anything and you won't lose more than 5% of your HP, even walking over every trap and enemy.
The other important aspect of this game is your
.
There are a bunch of different classes (maybe 9? didn't count), some melee, some ranged. You gain XP by killing enemies, and are able to spend 2 attribute points, and 1 skill point. The attributes are the same for all classes (Damage, Attack Speed, Damage Reduction, and Health). The skills vary from class to class, but there are a few common features.
Every character you create has permanent progression (leveling is permanent). However, as I said, items and potions are the most important part of progression, and those are contained in the run itself. Each character is also level up individually.
The
is more old-school than I was expecting, which I'm not sure it fits into what it's going for in terms of structure. But more on that later.
Most of it is passive abilities. Each character has 4 active skills, but they have a cooldown associated with, and while useful, they don't make as much of an impact as the passive ones. A lot of your skill tree is having a %chance of doing *action* when you attack. I actually liked that aspect of the game, but it also makes gameplay closer between classes.
With all of this, I can see people milking this game for hundreds of hours, between classes and different difficulties. However, it doesn't seem to be as replayable as, say, TBoI, due to its length. Each run may take 3 hours, and is long enough for you to get most of the items.
The game has many flaws (which I failed to mention), but it can be a fun game, if you overcome its difficulty. It's not expensive, so sure, give it a try!

Picked this game up for 10 bucks, and holy hell am I blown away. Easily one of the best games I've played in the FPS genre in a long time.
Typically, in single player shooters I get VERY bored, as the combat is generally repetitive and the story is usually too generic/"GET THE BAD GUYS!" that I can only stomach a couple of hours of it. This game was not the case for me. The gameplay feels so good, killing baddies is actually a treat. The storyline is also one of the most gripping I've played in ANY in a very long time. You actually feel a sense of attachment to each of the characters, and the bad guys are REALLY bad (they captured the brutality of the nazis perfectly). I bought this mainly because the E3 trailer for The New Colossus really peaked my attention, and at 10 bucks you'd be stupid to not buy this. 8.6 hours invested and I'm not even done with my first play through.
Only downside I've personally decided to make note of is that there are a lot of audio bugs plaguing the game. At times the sound of my machine gun will just stop while everything else continues, my footsteps will go silent, or an enemy will scare the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of my by just blasting my health down because I didn't realize someone was even shooting. I assume this may be a compatibility issue with newer hardware.
Overall, Wolfenstein is a solid 9/10 in my book. I dock the one point simply for the audio bug, it really breaks immersion sometimes.

A decent and interesting RPG with a decent amount of quests. It has a unique style of art (although I prefer photorealistic graphics instead of drawings), a decent range of weapons and good voice acting. It has many flaws for me to consider it a good RPG though:
-Inconvenient UI. All the windows seem clunky and restrictive (eg. opening the inventory or world map stops you from walking, and turns off your sprint so you have to press it again to continue sprinting). Because of this, it is annoying to navigate around given that every time I open the world map to see where to go, when I close it, I have to release W and press W again to start walking again, and release Shift and press Shift again just to start sprinting again.
-Not enough quests. I find myself stucked without quests very often (eg. My Lvl is 13 and the lowest level remaining quests are 15, which are almost impossible to do at my level).
-I prefer that they stick with the normal way of driving a car, WASD instead of W and A and Mouse.
-Looting items from the floor one by one is inconvenient.
-Glitchy/annoying AI. Often I'm browsing a shop in the town and I find that I'm losing HP, because a bandit or two followed me in and keeps shooting as if the town doesn't exist.
-Aiming a sniper rifle is rather annoying when it keeps swaying left and right when you're aiming it, meaning that you can only use it at most as a mid-range weapon.
I didn't complete it because I don't intend to grind on mobs just to bridge the levels I need to do the Lvl 15 quests.
Rating: 5/10

Story: You play Sashiro, a member of a kinda world police called World-Peacemakers, who hunts terrorists.

Endings:There are 3 endings, one of the endings is quite hard to achieve without"help"(will explain in the following soon)
I've played a lot of visual novels, in most of them there is a "good"(cool and satisfying) and a
"bad"(unsatisfying, short, strange) ending...not here in XorceD, all endings are cool and satisfying.
Also in most other VNs it is hard or even nearly impossible to get a desired ending without googling
a walkthrough, but in this game the developers solved this problem in a very elegant and lore-abiding
way, which ask you whether to completely reveal what to do exactly -or- just to give hints so you can
try to again yourself -or- to point out what you did wrong in the last playthrough.
Presentation: Arts are nice, soundtrack is ok which catches the situation.
PS: Don't skip the credits, there's bonuscontent after that. Bonuscontent is linked to every ending,
so you get total 3 different bonuscontent which is in my opinion quite entertaining!

PROS-----
- Very interesting characters.
- Sashiro, the main character, shows to be very mysterious within the first few chapters.
- Qi, a psychopathic sangophile who is also Sashiro's adopted brother.
- Janna, a medic and investigator who is just as mysterious as Sashiro.
- Ronald and Dan, both seem to be pretty interesting, though their faces were never shown (at least in Chapter 0).
- Plot's good so far-- nothing amazing, but it works.
CONS-----
- Short instrumental piano music clearly synthesized via FL Studio. I'm not really fond of how the melodies sound. The editing is a bit awkward, too.
- Not enough choices. The story is trying to give you multiple choices for each situation to make it more interactive but it's limited only to random conversations that don't have any affect on the plot.
VERDICT: The novel's okay so far. Not as good as I thought it was in my head, though-- but hey, I'm still on the second chapter when I made this review. My opinion might change. Just make sure you have the volume off so you don't have to listen to the music.

I have always liked kart games like these for their beautiful colors, goofy characters and creative weapons and this game nails those spots right on!
With beloved characters from the SEGA universe and some newcomers, this game offers a real nice variation of vehicles along with awesome and unique All-Star moves to go along with which lets you choose your way to devastate the track when you're having a bad day and watch you fly right past the competition in an awesome spectacle, may it be by the usage of rockets, soundwaves or bananas. The creative weapons are both amusing and rediculous and makes the races go completely out of control which is one of the charms of kart games like these. You can also find the usual powerups which lets you boost up to higher speeds or block incoming attacks, but with all the crazy weapons and powerups aside, this game can really offer you a test of racing skill to see if you got what it takes to go even faster by using risky air-stunts and powerful drift-boosts which, altough makes the game a little more difficult, also makes the game more thrilling and exciting and overall more fun. The race tracks are, what you would expect, tracks based on several of the SEGA character's original titles which definitely is a must for party games like these, and putting the "Transformed" in this game's title is the fact that in most of the stages there is a transition to race by both boat and plane during the race which puts more variety and challenge into the game.
So if you're a fan of racing games with elements of driving by car, boat and plane as well as neat combos you can pull off, or even if you're just a fan of Sonic and his friends I truly recommend and tell you that this game is for you!

Castle Crashers was my personal favorite Xbox Live Arcade game when it was first released back in 2008. The Behemoth continued to give this game more life with it's DLC of character's that had unique abilities, animal orbs that would accompany you throughout the game, and weapons that would improve your character's growth (or vice versa if you are looking for a challenge). The game was later ported to the Playstation Network with exclusive mini-games in 2010. Castle Crashers eventually was ported onto Steam, but was ported badly onto PC on launch; however, the game was redeemed to be fun and playable again after The Behemoth made necessary updates.
This title is a hack and slash RPG, and has been widely recieved by many gamers who appreciate the genre (even those who don't). The game can feel a bit tedious at times, but as you level your character(s) the gameplay will feel slightly different before it tends to get repetitive once again. However, the game keeps the game fresh upon every level with unique scenary, opponents, and even jokes. If you plan on purchasing this title it's obviously more fun to play it with friends then it is with complete strangers, so try to convince your friends (and if they've convinced you to buy it listen to them). Completing the title will be a mission, but personally I think that's half the fun of trying to unlock every single character, find every animal orb and weapons. Give this game a try by downloading the demo. If you find the game a bit pricey than wait for a discount (or a Humble Indie Bundle that has this game packaged with it).

This game has suprised me. It has elements of rougelikes, twin-stick shooters, and RPGs. I initially bought it when it was on sale over at
for something like a dollar or two. I thought, 'hey this will be a good hour or so' then 5 hours later I realised that this game had me hooked. Once the DLC for Act V and the Samurai came out I happily paid the $6 for it. This game is well worth that and even more.
The art style is charming and I've found that I really enjoy the asthetic of the monsters, player models, and all the effects. The UI leaves something to be desired though. These guys are constantly updating things and they listen to player feedback. Although, they can get a bit defensive at times. There are a few issues which make it a little bit frustrating at times. For instance if you view a relic that you don't want inbetween waves you have to push B (or the keyboard equivalant) to discard it. This will automatically trigger the next wave since the discard relic and start next wave buttons are one in the same. The reason this is annoying is because if there was a dungeon or crypt that you wanted to visit between waves, well, that's closed until the next wave now. All-in-all this is only a minor concern.
The game is completely addictive. Each run is over once you die but you level you character and become more powerful and your next run is even better than the last. As with many games with rouge-lite elements you will amass items in order to make your toon more powerful over the course of the run. This is reminiscent of The Binding of Issac. One run might not be very powerful and you might die early on, and the next run you'll be a god smashing through hoards of mobs with righteous vengeance! The addtion of online co-op and the inclusion of local co-op just enhance this experience. However, a word of caution; the MP aspect of the game is currently in a buggy state. While the devs are constantly working to fix it, it would seem that they are having a bit of trouble in that department. None-the-less, I still highly recommend this game.

This is a nice little game to pick up and play if you've got a handful of minutes to burn. Hero Siege is a roguelike hack 'n slash - the battle arena is randomly generated and you fight wave after wave of monsters, slowly getting stronger with equipment and potions. In addition to "per session" stats (which, as the name implies, fluctuate during a single run), you also level your character up over the course of several runs, and stats improvements gained this way are permanent. This means that the more you play a character, the stronger he will get. There doesn't appear to be a level cap, from what I can tell, so you can keep leveling up to make yourself infinitely strong. (However, leveling past 30-50 gets a bit grindy...)
Pros:
Cons:
Overall, I quite like this game as a quick pastime. There's a couple of glaring flaws, but for the price it's a pretty decent buy.
NOTE: I did not review multiplayer because I haven't delved into that yet, but from what I understand you need the DLC (Karp of Doom) in order to play multiplayer. The DLC isn't expensive, only 75 cents, but I figured it's worth mentioning.

Buy? Unlikely...Maybe. It's a space exploration roguelike, where you're expected to die often and your luck throughout the game is completely randomized. The goal is to accrue enough value through what you find in star systems, cargo. passengers, and equpment with in a limited. You start with a ship with inferior gear, and need to make trades or kill hostiles to get better weapons or more valueable trading goods. Usually, but not always, you will find a bird race early in your tavels that are willing to trade any item regardless of value, which helps you get better gear or more valuable cargo. You will encounter "unknown" beings at other systems, which more often than not are hostile encounters with enemies that will out gun you. You don't want to travel through nebulae as they take much time to move through, unless you have the proper equipment. This game has simplistic mechanics which actually turn out quite enjoyable, but my problem is that it's too damn random and you have to basically hope that the game gives you a good galaxy. I don't like the idea of wasting time dying and getting low scores because of "what mood the game was in" when it generated a world for me. If you're into space exploration and/or roguelikes, you might like it because there is enjoyable gameplay, but success through extreme randomness is not what I want to deal with.

Just play Crimes and Punishments or really any of the previous games first.
This game for one tries to be more like the modern "retellings" of Sherlock that have become popular, and as such is much more about flashy setpieces as well as pointless melodrama than the previous games.
It's also ridiculously short, and I had some complaints about how short Crimes and Punishments was to boot. At least in that game you felt like an actual detective, and most of the time the game didn't hold your hand in terms of having you figure out which suspect was correct - if you never used the cheat to tell you the right answer, you would never know if you were right or not. Not to mention the question of whether to have mercy or be vengeful was an interesting choice you had to make which was also seen in the books - multiple times Sherlock debates whether he should even tell LeStrade that the case was solved at all, depending on the circumstances.
But no, in this game, Frogware decided to go all about the spectacle, and of course, like BBC's Sherlock, all about "you know who," the guy from a grand total of two Sherlock Holmes stories who somehow has become The Master to Sherlock's Time Lord.
So no, I do not recommend this game unless you've played at least the previous two games and are reaaaaally in the mood for more.

Weird Worlds is another indie bundle game I stumbled upon. For a 2005 game, this is a pretty decent rouge-like space exploration and combat adventure game. After playing FTL quite a bit, it's pretty obvious where FTL got a lot of its ideas from. Much of the gameplay is very similar although the combat of Weird Worlds is overly complicated. It's kind of like SPAZ combat in some respects, but without the intuitiveness. The game does provide a combat simulator that allows you to practice as needed, but to win it's more about what equipment you  have as opposed to using any real strategy.
Weird Worlds biggest shortcoming is the lack of a proper reward system since you don't really have to earn anything. You just take items as you find them or if you find the right trader you can exchange some cheap trash for the best equipment in the game. Also you are not forced into combat and can retreat anytime. Where FTL creates an environment of urgency, Weird Worlds creates an environment of casualness and I'm not sure casualness and rogue-like is a winning combination. Essentially you are given a specific amount of time to explore and collect as much loot as possible and eventually get killed or retire and get a score based on several factors.
The randomness makes it fun from an exploratory perspective, but it's not really a game that captivates for replayability.

Train Town is a great game for young children (ages 4 ~ 10) who want to play with toy trains, but don't have the space or the finances for a real toy train set.  Instead of laying track, you set connection points for the track, making it incredibly easy for shaping the layout without having to worry about making realistic turns.  Various decorations can be laid out all over the terrain, including on the tracks themselves.  When a train collides with a decoration, or another train, both fly in to the air in a cartoonish mess with wild physics.  If you don't feel like making your own layout, there are various prefab layouts you can download and alter as you wish.  Older children may find the entire setup oversimplistic, or lack of realistic decor bland.  On the flip side, you don't need need to be a seasoned model railroader to pick it up and play it with your kids.

This is probably the weirdest fighting game I've ever seen. Built on a mechanic that seems preposterously simple and full of humor that takes heavily from martial arts, fighting game, and anime tropes before mixing in an appropriate dose of stupidity. I'm not disapproving at all, but it wasn't quite the game's tone that had me laughing so hard I had to stop playing for a minute and collect myself amid a raucous exchange of rounds. It was the intensity of trying to beat a much more experienced friend while frantically using just two controls (jumping and kicking).
That's the game, in a nutshell. You can jump up or back and you can aerial kick forward. It's a complete parody, but they squeeze a surprising amount of technique out of that format and it's harder to do well than it sounds. You're inside the classic fighting game 2D arena, with health bars for both players that are mostly part of the joke as you're KO'd in a single kick. Each character jumps a bit differently and kicks a bit differently, and there is a special ability that charges up for each character and innate abilities like teleporting or surviving one kick. One character's normal kick is a pro wrestling style dropkick that is almost too effective in the right hands, but each round he wins makes his head bigger (literally - it becomes comically larger with each won round, quickly enabling an easy headshot kick).
The game becomes greater than the sum of its parts when you play it with a friend you love to compete with (all the more so with real time voice chat). It becomes an absurd, intense, and hilarious fight to master two keys. One misstep- er, mis-kick and the round is over. There's also online play and a campaign for each character, complete with silly backstory. The humor might not be for everyone, and those looking for a serious or in-depth fighting game may want to look elsewhere. But the gratifying absurdity of this game lies not in its story or characters (though each of those elements here fits the game perfectly).
This game probably won't immerse you for hours, nor may you become addicted to it. But it just might inject some laughter into your night. For going a few matches in between other games with a friend of yours, it's a solid one to have in your library and quick enough that you can get a person to play even if they're not really down for games.

First person puzzle game, in the vein of Portal or Witness.
On each level you collect and use several types of tools ("jammers", laser connectors, carriable blocks...) to get to a puzzle piece ("sigil") for that level. Once you collect enough puzzle pieces, you piece them together, which then unlocks new abilities or more levels. Levels are embedded within huge beautiful worlds, 4-6 levels per map. There are shenanigans to be had and secrets to be unlocked if you manage to have one "level" somehow influence another (you can't carry gadgets through level entrances).
You also find various terminal texts, emails, book excerpts and System Shock-like audio-logs that slowly get you immersed into this world. All the lore is expertly written, full of philosophy and wisdom (I never expected this type of stuff from the authors of Serious Sam). The plot is refreshingly NOT cynical or misanthropic, AND it all makes sense in the end. I loved it (despite the grumblings in the spoilered peeves).
Visuals and interface are superb. I played all the way through and got all 3 endings after about 50 hours of playtime. I found the difficulty curve just right, kind of like Portal, and not at all like the Witness.
Peeves:
- I wish the game had a real save system. Several times I'd spend 5-10 minutes setting up a scenario, only to screw up and have the game reset everything to initial state. One quick save slot would do.
- The game has 5-6 different game mechanics / gadgets you can use. I liked all of them, except the one where you can create a recorded clone of yourself to help you out. Nothing objectively wrong with the implementation, I just found puzzles with this mechanic less fun than the others.
- There is a good number of Easter eggs you can unlock if you poke around a bit. These are done in the same style of humor as Serious Sam, which doesn't fit well with this relaxed contemplative game. I didn't like them.
- (Mild spoilers about the quality of the game's endings. No plot details)

A few tips for the end:
- The game has a "speed up time" button that is not bound by default. Bind it and use it.

Weird Worlds is another indie bundle game I stumbled upon. For a 2005 game, this is a pretty decent rouge-like space exploration and combat adventure game. After playing FTL quite a bit, it's pretty obvious where FTL got a lot of its ideas from. Much of the gameplay is very similar although the combat of Weird Worlds is overly complicated. It's kind of like SPAZ combat in some respects, but without the intuitiveness. The game does provide a combat simulator that allows you to practice as needed, but to win it's more about what equipment you  have as opposed to using any real strategy.
Weird Worlds biggest shortcoming is the lack of a proper reward system since you don't really have to earn anything. You just take items as you find them or if you find the right trader you can exchange some cheap trash for the best equipment in the game. Also you are not forced into combat and can retreat anytime. Where FTL creates an environment of urgency, Weird Worlds creates an environment of casualness and I'm not sure casualness and rogue-like is a winning combination. Essentially you are given a specific amount of time to explore and collect as much loot as possible and eventually get killed or retire and get a score based on several factors.
The randomness makes it fun from an exploratory perspective, but it's not really a game that captivates for replayability.

I'll give it... 7/10.  Let's start with that.  It's a great game and you should probably play it, but it's not life-changing.
First thing you should know: it's a puzzle game.  There are lots and lots of puzzles, generally involving the manipulation of a few objects through line-of-sight mechanics.  You get things like jammers to disable gates, laser connectors so that you can point lasers at various things, etc.  The puzzles range from "here's how the mechanics work" to some really interesting things later in the game, and a puzzle might take you from a couple of minutes to many minutes to solve.  I was skeptical at first, but they're actually a lot of fun, even some of the more annoying ones.  Generally, if you keep working at them, you'll make progress, at least once you've figured out the game's mechanics (there are some that are not so obvious until some puzzle guides you to them).  The story is also extremely interesting; I won't say anything about it here.
If this were it, this game would probably be a 9/10 or something.  The puzzles are pretty great and a lot of fun to work through.  The stuff in the late game is especially awesome.  But there are some things that I think bring this otherwise great game down.  First, there are some additional hidden puzzles required for the secret ending, and while maybe about 75% of them are fair challenges, a few of them are pretty close to impossible without a guide.  You're given fairly large worlds without a lot of visual differentiation, so it's very easy to get lost when all the walls and pillars and trees look about the same inside a level, and in this sameness you have to navigate your way around puzzle chambers -- which are generally not too big -- and the outside of the puzzle chambers, which can house those hidden puzzles without giving you anything but extremely subtle clues about where they might be.
On top of that, the story is distributed by means of lore, and... other than pure enjoyment of the story, there is literally no reason to go through any of it with very few (obvious) exceptions.  I feel like this isn't a spoiler.  Oh, there are things that are obviously puzzles hidden in the lore.  But these puzzles don't actually correspond to anything in the game; there's nothing you can do or get for solving them.  There are some puzzles that are I suppose larger than individual chambers, but there are also no meta-puzzles (using the sigils doesn't count).  Basically, the game consists of a bunch of puzzle chambers, which are awesome and interesting and the reason why you should play this game, the story, which is also awesome and interesting and the reason why you should play this game, and... that's it.  I think there should have been more.  I think there should have been meta-puzzles, locations within the levels that are more visually distinguished, and all that lore text should have contained real puzzles too, especially the non-story stuff that was kind of pointless.
I recommend this game because I had a lot of fun playing it and I think you will enjoy it as well.  But I also think it left a lot to be desired.  Don't get me wrong; it's very well-made.  The production values are fantastic.  The music is nice.  There are really cool easter eggs hidden pretty much all over the place.  But as a game, and as a puzzle game specifically, its approach to puzzling in general was underwhelming.
Was it worth the money?  Yeah, absolutely.  You could wait until the game goes on sale (I may have done this, I don't remember), but $40 is less than dinner for 2, and it lasts a whole lot longer.  I already forgot what we ate for dinner, but this game will probably stay with me for years to come.  But it's still a 7/10.  Sorry, devs.

Weird Worlds Return To Infinite Space is a strange collaboration of genres. On one hand the gameplay is based around that of a rougelike, with all the hardcore aspects like permadeath and randomized maps. On the other, it's built around the idea of 10-30 minute playthroughs making the execution feel almost geared towards a casual crowd. Yet this is not a casual game, nor would it be fair to say it is a hardcore game. It is a compilation of the two, trying to strike a balance and for the most part, coming out alright in the end.
Weird Worlds pits you as a spaceship captain out to explore the great unknown on a 10-30 year mission at the end of which you are awarded points based on your accomplishments and how much loot you manage to bring back. That is not to say that making it back is a guarantee, falling prey to hostile aliens and black holes is just as common if not more so.
Most of the game is spent in this galaxy view, you direct your ship to fly towards a planet and upon arrival is hit by a random event, you might run into a shop, a free item, friendly aliens or hostile aliens or many other things. As you progress through the game you slowly upgrade your ship with newfound items getting better engines, scanners and weapons and even occasionally added on a wingman to your entourage who is equally as customizable as your own ship.
Should misfortune strike and you encounter hostile aliens you are transported into a 2D battlefield where your ships do battle, your actions are limited to tell your ships where to go and who to attack and if you're lucky enough to have found any one shot ability items you get to activate those too in here. The battles are unfortunately fairly lackluster and you can do little to influence the outcome once you are committed, the only real decider being the equipment you have managed to scavenge so far.
Perhaps one of the biggest flaws of Infinite Worlds is also the reason for it's longevity. The randomness of the game might make every playthrough a little unique but it might also mean you run into the highest tier engine on the first planet you visit making this particular go-round a sure success whereas other times your first trip away from home will be to a soon to be supernova explosion.
All in all Weird Worlds manages to make a decent experience by combining the casual and the hardcore, in many ways it becomes sort of a solitaire for the Sci-fi inclined. A good way to waste 20 minutes every once in a while when you have nothing else to do.

Sherlock Holmes: The Devil's Daughter is a puzzle solving game.The puzzle being the various criminal cases that are presented to Sherlock Holmes.
The first case, Prey Tell, was interesting and well thought of. There is an interesting depth to the story and I won't spoil the ending.
Sadly, the second case, A Study in Green, was filled with glaring inconsistencies. Even the clues given contradicted what the game presented. The weirdest part is when voodoo magic is invoked and suddenly you are taken to a dream world where you have visions of the past and you can see everything. Instead of using facts to overcome fiction, which is the hallmark of Sherlock Holmes, you put in fiction in the place of fact. The general formula of a Sherlock Holmes novel is a fantasy crime shrouded in superstition and then solved by the intrepid analysis of Sherlock Holmes.
The logical inconsistencies make it a little irksome. Some parts that were advertised did not appear in the game at all. So, you can guess that the game was released incomplete. The final ending was kind of ho-hum for people who read the Sherlock Holmes novels as you know who they are talking about.
Conclusion, despite some flaws, the game is fine to play. I would recommend this game for players who want to challenge their mind on simple puzzles and weird deductive reasoning.
1. A Novel Form of Gameplay/Thinking
I feel like I'm thinking, even though there are glaring inconsistencies. Actually, I find myself thinking about how illogical the game designer designed the game and the inconsistencies that can exist.
2. Imaginary Pyramid Puzzle
I liked the one where the solution was to look at the face of Quiche statues. If it was angry, don't cross its path. If it was happy, you could walk safely through.
1. Stupid Clues in Case : Study in Green
After going to Charles Marley's foundry, you can obviously find an automation that can hurl a spear. However, the clues tell you it can't be done.
2. Inconsistencies In Study in Green
If Charles Wellingham did see a statue run away, did he see a pygmy run away? Did the game designer consider this inconsistency?
3. Fiction Instead of Fact
Finding clues from visions (the imaginary world) is not the hallmark of Sherlock Holmes.
1.Puzzle Solving Mini-Games
Most of the mini-games are not complex. They are about finding hidden pathways E.g. In the swamp, you try to find solid ground to walk on. In the imaginary pyramid, you look at statues and floor tiles.

Perhaps one of the best overall racing games that I've ever played, Sonic & All-Stars Racing Transformed is easily the best kart racing game that I've ever played. Mario Kart is commonly seen as the 'best' for this genre, but where as Mario Kart lets even the unskilled players win with last-place-powerups they get, Transformed instead still gives it's best powerups most commonly to the slowest racers, but makes them able to be dodged by the most skilled players. No Blue Shell stupidity here.
The tracks are all fun to race around, and the transforming vehicles turn this from 'just a great racing game' to 'one of the best'.  The car, boat, and jet all control radically different, and are all fun. The tracks 'transform' as well, most of them changing every lap to accomidate more the whole 'transforming vehicles' thing.
Every music track is a joy, wonderful remixes of classic Sega themes, and the tracks themselves follow a broad stretch of Sega franchises. Except Phantasy Star, goddamnit, Sega.
The online play is probably the best part, as the netcode works perfectly fine, and, last I tried, there was a pretty healthy community of players.  It's extremely unfortunate how many people avoid playing this gem simply because "I don't like Sonic." Anyone who even slightly likes this genre should love this game.
