There is no doubt that this game is a rip-off of Plants vs Zombies, as the game tries to advertise and describe itself as a hard-core version of that creative tower defense game that sold massively well.  I didn't expect it to be nearly as good, as imitators almost never are, but I hoped it would at least be competent, have taken lesson from Plants vs Zombies, and captured some of the same charm.  It didn't even come close.  For me, this game wasn't worth spending more than a few minutes playing the first two levels.  The graphics and models were shoddy and lackluster, the stage design is a cut and paste skin swap, and the mechanics were not refined or enjoyable.  They ripped off the parts that required the most work, and everything else they put in the barest level of effort possible.  If it wouldn't be against the law, I wouldn't have been surprised for this game to be called Zombies vs Plants, and just have a lower quality palette swap for the original game.  Not even worth .17 cents as part of a bundle I got this game in.  Save yourself 5 minutes if you got the same bundle and return it.

The things people shout when they lose are often hilarious, and the stories are a fantastic parody of the absurd writing found in fighting games.
All in all, a fun little game.

It's an insta buy for people that love FPS games.
The immersion in this game is the best. As many others have already pointed out, most of that is because of the sound. Masterpiece. When people use the local area voice chat you literally hear them as if they are 5 meters away from you, 10, or 15 meters away of you. If they are right next to you and speaking into your ear it will feel like they are right next to you in real life.
The multiple comms possibilities, the gunshots, explosions, everything makes it feel so real. The combat itself; the tactics you need to apply to win a game are amazing. Honestly, in this free weekend I achieved 2 things: I learnt how to actually shoot and the models of every faction (by the end of it I could actually get kills and ... stop being a medic all the time because I was bad at shooting lol, did not even see where the enemy was, hard to spot and hard to shoot at long distances in the beggining)
The second thing I achieved was my best experience in an online FPS. Got a good squad leader that knew how the game worked and competent squad members and we made our way through the enemy bases. It was AWESOME how everyone, including myself, were listening to the squad leader, staying together, dealing with enemy squads together, breaking into buildings and getting shot randomly when entering a room then squad members taking the guy out .. everything felt so real. We would get a target, we'd run on the other side of the road while being shot at, enter a building, clean it out, establish FOB or rally point and move on to the next target. Times where we were all spread out in a base, trying to capture the point, hiding in different buildings with another squad around and killing the enemies that were trying to enter the area to stop us from capturing; crawling inside small holes in the stone structure so we didn't get spotted, all of that felt like that's how real life combat would be if I joined the army. It's very much alike to how army fights rebels in iraq or other places in our world right now, I think. all of that happened in 1 single match which took around 1 hour and a half.
Best FPS experience that I had until now. This game is instabuy in my opinion, highly recommend it. Rarely you actually see communities where people truly teamworking in online gaming nowadays :)

A decent game, interesting puzzles with a good atmosphere to it all on the whole.
Contrary to many of the reviews on here though, I didn't find anything new or mind openening in the dialog with any parts of the system. It didn't make me question anything that my long term friends and I haven't discussed ad infinitum since we were in our teens over 20 years ago. In other words you can see what the game is getting at from within the first half an hour.
It also enforces a number of logical fallacies in order to get you to a pre determined point, and the computer is often flat out wrong.. for example there is one point in the game where you're asked to make a decision - I chose an option and went back to the main screen.. I chose the same option again and the computer spat something out telling me I was uncertain and just chosing every option possibe. I did nothing of the sort - I chose the exact same option I did the first time but I guess they figure most people wouldn't do that - thus the hard coded response with the expectation people would have chosen something different the second time around.
Its simplistic philosophical pretences aside, I'd still buy the game, the puzzles are for the most part well presented with a balanced learning curve  - and who knows - if your not naturally introspective and don't mix with friends who enjoy the esoteric then hey it might make you question certain things like it seems to have for a lot of others who've played it.

A group of teenagers spend a night on a deserted island; weird♥♥♥♥♥♥ensues. It's part macabre mystery and part Telltale style adventure. You have more freedom than in a Telltale game because the island is an actual environment to be explored, but the actual story moves forward in a linear way. Your dialogue choices inform your treatment by the other characters, and your ending, but I get the sense that the gist of it doesn't change too much. The characters rarely shut up and some other people seemed to find that wearing but I thought the dialogue was generally very well written and the characters deep enough that it was a big positive to me. The ending felt pretty rushed, especially after a decent amount of time was spent setting up the characters and the plot, but that's probably the only real criticism I've got and I really enjoyed this for the few hours it lasted. If you like the idea of the Telltale narrative adventures but would prefer something that gives you a little bit more direct control then this comes highly recommended and I really enjoyed my time with it.

As time passed, the DEVs stopped working on it. Content, patches and balance changes became rare, and, finally, the ceased completely.
This could've been a good MOBA. Maybe not to the level of Dota 2 or League of Legends, but good still.
Nowadays, you'll be lucky if you find a PvP match after 20-30 minutes. A big part of the community left when they saw that the developers were inactive, leaving this game to decay.
Hopefully, this game will make some sort of comeback at some point. That is if the developers don't focus on their recently published game, which happens to take a lot of models and content from Strife.

After playing this game for about 7 hours now I feel good about writing a review. First I'll answer some of the points from other reviews:
1. Have to wait hours for ships to be delivered.
A. The devs removed this problem fairly quickly, and now the longest wait for a Carrier is about 12 minutes, while a destroyer is about 3 minutes. This adds a different dimension to the game than other similar ones, and makes you think strategy when requesting units and budgeting. Also, while you're waiting you can earn more command points (CP, game currency) playing skirmishes. The skirmishes are a lot of fun because you can set the ships/upgrades however you like. It's a lot of fun to take some revenge after your ships get destroyed in the campaign by setting your ships up with all upgrades, and the enemy up with none =). A major flaw that still is exists is the repair times for ships.  Slight damage takes 10-20 minutes to repair, and you can earn some CP while you're waiting. My carrier just got into a firefight and it is going to take 7 hours to repair?
. BTW you can also spent CP points to repair your ships instantly, and deliver them instantly, but when you're trying to save CP's you don't want to spend them on rushing.
2. The game UI is difficult to aim properly.
A. Yes at first, but as your get used to moving/aiming your ships you get a lot better at it. There's also skirmish mode like  I mentioned earlier to hone your skills. Again, this is a different dimension to the game that makes it interesting. As far as blind spots being as big as cruisers, well like in real life, the closer you get the harder it is for all the turrets to aim together to one point. You have to take firing ranges into account in your manuevering. Larger ships have longer ranges.  Let me tell you there is no greater feeling that the first time you line up all your turrets on the enemy ship and blow it away.
3. You can only use one ship at a time on both sides, no matter how outnumbered the enemy is.
A. Yes, this one is a little annoying. You have 5-6 ships, your enemy has only one left, and while you get to use one ship, so does the enemy. So if you run 5 rounds letting all your ships have a turn, the enemy ship also gets 5 rounds. From a challenge point of view this is good, but from a realistic point of view this is way off. Especially when the enemy has a large ship left that can take some hits, and you lose a few destroyers trying to take it out. A good strategy to deal with this is remove the hardest hitting enemy ships first, but again it's not realisitic.
4. Game has no ship damage system.
A. It kinda does. You can hit the enemy engines and damage them hard enough that the ship will start spinning. However there is no way to knock out enemy weapons or subsystems.
5. The story is lacking.
A. No dispute there. There is just a quick paragraph of information before each engagement, and none of them have anything to do with the battles you are fighting. But it does give the feeling of being in a war, and the battles are all part of the larger conflict.
Now questions answered this is a fun game. It's pretty well balanced, and takes a fresh approach to a space strategy sim. Physics are in play and asteroids/other ships react to fire.  The graphics are fantastic, and run well with decent machines (I have a beast rig I built myself, and a 2012 Alienware laptop). I was able to run the highest graphics settings on either machine with no drop in framerate. Also, the game has not crashed/bugged once since I've been playing. That smoothness is appreciated. Ship designs are very familar to Starship Troopers/Babylon 5/Star Trek, and other well known scifi series. They look nice.
Overall, it's well worth the $9-10 they are charging for it, and will give you your monies worth in enjoyment, if you have the discipline to learn the controls.

I realized that my negative reaction to this game was because I going in with a very different game in mind and then being disapointed when it didn't live up to the image in my head. Watch the videos on the store page to get an idea of what your going into (and to act as a good tutorial, watch one move/shoot cycle and it'll give you a very clear indication what your getting and make it FAR easier to get into. This is a mobile-like casual game, not a Final fantasy tactics/front mission in space. That being said, the depth/gameplay is BETTER then I expect from a mobile-like game.
Great things:
Models are nice: to good in fact, it sent me in expecting a very different game. ALthough its not even, one race is EPICLY nice like AAA, and the other one is good and would be great in an indy game alone but along side the others they don't stand up as well.
Difficulty: Its neat, if you screw up and lose fleet, you can just do old missions at other difficulties to get the points to go back up. Theres also a thing about using skirmish to earn CP but I havnt really played with that.
Gameplay: Theres huge potential here,  the basic idea they have here is AWSOME, it just needs some refinement, and explanation which the videos can provide.
Music: Way better then I usually expect from an indy game.
Voice acting: Its very limited, but in a game thats also mobile you don't want to have meg upon meg of voice. But what there is is well done.
Complaints:
Long time to repair/requisition ships: The times are now MUCH more reasonable (order of magnitude better)
Controls are clunky: There was JUST a patch that makes it MUCH better (actual keyboard controls and some mouse integration)
Gameplay is simplistic: The 'tactics' and depth come from the upgrades on your ship in the 'upgrade fleet' menu. It's not as much as I was hoping for, but its a lot more then I thought there was initially.
New player experience: Watch the videos, one move/shoot cycle should BE the tutorial, it makes what the game is SOOOO much clearer and makes the 'what the hell am I doing' so much easier.
Story is simplistic: Only when compared to a AAA game, in its casual genera it has WAY more then would normally be expected.
There have been two patches very soon after release on this game that addressed the major issues people had.
CONCLUSION:
Its an awsome example of what its meant to be! Make sure you go in knowing what its meant to be!
OLD NEGATIVE REVIEW:
It has a lot of potential. There was a rather thin attempt at story. A lot of the ship designs are quite good. The combat system is very different take on things and is kind of an interesting idea that is a bit let down by the implementation.
Combat is one ship at a time with move and fire phases, full 3d movement you sort of pick a heading that’s going to give you a good firing line, move and then try to line up your turrets, you have 2 sets of turrets, one is up and one is down and its near impossible to either hit more than one target, or hit a target with all weapons.   Unless (and this is what I started doing) you spend your first few moves turning your ships on their sides allowing you to hit multiple ships. The ‘turrets fire in sets’ idea is interesting once you get it through your head you’re not going to hit every turn with every weapon, and wouldn’t be so bad if the top and bottom had separate side to side (Although that would change balance quite a bit)
Unfortunately the controls are clunky and can frustrating the tutorial/new player experience is really lacking.  I highly recommend watching the videos in the games store page both to see what you’re getting and get an idea of how the game play actually works. It’s not impossible to figure out but even once you figure it out your left with a 'eh...that’s odd' feeling. On mobile they might be ok but they completely ignore the mouse/conventions of the entire history of gaming on how to select directions. They are going in a new direction in terms of how to control things so its mobile friendly as well but there’s no reason the mouse couldn’t have been worked into that much better then clicking sliders (ala simulate touches) It really feels like a straight port of a mobile game.
The 'why am I doing this, what the hell am I doing' aspect is almost completely lacking. The story seems to come from another game and the world has a lot of depth. But the storyline is given as a quick ‘read this, ok now kill these guys’. Storyline is in somewhat unsatisfying glimpses.  Its missing a lot and it feels more like a mid to late beta where the main stuff is there it just needs a polish and fluff pass.
There are some bugs still like the campaign randomly losing your progress and selection of ships in repair menus but in all cases the game recovers to a sane state if you just continue to poke at it. I don’t recommend ramming as it just spins both ships and the firing here is actually check for round hitting model so that makes it VERY difficult to hit anything.
The whole wait for ships that everyone complains about it was removed in favor of using the in game currency to speed it up, it looks like an aborted attempt at a mobile pay for in game currency system. They fixed it for buying new ships at least at the time of this writing.
I really wanted it to be good, it has some excellent ideas but the controls need work. The damage/combat model needs a bit more depth (there’s even a bit of that with ships drifting/burning) but lacks the usual basic features like decals. The combat system itself needs more depth (like WHAT you hit mattering, separate left and right controls on upper vs lower turrets. A bit of an improvement to the AI. And more depth in terms of things like repair, initiative etc. It has the 'tactics' label but the only part it uses from the genera is 'turn based'.  The UI needs user experience testing, I'm sure it’s perfectly navigable to the developers but to someone that hasn’t seen it before...it needs a bit of work and a decent tutorial. A lot of potential neat features like replays are missing.   The controls feel to me like they were trying to make it work on mobile, but I can think of two ways to make it work better on BOTH platforms then what they came up with....(although what they have, on mobile probably acceptable)
The things I DO like are Ship designs are rather unique not just cookie cutter.  There are some 'inspired' type designs (somebody really liked the Normandy) but overall I really like them.  A lot of them I'd consider AAA quality with a few that aren’t quite there.  They made an attempt to avoid the Indy trap of boring menus by having backgrounds while doing things that actually matter. Very well done, but needs some polish. The 3d doesn’t always match the 2d. They tried something new with the actual combat system/UI with...varying degrees of success, but I applaud the attempt. They avoid the other indy trap of bad voice acting. I really think the person they used pulled it off REALLY well.
Short version is, this game is pure potential if this was early access I would have been happy with my purchase at three times the price and looked forward to exciting things to come. As a full released game like this is as good as it gets other than bug fixes....meh at best. I'm going to put some more time into it later on to see if it grows on me but the overall impression I get is a depressing 'aww, i wanted it to be good!
Or maybe my standards are too high for a budget game I saw a spaceship , the word tactics and a sub 10$ price tag and leaped without looking, watch the vids they are quite good and explain what your actually getting into.
(Also note that between my origional review this morning and this one in the evening the dev released a patch that fixed some of the bugs I ran into + some of the control issues, although I still think it needs work this might mean game is still in development and not to be given up on :) )

I'll start with a caveat: I usually don't buy greenlit/alpha games. I got lucky with Minecraft and burned a few times with some others. Despite it's pre-release Rimworld really knocks it out of the park. This game is fantastic. It's a wicked emotional roller coaster bound to completely drain all your feels and make you cry like a baby when the colony you've so lovingly grown and nutured completely burns down because Cobb the scientist can't handle researching day in and day out so he snaps and burns down all the buildings including the food in the middle of winter. Then a timberwolf happens to wander by and kills the beloved community dog Ursula. Then everyone is left standing in the snow, braving -20c, with no food, no shelter, and serious burns from the fire. The trauma of the disaster pushes Serph over the edge and he begins a murderous rampage just as you bail and exit the game. Then you feel a little dead inside and think about how everyone had to eat nutriant paste for a solid month and winter was just days away from ending. They almost made it! Just 20 days before everyone attended Chris and Tail's wedding, all hopeful the little colony would only grow and prosper. NOT SO.
But you'll come back tomorrow and restart. You'll mine stone and make those buidlings fireproof. You'll actively hunt timberwovles and never let anyone with a pyromaniac trait do any serious emotional lifting or research.
A great little game so far that really doesn't feel like alpha and will suck you completely into its all enveloping world simulation.
Pros:
-Random events make the game unpreticable and fun.
-Game feels pretty much complete.
-Offers a varied and almost endless approach to survival.
-Imperfect characters are fun and weird.
-Lots of choices for difficulty if you enjoy torturing yourself.
Cons:
-Random events shred your sanity and send your stress levels into the stratosphere.
-It's an emotional roller coaster where you are forced to never become too attached to any of the little dudes.
-Game isn't complete and it leaves you wondering/wanting more features.
-$30 price tag is kinda high for alpha.

If you're sick and tired of the BBC Sherlock but you still love Sherlock, look no further!
This is an incredibly focused game that captures the magic and mystery of Sherlock Holmes. Mini-games and puzzles abound, be ready to be challenged and somewhat frustrated, as all mysteries do. The graphics run well and give the gritty yet refined atmosphere that is England. The customization is great (especially if you're sick of looking at Benedict Cumberbatch) and the dialogue has a classic yet modern punch, as with the characterization.
Outside of the mini-games and puzzles, the game feels slow with all the walking and the not-as-fast sprinting. Luckily, there are a few quick methods to travel from place to place. Depending on your computer, the loading can be frustratingly slow especially since it's a two parter. Another flaw I'd like to talk about is the lack of a formal tutorial, as it may have frustrated me a little. For newer players, this may catch them off-guard but to veteran ones, it feels intuitive. I won't deny that gathering evidence has frustrated me, but since this is a mystery... You really have to observe your surroundings. And this game emphasizes it!
So if you want a TellTale lite game without any of the Tumblr crap, here it is.

This review is for season 1. I highly recommend that all fans of Borderlands-brand humor play this game. Tales from the Borderlands is just as hilarious as Borderlands 2 at its best, and both protagonists are as funny as they are likable. For the most part, the story is told in a sequence of flashbacks that revolve around a central objective: The Gortys Project. As you progress towards uncovering more of what got Rhys and Fiona into their present conundrum, you will encounter many staple Borderlands characters, and these encounters are often hilarious or otherwise memorable in some way.
Rhys, a Hyperion employee, has a gimmick that allows him to scan and hack various objects throughout the game, and much of the text-based humor is provided in this way. The other protagonist is Fiona, a con artist with a massive bounty on her head. She is able to loot crates, and much of her gameplay involves attempting to smooth talk her way out of multiple encounters, with the assistance of her sister Sasha. The dialogue and voice acting are top-notch, which is imperative to the delivery of the game's humour. The art style and aesthetic is exactly what you would expect from the Borderlands series.
Not only are the main and returning characters great, but nearly all of the new supporting cast completely fit in with the Borderlands style and humor you'd expect of the series. One of my favourite side characters is the highly passive-aggressive Loader Bot, who refuses to forgive and forget about my order to have him self-destruct earlier in the game. My biggest gripe with the game revolves around the lack of importance in a number of the decisions you make. Oftentimes, the outcomes will be the same no matter what choice is made. In one particularly egregious example, I constantly reacted negatively and antagonistically towards a certain character - the exact opposite to how a friend played the game - yet we both ended up with the same conclusion involving this character. This 'illusion of choice' was quite disappointing. That aside, the character interactions are a consistent game strength and the story will capture and retain your attention throughout. Quite welcomely, in Tales of the Borderlands we see the glorious return of the greatest character in the series' history -
Hail to the King, baby.

Very fun class-based FPS game. No need to spend money, the benefits of higher level cards are very small and can all be bought relatively easy with in-game earned credits.
Do you think Overwatch is too slow, and the gameplay relies too heavily on your "Ultimate" abilities?
Do you like that every class can top the scoreboard with kills, even the engineers and medics?
Do you like the real world guns from Arma or Insurgency but not the slow boring movement and gameplay?
Then Dirty Bomb might be for you.
The game is very skill based, with a high Time To Kill. Skill always wins.
Also the payment model is very fair - you can unlock weapons and mercs through credits earned in-game very easily. The rarer "loadouts" only offer cosmetic differences. (All loadout cards above "Bronze" rarity are ONLY different in how they look. They offer the EXACT SAME functionality. And bronze cards are easily obtainable)

OLD VERSION > NEW VERSION
OLD VERSION PROS
-Specific roles (Weapons couldn't just all be equiped, your role as a railer or smg is important because you dont have bots running around with every weapon equiped)
-Skill based (No auto healing and you have to be careful on how you build or design your bot)
-Healer Importance (Since you couldn't auto heal and regen your health you had to have a healer to help you and made their role a great importance to the battlefield)
-Awareness (Since you can only get healed by healers you have to understand what parts of your bots got damaged or criticaly damaged, like airplane aerofoils or thrusters and pilot seat)
-Requires more team work (Your not going to have people charge in without getting support or a healer since you have to be aware that you can only get healed by healers)
-Progression (Unlocking parts made it very intresting to play the game and leveling up felt rewarding, not just some crate that you can get that can give you crap or be earned easly through gameplay)
-Unbalance (Fliers get unfair adavantages, Flaks and Rockets will insta kill and you need to know that even SMGs and rails can bring you down so fast as a flier + Shotgun weapon that tears you down no matter what armor you have)
-Diversity (Cubes have different healths and different tiers for your bot. Different tiers ment you have to be aware who you are fighting and how your enemies will aproach you. They were also different tech tree paths which spiced the game up)
-Awesome rewarding system (RP/"Dust" would be earned through your skills on the battlefield and it doesnt give you a crate that just based on luck.)
-Mega bots (Just fun in general, a mini game where everyone works together to kill a high tier bot)

OVERALL 8/10

Nice feature is also that some of paid DLC's became part of standard digital key. Also the remaster works really well, even better on good-performing rigs.
I really enjoyed playing it for this short while, but as I know the game from console edition, I can give it rating of 8 with full confidence.

This is potentially the best kart racer ever made. It's a beautiful, fun and fast-paced game with great music, great characters, excellent race tracks and a unique gameplay concept. This is not just like any other kart racer, in this game you race with cars that turn into boats and airplanes in the middle of the race. These transformations are seamless and intuitive. All the vehicle types have their own unique handling, but at the same time feel similar enough to each other that it doesn't cause any disorientation. No matter which form you're driving, all the vehicles control perfectly. Rather unlike the luck-based whimsy of Mario Kart, the game is highly rewarding to skilled players; many of the items can be used strategically to attack or defend yourself from opponents' attacks, and there are even ways to evade attacks with homing items when one is unarmed. Snaking is not a terribly useful tactic in this game as it's very difficult to link multiple drifts across a straight. The game is more centered around thoughtful planning of boost charging and risk management.
There is a huge variety of game modes and lots of single player content to enjoy. You can go through the World Tour to unlock new characters and tracks, or play through the Grand Prix for a more streamlined experience. There are also multiplayer battle arenas with their own modes such as deathmatch, king of the hill or capture the flag (or "capture the chao" in this case). The gameplay holds true to Sonic's namesake as the vehicles move quite fast and the PC version moves along at a perfectly smooth 60 FPS, although it can reach even higher framerates at times.
There is a TON of Sega fanservice in this game, and you can telll the people who made this are really passionate about Sega's history. The characters and tracks are pulled from a large variety of Sega's franchises (such as Sonic, Super Monkey Ball, Space Channel 5, Crazy Taxi, NiGHTs, Jet Set Radio, Golden Axe and even Skies of Arcadia). On top of that there are many interesting guest characters in the game, such as Wreck-It Ralph from the Disney movie of the same name, and Danica Patrick, whom Sega is sponsoring in NASCAR. Not only that but the PC version gets several exclusive characters such as General Winter from Company of Heroes II, the Shogun from Total War: Shogun, Willemus from Total War: Rome II, and the Team Fortress 2 guys. More DLC characters are on the way as well, as Ryo Hazuki from Shenmue is already available to purchase from the store.
If you fancy yourself a fan of racing games, or just fun lighthearted multiplayer games in general, you will do yourself a great favor by picking this up.

An honest surprise of a game when I first played it during a free weekend. Was expecting some terrible Mario Kart clone with doses of fan service, but instead I got one of the best racing games I have ever played with doses of fan service. This even beats out Mario Kart in my opinion.
Gameplay is incredibly solid. The races feel really fast and intense, mainly due to the ability to turn into a boat and plane and the constantly changing maps mixing up the races. It never gets old.
The courses themselves are just plain fun to race on. All the maps(with the exception of the returning tracks from the first All stars racing) make use of the boat and air mechanics. Both the boat and plane offer different mechanics from the kart, forcing you to make the best out of all three if you want to win. There's also the constantly changing maps. It adds a more dynamic feeling to the race, and it makes you change tactics in turn of what happens. All of this, combined with well designed courses and a awesome soundtrack makes these tracks a joy to race on.
Graphics and preformance are amazing. This game is optimized to the point where it can run on a variety of different rigs. Graphically, this game turns out some amazing visuals. Many of the maps are utter eye candy.
There's also a large variety of characters to choose from that aren't Sonic characters. From more well games like to Super Monkey Ball to more underrated classics such as Vyse from Skies of Arcadia, and even some side characters that have no place in the Sega Universe (My main racer is Pyro from Team Fortress).
One thing that has to mention is that this game's difficulty mode is as advertised. Easy is easy, normal is normal, and hard is hard. Then when you spend enough time with the game, you unlock expert mode. I don't recommend you touch this mode until you're ready for it, to save you from frustration.
Overall, I would recommend you pick up this game when you have a chance. Quite possibly the greatest racing game to come out on PC and is great to play with friends.

Wolfenstein: The New Order resurrects the badass nazi killing simulator that is the Wolfenstein franchise in a big way. It takes the fast paced run and gun gameplay that the series is known for and adds just the right amount of modern FPS flavor to the mix. The game requires you to take cover and learn the battlefield or risk enemy flank, and it still rewards you for exploring with the same secrets you would find in the older games.
The story fits in perfectly with the game and you'll never end up wanting to skip the cutscenes. Though the story is a bit generic and sluggish in the beginning, with you just being another muscle bound marine in your squad of clones at first. You'll travel through all sorts of interesting locations ranging from hospitals, farms, German villages, and all the way up to the frontlines of battle.
The gunplay feels very smooth and satisfying with a weapon suitable for each and every play style, even stealth. The game now allows you to slink back behind enemy lines and take them out quietly one by one without alerting half of the Third Reich to your location. If you've ever played PAYDAY 2 or the older Far Cry games, the feel is sort of similar to that. It gets the job done and still feels satisfying, but it's relatively basic and leaves you wanting a little more.
The map design is near flawless in my opinion, but some things can be a bit confusing at first and will require a bit of figuring out. The game's visuals fit whatever is going in with the story at the time and provide great atmosphere, though they can be a little too dark and dreary at times. The sound design is great leaving the guns with a satisfying punch and further building upon the game's already amazing atmosphere.
Even at its base price of $20, I'd say this game is most definetly worth it.

Canyon is an arcade racer that consist of tracks that are somewhere between 20-30 seconds. You meet up online (or you can play against yourself) and everyone competes for the best time on each track. It's all about nailing those perfect drifts and jumps so you can shave milliseconds of your time. You can instantly restart at the push of a button.
It's a very simple premise, but it's is insanely addicting. Tracks are short and easy to learn, but difficult to master. You need to cut each turn perfectly to win against other people online.
You'll be saying to yourself: "Just 5 more minutes, I'll quit after the next track." And two hours later you're still playing. Highly recommended.

Borderlands is truly a classic. It brings in an innovative plotline, with twists, turns, and everything around. It also adds 87 BAZILLIONONDIEREST GUNS, allowing players to really shoot 'n' loot, and kicks a** in general.
Plot:
Borderlands isn't linear. You can choose your way through Pandora, and do whatever the crap you want. It has approx. 30hrs. of Singleplayer gameplay for ONE PLAYTHROUGH, and countless more for the 2nd playthrough, four characters and DLC maps. In addition, there are progressive enemies, scaling up so you're never bored!
Graphics/Performance:
Borderlands is widely regarded as gray, grey, brown and grey. While I agree, it does have some beautiful art, and amazing guns. It can run on the modest of computers (mine is 2GB RAM, and it worked well on low settings), but is also a monster on those 16GB Alienware computers. Lag is non-existent, and the stuttering you get from COD: Whatevercrap doesn't exist.
RPG/Skills:
Borderlands adds a plethora of things to the shooting genre; customize your character with skill points, and morph them into whatever builds you want! In addition, players can swap out elemental relics to customize action skils, and that decisions in-game result into different out-guns, largely allowing customization. The guns in-game truly allow personality, with four elements, and 8 different manufacturers.
Really, Borderlands is a great game. While it isn't Borderlands 2, it's great for those on a budget or Borderlands fans. GET THIS GAME NOW!

One of the best games I've ever played as well as the game that originally got me into philosophy, The Talos Principle is sure to exceed your expectations. Its graphics, plot, puzzles, and characters all stand out among the vast sea of one-dimensional characters, mundane environments, and mediocre, clichéd plots that are unfortunately prevalent in many aspects of media these days, and it offers a calming yet intellectually stimulating refuge from the monotony of daily life in a unique way. Except puzzles with mines. I wouldn't describe those as calming.
The Talos Principle offers a solid 40 hours of gameplay with just one file, and if you purchase the
DLC, that time will be bumped up to 50 hours. Through these 40 hours, you will consistently be challenged morally and mentally -- you will be forced to think about what makes a human, what it means, and the implications of establishing criteria for humanity, but while you're doing all of this, you will also be madly dashing around mines, serenely manipulating color-coded lasers, deactivating various futuristic devices, flying through the air without a care in the world, recording and playing back your own movements in a manner reminiscent of
, and listening (or not) to the voice of an omnipresent deity who calls himself Elohim. All of these elements converge to create amazing puzzles in beautiful environments based on the ruins of an ancient Roman or Greek city, ancient Egypt, and the castles and fortresses of medieval Europe, juxtaposed with futuristic devices such as floating mines, laser turrets, retro-style computers, and metallic cubes. Somehow the combination works together, and it creates beautiful scenery that rivals the real world's.
While characters are few, they are very well-done. Alexandra Drennan and Arkady are the only real traces of humans, and the only human voice you hear is that of Alexandra, whose voice actor in the English version is amazing, I might add. Based on her time capsules and her emails to various workers at the Institute for Applied Noematics that you can find in the archives, it's easy to visualize her as a modern human, and I almost felt like I knew her personally. When
, I could really feel the emotion and desperation in her voice, despite knowing that it's just a game.
Arkady's journals are uncommon, but offer interesting insights into the state of the world at the time and Alexandra's sacrifices to
. And we can't forget Milton, of course. At first, he acts innocent and robotic, but his true nihilistic worldview emerges when he begins debating philosophy with you.
The plot progression is very interesting and unorthodox. There are two main plots: how you came about and the actual series of events culminating in either you gaining eternal life,
, or
. The first is scattered about the world in archives and time capsules, some key parts not becoming available until much later in the game so you're left to wonder, while the second mostly depends on your interactions with Milton and your obedience or lack thereof to Elohim, and progresses linearly. I can't say I was a huge fan of how the first was executed, mostly because one of the most important pieces of information about
was hidden from you until you get all of the stars in World B, which some people might not even do. I ended up having to look it up because I can't stand to know such a huge event happened without knowing why. If the bits and pieces of information were placed about the world in a more linear fashion without requiring that you get optional rewards, I would've appreciated it, but at the very least, all the loose ends are tied up once you complete all endings of the game (of which there are three). It should be noted that the plot is great as long as you know everything about it.
Despite a few problems with the way the plot was executed, this game is absolutely amazing and I would recommend it to anybody who likes philosophy, sci-fi, puzzle games, or somebody who's not sure about their enjoyment of these subjects. On a scale of one to ten, I'd rank it at 9.5, taking off half a point for the scattered-about plot points.

I started playing this game recently and I've really been enjoying it. It is difficult but pretty fun and fast paced at the same time. As for the look, the levels look as if it's a "Dungeons and Dragons" game board combined with a theme park. Everything has a cartoonish look to it, even the giant spiders. This combines with a lot of blood and gore as well, kinda like tf2 now that I think of it, (Another great game by the way).

Basically a group of three players or "Heroes" come to a theme park run by the Dungeon Maestro, a some crazy guy who sends monsters and spells after them in the hopes of killing the heroes, wich he does quite often. As the heroes, It plays a bit like gauntlet if you've ever played that before. For the Heroes there are three classes you can choose. There is the mage, who provides support to the other players, the warrior, who soaks up damage, and the rogue, who can dish out a lot of damage, but can't take too many hits. Each of these classes has three different sub classes. The Mage has the fire mage, the ice mage, and the lightning mage, the warrior has the vangaurd, the lancer, and the defender. The Rogue has the assassin, the gunner and the archer. These different classes are made for fulfilling different roles on the battlee field. However, if you don't feel like being a hero, you can always be the "Dungeon Maestro". When you're the Dungeon Maestro your goal is to stop the heroes from advancing through the theme park. As I said before, you send you use monsters and spells to do this. the way you decide wich spells and monsters you will use goes like this. Before every run you begin by selecting cards. On these cards are the creatures, abilities, and spells you can use to thwart the heroes. Once the game begins, all you need to do is select the cards and use them on the heroes. However, if you use up all of your cards and are waiting for more, you can just posess one of your monsters and try to take the heroes out yourself.
I would definately recomend you to try it. On a side note, at this game's launch it was plauged by bugs and glitches that would occur frequently. That, along with its difficult gameplay may have scared off a lot of potential players. Despite this, the game has been patched plenty since, thus removing a lot of the bugs and all together making it much more playable. Even so, I will admit it still has it's bugs, despite this though, I have found ways to work around most of them and it hasn't really hindered the experience for me. It fun and free to download so if your willing to take my word for it, give it a try.
P.S. The game got pretty repetetive after a while, so you rnot exactly going to waste days on it. Still fun for awhile though.

There are essentially 2 reasons why you'll ever want this game:
Gameplay - think 'Portal' or 'The Turing Test': gameplay doesn't offer much more than that, but the challenge is still there nonetheless. There're a ton of puzzles that can challenge your brain matter without being a huge time sink, while each spurring you to 'complete one more': they are also quite forgiving in terms of starting puzzles over or attempting to retrace steps. Knowing your avatar is 'merely' a robot somehow nags at the back of your mind as you strive to solve puzzle after puzzle - would an AI have done this better (Especially the tetris bit)? If so, how am I faring against it? Thoughts like this blend into the next point...
Philosophy/religion - this was the surprise that they did not have to tack onto the story but still did so to amazing effect. Through countless 'random' articles and the brilliant recordings of Erin Fitzgerald you can't help but find yourself sucked into the metaphysical questions and conundrums the game raises...and at the end; a Soma-esque ending that left me devastated...and changed. If a game can do this to you, especially not even through it's main 'game' mechanic...why wait?
If you've tried and loved The Turing Test or Soma and want more of the same, this won't disappoint. Especially if you're currently pondering the point of your life, or of humanity, history and religion as a whole: have no doubt; this one is for you. It's actually better than Soma as it doesn't tip over the edge into Nihilism, which my tired mind truly appreciates. I cannot fully describe how the points raised in the game mirrored the ideas I had going in my mind for so long yet had no way to put a name to; or to know that it was something the whole of humanity actually feels: Existentialism.
Play for the puzzles. Stay for the insights.

The original TrackMania games were damned amazing and had a great following with tons of servers full of thousands of players at any given time of day. For the last ten months, the new TrackMania games have been dead. I paid full price for all three titles, expecting to have an even better time with the new games, because why not?
Well, as the days turned to weeks, I realized the folly of my wasted money as almost all of the servers remained dead across the planet and it continued to be impossible to find a choice of heavily populated servers. Whether it was the dumb choice to milk the players of their cash by splitting the game up into three separate releases (one for each environment) and requiring separate servers for each or if it was the decision to charge money for the new games, at all, the result remains the same -- nobody plays these.
If you reference
for Canyon, you'll find that the average number of players at any given time through all of 2013 was between 10 and 100. Across the entire planet - and most usually seem to be overseas (Germany, France, Russia, Spain, the UK), so if you're looking for a populated low-ping server in your region and you're in North America, you're going to have a bad time.
It's a very unfortunate situation. The game looks better than ever and it has a lot of enjoyment to offer if you like this style of game. It's a fantastic time waster when you need a break here and there. However, you ultimately need a player-base for a multi-player game to be enjoyed. Their business and release model for this series of games completely failed in this way, this time around.
Here's to hoping they give the franchise another shot in a couple more years and they correct their mistakes.

This game is a good game, I will give it a 7.5/10 or so. I want to break down my analysis into a pros/cons list for ease of understanding.
Pros:
+The background is good, I always found the wolfenstein alternate-universe where the Nazi's win WWII and dominate the whole world to be pretty intriguing. It serves to create a satisfyingly oomph-filled backdrop to the storyline of the game.
+Small details that further enhance the storyline: Such as the German Armstark's first moonlanding news clipping, or a news article on the hit-song "Das Blaue U-boot". It makes the game more immersive.
+The stealth aspect is quite fun, with knife throwing etc.
+There are some wild-moments and humorous incidents in the storyline.
+The hidden areas/secrets etc (Enigma Codes) are fun to look for and locate.
+Graphics and performance are pretty solid.
Cons:
-After such a well crafted and well-established background as the wolfenstein universe has at its disposal the actual storyline of this game is pretty cliché and lacking in depth.
-Side-characters are not developed sufficiently.
-Game is quite short - finishes in about 16 hours with all secrets etc. found.
-Enemies usually seem ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
-Combat becomes boring towards end-game. The areas where a stealthy approach is possible are MUCH more fun.

I'll start with a caveat: I usually don't buy greenlit/alpha games. I got lucky with Minecraft and burned a few times with some others. Despite it's pre-release Rimworld really knocks it out of the park. This game is fantastic. It's a wicked emotional roller coaster bound to completely drain all your feels and make you cry like a baby when the colony you've so lovingly grown and nutured completely burns down because Cobb the scientist can't handle researching day in and day out so he snaps and burns down all the buildings including the food in the middle of winter. Then a timberwolf happens to wander by and kills the beloved community dog Ursula. Then everyone is left standing in the snow, braving -20c, with no food, no shelter, and serious burns from the fire. The trauma of the disaster pushes Serph over the edge and he begins a murderous rampage just as you bail and exit the game. Then you feel a little dead inside and think about how everyone had to eat nutriant paste for a solid month and winter was just days away from ending. They almost made it! Just 20 days before everyone attended Chris and Tail's wedding, all hopeful the little colony would only grow and prosper. NOT SO.
But you'll come back tomorrow and restart. You'll mine stone and make those buidlings fireproof. You'll actively hunt timberwovles and never let anyone with a pyromaniac trait do any serious emotional lifting or research.
A great little game so far that really doesn't feel like alpha and will suck you completely into its all enveloping world simulation.
Pros:
-Random events make the game unpreticable and fun.
-Game feels pretty much complete.
-Offers a varied and almost endless approach to survival.
-Imperfect characters are fun and weird.
-Lots of choices for difficulty if you enjoy torturing yourself.
Cons:
-Random events shred your sanity and send your stress levels into the stratosphere.
-It's an emotional roller coaster where you are forced to never become too attached to any of the little dudes.
-Game isn't complete and it leaves you wondering/wanting more features.
-$30 price tag is kinda high for alpha.

There's potential for a good game here, and the coding is certainly competently executed, but the game is ultimately far too poorly-designed to be a success.
For starters, the game is too random (even by roguelike standards - sure, potions in Nethack are random, but the key difference - and one which the developer may not quite grasp - is that Nethack potions CAN be identified through various means before swallowing them) and certain elements are extremely poorly-thought-out (there's no "momentary invulnerability" on hit - so if you happen to wander into a patch of poison, you die pretty much instantly) or just clunky (it's too easy to get hung up on scenery, and sometimes traps can be spawned "behind" trees and other objects, rendering them completely invisible until you happen to get killed).
On top of that, the game is EXTREMELY grindy - I love a good grind as much as the next guy, but only when the game is fun and fair. "Fun" is in the eye of the beholder, but "fair" is not, and with its plethora of one-hit-kills and suicide potions, this game is anything but.

I must confess, I didn't want to play this game for the longest time, as it looked not like a sequel to the latest games, but as a standalone, with vanilaised characters, and something completely mainstream. And for the most part I was wrong. With summer sale up, I decided to go for it, liking detective games, and I am more than satisfied with the game.
It has really interesting quests and plotlines, even if somewhat of a fantastic nature, and I will lie if I will say I never was confused by the story, never made a wrong decision or haven't changed my mind a few times, trying to get to the bottom of the case. I loved to see the familiar apartment, familiar street, with familiar people, familiar Scotland Yard, and so on. It is a great sequel, and it fits rather nicely with the whole theme, even if I winced and spitted at the idea of Sherlock Holmes having a daughter. Foster, as it appeared, yes, but I just cannot see my childhood favourite sociophobe taking care of a little kid, even if he is responsible for her loss off parents, even if she locks her in the boarding school (which, by the way, is a norm at the time period it takes place), even if he is bad with parenting.
The amount of unique activity was amazing. I loved so much that, say, spying on a person, shoe-polishing, taking cover from bullets, or imagining the location of the crypt by the riddle were one-time activities and didn't look repetitive. My favourite, of course, is the reconstruction of road accident: very unique, very amazing, and it actually makes you feel like a detective, trying to piece together a long series of unfortunate events. The repetitive lockpick game and quick-time-events because of the amount of unique mechanics, didn't feel too much of a bother, although I must confess they were extremely easy to overcome, and didn't feel like a challenge at all. On the other hand, they shouldn't have been, since the main goal of the game is using your intellect and memory to make the right conclusion.
The slightly new approach in this main goal was also felt, as often times, solving the crime, you can find a lot of hints that either party is responsible, and only a few unmarked lines of dialogue or a small note will say that you are wrong. Such as, for example, the second case, where
- both things are not listed as important clues, and you have to figure this out yourself to make a right choice. This was a great improvement from "Crimes", where you had everything marked as important which made your investigation easier. In "Daughter" it actually feels like a challenge.
What was a major minus, and everyone is complaining about are the characters. I can only theorise that they were made more mainstream and "fashionable" after the success of "Crimes and Punishment", and bluntly because Holmes is a father now, and should be more relatable (I do not want to believe popularity of the BBC series has something to do with it, although two default suits of Holmes suggest otherwise). Therefore, he was made into a generic Hollywood hottie, with low manly voice; while Watson suffered from extreme case of metrosexuality, probably unnecessary for the person of his rank. Not only the designs, that were the main thing that turned me off the game at the time, but the voice acting suffered as well. Although British, Andrew Wincott (the voice of James Watson) sounds as if he struggles with British Accent, while Aalex Jordan (the voice of Sherlock Holmes) has too adolescent voice to be perceived as a detective in his forties or fifties. I must confess, I was actually looking for mods that would get the looks of the main characters back to what they used to be, instead of what they are now.
But, overall art looked very appealing. The (visual and sound) artists and designers really mailed the atmosphere of each building, whether it's the streets of London, the pub, or the opium-addict apartment, it all felt amazingly right. The game has some lightning issues, however, they are minor compared to the picture we got in the end. Every place had its own unique atmosphere and sounds, and this is the first game in the series with some very distinct music. In fact, I cannot remember if any of its predecessors even had any music in it, however, this one is extremely appealing, and very atmospheric, and even though it has a lot of modern notes, it transfers the feeling intended perfectly.
The final sequence was one of the best-made things in the whole game, and it left me slightly dumbfounded. The lack of the need to travel to your destination, and instead getting slightly phantasmagoric transfers in completely different parts of the city via simple doors added to the rush, and actually made my heart beat, as, combined with distorted sounds and visuals, it made me feel on edge and in a real hurry. So much so, that it was the only part of the game I used running for, as I felt that I had little time, and none of that time should go to waste. It sounds bad when you read it, but, if you never played the game, believe me when I tell in practice, it plays out amazing. Sudden transitions and rush as your character feels his life slipping away, is perfectly transferred by the game developers. However, I didn't understand if it was real or not until the very end, since we all know out main character is a drug addict, and up until the last encounter I thought it was a drug-induced dream, that will make Holmes rethink his attitude towards his daughter and a new neighbour. I cannot say if it was intentional or not, but if it was, I take off my hat to the writers and designers, as it was truly amazing.
Now, at the same time, the ending suffered a lot. This is the first game in the series that didn't put the full stop, neither suspension points. It just ended abruptly, and while the hopes were up about post-credit scene that will convince me it wasn't a dream, or that it, in fact, was, and show how the main character was able to overcome his fears and change as a person, there was none of it. The game desperately needs a good ending, and I don't mean a happy-one, I mean good story-wise, the one that will feel whether like an ending, or a cliff-hanger, while this one feels as none at all. It actually feels like if the production had to be cut abruptly, before the writers could finish the plot, or before the animators managed to lead the cut scene to the end.
Another thing I would like to point out as a great thing, - and again I am not sure if it was intentional or not, - was the character of the daughter herself. Katelyn's character changed for me as the game went. At first, her odd over the top girly attitude annoyed a great deal out of both me, and the main character. She was a minor annoyance to be brushed off before you get back to your business. But as every new encounter went down, it became apparent she is just a small child trying to get attention from her father. With a bit of jealousy kicking in, as she finds new friends around, you become more and more involved with the child, and like her a big deal. That is why the ending felt so rushed (but in a good way) - you start to care about the little girl that used to annoy you so much, you became frightened yourself of what might have happened to her.
Overall...* [read the continuation in the comments - I've run out of symbols]

By the time they get to a place where they're having a significant effect on how the character plays with zero artifacts, I've already grown bored of playing that character because of the lack of variety in the first place.
Used to be fun, now it's overly difficult to the point of frustration because of how random it can be at times.
EDIT: Went back to play the game once after writing this review. Had pretty low health and a wave had just finished. Dune rat pops out of absolutely nowhere and kills me. Yeah, I'll catch up with this game in another year or so and hopefully they'll have added some serious balance changes/QOL changes to it.

Borderlands is fun, fast-paced adventure in a game-world where hyperbole is exemplified in the explosions and the guns and characters that cause them.  The story is unique, clever, and makes the player feel like they are the only sane person in this post-apocalyptic dystopia.  The RPG component helps to immerse the player into the world by allowing an opportunity for the player to feel invested in the character as they make decisions that grow their character in a variety of branching directions.  The dialog is refreshingly quick and clever.  I wish more developers would spend time of the story component of their games instead of tacking on cliché dialog and overwrought cut-scenes that look like animated versions of artwork from the cover of video card boxes.
The only negative against the game is the lack of variety in enemies and vehicles.

I'm writing this review with a good amount of playtime, and I hope this helps others who plan to try this game out for themselves.
Dirty Bomb is very different from any shooter. It provides a new and unique field on which to play with a cool sci-fi post-modern setting it provides the explosives of today with technology of the future to create an amazing looking game.
My biggest highlight from the game is the selection of mercs (characters) to choose from and playstyles. There's almost a playstyle for anyone. The wide variety provides a great field. My first warning is that the draw back currently is there is a great amount and not all come free. There is a free rotation which helps in choosing your favorite merc.
The biggest drawback has to be balance. Plenty of maps lack proper design, with chokepoints located directly on spawns or otherwise. Making certain objectives on certain maps impossible to pass. The mercs also have a vast amount of balancing issues, with some being much better than others, and others giving more exp overall than others. The matchmaking is also something you should be wary about, and can be very disgusting. Guns themselves also have many issues, however due to new balance updates they are being improved.
The upside to this situation is the developers listen. They are also very active, and update almost every week. There is no shortage of changes, and the community grows. You can even catch special events for special cards!
I reccomend this game to almost anyone into casual shooters, or a free alternative to Overwatch or other types of games. This is a fun and enjoyable game.

I have spent a good long time attempting to digest this game and determine whether or not I enjoyed playing it.  Initially I was very angry with it.  It stole a full day of my life and really I was thoroughly convinced it was just a stunning setting cloaked in a philosophical (and often VERY preachy) robe.  But over time I have grown to appreciate it, and even miss playing it.  I loved the puzzles.  At first.  They are incredibly innovative and will make you call upon every iota of your brain as the Power Rangers call upon their Dinozords.  Furthering this awful analogy, you'll have some trouble getting through if you're not able to make your brain Megazord.
Initially this game was very jarring for me.  I was maybe an hour into it and still waiting for the actual game to begin.  Possibly my error, as I was expecting it to be a game *with* puzzles, not a game *of* puzzles.  That being said, the sheer volume of puzzles paved the Road to Redundancy under my feet rather quickly.  But then suddenly, vastly different visuals and new mechanics are introduced.  Unfortunately, traveling from Siberia to Egypt did not really change the content of the puzzles.  Still just doing the same old thing for hours.  And the new mechanics and items made the puzzles more complicated, but not necessarily more difficult.  A lot of them, though, really were very enjoyable.  It just went on a bit too long.  If the game had ended a few hours before it did, or if I didn't always have to go full completionist, I probably would have loved it.
A quick breakdown: The Talos Principle is really quite a beautiful game.  It ran seamlessly for me; never had any issues that weren't caused by me being a touch dense.  Equal parts intuitive and "seriously, who the hell actually thinks like that?" which was nice.  I enjoyed the story to a point.  The logs encountered throughout the game were very interesting, but in the end I was a touch let down.
In a perfect world I would be able to give this a neutral review, but since I cannot it gets a thumbs up.  It is a very well done and thought-provoking game, and the issues I had with it were mostly due to my personal preference and short attention span.

is the most thrilling and poignant puzzle game one could hope for. It is beautiful and challenging and in many instances truly arresting. The game does have one significant flaw that I think is worth mentioning to prospective players: there is a major lack of consistency where ledges are concerned.
Most of the time, accessible ledges (i.e. those that can be stood upon and/or used as jumping-off points) are clearly indicated with glowing footprints superimposed by the HUD. Jumps to those ledges are executed along preset arcs. In this sense, jumping is a decision to be made, not a skill to be cultivated, just as in chess, where a player does not win or lose based on how well she places her pieces in the exact center of each square.
, in a handful of instances, unmarked accessible ledges
are present and even required to solve a challenge. Sticking tricky landings is fun challenge in many 3d games, perhaps most notably in
and its sequel. But where
's austere environment and overall play style encourage players to explore vertically and test any potential foothold, the very rich environment of
strongly discourages such behavior. For every accessible ledge, there are
of promising looking but ultimately inaccessible ones. Does a player spend vast amounts of time jumping at every architectural ruin (with a 99% failure rate) or consult walkthrus? It's a frustrating dilemma.
Otherwise, this is a truly great game and deserves to be experienced.

The first Sonic & All-Stars Racing would have been the perfect kart racer if it weren’t for the omission of multiplayer on PC. Sonic & All-Stars Racing Transformed brings local and online multiplayer to Steam, but some of the magic has been lost. I fault the new multi-terrain direction Sega has taken the series for that. I don’t understand the need to take kart racing to the sea and skies. Controlling a speed boat or a plane is never quite as satisfying or responsive as controlling a car. Drifting is especially awkward when flying, but it can’t be avoided if you want to catch up with the horrendously unfair rubber-banding AI. A-class races are tough. You really have to know the courses to land first place, which can be hard to do considering many of them change with every lap. I like the idea of a course that morphs over time, but this usually means the whole thing catches fire or falls apart, leaving you air-bound for the final lap. As much as the new additions bother me, this is still a solid racing experience. The more car-oriented courses are a blast, the weapons are well balanced, and the graphics are as gorgeous as ever. I’m really happy to see this series revived because it’s just as good, if not a little better than that other popular mascot racer.

The Talos Principle
by Croteam
Genre: First-person puzzler
Release: April 18, 2017
-----
The Talos Principle is a strange game at first. Here’s what I’ve been able to decipher from my playings:
You are a strange robotic being in a strange, beautiful world. A gigantic voice, identifying itself as Elohim, occasionally speaks to you from above. You are tasked with recovering many blocks which resemble Tetris pieces (or Tetrominoes) from behind a series of increasingly complex puzzles. Also present are computer stands which contain, alternatively, bits of communication between coworkers in a modern-age computer center; slices of Wikipedia articles; and, more disturbingly, what seems to be a live intelligence who talks to you from time to time…
Something else you’ll find in the world is that the area you start in is actually only one of three major areas within a hub, all the levels (up to 10) within an area being accessed through teleporters. But take an elevator up to the surface from this area, succinctly named A, and you will find two other areas, B and C, as well as a fourth building, a strange, impossibly tall tower, with dark clouds and disturbing effects at its top. You are urged by Elohim to continue in the three main areas, but very strongly discouraged from scaling the tower, which contains similar puzzles as the individual areas…
From time to time you discover special items within the area hubs, which are locked behind puzzles. This is what your Tetromino-gathering leads up to! The graphics are beautiful, the sounds at turns relaxing and discordant (when Elohim is yelling at you, you know you’ve  done something wrong, or at least against him), the environments lend themselves well to the puzzles, and the slowly emerging story gives the impression that something… happened somewhere that wasn’t entirely good; discover it for yourself, I’ll say nothing else.
I most definitely recommend this game to all puzzle fans! Check it out!

Awesome FPS in a very interesting world.
PROS:
*Soaring high moments with a lot of badass fights, emotional highs, and cinematic experiences.
*GREAT gunplay
*Stealth is simple, and not perfect, but gets the job done.
*Looks beautiful (mostly)
*Feels like a good mix of modern and old FPS conventions (maze-like levels that encourage exploration, armor and health pickups, but with quasi health regen and a tighter focus on narrative than games like DOOM)
*Awesome cast of likeable characters that develop really well.
*The world of New Order is really fleshed out and clearly had a lot of thought put into it, it is brutal and foreboding while also strangely intriguing.
*Killing Nazis at its best
CONS:
*Weird melodrama at times
*Awkward sex scenes
*The tone gets a little much at times for my taste
*The perk system is interesting and a good idea, but not executed terribly well.
*Hit detection with the throwing knife can be god awful at times
*some minor graphics issues, the game doesn't play well with triple buffering and cutscenes tend to have this odd old-filmy grainy filter.
All in all, the pros far outweigh the cons. One of my favorite games of the last few years.

I love this game :)
It's a micro-management basebuilding game, where you control a group of people (it can be a group of one), trying to survive and build a spaceship to get off the planet. To get that far you have to build  a base, collect ressources and build defend the base against hostiles. But I guess you already know this, so I will just do a pro and con list:
Pros:
-Micromange or Macromanage. You choose how detailed you will control your survivors.
-Flexible game. There is alot of potential for Mods, and there are already alot available on Steam Workshop.
-Flexible game setup. You can choose several modes, and find more through Steam Workshop. This gives it alot of replayability.
-I love that you can give your survivors cyborg arms, legs and eyes. There could be other replacements, like ears, but maybe they will come later :)
-All setups are created from XML files (located at Steam\steamapps\common\RimWorld\Mods\Core\Defs). This means if you want rabbits to be super killers you can change their fighting abilities by changing the hitpoints and damage in the XML file, and presto!  Look, that rabbit's got a vicious streak a mile wide! It's a killer! You can also change the value of animals and alot of different things. It is recommended to take a backup of the files you change ;)
Con:
-Some random events can just end the game. Like dry thunderstorm when you only have 2  survivors, and everything burns down, leaving you with no ressources or base (true story). When you have enough survivors you can fight the fires off, but if not...
-Sometimes the random generated map will just create an awful starting place. When this happens I just drop it and starts a new game. Even if it can be fun to play a hard game, it usually means everything takes ALOT of time (for instance if there is almost no steel or almost no components, you need to buy it from friends).
-Some of the progress is too dependant of some specific ressources (as mentioned above). It would be cool if there where several paths through the invention tree.

Why, Frogwares ? I thought we were friends.
Some people may remember playing Super Mario Bros 2, a hundred years ago. Some may even have noticed, even as a kid back then, that "2" was a weird game compared to every other in the series. And then years later we all found out that the reason SMB2 felt odd and out of place was that it was a reskin of a completely different game, where they'd only replaced the main characters' sprites and
.
This is a bit what Devil's Daughter is like, except they didn't even use the right sprites.
Were the game titled "Fetlock Burns & The Devil's Daughter", telling the deeds of young american action hero Fetlock Burns, for some reason on holiday in England and staying at Sherlock Holmes' old address, it would be fairer to the player.
Because in no way, and from no angle, is the guy you move around Sherlock Holmes.
It would be bad enough if the difference (with popular culture) was limited to the looks (and the voice, and for God's sake the accent), but also gone are the wits, demeanour, dryness of analysis and lovable brand of light autism we all have admired and enjoyed for decades in Sir Conan Doyle's works.
Fetlock is just "some dude", and talks and acts like he's in a family sitcom on cable in 2010.
There is enough to say about Watson alone to fill a page, but I will let that one slide in view of all the rest.
In the game you lead him (Fetlock) in a series of events that are more tailored to Lara Croft or Batman than to a victorian gentleman (which is ok, since Fetlock is an american acrobat adventurer), while the screen is cluttered with the instructions for the current minigame - and it is a flurry, as these minigames just keep on coming, one after another.
Occasionally the flow of poorly jointed minigames will be interrupted by a brief session of guessing, where you will connect at times contrived observations and clues, through no particular logic, to form "Conclusions" which are too often open to interpretation. At any rate, you do more running than reasoning.
The puzzles themselves, that is the few that are not based on jumping around and avoiding traps, are too often absolutely arbitrary, and to "solve" them you have to guess by trial and error what the designer meant the solution to be. While this is an issue that plagues all puzzle games on occasion, in DD it compounds with all the other shortcomings to deliver a deeply unsatisfactory solving experience. Other times they are not puzzling at all, unless you can consider pressing clearly marked buttons in sequence from 1 to 10 "a puzzle".
The other kind of "puzzle", of which there is way too much for a SH game, is often padded and repetitive but never entertaining.
But enough of singing praise.
The game is short, less than 10 hours, and divided into 4 separate cases (the first of which you should guess the gist of within about 20 seconds), with some background noise-like "main plot".
The ending of each case comes up abruptly once you have collected all clues, and you have to pick a culprit among your suspects based on loose logic that you had no real part in devising or applying.
Loading times are pretty long, and you sometimes are made to go back and forth between locations with no real necessity. And frankly, Fetlock's book is (not that much) funny the first time you see it, but after 500 cab trips you have to wonder if he's learning to read from scratch from it, or if each time it has a different comic book hidden inside.
The writing is poor. I kept on playing hoping for the game to fall back by mistake on the right track, only to see Fetlock act out another uncharacteristic, american everydude dialogue. I won't even touch the plot, that is subjective and some may even like it. Stranger things have happened, like the mayor of Burgundy's self combustion in 1453.
In the end, if you make a real effort to ignore every time someone says "Holmes", and stick to thinking you're Fetlock with all your mental might, it is merely a poorly executed mixture of Tomb Raider and the CSI games, rather than a blotch in a series we have come to love and anticipate in spite of its slip-ups.
Couple of additional minor details that grate hugely :
- at some point you may find a map leading to money. On the map, there is a currency symbol. It is all but "£".
- Fetlock dresses like a hobo. A victorian gentleman would not dream of being seen in the street so attired.
What the game ultimately does is raise the question of why Frogwares would take such a dump onto an intellectual property that they seemed to hold dear all these years, with all its ups and downs.
Various reasons, that come arbitrarily to mind if I turn on my detective mode, may or may not include:
- a major wave of ministrokes
- the replacement of all writing staff at FW with people who have never read a book (never mind a SH book)
- the new publisher buying all FW's bank debt and forcing them to make this drivel against their will
- FW having it up to here with SH games and wanting to end the series in a way that would slight SH fans the most.
Graphics are good !
Worth acquiring ?
IF you are NOT looking for a SH game, maybe, and possibly if you are 13.

TL:DR
After Playing through this to the end, i have to say that this one of the best games i have played in the last few years. It was an extremely satisfying game with an  immense sense of atmosphere and intrigue. Despite a few bugs, some repetition in the gameplay and the graphics not being of triple-A quality, the game looked and ran beautifully. The game will grip you throughout and your choices do make an impact on the story.
Positives:
The game ran very smoothly, staying consistant for the majority of the time, with only a few framedrops at loading screens within levels.
the game did drop framerate a couple of times, but the game overall did still run smoothly.
The graphics were gorgeous, especially considering that this game came from a smaller development team to most
triple-A developers.
The voice acting was perfect, and each character in the game sounded unique and felt like there own person.
The gameplay was extremely fun, with a mixture of point-and-click and 3rd/1st person exploration.
There was plenty of diversity in the gameplay, providing much more depth to the game, and if you found something just too hard or boring, you can always skip it, which is a nice option to have.
The puzzles all took thought to accomplish, which felt very rewarding once you figured them out.
The game didnt hold your hand, but it gave you subtle hints that you could always refer back to. you felt like you were in control of what you found.

Although I've played through the "main" Borderlands games, I wouldn't call myself a huge fan, I found them enjoyable action games with a good enough story to keep me engaged.  So I didn't really know what to expect when I purchased "Tales from the Borderlands" during the recent Steam sale.  This is the first "Telltale" game I had ever purchased and I had a general idea that it more story driven than the other Borderlands, but beyond that I was clueless.
Well all I can say is "WOW"! This was perhaps the best gaming experience I had in quite awhile. I sat down to try it out for a few minutes and ended up playing through the entire first two episodes. When they say story driven, they really mean "story driven" this would have been a great made for TV miniseries. For those that have never played one of these "telltale" games, it's sort of like the old "choose your own adventure" books, where choices you make as the story unfolds effect how it progresses, although they are some button mashing action sequences, none of them were that difficult and were made to integrate into the story rather than detract from it, in fact you would pretty much have to try to screw up or not be paying attention to actually "lose".  Same for the puzzles, most are simple identify/use item with the purpose pretty obvious.  But the real star is the story, which so far is amazing. I can't wait for the next episode!
