Two of the episodes have been released at the point of this review being written, and as it stands Tales from the Borderlands could well be the greatest thing Telltale have produced so far. I have a lot of good things to say about it.
The Borderlands universe is already rich with interesting design and has a great aesthetic, and Telltale has not only nailed that style perfectly but they'd added to it with a wealth interesting characters, a dual narrative that is always engaging and excellent storytelling.
The cutscenes are very cinematic, even the interactive ones. This game may be the closest I've ever felt to being in an interactive movie which is a crazy level of immersion. There's great music throughout the game but in particular it really completes a lot of the cutscenes and makes it resonate with you.
Oh, and it's funny! Having grown up on games like Monkey Island and Day of the Tentacle, this is something that's really important to me. Tales has had me laughing plenty both at the dialogue and at events in the game.
There also seems to be a lot of divergent storytelling, I've not actually replayed it yet so I can't confirm but from my initial playthrough it feels you could get quite a different expereicnce depending on your actions.
If you have any interest in Borderlands, Telltale or just adventure games, you should seriously consider getting this game. It has a lot to offer.

I came to this game after playing The Witness and wanting more puzzle games. Initially, I liked it a lot. It had a compelling story from the beginning and puzzles with interesting and new mechanics, and seemed to be designed well that it taught you how to play without a tutorial. But as I got toward the middle and end of the game I just got bored.
There are 6 distinct puzzle mechanics that you unlock as you progress. It's totally reasonable that you don't like some or that they just aren't intuitive or fun to you. I personally despised the recording mechanic in this game. In The Witness, if you don't like a mechanic, for the most part you can skip it and go to another part of the game where there's something you like. But in this game you *must* complete (nearly) every puzzle using every mechanic. If you don't like it, tough luck.
The second complaint I have is the progression. The game's progression pretty quickly becomes tedious. You aren't doing the puzzles because you like them, you are doing them because they stand in the way of the rest of the game, and there's no alternative to it. Once all the mechanics are introduced, you know everything in the game, and then you still have a good 20 puzzles left to finish.
My final complaint is simply the level design. Some of the puzzles can be beaten through what seems to be a design oversight in the game. Using tools from other puzzles to help you out when it's fairly clear you shouldn't, or even just trying to find the perfect angle to save an item for a different part. Other times these goofy angles are the design of the level; there's no other way to complete it. It's a drawback of 3D puzzle games that a lot of extra work has to be put into perfectly crafting a level, but when so many levels seem really rough around the edges it just sometimes makes you wonder.
Oh and also in the end sequence of the game there was a bug I hit that made it impossible for me to progress and it should've been fixed a long time ago, since even I, a player of the game, was able to figure out why it happened (but only after it was too late).
Love puzzles? Get the game. It does well enough in that regard. But there are better ones.

Why did I wait this long before laying hands on this masterpiece of a game? I used to like Portal 2 a lot when I played it. I still do, but Talos Principle is so much more: it's the puzzle solving of Portal 2, plus a plethora of discussion on the human experience, viewed from the perspective of a third party, as your character is a bot. And in the (canonical) ending -- whereas in Portal 2 you manage to save yourself -- here you save humanity. But what moved me the most was all the bits of detail, collected along the way, that showed how humanity struggled to save itself. What a poignant story.
And do I need to elaborate again, as many reviewers before me have, on the superb quality of this game's soundtrack? Oh yes, I abso-♥♥♥♥in'-lutely do. Damjan Mravunac has done a tremendous job. Humanity's struggle for self-preservation is all the more saddening yet uplifting thanks to the work he has put into these tracks. And for five bucks you can get them all in lossless quality? That's like Christmas come early, at least to me.
Finally, a few words on some of the localizations. I first played through the game in English, then realized I made a less-than-preferable choice regarding Milton (the MLA), so I restarted from scratch in Japanese. Like in the original version, in the Japanese version the voice acting was mostly on point (Ueki Tooru did a great job as Elohim); but translation of some of the text is questionable at best. For example, during dialogues with Milton I sometimes wasn't sure if any of my available options made any sense, only to realize, upon loading up the original English text again, that the translation simply failed to capture the correct mood of those options. Then I finished the game again, and tried the Chinese localization -- only for a few minutes, before giving up. Not only did the (mandarin) Chinese version of Elohim sound mechanic; his lines weren't even translated into proper Chinese. I can only imagine what the voice actor was thinking when he was asked to read those broken sentences. I can't speak for all localizations, but if you're planning to play this game in Japanese or in Chinese, my advice would be to play it in the original instead, if at all possible. Still, I must say that rolling out this many localizations is no small feat for the developer (and they couldn't possibly have known the quality of each and every localization other than to trust the partners they worked with), so credit to them where credit is due.
(One more aspect of the localizations which I did't like, and this is an issue on the developer's side: when I first started to play this game in Japanese, I was quite baffled to see the captions out of sync with actual voice acting. Then I quickly realized that the developer probably didn't allow localizations to alter for how many seconds each line of caption was to be shown, and those values were fixed, optimized for the English version only. Another reason to stick to the English version, I guess.)

Easily the best shooter I have ever had the pleasure of playing, hands down.
You are William "BJ" Blazcowicz, American soldier in WWII. You are losing the war and mount a desperate mission to annihilate Deathshead, the mind behind the Nazi war machine, and critical centerpiece to their regime. The mission is a disaster and you are left in a coma for 14 years, and when you wake up, you find the world under Nazi rule. You won't stand for this. You'll fight the Reich alone if you have to. Thankfully, you have an array of fantastically written friends and allies who feel truly alive, and jaw-droppingly well designed enemies who you feel both respect and disgust with.
From the start of the game you are thrust into the action, and there is no hand holding tutorial like many games. You get minimal hints as they become relevant and are expected to figure out the rest, which I found highly enjoyable.
This game has lore written with such realization that is very rare these days. A true testament to the little used alternate history genre and what it could become. I was immersed in the world and people within it like no other game has done for me before, even beating The Witcher 3 for me at least.
The story is gripping and filled with unpredictable twists and turns, leaving you saying "Whoah, did that really just happen? Did I really just pull that off?" Your rising Resistance force goes from a small underground to a true terror against the dystopian rulers of this grim world.
The gameplay is one of the best I've encountered, going for more of a classic shooter feel than modern. You need to manage ammo carefully, and loot it from your defeated foes manually. Health does not regenerate, save for in 20% increments (If you're at 45 health you'll regen to 60 and no higher), leaving you to hunt for medkits around the map. Armor is similar fashion, though it's more common than health as many enemies drop it and you can break open many containers with armor components inside. Guns feel powerful but balanced, and each one holds a different purpose. Some are stealthy, some are powerful, some are in between. If stealth doesn't work for you, you can dual wield assault rifles, shotguns, sniper rifles, and more to obliterate anyone who gets in your way.
This game requires you to think a lot of the time, as some decisions can impact the story in different ways. Or you can find useful loot and upgrades scattered in hidden areas to increase your max health/armor, and collectible items that unlock bonus content such as lore, developer notes, concept art, and more.
Wolfenstein: The New Order is a true masterpiece of a game, and I cannot recommend it enough. I am truly excited for the release of its newly announced sequel, Wolfenstein: The New Colossus, which directly continues the story from the end of this amazing game.
You can't go wrong for the $20 maximum price on this. On sale, this game is a true steal for those wishing for a singleplayer adventure free from annoying children and smug teenagers.

I've given this game a bit of time in campaign mode with the advisors.  I've been playing in difficult mode.  It's a very frustrating and poorly designed game and I don't recommend it.  Here's why.
The Starting Phase
You settle a colony or two.  Then trade back and forwards to your home port.  That's it for an hour or more.  Very slow.  Once you start producing second tier goods, you start producing more cash and can do more than just keep up with you advisors' demands.
The Advisors
They regularly give you demands.  If you don't meet them, your reputation goes down - and in the end, you get replaced.  The demands are not well timed (eg. they will ask you to settle a colony when you are well below the minimum population threshhold for your next colony).  Sometimes they are impossible (eg. they ask you to send 50 soldiers to a colony that is less than 50 below the maximum limit).  Sometimes they are contradictory (eg. you are at war and one advisor demands you make peace and another demands you take a colony or destroy enemy ships).  As you progress and get your colonies going well with all the buildings they need, the advisors are left with fewer things to demand of you and so you get more of these impossible demands.
Battles
You can do these yourself or auto-resolve.  There is no tutorial.  Battles are complex and buggy.  Once a ship has been set to move in a direction, sometimes you can't change its direction - even if it means it hits a rock or another ship and sinks.  Often ships will file past the enemy without firing.  If a ship is set to attack the enemy, it will sometimes drift off and do it's own thing - drifting  far away if you let it.  Maybe there are solutions to these things.  There is no tutorial or explanation, so who knows - but I fiddled with most of the options and couldn't find anything.  Auto-resolve nearly always produces better results - particularly with attacks on forts.  The only downside with auto-resolve (apart from the fact that you are basically wasting half the game you just bought) is that you can't capture enmy ships.  But given the boarding function doesn't really work, that is not so bad.
There is one fight that is always auto-resolve.  This is when you attack a town without a fort.  This requires repeated attacks.  You lose each one until the defending soldiers are reduced to zero.  Then you win the next battle.  The town defends just as well regardless of whether it has 5 soldiers or 1000, so this is really tedious and a huge waste of ships.
War
Your advisors will ask you to do this, then hit you with repeated demands to make peace.  Even if you are winning the war, the other country will not make peace unless you pay them A LOT.  So you can get stuck in a long war.  Problem is even if you destroy the enemies ships, they survive, they don't get starved of cash, they don't go bankrupt.  Within the time it takes you to build two warships, they will have built 6 - soon they are picking off your convoys.  This affects your cashflow and once you drift into negative cash numbers, it's curtains (unlike your enemies).
The Economy
This works ok but is done so much better in other games.  Would have been nice to know that there is a tool to find the highest and lowest prices for goods.  Again, no tutorial, so I just stumbled upon this.  It would also be nice to be able to have standing orders to buy things and store them in the warehouses.  This would help deal with the constant demands from colonies for this or that good.  Otherwise - what is the point of the warehouses?  All goods seem to reduce in price and cost over time at a constant rate.  There is no fluctuation based on quantity available or demand.  So why would you put goods aside?  Basically, you want to make as much cash as possible, so you sell them as soon as you can.
You can't trade with your other colonies for price reasons.  You can't trade with the other countries except through one off sales through the diplomacy system.
Once you go into debt, that is basically the end.  You don't own the goods in your colonies.  You have to buy them (even though you pay for all the buildings that process the goods).  If you lack cash to buy them, you can't make a profit and you get killed by your fixed expenses (all those buildings you own that process the goods you then have to buy).  This can happen pretty quickly.  By 1540 your cashflow can fluctuate up to maybe 400,000 gold just based on the timing of your trade routes.  If you have a war and lose a convoy or two, it's game over  - and remember you can't make peace unless you have lots of cash and taking the other guy's colonies takes forever during which time, he will have twice the number of ships that you have.
Difficulty
I guess a lot of this is due to the difficulty level.  I have seen in these reviews that the normal level is a cakewalk - which is why I tried difficult.  Not so good if one level offers no challenge and the other is an exercise in frustration.
Winning
From what I can see - there is no such thing.  You play till 1650 and then it ends.  It's just a question of whether you can survive that many hours of frustration and monotony.  No thanks.
Overall, this is the skeleton of a game with lots of things missing and lots of issues.  It won't be worth playing until a lot more DLC is issued - and even then, not sure I would trust them given my experience thus far.

I bought it for 2.50 at a weeklong sale and have been playing it ever since.
It is a fun, arcade-like game where your movement is WASD and you attack with the arrow keys.
There are several Acts within the game. Each act has 6 levels with 6 stages full of Traps, Treasure, Monsters, Dungeons, and OP relics.
The game is randomely generated. No stage will ever be that same due to a random placement of Traps and scenery, as well as randomely generated monsters based on what level that you are on.
It is a wave based game with 30 seconds in between each wave so that you can buy things, hunt for loot that you missed, enter dark caves and dungeons or just wander around trying not to get skewered on the end of a spike jutting from the ground.
After 5 stages full of monsters you have to fight a single boss. The boss is randomely generated and when he dies a portal is created leading to the next level. There is always treasure at the portal. Either a single relic or several hundred gold peices to buy potions.
As well as the waves there are things like rat nests and such that spawn their designated monster every so often. Destroying these spawners grants lots of gold and XP.
Not all monsters are the same. There are already all of the random monster types and then they can get random buffs like Enraged, that just makes them all the more dangerous. Sometimes they will fire a giant ball into the sky when they die, that explodes upon impact with the ground and either sends fire, bullets or a giant laser to finish you off. Avoid these
Pros/Cons:
Pros:
-Tons of replayability
- Complete randomeness in acts and monsters
- Different Classes to play
- Traps
- Loot
- Leveling
- Skill trees and stats
- extremely insane when getting chased around a house by an army of skeletons
- Achievements
Cons:
-Have to buy updates
I also bought the karp of doom expansion. For those of you who play this I advise you to spend your hard earned cash on this expansion. It completely revamps the whole game. It adds in Tons of new bosses (as far as I can tell Hololo is one of them), Tons of new Relics to buff your character even more, an extra act, Multiplayer, Updates (this is the only part I find stupid, that you have to buy the chance to update) and the Samurai (he is just op woth all of his buffs).
Pros:
- New relics
- Higher chances of finding relics
- Samurai Class
- Next act
- Online
Cons:
- Costs money :(
*Final Note*
I think that this is a great game and if you have the money, Buy it. It is definately worth it. Lots of fun, replayability, and achievements.

2) It ignores rule 1 of Sherlock Holmes: there is never a supernatural explaination. Without giving too much away, you have to deal with the actual occult, magical puzzles that somehow draw you into a scale model, where you can look into the past and get the answers you need to solve a case.
3) Some lines of investigations are total red herrings, and are not at all explainable outside of "trying to make someone look guilty for no reason".
I myself rather enjoyed Crimes and Punishments, since it was finding out clues, and using those clues to further your investigation rather than "work out how to get across this tile puzzle" or "avoid this big rock", which have nothing to do with the case and you don't really feel like there's any point to except to fill out time and space where the devs couldn't be arsed to actually produce content.

One guy with malaria went into a psychotic state and I had to arrest him to continue his treatment. He survived at 99%, only to have his head blown off by raiders a few days later.
On my way through the ice shield my alpacas got so cold that their hooves froze off.
At one point I became a organ dealer because apparently that's the most lucrative way to deal with surplus colonists and prisoners.
I had a standoff between a rioting prisoner and a constructor repairing the door he was tearing down from the other side.
Another prisoner died because I tried to do a cold turkey with two addictions at once.
One moron shelled my own fighters during a siege, killing my best craftsman and source of income.
A wildfire opened an ancient tomb, releasing a bunch of angry mechanoids on my colony. The rescued people in the tomb were happy to be released, except for that one guy who went on to kill my best constructor.
Some old lady decided to settle alone in the wilderness for an adventure, only forgot she had asthma and no one around to treat it.
In an effort to appease hostile tribes by releasing healthy prisoners, two of them died of hypothermia or predation while leaving the map in shackles.

So I have played this game for a rather large number of hours now.
The game is fun - it's amazing, and it has vast replayability. Like Dwarf Fortress it is a game about how you die - or how it ends. Sure, if you play right you can get your little people in to space - but usually they die horribly, of cold, of fire, from bugs or pirate - or sometimes everyone just gets sick.
The game is an enjoyable simulator with a huge amount of depth - each colony teaches you something new about how to play, and the game can be as difficult as you want it to be. (Too easy? Try playing in the desert or the frozen north). You can crank up the difficulty if you enjoy fights, bugs and flu or you can keep it simple to build the colony you always wanted to.
I may have bought the game on sale - I don't remember. It's worth it.
You just have to remember this game is not to win - it's really just to play. If you like that sort of game you really can't go wrong here.

Commander: Conquest of the Americas is a flawed but still interesting game about the age of sail and colonisation.
You start your game as one of the European nations trying to colonise the new world, from the northernmost tip of Canada down to...The northern part of Brazil. Sorry South America, you're not allowed in here, this game is about the north only.
You are thrust into the role of the colonial governor and have to colonise the new world. To do so, you'll be sending out a fleet to find a place to settle, and then you will be bringing in new colonists and exporting the products from there to the old world.
In time, you will end up with multiple colonies and you will have to set up trade routes and pirate hunting patrols. You will mainly be doing this as you sit back and watch your new world empire grow, trying to make a profit and making sure your advisors are happy so they don't try to get the king to replace you.
The campaign stuff is limited, and somewhat repetitive. The AI nations do not really offer you much of a challenge, and it is easy enough to take out their new world holdings and fleets. Given a bit of planning and thinking ahead, you can turn a massive profit and conquer most of the world. You will then be pretty much just waiting for things to happen as your automated routes take care of everything else.
The game mostly does well in the ship battles, where up to 3 squadrons of 5 ships per side can join battle in a realistic simulation mode that I have not yet been able to find anywhere else. This is my main reason for saying this game can be a good recommendation for some. If, like me, you are a fan of more slow, simulation style naval warfare rather than action packed speedboats with explosive linings and machinegun-cannons then this is a good way to get your fix.
But being entirely fair, I can not really recommend it for other things. The campaign is nice as a way to lend some kind of importance to the battles, but it does not really do much else. The in-battle AI is capable enough that it won't just roll over for you, but it is not amazing either, and the detail of the simulation is still far from perfect.
Even though I like this game, and have probably spend way more time on it than I should, I can't really recommend it for anyone who is not a fan of the time period and simulation battles. It does decently well at the economy and trading parts of the campaign, but it is repetitive and you will find yourself speeding up time a lot until something interesting happens.

Well I'll be; somebody actually made a version of Tic-Tac-Toe that's legitimately strategic and challenging to play against a skilled opponent.  And the graphics are nice, too; I mean, it's not Unreal Engine 4 but for what the game is, it's great.
First off, to address the obvious question, yes the game contains traditional Tic-Tac-Toe if you want a little nostalgia; the game refers to it as "Classic" and it's just as boring as it ever was, although this time you get realistic chalkboard sounds to yawn along with.  The fun starts when you try "Classic Forget" mode, though.  Now you've got the same rules, but you only get to keep three moves at a time.  That's right, starting on move #4 your oldest move gets removed from the board.  I'd read the description but I kinda forgot about it as I twiddled with Classic for a bit, then played it, did three moves, whatever, then did the fourth one and saw my first move disappear and proceeded to spend the next 30 seconds staring at the screen, planning my strategy, at which point I stopped and smiled because I realized I'd just spent the last 30 seconds thinking hard about Tic-Tac-Toe strategy.
The titular "Ultimate" mode is where it's at, though.  While the instructions on how to play left a little to be desired, the actual gameplay is easy to grasp once you realize what's happening.  I'm not going to recreate the store page here, but in a nutshell the game takes the same basic ruleset of Tic-Tac-Toe and adds a meta layer on top of it, and you really will have to think to win.
There's also "Ultimate Forget" with the same difference as the classic modes (starting on the fourth move, every new move you make simultaneously erases your oldest existing move), but honestly that just seems like too much to keep track of; if you're looking for the Dark Souls of Tic-Tac-Toe, though, there you go.
So, 0.5 hours might not sound like a lot of play time to be making a review, but in this case it's justified.  The gameplay can be complex (especially if you're playing "Ultimate Forget" mode), but understanding the rules doesn't take that long.
At the end of the day, if you've got a warm fuzzy spot for Tic-Tac-Toe and you're intrigued by the idea of a grown-up version, you should definitely check this out.  It's got online and local (hot seat) multiplayer, and I'm thinking you could probably get a little mileage out of it as a party game with a bunch of people playing as a team against the computer...it's deceptive because you look at it and it looks like Tic-Tac-Toe and you're like whatever, this is easy, and then the AI beats you down.

The Trackmania series is pretty much a league of its own.  The various games in this series (Canyon, Stadium, Valley*) are quite similar in structure yet still have their own gameplay.  Canyon, like all other Trackmania games, have simple, highly-responsive controls.  You do not need a steering wheel or PC controller to enjoy this!  Despite the simplicity of the controls, the feel of the game is much deeper.  Powersliding around corners and launching off of ramps seem easy at first, but you'll have to think twice about your performance when another user beats your time by 1/100th of a second.  The precision needed to beat other (human) player will make you drop your jaw --only to have it slam shut after choking on their dust.
To add onto the play style game feels like it is trying to straddle hardcore precision as well as arcade (think Need For Speed: Hot Pursuit (2010), and it does a fantastic job at this.  Despite how frustrating it might be for trying to top the leaderboards, the game also has a little bit of a comical side; it can get very amusing playing on a server with 100+ other people and seeing many of them fall behind as you cruise on through.  ...  What?  100+ on a single server?  It is easier than you think!
Within all gamemodes, even circuit, there is no worry of server lag because times are handled more on every computer individually and there is no running into each other at all, everyone can play at their own pace --heck, you don't even have to run the race to have fun if you choose to go running off the track for your own adventure.  As for playing against other people, the leaderboards are the best I've ever seen.  You can see where you rank amongst other people globally, your country, and even down to your state/province/region.  Plus, there are individual rankings for single-player and multiplayer as well.
Hey, guess what?  I only told you what got me hooked on this game.  There is still more to Trackmania than what I have mentioned here!
*Valley has not yet been released, even for open beta, at the time of this Recommendation.

Game has some good parts, but the bad ones overweigh in my opinion. TL;DR:
- Almost nothing in the game feels satisfying.
- Deliberately vague evidence, making every conclusion logical
- Physical puzzles are poorly executed and annoying, they are pure filler for very short (~7 hr) game
- Annoying QTEs that add nothing to the game
- 80% filler
There are some good parts to this game, and some interesting puzzles and stories. But mostly, it feels.. lazy. The worst part is that almost nothing in this game feels satisfying. The idea behind adventure games, puzzle games, investigation games, is the satisfication of solving something. However, the developer of this game managed to mess most of it up:
- The evidence is often so vague that every suspect can reasonably be the murderer. Multiple people all have motives and have evidence pointing torwards them. Now, I understand the idea of red herrings. But this has to be well executed. There have to be subtle hints to the real culprit. These hints are, for the most part, missing in this game. Even if you re-read all the character portraits etc. you often times have to guess in the end. Sometimes the correct solution even fails to explain all the evidence (example with spoilers below)! This is bad writing.
- The logic puzzles in the game are often too simple to feel rewarding. Some are good however.
- They physics puzzles are absolutely bad. For a physics puzzle to be satisfying it has to be challenging either in execution or design. The physics puzzles in this game are neither. They are quite easy to figure out, only involve walking from A to B and pressing buttons and they take FOREVER. They are 100% filler. The game is short as it is, adding so much filler is just lazy. There was one physics puzzle in a forge that is very simple to figure out, but all the moving things around, climbing ladders, etc. probably takes around 15 minutes. 15 minutes of no interesting gameplay. The game is full of this.
- QTEs can be cool. If they feel rewarding. There are a couple that do that! But most are just minigames to make the game longer, like walking over beams very slowly. Or eavesdropping, or smithing something. This is all filler.
- Some parts are just absolutely lazy and hindered by the extremely clunky controls. For example lockpicking. Who came up with this control scheme?
For a short game like this, especially, I would expect good, tight, gameplay. But that's not the case. Quite the contrary, actually.

: Don’t let the Early Access tag put you off. RimWorld is as good as finished, but still expanding, and it's an engrossing and captivating colony sim, a labour of love that offers hours upon hours of playtime and is a must-buy for people who enjoy building a community from the ground up and watching it thrive in the face of adversity… or wither and die because of a few poor decisions.
: RimWorld puts the player in charge of a few crash-landed settlers, stranded on an unknown world after their ship crashed, because of course it did. After the player makes sure the colonists’ immediate needs are met, such as food and shelter, the real work commences, and in order for the colony to survive, it will have to evolve, expand and research, as well as trade with neighbouring settlements for the resources it desperately needs, or desperately defend against them.
What sets RimWorld apart from other colony sims is its colonist system. Colonists are all unique, and the player will have to make sure to keep an eye on what they’re good at, what they like and don’t like, and which colonists need to be around – or avoid – each other. Occasionally, enemy factions will attempt to raid your settlement, and you will need to keep evolving in order to withstand their ever strengthening attacks.
Meanwhile, your colonists will be busy crafting items, constructing buildings, tending to the animals, hewing stone, researching new technologies, sowing the fields, hauling lumber, and countless other tasks, which they execute more or less automatically according to the priorities you give them. A player who sets his priorities carefully, can take up a monitoring function as the colonists take care of everything that needs doing, if (s)he decides to.
: RimWorld has many very strong features, and one of them is the personalities it gives to your colonists. They are semi-randomly generated, with a diversity of looks, skills and traits, making them all unique and possessing an actual personality, and they develop social relations with other colonists, sometimes good, sometimes bad, and these social relations can lead everywhere from joining another colonist in marriage to starting a fistfight at someone else’s marriage. Keeping them all happy is involving without ever becoming a chore, and you just can’t help but care about every single one.
RimWorld’s gameplay is very solid, and the priorities and areas function lets you automate work, but still gives you a lot of control, eliminating the tedious parts of managing a colony but keeping the interesting ones. You can manually command colonists whenever you want, or even take full control of them when you need to give them detailed orders, for instance when they need to defend against a raid. Even better, while RimWorld is by itself already very polished, the game is fully modular, with an active modding scene which constantly delivers all kinds of content, ranging from small quality-of-life tweaks to big content-adding mod packs.
Another nice touch is that instead of simply choosing from a shortlist of cookie-cutter difficulty levels like “Easy, Medium, Hard”, RimWorld also offers you several narrators to choose from, who don’t really make the game harder or easier, but different. And yes, the narrators too, can be altered or expanded upon by mods.
Tynan Sylvestre and Ludeon Studios regularly update the game, often incorporating mods or acknowledging their ideas and including them in the base game, and so far, it seems like the influx of content, both official and from the modding community, is showing no signs of stopping anytime soon.
: There is really very, very little that is wrong with RimWorld, but the one thing that I did notice was that in the late game, you’re often forced to remain mostly static as you wait for opportunities to get a hold of some of the resources you can’t grow or craft yourself, like plasteel and uranium, and that’s a bit of a shame. But honestly, even static time in RimWorld is enjoyable.
: RimWorld is well-deserving of all the gushing reviews. It’s one of those rare jewels: an indie game crafted by a developer who kept going strong and never lost interest in the project, made with pure love for the craft. It really is one of those games you sit down to play ‘just for a half hour’ and before you realize it, it’s three in the morning, your tea is cold and payment of your taxes is four weeks overdue.

PS: Pardon if you are the devs and are spending time trying to balance out and make this game better, just ignore my review and go on with your lives, work hard and make it a good game so I can recommend it. I will correct this review if the game makes up for my expectations in the future.
PPS: This review will present some terms adherent to MMORPGs, other games, or just terms that I created since I am lazy to look out for the correct terms to be used. I am going to start this review by poiting out the good sides of this game and why someone would buy it. Then pointing out my opinions (which are mostly negative) on this game based on other similar games I've played, or games with similar mechanics that are pretty referenced within this game.
First of all, this game looks very promising, it has many mechanics that may work in the future if more polished, it has many things that would work if the developers spent more time on it  has a pretty good presentation and a good amount of references hidden within, the Character creation looks like Diablo 2, the skill builds work similarly to Diablo 2 too, both mechanically and aesthetically, the way the light goes through the stage after finishing it looks a lot like the Den of Evil from the same game, the game makes lots of references of The Binding of Isaac too, which is another roguelike that has many similar mechanics. I would point both of them as being the main drivers of this game, along with Diablo 3, that has many mechanics "referenced", such as the elite enemies, some of them have similar powers, such as Cold Enchanted freezing the player character for some seconds that may kill him, while others may explode and send out a globe of laser that (will, most of the time, if unseen) kill the player character too. I like the way the developers tried to create many classes and how they try to work differently, the necromancer summons minions to aid him, while the Viking goes straight for melee combat doing hard crowd control. The game is separated in acts, just like the now-so-famous Action RPGs, it also resembles old time games such as Smash TV, you wait for the monsters to come, and exterminate them while trying to dodge them and stuff like that. Okay, end of the positive parts.
If the developers were trying to make their game similar to The Binding of Isaac + Blizzard Stuff + Pixel Art + Original Ideas
Gold feels useless for most of the time, while crystals are just "cash" that can be used on some pretty cute/cool stuff like hats, it is also used for resetting the character or renaming it, these character features should be free or with small work needed by default to incentive players to change names and try new different builds, but are pretty expensive.
Damage done by the player is extremely hard to see, numbers are small and travel too fast, and are also decimal.
Hidden traps can be utterly strong without previous knowledge since the player couldn't see them, and are mostly luck based when they spawn, if it hits the player, the mobs or nothing. Grabbing potions on the ground may mean player's death if she happens to grab one that is among the gold/loot while a blood maggot/other strong mob is shooting at you. Since the players stops all animations for extremely valuable 0.5 sec.
Some bosses will 1 shot a squishier character with no way to read how much damage they would deal, just like the "girl spirits"  Annie or Samar, they just spawn going lightning speed toward the player while dealing like 50% damage in 1 hit, no clue what happened and just died. Also, their projectiles don't look like dealing THAT much damage.
Voice acting is terrible, wish there was a way to shut it down completely, because there is no way.
Now for the main part:
The Game feels totally incomplete and unpolished, at times I thought it was a Early Access and had to go to the Store Page to check if it really wasn't. Most of the Controller based commands feel incomplete, e.g.: "B" is used to call a new wave, while "B" is also used to close the level up menu, if you press B to close the level up menu while you are able to call a wave, it'll do both.Trees and most of the props are just hindering player's vision too much, just too polluted, I know that the intention was to hinder the player, but since the player can't tell what is behind 100% of the trees, sometimes there is a ultra-strong 1 hit killing turret/statue trap and the player can't tell it, just killing the player by full surprise.
Most of the "spheres" that monsters throw to the sky when dying are broken, blue, red, yellow, they are always off screen unless the player is north of the monster that throws it.
Sometimes monsters have "0" HP on their bars but still alive, some monsters get stuck on their own paths and cannot reach me going forwards and backwards non-stop, some
some bosses are ridiculously easy, like Beketamun, while others need extremely high skill from the player to be able to kill him, like ones that laser around non-stop, bosses like that need a open-area for the player to be able to move, but they walk after the player and sometimes it just means death if summoned on the wrong place. Such as near a Statue Trap.
dungeons are like rolling a d20 to see if you get out alive or not, some dungeons may present you with a screenful of godlike enemies on the instant you enter it, the area that the player has to deal with bosses inside dungeons is also pretty small, there is nigh-none space to fight bosses, and there are also bosses that are summoned that are ultra-strong for particularly enclosed spaces. There are also other dungeons that may be empty with a free treasure for the player with just some small puzzle before it. Entering dungeons is just too high of a risk for lower leveled characters, since the chances of dying because of a unlucky boss or unlucky room are very high. While it may present free relics for higher leveled characters, it just stacks with the grind needed to become "successful".
So far most of my deaths have been to the Blue Sphere on-kill effect from monsters, I've played plenty of Diablo 3 to know where this mechanic came from, so, In Diablo 3, sometimes monsters had the "Arcane Enchanted" property, which happens to be a similar mechanic, when they die, they leave a purple sphere on the place of their death, which exists for 1 second before firing a "laser needle" which spins and deals huge damage, the main problem with Hero Siege's "Arcane Enchanted" is that it is only a sphere that's thrown out of screen at the monster's death, when it comes back it is already firing the laser, seeing the shadow of the ball is pretty difficult considering the amount of trees, grass, monsters and shots on the screen, most of the time it is instant death for the player if it happens to fall on his head, that is if no traps spawn on the player's feet insta killing.
- It seems to me that the Devs didn't play their own game before releasing 1.0, or if they did and enjoyed it, they must have a pretty taste for artificial difficulty. Some bosses can kill you while on their death animations, due to the lightning globes that keep spawning when the player damages them while they are dying.
most sprites are far from being user friendly, since it's hard to tell what's "friendly particle" to a "foe particle".
- There is no catalogue to check the item list, I know that the Twin Blades give me Critical Chance, but how much Crit%? I can't even see my critical chance on the menu in first place. If this is intentional, it feels pretty odd when playing.
There is almost no room for faults since most of the stuff will 1-hit the player, I know that the developers must've made it their way, but when playing on hardcore it is just too unforgiving.
tl;dr: dont buy it, too luck/grind based instead of skill, unpolished, broken mechanics sluggishly borrowed from other games. My tip, go for Risk of Rain for roguelike, Path of Exile for action

This game is a huge step up for the Wolfenstein series. Not only it brings a wonderful Nazi-killing experience, but also a very good story!
The character, like always, is B.J. Blazkowicz, but this time, he shows meaningful emotions, connecting with the player in several ways.
The levels are quite linear, there are usually stealthy and guns blazing approaches, and both are enjoyable. Unfortunately the game is not a very good stealth game, as you can kill a guard right beside another guard just fine if he is not looking, and then he will just turn and walk over his team mate's corpse like nothing happened. As for the guns blazing approach, the game lets you dual wield machine guns, shotguns, and so on, allowing you to become an unstoppable Nazi-killing machine, and the game being gory adds a lot to the fun.
The story takes you to various locations in different time spans, and the game is not only about shooting, there are different kinds of levels with different quests.
The graphics are very good, unfortunately the engine is not able to maintain a stable FPS if you uncap the framerate, but it should not fall under 60 fps very often if you do.
There are lots of collectables throughout the game, but getting them all is not worth it in my opinion. It unlocks extra game modes for you to replay the campaign, but it disables a lot of the perks that you earn throughout the game.
I highly recommend this game, it honors the Wolfenstein name and is very fun!

Battle Ranch: Pigs vs Plants rests in a subgenre of Defense games that is most often represented by Plants vs Zombies, which I'm embarrassed to admit, I still have yet to play.  Even so, that shouldn't keep us from discussing Battle Ranch on its own merit.  Because, even though it's not a game I would have actively sought out, thanks to Epic Quest Games, I was given the opportunity to play Pigs vs Plants to create my own opinionn of a game which receives very little hype.  Having been a steadfast fan of defense games since the iconic Defense Grid: Awakening came out, Pigs vs Plants comes as my introduction to this style of defense games where you play on a game board and enemies move from one side of the field in order to destroy your resources and reach your base at the close end of the field.
It might be thought of as simpler to the full field style Defense games, but not without a similar brand of frantic pace in getting your own defenses in shape in preparation for the onslaught.  You still have different types of towers, even if they aren't upgradable, and tools to slow and stop the enemies.  The other element that isn't present in traditional defense games is how your resources are generated.  You must plant crops and harvest them, rather than generating points by killing enemies.  This adds to the exceitment by giving you the additional dimension of managing your crops.  Not only are there a number of towers at your disposal, this is also a pretty good variety of tools, and an in game store that allows you to buy tools, unit slots, and other things that come in useful to help you fend of the enemies.
When you first start the game, one of the more notable aspects is the art style.  It has a comical, fun style that is easy to appreciate, even if not ground-breaking.  I have to give credit to Playboom, an unknown developer for putting together something that is fun, challenging, is incredibly addictive, all for a remarkably low price of $1.99.
If you're looking for some mindless entertainment and don't require something that represents the high bar of technology, you might just want to give Battle Ranch: Pigs vs Plants a try.  For all of the things that it does right ?I recommend it.  My final score is a 7/10.

Well, well, well. I played Sonic & SEGA All-Stars Racing (the original) first. I REALLY liked it, I wish the online wasn't dead on the Wii. Anyways, I liked the drifting the All-Star moves, the Items and the tracks in that game, I can't really say a track I didn't liked in that game. Well in this one, there's a lot I don't like, and not because of the transformation, boat and air portions. I HATE the Zombie (I can't remember the name) stage, and Race of Ages is very hard for the first time (and lot more tracks). You need to play a little bit, and discover the controls and such, because these physics are so different from SSASR. Sometimes the water mechanics bugged out, you can fall through thw world a lot of times. You need to learn the flight controls. I didn't liked the drifting mechanics, it was faster in the prequel. I didn't liked the crashes either, they happened quite frequently for me. The online play is kinda dead here as well, I only had normal races online, I haven't found a lobby in any other types of races online. But let's say some good things about the game right? I've started with the cons, weird. I liked the character "customization" a lot. The mods gave us a lot of combinations and gave our favourite character different abilities. Levelling up is also fun. I wish it wouldn't stop after level 5. The characters are nice, and there's a lot of them. Some tracks are very creative. The graphics are amazing. I receommend playing it with a really good and precise gamepad, Xbox 360 controller is very supported, PS3 and others are good. I'm playing it with a lesser-quality gamepad, it's ok. Keyboard is okay too, just have one, what can recognise more than 3 buttons, and set it up comfortable. Music is repetitive for me, not really special, I liked it more in SSASR. Menus are good!
So, I would gave it a 7.5 out of 10. Maybe I would gave it a higher score, if I didn't play the prequel.

First, of all let me say I'm a huge Sherlock Holmes fan who knows all of Conan Doyle's stories almost by heart and has played all Frogwares SH games throughout the years on various platforms.
Despite giving it a thumbs up, what irks me about this game is that it could have been so much more - less minigames about balancing on wooden beams and more old fashioned deduction, especially when interviewing witnesses and suspects (more like Crimes and Punishments or LA Noire for that matter).
There are touches of brilliance in there, but they've been overshadowed by annoying mini games (climbing a chimney, I mean really) and  inconsistencies, as cases vary in length and difficulty (there's only one small nod to the original SH stories).  Some cases contain great puzzles inside, but I was expecting more overall consistency and sometimes more mental effort - Holmes analysis table was barely used, for example.
Despite this well meaning criticism I truly believe you should buy this game on a Steam sale (I bought it at a 50% discount), as it's generally a very pleasurable experience for the fans of the genre, despite it's uneven rhythm. Also, I was greatly impressed by voice acting and the graphics.

Like I said, the only frustration is that it could have been a brilliant game, not just a solid one.

FALL is a physics based game. I'm not sure how else to classify it. It's got very poor quality graphics, and yet it somehow has charm. You control your ragdoll by using WASD and the right mouse button for the jetpack and jet boots. Currently, there are three game modes. None of these are explained in game, so I'll explain them now from what I have gathered. Time is a game mode where you try move from one level to the next as quickly as possible. Score is the same as time, except you get score for killing enemies, and the last Depth, is similar to an endless runner game like temple run. You have to go as far as possible as fast as possible. Now that I have summarized the basics, I'll now move into pros and cons.
Pro:
-Odd graphical style that has charm
-Satisfying physics. It's always fun to plow through a building and turn around and see the hole I left.
-Good animation on the giants.
Cons:
-Poor graphics that are most likely assets of some sort.*
-The game literally can't handle its own physics. If you turn the graphics up to super fine and set off a shockwave, it will crash. Nukes crash the game regardless of the graphics.
-Alt-Tabbing will crash the game
-Your character resets his animation every time you shoot while flying or falling.
-Oh God, the music. Please have mercy on my ears.
-The monster noises and design are appalling.
-No explanation of ANYTHING
*I know I just praised the graphics, but it charm doesn't excuse garbage because it isn't a stylistic choice, it's just barebones. This is likely due to the developer's shortcomings.
TL/DR: Even though the pros I listed are outnumbered by the cons, it's still FUN. Fun, in my opinion, is the most important part of any video game. Although it has its flaws, I would definitely recommend this game.

I don't feel much comfortable criticising a beautifully-made game like this but when you compare it to the previous Sherlock Holmes title, Crimes and punishments, you realise that this is mostly an exact replica of the previous near perfect title, which of course is not a bad thing when it comes to copying an already successful formula developed by the same developers at least for quite a few times considering the excellent story to the game, but they have made a few tweaks to the gameplay and I'm afraid to say all of them are total disasters especially when you try to play the game on a PC.
I mean this is supposed to be an adventure game dealing most of the time with brainwork and the power of analysis and deduction while you mostly must deal with fast-paced action scenes in game that was not originally designed to be an RPG. I mean how you're supposed to enjoy the usually slow and careful flow of an adventure game when you are bombarded with ridiculous scenes time after time when you must keep your balance on a narrow piece of plank up in the air using a funny crappy combination of movement keys and your mouse at the same time? Why not leaving those kinds of gameplay to the guys behind Tomb Raider series and stick to develop an adventure title instead of trying miserably to include action elements into the gameplay? I have spent almost the same time to complete this as I have spent previously on Crimes and Punishments but to be honest it happened just because I had to play the action scenes multiple of times to beat them not thinking about solving puzzles and deducting things like an adventure game is supposed to be.
The logic system of the game has an obvious regress compared to Crimes and Punishments with most of the deductions the game wants you to make or considers to be the right ones lacking the logical justification or following strange hardly acceptable logics. While both Sherlock and Dr Watson had a complete plastic surgery to look more like modern guys which may be desirable by the younger audience, old school gamers like me who always known Holmes and Watson by Jeremy Brett and Edward Hardwicke still prefer the original faces over these stylish new looks, after all these guys were Victorian era characters for God's sake. Despite all the disappointments, I still recommend the game to adventure lovers considering all the effort has been made to copy as real as possible of a Victorian London atmosphere and the beautifully made graphics and artwork. The story is rich and entertaining with a twist or two and the voice overs are incredible.

Our five were all that was left of our tribe, the rest killed when the mechanoids fell from the sky. We took what we could and fled into the night, far away from from our homeleands. We settled in a mountainous forest region, and dug into the side of a mountain for protection and shelter. We planted our crops of potato, rice, healroot, and smokeleaf in the valley in front of us.
The first challenge was a minor raid, nothing serious. Soon after a wildfire raged across our valley, pushing us to the brink of exhaustion keeping it from reaching the crops. We picked up a new member being chased by pirates, and soon after faced our first large raid. A blight struck just before our first harvest of healroot and smoke leaf, setting us back. But things improved.
Three raids later our hunters and warriors were armed with sniper rifles and hunting rifles. We had armor, grenades, machine pistols, and a shotgun prepped and ready for the next raid. We had stockpiled vast quantities of food, and it even looked like our healroot would be ready for harvest before the growing season ended. Things were looking good, we were harvesting and hunting all that we could in preparation for the coming winter.
Then everything went horribly wrong. A group of boar charged into our home, attacking our farmers. The hunters responded, but in killing the boar three of our own were seriously injured. Just as we began rescuing everyone, our tender Banastra died from her wounds. Her bonded animal, a warg named Crazy, snapped and went manhunter. He savagely attacked our three remaining people, bringing them low. Our old healer Locust regained his feet, bleeding out, and managed to stop Crazy with his club. He collapsed soon after dragging two friends to hospital beds.
The next few hours were insane. People regaining their feet and dragging friends to beds only to collapse again. Those who could healed others the best they could while bleeding out. Everyone was in a constant state of pain and collapse. And before we had a chance to pull through, our scout Viper died from her wounds sending her bonded cat Ouija into a manhunter state as well. Before anyone could react Ouija was on them, savagely mauling anyone left standing and bringing them low. She roamed back and forth, attacking anyone as soon as they regained their feet. One by one the members of the tribe died from blood loss until only Dinosaur the loner remained, surrounded by the bodies of dead friends, bleeding out, and fading away as she listened to the cries of the cat roaming the blood soaked halls of their home looking for more victims.
That's Rimworld for yah.

tl;dr - only the graphics are good
It's another two-stick shooter where you try to survive waves of enemies and level up your abilities. The decent art disguises how amateurish the game feels. I tried playing as the redneck class (to take back 'Merrikuh from the monsters). There was no description of how the different classes play, so I was confused to find my controller vibrating at full power and the attack button (there IS at least a controller map) not working. I was eventually able to start attacking (the redneck swings his chainsaw just like a sword... did I mention how limited the animations are?) and figured out that the redneck has to take a minute to pull the ripcord on his chainsaw at the start of a fight. I think. Again, there's no warning about this, no cord-pulling animation, no proper sound effect of a chainsaw starting up, just vibration and a disabled attack button.
Oh, and I unlocked a molotov cocktail attack that you use by aiming with the right thumbstick and then launch by clicking in the thumbstick. That sounds like a terrible, awkward way to aim an attack because it *IS*.
I enjoy other games like this in small doses, and I don't mind simple graphics (I bought both of the Zombie Estate xbox indie games) but this has severe design flaws and just isn't fun. Many of the reviews are positive and one specifically mentions that it takes a few hours to get the feel of this game, but I'm not going to give it the benefit of the doubt.

This abandoned free to play game that allows you to torture your friends in a dungeon of madness (and possibly bondage, if your into that kinda thing) while throwing bombs, traps and minions at their faces.
It's easy to learn, fun and very hard to find a game due to the player base being next to non-existent in the player department. The game developers have also neglected the game completely, giving up on updates and any further content. This also means they have taken down the servers, forcing you into the old fashioned way of creating a lobby and waiting 30 mins for someone to join.
Aside from all that, the gameplay can be very fun for the first couple hours, but soons dies out because of the ease of unlocking content, but I'm getting ahead of myself.
So four people play in one game, one is the dungeonmaster who has mana and cards that act has abilities and your resource, this recharges over time and when the heroes reach certain checkpoint, it will recharge instantly and give you a new hand.
Now there are three different heroes, the Rogue, the Mage and the Warrior. The assassin uses high amounts of damage to kill stronger minions while the mage uses a mix between damage magic and helpful shields to prevent your allies from being knocked down. Last is the warrior, who is meant to take a beating from the dungeonmasters cruel and kinky toys of war.
The heroes must survive with only several shared lives to spare, forcing you to revive at all costs in order to complete the dungeon. If the heroes manage to make it into the boss room, they will have a bit of a problem keeping their sanity as the dungeonmaster controls the boss and will easily kill you on any difficulty higher than easy.
Decent monster variety, with the dungeonmaster being able to possess them if they have the correct talents.
Now, the cards the DM uses are unlocked with a currency you earn from playing bot or real games with players. You apply this to buy different minions, traps, bombs, turrets or bosses. These are much to easy to obtain, making the game pretty short and currency near worthless.
It's free, it's dead and it's a good game to play for an hour or two, by yourself or with friends. Give it a go, but don't expect anything in the long term.

You loved the original and want an untainted remix on your modern machine... only with sharper graphics, stronger AI and more maps! Or, if you're new to the scene, want an RTS which balances the build-up of an empire with decent-paced games (and you can stomach how old it is)
A fine example of a remaster done well! If you have the burning taste of nostalgia for Age of Empires - this is easily the best version to go for.
It's a clean upgrade of the original game and its expansion, Age of Conquerors - bringing in very welcome improvements: Sharper graphics, smoother movement, stronger AI... all whilst leaving the fundamental nuts and bolts very much alone and un-fudged with. There's no attempt to 'reimagine' here, it's exactly what you loved, only better. (Well... except the new fire, but there's a mod for that). There are also balance changes; but these have, thankfully, been honed over thousands of hours of top, competitive play... so are not the result of horrifyingly whimsical "hey, I think Teutonic knights are too slow.... You know what they need? Bazookas".
For a veteran who wants to see life breathed into one of their favourite titles - this one should tick the box nicely!
Now... if you're
to the series, this is where it gets a little tricky. The game will undoubtedly feel dated to the likes Total War, Dawn of War or Battle for Middle Earth. So a few things to bring your attention to when pondering this game:
Its strength though is, to me, its balance. You have decent-scale base-building, resources to harvest, scouting, harassing and all-out combat. The progression is paced brilliantly so that the defender starts with the biggest advantage but, over the 4 ages (akin to 'tiers'), the balance swings more in favour of the aggressor - providing a nice build-up in games that can last anywhere from 40 minutes to a few hours (in general). I find the larger focus on economy makes for a refreshing strategic change, especially in late game where it opens up more opportunities for thwarting your opponents with your medieval shenanigans. The trade-off is that you do not necessarily get epic clashes of armies, but more ongoing skirmishes.
For me, it's fundamentally the enjoyable balance of economy and military. You get the fun base-building and build-up of an empire, married with a decent pace of play... Kinda like a pocket-Total War, if you will (albeit with considerably fewer units). Empires in a 2 hour slot. If the pace piques your interest - it might be worth a spin!

Every battle with a bot is epic, from the first sound of a chalk-board roar, to the glimpse of a cross through the gridline, to the fantastic swoop and crash as the monster lands and draws its cross. The art, animation and sound design for the game is stupendous across the board. At first the noughts look generic, but closer inspection reveals fantastic subtle details in their anatomy. Our favorite aspect, though, is the sound of their chalk-scraping, which also has a secondary sound like a giant flute, providing musical character and power to these mighty beasts.
Because there is no legitimate reason to not defy the laws of physics.

I don't know if I've missed anything, but this game is so uninspiring it's hardly a surprise that I don't especially care. Do not pay any more than $2.50 USD for this title.

•	   Having your vehicle transform into four different shapes gives the game a great deal of variety. That, combined with the fact that most of the tracks change every other lap, makes it so that you don’t feel like you’re always doing the same thing.
•	         Having seven different mods for every character makes it so you can use whatever character you like, even if you can’t deal with the way it initially plays (lack of handling / acceleration / speed / etc).
•	         Has a decent amount of tracks (and of course, mirror versions) but could use some more. One of the DLCs added an extra track, but since not everyone has it, it never gets selected in online matchmaking. In addition, the new track feels pretty bland, there aren’t many obstacles or variety at all.
•	         S class is pretty damn hard, mainly due to abusive amounts of rubberbanding. But once you master those tracks, it’s an awesome challenge and feels pretty rewarding to win. However, even S class isn’t much compared to online matchmaking, especially if you put yourself in a lobby full with players with their ranks in the 1500’s or above. S class challenges are also pretty difficult and require practice most of the time.
•	 The online matchmaking itself works pretty well and it’s fun, but there’s (arguably) too much time between races. Ten seconds to vote for one out of three tracks, and then forty-five seconds just to choose a character is too much. Also, don’t make me choose my character after every race. Just give me the same one I used in the previous one by default. If I want to change into another one, I can…after all, I have forty-five seconds to do it….
•	         Speaking of characters, the AGES character comes as a pleasant surprise, with its unique sounds and transformations which you’ll no doubt recognize. On the other hand, having NiGHTS and Reala in the game AS THE vehicle feels like a bad joke. At least their All-Star transformations look good.
•	         There’s a healthy amount of achievements, even though it would have been cool to see every in-game sticker have its own. Some achievements involve playing with four local players, which is not a good idea. Not many people have that amount of controllers, not to mention the fact that split-screen multiplayer is becoming a thing of the past. It would have been more sensible to make these achievements doable with Steam/PSN friends.
•	         The game runs great and looks amazing and crisp on PC, but as usual with sonic PC ports, there’s a specific zone (in this case the Samba Studios track) that tends to drop the framerate. That being said it’s still a pretty good port, but still suffers from the same problem as all the other sonic PC ports that came before it: the graphical options menu is in a separate executable and must be run before the game. Also it forces you to skip through a bunch of stuff before you get to the main menu every time you launch the game but at least on the PC, there’s a fix for that.
As a conclusion, this is definitely an extremely satisfying and challenging game, especially if you have a couple of friends to play online with. SEGA will certainly milk this game some more by slowly adding more characters as they’ve been doing in the past. This is reinforced by the fact that the game is still selling and the online community is still pretty active.
The game isn’t expensive and has been on sale again and again, with prices reaching under 7€ at times. Definitely a good buy for any fan of SEGA and/or kart racers.

Cons

I'm still annoyed at this one scene where some Nazi gets his head cut off with a chainsaw off screen >:(
I get that the Campaign was the main focus but why not implement some extra features like multiplayer death match or coop extra content never hurts

Also none of the cut scenes are skip able
This game has a pretty horrible hacking/lock picking mechanic from what I've gathered there's an alternative method for this but instead of giving you an option it gives you 1 moral choice at the beginning of the game that affects how you hack/lock pick and a few bits of the story
I don't think this game gives you enough ammo to work with it just seems to max out to easily

This may seem minor but trust me some of these reload animations go on way to long
This game only features one double barrel shotgun for one level that can't be dual wielded and can only fire one barrel at a time :(

There's a hidden Wolf 3D level in this game which is cool but like DooM 4 with its hidden classic levels this also seems pretty clunky with how the classic levels just don't merge to well with all the modern touches although its not as bad as DooM 4 in this regard
This doesn't really feel like a classic fps with a few modern touches rather it feels like a modern fps with a few classic touches and the end result just isn't that good
So overall while I did have fun with this game it's still fun to shoot Nazis but I feel like this game just has way to many flaws for me to honestly recommend it if you must buy it just to keep your Wolfenstein collection complete then I'd say wait for a sale it's not so bad that you'd be better off completely ignoring it

Since I'm not typically interested in these sorts of games, I was pleasantly surprised when Oxenfree exceeded my expectations.
The main strength of this game is that it tells a compelling story complemented by voice actors who do an excellent job of making the characters and their interactions sound genuine. Furthermore, it has good sound effects and features a quirky but interesting soundtrack to set the tone of each scene. The environments are also visually stunning and filled with details, and the art style does not seem to affect exploration or gameplay in any negative way.
The only downside to this game is that there isn't more story to enjoy (It's approximately 5 hours), although it makes up for this with replayability, providing a vast selection of choices and outcomes to go back and explore, and even by making subtle adjustments to the story the second time around.
Overall, I found Oxenfree to be an incredible and thoroughly enjoyable game. If you are still on the fence about it, I'd strongly recommend using the game's trailers to determine if Oxenfree is for you, as I feel they are a good representation of what to expect in the game.

I bought this game on a whim at full price out of boredom and wanting something different. I never got into Prison Architect and this looked similar so I was very skeptical about it from the get go. I thought that a game like this isn't one that you can tell whether you enjoyed it or not accurately within the first two hours of play, but I was very wrong on that front. At first I attempted without the tutorial, but immediately decided to try the tutorial within 5 minutes because it wasn't self explanatory as I had expected. This was not a bad thing. The amount of depth within this game is insanse. Always new things that I'm learning.
As of writing this review I have 300 hours in this game and I can say that almost every time I start it I learn something new. When I purchased it, it was on Alpha 15, now it is on Alpha 16. It says that this game is in Alpha and early access, but this is the first game that I've bought with such a disclaimer that feels like a finished product. Updates may not come every week, but they seem to be substantial in size. Even if the developer left the game right this moment, I wouldn't give this game a negative review. The amount of depth is staggering.
The modding scene is amazing and I love the Steam workshop as well. If you have any qualm with any aspect of the game bychance there is a strong chance that someone has made a mod to change that part of the gameplay. There is a overhaul mod that turns the game medieval only with extreme depth added to that part of the game. I figured that around 100 hours I would get bored of the vanilla game and install that mod to spice things up. I still haven't installed that mod and I'm sure that it will give me another hundred or more hours of gameplay when I decided that I've finally had enough of vanilla gameplay.
I cannot recommend this game enough, even at full price.

Rimworld is unexpectedly great, and has ruined all other colony management games for me.  You can't see the best part in the screenshots, because it is the game director, which chooses when to create game events like disasters, raids and other threats to your colony. The rest of the game is good, combining standard features of colony games to make what would be a satisfying game, with colonists that have distinct personalities and preferences, enough that I remember them by name, work around their problems and get the most out of their best skills.
There are some less-great parts, like the UI has some bugs and is confusing or frustrating at times, but overall, this Early Access game is superior to all the released colony games I have played so far, and sets a new bar for all the future ones.

The great strength of this game is in how easy it is to get everything up and running for fast-paced multiplayer. Drop in and drop out online co-op and mechanics that are basic enough that any skill level can start playing and get something out of it. Everything is shared and the gameplay is all about working together and helping each other out in order to survive. Difficulty is also quite flexible, though I think there should be a "normal" mode added.
Something important that is understate though.. you don't level up, there isn't loot, and the weapons/armor to buy is all for show. This was very jarring to me at first since even pure action and hack n slash games often dabble in at least some of these elements. Dungeonland makes use of certain accessory slot items that create new, sometimes a bit convoluted abilities and passive skills for characters. Those, along with truly mastering how a character controls are key to being successful in this game. There isn't an RPG-like focus on growing and getting stronger. You grow and get stronger by becoming more proficient at controlling your character and working well with others.
While I am terrible at it, the dungeon master mode must also be mentioned because it's unique and rather amusing. Basically you can become the "bad guy" and be in charge of dispersing enemies, traps, and goofy manipulations of your foes (bots, or other players in co-op) on the battle field. Oh, and there is a button to press to laugh maniacally just for fun. Most of the more interesting unlockables are located in this mode.
As for whether the all access pass is worth getting.. it definitely is. The free to play version has substantially less worlds and you'll see more interesting battle scenarios (being able to ride creatures, deal with more environmental hazards, etc) and much more varied graphics and enemy types by going all-access.

Overall, a recommendable game.

A classic game so many of us grew up with, Age of Empires II was a fantastic game for its time. However, I only ever played it casually, a few skirmishes here and there, since its contemporaries included such gems as Homeworld and StarCraft. As such, I have no real nostalgia for this game.
Even were I to judge it against its contemporaries, to say nothing of the multitude of games released since, AoE2 doesn't seem to hold up all that well. It's a game of micromanagement with very little action queuing and even less AI. The units in AoE2 need constant attention in order to perform well - some may find this exciting and "skilful" but for me, it seems like a completely unnecessary burden on the player. There's not even an auto-explore option for scouts. Resource collection could likewise use with significant automation as well. I don't generally consider babysitting my peasants to be fun or engaging gameplay. Yet, in AoE2, if you don't keep an eye on them regularly, you'll wind up with much of your workforce idle and you'll fall behind your opponents. I'll pass on that.
Homeworld had a beautiful 3D map that allowed players to develop tactics in three dimensons, using different approaches and forcing one's opponents to expect attacks from all directions. StarCraft had three distinct yet balanced races, and while it still relied heavily on micromanagement, it felt like less of a chore.
There seems to be a cultish following for AoE2 that I don't really understand. It's a product of its time, and I'd understand its popularity far better if there weren't significantly better games available even around the time of its initial release.
Buy this only if you want a hit of nostalgia. There are better RTS games out there. Many of them.
