I do not know many games that tried to emulate and challenge the original master of the line tower defence, Plants vs. Zombies (
). Battle Ranch takes the same basic principle and, frankly, merely does it again. They should have at least made the turrets something else than fruits. Still, there are some differences for its own merit.
Every level throws a bunch of different zomb... uh, I mean freaking boar vikings at the ranch and you have to defend it by planting defensive turrets. There are both fast-loading pea shooters and burst turrets with longer reload-times, turrets with slowing capabilities, debuffers and outright defensive plants that block enemy movement or projectiles from hitting your plants. There are single-use items like bear traps and different area-attack bombs all the way to the slowly replenishing banana missile silo. Mobs sometimes drop special single-use items as well. Defences are no real innovation in tower defence but adequate enough.
There is a good variety of different enemies from the basic grunt through more enduring varieties to ones with special abilities like flying, fast moving capabilities or tunneling under everything. There are several tanks too. Alas, within these special capabilities the boars do not differ more - every boar of a certain special type looks and behaves always exactly the same way. It would have been nice to see some variation or maybe stronger or weaker types of the specific specialities. However, noting that almost all the game graphics files are plain images, some crazy graphics mods might become available in time.
Different from
the six-row field is divided into two separate parts: the garden and the turret field. Field hosts your defensive capabilities while in the garden you play a constant mini-game of planting and harvesting fruit for score that's used to buy turrets. There are 18 different garden plants, one for each turret type. They differ from each other with their reharvesting times and score production rates, and in addition few of them have to be replanted after harvesting. You get a full score (i.e. a star) from a level if you harvest all of the fruits required by the level.
One thing that's nice is that you don't have to click every single fruit you harvest - simple slide by the mouse cursor is enough. However, annoyingly enough the frame rate appears to be locked to 15 FPS, resulting in clunky animations. Also, the PC port (Battle Ranch was originally a phone/tablet game) has merely one resolution available, which is a huge oversight. The early levels are also super-easy so I'd wish there was a turbo button to speed things up. That or it should generally be slightly faster paced. Also, you can't redo levels: you have to play through the whole thing again if you miss a star for that season perfection achievement.
The story mode has 50 levels divided into five seasons (the regular ones + unpredictable) plus a couple of special levels for each season. The only differences between the regular seasons are the fruits and the obstacles that you have to clear to fill the whole garden: grass, stones, tree stumps and snow are just reskins of the same stuff, as are the "tools" required to clear/harvest them. In the unpredictable season and bonus levels between stages some special effects can affect the garden and your plants, like rain grows more grass to block the garden (minor annoyance) or localized tornados destroy plants in random locations. Unpredictable season is clearly the most challenging (and suitably, the last one) of the otherwise easy story seasons.
After story you can hurl yourself into the bonus games and mini games: there's a pure gardening mode and a long defence mode with several stages of enemies with the same fruit defenders. It's a shame there were often just one or two levels of the more intriguing mini games like the one where the field is filled with treasure chests, each one containing either a boar or a weapon to use againts them, a click opening the surprise. Myself, I found the puzzle levels of Boarmania the most interesting, for in those the roles are reversed: you are given a set amount of boars and you have to destroy the gardens behind rows of defensive plants. There were 15 levels of these but I wouldn't have minded having more.
Like any farming game, this one also has a silly garden for you to waste hours with. Any garden plants can be planted there with a set fee and you'll get some money for the plants thus harvested. This is probably the most viable way to get the two grindy achievements (get 1 million dollars and harvest 100000 fruits). Fortunately, you can hire a slow-walking but tireless farming gnome to do the harvesting for you and let the game run on the background while you play something else. Nevertheless, it's still going to take a lot of time if you want them. I've effectively AFKed some 50 hours of my game time and silently grinded the fruits in the background while actually hacking away at knights or ruling vast kingdoms elsewhere. Oh, and there's also a barn with potential (and quite expensive) cows and chickens and stuff but I figured it was a waste of grinding time to grow chow for animals (unintentional shout-out to vegetarianism).
In effect, there's about 30 hours of real playing involved. I'd call it Above Average and in my opinion it's worth its list price of 7 euros especially if you loved
, maybe about half that if tower defence still tickles your fun bones. The oversights in porting it to PC dull the outlook, though the devs have said they are at least looking into the resolution matter. Modding might make it more interesting even though there's no Steam Workshop at the time or (AFAIK) planned out.
If you're sceptical whether you'd like it, there's a demo on the game's Steam Store Page. Initially I tried it and was satisfied to buy it at launch, but it's also a good way to see whether you can put up with the resolution, clunky animations and the similarities to
. It's convenient that you can continue the full version from where you were left in the demo.

Alright, so to be fair, I managed to nab this game for free from galagiveaways, however I'll try my best not to let that influence my review by any means.
The game comes across as being a PvZ clone based on what you'd see, but there's actually a lot of differences that made it stand out to me. First and foremost, you can't just plant down your growth plants and expect them to instantly generate your resources. You end up having to water them first, which adds to another level of management, aside from placement of defenses. In addition to that, there appears to be a mechanic that involves collecting a certain number of fruit or vegetables from those plants in order to get a star for each level, though to be honest I'm not entirely sure what that adds aside from a sense of completion.
The watering mechanic seems to come further into play during later stages of the game from what I can tell, and... Well, actually makes for an interestingly frantic gameplay compared to the relatively slow looking animation of the pigs you're fighting. There's a lot to keep track of at once, but it never feels too disorienting, just... Like there's a lot to do and keep track of which is actually pretty good.
So, if I can edit, I will once I get further into the game, I'm only up to the level at which the player can unlock the greenhouse, so please bear with me for now. The greenhouse is about what you'd imagine from similar games, allowing the player to generate some coins and... In my opinion being a rather fun gameplay mechanic, but more likely than not that opinion stems from my appreciation of idle/incremental gaming.
So far, I'd give this game a 7/10, it's not perfect, the animations feel somewhat awkward in places and the art style isn't necessarily the most pleasing, but the gameplay itself is really solid and it's definitely worth picking up if you're a fan of similar games. Seriously though, it feels like there's a lot of content I'm missing, all things considered, so it's safe to say it's pretty packed with enough to keep you entertained for a while.
Thank you for reading if you did, and sorry for this being so drawn out.

I liked this game quite a bit. It does the whole trade thing pretty well. It's definitely one of the better economy games released recently. It not only allows you to build ships and set up trade routes but also allows you to build colonize and maybe be a pirate if you want. I'll go into some pros and cons:
Pros:
-You aren't stuck playing the economy game. You can play a military game by being a pirate or fighting with other countries.
-The game does the trading really well. The amount of resources aren't overwhelming (although the amount also isn't very impressive either). It's easy to just jump into the game.
-There is a good amount of ships and you can customize each one you build by spending a little extra money.
Cons:
-The colony management is a little too simplistic. It does add to the game but it is only picking a building you want to build from a list.
-There are only limited colony spots that you can build colonies on. I would've liked to just see where the resources were and build a colony accordingly.
-You have to buy the resources from your colonies to sell them in the Home Country (Europe) and, as far as I can tell, you can't trade with other colonies. Instead you trade resources via diplomacy but those resources can only be traded via diplomacy and you cannot sell them in Europe. Because of this it is very possible to go negative and you can't do anything about it.
All in all it's a fun game and I would recommend it. Especially now (11/27) with a sale going on. Certainly worth the $4 for the base and $6 for the complete.

Although I'm not 100% sure exactly what this "ManiaPlanet" service is that Nadeo is providing with all of their games, the latest iteration of Trackmania delivers high amounts of fun and nearly infinite replayability for a good price. This racing game feels like a direct sequel to the DOS game Stunts. The focus is on over-the-top fast-paced racing on impossible tracks with flips and loops.
There is a robust track editor that allows you a nearly absurd degree of customization, and you can share your tracks online. Some servers I have seen have upwards of 200 tracks, and no repeats. There is a seemingly robust car editor, but I have been unable to get it to do much other than make solid color cars.
The control of this game is fabulous, and it allows you to seamlessly switch from controller to keyboard. Offline split-screen multiplayer is present as well, by the way. There's lots of good drifting action to be had, and some of the maps I've seen online have been fabulous high-speed adventures.
The gameplay centers around playing a map and getting the best time possible. You have zero collision with the other cars/ghosts that are racing. It's all about your performance on the track.
Unfortunately, this game is bundled with some program that Nadeo calls "ManiaPlanet" that seems to deliver absolutely nothing. I can view my Nadeo games in a Wii-like format, but for no reason. I have some weird currency called "Planets" that I seem to get awarded randomly, and I guess I can buy things with it or donate it to servers? It's very unclear and nebulous, honestly.
The signature insane amount of clutter that servers seem to throw on your screen is present as well. If you are a useless-stats freak, you'll love being able to see your personal best, the personal best of everyone else playing, the time, the local time, the time the moon will rise, the personal best of the author, all the medal times, how many times the track has been played, the song being played (which seems to be an awful lot of Guns and Roses), the amount of people playing, the ladder ranking of people playing... etcetera. There's just too much damn clutter on the screen that you can't seem to get rid of.
You might want to wait until it's on sale. If you're not sure you'll enjoy it, there's a free version of Trackmania on Steam called United Star Forever or something stupid like that. There's probably more people playing the free version, even. I'm in the top 1000 players in the United States and top 100 in California after six hours of playing the damn game. There's nobody playing.
Overall, damn fun, but needs a community.

This game isn't super bad, but still I feel like I can't recommend it.
The Devil's Daughter is a detour from the traditional point-and-click style of former Sherlock Holmes games from Frogwares. This may cloud my judgement as I am used to the style of the former Sherlock games, but it is clear that they have tried to mainstream the game series to get more action-oriented gamers onboard. This may have worked, but in the process they made the puzzles less interesting and the plotline obvious. The "twist" in The Devil's Daughter is very obvious and the daughter is a very unsympathetic character, making the main story fall a little flat for me.
I enjoyed the earlier parts of the game more than the latter parts. Some of the new mechanics are interesting (like a minigame where you have to stalk someone or another where you have to run away while simultaneously making decisions on your path based on Sherlock's information), but later in the game, a lot of the puzzles become long and tedious even after the point where you have figured out how to solve them. It actually feels like some of them have been made extra long in order to stall time to make the playtime longer.
Buy this game if it is on sale, you have played all other good point-and-click/adventure games and are looking for an okay puzzle game with some quick time events (or if you are new to puzzle/adventure gaming and looking to ease into the genre as this has some action elements), but I would not buy this at full price.

A lot of people have seen this game on youtube, perhaps even on steam in their "recommended" games list. Plenty of high reviews out there.
They don't do it justice.
From the fantastic AI that is only improving with each update, to the ever-growing content within the game, and coupled with the attention to realism, this is a colony simulator that trumps all simulators.
From having to go from crash-landing on a planet with nearly nothing, trying to survive with Neolithic methods to create food sources, shelter, temperature control, and defending your fledgling village from feral tribes, to having an advanced base with hydroponics to grow food, advanced climate control to scoff at the vicious blizzards and heat waves outside your walls, to laying down blistering energy barrages against terrifying advanced foes that want to annihilate all you have built, Rimworld has something for everyone. Your colonists' needs and wants play a part as well, as you must keep them sane as they brave all these dangers.
Nothing I can write does this game justice. My advice? Buy it. While listed as "Early Access", this game is far from just playable. Rimworld is already a polished product. It only excites me more knowing that the developer still thinks they need to add more! Well worth the money, and the Steam Workshop support only adds to the fun.

$1 Ride is a simple arcade game that is not worth your time even at $1. The aim of the game is to keep your speed going by collecting speed upgrades while also collecting point items. You're supposed to balance your speed and non-speed pickups, but you can only get 1 non-speed pickup before losing all speed. This means that in order to score high you have to constantly speed up and slow down which isn't very fun - the game would be more fun if the point items were scrapped and score was based on distance.
There is an item in the game called the rocket which destroys asteroids. The asteroids take away 1 hp and slow you down - if you're going at full speed these won't slow you down and you'll live so they're not a huge threat. The other obstacle, the black hole, will always kill you if you run into it regardless of your hp or speed and for some reason rockets will not destroy them. This just makes the rockets feel pointless, the health pickups increase your speed and health while the rockets destroy asteroids which won't kill the player...the whole game just feels poorly designed.
The presentation is decent, I suppose. I wouldn't recommend paying $1 for this game as there's not much to do, there's a checklist of achievements and some unlockable ships, but it does not tell you how to unlock these ships and I swear that half of the achievements are broken. Avoid this game unless you really want the badges, that's the most I got out of it.

Hero Siege is a great 2-player local coop game.
In Hero Siege, you fight wave after wave of enemies, then fight a boss, then do it again in the next world.  While that sounds like a game that has been made 1000 times before, Hero Siege does it really well.  Each player can choose one of eight heroes, each with their own special abilities.  You level up your hero by killing enemies, increasing your stats and learning new abilities.  Those stats/abilities are permanent.
Additionally, in each playthrough you find gold and artifacts.  The gold can be used to buy potions or increase your stats more (for that playthrough only), and the artifacts give you further stat-boosts, or sometimes special abilities.  These temporary stat boosts count much more than the permanent ones.  The net result is that, while leveling up your characters definitely does help, the outcome of a given playthrough depends much more on how well you played.  It's entirely possible
to beat the game on your first playthrough.
There are enough different artifacts/enemies to keep the game interesting through multiple playthroughs.
The downside is that the game is currently extremely buggy.  During 10 hours of gameplay, we encountered 3 game-breaking bugs which set us back several hours each, along with countless other less serious bugs.  We played local-coop; the developer recently (mid-July 2014) released an experimental online coop mode, which I've heard is even buggier.
Fortunately, the developer is very active on the forums, and has promised to continue fixing the bugs people find.  The latest bugfix was currently 4 days ago, so he seemed to be making good on his word.
We tried playing again today.  The majority of the bugs we found a year ago have been fixed, but have unfortunately been replaced by a whole slew of new bugs.  The game is
unbeatable, entirely because the game still crashes after several hours of play, and doesn't correctly save your relics.
The developer still seems to be active, which is good.  And this game is a TON of fun.  Just be prepared to lose your game at any time due to the massive number of bugs.

This game is really underappreciated. Dungeonland has the gameplay of Diablo, and a lot of co-operation is a must. Every game starts with a team of three players, and there are three unique classes to try out, with unlockable branches for each: The Warrior, Rogue, and Mage. It's essentially a dungeon crawler, but each one is challenging, and can be done in bursts of about 15 minutes each. The vibrant cartoon-like style of the game is quite refreshing among all the other darkly-styled games in the Free to Play section. There are also unique abilities and perks that you can buy in-game, and there are creative and unique hats and clothing items for your characters, as well. Finally, if you're tired of being the hero, you can play the role of the villain with DM Mode, where you control the enemies and monster spawners, and your goal is to brutally murder the heroes in your dungeon in the worst ways imaginable. It's a great, creative game. I highly recommend it.

It's tic-tac-toe. Noughts and crosses for those in the UK.
This rendition is a free indie product, so at least it has that going. The base game's also free if you have pen and paper, so there really wasn't a choice regarding pricing if the developer wanted to stay competitive on the market. I genuinely dig the freeware aesthetic it has going on, sort of like something you'd find on a '100 Games!!' CD that actually cared about itself. I find those collections pretty damn sad, though, so I'm not aware of any that actually do.
As I said earlier, this is tic-tac-toe. If you actually find someone in multiplayer, or invite someone (to find you in matchmaking, of course, since there's no discrete room creation here). you essentially try to make them screw up. If you play against the computer, you set the difficulty to easy if you want any outcome that isn't a stalemate, and even then it's not guaranteed you'll not stalemate.
There's new variations of the game, which is where things get a little crazy. The titular 'ultimate' mode replaces every square in a standard tic-tac-toe board with its own little board. You try to mark the little boards and win them to make a mark on the big board. The crucial thing here is that you're not actually told that marking the top, middle or bottom of a small board dictates where the next player has to play on the big board. In this case,
, a tutorial that you'll only find in the
. It also doesn't help that the variations in small board color that let you know whether you can play there or not seem to be designed to frustrate colorblind people and those who use any sort of screen dimming whatsoever.
'Forget' mode erases the last move made that's four moves old. It's interesting until you realize that it basically means any mark that would let you win is erased so the AI can eventually win instead.
The Steam achievements - for a tic-tac-toe game, I will remind you once again - include ones for various flavors of winstreaks and for reaching 'level 50'. They also don't work in classic mode for some reason, but I digress. The worst thing about this game, really, is that according to the minimum requirements it won't run on Windows XP. That's a bit more flattering: this game is also like something you'd find on a fresh install of XP, except not quite as polished.
Despite the detached, sarcastic tone I affected throughout this review, there's genuine value to be had here. If you know someone, whether a Steam friend or an offline friend you communicate with long-distance, who you'd like to mentally wrestle while you trash-talk them via Steam (because I'm not sure this game even has a chat feature), this is for you. If you're a masochist who thought chess against Deep Blue's extended family wasn't painful enough, you'll like it too.

This game has a very hard learning curve and can be very stressful to understand on your first play through even if you were doing sandbox mode. However, overtime this game becomes extremely addicting and is well worth it's price tag. In short, I can describe the game in three vital areas:
- Building, maintenance, and development of a studio and facilities that contribute to your publicity and production
- Very detailed 6-phase production of a movie (can work on 6 movies at a time, though it is very difficult to do so if you're trying to make 6 star quality screenplay) Script-writing phase, casting (Even the Producers and Directors you choose matter) , production, marketing, and release.
- After all of your production work, then it comes to release. How did the audience like it, critics, did it make or lose money, where did you open it, what was the appeal? Then there is several award ceremonies that occur over the course of the year (this game is turn-based on a monthly scale) and your movie winning an award can increase home release sales if you choose to market it - adds prestige to your studio - and you can create a filmseries that makes even more money as you attract a fanbase to that series. Huge emphasis on this point, it's very fulfilling too after all of your hard work
Overall, this is a very addicting turn-based-tycoon-style game that really makes you feel involved in the Entertainment Industry.

After Frogwares' excellent
(
) in 2014,
is a big letdown.
The investigation and deduction mechanics are still excellent ... but there are fewer facts to be gathered, and far less secondary information available to lead an attentive player to the correct conclusion of a case.  Unless I was missing it all,
simply throws a bunch of suspects at you and has you pick one.  If you choose incorrectly, it makes no attempt to convince you that you may have been right, and instead practically insists that you replay the ending and throw another dart, until you finally get a case-closing cutscene in which the criminal screams his confession in 10-foot-high letters.
This lack of subtlety is perhaps due in part to
's new emphasis on action and minigames.  Previous games had some of this to break up all the dialogue and text, but in this game, minigames are the meat and potatoes and the actual investigations are reduced to dressing.
Characterization is disappointing as well.  The coldly burning brilliance of the previous games' Holmes has been replaced by the amiable blandness of a "rebooted" everyman character.  Holmes' delightful arrogance is gone, and we are left with a nice guy who is pretty smart, but just isn't special any more (unless it's in his ability to take several rifle shots to the chest without apparent discomfort later).  Then there's the precocious adoptive daughter character who cuts down Holmes even more.  I don't care who her father was; no one wants to see Sherlock Holmes lose an argument to a 10-year-old.  Who plays a Sherlock Holmes game to see a heartwarming sitcom about a clever criminologist who's got a lot to learn about parenting?  Who is this for?
These are not the only faults in the writing.  The cases themselves have gone from very personal to goofy and outlandish.  The cases in
were, as much as they were about gathering evidence, centered around
: their passion, madness, greed, jealousy, and more.
is about jumping from flagstone to flagstone fast enough to escape the deathtrap in an ancient temple, or guessing whether a murder was committed by a robot or a ninja.  Not joking.
A
silliness is acceptable and even to be encouraged; after all, the Doyle Holmes stories used such devices as a poisonous snake trained to crawl through a ventilator as a murder method; but
blundered way over the line here.
Could the new publisher be to blame?  Did Bigben Interactive insist on a friendlier Holmes, more action, more QTEs?  Or did Frogwares themselves change their minds about what these games should be?  If the former, perhaps it's best if the next game (if there is one) be published by Focus Home Interactive, who produced
.  In any case, I hope Frogwares brings Holmes back down to earth, with sensible cases painted from the motivations of believable personalities, plenty of secondary information available to encourage thoughtful players to reason out the solutions, and sparse use of action to break up the investigation, not the other way around.

Fun, addictive, cynical movie production simulator!
It's quite a simple process - you pick name, genre, subgenre and themes for your film.  Then you pick writers, actors, directors and producers to create it for you, based on their experience, talents and fees.  Then you find out how it did!  Did the public like it?  Did the critics like it?  Did it make you money?  Then you make the cynical choices like producing 10 sequels to your terrible action movie series in order to fund your serious movies.
Don't expect this to be like The Movies, where you actually get to see any of your film animated.  You also don't have floor plans and rooms to manage, it's not that kind of sim.  Take a look at the screenshots - that's pretty much what you're getting.
It looks simple, but it's a lot of fun!

You know, I love Rimworld. After getting to grips with the new engine (used by another very popular game of this genre) and the fact that the people have no feet or legs, (it seemed odd to me at first, but I got over it in the need to plant some corn!), I've clocked up over 600 hours of gameplay and I will recommend the game highly to anyone who asks my opinion of it.
However, I have one bugbear that I find very frustrating, and that is, that every time the Dev releases an update, my established colonies are unplayable. I have to keep restarting, and since it is not a 'quick-play' type of game, in fact, it might take you weeks of gameplay to finally get to end-game, ie. building that spaceship to be able to get your colonists off the planet and back home where they belong, I've come to the conclusion that I might never get there. The stability of the framework seems shaky, and I never know when I log on, if I'm going to be able to load my current game or not.
That said, I have soldiered on...
because the actual gameplay is stable. I'm not experiencing mid-game crashes or other weird stuff happening.
The stories that are created, as much by you as by the game itself, are always unique and entertaining. You just cannot make some of this♥♥♥♥♥♥up. :}
It is also a builder, crafter and farmer's dream, particularly if you have signed on for a couple of the *choice* mods that extend that content. Lots and lots of equipable items for your little blobbies too.
And, if you're a bit of a p*ssy like me, who doesn't like to wake up to find foaming-at-the-mouth hordes coming over the horizon while you stand there thinking 'Oh SH*T!!' then you can play in any number of more relaxed modes too, from 'peaceful' to 'OH MY GOD!'. Suits me just fine because it doesn't exclude me on the grounds of not wanting to have my colony's guts ripped out and handed to me in a bag after two weeks of carefully building my palatial base.
Your environment presents a danger too. I always like that attention to detail in a game. If a polar bear is hungry, he'll definitely be on the prowl for man-flesh. If it's snowing, your people will need warm clothes. If you mine just anywhere, you might hack into a secret cave full of mechanoids who can annihilate you where you stand.
Lovely fun. All of it. Just find a way to stop breaking my games with the version updates, please. I feel quite stuck on repeat here, and it gets old eventually.

The Talos Principle is a Christian puzzle game. And yes, you read that right.
Gameplay: You basically have to connect beams of light, with an increasing number of tools to your disposal. The actual puzzles are among the better ones in the industry but sometimes lack a real challenge.
Story: Mankind's extict. You are a robot AI trapped in a virtual garden of Eden. Your task is to preserve "humanity" by becoming as human as possible. So why is this a puzzle game? The game itself answers this question by stating that "curiosity is the most human of all traits." But what "being human" really means is up to your interpretation.
Philosophy and humor: During the game you read remnant messages from the last surviving humans and debate with Satan about God's motives via... instant messenger. This may sound weird, and at first it feels odd. But after completing the last chapter you experience the most amazing depiction of the devil in... well, basically ever.
Is this game still enjoyable for non-Christians?
To a degree. It has some excellent puzzles and is genuinely funny. The questions about what makes us human is interesting no matter your religion. But to fully understand the central message of this game you should at least know what the book Genesis is about.
It will violate Newton's first law of motion... and your wallet.

Sierra games are known for being ridiculous and scummy in some aspects. In spite of this, some of them still manage to be enjoyable -- but not the Space quests. Too many puzzles are based on random bruteforcing rather than logic, too many problems with silly solutions that you'd think could be solved in a much more straightforward, better way, too much cheesy, dumb humour. If you'd like to play a much better game in the exact same genre from the same company, the King's Quest series is a much better choice: and it even has the first three games available as free remakes.
If you do get this Steam version, be warned: the included manual provides copy protection solutions for Space Quest I and V, but doesn't give you the copy protection solution for Space Quest 6. Has pretty much everything you want out of a kart racer:  balanced power-ups, great level design, large cast of characters, plenty of challenge, smooth online play, local multiplayer, and some fantastic visuals.  If you can look past the fact that you might not recognise some of the racers then you have no reason not to give this game a try.  Seriously, it's easily one of the best kart racing games ever made... it's up there with CTR, Diddy Kong Racing, and whichever Mario Kart you prefer.
I know it can be easy to write this game off.  After all, how many Mario Kart clones did we see after the N64 version blew up?  But instead of merely copying another franchise and putting a Sega skin over everything, you'll quickly notice that the developers genuinely tried to take full advantage of every licence they got.  Putting as much detail as possible into each racer's kart and respective tracks.  The tracks are really well designed; they never get too long or feel too short, they contain plenty of variety thanks to the ability to jump between car/plane/boat, and often change dramatically as the race progresses.  The gameplay itself is a sweet mix of CTR and Diddy Kong Racing, but with their own unique take on the two.
The game's one weak point (outside of maybe the initial learning curve) is some of the character selection.  While they do try to include plenty of female characters, a few of their choices are kinda lame side characters, but it's a minor complaint and the roster is otherwise very creative and varied.  Plus the PC version has 31 (!) total characters, which is great.
If this is a style of game you enjoy or have ever enjoyed previously, I highly recommend picking this up.  If you can manage to play it with friends then you are in for some competitive gaming bliss.

This is my favorite style of horror game.  It doesn't bombard your eyes with graphic and unpleasant imagery or gory scenes, but with unsettling dialogue and eerie atmosphere.  It's scary, but scary in the sense that you don't understand what's going on, which drives you forward in search of the truth.
This style of games reminds me a lot of Life is Strange, and I'm happy to say that this game does a much better job of filling the dialogue with authentic-sounding "hip teen" language.  While the voice acting isn't perfect in
situation, it's generally very well done and feels very realistic for a group of teenagers in such a situation.  The cast in endearing and well written; the shortness of the game precludes any great depth of characterization, but what is there is enjoyable and there are enough twists and turns to keep you interested for the length of the game.
This isn't really a style of game where graphics are a huge factor, but still they're quite nice.  The backgrounds have an unique style that give the world a bit of a surreal touch, but the special effects are very nicely done.
The music is in the background and forgettable for most of the game, but the two or three points where it rises to the front are effective.  It's a good soundtrack if you like ambient synth, as that's the best way I can describe it.
If I had a critisism, I'd say that the game slows down a bit in the last third of the game, and loses a bit of the scaryness - too much is explained and it detracts from the unnerving scenes that were pulled off so well earlier.  The game is definitely worth finishing though, as there are some great twists.
If you like adventure games, horror games that are more atmosphere than gore, and even a fair bit of comedy, you should definitely pick up this game.  You can probably finish the entire thing in a day or two, depending on how deeply you dig.

This is a tentative thumbs up. The Devil's Daughter retains the strengths of Crimes and Punishments: the interesting and ambiguous cases and the clever deduction system that actually makes you feel like you're solving a mystery and not just following bread crumbs to a single solution. However, it also retains and exacerbates the weaknesses of its predecessor: QTEs, minigames and an awful ancient temple section. Yes, another awful ancient temple section because the one in the previous game was so well-received... seriously, I'd love to know what the designers were thinking when they decided to add tomb raiding to a Sherlock Holmes game. I understand the desire to appeal to a broader audience but adding a bunch of poorly-implemented elements from other genres is not the solution.
Thankfully, most of the QTEs, minigames and out-of-place puzzles can be skipped on the normal difficulty. I still completed them all but if you have a very low tolerance for such things, you can avoid them. I just hope that the next game focuses more on the sleuthing and less on the "visceral" elements. If I wanted action, I'd play an action game, not an adventure game.

It says that this game is in Alpha and early access, but this is the first game that I've bought with such a disclaimer that feels like a finished product. Updates may not come every week, but they seem to be substantial in size. Even if the developer left the game right this moment, I wouldn't give this game a negative review. The amount of depth is staggering.

If you have any qualm with any aspect of the game bychance there is a strong chance that someone has made a mod to change that part of the gameplay. I figured that around 100 hours I would get bored of the vanilla game and install that mod to spice things up. This game is by far one of my favorite early access/in development titles out there. It's not a finished game, so don't buy it expecting 100% polished graphics, controls, or a game free of glitches and bugs. That being said, if you enjoy tactical realism in your games, but don't want to or can't get into a game like ArmA, Squad is perfect for you.
Initially, I was part of the free play weekend offered (time of writing this is April 2017). I had been wanting to play Squad for a while, but I wasn't sure if I'd enjoy it. I should've played this game a long time ago. It's fun, challenging, and immersive. Squad is the perfect blend of the fast, frantic action of a game like Battlefield combined with the slow, tactical planning of a game like ArmA or the Project Realism mod.
Some suggestions and a pro/con list follow.
SUGGESTIONS
-Do not buy this game expecting constant gunfights and explosions. There is a lot of walking, riding in vehicles, and travel time in between fire fights.
-Try not to get discouraged if you die. You will die. A lot. And often times have no clue from where. There are no kill cams, radar hints, or damage direction indicators. This game is realistic in that regard.
-Take some time when you launch to go to the Firing Range, practice aiming and movement there first.
-Listen to your squad leader.
-Have a mic. This game requires a mic.
-Remember that friendly fire IS on.
PROS
-Immersive gameplay.
-Challenging yet rewarding difficulty experience.
-Servers are stable.
-Gameplay is tight and tactical, while still offering adrenline rush moments.
-Weapons handle and behave well, gunfights feel right.
-High replay value, with a variety of different modes to choose from.
-Sound quality is very high.
CONS
-Optimization needs work. Even on high end rigs you'll experience stutter lag and load time issues (very minor)
-There is no customization available, so there is no feeling of progression, despite having a scoreboard.
-If you use a controller (either Xbox or Steam) prepare to have to fiddle around figuring out the bindings. For Steam gamepad, I would suggest taking the time to set up a custom profile.
-Currently there are only a few different "roles" but I know the developer has plans for more.
TL;DR: Buy if you want a game that combines Battlefield and ArmA. Avoid if you don't like games that are challenging and require practice and critical thought.

I don't have much in the way of experience when it comes to writing long serious reviews. But I firgured since this review was getting more views I might as well redo this whole thing. So here it goes:
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Tales of the Borderlands is a choice-driven adventure game (in Telltale's signature format) in which you play as either Rhys, a Hyperion employee with big dreams and Finoa, a local con-woman ready to make her biggest con yet, taking place after the events of Borderlands 2.
In the first episode Rhys's promotion and all chances of moving up in the company are ruined when a rival steps in and becomes his new boss. Rhys then comes up with a plan to get back at them by stealing the vault key, an alien aritfact capable of unlocking great wealth and power, which led to his rivals promotion from right under their nose. With the help of his two best friends, Vaughn and Yvette, he makes his way to possibly the most dangerous planet in the galaxy, Pandora. Meanwhile, Finoa in her home town of Hollow Point on Pandora is preparing for her greatest con yet. Helping her she has her sister Sasha and their mentor/foster father Felix. Events unfold and the two must work together to discover a treasure of epic proportions!
People who have played any of Telltale's games will know what to expect in terms of gameplay. Small areas to navigate in which you look and interact with the enviroment with simple puzzles along with lots of cutscenes with many quick time events.
Needless to say, the game's main focus is on it's storytelling which it does very well. People who have not had the pleasure of playing any of the first two Borderlands games might get lost in terms of the lore (as well as a few jokes) but it is not needed as the game does a good job on focusing more on the central premise of the story. People who are familar with the Borderlands games will enjoying getting to see Pandora from a whole different view point (rather than just running around shooting everything). There are plenty of humour to be found in the writing even if you are not a fan and action cutscenes that are throughly entertaining!
So in summary: If you are fan of Telltale's adventure games then this is basically the same thing you are used only in a lighter setting and I highly recommend.

Definitely a recommendation for everyone who likes to think a lot about stuff (either solving puzzles or answering some philosophical questions, its up to you)

This is my favorite style of horror game.  It doesn't bombard your eyes with graphic and unpleasant imagery or gory scenes, but with unsettling dialogue and eerie atmosphere.  It's scary, but scary in the sense that you don't understand what's going on, which drives you forward in search of the truth.
This style of games reminds me a lot of Life is Strange, and I'm happy to say that this game does a much better job of filling the dialogue with authentic-sounding "hip teen" language.  While the voice acting isn't perfect in
situation, it's generally very well done and feels very realistic for a group of teenagers in such a situation.  The cast in endearing and well written; the shortness of the game precludes any great depth of characterization, but what is there is enjoyable and there are enough twists and turns to keep you interested for the length of the game.
This isn't really a style of game where graphics are a huge factor, but still they're quite nice.  The backgrounds have an unique style that give the world a bit of a surreal touch, but the special effects are very nicely done.
The music is in the background and forgettable for most of the game, but the two or three points where it rises to the front are effective.  It's a good soundtrack if you like ambient synth, as that's the best way I can describe it.
If I had a critisism, I'd say that the game slows down a bit in the last third of the game, and loses a bit of the scaryness - too much is explained and it detracts from the unnerving scenes that were pulled off so well earlier.  The game is definitely worth finishing though, as there are some great twists.
If you like adventure games, horror games that are more atmosphere than gore, and even a fair bit of comedy, you should definitely pick up this game.  You can probably finish the entire thing in a day or two, depending on how deeply you dig.

This one's actually pretty easy to sum up in a review, unlike other reviews I tend to do.
It
have a good story. It can be hard to parse at times, but things are more or less clear. The way dialogue is treated is interesting as well, even though the game suffers from the Fallout 4 school of limited sentences conveying multiple intentions. Or like LA Noire. Basically, expect to pick one dialogue option in one scene and get a completely different reaction and read than what you were expecting.
The art is actually very good. The 3D character models are more than a little janky, and the animation is passable at best, but that's largely drowned out by the great aesthetics and the camera that (wisely) chooses to remain distant from the characters.
Sounds design is actually top notch as well, and aside from some muddy mastering for some of the spookier voices does an amicable job at conveying what you need to know. The voice acting is delivered very well, and the character writing is on point for the most part, but expect characters to change emotions quickly if you interrupt an intense line of dialogue by making a joke about a statue you just looked at.
It IS an indie game, and I think that goes a long way in forgiving the very real flaws the game has. Having said that, it's kind of unfortunate that the game didn't have some better polish and time in the oven for the designers to think about how best to deliver the story.
One of the biggest problems with the game is just how slowly paced it is, as well as its reliance on backtracking, having a slow walk speed, even the radio - the key item for solving puzzles in the game - forces you to scroll through it so slowly so you don't miss the one frequency you need to open a door. Perhaps if the game was done in a first person perspective, or had a closer camera and better situational sound, a slower pace would add to the tension. Instead, the zoomed out look and colorful palette does the insistence on slow-paced gameplay absolutely no favors.
It actually makes you realize just how well designed the similar Firewatch is compared to Oxenfree. Firewatch also has a lot of walking around, talking with people and spooky conspiracies layed over character driven neurosis, but where Firewatch moves at a brisk pace and never felt like it wastes your time, Oxenfree can be a chore to get through. Double-damning is the game's use of New Game+ and multiple endings to fully understand the story. For that, I'm comfortable uninstalling the title and just watching someone on YouTube explain the story to me.
All-in-all, a great game that's worth the price, especially because of how constantly it's on sale. And a great buy if only to promote more games like this in the future. Let's just hope that whatever Night School Studio decides to do next, they hire a UX designer to trim the fat.

This is a departure from what made Crimes and Punishments so good - focus on decently good pacing, a compelling overarching narrative, enjoyable "deductive" gameplay and a fairly challenging moral conundrum in every case. The new additions and elaborations - drawn-out action sequences, QTEs, action puzzles - are mostly unnecessary. It's especially galling how every episode had to have them, even if it was shoe-horned in, just to make Sherlock more of an action hero (to go with his relatively youthful style in this game).
If I had to choose between playing through those sequences and having control taken away from me to watch a cinematic, fully scripted set-piece or even an Uncharted-style walking/running sequence without QTEs or button-mashing (e.g. the lost in the desert segment in U3), then I'm happy to choose any of the latter. The Wiggins sequence in the very first case was far too long - it felt like padding after the first minute already! That said, the ability to "explore" neighbourhoods also added very little immersion (hearing people say banal things in Cockney, woo!) and again, felt like padding.
In terms of "content," there are actually four cases to solve, plus a couple of mini-ones (at the start of Infamy and the overarching story is really a mini-case). The cases were varied and interesting (I enjoyed the fourth the most, though the moral conundrum of the first two were best). The overarching story wasn't bad but the reveal was disappointing, the identity and motivation of the "villain" were telegraphed and their plan didn't make a whole lot of sense in restrospect.
I didn't experience any bugs or glitches, and the only two times I was genuinely stuck for what to do was before I realised that a fully green "reticle" on an object means that you've finished "exploring" it completely. I enjoyed the graphics and details (as well as the written content and dialogue, as brief as it was) so props to Frogwares for that.
Overall I'd give this game a 7 out of 10. I want to not recommend this game to let Frogwares know that they're straying from what made C&P good and that they should focus their efforts elsewhere (than action sequences) in terms of developing the series but it would be like punishing the horse for the jockey's choices I guess. 7/10 is fair to me - DD is an enjoyable game if only for the cases alone, and definitely one to pick up on sale. Those who enjoyed C&P or Sherlock games in general will likely buy this regardless but just don't expect it to be as good as C&P!

let's write a review for the steam awards!  okay!
i played this game for about six months straight when it was released, but left for the better part of two years and recently came back to the game this summer.  not a whole lot changed with the game in that span, sad to say, but things have picked up.
dirty bomb is a fun shooter and a good game overall.  it's completely free to play, there's no advantages to be purchased in any way.  will it take some time to unlock every merc and preferred loadout card for them?  yes.  but it's not a heinously long grind, especially if you make sure to do as many of the credit missions as possible.
on the downside, if you're looking to craft a specific loadout it's a real nightmare.  and event skins can be quite elusive despite a real effort to grind for them.
there's also the playerbase itself.  be prepared for anything with the quickmatch.  newish players with no real idea what they're doing.  griefers just running around being useless.  stacked teams steamrolling the other side.  it can be pretty frustrating to deal with.
but even with those issues, it's still a lot of fun.  if you're looking for a quick paced shooter, and for free; i recommend giving dirty bomb a try.

I don't have much in the way of experience when it comes to writing long serious reviews. But I firgured since this review was getting more views I might as well redo this whole thing. So here it goes:
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Tales of the Borderlands is a choice-driven adventure game (in Telltale's signature format) in which you play as either Rhys, a Hyperion employee with big dreams and Finoa, a local con-woman ready to make her biggest con yet, taking place after the events of Borderlands 2.
In the first episode Rhys's promotion and all chances of moving up in the company are ruined when a rival steps in and becomes his new boss. Rhys then comes up with a plan to get back at them by stealing the vault key, an alien aritfact capable of unlocking great wealth and power, which led to his rivals promotion from right under their nose. With the help of his two best friends, Vaughn and Yvette, he makes his way to possibly the most dangerous planet in the galaxy, Pandora. Meanwhile, Finoa in her home town of Hollow Point on Pandora is preparing for her greatest con yet. Helping her she has her sister Sasha and their mentor/foster father Felix. Events unfold and the two must work together to discover a treasure of epic proportions!
People who have played any of Telltale's games will know what to expect in terms of gameplay. Small areas to navigate in which you look and interact with the enviroment with simple puzzles along with lots of cutscenes with many quick time events.
Needless to say, the game's main focus is on it's storytelling which it does very well. People who have not had the pleasure of playing any of the first two Borderlands games might get lost in terms of the lore (as well as a few jokes) but it is not needed as the game does a good job on focusing more on the central premise of the story. People who are familar with the Borderlands games will enjoying getting to see Pandora from a whole different view point (rather than just running around shooting everything). There are plenty of humour to be found in the writing even if you are not a fan and action cutscenes that are throughly entertaining!
So in summary: If you are fan of Telltale's adventure games then this is basically the same thing you are used only in a lighter setting and I highly recommend.

This is an enjoyable game.  Most of the down votes are because the game has changed over development...well...that's how development works.  There used to be a research type progression that has been removed and replaced with a crate loot and forge system.  If you have not played it before you won't know the difference.  Here is how I feel about it.
Not pay to win.  You can get premium membership which allowes faster leveling, extra crate loot, more paint colors, and more crates overall.  I just play for a week or two for free then pay for 1 day of premium so I can sell my stuff at top dollar.  One day of premium is a buck.  Even if you are premium you just get stuff faster.  Anyone can get anything from the crates.  Second crate I opened had an epic gun in it and I pounded people with it for quite a while at lower levels.
Matchmaking is very even.  Player enemies will get harder as you level up.  Ranked matches the players within a few points of each other.  It's not perfect but it's good.
Any items you want you can forge when you get enough in game cash if you don't get what you want from crates.  You get in game cash from crates after matches, recycling parts (premium get much better recycling prices so that's why I do it once every week or two), and selling your bot designes.
Robot design is fun.  If building stuff is not your thing, don't let that stop you.  There are tons of player made bots to choose from some that are fairly cheap.  There are tons of parts and weapons and movement types to choose from.
Several game types.  TDM, a Domination like mode, practice with AI, a brawl that changes the mode frequently, and you can make your own custom games with friends.
There are limited maps at the moment, but they are well balanced.  Both teams seem to be able to get to the objectives at the same time.
Overall worth trying out.  It's free.  Not pay to win, just pay to get things done faster.

The way Bethesda explore an alternate future under Nazi rule is a world well worth exploring. There is even a couple of points in the game where the game asks you to make choices that have serious consequences on the story - not something you'd expect from a game in this genre.  The gunplay is frantic and heavy duty - the guns are satisfyingly robust and the stealth elements of the game were well executed. And the smile I had when I was able to control a mech was something to forget.
There are some definite spikes in difficulty that caused a few rage quits but that made finishing the game all the more satisfying. The visuals are clean and look great - I ran this on an i7 with a 960GTX @ 1080p with no difficulty whatsoever. All in all it's hard to fault this game - I strongly recommend it!

After having accumulated 10 hours of gameplay on this wonderful take on Arcade racing, I can safely say that it's done everything right! I never played the original S&AAR, but while this may seem like an expansion for it, it has an innovative mechanic: the ability to drive (or fly) on land, sea and air, sometimes all in one race!
To start, there are several Characters, namely ones like Sonic, but others too, like Joe Musashi from Shinobi. They all have different stats, and are best suited to personal preference. There are many you can unlock too! They all have unique sounds and quotes, and some of their cars are insanely awesome to look at!
It has 4 levels of difficulty, the last being unlockable, and after you learn how to play efficently without crashing into walls or falling off, it does seem rather easy, even on hard. Expert is a real challenge, the AI can keep up with you in rather tense races. The track design is inspired by levels from various SEGA games (hence the 'All star), and they are very original ideas, with each lap (normally of 3 laps) changing the track itself! You can find yourself on a simple land track at first, but all of a sudden: the track retracts and you're on water! The actual transformations happen rather fast, but still cool.
The single player consists of a 'Single race', which is 3 laps and not tournament based. Career, which sees you progress by earning stars and going through a path of races. That being said, the game offers many varients of racing, such as traffic challenges, drift challenges, Versus and more! The Career is a bit shortwinded, however. Of course, 100%-ing it will take a lot longer than I have played, but to get to the end itself doesn't take all that long. The idea is to progess through the different Cups, and you unlock characters on the way.
For the cars (planes, boats etc), you can alter their attributes by levelling characters through an XP based system. You will unlock 'mods' for the Vehicles, which can, for example, improve Handling, but at a cost of speed. This is useful depending on what type of race/track you're on.
The online seems to be dead, through no fault of the games, but no-one seems to play it, which is a huge shame as there is an Arena mode! That said, if you have family/friends, get them a controller (or keyboard if you're feeling like that) and play together! A controller is definetly superior for this game, more precise speed/accelaration and handling. I use a keyboard, and fortuneatly, you can rebind. You don't need the mouse for this which is cool.
Finally, the Graphics in the game (at max) are beautiful! For some reason, my game locks itself at 55fps despite V-Sync being off. It is well optimised and a smooth experience and you don't need a monster PC to run it, not at all! Loading times are good, the menu and in game interface are well designed and easy to use.
I think I covered everything, please comment if I left something out. Overall, 9.5/10!

Very fun kart racing game. The single player is pretty fun, but playing muliplayer with your friends is awesome.
There are 30 different characters in game, in with a different standard style of driving. Each racer has 6 skills - Speed, Acceleration, Handling, Boost, and All-Star. As you level up your racers you unlock mods which change how those skills are spread out. The different tracks and gamemodes can call for a different setup, so you can usually use your favorite racer with a different mod. (And of course Football Manager is the best racer :D )
The tracks are based on old Sega game, and most of them change throughout the 3 laps. There are also sections where you transform into a boat or a plane.
There are a few different game modes - SP has a World Tour, a Grand Prix, and single race modes. For MP there are:
Standard Race - Race for the top position while utilizing power ups.
Battle Arena - Fight to survive using power ups. All players start with three hits. Once all off their hit points are gone, they are out. The last surviving player wins.
Battle Race - Fight to survive using power ups. All players start with three hits. Once all off their hit points are gone, they are out. The last surviving player wins.
Capture The Chao - A Chao balloon and a capture point spawn in random spots. Bringing the Chao balloon to the capture point adds to the players score. Reaching the target limit or capturing the most before time runs out declares the winner.
Boost Race - Race for the top position. There are no items to make use of, only boost pads will help racers in this mode.
The boost race isn't that much fun, as using powerups to slow or stun your opponents is the best part of playing a kart game.  The other modes are all very fun though.
This is definitely worth picking up during a Steam sale, and if you like kart or racing games $20 isn't bad either.

A casual, interactive piece. While undoubtedly a video game, there isn't all that much to it. It's mostly an abstract, physics-based platformer, where you jump around using momentum to collect objects. You can swing around, you can jump, you can fast fall and you have some control over your aerial momentum. The goal is to spread pollen to activate plant seeds, which in turn become platforms for you to launch yourself from to collect Spectra - the major collectible (think Stars or Jiggies, although this is not the same kind of game). Each time you collect one it boots you out and you must reenter the garden. Every few Spectra you open a new garden, which must be 'stabilised' by collecting at least one Spectra. Playing with mouse, the game is responsive and pleasing to move around in, once you get used to the particular nuances of the physics.
While visually pretty and aurally pleasing, with use of simple shapes, flat contrasting colours and a casual chill electronica soundtrack, the game doesn't really amount to much, in my opinion. Good much in the same way a game like Flower is, in that it would be a good game to relax or unwind with, spend some quiet time lost in this little world, but not something I would sit down to actively play, enjoy, and experience.
If it's the kind of game you're into, a casual, relaxing experience to lose a few hours in every now and again, then you'll definitely enjoy it - maybe pick it up on sale. If you want something more exciting or something to really sink your teeth it, I would suggest looking elsewhere.
Ultimately, I believe it sets out with a specific goal and achieves that goal quite well.

A great, balanced MOBA that only suffers from a few major issues. Here's the overall stuff I found as food and bad.
Good:
1. Balanced game play, none of the characters seem OP from my experience.
2. The single player against bots isn't too bad
3. The single player campaign is great, for what's there (which isn't much, see cons #3).
Bad:
1. Dead community. It takes hours to find a game. Usually I give up and play a bot round
2. Devs gave up. There haven't been any updates in over 5 months, and no word from the devs  on why. This leads me to believe that the game has been left behind, which is a real shame.
3. Short campaign. This is mostly because the devs have up, but the campaign only lasts about 2 hours, with more "soon to come" as of April 2016.
4. Microtransactions EVERYWHERE. Want more abilities? Pay money. Want a new pet? Pay money. Want an alternate skin? Pay money. Granted, this is a big problem with most MOBAs, and devs have to make money somehow.
Strife is a great entrance level MOBA with great gameplay. The only things holding it back are a dead community and lack of updates. These two problems have killed the game. I'd give it a try, still, because it's free and fun, just don't expect anything extraordinary or anyone to play with. It's a shame the devs gave up.

I bought this game on a whim at full price out of boredom and wanting something different. I never got into Prison Architect and this looked similar so I was very skeptical about it from the get go. I thought that a game like this isn't one that you can tell whether you enjoyed it or not accurately within the first two hours of play, but I was very wrong on that front. At first I attempted without the tutorial, but immediately decided to try the tutorial within 5 minutes because it wasn't self explanatory as I had expected. This was not a bad thing. The amount of depth within this game is insanse. Always new things that I'm learning.
As of writing this review I have 300 hours in this game and I can say that almost every time I start it I learn something new. When I purchased it, it was on Alpha 15, now it is on Alpha 16. It says that this game is in Alpha and early access, but this is the first game that I've bought with such a disclaimer that feels like a finished product. Updates may not come every week, but they seem to be substantial in size. Even if the developer left the game right this moment, I wouldn't give this game a negative review. The amount of depth is staggering.
The modding scene is amazing and I love the Steam workshop as well. If you have any qualm with any aspect of the game bychance there is a strong chance that someone has made a mod to change that part of the gameplay. There is a overhaul mod that turns the game medieval only with extreme depth added to that part of the game. I figured that around 100 hours I would get bored of the vanilla game and install that mod to spice things up. I still haven't installed that mod and I'm sure that it will give me another hundred or more hours of gameplay when I decided that I've finally had enough of vanilla gameplay.
I cannot recommend this game enough, even at full price.

One of the very basic logical games we all learn to play in the early childhood, noughts and crosses, fixed to the state where you need to actually planning your strategy and where crosses not always prevail with their starting advantage.
Speaking a little more specifically, an "ultimate" Tic-Tac-Toe have 9 squares of usual 9-cells Tic-Tac-Toe playing field, and you gotta use them all, turn by turn. The main catch is that your move predetermines the next move of your opponent. Like if you hit the upper left cell, your opponent have to play on the upper left square... That's longer to tell, than to show, but in the end, we've got our well-known game quite updated, so it is playable again, at least, for some time, until you get the vibe.
Which is more, there are another new option: draining moves. If you choose this one, in order to win, you have to construct a line of 3 with exactly three hits. If you try to set a trap, and win with 4th step, alas, you 1st hit will be drained from the field, so you have to change your usual moves one more time. It is fun even with the basic single 9-cells field, but when you adding this draining feature to the "ultimate" version, now the game can run for hours, if you and your opponent both skilled enough.
Above all of it, the game is freemium one. And it is quite easy to get a gold with achievements there.
I strongly recommend to give it a shot. That's not the only possible variation of Tic-Tac-Toe, and probably not the best (I still like more the one I've played in the schooltime).  But it is a fine little logical game, to catch a breath after working hours, and without killing everything on the screen. Peace, people. Try it on!

Game Maker is a tool, and like any tool, you can use it well to create fantastic things, and you can use it poorly and make utter trainwrecks. The fact that I'm explaining this means you probably know what side of the line Hero Siege falls on.
Hero Siege wants to be Diablo, on a basic level. It wants this BADLY. It breaks itself into 'acts' (with a new, fifth one in DLC form!), it has a bunch of classes with skill trees of their own, it involves semi-random world generation, and loot plays in heavily, with a smattering of crafting. Heck, it comes as close to ripping off the Diablo font as one can without a C&D being involved (if it's not actually just stolen outright - I haven't compared directly). The big problem is that the game's everything is a muddled, broken husk.
The gameplay isn't mouse-based, and in fact, the mouse barely functions in the game. It's more like a twin-stick shooter, except you only have the four cardinal directions to work with (you can combine them to move diagonally, but if you can fire diagonally in any way, I didn't get it to work). Random 'traps' appear on the ground and around the world, and this is problem number one: the art doesn't convey things well. Things which appeared to be scenery would suddenly spit out a bullet and BAM, half my life gone. Even worse: bullets don't appear as the top layer of graphics, meaning they might hide behind other objects and suddenly go right through you. Instead of exploration being key, you're mostly in arenas which spawn enemies in waves. Sometimes you spend gold on items between, or level up with an incredibly pedestrian character skills tree here and there. (Fun fact about the level up screen: tooltips do not always work, so have fun figuring out if something is a trap or not!)
To top it all off, this week there was DLC released for the game, which adds multiplayer. "Early Access" multiplayer, according to the in-game menus, but really the entire DLC is half-baked: for most of us, it doesn't work. At all. You can purchase it but if it doesn't allow you to unlock anything? Well, according to the devs, that's Steam's fault. It totally happened to a dev's copy of Indie Game the Movie, so that means they didn't code things poorly, you guys. (This is an actual excuse.) You don't want it, just like you don't want this game, but I really figured the technical problems were best summarized by that. Or the fact that options don't save/kick in unless you visit their screen, in which case it remembers "Oh yeah, you turned the volume down" or "Oh yeah, I'm set to Windowed mode!" and suddenly picks up on the thing that it saved to a file it refuses to load on boot? Also be careful dying if you're playing with keyboard! The mouse cursor can vanish (read: stop working entirely) on the death screen, making you force-quit the game to reload.
I know I'm a harsh grader sometimes, but this is an honest plea from me to you: Hero Siege is a bad game made by people who are, at best, first-time developers way in over their heads. Please do not buy or support this title. It has been in enough bundles I've given out around 3-5 keys on my own now, if you MUST play it, wait for another deal of that sort. It's very bad, and not in a funny "it's better with friends" way. (Remember: online multiplayer is a DLC-only feature, so you're getting overcharged to screw around with pals who aren't at your place.) Everything it attempts is done better by another game, and most of those are just as cheap or entirely free.

Borderlands is a game about loot. You want to find the Vault. Why do you want to find it though? For loot. There's a secret area  over here, what does it contain? More loot! Guns, shields, class/grenade mods, all different kinds of loot. Keep this in mind when starting to play Borderlands or it's sequel. The gunplay feels a little bit iffy sometimes, but it works plenty well enough. The main issue is that the game treats every bullet you fire as a really fast projectile, so sniper rifles aren't as incredibly OP as you might think at first, but they're still one kind of gun you're very likely to have on every character you make.
Speaking of characters, you can play as one of four classes, each with a different action skill and skill tree. Berserkers have. well... Berserk. They start healing a lot, and opt to punch things instead of shoot things. It's a great skill to just pop in a safe place and heal up for free, and it's always fun to just go on a bloody rampage with it, but be wary of charging into too many gun mooks with it. As far as skills go, the berserker is mainly a tanky brawler character who revolves around getting up close to soak up the damage for the rest of your team while still making a dark red mash of your enemies up close with his action skill. His Berserk tree is all about making Berserk more effective, making Berserk's cooldown shorter, increasing your sexual endurance. However, if you want to Berserk all the time, you need the beefiness that his Tank tree offers, It's all about making you tougher and making enemies do less damage to you. The last skill tree is Blaster. It's mostly based around explosive damage and Rocket Launchers, which are meant to be the Berserker's "choice" of weapons. However, either do to an error in the game, the port, or maybe i'm just using them wrong, rocket launchers are incredibly underwhelming, unless they have a powerful elemental effect tied to them, mostly ones with x4 of an element. The only time you'll ever really get any real use out of explosive damage in Borderlands 1, maybe outside of grenades, is when you get lucky enough to find a weapon with a rare attribute that changes it's bullets to rockets, and even then the unreliability of those weapons will likely make you replace them somewhat soon after. It's possible you'll be able to make explosive damage worthwhile with this skilltree, but the points you'll use to get to that point are much better off used in the other two skilltrees. However, respeccing is cheap in this game. Really really cheap, so feel free to experiment and prove me wrong! Also with all of the DLC and a patch that was put out at some point, the maximum amount of skillpoint you can ever get on a character is 69, so this tree will likely get some use late-game just to make these weak weapons more reliable and make your grenades more awesome.
Sirens can phasewalk, which basically makes a shockwave around you, damaging enemies and making you invisible and fast for a few seconds. Use this time to move up to someone and melee them to make another shockwave, bringing you back to normal and repositioning yourself. It's much more powerful once you have an elemental effect added onto it through elemental artifacts you find, but even at it's weakest it can save your hide in a tight spot. The siren's skill trees are Controller, which is based around messing with your enemies, mostly by Dazing them, making them slower and making them aim like a Stormtrooper. Next is the Elemental skill tree, which is based around doing lots of elemental damage and decreasing the amount you take. The last is Assassin, which is based around letting you phasewalk in to get an easy kill on an unsuspecting enemy, and using the momentum from that to wipe out the rest of the crowd while getting to your next Phasewalk faster.
The Hunter class has Deathwing, his pet bird who will fly out and attack an enemy, along with a number of other things, depending on what skills you have. Deathwing is fairly weak early game, but he/she becomes a force to be reckoned with  later on. Also, a note on using Deathwing well, she has a tendancy to fly around in circles like a moron if you aren't looking at something for her to target, so she's not very good for tossing out from behind cover. This got infamous to the point that they make fun of it in Borderlands 2. Deathwing is still nice to have though. Anyway, the hunter's main focus is sniping, be it with Sniper Rifles or Revolvers. His Sniper tree is just what you'd think, making him wreck faces with Sniper Rifles. However, a word of warning, sniper rounds are capped fairly low due to how powerful they can be, so don't forget to have good weapons of other types to boot. However it's an amazing tree if you're playing with other people since you can stand back and melt the enemy opposition. Rogue is the tree based around Deathwing, and making her into a killing machine, while also making you get more loot for your trouble. This is a great tree to use for solo play, since it can keep you alive and give you ammo you might be in need of, and more loot is never a bad thing. His Gunslinger tree is a somewhat general tree based around critical hits, and giving you the chance to get random crits (under different names, like "killer shots" so they don't trigger crit bonuses)
The Soldier has the Scorpio Turret, which basically works like a decoy that does damage. It's not very powerful on it's own, but it does set up a very temporary spot for you to regroup and attack the distracted enemies. It's more useful than it sounds, don't worry. Infantry is a skill tree based around making the Soldier and his turret more deadly, and making him able to use it more often. It's fairly straightforward, and while I wouldn't put all my points into it right away, it's certainly worth easing into over the course of your playtime. The Support tree is all about making the turret work as a mini resupply station. some skills let it give you ammo, and there are some general defensive skills to help you get a foothold in a rough situation. His last skill tree, the Medic skill tree, is just what it sounds like. It gives you and your team a lot of different ways to get healed up, from a healing aura around the scorpio turret, to being able to heal teammates by SHOOTING THEM. Just keep in mind that some of these skills will be useless in a solo game, so if you want to play a support soldier, make him a seperate character instead of trying to shoehorn in some great skills into a character that can only use them occasionally when playing with other people.
Now for a big issue, is this game better or worse than Borderlands 2? It's not such a simple question. Borderlands 2 has more solid gunplay, and much better presentation and characters, however Borderlands 1 has a better loot system, and it's a fair challenge to solo players as long as they're willing to put in the time to get better at the game and put together a good build, whereas Borderlands 2 has bosses similar to Crawmerax that are nearly impossible to kill solo without an extremely specific build, which leads into my next point. Borderlands 2, while it does have room for different builds in it, mostly has specific skill combinations that are simply better than the rest, which is made worse when most of the legendaries seem built to work with a certain playstyle, especially the legendary class mods, which, to my knowledge, always give boosts to the same set of skills. And it's not that Borderlands 1 doesn't have skills that are just flat-out better than others, but it doesn't force you to use them late-game. You can have a weird build that doesn't focus on anything, as long as you have a few specific skills for late-game effectiveness, such as Tresspass on the Hunter. Also, BL1 has a more fair loot system, not based all around legendaries like BL2. Sadly, character limits cut this last point short. I suggest BL1 over 2 overall.
