Okay, so this game can be really buggy. And if you're expecting something like Lionhead's "The Movies," you're going to be disappointed. It's pretty much a text-based sim. It really reminds me of Extreme Warfare Revenge, the wrestling promotion game.
First, the bad stuff:
The interface is TERRIBLE and fairly unintuitive.
Sometimes you have to click (+) or (-) buttons or use a slider instead of just typing in the value you want.
The game will occasionally crash, so make sure to save.
Speaking of, after you select a save slot, the game will tell you that autosave is now enabled. It isn't. Go to the options and enable it manually. Oh, and you have to make your first save manually before you can do that.
Then the good stuff:
It's just fun, and fairly addictive. Once you get the winning method down for producing movies, it's not a hard game.
I released a series of big-budget action flicks that made me BILLIONS of dollars. Then I produced a horror movie based on Gulliver's Travels.
All in all, despite its flaws, I'd still recommend this game.

Sherlock Holmes: The Devil's Daughter (SHD), developed by Frogwares, is a very curious case - a mystery worthy of the sleuth himself. Since I'm clearly not Sherlock Holmes, my investigation is going to be rather more mundane, so let's go over the basics (for PC):
a) Priced at 45 euro/dollars*, it immediately raised (my) expectations as to content and technology and inevitably invites comparison with other games/franchises in this price range, e.g. Tomb Raider and Metal Gear Solid. Based on UnrealEngine4, it is painfully clear that SHD has no business in this league in terms of technology and user-friendliness. It feels more like a pumped-up HOG from Artifex Mundi (which I happen to like enormously): In 'A Study in Green' this becomes so glaringly obvious that if you've ever played an HOG, the piled-up temple puzzles should pose no problem for you. But it's not what I'd expect in this price range!
b) As for content, well, most of the story-line has already been provided by Conan Doyle - all you have to do is to figure out some new angles and twists based on that solid foundation. And Frogwares just barely manages that. The cases themselves aren't bad, and I particularly like 'Chain Reaction', but a total of 4 cases and a tepid finisher ('boss fight' isn't quite the word...) does feel a bit cheap, not to say downright lazy.
c) Interaction is a nightmare, and I'm not talking about the difficulty level, which doesn't seem to change anything. The character analysis, while certainly an entertaining novelty, seems oddly redundant. Mouse/keyboard operation is frustrating to say the least: The balancing acts and eavesdropping maneouvres are insanely annoying, and I spent way too much time trying to figure out when to press [W] or [A] etc. to jump from a chain or activate an action (e.g. the exorcism in 'Infamy'). And it never made any sense to me why the keyboard buttons need to change randomly. It just seems an easy developer solution instead of devising a more clever approach.
d) The graphics are decent, for a UE4-based game, but the way Frogwares created the characters seems rather odd: All male characters are splendidly detailed and realistic, and I particularly like Tom Hurst's appearance and gestures. But most female characters, excepting very old ladies, are scary as hell - especially Kate: With the head of a grown woman placed on the body of a pre-teen schoolgirl, Kate does look like she could be the actual daughter of the Devil himself, although I doubt that was the intention. Frogwares also captured the mood and atmosphere of late 19th-century London very convincingly in all its class-based discrepancy and misery.
e) So, final words: Is SHD worth your money and your time?
NO, not if you expect 15 hours+ of fast-paced action or stunning scenery with lots interactive options and progression (at 45 euro, that wouldn't be an unreasonable demand).
YES, if you like Sherlock Holmes as a literary figure and also like medium-strength puzzles AND you happen to have 25 euro to 'donate' to Frogwares on top of the 20 euro that SHD should have cost to begin with.
Personally, I don't regret buying SHD too much, but I'm definitely not going to buy another installment. Replay value is so-so, and I'm down to 7 hours, but at least 1 full hour is wasted on loading screens.
* At the time of writing, 1 euro = 1 dollar.

So there I sat behind my desk as the head of Complex Melon Studios. I had started the company with a hundred million dollars and turned it into a multi-billion dollar company. I sat there smiling to myself. I was cocky, arrogant, but also humble as my many pictures of myself hung on my walls proved. I started looking over some ideas for future movies; perhaps more sequels were in order since the previous sequels of my several series had all done well. Just as I was thinking about it, my main writer burst into my office. Her name was Francis…something-or-other. I’m a busy man, I can’t be bothered to learn names.
She looked me dead in the eyes and said, “Sir, I have a slight complaint, if you would be so kind as to indulge me.”
I nodded and motioned for her to sit down in the chair in front of my desk and she obliged.
I smiled at her and said very sweetly, “What seems to be the problem?”
“It’s your movie summaries, sir, or should I say lack thereof?”
“I don’t understand.”
“Your movie summaries don’t make any sense. Take for example this one script you gave to me not too long ago. You titled it ‘Little Doggy Choo-Choo’ and your movie summary was simply, ‘Da fuq?'”
I chuckled to myself, “Yeah, that’s because I had no idea where that title came from.”
“Right,” she said, still perplexed. “But how am I supposed to write a screenplay when you haven’t given me anything? Is the dog’s name Choo-Choo? How little is he? What does he do? ‘Da fuq?’ is not very helpful.”
“You’re the screenwriter, you make it up.”
“Okay, but how about this one? The third movie in the ‘Deception’ series has the plot summary: ‘No one asked for it…so here you go.’ Do you actually want me to write something here?”
“Of course. I gave you a title, didn’t I?”
“Yeah, a pretty bad title. ‘Deception 3: Deceptiest’? There’s no such word as deceptiest.”
“There is now!” I said, smiling.
“I have another complaint,” she sighed.
“Oh?” I asked, sitting up straight.
“Yes,” she said, “Whenever I give you a script, you always give it to someone else to do slight revisions. Now I don’t necessarily have a problem with that, but, for some reason the entire script winds up being credited to this other guy even though he just did slight touch-ups and I still did basically the entire script.”
“You still get paid, don’t you?”
“I guess.”
“Then why do you need the credit? Who cares if it’s credited to you or this other guy? Do you think people actually pay attention to who the screenwriter is?”
“It would be nice to win the award for best screenplay for once, that’s all. When I see that my movie won for best screenplay, and this other guy who did barely any work on it at all is accepting the trophy, it kind of angers me a little.”
“He doesn’t get paid nearly as much as you do, let him have the trophy.”
She sighed and I thought I was done, but just then another screenwriter burst through my door.

Wolfenstein: The New Order is a story-rich and reasonable first-person shooter. As we can expect of modern FPS games, its difficulty tends toward the easy side; hard mode feels like normal mode, so gamers wanting a challenge would be best suited to Uber difficulty.
Perhaps the best part of the game is the lore and story. The Nazis are portrayed as visceral, genocidal, sadistic and thoroughly inhuman - their thirst for progress, exemplified by their obsessive construction of concrete infrastructures, provides for both an evocative environment and narrative. Perhaps bravest of all was making the primary villain convinced of his own nobility in spite of having murdered so much of mankind; this delusional aspect helped accentuate his inhumanity.
The plot isn't without structural weaknesses. For example the mission to gather a piece of moldy concrete for research had no real consequences down the line. However on the whole it was a solid hero type story, bolstered by bits of lore in newspaper and document clippings you may read as you go. I could see the influence of Half-Life 2 and Dishonored in the enemy and stealth elements, respectively - two apt and worthy sources that helped the game greatly.
The New Order's longevity was an issue; I finished a playthrough on hard mode in 10 hours. There was no compelling reason to replay the game other than to find collectibles. In terms of gameplay there were a few frustrating moments, however I found that these difficult sequences could simply be sprinted past, speedrun style. Some elements are needlessly easy; for example, the Laser Kraftwerk energy rechargers being infinite use, rather than limited like their equivalent in Half-Life 2, was an oversight.
In terms of design and challenge, the final mission was a particular dissapointment; a series of unimaginative, symmetric, Quake Arena style maps filled with enemies. The concluding bosses - like most bosses in the game - are based upon a sequence of actions which, with a couple of tries, can be accomplished pretty easily. I got the sense that the conclusion was somewhat rushed, as despite being set in an enormous place it ranked among the shorter and easier of chapters - and not simply because I was used to the game's mechanics by that point.
Overall Wolfenstein: The New Order is a fun, if somewhat brief, experience. Given its brevity, I recommend picking it up when it is on sale; as it has been a few years since the game's release, such an event is now regular.

I am in love with the art direction in PixelJunk Eden. It has become my go-to game for when I've had enough of killing things, blowing things up, and other related virtual mayhem. Or, after rage-quitting the last five games in a row because they are deliberately obtuse or sadistically difficult, it serves as a good reminder of why I play games in the first place; to have fun and feel good about myself. PixelJunk Eden has those "Man, I'm good" moments when you clear an area, in the same way that very well done puzzle games do. It can have it's frustrating moments, like falling 50 stories after a long and complex climb, but they are always user error and not the fault of the game design. Difficulty progresses naturally and not without commensurate upgrades and new abilities. Time is made a valuable, albeit renewable, resource. It has the perfect balance of relaxing and challenging that makes it highly addictive to play. Adding to replay value are the achievements for clearing an area a second time or for activating all of a certain interactive object. The soundtrack is generally pleasant, in a techno-jazz kind of way, but I occasionally found it irritating and so played that area in silence. And as I've said, I do love the art direction, although some screens in the higher levels are downright hard on the eyes. It is still one of the most fun, refreshing, satisfying and addictive games I've played in a while, well worth the full price.

This is quite a simple game... quite: You "fly" a spaceship, and collect one of the multiple of items during your flight. Items come in lines, and you have to choose 1 item from the line, moving your ship in that item's way using arrow keys. The ship moves at a certain speed that drops off as you go, and you have to collect speed boosts to keep on playing. Once the ship stops, it is game over, and you have to start over.
There are 3 types of speed boosts, and 2 of them will only get you safely to the next item line, while the third allows you to pick up "money"(it only adds to your score, no upgrades in this game) or missiles. This means that, if you are lucky with the random item generation, you will have to pick up a speed boost every second item lane, and sometimes you will have to collect speed boosts few times in a row, just so you wouldn't stop. The misslies are used to destroy one of the obstacles: the meteors, and it is really unvieldly, since it fires automatically, and it sometimes uses the missile while you are switching lanes, even though you werent going to hit the obstacle. The other obstacle, black hole or something, stops your ship completely, regardless of your ship speed. This is the game over item. I can kind of understand why this works that way, since the slower your ship goes, easier it get's to pick up the right item, and having no abrupt game enders would mean you could go on forever. It is not super easy to get high scores, which is good. Note: There are apparently 3 different ship designs in the game, but I haven't been able to unlock the other 2(so I can't tell if they change anything in the gameplay).
Is it worth the 1$? Honestly, that is not a lot of money in general, so I would say yes. The only problem with this price I have is the fact that this game is the kind of game that you would go to the internet 10 years ago to waste some time, playing random flash games for 5 to 15 minutes at a time, until you got bored and got on another one. Those were free(and there still are plenty of those around on the internet). So yeah, if you want a cheaper(read: free) alternative, search the internet for all the free to play flash games. On the other side of the coin, you can probably find 1$ worth of money by walking around your neighborhood and looking at the ground, or by saving change when your are buying stuff from the store.

Surprisingly good - this is the best way of describing RimWorld.
The last time I played an indie game with as much potential for replayability was FTL.  If you liked FTL, I'll take a leap here and say you will like RimWorld.  Very different in its concept, but similar in it's addictiveness and replayability which for me is really important.
Each time you start a new colony the experience is slightly different.  Obviously there are similarities between games which have had me sighing a little when a colony goes wrong and I have start a new one, but on a whole its quite fresh each time a new game is started.  You build a base from scratch and collect resources, but the little people you start with have real vices and personalities, some are hard workers, some lazy, some hate each other, some spawn new little people if they get together!  Pets can be trained if you have a animal friendly little person too, and they can help fight off attackers or fetch resources.  This can sound gimmicky and a little micro-management heavy, and I was a little sceptical when I read about the AI story teller, but actually it really does work and is fun and balanced.
If you're like me and prefer a permadeath game RimWorld comes with that option, and its great, knowing if something goes wrong (and it often does) you just have to keep going till your team recover or all is lost, and that makes the experience deeper, because sometimes you start to feel the journey with your characters, particularly if some get killed or maimed.  I actually got properly sad once when one character died and then his pet dog died defending him afterwards, I ended that game, and that was the end of that story.  The beauty is, you can then start again with new people and have another 'largely' unique adventure.
Give it a go, it’s worth it just for the experience, it’s quite a unique game.

You have to keep winning.
I played the predecessor "You Have to Win The Game" a while back. If you're on the fence about buying this one, give that one a try. It's also available on Steam (for free!). There's more meat to this game, but there are also more downsides.
The king is cursed, and the only way to save him is by doing a whole bunch of platforming. There are several dungeons to explore, and you'll find treasure and powerups which will grant you access to additional areas as you go back and forth.
I wasn't a big fan of the inclusion of an overworld map. If you like to explore, it's easy to wander into an area you can't pass through because you lack the requisite powerup. It's frustrating to travel back and forth between areas, searching for someplace to progress. It's especially painful when crossing a bridge on the map just brings you into a platforming segment representing the bridge (which must be completed every time you want to cross). I feel like the inclusion of the Subcon travel network (and some other shortcuts) should have rendered the map unnecessary.
There are a few towns scattered throughout the game, and most of them have a resident Fortune Teller. This person will give you a free hint as to where you should head next in order to advance. I didn't use this feature until the late game because I wanted it to be a last resort.
The keys were a bit confusing to me at first. You can find a couple of single-use keys to open locked doors. That's simple enough. You can also buy more keys by spending the gems that you find, or save up more gems and buy an infinite-use Skeleton Key. If you're completely out of keys, you can also get keys on a credit system from people in towns.
The speedrun trials were a fun idea, but the courses felt more like a test of trial and error & memorization rather than speed and motor skill.
I enjoyed the feeling of discovering new secret paths in areas I've already visited (or finally being able to reach That Ledge that I had to keep passing by earlier), things like double-jumping and wallclimbing are satisfying and responsive. I had a few deaths that felt cheap, but the huge abundance of respawn points meant I never really lost progress.
I do like the game overall, and despite my minor complaints I think it's a successful expansion on the original.

When something is called Pandora, you can bet your marbles something bad is going down.
For those of you who are not so well versed on the subject of Greek mythology, Pandora was the name of woman who was sent to earth by the gods as punishment for their disrespectful actions. Pandora was moulded by the smithgod and endowed with all the desireable traits anyone would want in a person. Lastly they gave her boundless curiosity. She was then given a box (or an urn depending on your textbook) and sent to earth with the simple message to never open the box. What was in the box you ask? Well...despair, terror, disgust, disease, death, pain, agony, greed, lust and lastly: hope. Pandora opened her box and the world was made miserable and the only respite was the tiny bit of hope at the bottom.
Now that we have a context, can you image what is hidden on a planet called Pandora? Há! Wrong! It's guns! Guns and bullets and rockets and bullets and bullets. There are so many bullets on Pandora you'll be wondering why people are still paying with cash when you can get bullets and guns from everywhere. The whole point of the game is to open a mythological vault (Pandora's Vault. See where this is going?) On your way you'll be beset by all manner of horrors and fiends. So it is nice that you can pick up guns everywhere and share your bullets with everyone. Obviously I meant: shoot at everyone. Stuff gets a bit blurry after a while cause the game is so vast, so huge, you'll be dragging yourself from one end of the planet to the other over and over again, and everything looks the same. This is my chief complaint with this game: It is huge, but doesn't offer much in the way of streamlining. There is some fast travel possible, but only from certain places. You can also rent cars, but arbitrary barriers stop you from driving them all over the place. So if walking is not your thing, steer clear.
However, if hearing the screams of bandits, as they dissolve into a sloppy pile of green goop after you shot them with a round filled with acid then you are in for a delicious treat. Borderlands drops a lot of weapons. You can compare and contrast to find what suits your class best and go to town on people's face with it. Zap 'em. Burn 'em. Melt'em or Blast them into tiny bits. All off course accentuated by delicious screams of pain and horror. What do you mean "thats grim?" That isn't grim at all. That's life on Pandora man. You better get used to it, cause you'll be doing it a lot.
A funny thing about how the game presents itself is its classification system. A normal wolf-like enemy would be a normal wolf. A big one would be an Alpha Wolf, and a giant, burning and barking monstrosity would be a Badass Wolf. This trend developes, and it makes it easy to gauge what you can deal with, and what will certainly kill you. Dying then triggers a short moment where you can save youself by killing anything on the screen to prevent a hefty ressurection fine. Of course, you can mitigate all of that with the help of some friends.
You can play the game with up to three friends at the same time. Everyone helps both eachother and themselves when completing quests. However, don't think it is weird to have all out brawls over who gets the good loot. It is a veritable melee of conficting interests that will inevtitably result in the death of many enemies who simply stood in you and your friends way of riches and glory. Unfortunately, the game is connected with an archaic netcode, to actually getting together might be a pain. However, there are workarounds, but it would have been nicer if it would have worked straight out of the box....

Summary: Alex and her new step brother Jonas; go to Edwards Island to meet Alex's friends for a beach hangout. As Alex and Jonas enters the mysterious caves; they shift to another dimension of the island and discovers dark secrets that the islands hold. Oxen-free is a decision based game where your decisions will change the story as well as how other characters will progress.
Review:
10/10 - OXENFREE (in my opinion) WAS AMAZING FAM. I love story-rich games that have immersive unique character and oxenfree had a ton of it. I can’t explain how good the character progression was in this game. I finished the game in a day because I just loved the conversations between the characters.
There were many things I didn’t like about this game; from bugging out to an unfulfilling conclusion but it honestly deserves a 10/10 for character development and dialogs.
The story was great too. The idea behind the radio is unique and plays well with the historic concept of the story. The history of the island is interesting (but I'm sad that they didn’t do more with it).
The story includes time-travel which is great. And don’t let steam-tags fools you; the game is low-key horror. No jump scares or anything crazy like that just the everyday ghostly satanic things.
The voicing was great, and the graphics were amazing. The game has a comic book movie feel to it. You could say its sort of like a walking simulation cause there’s not much actions. But I feel like that’s the point. The game wants to tell a story about these teens and their lives.
Reasons why you wouldn't like this game:
Like I said its kind of like a walking simulator. (very similar gameplay to: Night in the Woods). And the walking is PAINFULLY slow. There’s not much to do other than walking around and picking your dialogs. So, if that’s not your thing you might not like this game.
Sometimes when you pick your dialogs; it ends up being something that you didn’t want them to say. For example, maybe you'd pick "Ask for forgiveness" and the character says: "hey i think you should say sorry" instead of "hey can you forgive me". It rarely happens but I just thought that was annoying.
The ending or the final scene is unfulfilling. I felt like there should have been more there but the whole thing was resolved so easily. TOO easily, to the point where the whole journey felt like it wasn’t as intense or kind of exaggerated. Kind of like you’re fighting an evil bad guy for like an hour and then you say something like "hey man, stop being bad, that’s not cool" and he's like "tru" and the fight stops. IDK its weird and I just thought the final scene would be more intense.

I got Showtime! in a bundle, and was interested in the concept - I had really enjoyed playing Game Dev Tycoon, and any other management simulator-style games. I was very satisfied with this title.
If you are interested in a movie studio simulator and do not mind a lack of animations (gameplay is all text-based), then you will most likely enjoy this game. For some mindless, casual playthroughs, this is the game for you.
The aesthetics are decent - since the game is entirely text-based, you will encounter numerous menus and backgrounds. When you make a movie, you have the option of selecting an ad poster from a small pool of premade templates, however, you can also load any other image you have saved on your computer. You can customize the lettering on the poster a bit, like manipulating the font and color. There is no music, so I play my own. The sounds when you click things are okay, but can get repetitive fairly quickly (I turned all audio off after about 2 hours).
You will use the mouse to click on different buttons and menus, and the tutorial is very helpful at showing you everything you can do in the game. The learning curve is mostly minimal to (maybe) moderate, depending on your experience with management simulators. You can adjust the difficulty accordingly by changing how much money you start with and/or what year you start in (more modern years give access to the latest cinema technology).
Gameplay consists of you making movies and conducting research to give you access to the latest technology. When you make your first movie, you will have the option of customizing the scripts you'd like to use (or, you can buy scripts offered by hopeful prospects). You may change the themes you'd like in your movie, and this part is very interesting, because it will affect the target demographic, and is also sensitive to the time period you are currently in. For example, lots of adult themes and profanity will most likely give you a 18+ (or higher) rating, and lots of violence will be very, very controversial if done in the early 1950's.
You will need to fill your movie with actors, actresses, supporters, directors, and producers. You can hire accordingly, or you can sign contracts with people if you want them to be exclusively yours (for a time). The contracts will expire after x movies have been made with the individual, or after x years (whichever comes first) - higher values will cost you more money. If you are careful and experiment, you will realize that signing contracts is much more cost-efficient in the long run, but ONLY if you are intending to repeatedly use the individual(s).
As your movie is being made, you can invest your networth in things like better sound stages, more advanced technology (you will have to keep up as new technologies arise with time, or lose market share to your competition), and better working conditions.
The game plays a lot like Game Dev Tycoon, where you can select from a large number of movie genres (as well as sub-genres if you desire). From here, you will have to do a bit of matchmaking, as different individuals are more proficient at certain genres, and certain themes are better fit (for example, you won't necessarily want a lot of violence in a family film). Balancing these different elements will help you get better ratings, which lead to more viewers, and also more revenue.
Pretty frequently, you will be invited to attend various award shows, however, you do not have to attend (it can be a waste of time if you know with certainty that you won't be nominated). Getting awards bolsters your studio rating, and higher studio ratings allow you to hit a larger target market.
Although your playthrough can get very repetitive very quickly, it is still worth giving this game a try if you are the least bit interested in movie studio management. The gameplay is very casual and not at all demanding, so it plays well for a time-filler, or as a break from your more intense games.
Recommend!

Some things though seem to make little difference.  The city chose to make a film or some of the film or sound quality do not make much difference.  It would be great to automatically retain case and director on a re-make/sequel. Also would be great to see how many films a particular actor has been in (one actor I used was a low level actor, after the first film he jumped to A-List status demanding 30+ million dollars, so I assume he also made other films, since mine was a mediocre success).
Other than that I think overall the game is worth it.  You will probably burn out after 2-3 hours.  But it's a game you can come back to later.  Because of this it is within what I would classify a THUMBS UP game.

At 21 hours, I've finished the game. There are no side quests, and the areas to explore are quite small and constrained. I agree with most of the criticisms from others regarding the gameplay. Here are my main beefs:
- Action suequences simply depend on hand-eye co-ordination - nothing to do with detecting. This is made even worse by the poor sensitivity mapping of the right Steam Controller pad to the right joystick, making them often almost impossibly hard. I had to switch to my XBox controller for most of them.
- There is no explanation of the mechanics of the deduction chains - you just have to figure them out. This does not add to enjoyment of the game - it's just annoying. Either add a manual, or add in-game help to explain in more detail how it works.
- Deduction chains often don't have enough evidence to choose the right answer. The choice of "right" answer is often arbitrary.
- The the way facts join to add a point in the deduction map has little to do with detection, as the logic behind them is often sparse. Rather than trying to figure them out, it's faster to do trial and error.
- Both the main story and the side cases that you have to solve to get to the end have gaps in them, so that things don't entirely hold together.
On the good side, the graphics are pretty well done, and the story is moderately interesting (if you don't already know them). Saves are automatic, and granular enough that it's not too hard to find a save point to go back to where you can redo a sequence that you got wrong.
However, this may not be apparent at first - I did not figure it out until the last case.
I'd give this 5/10, and add that even at the discounted price I paid, it was not great value for the money. Since Steam only allows my to choose either Yes or No, I pick No.

This game was a fantastic experience. As one who plays many mystery/fantasy adventure games, I rate Devil's Daughter in the top three. Here's what they did right:
1. The designers changed up the challenges and situations so thoroughly that absolutely no situation in the game felt familiar or repetitive. From a quick five minute mystery to a long Mayan struggle, it was all fresh. This is the most masterful aspect of the game.
2. I was surprised at how engaged I became to the characters and suspects. That normally does not happen in a mystery game, but I was at times making decisions purely from the empathy for a certain character.
3. For this type of game, the graphics are excellent. We compared to the old Sherlock games, and laughed.
4. The game felt intuitive. In most mystery games, there comes a point (or two) where you are at a loss for what to do, mainly because the game did not serve it up well. Did not happen here.
5. Finally, but for one, the series of mysteries were rock solid. They contained the perfect subtle clues that, if you were paying attention, you catch and become confident. Very well done.
6. Sherlock can die horribly. This adds an intensity to your actions and choices.
7. Watson is young and hawt. And he shows up when and how he should.
BTW, this game is perfect for group play. Most of the work in the game is brain power, so a small group of players are actively engaged in the game and discussing/pointing out/solving the mysteries, even though one is controlling. It's becoming one of our favorite group night activities.
Bring on the next one.

(Buggy and unpolished especially by today's standards, but what can you expect from a studio's 2nd title from 2006?
Crashed a lot for me, but that's likely due to bad Windows 10 optimization.)
PROS:
>Intricate combat. I only played melee, but magic can be very helpful and feels powerful if used well.
>Good level design. Can feel like a maze, but it's really just many roads to the same place.
>SMART level design. Many solutions to a given problem.
>Kicking and throwing, while funny, actually play an important role, and it feels good to utilize.
>Engaging item system and skill tree gives you choices with how to play.
>Gods-darned Fire Sword. There's a fire sword. Aaaaaah! Can't figure it out? Google it! Get it! Use it!
MIXED:
>Entertaining but cheesy story. Fun to either make fun of or just competent enough to get by. Nothing special.
>Voice acting. By and large, a crapshoot. Some characters are alright, and even the bad ones have some alright lines. Overall endearing, yet... amateur.
CONS:
>Hard Mode is not recommended. This is a game where hard simply makes certain bits tedious and unfun.
>Untelegraphed attacks. I found myself taking damage when I thought the enemy was done swinging, and it feels more likely a result of jumpy AI than intentional design.
>Inconsistent combat. Enemies knocked down may stay down for 5 seconds- may stay down for 1. I found myself dying even though I was blocking, and the enemy appeared to have done nothing. Perhaps this is folly on my end, but bear this in mind. In addition, hit detection can be wonky. Infrequent, but still prevalent enough.
>Hard Mode SUPER not recommended. The above problems probably left more of a mark due to me playing on Hard Mode.
---
OVERALL: If this game was revisited and rereleased today, built from the ground up (with new voice acting), and with a good chunk of technological errors ironed out, I'd give this a solid 8/10. Maybe 8.5. From start to finish, despite suffering through Hard Mode, I was entertained enough to keep playing. Worth $10 for anyone who likes old games or wants to try out the addicting combat, but nab it on a sale if you can help it.

Several gripes come from an overuse of puzzles (especially in an Mayan temple segment) and an almost criminal under use of Holmes' faithful ally Dr Watson who doesn't get very much to do here. Despite this, the game is pretty fun, challenging and a must play for many Holmes fanatics.

I got this game in a humble bundle years ago., if you don't own this game yet, you are missing out by miles.
I have since sampled the other pixeljunk games and I conclude that this is their magnum opus.
The game itself is simple in its operation: jumping, spinning, web-slinging and ground (or sky) pounding your way through an Eden of sound. The more life you spread through the area, the more intense the music becomes, the higher your score gets. The interplay between light and sound in this game is simple, pure and effective, making what might otherwise be a monotonous game into a true gaming gem. The artful style of this game shines high above pixeljunk shooter's comparably infantile gameplay and the overly simple faced pixeljunk monsters. But the style alone does not make it great, the gameplay too is razor sharp. Simple controls allow for intuitive movement through the levels, using momentum and quick reflexes to reach speeds and heights neccesary to awaken the furthest reaches of each garden. The control of the game allows anyone to get into the game proper, and ride the difficulty curve as they please. This is a fairly low-stress game, as long as you keep an eye out for nasties and try not to fall all the way back down, you'll find very little pressure from the game to be fast, or efficient. There is a draining health bar, but suppliments are so common in-game it serves most purpose during combat. It does also create that special spark of drama, leaving a combat on low health and half-way up a garden, and urging you to find more dust quickly. The soundtrack is also one of the best I've heard in a good long while, featuring cool and relaxed electronic music, that provides enough rhythmic backbone without being overly intense or dramatic. The game as a whole is fairly clean from modern gaming cliche and is a welcome change from pretty much everything.
So, if you are looking to relax into a hypnotic electronic music arcade game art world from an arena of high-maintenence, major league, time-limited, bland and corporate gaming, Pixeljunk Eden is the game you need to buy.
PS, it has world and friend ranked leaderboards if you didn't want to relax ;>

The Talos Principle is one amazing game.
When I started playing, I expected this to be a bunch of puzzles I'm supposed to solve to proceed to the next level, but quickly enough I realized there is so much more depth to this game. What started as a simple puzzle solving, quickly evolved into deep thought provoking philosophical discussion with myself, I wasnt even sure what do I believe in anymore.
Puzzles itself are not that hard. They consist of several game mechanics interlinked together. Game mechanics like reflecting laser beams at certain angles, disabling force fields and turrets with certain devices etc. All of them all straight forward and you don't really need to glitch your way trough the level or hit those exact impossible angles. Even if you're not into puzzle solving games, you will be able to finish this game. Completing the game 100% is a little tougher and will require you to think "outside the box", but its much more rewarding in the end as it helps to reveal more information about the game.
Trough the game, you are gathering pieces of informations, trying to put them together to discover whats it all about. There is this feeling of grand mystery you're trying to reveal and it sticks till the very end.
Game itself is full of easter eggs, references to history, philosophy, popular culture and so on... Trying to solve them is a mystery of its own.
I nominated this game for the "haunts my dreams" steam award in 2017. This game was trully haunting me, I couldn't stop thinking about it and still can't.

Space Quest Collection on Steam is a digital rerelease of collection from 2006. It had 6 main Space Quest games in it, brutal comedy Sierra adventure games that have excellent humor but you probably should use walkthrough and many saves. Spans from 1986 to 1995, so you will see a bit of evolution here. But it's not complete compilation.
It doesn't have the original EGA version of the first Space Quest, only VGA remake version. And Space Quest 4 that is included here is a CD version. It also comes with shortened manual of SQ1 to SQ6 which is important as some of them have copy protection that requires reading manual. If forget that it doesn't include the second manual "Popular Janitronics" for SQ6 that contained important instructions for in-game puzzle. Just Google it out.
It was 2006 collection, so it doesn't come with any Space Quest extras, like game that includes every mini-game from the series. No development video. No other fun videos. No cheaply done CGI teaser of Space Quest 7, you will have to YouTube it all out. Oh, and search for Space Quest 3 Promo while at it. Good fun.
EDIT: Well, Legacy collection has VGA remake of SQ1 while new updated has original instead.
As for games themselves, those are mostly credited as being job of Two Guys from Andromeda from Sierra, will have you follow Roget Wilco, a janitor and idiot who is clearly not a responsible adult. And he has dumb luck. And series had one great humor to it, coming from announcer and death messages. Yep, lots of death scenes in this one. Not to mention that games were generally good for Sierra games, with nice world and nice puzzles here and there. But it's Sierra games which means that it aged. I mean, it's fun to have death scenes, but having dead ends because you forgot item around hour ago is a big no-no for me. So eh. I just used walkthrough in this one.
Still more fun and safer than King Quest though. Hm, collection of that one went off Steam recently though. Anyway, off to drop quick comments on each game.
Space Quest 1 VGA:
A pretty short adventure on very few locations with no ability to backtrack. In this one you will have to rescue Star Generator from hands of aliens race. Well, this one is VGA remake from Space Quest 4 era. Sierra tried to remake a few of first games of their Quest series. Yes, it has dead ends. At least it helps that you have icon interface instead of text parser. Remake even has cheat-device to make annoying gambling part impossible to lose. Yes, original included machine on which you had to gamble and try to get a certain amount of money.
And hey, humor is there. And death messages humor. And somewhat gory deaths occasionally.
Don't forget about copy protection in manual. And don't forget to pull catridge back after you use it in the middle of a game.
Also, it has strange bug with speed setting. It doesn't affect everything in the game. You have to crank it up to be able to overrun walking droid mine in desert area.
Oh, and there are 3-issue comics that were made by Malibu, I think. Can be worth to track those down. No, it's not in-game thing.
Space Quest 2:
Came out in 1987, this one will show you the meaning of retro adventure, with parser command and walking with arrows. Actually, it will show you all the bad about them too. No regret of using walkthrough. It has dead ends, deaths, having to navigate through maze with pixel-accuaricy or die, having to guess with no big hints what to do, obscure puzzles, tedious walking, barely any characters, boring locations and huge maze where you can see small area around your character, oh my. Oh well, death messages are there. And you are now stopping a new villian, Sludge Vohaul. Stopping him from ending civilization by sending salemans. Yep, it got a bit less serious.
Space Quest 3:
Came out in 1989, was one of the first games to use Sierra's new engine that at this state allowed dumb straight movement by mouse, had a lot of cool effects for EGA game and was one of the first games on PC to use soundcard, with nice music here and there. The thing about this one is that it feels a bit like developers were running out of inspirations and just decided to do straight jokes. I mean, you can read easily from manual that you are supposed to save two personas of two main developers from evil ScumSoft corporation. Well, less Space, more jokes.
From one point it has some interesting setting and stuff, like getting chased by Arnoid. Or having to play horrible arcade game. But then you are also often left wandering around aimlessly at some point of a game.
It also has most gory deaths in series. I couldn't giggle at message because I was feeling too squishy.
That, and I would have never figured out to grab something that is few times bigger than main hero and isn't even visible in the current screen.
Space Quest 4:
It's time to be Time Ripper and kick butt of Sequel Police. Wait, you should be afraid of them actually. Anyway, this is beautiful VGA game now and has icon interface. Came out in 1991. Ask any fan, and they point at this part as their favourite. Though in this case, for every good thing, there is a bad thing somewhere else in the game. Still, most important thing, humor is at the peak there, alright. Actually, since it's CD version, you will be able to hear speech. And that announcer has one awesome announcer. Even "don't touch it!" will make you smile. Though they say that CD has slightly worse graphics than floppy, less animation, they say.
Sadly, it has painful parts. Not sure about dead ends now, there may be some. In one case, you are punished in the beggining at some point because you took one item some time ago. I know that announcer keeps warning how bad this item is, but we are potty-trained to grab everything. Also, Skate-O-Rama. Save tons of times and try to move in zero gravity in such way that police will miss you. Good luck.
Space Quest 5:
A little more on parody of Star Trek, this one was given to Dynamix to make and release it in 1993. It was floppy only release, so no speeches this time. And oh my, this one steps up in adventure games design. I am still not sure about dead ends, but this one has interesting narrative, that will actually make you interested to go into various place and progress in the game all time, as you command fleet and stop mutation. Humor is still there, althrough not as extreme. That first puzzle feltd hiralious for me. Old comics style is awesome.
Just don't forget to look into manual for coordinates.
You know, I actually could recommend it to modern gamer and almost regretted using walkthrough... Until I got to the maze part.
Dammit Wilco, you dummy-butt, you was so close at being best!
Oh well, you are just a janitor.
Space Quest 6:
Released in 1995, this one was done almost without original developers. Which means that a lot of puzzles had no needed hints and were obscure. That, and art style will turn off many people, looking like high-animated Microsoft Paint characters drawn on top of early CGI. And you would start in the dark ugly area with no directions and not much interesting parts. And try to solve obscure puzzle where you really should know what to do to begin with.
Ehh, it's not awesome. Get a bit better and a bit worse.
Actually, it has a glitch at tape worm screen near the end of game. Have to disable scrolling in options there. Vertical scrolling messes up.
Don't forget to find "Popular Janitronics" manual for puzzle.
It also had demo version that has different plot. Can be worth to check out.
Anyway, use walkthrough, but play these.

I did not know what the hell this was in my library, but now I know.
It's a game where you either move left or right, that's it. The catch is that you need "speed" to continue forward. The moment you can no longer move forward, your game is done. You have obstacles that either decreases your speed, health, or both. You have pickups that help make things easier, such as the speed boost that will help you progress to each group of items, or "big boost" that will help you pass two. The big boost is helpful for it allows you to pick up score instead rather than the speed boosts, the goal of the game. There is also a shot pickup that basically allows you to automatically fire if you by mistake hit an asteroid which would slow you down and give health damage.
This game concept could have been interesting, but the items are not scattered, they're all aligned in a row that's boring and repetitive. It's not something you'll get your money's worth unless it's cluttered in a bundle or you get it on sale here. The "upside" is it has trading cards, 15 cents worth, costing 25 cents overall to get a badge for the game.

This game bored me so terribly much I couldn't even finish it.
As far as Metroidvanias go, this one is so barebones and basic that nothing that would make this game worth being played really remains. Everything you would expect in that kind of game is there but in its dullest, most basic form. Metroidvanias thrive on a sense of exploration and curiosity, but if everything is run-of-the-mill and you're seen every single solution being done in much more creative ways before then there is zero payoff.
There is no combat nor any way to kill enemies so you're confined to a "move and jump" kind of gameplay that gets old really quickly considering how lazily designed the levels are. The game is not challenging and the parts that are, are more annoying than exciting.
The world is not nearly as "massive" as advertised, by the way. A few hours in and you've seen it all and are pretty much walking back and forth to the same places to get to new areas. Also, exploration is incredibly underwhelming since aside from the important items that get you to places, your rewards are pretty much just gems and keys that get completely obsoleted by one skeleton key you get when you have enough gems.
The "dream" scenes are completely pointless as you have no idea at all what's going on with the hopelessly unengaging story of the game so they just look like nonsense and an unnecessary hault to your gameplay.
The music is TERRIBLE and quite possible the worst aspect of the game. Seriously, I love 8-bit style music, but the soundtrack of this game is pretty much unbearable. It is at the same time saccharine and souless, and utterly ruins the mood of whatever was attempted to be accomplished here. It made playing the game a depressing experience more than anything else.
This game is cheap and all, so one is tempted to cut the game some slack, but honestly this game was just a waste of my time and I urge anyone to make a better use of theirs playing something else.

While it's not consistent throughout the series (mostly SQ VI, which isn't bad, but isn't great, either), the highpoints are tremendous. My favorite is easily SQ IV, but SQ I-III are also fantastic with the same sort of humor (I haven't played SQ V enough to rule on it).
It's important to mention that this collection is missing the original version of Space Quest I, which is an EGA version with a parser instead of point & click. I personally missed it since I have nostalgic memories of playing it. It's also important to note that this collection has compatibility issues. EDIT: I believe this has since been fixed. The non-Legacy edition worked on Windows 10 for me. I still prefer downloading ScummVM (a client program which allows you to run old Sierra & Lucas Arts games) and manually adding the games that way. ScummVM has plenty of options if you're a stickler for various graphics & sound options (it can emulate the Roland MT-32, a legendary sound device back in the day, however, you will need the ROM for it). You can also get the GOG version which has the original version of SQ I instead of the point & click remake.

For over two years they fought and won slowly advancing their technology till they had a stable industrial base and had upgraded their spears and arrows to machine guns and rifles.  The pirates had had enough banging their head against their fortified position and decided to setup a mortar bombardment instead... again.  The tribe had grown to around 20 at this time and prepared to counter attack and destroy the morter emplacement when half the tribe was struck down with plague while a toxic plume went up miles away and poisoned the air. Borderlands has boiled the basic mechanics down from a Diablo-style loot system and inserted them into a cartoonish and fun overworld populated by psychos. The drive and enjoyment here from from constant reinforcement and progression. Every single bullet pushes you further up the skill tree, giving you new perks and letting you cause damage or havok in new and interesting ways. The four classes can all use any of the weapons in the game, though the skills complement some combinations more overtly. The bosses are generally challenging enough to be fun, and the penalties for death are annoyance but not frustration. Nearly any encounter can be overcome with enough thought and preparation.
The game does get repetitive at points, and there are a few too many quests that tread into the fetch 10 pelts territory that MMOs are so fond of, but if you can slog through that it is well worth it. And if you can bring a friend along, you will hardly notice this anyways as you push to the front and squabble over who needs the gun with exploding fire bullets more.

Is a solid title that surely succeeds in captivating the player, but tries very little to improve upon the previous entry.
I've followed this franchise since "the testament of Sherlock Holmes" and I've loved every entry since then, but if you are expecting a new step forward like "crime and punishment" was for mechanics and graphics you will be a little disappointed. Aside the lack of innovation, the title is really solid and, in some areas, is able to surpass its predecessor, showing more positive aspects than negative ones.
Pros:
- Every case feels different. This is a huge relief, especially if compared to the previous title.
- Solving a case isn't a roll of dice. The previous title lets the solutions quite open, so open that sometimes there was no logical reason to prefer one culprit to another. This time feels different, little clues can effectively help you figure out what happened.
- Puzzles are well balanced, not too difficult to break the experience and stop the fun, not too easy to solve mindless. No puzzles seems out of place.
- No technical issues and beautiful graphic.
- Interesting characters.
Cons:
- Very few puzzles, especially if compared to previous titles.
- lack of innovation.
- The devil's daughter subplot is quite rushed. This is unfortunate especially if you choose it as the game title. Throughout the game you get little glimpses about that story only to face it as your last case.
- Shorter than previous entries, fewer cases.
- Skin textures are really low quality.
Depending on taste:
- Mini-games to break the monotony.
- A Sherlock Holmes able to have feelings
In the end is a good title, fun and solid. If you have never played another entry of this franchise you will be amazed, if not, the comparison with "crime and punishment" is obvious. Don't expect a huge innovation, expect a good game.

I can highly recommend this game! While I played Mario Kart a couple of years ago at a friend's house and didn't like it too much, because I felt winning relied too heavily on chance, I thought I would feel the same in this game. Sure enough, I did at first felt that, but after getting the hang of it after a couple of tries, I soon realized that it was mostly a skill-based game. Sure, there is some luck involved, but it isn't a key-factor to finishing first.
Whether you are familiar with Sega's games or not (I recognize most characters, but haven't played all games), this game should be a ton of fun if you enjoy arcade or kart racing games. Your vehicle transforming from car into boat or airplane and back isn't a gimmick, but really adds to the diversity of the game and the difficulty to master it, as cars, boats and planes each handle differently. Each character has different stats, although modifications for each character can be unlocked (just to be clear: visually customizing the karts/boats/planes is not possible). But the most fun feature of the game is that the track changes each lap (with some exceptions, depending on the game mode and type of race). Seeing that the tracks are all well-designed, this is a huge plus! There are also some different racing challenges, among which drifting, maneuvering through traffic, flying through rings, boost races, 1-on-1 and destroying a tank. That combined with a Hard mode that provides plenty of challenge for experienced racers, as well as the later unlocked Expert Mode, you'll likely be putting many hours in this game.
Although great fun, visually stunning and sufficiently challenging, you might still encounter a bug or glitch here or there, but they seem to be rare and don't break the game. The only semi-annoying bug I found is one where the button "Retry" is highlighted, while really the button "Quit" is being activated after pressing "Enter". I have noticed the same happening with the options "Continue" and "Play Again". I'm not sure what triggers this, but it can be easily solved each time by pressing up or down a few times.
This is without a doubt one of the best arcade/kart racing games available on PC. For me, the only real disappointment is that not all Sonic characters are in the game, but with 20+ characters throughout the Sonic games, that is something to be expected.
All in all, I'd give this game a 9 out of 10.

Overall, The Devil's Daughter is a decent Sherlock Holmes game but it fails to deliver on the promise that was established with Crimes and Punishments.
The cases presented have certain interesting points, particularly the 4th one but don't quite measure up to the five fascinating cases of Crimes and Punishments. The results are often too ambivalent to make a player confident in their deductions and there's always a sense that you've missed something even when you've found all the clues.
The attempt at an overarching plot and Holmes as a father sadly falls rather flat despite its best efforts. The game doesn't incorporate enough cues to pique a player and frankly, the plot breaks Frogware's previous assurances that the games following Crimes and Punishments were not part of the previously established timeline.
The gameplay remains quite solid but the prevalence of QTE rather spoils a neat little experience.
I'd recommend this for SH and Frogwares' games fans but hold off until a sale.

I don't even know why I'm writing this. Even my grandmother knows what Divekick is, and if you're reading this, you've already seen a couple screens of it and probably skimmed a couple other reviews.
I organize my steam library by genre, and when I went to sort this one, it gave me pause. Sure, it's kind of a fighting game, but it's also a bit of a strategy. Mostly, it's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
The worlds first two-button fighter (and it means that literally. No analog stick movement at all. Dive. Kick.) comes to us from Iron Galaxy games, and maybe it should have stayed there. Previously a developer for Dungeons and Dragons digital titles, they moved to a heavily meme-inflated "fighting" game where you first dive (or 'jump', but whatever) by pressing one button, and then, while in the air, kick using the other. That's it. There's a cast of characters to choose from, most of them harkening back to inside jokes.
It's moderately funny, I guess, but that's hardly a reason to spend 10 bucks. Basically if you have Divekick, it's because you got hyped on it (or in my case, someone gifted it) and spent maybe as long as I have playing it. Poor replay value outside of sheer novelty, poor gameplay attibuting victories to luck rather than any variant of skill, and after the third or fourth time he holds up the, "I don't hug white girls." sign, the joke loses its luster, and I quit out to go play a fighting game with more than two buttons.
Should you get it? Do you make enough money to literally waste ten dollars? Sure, but if you're even a tiny bit iffy about it, wait until the next time it's 90% off. In the meantime, there are better ten dollar games.
Hell, there are better FIVE dollar games. Get two.

Dark Messiah of M&M is a decent game, that has held up pretty well over the years.  I played through it recently on a Ryzen 7, with a GTX 980 Ti and Windows 10 Fall Creator's Update -- worked well, except that it crashed now and then (usually when changing regions), and every time I exited the game (which wasn't a big deal).
The game's graphics scale well to high resolution (QHD, UHD) displays, and the animation, ragdolls/physics, etc. are all pretty good.  It even looks good when put under psuedo-HDR modes of HDR televisions that can artificially create HDR for image sources that don't have it natively.
The combat is pretty fun, although not too much more complicated than games like Skyrim (which this game predates by several years).  The infamous kicking is just as entertaining as all the reviews state, as are slides, etc. caused by ice effects.  The game is relatively easy, overall, on "normal" difficulty.
If you can get it for $5 or under, don't hesitate -- it's worth it just for the kicking and ragdoll physics.  Even at the full price ($9.99 at the time of this review), it's well worth it, if you're okay with cheezy voice acting, and a moderate campaign length (15-25 hours, depending on how thorough you want to be).

$1 Ride is a new take on an old trope. You'll pilot your ship that, contrary to what physics would tell you, can't maintain its speed  to save it's life. Replace space with Honey and that's what the flying feels like. The only buttons you'll use are left and right arrow or "A" and "D". Flying left or right you'll attempt to pick up speed-boosters, rockets or money. Which is the right choice is dictated by your speed at the time. If you're flying full speed, grab some cash/rockets. If you're a bit slow, you're going to need that speed boost. Contrary to what you might think you have no real control over the rockets as they are fired automatically to take out obstacles. I'm going to have to echo what a couple of the other reviewers have said here and say you should only pick this game up if you're getting it for free or as part of a bundle. It's not a bad way to spend half an hour, but In my opinion it's not worth the one dollar asking price.

This is a game where you could judge it quickly by face value, but you really need to stick with it to understand and see the beauty of it. It is a REALLY good puzzle game.
The objective is to control a bug through spinning and rolling and make it hit spores and then collect the pollen so that it germinates nearby seeds which will grow further branches which you can now latch onto. You must navigate each map with your grappling silk hook and find five spectra (glowing bulb spirits) so that you can unlock more maps. There is a total of 75 spectra in all. The game is visually impressive with it's abundant in  your face vibrant colors and patterns and it's comprehensive list of trendy instrumental music scores. It's peaceful and relaxing, but it is also very fast if you are to take on the challenge of getting the whole five spectra in a single course in a single run. There is no dillydallying then. The further you progress the more interesting the different mechanics of the game.
What I love about this game is that there is NOTHING like it. Well done to the developers for producing a UNIQUE product and visual. It's constantly on sale and I would say it's worth more than what it goes on sale for. High Praise.

Initially it wouldn't run on my Win8.1 PC after installation - it would seem a bad dosbox configuration or possibly an issue with the emulator?
Anyways - if anyone else has the same issue, these steps might work for you as well.
1. Right click the game when in your Steam Games Library > "Properties" > Click the tab, "LOCAL FILES" > Click "BROWSE LOCAL FILES..."
2. Open ".\dosbox-0.63\dosbox.conf" for editing in notepad..
3. Find (CTRL+F) "core=" and change the value from "dynamic" to "simple" and save your changes (CTRL+S)..
4. Launch the game.

Personally, this isn't as good as you have to win the game.
First, I didn't like the "open world" style as it lost the intertwinedness of the original game. everything was too far spaced apart and the zones were bland and mechanically the same. Because of this open world idea, this means there is a LOT of backtracking. far more than in the original, and I felt that the backtracking was a lot more fun in the original. In this game, it's walking around every dungeon in the world until you find that one hidden door that takes you to the gem, but in the original, it was more of a test of your skill and determination. Which brings me to
Point 2: It wasn't hard enough. This is my opinion, but the level design seems lazy when compared to the original. The original had a maze-like a dungeon with challenging tasks. This game was way too easy. The only hard part I found was the path to the arcadian's mask. The rest was more tedious than hard.
Also, the graphics and story were not that great. This game blew up everything which made levels a lot easier, but I guess this is okay considering some of them scroll. I would have liked something that would have come off the snes, akin to Metroid style graphics. And Stemmons community looks really out of place. the CRT simulation on this was way too overwhelming and the story was subpar. in the original, you just fought the hollow king. you didn't need to know why you were doing it because the gameplay was solely on mechanics. adding villagers and a story seemed like wasted potential. There probably may have been a way to do this right. also, the music, while catchy was very short, and could have been done better, like in cave story.
What I did like about this game were the speedruns. I liked competing against other players and some of the dungeons, while not that hard, were a little tricky. If the speedrun levels had been longer and more fleshed out I would have really liked it
Overall this game is not worth 8 dollars and would have been really good if they had put more heart into it, and made it more akin to the original.

Original Review: 7/18/14

Hero Siege, the game about killing stuff that has more health than you.
Then again, what roguelike isn't about that?
After 3.5 hours of gameplay, I can strongly recommend you buy this title. Its not easy but not hard difficulty keeps you from sliding right through a level, but it also doesn't have you on your knees begging for mercy. The classes vary from something traditional like the Pyromancer, to something not so traditional, like the Redneck. Crypts, dungeons and statues can apprear, giving you chances at gold, keys to open chests, and experience to level up. I can't imagine the time it takes to get to level 210 (as seen in the screenshots), my Pyro is only a level 17, after 3.5 hours of playing.
But here's the thing about roguelikes: no matter how much you play, or how much your practice, you're still going to suck. With a game like this, you just have to hope and pray you don't get hit with an arrow of get a potion that brings you down to no health. If you get hit by an arrow, that's it. You have to find some health or you'll get hit by another and die. Aside from that, no matter how many times the game pulls a kill out of it's ♥♥♥, the satisfying feeling of leveling up or killing a boss will always make up for it.
Even after throwing my mouse at the wall, or tearing my headset off and throwing at my PC, Hero Siege will hold a place in my gaming life, known as the game that broke me. It will forever hold a place as my least favorite game, the game i play all the time.

Echoes+ is Free for all Steam users, so you're better off playing it yourself than hearing me ramble.
But if you want a quick rundown, it is something of a hybrid of classic Asteroids and beloved Geometry Wars, made to showcase the ability of the AppGameKit engine it was made in. There are five modes that are well described on the store page. My personal favorites are Meteor Storm, where a line of astroids come from one side of the screen and your strategy is to dodge them and rack up multipliers, and the standard Echoes modes, which puts you in a rectangular arena where you are shooting against various sizes and types of asteroids while increasing your weapon power and score and trying to avoid damage or restore health from pick ups. I've never cared for Time Attack/Survival modes in most games, so I don't care for them here either, and the Asteroid Belts Mode (where snake like strings of rocks home in on you) features my most hated "enemy" of the game - so simply don't like it.
You can do worse for free on Steam and you can probably learn a bit about game development by opening this in AppGameKit. It is a decent twin stick shooter, but personally I prefer Waves and most people prefer Geometry Wars.

tl;dr A promising game that runs well. If you are looking for mil-sim, or something between BF and Arma on the hardcore spectrum, this could be it.
Squads soldiers are the best I've seen in a while. Not as clunky as Arma soldiers, but they don't feel like they are on ice skates like in CoD.
As for the game itself, well it beats Arma in that department too (as far as hardcore mil-sim goes). Runs better than Arma but still lacks the AAA graphics (so even with Arma). Idk what the usual server pop is like outside of a free weekend, but I've been able to jump on pretty much full servers within 1 minute. I hope they improve the server browser in the near future, as trying to find servers you have played before is difficult.
I played without a mic so I didn't get the full experience, but if you find a decent squad leader you can have a fun time.
Whilst you may not rack up the kills and it may take awhile to find action (hope you like running!), when you do get to the front line it can be pretty hair raising. 10/10 audio + screams of my dying comrades.
Also you need good eyesight, and those cheeky Russian soldiers are dressed up like US ones so be careful (unless you are VS the militia in which case it's easier.
Guns - The guns are great to handle, I wish there was more kit customisation but what they provide is sufficient compared to Squad's competition (looking at you Bohemia). The gun sway isn't too bad, but neither it easy to shoot at first.
Maps - The city based map was awesome, I'm pretty sure every building can be entered and there could be an enemy around every corner. The sparse desert/forest maps were great too, albeit not as forgiving to a newbie.
All in all I look forward to seeing what this game becomes. Project Reality has come a long way.

I was able to "update" my AMD driver to 17.5.2, which fixed the issue (thank you comments that pointed me to the right solution). As such I will rescore the game.
For starters, the game had a much deeper story than I would have expected a Wolfenstein game to have, and BJ certainly gets much more exposition via either cutscenes or frequent internal monologues. Frankly, most iD games can be shortened to "you are DOOM guy, kill everything you see". This game has that (as expected), but with some added dimension. The villains can be sadistic (Deathshead early on is a complete psychopath), or just distrubing in the way that only a cold disregard for human life can be.
The stealth system is simple, but functional. The AI isn't fantastic in this department; bad guys have Skyrim-tier perception, but it is hard to truly stealth entire levels unless the game WANTS you to stealth. At the least, it means you usually can catch enemies off-guard, and the game is good at offering multiple avenues of ingress to a given area, whether you prefer to just charge in or take a side path like an air duct. This is particularly important on higher difficulties, since health has only limited regen capacity and at higher difficulties enemies are much more capable.
The setting is well-done. Nazi brutalism dominates, architecture-wise. Lots of propaganda, and it is a very interesting sci-fi twist to "what if". The graphics serve to accent this; its a good-looking game, even on my relatively spartan 2gb video card. Enemy models are great, they look like stormtroopers from Star Wars with a black color palette, and they can be quite aggressive at attempting to flank when in groups. However, their individual AI can do quite questionable things, such as allowing themselves to get pinned when they find cover at longer distances. When up close, they tend to move around a lot more. Controls are likewise responsive, with a decent lean-mechanic. Simply put, if you try to aim when near cover, you will lean over or to the side of it. This can be manually overidden with the alt-key, allowing you to always be in the right position for a shot.
Gun play has always been a strong-suit of iD software, and it really is here as well. The guns all have distinct flavors, depsite their relatively few number. There are shotguns, lasers, assault rifles, machine pistols, a marksman's rifle, etc., so all the general FPS bases are covered. If you want a game where you can dual-wield auto-fire shotguns, here it is. If that doesn't sound great to you, i'm not sure what would.
Collectibles also exist, should you wish to pursue them. While I am not a perfectionist myself, some may enjoy the challenge. Many of the collectibles are not just "piece of intel 1/3", some are letters or momentos that players may find more interesting. However, replay value is not phenomenol. Playing a campaign every year or so after watching "Man in the High Castle" may be fun, but it doesn't have much to offer. This game will not be racking up scores or hundreds of hours like Skyrim, Fallout: NV, or Witcher 3 did.
This is not a game that bases itself in complete realism. The protagonist is himself an unstoppable one-man army, effectively time displaced and filled with anti-Nazi rage. He can get shot, take on giant nazi mechs, and gets laser weapons. But the iD factor shows through; they take "rule of cool" very seriously, and it makes for a game that is, at its core, fun, if at times rather challenging. If you want a difficult FPS grounded in more realism, I'd suggest something like Ranger Hardcore Metro 2033/Last Light. But if you want a game that combines some of the more arcade-y elements of early FPS games with some of the more CoD tactical gameplay, Wolfenstein: The New Order shows that even old IPs can breathe fresh air into a VERY saturated market.
8.5/10, certainly worth the half-off price. Some deduction for it not working without hunting for AMD patches. If you see a Wolfenstein: Old Blood and New Order bundle for $30 or less, it is certainly worth getting them if you enjoy FPS titles.

The combat is where this game shines. There is also a nice tutorial system. You learn as you play the campaign, which is perfect for people who don't like long introductory training sessions. I only had to look up a tutorial on how to beat one boss and it was the final one and (technically a spoiler) It was because the last boss involves a dragon and the wood along the ceiling had me believe you were suppose to go up there so It confused me but it turns out all you had to do was hit or shoot him, cause every other dragan before you had to kill with either a ballista or by using a trap so I thought this was going to be the same.
Non-Linear Classes:
You can go with the Warrior, Thief/Rogue, and Mage. Archery isn't really a class and it's more of just a secondary weapon that you can count on. You don't actually select your class, you just put skill points towards things that help you use what ever type of weapon it is you like. So if you like Daggers you'll put it all into Stealth and stealth assistance, and archery probably. If you like Swords you'll put it into strength and endurance. If you like magic you'll put it into mana, but you can switch between roles simply by switching weapons, so if you put a few points into stealth and you wanna backstab someone you can and then you can slaughter the rest with a sword.
Weapons:
Well you have a few kinds of weapons but with several variations that I won't all list but will give a few examples.
Swords, Daggers, Staffs, and Bows.
Swords are the top of the food chain for melee combat, they are well balanced between speed and damage. Swords can be paired with a shield, which makes them even better, as shields can be used to bash enemies, this means you can lay down some sick and hefty combos, especially on solo enemies. I forgot to mention the kick, which stuns and staggers enemies and can send them flying if they are in the right spot. So basically with swords you would block and let the enemy hit you and then you want to shield bash right after or kick them then when they are stunned hit them with a heavy attack and then repeat. You can do it your own way if you want. After a while you get used to the combat and you learn to predict attacks.
Then you got daggers, which is what you want to use if you're doing a stealthy Thief/Rogue type of playthrough. Daggers are extremely fast and versitile. They typically hit in burst and are super fun to use. A power attack from daggers will hit in a double swing burst, so the first might stagger the enemy and the second will pound them into the ground, then they'll be easy to stab while they're down. You can also throw daggers if an enemy is fleeing or if you have full adrenaline.
Staffs...
All weapons can impale a person while they are down (except bows, duh.)
Adrenaline allows you to use a power attack that can instantly kill one or two enemies depending on which attack it is.
Swords sometimes will do a dual swing which can be used to hit more than one enemy if timed correctly. Sane could be done with daggers but less effectively (most likely.)
Archery is somewhat underpowered but very useful against an unaware enemy. A headshot against an enemy who hasn't noticed you will kill him instantly (90% of the time, sometimes the hitbox is sort of deceptive or the gravity on the arrow will screw you out of the kill and will instead just trigger the enemy and♥♥♥♥♥♥everyone in the room off.)
Some areas of traps which are practically invisible unless you have a special ability or if you die to it and then know where it is. You can trigger a trap by shooting it, Just aim for the shadow on the ground. You'll walk into these 90% of the time and they will scare the living♥♥♥♥♥♥out of you for 5 seconds because you'll be walking up to some cool as loot all happy and♥♥♥♥♥♥and then BOOOM! Huge ♥♥♥♥ing explosion from out of thin air will instantly kill you. It took me like 5 times to realize they were traps. I thought it was some cheap♥♥♥♥♥mechanic to keep me out of an area.
Exploration, not much to say about this. There's a lot of hidden areas and if you find them they can contain some godlike loot which is extremely useful. I'm going to tell you right now, when you realize you cannot use the "Sword of the Dragonclaw" DO NOT THROW IT AWAY... Trust me. It's an end game weapon and if you keep it with you that whole time you'll be able to use it if you decide to purge Xana from your soul.

I'm a fan of these kinds of srategy sims. But I have a couple gripes that I think are easy to fix:
1. This game suffers from a lack of clean step by step instructions. There is a tutorial, pop-ups, but it is timed rather than screen based. If you get ahead of the tutorial the only way to get past certain screens was to click on the pop-up which made it go away. So I ended up wasting several months in the game not knowing what to do to release a film. I recommend that there be a clear pathing for each movie so that you can click the title and it will immediately take you to the next step. That way you can't get lost. I also recommend an icon next to each movie in your queue to clearly state where they are visually instead of having to click them and read.
2. In order to set up auto-save to start you have to create a save game first. I think that's backward. It should auto-save to start in my opinion.
Overall, some technical issues hold me back from recommending this game at this time. However, the dev is actively looking to improve the game so with a dev like this and a game that has almost everything you need I am willing to thumbs up this game.
