One day after another raider attack, Lupos was shot, there was seven of us at this point and none of us but the Doc had any medical skills, it was looking like a pretty sorry state of affairs. Weeks told us some rubbish about reading some off-world med book. No idea if he was lying or not or he just wanted to help the person who had patched him up countless times. He managed to save Lupos and from that point forward he decided medicine was his calling.
He built a wooden shack out back with 4 beds in it and put a red light in there, no idea why. Every raider attack from then onwards it was like he couldn’t wait for his new guests to arrive. Most of them died, the lucky ones. The survivors were taken to Weeks cabin, let’s just say no one who went in came out the same way they went in. He would go into “treat” them, their corpses would come out with legs amputated, replaced with stumps of wood, their jaws removed and often missing several organs. He would store the remains in the freezers with the food, what the hell!
The thing was he became good, almost as good as Lupos so we let him be. There must have been at least 40 graves out the back of that shack by the time things went belly up. Another day another raider attack. Bloody genius who thought mortars were a good idea for base defense, almost killed us all. Lobbed a mortar shell right into the hospital where Lupos was treating patients.
Weeks quickly tended to Lupos' wounds and then went to play in his shack with his latest friends. It became apparent that Lupos right leg had been maimed due to the mortar injury. You would think after performing countless amputations and peg leg attachments on his victims Weeks would be able to do this.
No the idiot failed five surgeries to help poor doc, not to mention stabbing her five times in the torso and chest. What the hell is wrong with Weeks. A few days later both Lupos and Weeks contracted severe malaria. None of us knew what to do, both doctors were dying. Irony or not Weeks died roughly one Week after contracting the disease, I threw his corpse in the newly made cremater, no one wanted to bury him out back with his victims.
Lupos is a tough bird, she pulled through but was still missing a leg. I thought screw it, how hard can it be and with my none existent medical skills managed to pull it off. Lupos was up and walking again. We agreed the next time a trading ship came by with some synth legs we would get one for the doc. Sadly that never happened, the boomrat plague happened. There was so many and they came so quickly. The stupid dog Silver, who was Weeks loyal pet went into a frenzy opening the main door to the base and mauling one of our crew. We had to put the poor mutt down. It was too late though, the boomrats poured in. People panicked and stabbed them causing explosions everywhere.
Only I made it out of the inferno, Lupos was too slow now that she had a wooden leg. I made it offworld in the escape pod we had built. That was the end of New Havenbrook. I leave this as a record for the poor souls I left behind. I probably won’t survive to tell the tale, I got burnt pretty good and I’m bleeding out it’s only a matter of time now. I wish Lupos was here.

Full disclosure: This is the only Wolfenstein game I've played, and I played this right after I played DOOM (2016) so my expectations may not have been proper for the game.
I'm conflicted; I like different parts seperately but feel like they didn't fit together well as a whole. I like the character development and story arcs that are in the game but at times it feels like it slows the game down too much (didn't much care for the time sponge missions in the resistance hideout). Mechanically, the inclusion of stealth was fun (felt like Elmer Fudd during Nazi Season) but I would have rather seen more time spent on polishing the shooty mechanics.
All in all, I did enjoy myself, howerver I will not be making an effort to replay it.

I was able to "update" my AMD driver to 17.5.2, which fixed the issue (thank you comments that pointed me to the right solution). As such I will rescore the game.
For starters, the game had a much deeper story than I would have expected a Wolfenstein game to have, and BJ certainly gets much more exposition via either cutscenes or frequent internal monologues. Frankly, most iD games can be shortened to "you are DOOM guy, kill everything you see". This game has that (as expected), but with some added dimension. The villains can be sadistic (Deathshead early on is a complete psychopath), or just distrubing in the way that only a cold disregard for human life can be.
The stealth system is simple, but functional. The AI isn't fantastic in this department; bad guys have Skyrim-tier perception, but it is hard to truly stealth entire levels unless the game WANTS you to stealth. At the least, it means you usually can catch enemies off-guard, and the game is good at offering multiple avenues of ingress to a given area, whether you prefer to just charge in or take a side path like an air duct. This is particularly important on higher difficulties, since health has only limited regen capacity and at higher difficulties enemies are much more capable.
The setting is well-done. Nazi brutalism dominates, architecture-wise. Lots of propaganda, and it is a very interesting sci-fi twist to "what if". The graphics serve to accent this; its a good-looking game, even on my relatively spartan 2gb video card. Enemy models are great, they look like stormtroopers from Star Wars with a black color palette, and they can be quite aggressive at attempting to flank when in groups. However, their individual AI can do quite questionable things, such as allowing themselves to get pinned when they find cover at longer distances. When up close, they tend to move around a lot more. Controls are likewise responsive, with a decent lean-mechanic. Simply put, if you try to aim when near cover, you will lean over or to the side of it. This can be manually overidden with the alt-key, allowing you to always be in the right position for a shot.
Gun play has always been a strong-suit of iD software, and it really is here as well. The guns all have distinct flavors, depsite their relatively few number. There are shotguns, lasers, assault rifles, machine pistols, a marksman's rifle, etc., so all the general FPS bases are covered. If you want a game where you can dual-wield auto-fire shotguns, here it is. If that doesn't sound great to you, i'm not sure what would.
Collectibles also exist, should you wish to pursue them. While I am not a perfectionist myself, some may enjoy the challenge. Many of the collectibles are not just "piece of intel 1/3", some are letters or momentos that players may find more interesting. However, replay value is not phenomenol. Playing a campaign every year or so after watching "Man in the High Castle" may be fun, but it doesn't have much to offer. This game will not be racking up scores or hundreds of hours like Skyrim, Fallout: NV, or Witcher 3 did.
This is not a game that bases itself in complete realism. The protagonist is himself an unstoppable one-man army, effectively time displaced and filled with anti-Nazi rage. He can get shot, take on giant nazi mechs, and gets laser weapons. But the iD factor shows through; they take "rule of cool" very seriously, and it makes for a game that is, at its core, fun, if at times rather challenging. If you want a difficult FPS grounded in more realism, I'd suggest something like Ranger Hardcore Metro 2033/Last Light. But if you want a game that combines some of the more arcade-y elements of early FPS games with some of the more CoD tactical gameplay, Wolfenstein: The New Order shows that even old IPs can breathe fresh air into a VERY saturated market.
8.5/10, certainly worth the half-off price. Some deduction for it not working without hunting for AMD patches. If you see a Wolfenstein: Old Blood and New Order bundle for $30 or less, it is certainly worth getting them if you enjoy FPS titles.

As a gamer who played Return to Castle Wolfenstein and Wolfenstein: Enemy Territory while growing up, I must say that this game impressed me in terms of how they managed to recreate that feeling that only Wolfeinstein games manage to produce (this maybe a fanboy speaking, just so you know).
Everything about this game is worth it. The music, story, artwork, collectables, lore, refferences to some other games, hidden mini games, weapons, perks and challenges to unlock them, the badass feeling while you bring destruction upon your enemies. The characters make you feel like they are alive even if they are just a bunch of pixels on your screen.The emotions they managed to put in all characters is great, they are not lifeless and there just to fill the space, and your character is not a mute, Blasko has his own thoughts as you move forward with the game. AI is not dumb, they dont just camp and wait for you, they overwhelm you if you wait for them too much and dont let you breathe if you give them space to do so.
This game was very very well made, the only cons I could think off is maybe that stealth is sometimes too easy but AI is not dumb enough to not see you if you are in front of them and not in cover, they are well aware of stuff that is in front of them. The other problem was horizontal screen tearing where vsync didnt help and changing various settings in the nvidia control panel etc., but that may as well be my graphics drivers.
Anyway, worth your money and your time. Buy it.

This game is really fun platformer and I recommend it if you liked its predecessor, You Have to Win the Game (get it; it's free on Steam!). The gameplay is a lot like the original, but in this game there are towns, more secrets, and an open world. The game world works like Zelda ii, the overworld is top down, but all the actual gameplay takes place in 2d areas. If you play the game, I recommend collecting all the gems (and maybe all the achievements if you're into that). This game has a unique crt display style which might annoy you because it makes everything look blurry, but the game looks horrible if you turn it off. The soundtrack to this game is absolutely phenomenal. It is my favorite video game chiptune soundtrack ever. (If you like to buy the soundtracks to video games, you should know that it can't be purchased on Steam separately from the game) My biggest complaint is that the game is too easy, especially when compared to its predecessor. There are a couple of really difficult areas, but they can feel a little out of place because of the shift of difficulty. I would recommend this game overall, but the execution could have been tighter.  Starting off on a positive, the game's graphics are actually pretty unique as it has been programmed to replicate the graphic style of playing an NES game back in its hey day.  It has so much detail that if you look at the edges of the screen it's rounded off and reflects the side of the screen, just like the TVs did from that era.  It really reminds me of playing games back in the 90's, though it can hurt your eyes after a while, especially since you'll be sitting closer to your computer monitor then you would have sat next to the TV.  I didn't adjust any of the options for this myself, but there are several graphic options you can adjust if you weren't a kid of that era and don't want to strain your eyes like that.
The game opens with a basic tutorial showing you the mechanics of the game, but otherwise it just dumps you in the middle of nowhere with no explanation as to who you are, what your mission is, or where anything is.  You actually don't even get a name in this game; you're just called Wayfarer.  I've noticed this is pretty common in many indie games, and while I don't mind it that much it doesn't build up the story very well or give the player any sense as to what it is they're trying to accomplish.  It isn't like the old days where we'd have an instruction manual to browse through.  However, this is somewhat dealt with by the fortune teller system.  Merely speak to one of them in any town and they'll tell you the next place to go, which is very helpful, as otherwise there's nothing else to guide you on your mission.
This proves especially meaningfully in certain areas of the game.  For instance, while exploring the desert area, if you pay attention to what the Arcadian in that area says, they tell you about a secret cache to go to in order to get an important item.  After getting that item and leaving the area, if you continue going East, you'll hit the edge of the sea, and you're able to walk across it and access an island (which is never explained or accounted for how you do that).  No NPCs mention this area, so it is somewhat obtuse to find, especially since nothing draws your eye to that set of islands; I feel like I was pretty lucky to have stumbled upon it.  What really aggravated me though was when I was there, I explored around the island to see if I could go further, but I must have missed the one place I could have done so.  With absolutely nothing even hinting at this secondary secret area, even when I thought it might have been there, I do think this is a flaw in the game since others might not have even found the first island like I did.
This also happens while exploring different dungeons, as hidden areas are secreted away throughout.  Some of them have very good clues cueing you in to subvert your expectations and try something different, such as jumping through a wall of spikes because there's an arrow pointed towards them.  Other areas, however, don't seem to have any clues whatsoever.  In the very first dungeon you explore, it turns out there is quite a bit more there then you first expect.  After exploring for a while with greater power-ups at my disposal I was able to see an area I could platform through, but had no idea had to get to.  It turns out, all I had to do to access it was to walk through a solid-looking wall.  I could have done that part much earlier, but with no visual cues or hints, I had no reason to attempt that, which is a real problem in a game like this.  The player shouldn't have to be of the mindset to check every wall on the off chance it contains a secret; they should be rewarded for noticing the clues laid out around them, not for blindly jumping against every wall possible.
Another area that lacked polish was how the game distributed its hidden items and the usefulness of its power-ups.  Early on, with many of the collectible gems out of your reach because you lack power-ups, they feel very well distributed and tucked away, with some being easier to obtain then others.  However, in the late game, after you have all of the power-ups, many of them just seem to be tossed around randomly without much thought, as if they wanted to make sure they hit a certain number or just wanted to get the game finished.  Another example of this issue is how you get missions from NPCs to explore an area or get an item, making you think this might be a recurring theme through the game, but this only happens four times throughout the whole game.  It happens so infrequently that if you took it out entirely nobody would have noticed, especially since the main quest overshadows them.
Similarly, one of the early power-ups you get in the game (if not the very first one) is a red block to help you platform in certain areas.  It's useful, but later on it becomes completely unnecessary, as you gain a double jump and the ability to slide and jump alongside walls.  If it weren't for an NPC rewarding you for getting the item, you wouldn't actually need it at all throughout the entire game.  Even if it there were areas it was necessary to use, these blocks show up in only a few, scarce areas, making it seem all the more pointless, especially since there are two versions of these same item.  In order to gain an achievement in the game you actually have to get rid of these two items.  I really think this needed a bit more thought since its existence in the game is so moot.  Another item that didn't seem to serve as robust a purpose as it could have was the mask that showed you invisible items.  It was immensely useful the few times it was used, but it could have served a greater purpose in showing you hints to find secret areas that wouldn't otherwise show up.  Such a shame they didn't do that as it would have removed one of my bigger complaints about the game.
A simple aspect in the game I found lacking was never getting an ability to engage in combat with the enemies.  I have played games like this before where you always platform and dodge around your enemies, but somehow in this game I found myself craving it more than usual.  I think it's because despite the game providing you with ample checkpoints so you can quickly retry areas if you die (very good job in that regard), the game has several enemies that are very annoying to dodge and avoid.  Namely the flying skulls and the giant eyeball; I craved a means of destroying these guys so badly by the time the game was over and was so disappointed it never came up.
The last thing I'd mention is that the story of the game is quite abstract and I would suggest fairly dark at that.  Nothing horror movie level, but I felt like I was reading the quotes of someone struggling with writer's block and depression that their life isn't going in the direction they want it to.  Not really what you'd expect with a game title like Super Win the Game.  I don't mind it being there, but I'd kind of like to play an indie game that didn't have this darker overtone laid over the gameplay.  There's a reason people love Nintendo so much; the platforming is happy and upbeat.
Overall, I would say this game probably isn't worth its full asking price.  With a few hints and pointers, I was able to beat the game 100% in just under six hours and I know others could do better then that if they had looked up stuff earlier than I did.  I picked it up while it was on sale and would recommend you do the same, as it does merit its overall favorable reviews.

Super Win the Game is a retro 8-bit adventure platformer, taking inspiration from games like Link's Adventure with its wide open overworld that houses individual side-scrolling action segments.  Unlike the first "You Have to Win the Game", Super focuses much less on high-precision difficult platforming and trades it for a much larger, more explorative game packed with secrets.  It loses much of the minimalist charm the original had and is ultimately an unmemorable game, but is nevertheless enjoyable and a faithful tribute to the NES era.
There is no game more relaxing, philosophical, well-crafted, and simply good than this game.
True to the original, great support and an active online community. A must buy for any former or new player.

The game (or Episode 1) - or more interactive story - is enjoyable and well done. It will make you laugh and think about choices in some areas. It stays true to the Borderlands canon and will have you wanting more.
While I will recommend Episode 1, I have to point out that this is for a 5 episode series with only 1 released so far. Typically, episodes are delivered in a 4-6 week time frame (6-8 for longer episodes) but, for this series, it has been 13 weeks and still no word of when Episode 2 will be available. While the game is enjoyable, the communication from the company is extremely poor and can frustrate many waiting for a game to be delivered that was already paid for. If they continue to take as long on each episode, the full game (all five episodes) will not be done until early 2016 (about nine months later than normal).
If you are the type frustrated with long waits in between episodes, I would recommend waiting until all five are available. If you don't mind the wait, then I would recommend picking it up now.

+Perfect blend of Telltale and Borderlands humor
+Dynamic choices that make you think
+Unique and quirky characters
+Captures Borderlands series' atmosphere well
+Two playable characters
+Anti-hero protagonists, a Hyperion employee and a Pandoran thief trying to get rich
+Excellent voice acting, including Patrick Warburton (Brock from the Venture Bros.)
+Cool additions to the Borderlands universe (Echo scanner eyes)
+Many references to the Borderlands games, including some surprise characters that I will not spoil
-Untimely updates. Come on Telltale, it's been three months.
The last update from TT was on February 22nd, claiming the Episode 2 will be big and on its way, but still no release date after an extra month of waiting. It's a shame that Telltale is neglecting this game, because it actually is my favorite from them. So far, Episode 1 was a blast to play. While the moral choices and dillemas never come close to The Walking Dead game, the humor and storytelling are definitely my cup of tea. As a huge Borderlands fan, this title definitely does the series justice. The only issue is that Telltale isn't giving this title justice. If you're a fan of the Borderlands series and its trademark humor, and enjoy the choice-based gameplay of Telltale games, definitely pick up this game...once all of the episodes are released.

Rimworld is a game that I wish I could give a nuetral rating.  Is it a bad game? Nope.  Is it a great game? Again, no.  This game is similar to another indie title called Banished.  Although the planet you crash land on is about a thousand times more dysfunctional and so are the colonists.  There is a bit of the Sims mixed in with mood and needs counters.  When your mood becomes to low, your colonists will end up having psychotic breaks, which can cause them to wander aimlessly or start fights with other colonists.  While it is neat in theory, if you roll certain colonists or if some join with a number of mental issues, you're gonna have a bad time.
To sum this game up, it's pretty much: start a colony and wait for random events to kill you.  Literally.  Random event after random event, and it gets to the point where these events start to pull you away from the game and sit in your chair and wonder?  How in the hell can a plague, solar flare, raid, and lightning storm happen all at once?  By the way if you get that combo, you are pretty much dead.  These are great ideas on paper, but after a while they really detract from the gameplay just because of how often they happen and the right combination WILL destroy your colony, no matter how good you build it.  And if it doesn't, you are left with one or two colonists and have to pretty much start all over again.  It gets old, very very fast.  Oh and don't even get me started at how stupid the AI of your colonists can be...(but overall the AI is pretty good)
Don't get me wrong though, it can be fun.  But I think they should have added some more variety of play other than just random event after random event.  And you can end up with colonists that are so mentally fragile that the littlest thing will set them off on a psychotic break.  This game is so deliberately and obviously trying to hold you back from finishing the game that you feel it.  You will eventually stop enjoying the game because you know, that there isn't one thing in this game that is trying to help you...well...maybe cargo pods and ship debris.  But this overall sense can really detract some from the whole experience and I think that that is the games biggest flaw.
Overall I'd say it is a game worth trying if you liked games like Banished, otherwise I wouldn't get my hopes up to high.

This game is, without a doubt, a fantastic looking game, the graphics are extraordinary.
The very trivial things like being able to walk out of 221B and walk along Baker Street reveals itself to me as... well... nostalgic in a way.
The gameplay is very similar to that of Crimes and Punishments, with an addition of stealthing, tailing, lockpicking and safe-cracking. While they are great additions, some of them were quite a bore, while some were decent to say the least. One thing that I like was how character portrait can be imprecise.
This game takes place after the Testament of Sherlock Holmes and we see Kate Holmes who was adopted by Sherlock Holmes after the events of Testament of Sherlock Holmes, the over-arching story in this game revolves around the idea of Kate finding out her identity as Moriarty's daughter which is interesting but brings some issues to Sherlock Holmes as a character. Don't get me wrong, seeing development in Sherlock Holmes is fascinating but he doesn't feel like THE Sherlock Holmes, especially when we see him facing emotional issues with Kate.
The cases in this game were... interesting yet somehow lack the satisfaction when you have deduced the culprit. They also have these puzzles that are not as interesting as the previous titles. All I can say is the cases in Crimes and Punishments were better.
While the voice acting in this game was about a 7/10, the lip syncing with the voices are inconsistent. Sometimes it matches perfectly while other times it doesn't, this isn't much of a problem but it can break the immersion.
I gave this game an 8/10 which is pretty high but it is not as good as Crimes and Punishments which I enjoyed far more.

Mechanically, this game is identical to its predecessor, You Have to Win the Game. So far as I can tell having almost beaten the game, there are no items in Super that were not in You Have to, meaning that for gameplay, you're in for much the same.
Coming from someone who really loved You Have to Win the Game, I found Super Win the Game profoundly boring. The charm and variety found in the original game has been shirked here for an "open world" style akin to Zelda II, losing the great sense of connectivity in You Have to for not much in return. In theory this means that Super can have varied environments in a way that You Have to never could, but in execution I more often than not found myself bored with the environments as they were something I had seen before in other better games, and I longed for the tubey VVVVV style world I loved in You Have to.
Maybe with better spritework and environment building Super could've been better than the original. As it stands, You Have to is a much leaner, tighter experience with none of Super's fluff with more pleasing aesthetics and less aimless roaming.

This game left a mixed feeling but it's probably my own fault for not reading the comments properly.
I read "Zelda II-alike" and jumped the bandwagon immediately.
This game is
a copy of Zelda II on the NES. Sure; the graphics, music and controls are strongly reminiscent of the NES era (think about the last world of Mario 2 when you walk through the Sky Pillars, for example) but this game is 'only' a platformer. There is not combat, the game takes 5 hrs to beat and the story is somewhat inexistent. There are some books to read here and there but it's mostly gibberish and irrelevant to the adventure. So if you try to compare with the 'Nintendo-hard' games from the 80's, you're nowhere near the ballpark.
So make sure you know what to expect: it is a nice platformer (again, no combat) with a bit of challenge if you try to clear all the achievements. Still worth the price tag but if you can get if during the Steam sales, it's a good bargain. I'd give it 7/10.

Rimworld... what to say.  Well I'll just tell the story of my last colony.  They were tribals fleeing the death of their village.  They had a rough time of it with opposing tribals and a local pirate group constantly launching raids on them.  But they did have a strong defensive position in a mountain valley on the coast with only two approaches which where easily protected.  For over two years they fought and won slowly advancing their technology till they had a stable industrial base and had upgraded their spears and arrows to machine guns and rifles.  The pirates had had enough banging their head against their fortified position and decided to setup a mortar bombardment instead... again.  The tribe had grown to around 20 at this time and prepared to counter attack and destroy the morter emplacement when half the tribe was struck down with plague while a toxic plume went up miles away and poisoned the air.  They launched the attack and while many where wounded and sick from the bad air they where victorious without any dead on their side.  That's when the scarabs infested the storage cave with all the medical supplies.  Sometimes no matter what you do you just get boned. 10/10.

This game was released on November 25th of last year. Episode 2 was told to be out in about four weeks, and then they said it would January. It's been a month late and there's not even a release date in sight. Telltale is working on many projects at the moment (e.g. Game of Thrones, Minecraft: Story Mode) and I guess they simply forgot about this one. Tales from the Borderlands is a great game, but we've all been tiredly waiting for the second episode to come out and so far Telltale has come up short. I will not recommend this game until Telltale becomes timely with their episode updates.
+Perfect blend of Telltale and Borderlands humor
+Dynamic choices that make you think
+Unique and quirky characters
+Captures Borderlands series' atmosphere well
+Two playable characters
+Anti-hero protagonists, a Hyperion employee and a Pandoran thief trying to get rich
+Excellent voice acting, including Patrick Warburton (Brock from the Venture Bros.)
+Cool additions to the Borderlands universe (Echo scanner eyes)
+Many references to the Borderlands games, including some surprise characters that I will not spoil
-Untimely updates. Come on Telltale, it's been three months.
The last update from TT was on February 22nd, claiming the Episode 2 will be big and on its way, but still no release date after an extra month of waiting. It's a shame that Telltale is neglecting this game, because it actually is my favorite from them. So far, Episode 1 was a blast to play. While the moral choices and dillemas never come close to The Walking Dead game, the humor and storytelling are definitely my cup of tea. As a huge Borderlands fan, this title definitely does the series justice. The only issue is that Telltale isn't giving this title justice. If you're a fan of the Borderlands series and its trademark humor, and enjoy the choice-based gameplay of Telltale games, definitely pick up this game...once all of the episodes are released.

However, let me give you some background first before I review this product:
I was born in a town of some of the most hardcore tic-tac-toe players around the globe, where we all settled our disputes with a simple 3x3 tic-tac-toe. We developed our own culture based off this game, and if you didn't have the skill, you did not belong any where in that town. I went to various tic-tac-toe tournaments across the country, winning all of them. However, the decline in interest in surrounding cities led to the popularity of my hometown to nothing, leaving it in shambles.
Untill this game showed up on Steam.
Ultimate Tic-Tac-Toe completely revives the basic tic-tac-toe formula, but adds a new twist, adding layers upon layers of in-depth strats and tricks. This game includes various game modes, that are sure to pique your intrests.
Those modes include:
All of these modes are available against a bot, local multiplayer, multiplayer LAN, and multiplayer over Steam.
In conclusion, this game is a great masterpiece that expands upon normal tic-tac-toe, and adds a new layer of complexity. This game does not have a very steep learning curve, allowing begginers to enjoy, as well as hardcore gamers, such as myself.
Total Rating 10/10

You will be severely disapointed to find out that combat is not as fluid as people say, and the game wasn't quite thought as well..
Firstly the level design is a solid. In most sections its really good (complements gameplay extremely well and makes the combat much more fun/challenging) but sometimes it doesn't fit the gameplay at all. There was this very annoying bit with a dragon in the desert, in which you need to run for your life, but your NPC companion got in the way every single time, resulting in some very cheap deaths..
Which bring to my second point.. Cheap deaths and cheap gameovers... This game is full of them, and 90% of the time its not going to be your fault. Sometimes its the level design, sometimes its the friendly AI, sometimes its some bug that still wasn't fixed.
And that is not all. Archery is extremely underpowered, there is no point to using stealth and the swordfighting is not very fun.. The only thing saving the gameplay is the magic system and the famous 'kick', which are indeed very fun but makes you wonder what the point of everything else is.

Gameplay is overall broken, the story is generic, the character development is as awful and forced as the voice acting. Multiplayer is dead in South America so I couldn't test it.
Overall, I don't get why people like this game. Its a broken mess. Maybe its the kick meme, maybe its the forced boob material, maybe its the cheesyness (none of which i have a problem with... when the game is good). Fortunately Arkane moved on to bigger and greater things and made some spectacular games like the Dishonored series. As for this thing, just keep in mind what you are getting into.

Oxenfree is the weird combination of PG-13 horror tropes, the unfiltered nattering of self-important teens, and walking. It has a story to tell; a tale of lingering death, lost souls and just who’s going to the senior prom with whom. It shouldn't work - it has no real right to work -- and yet, strangely, it does so anyway.
It’s a familiar tale; a group of teens stow away to a near-deserted island to guzzle down beers bought on illegal IDs and create some memories with the friends who'll soon scatter to far-flung colleges to forget just how hard they promised to stay in contact. Only, for Alex, the entire experience is a fair bit weirder than initially expected. She has a new step-brother in tow who she’s only meeting for the first time that day, and her best friend’s reason for going is less about one last adventure with his BFF, and more about creeping on his new crush. The group’s rounded out by the resident socialite whose energy is laser focused on snark and ♥♥♥♥♥ery.
The island exertion is a tradition of sorts, complete with exaggerated ghost stories and carefully cultivated urban myth. Edwards Island is a creepy place, resplendent in abandonment, decay and disaster. The skeletons of a military base litter the landscape, some buildings left to rot, some half-renovated in a doomed restoration project to make the entire location into a museum. The island has lore; mysterious deaths aplenty to gossip about over a campfire in a heartfelt attempt to terrify your peers on the last night you’ll likely spend together as classmates. Its speciality rumour is that using a radio in certain spots allows you to tune in to weird stations that don’t actually exist. And it just so happens that Alex has a radio.
That turns out to be a mistake, and Alex tunes into to something she probably shouldn’t have, transforming their once innocent coming-of-age sleep-over into a coming-of-age scramble for survival. There’s suddenly voices to be found in the static or residing a little too comfortably in the group’s heads. People are no longer where they should be, or have stopped being a reliable approximation of the person you remember them as.

I enjoyed most of it, though I found the tone to be somewhat off for the Borderlands universe. There are plenty of jokes, but it still somehow manages to take itself too seriously. For one thing, most of the main characters, even the ones from Pandora, seem far too reasonable. I couldn't help feeling like they were tourists from a different game series cracking jokes about how quirky Borderlands is, and that people like them would probably be devoured by psychos in their first five minutes. At the same time, the characteristic, gruesome, dark humor felt less humorous and more dark.
The other issue might be the format itself. Telltale makes games about meaningful choice and consequence, and dramatic interpersonal relationships. It's hard to bring that into the nihilistic Borderlands, with its comically random death and destruction, without the characters seeming a bit too sentimental, or even whiny.
The action was fun, especially with Rhys, but I'm hoping for more puzzles in the future, especially ones that make use of the characters' unique abilities.
I don't know if this qualifies as Telltale's best work, but it's a good chance to get more out of the Borderlands universe. Seems like it would be strange as an introduction to it, though.

This is one of the best games I have ever played. While updates come slowly, they are full of content and incredibly well polished. I have never once had a glitch in the vanilla game. Which, of course, brings me to the fact that this game is great the way Skyrim was and is. It has a deep vanilla experience, but playing the game vanilla is wrong. The correct way to play this game is modded. Due to this, I am trying to keep the content of this review to the content of the base game.
This game achieves levels of ridiculous usually reserved for mods. I had a chicken get struck by lightning at age 4 days, get lit on fire by my resident pyromaniac at age 5 days, and live to the ripe age of 4 years with nothing but a burn scar on his left eye. He died heroically when he strayed too far from the base and was eaten by a cougar. That cougar was summarily killed and turned into kibble for my other chickens. Also, dogs will not stop drinking beer. I had a pregnant, alcoholic husky that gave birth to an alcoholic son. I was given the notification that my new husky was downed, and I quickly checked to see what was wrong with him, and I discovered that at the age of 12 hours, He was hammered drunk, had a massive alcohol tolerance, and had developed cirrhosis of the liver.
The Storyteller system in this game is brilliant. Every game has a difficulty setting, such as easy or hard or what have you. But besides this, you select a storyteller. If you only play with one storyteller it doesn't seem to do anything, until on a different playthrough you use a different storyteller. Phoebe Chillax is exactly what she sounds like, a relaxed storyteller more inclined towards peaceful basebuilding. Then there is Cassandra Classic, who gives you a fairly standard base building experience with difficulty that scales with progress. Finally, there is Randy Random. Randy is a vengeful, hilarious god of the Rimworld community. Most players have a story of that time that Randy sent them a psychic ship (a mid-to-end game event) on day 2. My personal favorite Randy example is on my current playthrough.
Alphabeavers are one of the potential events in Rimworld. In it, a pack of ravenous beavers enters your section of the world and begins to devour every tree in sight, depriving you of valuable building resources. They are not a particularly difficult event, as they usually won't fight back if you hunt them, but they can combine with other things to cause lots of mayhem. In my current playthrough, Randy has sent me 10 alphabeavers in 2 years. Previously, I had never had more than 2 in a single playthrough, some of which stretched to 5 years in game. At one point, to finish a month of 4 alphabeaver swarms, I had 2 in the same in game day.
This game's only fault is that it isn't as deep as it will be soon. Many features that fans of the game ask for are clearly in the works, and the developer, Tynan, is active in the community and listens to what people want and seems to try to implement the better ideas into the game. However, this is not to say that the game is not very deep, it is not as complex as dwarf fortress but then neither is rocket science. This game does not yet live up to its potential, because its potential is so immense.
TL;DR this game is amazing, polished, full of content with more randomness and chaos than a vanilla game has any right to, and the only downside is that it doesn't have nearly the amount of content that it will have when it finally achieves full release.

Divekick is based on a joke, that was turned into a simple game.  People liked the idea of the joke, and the simple game became a much more complicated game and was given a $10 price tag.
Divekick is full of in-jokes and references that most casual gamers will miss.  The game itself is somewhat tiring, limiting how often people are willing to play.  Design-wise, balance appears to be handled through counter-picking rather than attempting to make all match-ups even.  For a $10 game, it is fairly no frills.  As a $10 game, it is overpriced.
NOTE: It is possible that Iron Galaxy Studios have abandoned this game.  A 2014 update introduced an issue where the game crashes during Redacted's story mode, which has yet to be fixed as of May 23, 2015.  The game's non-Steam forum, where a pinned Steam topic sends people with support issues, is overrun by spambots.  A Steam post on December 25, 2014 acknowledges both the crash bug as well as the spam issue, stating that everyone was on vacation for the holidays, and that both issues would be looked at when they returned.  Five months later, the crash bug remains and the non-Steam forums remain overrun by spambots.

Quite a few of the NPCs are lacking portraits, and I don't care what their visual appeal stat is, I have a real block against hiring a leading actress when I have no clue what she looks like. It really bugs me. The backgrounds available aren't well themed or much use in creating memorable posters, and I just make too many movies to want to make them separately and import them. The tutorial really needs a grammar check, and numerous glitches in the awards ceremony (actors under contract to me getting nominations for films from other studios, the same film apparently competing against itself...) are mild irritants.
So. It's good, cheap, addictive fun. I can forsee wasting many more hours on it. I just wish the care that went into creating it had also gone into sending out a polished product.
Now I need to go back to establishing a top selling animated series about two girls in love, filmed in Adelaide, Australia.

This is mario kart on crack. If your a fan of "kart racers" or arcade racer, whatever the proper term/s is/are, games like mario kart, diddy kong racing or crash team racing, you'll more than likely love this. This game consists of a few types of movement; driving boating and flying. The majority of courses use 2 or all 3.
The World tour mode is pretty nice. Its a combination of traditional single course races as well as different challenges such as drift and boost challences or boost races. Continuing on the single player aspect, you've still got the standard grand prix and time attack modes. Matchmaking is nice, and I personally haven't had many issues.
This game also has a large amount of characters to chose from. You start with a few and unlock the rest in world tour. Each of the characters also has a few mods to change their attributes like speed and handeling. You unlock most of these by leveling up that character, and you get experience by playing as them in just about everything. The final mod, called console mods, are unlocked in world tour.
The only problem I have is that the AI can be quite a challence; they seem to have a slight bias against the player. Its not impssible to beat them, but until you truly master this game and can drift-boost every single turn and never crash, they will pose a challenge on the A and S class.

CONTAINS SPOILERS FROM BORDERLAND'S SERISE
Now I am a huge fan of the Borderlands serise, espically the main story, apart from the shoot em' up. Borderland's story kicked up when the second game came out with the main villian being the leader of a company named Hyperion, Handsome Jack. His goal is to find the Vault and to awaken the monster within it, The Warrior. Whilst doing that, he is there to remake Pandora into a world he dreams and not the savage planet it is. However four Vault Hunters, Axton, Zer0, Salavador and Maya defeated the masked man which they end up taking his life. So it seemed...
Tales from the Borderlands take place on Panadora after Jack's defeat which makes this the last game in the serise [Borderlands, Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel, Borderlands 2 and Tales from the Borderlands]. However unlike most Telltale games you take the role of not one but two main characters.
Fiona:
A Con-Artist who has grown up on the bandit ridden planet Pandora, with her sister Sasha and their father figure Felix. She takes deals seriously and her personality is professional and caring to the ones she loves.
Rhys:
Is a Hyperion worker who was currently demotted to trash duty by his new boss, Vasquez, which he wanted to what he desvered. He and his partners Vaughn and Yvette team up to help Rhys by ratting out that Vasquez buying a Vault Key. His character is funny and he is your typically geek character which I love!
The story follows the two teaming up despite their differences. Players are put into both characters shoes, choosing to hate or stick together the two. Telltale is well known for making players grow attached to their characters and stories which they did espically in this. If your a person who loves story based games this is most recommended espically! Trust me your will feel so many emotions in this game it isn't funny, well the game will make you laugh.

It breaks the succeeding formula of the SH by trying to mix in elements from successful action games using quick time events. At one point you are following a guy like in Assassins Creed. Another moment you sneak by guard like in Metal Gear Solid. Tons of quick time events. Few cases with boring stories, with sudden end and sudden start. Characters with no facial expressions, requires no real slueth skills and even the underline story of your so called daughter is appealing as watching a hair grow.

They won't address a larger audience but there are enough action games and open world games that are doing that and trying to hybrid that with a detective game is a disaster.

To sum up, don't buy this. It's not worth 50$.

A bunch of teenagers, stranded overnight on a small islet, haunted by ghosts of the past (both literal and personal) - that's Oxenfree in a nutshell. Wrapped in very nice hand-painted graphics and written by a skilled scriptwriter, this indie 2D walking simulator offers the best of teenage horror stories from 1980s. Think
, or, more recently,
. The story is interesting and well-wrought, influenced by the choices you make in rich dialogue trees, and taking quite a number of unexpected turns. Of course, it falls within the given genre and is not completely innocent of exploiting dated clichés, but compared to the myriads of other horror games out there, this one has at least some fresh breeze about it.
However, there are some things that annoyed and bothered me. The length was one of them. It will take you 4-5 hours to finish the game for the first time (if you're not rushing it), which is a little too long for a one-time-run and a little too short for taking a break. Moreover, the story eventually gets really gripping, so that you want to finish your playthrough in one run, but on the other hand you feel that your attention is slipping. Also, it doesn't really work in regard to the characters, who are well-written enough, but get too little space and you know them for too short a time to genuinely care.
Another strange designer decision concerns the only game-y mechanic in the game - your pocket radio. You tune in different frequencies, pick up strange signals, listen to the strange mix of music, noise and coded messages. Cool. But somewhere halfway through the game, you get a better radio with expanded frequency range... and you can go through all the locations and hunt for the signals AGAIN! Not cool. Especially since other characters are rushing you to conclude the story and your completionist detours don't really make much sense.
Finally, if the authors decided to make an artsy-looking indie game with beautifully stylized backgrounds, it would be nice to stick to the same style also for character design. The 3D character models you get mismatch painfully the overall style of the game. True, they are most of the time too small to notice, but when you DO notice, you can't help asking why.
If you like teenage protagonists and a good ghost story that relies on thick atmosphere rather than cheap thrills, grab a six pack or a bottle of wine, shut the doors, get Oxenfree and delve into the mysteries of Edwards Island. Allow yourself at least 5 hours of time, don't try to perfect the game, follow the story and you won't be disappointed.
P.S.: I can't wrap my head around the title - Oxenfree. What does that even mean? Sure I haven't seen a single ox in my playthrough...

This game is a classic. Among RTS games, many of them only have two or three playable factions, each with a vastly different way of developing their base and a completely different strategy of how to use military units. This game does the same thing with over a dozen. Each of those civilizations share generic unit models, but by restricting which unit types and technologies each civilization gets and granting bonuses to resource gathering and unit statistics, it is able to completely differentiate each civilization and encourage a strategy that the civilization is best at while also giving the player freedom to completely go against that strategy. Furthermore, there is no such thing as a "final super unit". The game is balanced by giving every unit in the game a weakness and often a counterunit that can nullify any basic strategy if played correctly. The game also requires careful resource management, as there are four different types of resources as well as population that must each be managed carefully to continue building armies. The game is unique in that it rewards players that build their economy carefully, and not just who can build the most mineral harvesters. The graphics are also pretty good given that the game was isometric and made in 1999.
Overall, I would say that this game has aged phenominally well and is the best of all of the games in the Age of Empires, without hesitation. The freedom available to the player to pursue dozens of different strategies depending on the map and civilization gives this game tremendous replayability. I would definitely recommend this to anyone who is looking for a strategy game of any kind.

A tough recommendation.
Pros:
- Fantastic combat design. Kicking enemies and the overwhelming amount of physics interaction is top notch. Throwing boxes at people is stupidly fun.
- 'Old school' clunky but engaging design. Controls are dated, but still do the job.
- Fun level design. Lots of interesting locales, with many side passages and secrets that feel rewarding to find.
- A fantasy game where magic can be fun, useful, and isn't just about throwing fireballs.
- Writing gave me the occasional chuckle. Some of the 'sexy' dialogue made me roll my eyes, but it was all in good fun.
- High level of difficulty. 'Normal, 'Hard', and 'Hardcore' are appropriately named.
- Light RPG mechanics and skill tree, that combined with multiple endings, gives good incentive to replay.
- Very strong starting levels.
Cons:
- The absolute worst offender of "Where the ♥♥♥♥ do I go?" I have played in years. I couldn't play 30 minutes without getting stuck at least for minute or two. A lot of the 'core path' was more hidden than some of the secrets.
- Repetitive locales. Aparently there are two spider-themed dungeons on two different islands.
- Predictable plot that blows its load on the interesting twist about an hour and a half in.
- Ludicrous difficulty spikes. Late-game enemies that kill you in two hits, come in packs, cannot be stealthed past, and can seemingly attack you through your block. Whoever designed the worm sequence, and the lightning dragon fights, need to be shot.
- Poorly balanced. Stealth is useless until the final upgrade. Health upgrades become essentially mandatory late game.
- Controls can be unintuitive, leading to frustrating moments. You can't seem to throw something if you're sneaking. Your chracter can't survive a 15 foot fall. Kicking enemies into spikes has a weird success rate.
Seems like a 6.5/10

Do you have trouble kicking people? You've come to the right place to learn!
The jokes are all true. Your foot may be your most used weapon in this game. When playing on the hardest difficulty, I found that it was almost impossible to take on multiple enemies in a sportsmanlike manner, so I would kick them around until I could face one at a time. Sometimes that meant kicking them down a set of stairs. Sometimes they would die from that. Sometimes it meant kicking them into a conveniently placed wall of spikes, in which case they always died. (Side note: I was so smitten with the prevalance and utility of wall spikes that I'm having them installed all over my house! Orc invasion? Spike wall! Goblins giving you trouble? Spike wall! In-laws won't take the hint? You get the picture.) Sometimes I just kicked them into an abyss. Not sure how they ended up but I never saw them again.
Really though, this is actually quite a fun game with a surprisingly long playthrough time. There are multiple ways to approach most combat instances (the boot is only almost all-powerful), and the environment is semi-usable, whether you're throwing barrels or causing 4x4 posts to collapse by shooting arrows into them. The rope bow can make things interesting from time to time, but I've never figured out why it gets infinite ammo and where you are keeping all the rope. The storyline is good by video game standards of its time, but the female dialogue is at time cringingly awful. The variety of monsters isn't great, but they are well-modeled and on average the AI is good.
For $10 you can't go wrong buying this game.

Space Channel 5: Part 2 is a really memorable novel game that is loads of fun. The basic premise of the game is to repeat the inputs from the enemy rhythimically and in-time to save humans from the Rhythm Rogues, and to destroy their robots.
This game looks very dated but has a really fun early 2000s style that will sure to delight. The game is capped to 30FPS due to its rhythm gameplay, and many low quality FMV cutscenes are used which do age the game quite a bit. Facial animations really don't exist and animations are flat-out akwards, but this somehow helps contribute to the game's quirky nature. On the technical side there are no options to adjust for input lag which plauge some plahyer, and frame tearing still seems to happen even with V-Sync on.
As a rhythm game this soundtrack is groovy, and screams music from its era. The music beautifully combines with the gameplay with distinctive beats making it easy to input commands. However, in some locations in-game characters can speak rather accented like the Space-Bird Mistress meaning you can get confused between left and right (and not break down laughing).
You play as Ulala, a news reporter from Space Channel 5 trying to save the galaxy and get a scoop on the Rhythm Rogues which are trying to kidnap the Space President and create a weapon of mass-dance destruction. Enemies will shout a directional input or 'Chu/Hey' in a rhythmic pattern and your job is to copy it to win. Sometimes you'll have to play instruments by hitting down on the D-Pad or analog stick. Once you beat the rather short 2-3 hour campaign, depending on whethever you can clear stages on your first try you'll unlock EXTRA reports, a repeat of the main game but with different harder button inputs, plus you can unlock secrets on each song by 'Heying' indicating by a flash inbetween dance battles. Ulala's Dance is a mode where you have to beat 10 levels of increasing difficultly without failing once - not for the faint of heart. You can also also unlock costumes from doing well in game letting you dress up like a Space grandma, to a security robot of Ulala.
The difficultly curve of this game is rather strange and this game can be quite difficult to newcomers of rhythm games, with stage 2 definetly being a killer in difficultly. Your short-term memory will be tested!
Multiplayer is avaliable which allows one player to input directional inputs and the other player to input Chus and Heys. This runs into some problems where you cannot use two controllers, only a controller and a keyboard unless you want to fiddle around with a remapping program such as AntiMicro or Xpadder.
Space Channel 5 Part 2 is a short and sweet game ozing in quirky charm and solid simplistic gameplay which can be beaten in a single sitting. This is a must play for people that love rhythm games and if you want to try one this is a pretty good one to start with. $7 is a little steep for a short experience although this game goes often on sale during Steam Sales so its a good idea to pick it up then.
TL;DR: You get to save Micheal Jackson and scream Woo by playing rhythmic Simon Says; did I mention the part with the tentactles?

Look. Bottom Line. Great Game. Perhaps it would be better if they would release a new episode someday, but great game.

The Borderlands game are generally known as FPSRPGs with a heavy focus on the collection of ‘loot’. They are witty, aware of themselves and very entertaining, despite an overall lack of deep story or meaningful characters. That is why, when I heard Telltale Games was working on a story driven game for the franchise, I had some minor skepticism, but overall excitement. What they did with The Walking Dead and Game of Thrones games was a wonder, so you can imagine that I bought this game a soon as I could, and was not disappointed in the least.
Jumping in, you are a young Hyperion employee, living life and up for a major promotion. This doesn’t work out, unfortunately, as your rival (voiced by non-other than Kronk) has taken your place. Without getting into much spoiler territory, you definitely will be unable to seize the promotion. Obvious course of action? Vengeance in the form of intercepting a deal down on Pandora for a Vault key. Wacky hijinks ensue, and it all feels very much like a Borderlands game.
Beyond the story of the Hyperion employee wronged by the boss, you also play an intelligent con-women who lives on Pandora. Both main characters have people in their lives around them that make appearance in the game, and are incredibly interesting characters. In the short 2.5 hours that made up the first episode of the game, I found myself attached to each character and generally worried they were going to die at some point. This degree of writing is something to be cherished in the shoot-em or generally weak writing that make up the reality of today’s gaming world.
Overall, this game is worth it. It is entertaining, well written and a fun delve into the world of Pandora. Buy it now, buy it tomorrow, but no matter when, buy it and have a hell of a good time.

Oxenfree is a story driven game in which your actions and words have a big influence on the characters around you. Oxenfree is one of those experiences that you can only have once, so I urge you to play it for yourself before watching a gameplay video. With that in mind, I wrote this review with as few spoilers as possible.
- This game is designed spectacularly. The visuals, audio, and especially the story and character interactions are superb. It is thrilling, terrifying, and tragic.
- The characters are actually interesting and the voice acting is spot on.
- Things change when you start a new game. I thought the added interactions were very clever.
- Loved the idea of carrying around a radio. You can actually tune in to music, information (lore), hints, and more while walking around.
- Optional collectables and integrated hints that guide you towards them.
- You walk slowly. Too slowly in my opinion. I can imagine the developers chose this pace for two reasons. 1. Many conversations happen while you are walking around, you walk slowly so you have time for character and story development. 2. So the player can appreciate the size and beauty of the island. Regardless, I often felt bored when there were no conversations and when I had to backtrack.
- I encountered a glitch three times when I tried to move to the next screen and interact with people at the same time. My character would then be unable to proceed to the next screen. This is particularly annoying because the game only saves when you enter a new screen. In the worst case I had to reset and replay 20 minutes of interactions before I could continue.
- I would have preferred if you could fast forward conversations. In other similar games, you can often click to skip what is currently being said, speeding up the gameplay. I can understand why this isn’t allowed in your first playthrough; however, it should be unlocked (or at least an option you can toggle on) after you finish the game for the first time.
Despite my criticisms, Oxenfree is great. It has been a while since I actually felt invested in characters. The story and character development makes this game worthwhile, enough for me to play through it twice. If the developers want me to play it a third time, however, I would suggest that they address some of the issues I mentioned.

is a well-written interactive-fiction game that, while not without its flaws, is a worthwhile experience.  You play as Alex, a high school senior who goes on an overnight excursion with her friends to an island that has become the stuff of local folklore.  When you perform an urban-legend ritual, the night quickly begins going off the rails, requiring you to use your wits, and pocket radio, to get everyone off the island alive.
The story is well-told, and if you enjoyed the story of
, you'll like the story in this.  The lore of the island is well-fleshed-out, the characters have somewhat uncomplicated but effective personalities, and the plot manages to throw a number of curveballs (and a handful of punches to the gut) while still mostly making sense.  The dialogue occasionally has its issues--a number of times the player is forced to choose a dialogue option before the previous speaker has finished speaking, and it can sometimes be difficult to know just how much time one has before the game will force silence (a more informative dialogue timer, like those found in the works of TellTale Games, would be very welcome here), but it's hardly a deal-breaker.
There isn't much in the way of gameplay--the lion's share of it involves tuning the radio and similar activities that are more ways to occupy time than provide a challenge.  But these activities do have immersive value, and the real "gameplay" is making decisions throughout the game.  The controls when moving around also feel like what you expect from a Unity engine game, but this is not so much a gameplay hindrance as an annoyance, and it's not enough to keep me from recommending it.

This game isn't very good. It's a casual game that falls flat in the gameplay department.
Basically, the gameplay hasn't been tweaked and balanced enough, or possibly at all. Basically, you switch between lanes trying to avoid obstacles and pick up speed boosts that appear in a row ahead of you. The biggest problem is that it's grossly unforgiving- hit one obstacle and you're done for. If you miss a boost, you might make it to the next row but your ride is going to be painfully slow and it feels like you're barely creeping to the next row. The second biggest problem is that anything except the boost is basically useless. You can pick up health, but anything that damages you will kill you by slowing you down anyway. You can pick up money, but there aren't any upgrades so it's basically just for score. You can pick up rockets that destroy the obstacle in front of you- automatically and before you see it- making them next to useless.
Once you get the hang of it, it's easy and boring. There doesn't appear to be any difficulty ramp or surprises.
The game is kind of unpolished- a lousy menu system and next to no options, as well as music that doesn't perfectly loop- but that's excusable for a $1 game. I feel this would make a better mobile game than a desktop game as well.
With a little more work, this could have been a decent game, but even for $1 I can't recommend it.

Alright... So...
I don't believe this game deserves as much s*** as it's getting, it really is a very unique and cool concept and it isn't trash as some of the other comments you will read would have you percieve.
Robocraft is basically a gladiatorial arena game in which you pit your robots against your enemies' robots. Each of these robots are built before battle in nearly any way you please, like building a 3D puzzle which you will then pilot to destroy other player's 3D puzzles. Your crafting will be limited to the amount of materials you have in your inventory, which you get either at random in an after-battle reward crate from playing the game or from purchasing from in-game currency in the part shop.
If you find that you aren't very good at building robots, or if you really would rather just get in there and fight, there is a robot shop where you can find other player's robots that have been pre-built and uploaded to the shop. When you purchase a robot, the creator will recieve payment from you based on how much you spent to purchase that robot (you can reduce the cost of building other player's bots by having some of the parts that are required to build the bot).
I believe this game is fun, sometimes when you are in the mood it's like playing with legos. Sometimes you want to build a bot that's like this, or like that, or a replica of a chicken or Star Destroyer, or a shark with friggen lazer beams attached to it's head. And you can do that.
The main downsides to this game, in my opinion (in it's current state), are as follows:
1) Matchmaking
-Currently, there are problems with everyone queued up for a game, and once enough people are queued up ONE player fails to connect due to a bad computer or internet, and it sends ALL players back to main menu. Stop it. (When you play more than a few games in a row, this tends to happen more often and is much more of an annoyance.)
-[They said they are fixing this with the update that comes out later today...]
-Another problem: When you get into a game, players are stuck with whatever they have on their team. So that one bot with a single low tier weapon on a tiny platform that doesn't move? Prepare to carry their weight. A team with nothing but fliers? Okay... how strange... A team with nothing but fliers against an enemy team with nothing but aeroflak and missile launchers? GG.
-I believe this can be fixed by allowing a kick option (with the ability for other players to join your game-in-progress) to boot those who won't do much but weigh you down, and also a mid-game bot selection option for when your team really needs a healer, or air support, or a freaking tank, or whatever.
2) Meta/Balancing
-A lot of people complain about meta. Hell, I've complained about meta. The most recent time I can remember complaining about meta was when the propellor update came out. It wasn't exactly the propellors themselves... but the propellor drones that came with them. Damn things were near impossible to shoot down, moving erratically but still somehow shooting you like they were standing perfectly still even though they're flying like a bee drunk on vodka. Then, if you got 'em right, they would have nothing but their propellor and fly off into the sunset. Why? Because the propellor had too much health. The devs definitely need to work on their speed at fixing issues like these.
-There will always be a meta, there are metas in a lot of games. Don't like the current meta? Find a way to counter that s***. Can't beat 'em? Join 'em. (This may also be helped by adding that choose-a-bot feature I mentioned earlier)
3) Leveling System
-I am currently level 122. When I level up: Oh hey. Another crate. When the update hit that started giving you a crate per level, I was already like... level 98. So I've missed out on 98 levels worth of crates? That's ALL I get? Just another crate every time I level up from now until level 500+?
-Better rewards for leveling... We used to get cpu increases or access to new parts, now we just get crates that we can get from playing a match.
4) A Slight Lack of Variety
-I'm not talking about the bots, the bots are fine. But maps and gamemodes... There aren't that many...
-Each of the 8 maps are on one of the three planets, and the maps reflect that planet in one of the following ways. Earth (green with plants with large broken thing in middle that you fight in; 2 maps) Mars (Rocks, canyons, mountains; 3 maps) and GJ 1214b (Icey bluish, ice mountains; 3 maps). That's it.
-There are currently "5" gamemodes, 3 of which are relevant. There's basically only two gamemodes: Team Deathmatch and Battle Arena. There are two forms of battle arena, one which is normal and the other which is League (a ranked mode which puts you aginst others of your skill level and gives you more experience and rewards so no reason not to play it over the other). So really you should only be playing Team deathmatch or League. Even though Team deathmatch only gives you half the rewards of League so you really should only be playing League. So only 1 relevant gamemode. Get the point?
-We need more gamemodes... You took away elimination and the pit, we went down in gamemodes! We need to go up! We also need more maps in my opinion. Look, off the top of my head: Some sort of planet that's underground, with holes in the ceiling that allow drop from mothership and for lighting. A darker, green, forest planet with strange glowey plants for lighting. Mercury, a hot af red planet with lava or something as a natural hazard. Saturn with stormy skies... etc. More planets, maps, and gamemodes, please.
Now, after reading all of that... Let me remind you that this game is in alpha. Let me remind you that this is an indie. Let me remind you that this is FREE. This game plays amazingly for a free indie game that is still in alpha, it has so much variety for what it is, so much fun to be had. Don't let these negative comments stop you from trying a free game.
I highly recommend getting friends to play this with you, having your own squad is amazing with the combos you can pull off. Also, some people call this pay to win/play. I don't agree. Sure, I've bought premium for life. I didn't feel like I NEEDED it to play the game. Did it help? Hell yes. If you played the first level - you will get that old Wolfenstein feeling back. And to be fair - no, its NOT that fun, It can be overwhelming to be thrown into the action from the start, and a bit exhausting cause "here we are again", killing Nazis and blowing up everything in our way. We've been there already. Its not a bad chapter, but it is slightly different than the rest of the game. ON PURPOSE.
The real New Order actually starts after that level. Everything will change, the story, the characters, the tempo, Blasko himself, the timeline (14 years between 1st and 2nd level) and suddenly game will develop depth in every aspect. And that depth hasn't been seen in old Wolfie games at all. You will start to care for the story (it still is about Nazis dominating the world but hey you cant change that premise), you will develop the interest for the people around you, you will start to notice all the little pieces of information thrown around the levels, and you will see the narrative of the game going only upwards. Right until the end. And what an ending it is.
The New Order tried and succeded  to tell us a story. It still is crazy fun to shoot and kill, but this time - it seems like there really is a bigger purpose. Shooting is great, stealth has its ups and downs, but overall - the flow is just right. One of the most overlooked games. Big recommendation.

Do you like platformers? Do you like games that feel they are from the early 90s? Do you like Winning the Game? If so, this game is for you.
It looks, sounds, feels and plays like an old NES/Master System game. It's your basic faire - run around, collect gems, avoid enemies, and win the game - much like it's predecessor, except this time, there's a huge world to explore, connected by a Final Fantasy I-style world map.
You Metroidvania your way around the world, finding powerups to open doors in previous locales. If you rush through it, you'd probably be done in a couple of hours, but if you want to 100% it (which isn't too hard - there's no No Death/Speedrun achievements this time around), it'll take you 5 or 6.
There's also a great bunch of guides for when you get stuck finding those last 5 gems. So, whether you want to explore it all yourself, or just want to 100% it in a speedy fashion, there's options for all kinds of gamers.
So, all-in-all, very reccommended.

One of the best games of its genre. Which is... hard to define, really. It sort of feels like Oblivion or Skyrim, only with levels to complete rather than an open world, parkour and a very neat physics engine for its time.
The campain will last about 10 hours + but there is a huge replay value as you can develop your character in stealth skills, fighting skill, magic skills or a mix of them all. You'll even find yourself quick saving and quick loading to replay the same room over and over again and try different approaches. The environment is heavily interactive with traps, holes, levers, things to climb, objects to pick up,... Once you learn how to kick and play with the physics, there will be no end to your enemies' suffering... The level design is beautiful and lets you play the same level in many different ways with tons of secrets to find if you take the time to look around.
Storywise, you play as Sareth, a talented young apprentice on a mission to recover ancient artefacts to stop the advances of the armies of demons and necromancers in the world of Ashan. Many powerful people seem to take an interest in you and perhaps you will learn more about your past and what's really going on along the journey.
I would also highly recommend playing Heroes of Might and Magic V if you are interested in the story since the games are related and the events in Dark Messiah take place about 20 years later after the end of Heroes V's campain. An FPS, sequel of a strategy game ? I know, cool, init ? :)

Still one of the best, quirkiest music/rhythm games ever made - and by the legend/team who went on to develop Rez, now finally available on PC as Rez Infinite.
Space Channel 5 (Part Two)tm remains magically potent and fresh.
That its gameplay hasn't been cloned to the point of becoming a genre is something of a mystery, but imitators could probably never top the mix of music, art and writing that leads to cult status.
There's another, hidden-in-plain-sight level of gameplay right in front of you from the start (like The Witness), it has the short playtime, beauty, emotional rollercoaster and Flow state of a Journey or Abzu, the visuals are all cued to the music like an Amiga demo and it's bonkers in a way that only Japanese developers seem to know how (no homo).
It's a mashup of the quirkiest musicals in terms of plot, structure and variety - if Little Shop of Horrors, Rocky Horror Show and Michael Jackson had teamed to do a Sci-Fi themed stadium tour in the 90s this would be it.
And to anyone who's experienced the thrill of playing it, the phrase "chu! chu! hey!" will always bring a smile.

I am into music and often snap my fingers and bob my head to the beat of a song so succesfully doing things to the beat of a song in a game feels really rewarding. Of course there is a small subset of people who just don't have the sense of rhythm required to play a rhythm game. I can't really say that those people are missing out by not playing this. But as a small 3h experience I think Space Channel 5: Part 2 is *totally* worth the asking price.

If you have a dollar collecting dust in your Steam wallet, go for it. The game does exactly what it claims to. You don't need a huge open world or an in-depth character-driven story to have fun. Sometimes lazy button tapping is all you need. I can easily see this game being in an arcade, myself dumping quarters into it, and grinding for that elusive high score.
That said, I have a few complaints. Nothing deal-breaking, but I hope the developer sees this and takes notes.
Number one: the options menu. You've got music and sound on or off, and windowed mode. This game doesn't need the huge amount of options like most games, but it could use a volume slider at least. I like to listen to podcasts and audiobooks while playing games. I still like to faintly hear the game, but the only way I can get the game at the appropriate volume will make anything else too quiet.
Number two: gamepad support. There is none. I'm not a developer, but how hard could it be to get a simple game like this to recognize left and right inputs from an analog stick or D-pad? The keyboard controls as-is are satisfactory, but the extra option would be nice.
Number three: gameplay. The two necessary changes that stick out to me are balance and the lack of a quick restart option. When your ship runs out of speed you lose. This automatically takes you back to the main menu. It is only three clicks to get back into the game from the main menu, but it would be nice if instead the game gave two options at the failure state: to restart with the currently selected ship or to go to the main menu. A single round doesn't last too long, so those three clicks can get tedious after a while.
I haven't unlocked the two other ships, so maybe this criticism is addressed by the attributes of these ships, but it feels too easy to lose with the default ship. I don't think it's possible to recover from the 'big slow' obstacle, even if you were at the maximum speed. If it is supposed to be a 1HKO then just end the game immediately when it's hit.
Number 4: menu controls. You can control the ship with A D, right and left arrow keys, and the mouse, but the menus can only be selected with the mouse. This leads to having to awkwardly move the mouse cursor out of the way after selecting start game, if you play with either set of keys. Again, it's not a hinderance to fun, but it's one of those small things that make the experience more enjoyable. Menu movement with W S or up and down arrows and selecting with the enter or spacebar keys would solve this problem in a jiffy.
So despite these issues, I wholeheartedly recommend this game for one dollar. It's not going to be the most breathtaking, exciting experience ever, but great in its own way. A nice, humble little game to relax and unwind with.
