Overall:  I enjoyed this game a lot.  I got it on discount for about $35 and I feel like it was worth it, but you should know what to expect before deciding whether to buy it.  It takes after Crimes and Punishments and throws in a fair amount of action sequences involving quick time events, a bit of stealth, some box-pushing puzzles, and even avoiding traps by figuring out where to step.  Also, there are far fewer minigames compared to in the previous games.  It's also very straightforward where you're supposed to go next, so there's not that much exploration but also very little tedious backtracking compared to earlier games so it's a draw for me whether that's good or bad.
Cases:  It is broken down into cases like Crimes and Punishments and has a similar format where you need to find evidence and make deductions to figure out who the real culprit is and then you can choose the person's fate.  I had similar feelings on it here as I did in that game.  Namely, I loved finding the clues and trying to figure everything out, although I felt each case ended a little abruptly.  I wanted to interrogate the suspects about new evidence I found later on in the case, but that usually wasn't an option so it felt like too much of a guess to accuse someone.  I did enjoy each mystery though, and I cheated a little bit and checked if my answer was right before moving on in each case (it doesn't tell you on hard mode, so I checked online).
Action:  Speaking of which, I played on hard mode and there are a lot of action-y sequences that might or might not be there on easy mode.  Some of them were pretty fun and some were a little annoying, but there wasn't anything that was horribly frustrating for me (keep in mind I also play a lot of action/adventure games which have had far worse action sequences, so the Sherlock ones might be frustrating if you don't usually play action games).  However, the quick time events were clearly designed for a gamepad so they are a bit difficult with keyboard and mouse, especially the one to concentrate (you have to use WASD to keep one icon centered in a circle while simultaneously using the mouse to keep the other icon centered in another circle, and it seems clearly designed with analogue sticks in mind).  I found these to be very tense, but I usually passed them on the first try and it lets you redo it without repeating too much if you miss it.
Story:  In terms of the overall story, I'm a little puzzled why they changed the faces and voices of Sherlock and Watson.  They looked and sounded more distinctive before.  In this game, I kept getting confused who was speaking because I'm so used to the previous voices (I do like that Watson is more serious now -- I felt really bad for him in the previous games because he was always played for laughs).
Due to that I thought it was supposed to be a reboot, but it is clearly in the same continuity as the previous games.  It picks up from the endings of both Last Testament and Crimes and Punishments (as well as including easter eggs to some of the other games and of course the original stories).  The game starts off by introducing the neighbor mentioned at the end of Crimes and Punishments, and then the girl from Last Testament appears (apparently she was at boarding school during the previous game).  There's an overall story involving them which gets gradually developed through the cases and then gets resolved at the end.  So, there are pretty much four separate cases plus the last section which wraps up the main story.  The main story was a bit predictable, but I enjoyed unraveling the details of each case on its own.

Where to start with Borderlands? It is a ridiculously addictive FPSRPG...with limited RPG elements. You pick which character you want to be, then level up accordingly to your gameplay style. Best enjoyed as a 4 player co-op with friends. You can try to join an open online game, but this may end up with people running off without you to level up their own characters faster. Single player is solid, mindlessly repetitive, yet somehow deliciously satisfying. The story is practically non-existant, simply, you're a vault hunter...go find the vault, with a load of side missions attached. The ending is horrifically unsatisfying but then what do you expect from a game with no real plot?
HOWEVER! That being said, I did enjoy this game! It is thoroughly addictive and it's the game I've put most time into in my Steam collection. So if you have friends to play with, it's amazing, if it's just you, it passes the time very enjoyably! Just don't come here if you're expecting a revelation in FPS story telling. Come here for the fun, and the bazillions of guns!!

Frogwares is known for their games about Sherlock Holmes. They had their upps and downs, but the latest one, Crimes and Punishment has been the best one in the series so far. It's hard to follow it up, but they tried exacly that with The Devil's Daughter. Did they succed? Well, if you played and liked C&P, you'll probably like Devil's Daughter.
You can absolutely see why many people compare the two. Gameplay has been largly recycled but there are also a decent amount of improvements. It is clear that Frogwares has realized that they should make the game more open to newcomers to the genre and as such, the lowest of the two difficulties tends to hold your hand and correct your mistakes.
The star of the show is of course Sherlock Holmes. There is also a number of other important characters, trusted companion John Watson, Misses Hudson (only seen in cutscenes), Sherlock's adopted daughter Kate and an innocent looking neighbour that is actualy more than meets the eye. You'll mostly be playing as the great detective, however you do occasionaly take control of other characters for a short amount of time.
Exploring and research is simmiliar to its predecessor, however there are a couple of improvements. You rely mostly on your trusted notepad, which is used to save and access clues and evidence but also serves as a map. As such, it's a vital thing during investigation. Once you've gathered enough clues and evidence, you can combine different facts in a seperate window, which leads you to a conclusion. There are multiple solutions for every case, so it's better to gather up as many clues as possible before making a decision.
I really liked the fact that when you meet a new person, you'll often be allowed to found out more about them in the form of characterists. You always have 2-3 of them where you have to decide between two facts, which means you have to choose which one is most likely to be true. It really makes you feel like Sherlock Holmes, as he's known to notice every little detail about everything.
Another thing that often comes to play are different puzzles and mini games. They are quite varried (including a lockpicking mini game which I wouldn't mind seeing in other games) and don't become cumbersome. A couple of them are however simple QTE events, which can be annyoing for some. There is also a decent amount of puzzles, which range from  It's still not that big a deal and they usualy don't apear twice, however it's still worth to be mentioned. Action sequences work simmiliary but are kind of clumsy. They are still fun to play, however some of them do drag a bit to long for my taste. There is an "skip" option, if you get stuck, which is quite usefull, however I've still found it to be more satisfying to spend some time thinking up a solution.
The game looks really nice. It is up par to the newest releases, however this comes with a huge downside. While it did run at 60fps most of the time, I've noticed that it tends to have huge drops for a couple of seconds when you enter a new area and sometimes in large, open areas. Another problem lies in long and common loading screens, but you get the option of checking your notebook and connecting facts during them. It's like a band aid on a sliced artery, but it does help a bit.
Conclusion: Devil's Daughter is plays simmiliar to Crimes and Punishment. If you liked the previous game, you will most likely like the new adition too, as it comes with a couple of interesting casses and provides solid 10-15 hours of "fun". I  recommend getting it on a discount if you don't mind waiting a bit. (judging from Crimes and Punishment).
Final Rating: 7.5/10

An honest review. (UPDATED 2)
I wanted to like this game. I wanted to, because I'm a fan of Sherlock Holmes, as imagined by Arthur Conan-Doyle. I've just recently played Crimes and Punishments for the first time and boy did I enjoy it. Obviously, I said, The Devil's Daughter will continue the same excellent formula of its predecessor. Boy, was I wrong.
So with the good first - the graphics are excellent. Everything is as good looking and better as C&P. Dynamic lights, shadows, beautiful locales, a lot of style to it all and it's a pleasure to the eye, for a while anyway. The deduction board is there, and so is Toby.
The problem with this game is the actual gameplay. The cases are simple and poorly written, especially compared to C&P and the Testament of Sherlock Holmes. In fact, there is barely any actual "detecting" going on, as the game pretty much leads you by the nose through rushed stories, increasingly annoying QT minigames which invoke images from Indiana Jones in the most unfortunate of ways, that are clearly there as a filler for otherwise poor writing that lacks depth and development.
Conversations are stubs, it's almost a throwback to the 90s; Holmes and Watson may as well be perfect strangers as they barely exchange words with each other. There are no interesting puzzles, most of them will make you wonder why you're playing these run-dodge-dodge-run games on bridges and forests and collapsing floors. This does not have RD Jr's charm, and after a couple of cases you start asking yourself if you even care, and you will end up skipping more "puzzles" than you solve. For a game about Sherlock Holmes, it's shockingly uninspired.
The voice-work is barely passable, and a big step down compared to the excellent voice-work done in the previous games in the series. The dialogue is very bare-bones, and lacks depth. Lacking depth seems to be the best way to describe The Devil's Daughter. Such a shame.
I don't know if the developers read these reviews, but if they do, I suggest they sit down and re-read Sherlock Holmes. Maybe that will put them back on track of who and what Sherlock Holmes is. This, unfortunately, isn't it. This almost feels like Frogware just said "f#$k it, they will buy anything we give them". Oh, and Holmes in this game is just a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Not even a charming one.
UPDATE 2: age of characters
It is true that in the source material Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson DO meet each other first when they are most likely in their early 30ies. But let's not be distracted by this fact - the real reason for younger characters in this game is to justify the running/jumping sequences, that for obvious reasons wouldn't be possible for older characters. Chronologically, this makes no sense either. Trying to channel Guy Ritchie's Sherlock Holmes movies is a dumb idea. If I wanted to play running and jumping in Victorian London, I would be playing Assassin's Creed Syndicate. But this is a Sherlock Holmes game. SHERLOCK HOLMES. It should be a game of wits and rich dialogue, not jumping obstacles.

I DO NOT recommend this game. Buy Crimes & Punishments and Testament instead.

Super Win The Game is an adventure-platformer, with an overworld map linking together multiple short levels and some bigger dungeons.
Little bells are found very frequently, they are checkpoints and prevent the difficult platforming from being frustrating. The difficulty is not extreme, everything is manageable without being easy either.
However, what is frustrating is the backtracking and the adventuring. The player can unlock new abilities (survive underwater, survive in lava) which permit access to new parts of the levels. So the player has to go back to each previously completed dungeon, and try to find out where such a restricted area was located, then explore a few new rooms, then backtrack to another dungeon in search for other areas. In a similar manner, there are different entrances to dungeons (main entrance or doors from a HUB), but these entrances are not even located at the same place. In consequence, all the dungeons are confusing and the game is hard to navigate. What would have been better is one huge castle with teleporters, like Castlevania, with a map that is easy to read and finding the areas that have not been accessed yet is not a pain. Another level design mistake is to have areas important for the progression be hard to find, almost like a secret (I am talking about the Swim ability in the desert).
The different abilities to unlock include double-jump and wall-jump. Those are great, the character is a joy to control as he reacts instantly to the touch of a button. Way better than any Mario and his inertia. Win The Game really has the best platforming feel I have ever experienced, thanks to the excellent controls.
The graphics are mostly hideous, especially the caves. Thankfully, the engine with (customisable) CRT effects is great and gives a nice touch to the game that the graphics could not achieve alone. The music is so repetitive it becomes annoying, not enough tracks.
The story was not appealing to me, in the end it is almost as if there was no story but it does not matter as I wanted to play a good platformer and that's what I got.... When I was not being annoyed by having to walk back and forth to uncover newly unlocked areas. So in conclusion, I liked the engine and platforming of this game, but I hated the adventuring and the graphics. So I recommend more You Have To Win The Game, the previous free game from the same developper. This game.... could have been so much better, Oh, I really liked the extra speedrun dungeons because they are self-contained and do not require to switch from level to level. Their only issue is that it is not possible to exit a level without completing it.
So yeah.... it plays super well but moving around killed my fun. Thumbs down because I cannot recommend it blindly. I wish there was a "neutral" button instead.

This is an absolute must-buy for fans of the previous game ("You Have to Win the Game", available for free on Steam). It follows the same basic formula of platforming (there is no combat at all), exploration, and puzzle solving. Similar to the original, the look is retro, only this time around the inspiration is more from the 8-bit console era. In fact, the majority of the aesthetics are pretty blatantly, err, "borrowed", from Zelda II. While this might seem a bit shameful (and I suppose it is in some ways), it touches me smack dab in my happy nostalgic gaming place. This is pretty much a perfect game for someone like me who still looks fondly on those old days of gaming and wishes there were more games in that vein. The gameplay consists of exploring a top-down overworld map, and then exploring several side-scrolling locations (towns, caves, dungeons, etc) to solve secrets and collect the items needed to win the game. There is not a lot of hand holding, and there are lots of secrets, so you do have to pay close attention (or be very thorough exploring) to finish the game, which is something I really enjoyed. The bulk of the game involves platforming and solving platforming-related puzzles. The difficulty is mostly reasonable throughout, with just a handful of really tough spots, so it's a decent balance. Although it can be quite challenging at points, checkpoints are plentiful and there is no penalty for dying, so it's not too frustrating overall. I would not recommend it if you don't like platformers at all, or don't have a good controller, though. But otherwise, I think it is an excellent game for those who like old-school and/or challenging platformers.

This game left me very conflicted.
Let me just start with the things i loved about it. The atmosphere paired with the sound track left me on the edge of my seat almost all the time, it did a good job to bring out a eerie atmosphere. The art style is interesting and the voice actors sound amazing. The fact that it have multiple endings also promote replayable (although i doubt i would be returing to this game in the near future).
Now its talk about character design, I find them all of them very unique. The relationship between Ren and Jonas is interesting and choosing between Jonas and Ren can be hard at times as one is your best friend and the other is your new step-brother. The relationship between Nona and Ren was also interesting and the flashbacks of Alex and Micheal also made a big impact in me activtely trying to change the past and save Micheal. However i felt that Clarissa was sorely underdeveloped. She's just a typical annoying whining character and while she was no doubt created to be the character everyone hates, i find that the lack of things to like about her made me sacrifice her without much heistiation. There's just no reason to like her and therefore it is hard to connect with her.
Optimisation was...... horrible, i know its not fair to expect too much from a indie dev in this aspect but cmon... you cant just release a game with ONE graphical setting. Especially when the game is not well optimised. I also ran into various bugs like the camera not panning when using certain resolution.
I actually liked the map but still feel that there's just a little too much walking around without doing anything, bare in mind, i like most walking simulator type of games. Just some minor distance changes would make it a perfect map.
I find that jumpscares are a cheap way for horror games dev to invoke creepiness and shock into the game. Its such a boring mechnanism, you find it in every single horror games. The best horror games are those that use the atmosphere and soundtrack, not jumpscares to invoke feelings. This was quite a big let down for me.
Now the story, i felt like i didn't fully appreciate it and i would probably like it better if i did a replay of it. With that said, the fact that they were still stuck in a time loop at the end is a HUGE deal breaker for me. It just felt like..... the whole play through resulted in nothing and i frankly hate games that do this. You need to let the player feel like they made a difference, this is the complete opposite. It was however, satisfying to know that I ended up saving Micheal and that really made me really happy (until 5 minutes later, the game flips me off by telling me its a ♥♥♥♥ing time loop)
This game reminds me of Life Is Strange in many ways, but it have some deal breakers and is so not very polished and these factors really turned me off.

Robocraft is the epitome of a game whose developers didn't know what to do with it. They had some great ideas, some bad ideas, and overall just can't seem to solidify its design. The game itself, in the end, suffers- it's fun at its core, but the plethora of issues snowball into a massive tidal wave of problems that just can't be ignored. I certainly can't ignore them anymore.
A lot of reviewers seem to suggest the fault lies in a few simple decisions that FreeJam made- such as removing tiers, removing megabots, adding crates, etc. The truth is, those actually weren't that big of a deal- yeah, they may have removed some features some people liked, but those were probably some of the few GOOD decisions they ever had (minus the crates, but we'll get to that in a minute).
So what is it, you ask? What makes this game virtually unplayable now? Well, in order to answer that, we've got to get into... basically everything. Almost every element of Robocraft is faulted and never fixed. While the idea of Robocraft is fun, the way the game works certainly isn't.
#1: The building
Robocraft is a game that's primarily about building a vehicular robot, then fighting other players' robots in a small handful of game modes. Basically, it's that idea you had as a kid- "What if you could make your own lego tank and fight other peoples' lego tanks?". A cool idea on paper- and certainly one that COULD be executed well- but not one that Freejam seems to be able to accomplish. The way the game plays out in practice is more akin to a MOBA- only instead of having a plethora of viable characters and builds to choose from, you can instead use your hand to count how many viable types of robots there are.
You have a lot of options, it would seem- wheels, various types of legs, tank treads, wings, hoverblades, helicopter blades, etc. They add in things that LOOK or SOUND cool, but certainly don't work in the regular game. Want to fly a robot with wings like a fighter jet? Too bad, drones are better, and you'll get shot down faster than somebody suggesting a good idea to Freejam.
Now, as of writing this, the developers have stated they intend to balance out the various types of robots. They're rolling out an update for wheels and have said they're interested in re-balancing wings. Still, this feels like a bandaid- it's something they should have done from the very beginning. To be honest, I don't have much faith it'll work- almost every supposed balance update seems to just shift the meta, rather than balancing it. Because, again, the developers don't seem to really understand HOW to balance it.
What's worse is that all the promo material and pretty pictures give you this idea that you can play these really cool looking things. Sure, you CAN.... if you want to be a useless team member who gets destroyed every game with ease. The reality is, only a small handful of robot designs "work". I'd be willing to accept that some reasonably work better than others- a lazy "cube" shouldn't work as well as a masterfully crafted tank. But that's not the case- literally almost every 'bot shown in the store screenshots and promotional material are worthless.
This turns the game into a min/max fest which seems to appeal to only a very small minority of players. The rest of the players- long time veterans, or new players alike- get left in the dust. The sad thing is, it doesn't even work as a competitive game- at least fighting games or MOBA's like League of Legends (which also have some character balance issues) have a competitive edge, but Robocraft can't even accomplish that.
#2: The weapons
As with the robot types, weapons have horrible balance. Right now, the short range options seem like the only viable choices- namely, the shotguns (or "Ion" weapons). Of course, it wasn't always like this- once upon a time, it was the opposite, and the long range options were the only option (Railguns, Lasers). That's the problem, though- it's never at a point where all or most options are viable.
You're just left with the un-said but clearly received message of "Well, you COULD choose things other than what works... but have fun fighting an uphill battle". It's frustrating to be a clearly more skillful player, yet get absolutely trashed by players who are using the "right" equipment. Not even what should reasonably counter your weapon/robot loadout, either- the close-range ion users have absolutely no problem wrecking the long-range railgun users.
Again, I'm sure this will change- but it will only CHANGE, not get better. That's the problem.
#3: Crates
Robocraft seems to have taken a hint from CS:GO and decided to change its match reward system to a "crate" system. Your performance reflects the type of crate you get, which is great... in theory. The problem is that it's all still randomized- you'll very often just get total trash from crates. Recently, they seem to have updated the game to finally include the ingame currency again, but that's still just a bandaid. You're still left with swathes of content beyond your reach without grinding for AGES and selling the useless parts you constantly get (boy, I sure am glad I got another honeydew horn).
#4: Terrible matchmaking
Again, Robocraft is a multiplayer game- its matchmaking system should be its strongest point, but it's not. Not only does it take forever to get into a match, but players can (and often will) leave matches or disconnect randomly. This wouldn't be such a big deal if they could reconnect, or other players could join in- but they can't. Once a player leaves, that's it- the game is basically already over with.
Furthermore, there's absolutely no matchmaking balancing. At all. You're left with terrible matchups, where one team can be almost entirely anti-air, and the other team is all aircraft. You can see how this doesn't work out very well. It's a joke- a bad one.
---
All in all, I can't recommend Robocraft anymore. I did, once upon a time, because it was fun and showed promise- but not anymore. Unless the developers make a total 180 and really balance the game all at once, it's going to die. Don't bother even wasting your time on it- you'll be left yearning for "what could have been" rather than ever getting it.

Most infuriating "zen" game I've ever played.
Think of this like one of those old nes "tower platformers". Your goal is essentially to get to the top of your garden, but if you miss a platform or the physics engine is bored, you'll fall to the bottom and have to work your way back up. The physics of this game make me cry. The platforming is sticky, but really, REALLY floaty, to control yourself in midair, you have to hold down the mouse button, but if you want to land on a platform you have to let go of the mouse button before you reach the platform. Trust me when I say this is far more annoying than it sounds. You'll more often than not have the floaty controls send your little dude plummetting to the ground, which should cause you to not be very "zen".
The physics are slightly broken aswell. If you're on a spring board, and are being pushed upwards by the kinetic force, if you then JUMP as the spring reaches its apex, you should be launched into the air, right? haha, no. In Eden, that is the WORST thing you can possibly do, as this will make you fall through the platform. To get the biggest air you need to press the jump button when the platform has the most POTENTIAL energy, in other words, springboards in this game work the exact opposite of how they work in real life.
If you can get used to the appauling physics and infuriating gameplay though, Eden is actually pretty fun. Solid idea, pretty graphics, rewarding completionist title and great soundtrack. If you don't have a heart condition or anger issues, please try this "zen" game.

There are a lot of great things about this game, but there are also some huge problems. Here's a breakdown, with some content spoilers but no endings.
PROS:
- The graphics and animations are the best in the series. Small details like Sherlock's archives and apartment have callbacks from older games. There also seems to be a more cinematic flair in the cutscenes.
- John Watson looks like Jude Law now.
- The mysteries were all engaging and unique. Some of them were actual moral dillemmas!
- Like "Crimes and Punishments," the game is in an episodic format, and you get to test every conclusion at the end of every case. Unlike the previous game, there is unifying storyline as well. Personally, I liked this combination.
- There were some really inspired puzzles. For example, piecing together the  events in chain reaction was really fun. The bar fight in an earlier case sticks out as well.
- The finale was really well done. Raised stakes, hit great emotional notes, creepy atomsphere. Loved it.
- The skip button exists.
CONS:
- The developers at Frogware are masochists. Some of the puzzles require you to die over and over before you can figure out the rules. Others are just so tedious they aren't even worth doing. Luckily, you can skip them.
- THE GODDAMN MAYAN TEMPLE. It felt really hamfisted for Sherlock to explore a Mayan temple IN HIS HEAD, especially since the last game sent him to a real temple already. I think Frogware just really wanted to put him in a booby-trapped temple situation without sending Sherlock out of London. Even if it made sense narrative-wise, the puzzles were hands down the most frustrating part of the game. I skipped every one that I could.
- There are some jumpy transitions. Once you send Sherlock to the forest to question a suspect, you skip straight to Sherlock running for his life. What happened inbetween those moments? We don't know. The game also ends abruptly after the final confrontation. The developers, surely crunched for time, abandoned the artistry they showed in the very first scene.
- The game isn't optimized for extremely wide screens. I tried to play it on 1440p display, and the cursor became unaligned.
Overall, I enjoyed the game and would recommend it to others. I just suggest a liberal use of the skip button when puzzles frustrate you.

In a trend of generic named games comes Super You have to Win the Game, which is the sequel of a free 2D platforming adventure. Its a game that looks like another popular Nintendo game, but it plays different. There is no attacking, only platforming. One hit and you're dead only to spawn at the last checkpoint bell.
What's super about the game is that its in color and geared more toward the original Nintendo nostalgia rather than the Amiga nostalgia. With the old Nintendo naming conventions, "Super" was always relegated to those of the sixteen-bit console rather than the eight-bit. The game plays the same with more frills. You'll still explore and find new abilities like the double jump and wall cling, that let you get further.
I enjoyed the predecessor, but SYHTWTG feels bland and generic as its name. The only thing fresh now is a color of paint, overhead maps and towns that offer hints and other frills like buying keys, loaning keys and buying skeleton keys. The keys are a tough sale for me, because you can find them out in the open and every door you unlock leads to either another door or something you need later in the game. You can find keys, but the skeleton key is your best value since all doors can open.
The game's currency is jewels. I would say diamonds, but since they have color they're jewels. You're told there's 128 in all and there are fortune tellers in town that let you know how many you've collected, how many deaths you've had, how much debt you've been in and where your next goal is located. Some might think being told where to go next is a cheat, but in an open world game where you need to return several times to previous locations is a welcome treat for anyone stuck. Its optional to speak with the teller.
Your objective is to obtain six pieces of a king's heart. By pieces the game shows entire hearts rather than fragments. There's no sense of direction since the game is open world. You can invade any palace with your only restrictions being keys and abilities. There are a few palaces and a few dungeons here and there that look taken from a more popular game from the 80s.
This is a game about traversal, exploration and restriction. You will find things that let you turn hollow blocks into solids of specific colors. Gain the ability to swim through poison swamps, lava and sewage. Under water you have a high swim jump and a double jump to go along with it.
While there is an over world map to get from place to place, the game also has a backdoor area that connects the first town and several key dungeons. You still need to find the dungeons before you can unlock the doors. Its a quick way to get back and forth instead of walking in the over world map, then crossing every bridge, going through every cave to find the dungeon you need.
At the end of a dungeon, once you have found whatever item you were there for, there is a book that puts you in a dream land. This is a surreal dreamland with a monochromatic look where you can jump on invisible platforms, wall climb invisible walls. It feels closer to the previous game and maybe that's why its here, to bridge that gap between the basic graphics and the full color.
There are a few towns and settlements, each has the same shops selling or loaning keys and fortune teller. The towns are for hints. You can find a few castles and a few quests, such as get me this item that gives you an ability. Then when you bring it to them they give you a jewel and let you keep the item.
Everything feels so basic and maybe it did in the previous game too. The enemies are basic. Bats fly left and right, crabs, snakes and scorpions and snakes move left and right. There are spikes and death traps everywhere. It feels like the bare minimum of effort went into the game. Perhaps to make it feel as old school as possible. It still feels engaging, fun and challenging.
I have had a few issues such as spawning on a checkpoint bell only to get killed again and again by a nearby enemy. Walking left when I died, only to spawn walking left and plunge into lava. Things like that. There's little to no wait between spawns. One good thing about the spawns is if you died getting something, you still have it. Which makes it a spawn rather than a restart.
For extra frills there are speed run challenge maps. Going into one of these rooms via a town map strips you of all abilities. You can regain abilities in the challenges as you find them again in the maps. I gave one a try, but it seemed to loop. I tried for eight minutes to find my way out, but I failed. There is no way to get back to the town where you originated, instead you need to exit out of the game and hope that alleviates the problem.
There is also a portal that will take you to an alternate land that feels like a bunch of small challenge dungeons. Go into each dungeon and find an icon to unlock the bridge in the map that leads to the next dungeon. It feels like stapled on content rather than part of the game, even if its still in the game and you keep all your abilities.
The sprites and look could be a lot better. You are a green elf sprite without arms. At a higher price, this would be tougher to recommend and even now I'm on the fence about it. For everything bad I've said about the game, its still tough to put down. Its easy with tough moments. Its a game we've all played before and it does it simple, but well.

While I'm not a big Borderlands fan, my friend convinced me to buy this game. The first episode was really nicely done. I'll get started on my review.
Sections
1. Graphics
2. Controls
3. Audio
4. Optimization
5. Story
6. Overall
1. Graphics
The graphics for this game are the average Telltale kind, but mixed with regular old Borderlands as well. They aren't realistic of course, and they aren't too cartoony, putting it in a nice little spot in between. It looks beautiful on high settings and the colors are fittingly vibrant. The lighting for Pandora looks very close to the lighting as in the regular Borderlands games, being the same old sunny desert-like planet. I wish the mouse color would be brought out at more points, as it is usually clear and I can sometimes not find it.
2. Controls
I don't have to say much for this, considering the controls are about the same if not the same for the other Telltale games (As far as I know). For those who don't know the controls, the games make great use of the WASD, arrow keys, Q & E, along with the mouse. Not much else, but you won't really find yourself using other controls often, if at all. They're amazingly easy to use and if you're used to the keyboard (Which you should be) then you'll be fine. As for points it needs you to click, you simply drag the mouse over to that point, which is shown by a bright red circle on it. You won't have to worry about remembering lots of buttons.
3. Audio
The audio is nicely done. I love the music and sounds of the weapons, voices, cars, etc. They are all put at a nice default level. The audio is a big part of this game as it sounds so good. I can only wish that many games in the future have as well done audio as this one. You'll rarely notice yourself having to strain your ears to hear voices, and even if you have that problem you can simply turn on subtitles. The audio all fits together, where a character's voice is still hearable but  a little shut out by loud sounds, giving it a realistic like feeling.
4. Optimization
The game is incredibly well optimized and should be able to be played on nearly every computer from as early as 2009-2010. My computer isn't as strong as most but I can still play on high settings at an average of 50-60FPS. I haven't noticed any large dips in the framerate, even in action packed moments, where the framerate stays steady but can go down to 40FPS or so. The average computer should be able to play this game on at least medium settings.
5. Story - NOTE: Possible spoilers.
Tales From the Borderlands features two main protagonists, Fiona and Rhys. Fiona, a thief born on Pandora, is a con-artist taught and raised by a pro. Rhys, on the other hand, is a Hyperion employee working to become the next Handsome Jack (As the game is based after the events of Borderlands 2). However, a twist in his plans comes along, where a man named Vasquez takes over Hyperion, killing the former boss, Mr. Henderson. Vasquez then proceeds to demote Rhys extremely, cruelly taking the position Rhys was about to be given. Rhys then begins to work against Vasquez, with the help of his friends, Yvette and Vaughn. After a deal goes wrong, Fiona and Rhys must work together to  get what they want. Your choices, with both characters, matter very much so. Your friends will look at you differently depending on your choices, as in all of the other Telltale games.
In my opinion, the story is well constructed. They definitely thought it out a lot and it seems like it will influence the total future of Borderlands. I can't wait to find out what comes next.
6. Overall
Here's where the points come in. Using from what I've seen from the first episode, I'll give my review. This review may be updated in the future, possibly for the better or worse.
Graphics - 9.5/10 - While the graphics are nice, I feel like there could be a little more detail. It might just be me, though. The graphics were put in a nice place between realistic and cartoony.
Controls - 8/10 - I'd like a little more use of the controls and I can sometimes feel trapped. I'd like to adjust the mouse sensitivity so I can make my decisions before time goes out, especially since I struggle to find the mouse on the screen.
Audio - 9.7/10 - The audio in this game is great. There may be a little tiny bit more they can do, and I know they can improve it a tiny bit more. Otherwise, the audio is absolutely great and is some of the best I've ever heard.
Optimization - 10/10 - I see no problems with the optimization. The game can run on such a wide variety of computers that it would be hard to find someone with a computer that fails to run this game.
Story - 8/10 - There's some more detail they could add, like a little backstory or even some character profiles would be nice. The feeling of characters betraying each other and the greed they're driven by can be easily felt by the player, making you feel for the character(s) at points. I'm impressed.
Overall Score - 9/10 - The game can still offer more to the player, even though what is already included makes me very close to satisfied, just a little more could help in my rating being boosted. As I stated before, I'm not a big Borderlands fan. This game, however, made my relationship with the series improve and I hope it continues to do so. I highly recommend that you buy it. You'll get laughs, sadness, and feelings in between, along with a sense of accomplishment.

If you're not afraid of RNG, frequent change, and PVP balance issues, I suggest you try this out.
However, I will caution you that the game has been on a bit of a downhill recently. There's less of a skill ceiling, and the economy has become a loot crate system. Furthermore, the current matchmaking is not new player friendly, as robots of all sizes are matched together. These problems have been getting worse, so I would caution people from becoming to invested in this game.

I got this for rather cheap so luckly it paid for itself but at its regular price just be careful.
In this game you fight waves after waves of monsters using a rather scant diablo like set up, and hillariously terrible voice acting which is a plus (though judging by the lumberjack with a chainsaw, that may be intentional). The monsters generally just walk into you and deal their damage, they don't attack you so to speak. After completing enough of a stage certain features will open up such as dungeons and level features, inside they are usually puzzles, boss fights, and trap guantlets.
Each character has about 4 action skills (mostly attacks) and usually a few buffs that either enhance their attack or one of their skills. Some of the characters are pretty creative with their attack skills and some feel oddly basic. Don't expect long and complicated trees.
But the shortcommings of this game make itself apperant. Some abilities do not have an obvious use but most of all what should be a serious test of skill. Difficult enemies almost always have a death attack that is difficult to avoid, in otherwords to make the game tougher they intentionally try to get a few cheap hits in. There is no real inventory to speak of... You can do the dungeons but they might just outright kill you with no hope for you to win. Collecting potions is the most deadly thing you can do as you will stand still for a second, enough time to be hit by a trap or boss.
Add in that this game has a cash shop, and you will see where they will be trying to earn some cash off of you... and a lot in this game costs crystals and they constantly have it up in front. For example renaming your character costs crystal and respecing your character costs crystal. You can earn crystal in game but don't expect to earn anywhere close to enough. You start off with a generous amount, assuming my 750 was typical, so getting to the end of the game and then respecing might be a good idea. The fact that 50% of the options menu is cash shop (with bright flashing crystals showing to draw your eyes)... can get on your nerves.
All in all this game is alright... but there are a lot of diablo-like games and even "Waves and waves of enemies you must kill" and even "trap guantlet" games that do this genre so much better that even for the price I got it for (a dollar) I can't recommend it.
However, this feels like a game that I dislike but that others will enjoy. So please consult other reviews.

I haven't played any Sherlock Holmes games before this one, except for a demo of one really old one and the first one which only lasted me a few minutes before I couldn't handle its age.
This is a fun game, not particularly challenging, as it lets you skip the puzzles you struggle with, but if you actually ignore that temptation, there are a few fun to solve puzzles (and a few not so fun ones). Some are easy, some are a bit more challenging, but none are really hard.
In terms of investigation, you need to use the information gathered to draw your own conclusions (as long as they fit within the very thick lines drawn for you). Usually a case has 2 to 3 possible suspects, it is up to you to decide who is the guilty party. Sometimes you can end a case in like 5 minutes if you don't particularly care about being thorough and correct. That's an interesting idea.  These decisions are nice and all, but they don't particularly have any impact, as there is literally a button to go back and make a different choice when you see that you were wrong.
There are some stealth sequences, but I managed to finish them all first time without failing, so they are quite easy and not really tedious at all. The only irritating one was one of those terrible Assassin's Creed-like follow the suspect sequences, where the guy constantly turns around to check for followers. Nobody does that. Video games pls.
All in all, it's a fun little time, you'll get about 9 hours out of it, solve some interesting cases, meet some interesting people, do a few QTEs, solve a few puzzles and then be vaguely disappointed, but not terribly so, by the ending. You might even like the ending, but it just seems like it could've had a little more build up to end in a slight bit more payoff.
You might like this if you:
- Like those old CSI games.
- Liked the previous Sherlock Holmes game (Crimes & Punishment, I believe it was)
- Liked LA Noire but would've preferred for the open world to not be there.
- Are a superfan of anything relating to Sherlock Holmes.

I think that somewhere hidden in this game is the implication that you are a sort of bee/spider-angel spreading pollen for God in the gardens of Eden. This game had high expectations as the sequel to the popular 'You Have To Win The Game', a retro-style indie platformer / MetroidVania available for free right here on Steam. Personally, I think it delivers.
Gameplay wise the game is an extension on the original, with a greater variety of areas to explore, as well as a new overworld map for travelling between areas. There is also a more structured attempt at a storyline this time around. I think this game was a little easier than the first, although there are still some very challenging areas that will take multiple attempts to progress through.
The game retains the MetroidVania style item-collecting and backtracking through previously visited areas with new abilities in order to collect missed stuff and reach more new areas. The game itself is not too long (although much longer than the original), so it never felt boring having to go back to areas too much, I finished it in about 5 hours although I think it could be done much faster than this if you know the path to take, and like the first game this could lend itself well to speedrunning.
Graphically, the game is a near-perfect homage to the NES era of home consoles, the visual design has not-too-subtle hints of Zelda II (not to mention the overworld map and the layout of towns and dungeons are clear references to this game). The game looks lovely on it's own, but I have to commend the developer for their CRT TV simulation which is even better than it was in the first game, and really adds to that retro feel.
I have to highlight the music in the game as well, which is just wonderful, anyone who likes retro game music or chiptunes in general will absolutely love this soundtrack.
Overall I highly reccomend this game, and would urge anyone that had fun with 'You Have To Win The Game' to check it out!

This game left me very conflicted.
Let me just start with the things i loved about it. The atmosphere paired with the sound track left me on the edge of my seat almost all the time, it did a good job to bring out a eerie atmosphere. The art style is interesting and the voice actors sound amazing. The fact that it have multiple endings also promote replayable (although i doubt i would be returing to this game in the near future).
Now its talk about character design, I find them all of them very unique. The relationship between Ren and Jonas is interesting and choosing between Jonas and Ren can be hard at times as one is your best friend and the other is your new step-brother. The relationship between Nona and Ren was also interesting and the flashbacks of Alex and Micheal also made a big impact in me activtely trying to change the past and save Micheal. However i felt that Clarissa was sorely underdeveloped. She's just a typical annoying whining character and while she was no doubt created to be the character everyone hates, i find that the lack of things to like about her made me sacrifice her without much heistiation. There's just no reason to like her and therefore it is hard to connect with her.
Optimisation was...... horrible, i know its not fair to expect too much from a indie dev in this aspect but cmon... you cant just release a game with ONE graphical setting. Especially when the game is not well optimised. I also ran into various bugs like the camera not panning when using certain resolution.
I actually liked the map but still feel that there's just a little too much walking around without doing anything, bare in mind, i like most walking simulator type of games. Just some minor distance changes would make it a perfect map.
I find that jumpscares are a cheap way for horror games dev to invoke creepiness and shock into the game. Its such a boring mechnanism, you find it in every single horror games. The best horror games are those that use the atmosphere and soundtrack, not jumpscares to invoke feelings. This was quite a big let down for me.
Now the story, i felt like i didn't fully appreciate it and i would probably like it better if i did a replay of it. With that said, the fact that they were still stuck in a time loop at the end is a HUGE deal breaker for me. It just felt like..... the whole play through resulted in nothing and i frankly hate games that do this. You need to let the player feel like they made a difference, this is the complete opposite. It was however, satisfying to know that I ended up saving Micheal and that really made me really happy (until 5 minutes later, the game flips me off by telling me its a ♥♥♥♥ing time loop)
This game reminds me of Life Is Strange in many ways, but it have some deal breakers and is so not very polished and these factors really turned me off.

I do appreciate having some more cases to play and they are alright but this game is somewhat lacking.
Lack of Content considering a lot of asset reusage from the previous game and it having considerably less cases (the last case barely counts as being a case) than the previous.
The game has 3 bars. 2 are the same with some rearranged furniture.
And yet those 2 are actually from the previous game.
Scotland Yard is actually 1:1 from the previous game. Except there now being an exterior that you never visit in the story.
You may only find it if you use the door expecting a prompt to the map screen like in the previous game and then you suddenly end up outside.
There are also 2 hospital rooms which are also very similar with just a bit different props. And yet I suspect to have seen this one in earlier games as well.
Baker Street is also almost entirely taken like this from the previous game.
Most NPCs are 1:1 from the previous game.
Lots of props and other odds and ends were reused.
Even most of the new clothing is literally just ported from various NPCs to Sherlock, and yet some iconic Outfits that were present in previous games are suddenly gone.
Additionally the entire interface is also from the previous game.
So considering all of that the game should have definitly ended up bigger and with more content since most was already existing before release. So this definitly should have lead to a more varied and even bigger game than the previous. As such I am disappointed by what we got.
Most of the time you spend in London and in a very small area and most of your cases are in same looking urban areas.
The only highlights are a foundry, Gambling Den, a Graveyard and a Bowling Club.
There are other highlights but they do not feel like they are highlights. Mainly because you don't actually investigate there. Meaning you don't look for clues etc. As such they become easily forgetable.
Consider that the previous game had a Temple, 4 Railway Stations, a House with a nice Garden, a Roman Bath, a Digging Site, a Lake, a Beach, a Mine Entrance, a Bothanic Garden (huge), the Mansion of Noble (big) and more.
And most importantly you also investigate there.
So all in all you are better off to get Sherlock Holmes: Crime and Punishments and if you want you can then get this game for some okish extra cases. It however doesn't really contain anything amazing.

Today I bring you Oxenfree, a 2D Story Driven horror game. You play as Alex who is currently on a trip to a Local Island with her life long friend, Ren and her recently met Step-Brother Jonas. Actually so recently that today is their first day officially meeting.
Ren is a socially awkward stoner, who is a huge history buff and knows pretty much everything about this little fictional island known as Edwards Island.
They meet up with the rest of the group slightly after reaching the island. Here you meet, Clarissa, Alex’s dead Brothers Ex Girlfriend, and as much of a spoiler as that sounds, it’s really not. You find out in the first 5 minutes so don’t worry about it. Clarissa is very short and snappy towards your character, she’s the classic pretty girl in every Horror movie.
At this point we also meet up with Nona who is friends with Clarissa. Nona invited Clarissa behind the backs of the other characters to the island. Ren also has a huge crush on Nona.
They sit around and talk for a bit and then Ren decides he wants to head to check out the Caves. There’s something spooky and weird going on in the caves. You carry this radio and can tune into certain frequencies causing voices as well as portals to open up.
That is basically as much of the story as I want to tell because anything else would be spoiling you guys on experiencing such an amazing game. Lets talk about the actual gameplay for a little bit.
Oxenfree is very story driven. You can respond to questions and talk with a choice of three responses, pretty much exactly the same as say the walking dead, or Life is Strange. These responses are timed, so you can choose to pick one of them, or just skip the whole deal. I was completely involved in the story of this game from the moment I started playing. They characters dialog usually goes on longer than the walk time to the next destination, but I always found myself sitting around listening to them talk about nothing that actually directly impacted the story, just because I wanted to learn as much as possible.
There are Items in the world that are Highlighted with a little circle that you can click on which provides more dialog, and if you watched my Firewatch review you would know how much I enjoy games that let me learn about pretty much every object in the game. The neat thing about this game in comparison to The Walking Dead game by Tell Tale, is in this game the choices actually matter. People will remember what you say, and it impacts the ending, having huge differences. Not just one replaceable Character being at the end over another Replaceable character.
You can also choose who accompanies you for most of your journey by making specific choices, but no matter what choices you make you’ll end up hurting someone. It’s like in real life, you can’t win all social situations. Sometimes your end goals don’t line up with everyone elses. It helps to keep the story grounded.
The game is also pretty damn terrifying, there was always this really creepy feel to the whole game, the voices in the radio, the “Jump Scares” and I put them in quotes because they didn’t feel cheap and ♥♥♥♥♥♥ like every modern day horror movie. They were there for a reason, and had solid backing. It keeps you on edge the whole time you’re playing it and I freaking loved it. I can’t believe I used the Edge line it’s not like this is a review, but it is a 100% recommendation and I really think you guys should pick this one up. It’s currently available on Xbox One, PS4, PC, Android, IOS, and it is launching later this week on the Nintendo Switch!

So I had just established my young but promising new colony, Ashton (a quite ironical name in the end ...). The basic needs were all covered, everyone had a nice place to sleep, decent clothing, enough to eat and time to relax. The people of Ashton were prosperous. They lived in harmony with nature and each other. Their wide fields provided them with plenty of food and they sold the surplus to the passing by caravans.
Now and then a few warriors of a near tribe, the Pig Face Men, attacked the settlement, but the people of Ashton were safe, relying on the strength of their automated defence systems. And so the colony grew and I thought: This is it, I finally have a colony which doesn't collapse after a few hours.
As if ...
Remember when I told you about the harmony between the people and with nature? I meant there were no rivalries between the colonists, most were friends and there even was a married couple, Tali and Waltz.
The harmony with nature also seems pretty coherent; the people relied mostly on their crops, eating only those animals which died by natural causes (e.g. old age or other animals), so the animal population in the near forests remained stable. So far so good. But taking those dead animals in meant of course someone had to leave the safe area of Ashton and wander through the wilds. Normally that wouldn't have been a problem, everyone was equipped with guns and armor of the Pig Face Men so they were quite ready to take on anything coming in their way.
Waltz left Ashton to get the still fresh corpse of a chinchilla which had been killed by some other animal. So Waltz has just grabbed it, when a tortoise nearby turned mad. I thought ok, those aren't that fast, Waltz will be able to safely carry the chinchilla inside and the turrets will take care of the tortoise.
I'm not quite sure what exactly happened, maybe this animal was on speed or something like thak. Anyway, when it saw Waltz it charged at him at a horrifying pace. Waltz had just lifted his weapon when this damn creature reached and hurt him badly. However, its hard shell was no match for Waltz' gun. And so he came back home, injured but happy, that now there was even more meat than expected. But the wraith of the tortoise was unforgiving. The bite wounds in his upper body infected themselves. The medical treatment didn't work and he got weaker and weaker. If the infection at least would've been in one of his limbs, that might had saved him, but you can't just amputate someones chest.
At last he couldn't fight any longer, the infection overwhelmed him. Tali, his wife, carved his story in the sides of his sarcophagus. The burial ceremony was heartbreaking. Everyone had come: Tali, his sister Julia, his friends Vas, Jones, Stephan, Boyd and Leia, Vas' tame wolf Nevile and Bacon 1 and Bacon 2. In the light of the evening sun they all waved a last goodbye to their fallen husband, brother and friend, before the people of Ashton went to bed. With Waltz dead or not, they had to cary on.
But apparently it was all too much for Tali, not very surprising if you think about it. There was only this one little problem: She was a pyromaniac. When the rest of the colony slept, she left her big and empty bed. Driven crazy by grief, she did the only thing able to ease her pain. She set the forest on fire. Finally, exhausted almost to unconciousness, she fell back into her bed again.
While she slept, the others, waken by the crackling fire, desperately tried to put out the flames which already started to spread over to the buildings. But they simply weren't enough, they could either try to save the buildings or the forest, not both. Of course they tended to the buildings, to the food storage to be exact. However it gave the fire the chance to spread through the forest, completely sorrounding the settlement.
In the end it was all too much.
Tali died in her own fire that she refused to extinguish, Jones and Boyd followed when they collapsed in the infernal heat. And then, when no hope was left, the gods, the ancestors, the Flying Spaghetti Monster or whatever thi people of Ashton believed in, heard their cries. Rain started falling down, putting out the fire. But it was too late. More than three quarters of the colony had been taken by the flames. Vas, Stephan and Leia were unconcious. Julia was the only one still able to stand. She did what she could, but with all the medicine burned she had no chance. Leia died first, Vas second. This caused his wolf Nevile, who had been laying loyal by his side, to turn mad like the damn tortoise and he ripped the still unconcious Stehpan into pieces before he went on attacking a herd of muffalos (some kind of marshmellow like buffalos) which was his end.
Traumatised Julia, who managed to flee when Stephan was killed, wandered through the burnt ruins of Ashton. Blackened stone walls and pieces of charcoal everywhere. All the food they stored for the winter was gone, the fields empty. With no medicine left and her own wounds hurting worse and worse, Julia found a last smokeleaf joint in one of the destroyed buildings. She leant against her brother's sarcophagus and lit it. So she didn't feel anything when the Pig Face Men attacked. With the solar panels a loss to the flames, the turrets didn't react when Ashton's last inhabitant finally exhaled her last breath.
12 / 10 - Creates more immersive storys than many RPGs; looking forward to my next colony (and possibly its desastrous destruction ...).

Pixeljunk Eden made its way into my library on a whim and it turned out to be a solid decision.
This is a good game to play for relaxing and quiet time. Gameplay consists of leading a small creature from plant to plant or to rocks via jumping or spinning. In later gardens there are additional movement and puzzle mechanics which complicate the game in a positive way. The game introduces new mechanics slowly, which keeps frustration to a minimum. There's some need for planning and quick movements at times, but it's not a game that relies 100% on twitch reactions. The main goal is to find all 5 spectra in each garden and there are additional challenges such as collecting all 5 spectra in 10 minutes or unlocking all seeds in a garden. You can go as quickly or as slowly as you want through gardens, which is a very attractive freedom to me. It has an odd graphic style which is pretty fresh. Each garden has its own graphic style and color scheme, which change as you collect spectra. The music is made by an independent Kyoto artist and is a good selection of electronic trance with light beat (get the soundtrack bundle, it's worth it).
Overall, this is a solid puzzle game that has a lot of fresh and interesting attributes - a great thing to play and just relax with.

Sadly, this game was a step down from Sherlock Holmes: Crimes and Punishments.  In Devil's Daughter I could probably count on one hand the number of times the game put a puzzle in front of me and made me think logically to solve it and then had me feeling smart because I did.  Unfortunately most of the puzzles in this one are just arbitrary or lack a logical system to make them work.
Even one of the best puzzles in the game, which was figuring out how exactly a massive accident happened, was ruined because of a lack of logic in deciding the order that the contributing factors happened in.  Example: a banner fell down on top of 2 separate horses eyes, causing them both to crash the carriages they were pulling.  How do you know which order to put them in and the subsequent events that happened as a result?  There's no logical way to decide other than trial and error as the game makes no mention and leaves no discoverable evidence to help you decide.
Otherwise, puzzles were either a too simplistic "follow the bread crumbs" type or they were arbitrary tile slider types.  On one case there were 3 tile slider puzzles in a row.  There also seemed to be more quick time event action sequences than in games' past.  I don't mind those here and there but ultimately Sherlock games are supposed to be about solving puzzles and making you feel like the smartest guy in the room in the process.
They brought back the system of observing people before interviewing them to notice details which can then help you catch them in lies, etc.  For the most part these were fairly easy to figure out if you are paying attention to the other contextual clues you are given, but at times it's literally a coin flip.  Example: you notice a gang member has red knuckles.  You have to decide whether it was from a fist fight or from boxing work.  There are no other clues to help you decide, and both options seem viable.  Make the wrong choice and you're stuck with it, even if you later learn things that would have helped you determine the correct choice.
The graphics are passable but certainly not pushing the envelope of next gen by any means.  The voice acting is decent enough.  The story is actually fairly interesting, although Sherlock's "daughter" is a completely unlikable spoiled brat.
I almost got the feeling that Frogwares kind of rushed through this game just to get it over with as they stated they were eager to get to work on a new open-world Cthulhu themed Sherlock game.
Again, it's not a bad game by any means, but I was looking forward to Frogwares raising the bar even higher just as they did with Crimes and Punishments, and instead the bar got lowered a bit in my opinion.  Buy it on sale if you're a fan of puzzle and adventure games.  If you're not, skip it entirely.

#LinuxOnly
Zelda II, Metroid, and Super Mario without swords or any weapons, epic music, extra lives, boss battles, life meter, destroyable enemies, cutting edge 8-bit graphics, or magic. What does it add for the things it lacks?
Optionally, it can be experienced in CRT mode. CRT mode is everything bad about playing on old style TVs. Fuzzy moire hexagonal screen pixels, color bleeding, curved screen distortion, invisible overscan and rounded off image corners, motion blur/phosphor burn, reflections on the CRT frame. Even rolling screen, RF interference, and static make an appearance. But it's nostalgic... I think this might well be the only Linux game that has "action safe" and "title safe" design (google it). CRT mode is also tunable to better match the old TV players used when they had no other choice. Personally, I found CRT mode to be worth 15 seconds of enjoyment, then I switched it off. But, that's just my personal preference. Turning off CRT mode does not result in 'modern' graphics. Without the CRT mode, this game is about gameplay only.
It also ads some sort of quasi-bonus, playable dream segments. Same gameplay but confusing transdimensional level design and dialog I cannot make any sense of. The author admits that the dream segments are about something deeply personal. With that, I expect few would understand. This is OK, the dream segments don't require the player do do anything except progress through them and the author hasn't decided to leave the gaming industry or threaten to (like some others have after their deeply personal game designing went uninterpreted).
All sorts of game mechanics make up the game. Double-jumping, wall clinging, wall jumping, invisible structures, switch-on platforms, etc... Each one needs to be earned. Each new ability opens more areas to explore and more places to discover when revisiting. And to make 100% completion, full expert use of each mechanic will be required.
There are no map spoilers. Get out your oldskol grid paper and start making checklists if you want to do a 100% completion of the game. Once again, this seems a deliberate feature to invoke nostalgia.
Speedruns are also added to the mix. Complete with online leader boards.
Finally, death is instant but not costly. Everything kills the player without HP, shield, or mercy. The player cannot eliminate enemies at all, only earn better methods to avoid them. In contrast, pretty much every door is a retry point.
In short, I you like(d) NES games, or have never tried NES games, SWTG is for you.

The game deserves all my praises, however some of the puzzle sequences (looking at you, temple scene) dragged the game out to a bore and did not require much brain work (puzzles that belong, and are, in games such as Uncharted and Tomb Raider).
Overall, I enjoyed both The Devil's Daughter and Crime and Punishment.  I will see about playing the previous Holmes games, and look forward to the next games release!

This game was such a vivid part of my childhood I was overjoyed to find it here. The animation style is slightly more 2 dimensional without the distinct shading I remember but that really doesn't take too much away.
This is a delightful game that progresses through difficulty levels in such a way that anyone of any age can enjoy these pattern based problem guiding the zoombinis to their goal.
It combines lush, muted backgrounds with a variety of funny characters and then there are the zoombins themselves. My brother would select their attributes randomly but I was a stickler for doing them in a precise order but you'll fall in love with this queer race and take pride in guiding them to a better life.
It may begin blandly easy but that will soon give way to some real challenge. The mirror game I remember however being a bit of a pain because it's more of a chore on the easiest setting and I kept failing to achieve a higher difficulty because I tried to make it fun by doing it as fast as I can.
Cute and charming and quite blatantly one of those games meant to be used in an elementary classroom this still provides delight for me now I'm in my mid twenties and I vow to beat it one day as you do actually have only so many zoombini parties to complete the game 100% (all difficulties unlocked and beaten; more of a personal challenge but one I must do!).
Sweet, challenging, non-obnoxious bit of puzzle gaming with great emotional investment but never too heavy.

I've played this though before on iOS and just recently on PC. Honestly, this is one of the better story-driven games I've played in a long time. The whole setting is generally eerie and, at some points, genuinely disturbing. This isn't one of those games you can just play once to get all the details. I won't go into any spoilers: I think this game is best played blind.
The only annoyances I have with the game are the slow walking/running speed of the main character and the often confusing map layout. I'm not sure if the latter is intentional or not, but looking at the in-game map and the paths available in game, it's not always clear which direction you should be going.
But, everything feels real with this game. The voice acting and writing is spot-on, even though they sounded more like awkward freshmen college students than awkward high school juniors. The characters feel alive and react to the world and the choices you make in a believable way. If you like games like Life is Strange, it's probably worth giving this game a shot.

There are a lot of reviews I saw-- and that you'll also see-- talking about how this is a bad port and how there are a lot of bugs and how it may even be unplayable. There are some bugs, and I've had a few issues here and there, but overall I think I fixed them. Read more info below.
tl;dr, even though there are some bugs, I really recommend this game. If you can get it during a summer/winter sale, even better. It's a lot of fun!
The first thing: even if it's set to english voiceover, it won't always be... well... in english. In configuring, I just hit right to Japanese and then right back onto English and that fixes the problem. Found this fix in the guides page.
The second thing: Lag. Especially in report 2, there's a lot of lag that I thought made the level unplayable. I went from 1280x720 60hz to 1280x720 40hz and that solved the issue. As far as I can tell, the audio is synced up right, because as long as I wasn't looking at the screen I did alright even when lag was an issue.
Lastly: input lag. Haven't found a fix for this yet, but sometimes my inputs don't work quite right. It makes a perfect report hard, but it's not often enough to really frustrate me. I can do the consecutive dance mode no problem.
So hopefully this helps if you're having some bug issues. Have fun!

This is unquestionably the greatest puzzle game I have ever played and probably even one of the greatest games in general.
It almost never tells you explicitly what to do, opting instead to be more respectful of the player's ability to explore and experiment to find solutions and secrets on their own.
Gentle music serves as a background to a solitary journey through more than one hundred puzzle rooms carved into photorealistic ruins. It is not a funny game like Portal or an immersive game like Amnesia, it is a quiet and meditative experience.
The conditions to solve most of the puzzles are quite flexible and often have multiple solutions or can even be beaten by "breaking the rules". This gives the game great replayability even after you have solved a puzzle the first time.
The plot is basically optional--if can ignore a beeping terminal as you pass by. If you do choose to interact with the terminals you will find an interesting philisophical story that questions your beliefs on being. Because your responses to questions are limited to options in a list the edges of the dialogue tree become very apparent in subsequent play-throughs but at least the first time through the game it feels like you have a lot of agency in your responses.
The Road to Gehenna DLC is also excellent and highly recommended as it adds puzzles of greater size and complexity than typically found in the base game.
The Serious DLC is also good for a laugh on your repeat playthroughs (don't ever enable it for your first playthrough) but is probably only worth it for most to get while on sale.

Hero Siege is a pure grind for skills and upgrades RPG with rogue like randomness. You play on a battlefield that is about 12 times larger than the screen, each time the locations of elements are randomized and there are a few things you can count on but the rest is randomized. Ever now and again you will find a dungeon or keep which forces the camera closer to your character giving you linear levels with puzzles and boss battles to break up the monotany, these can vary greatly in difficulty, but always worth the risk unless you get those rare super difficult ones.
This game is addicting and well thought out, but there are problems. The randomness lends itself to you dying for very stupid reasons, like triggering a laser blast that drains your health in a few ticks of the game time while against a tree or simply grabbing a potion at the wrong time. No game is perfect, but this game is a little more varied than I am used to and comes with a few bugs that don't break the game, but should be very easy for the developer to fix.
- Clothing options don't actually show the characters you have assigned to the slots
- Clothing options reset every time you use them
- Some stats don't add up correctly when you have multiple items (vague but it seems to happen ever few games)
- Sometimes it seems like if you have a skill that fires 5% of the time, it will fire 5 times in a row for every 100 shots... weird.
Some of the characters are kind of broken when compared to the others like the viking and the necromancer.
The Viking's skills are geared towards charging enemies, but running at them might be a death sentence. Some bosses are near impossible to beat with the viking as he has no long range attacks. Giving him regeneration or the ability to redirect damage would fix him in some respect, but right now, he is about the worst character.
The Necromancer's minions fall off the screen often... always when you don't need it. Almost impossible for the necromancer to beat some dungeons because of this.
The rest of the characters are fine, but those two need the help of a coop partner, which brings this game up several notches in enjoyment.
There are problems, but this is a great game to just have fun with someone else and grind. The fun is finite, but for $6 it is worth it. Grab a friend and two controllers and start slaying monsters in mass. You can amp your characters to the point you are destroying everything on the screen with little effort, but the curveballs this game throws at you always keep you on your toes. DO NOT DRINK POTIONS YOU DIDN'T BUY ON YOUR OWN!!!

Sherlock Holmes: The Devil's Daughter is the best Sherlock Holmes game so far. It is a real joy to play it and I highly recommend it to anyone who loves detective games and breathtaking stories.
Before I played this game, I thought that nothing could be better than Crimes and Punishments but I was wrong - The Devil's Daughter is an amazing game. This game has far more complicated cases which require you to take real decisions and you have many moments where you can make a mistake. However, the game is not too hard to be able to complete the cases correctly, you don't need to be the real Sherlock Holmes to make it out - YOU JUST NEED TO THINK, which is the most beautiful part about this game.
The Devil's Daughter has got some cons and I will point them out here and hopefully the developers will fix them with the next game.
1. Unreal Engine 3 looks outdated. No matter that rooms, objects and faces are well-made, it is 2016 and Unreal Engine 3 is not what I expect from a 2016 game.
2. The action scenes where you have to do certain things in order to proceed are a great idea but it hasn't been completed properly. These moments can be annoying because there is only one thing you can do to proceed and sometimes it is not that obvious at first sight which makes you start the scene all over again many times until you find it. This is not fatal but it can be annoying.
That's pretty much all I can think of as cons. Everything else is great - the story, the cases, the setting and etc.
Keep up the good work Frogwares, I can't wait for your new title!

I've played this though before on iOS and just recently on PC. Honestly, this is one of the better story-driven games I've played in a long time. The whole setting is generally eerie and, at some points, genuinely disturbing. This isn't one of those games you can just play once to get all the details. I won't go into any spoilers: I think this game is best played blind.
The only annoyances I have with the game are the slow walking/running speed of the main character and the often confusing map layout. I'm not sure if the latter is intentional or not, but looking at the in-game map and the paths available in game, it's not always clear which direction you should be going.
But, everything feels real with this game. The voice acting and writing is spot-on, even though they sounded more like awkward freshmen college students than awkward high school juniors. The characters feel alive and react to the world and the choices you make in a believable way. If you like games like Life is Strange, it's probably worth giving this game a shot.

Though I liked You Have to Win the Game more than Super Win the Game, I enjoyed this one a great deal too.
Super Win the Game is an exploratory platformer. You have no attacks and there are very few enemies. It's all about navigating the levels and avoiding the obstacles that can kill you.
Instead of one map with a metroid-vania like lay out, Super Win the Game has an overworld to split areas up, much like The Legend of Zelda 2. I feel like it's more of a hinderance than anything else because it's sometimes hard to know exactly where you are on the map, where you're going, where you've already been, and where you need to go.
That gripe aside, I highly enjoyed the game and I recommend it to anyone who is a fan of this genre, especially on sale for a few bucks.
Pros:
Levels are well designed and fun to explore
Some areas offer a bit of challenge but the game is pretty easy
Snappy music
Map is a huge help
CRT effect can be modified or turned off completely
Speedrun courses and gems to collect for those who want a bit more to do
Cons:
Can be difficult to know where to go next
Overworld map is a bit hard to navigate
