Let me tell you the short story of Sactuary Colony:
Ten colonist set up a lovely little community, they have a thriving farm, two of them hunt animals for food and make clothing out of the leather, another man spends his days making swords to trade with the local tribes people. They even had a couple of pet giant sloths for company and security.
This all changed when one of the team, a wanderer who joins the colonists had a mental breakdown due to drug withdrawal and went on a rampage, causing him to be arrested and locked up in the colonists jail. Shortly afterwards a heatwave hospitalised 7 of the remaining colonists. This left two healthy colonists to tend to the ill and look after the crops. Our pet sloth then went into a bloodlust, killing the two healthy colonists while the rest died of heatstroke in their beds. Our crazy prisoner then died of starvation in his cell.
A fun game with a great challenge and interesting stories for each colonists, just don't get too attached to them. Would definitely recommend.

Hero Siege is a pure grind for skills and upgrades RPG with rogue like randomness. You play on a battlefield that is about 12 times larger than the screen, each time the locations of elements are randomized and there are a few things you can count on but the rest is randomized. Ever now and again you will find a dungeon or keep which forces the camera closer to your character giving you linear levels with puzzles and boss battles to break up the monotany, these can vary greatly in difficulty, but always worth the risk unless you get those rare super difficult ones.
This game is addicting and well thought out, but there are problems. The randomness lends itself to you dying for very stupid reasons, like triggering a laser blast that drains your health in a few ticks of the game time while against a tree or simply grabbing a potion at the wrong time. No game is perfect, but this game is a little more varied than I am used to and comes with a few bugs that don't break the game, but should be very easy for the developer to fix.
- Clothing options don't actually show the characters you have assigned to the slots

For being 'just' "a bunch of puzzles the devs thought to be too hard for serious sam", the Talos Principle is a very well polished experience and quite the mindbending puzzle game.
You play as one of the children of ELOHIM, who assigns you the task of solving challenges in his garden of worlds. This garden is divided into different areas, each with their own beautifully crafted environment. Each area is further divided into smaller levels with multiple puzzles contained within each. Puzzle elements are intuitive and easy to learn, but hard to master.
The game challenges wits, combinatorics skills and spatial reasoning with a multitude of puzzles ranging from walk-in-the-park easy to bashing-the-head-on-your-desk hard. While the early sections are rather easy and only require one or two different things to be done to arrive at a solution, the later sections combine various elements - turning them into tough nuts to crack.
What sets the Talos Principle apart from many other first person puzzle games is that it makes carefull use of psychology: Sometimes, you will not be able to solve a puzzle, move on, solve another puzzle and return later to find that the things learned in the other puzzle help you solve the former. The game also contains a bunch of meta-puzzles, which require (ab-)using and combining elements from multiple puzzles in the same area. I often had no clue as to the solution of the puzzle at hand, but I never felt lost or unsure about what to do.
The game is a bit heavy on religious motifs, but given the way the story unfolds, it makes more sense later on.
The games the Talos Principle most closely resembles are Portal or Antichamber, but without the portal gun of the former and without the wtf-am-I-supposed-to-do-factor of the later.
I love it. many thanks to the ROBOCRAFT team ;)

A very fun (even if frustrating at times) game with interesting visuals, simple mechanics and a great soundtrack.
Each level feels different from the others, and most of them have unique conditions and configurations so there is variety within the simple frame of the game's mechanics. A few of the levels also feature puzzles that make completing them more challenging.
Upon collecting a spectra in a garden (level) the game will pull you out of the garden and it may unlock a new garden to visit even before completing a previous one. After you have fully completed a level, you can play it again to collect all 5 spectra with no interruptions, or to try to activate all seeds and earn the corresponding achievement.
The "menu" interface is also unique, since it is an actual garden (Eden) that you have to navigate in order to reach a the game level you want to play. An "encore" garden is also unlocked after you have collected a certain number of spectra, and in both vanilla and encore Eden gardens there are ...secrets to be found if you explore them after you have collected all the respective spectra.
I've had much fun with the game, even though at times (especially before mastering the game)I was frustrated by not being able to properly navigate my avatar (miscalculated jumps, failed to grasp branches or grab onto a rock). The game even offers a mechanic to counter miscalculated platforming at the expense of some "energy bars" which can be replenished by (generating and/or) collecting crystals.

So verdict- not perfect game, has some good but underutilised ideas, maybe more streamlined than c&p, but is this game worth it? definetly.

A very relaxing, casual yet challenging game utilizing simple swing, jump, and warp mechanics to collect glowing plant-shaped things called 'spectra'. Within each garden, the player is fighting against time (shown at the bottom as a slowly depleting bar) to find spectra. The player has to collect pollen and grow plants which acts as platforms which the player can utilize to gain access to previously unreachable areas.
The beginning of the game may feel confusing as there are no clear directions and spectra may be frustratingly hard to find. Controlling the little character can also be quite infuriating at times especially when a failed jump may delay your progress substantially. However the objective of the game IS to explore and find these spectra, so the lack of direction is just part of the game experience in my opinion.
The art in this game is very pleasing to the eye, composed of a fusion of various shapes and colors. The music is calming and somewhat mysterious, very fitting of the visuals. Overall the game is rather enjoyable and something I would definitely recommend to try. The price may be a little high for some, buying it when it is on sale would be wise.

In simple words, Dark Messiah of Might and Magic (DMMM, I guess?), is a good, but flawed game. That being said, its flaws are no small matters, at least they weren't to me.
Let's start with something simple: the story. Now, some stories are anything but simple, but not this game's. While it has a few... okay, maybe one real big twist (which is actually not very surprising), DMMM's story is simple. You are the apprentice of the wizard Phenrig, and you have gone to Stonehelm to help an associate of his obtain a powerful magic artifact. Needless to say, things do not go as planned. Of course, that does not mean the story get's more complicated or less cliched.
Now, without going into spoilers (I don't care if it's  ten year old game or not), one thing I do actually really like about the story is how you actually can choose what to do. Now, this is no Telltale game, nor is it a Witcher game. You don't have great dialogue trees and many choices, big and small. You essentially make handful of choices near and at the end of the game that determine the outcome of the story. I'd say that only three of them have any real significance, but they are still there.
My favorite part of the story is how there isn't really a "bad" or "good" ending. I mean, some endings lead to more or less innocent lives, but who cares about the mindless masses, anyways? In this game, you can choose to be the bad guy, and it does not punish you for it. I really can't say more without given even more away, but let's just say you aren't forced or really encouraged to be the good guy in the end. Hell, I'd even say you have more reasoning not to be.
But with the good comes the bad. Aside from what I have already spoken about, nothing else in the story stands out much, or if it does, not in a good way. All of the characters are mostly forgetful except for Sareth (you) and Xana, the pretty lady who get's shoved into your head twenty minutes into the game. But they're only memorable because they are a constant throughout the game. Other named characters are not only few and far between, but also rather lackluster. Sitting here, writing, having beaten the game a few hours ago, I cannot recall the name of the wizard Phenrig sends you to help. I also had to double check the main character's name because I thought it was Saref, not Sareth. That's not a good thing.
The story is also not very well written and is predictable, which isn't great, either. It's saving (or damning) grace is the voice acting. While some of it comes off as plain annoying, and all of it is bad, some of it is so bad it's great. Xana's lines, while I can see what the writers were going for, often made me feel uncomfortable or were simply hilarious without intention. Sareth was just an accepting deadpan without much conviction (save towards the end), and Leahnna (Leanna?) was kind of there and awkward. The enemy necromancers are the best because they all kind of sound like Skeletor.
The game's real boon, however, is the combat. The first person melee combat is incredibly satisfying and surprisingly in depth. Swords, daggers, and staffs all handle differently while feeling visceral and impactful. Magic, while I only fiddled with the healing spell to fuel my cleaver swinging melee character, seems to have a nice variety and balance of power, though I was finding stupid amounts of mana potions despite depleting mana and using my own potions in fights for healing. Archery is, you know, archery, and stealth is, you know, stealth.
DMMM also has a skills system, but it is simple and straightforward, which is not a bad thing. It keeps you from being bogged down while also having you specialize without limiting you via class options (which are nonexistent). The game does not give you enough to unlock all skills, so you need to chose whether or not you want to be a powerful melee combatant, a powerful mage, or a great archer. I went for the melee fighter and managed to be as powerful as I could while still having healing magic and being able to pick locks, so you aren't too stringently locked into one path.
Still, with the great and not great out of the way, let's get to the real issues the game has. I had only two really major gripes, but each gripe threatened to put me off of the game on their own. The first and most noticeable is the game's technical shortcomings. DMMM runs on Source and looks fine (great for 2006), but it is buggy as hell and, worst of all, unstable as a half hour game of Jenga.
Aside from crashing on exit (which the game did every time I quit of my own volition) I probably experienced around twelve or thirteen crashes. Some had error messages, such as "ran out of memory," others simply said the game stopped working. I crashed three times in a row on the same loading transition. There seemed to be no rhyme or reason to it. I wish you could hear my tone while I write this; I am INFURIATED by these crashes. I have a modern system and am playing a ten year old game. It's unforgivable, and it seems it has been this bad since it's initial release.
My other major issue I had with the game was it's platforming. That's right, you heard me. This first person hack and slash RPG has platforming elements; and they are god awful.
Don't get me wrong, this isn't a bad thing in of itself. Dying Light and Mirrors edge are first person "platformers" and the former even has RPG elements, too, and I love both these games to death. But DMMM does it so poorly that I find it difficult to recommend this game, since it forces you to do platforming throughout.
Sareth has a feeling of moment to him. This is great for when you are walking about, but not so great when trying to jump from platform to platform. Because instead of feeling like a maneuverable mass of a person, you are nothing more than a brick. If you don't sprint jump, you basically go one foot and fall. If you do sprint jump, you go flying through the air with little or no control.
You can also climb up ledges. This is done by holding the jump button next to a ledge. Of course, it is unresponsive and only sometimes wants to climb a ledge, and when it does climb, you have to actually hold the jump key until Sareth has finished climbing or you ♥♥♥♥ing drop off the ledge like an idiot.
I would sometimes pull myself up and let myself go three or four times in a row before I could get a feel for the strange length of time the game wanted me to hold the jump key for before I was "up" a ledge. It made me angrier than the damned crashes, at some points, and is truly the worst platforming I have ever seen in a video game. I despise it.
But, with everything considered, I give Dark Messiah of Might and Magic a recommendation barely. But be warned that this is strictly for its combat, and its combat alone. Everything else in the game either left no impression or actively tried to prevent me from actually play the game. If its combat wasn't as good as it is, I would tell you not to by it. Thankfully, the combat is that good. For the hell of it, I would give this game an uneasy 6/10. Don't expect another Exanima here, but don't pass it up if it is on sale or something.

Zoombinis is a classic in the edutainment genre. While the sequels were good in their own ways, they never truly captured the magic of the original. Unlike most other games, which mostly focus on concrete skills like math or spelling, zoombinis focuses more on abstract skills and critical thinking. This has the side effect of making the game still fairly enjoyable and difficult at higher levels, even to adults. The zoombinis and their journey to escape the horrors of overreaching capitalism are full of strangeness and charm. This remake is generally a good version, though a few bugs (most notibly the final puzzle, which doesn't always give you a way to save all of your zoombinis) mar it from being quite as good as the original version. Still, it's an amazing game, and is definitely worth a try, especially when it's on save for $2.50.

a lot of people might pass on this game. yes, there are a lot of indie 8-bit platformers out there, and yes, super win the game certainly is one of them. but the problem many games in this "genre" face is poor game design, often favoring what made NES-era games visually appealing over what made them fun to play. super win the game - like shovel knight, 1001 spikes, cave story, VVVVVV, and a few others - is a great example of what's possible when gameplay is given just as much emphasis as retro visual flair.
super win the game (swtg) is a metroidvania game with no combat. your goal is exploration and discovery. its visuals and design take some clear influence from zelda II, interestingly, but the resemblance stops there. in my opinion, swtg is a vast improvement on its free predecessor
- its diverse locations and overworld map give swtg more variation and a stronger feeling of adventure. on top of its main story and objectives (which can be kinda heavy-handed at times, i have to admit), swtg is packed with mysteries to solve and secrets to find, but never anything obtuse or unreasonable. it's one of the few games i've ever bothered to 100%, out of sheer enjoyment and a desire to keep playing. with a game like this, there's always a chance of boring or annoying a player with uninteresting/obnoxious music, but swtg's soundtrack is pleasant and nicely composed, and never wore on me over the hours i spent wandering around the game world.
the solid design work and fun gameplay make its NES-inspired graphics and impressively realistic (and very customizable) CRT emulation feel like charming additional polish rather than pandering retro ♥♥♥♥♥♥y. it's an impressive and vastly underappreciated game all around, and i wish more people would give it a chance and support its developer.

This is my first review, so if my review is poor, my apologies.
Space Channel 5 is a rhythm game made by SEGA. I first heard about it through Project X Zone on the 3DS. I'm glad I did, I enjoyed this game quite a lot despite me not being too interested in rhythm games or SEGA games. I say all of this because it helps explain that I'm playing this game, not as an expert, but more of a novice or amateur.
A general rule of thumb for me is that gameplay is most important, and neither voice acting nor visuals usually matter. My visual preference is cartoony, not realism, and so I feel that I should leave it off to limit bias as much as I can (Although, isn't bias the whole point of a review?) This is how it works for me specifically. Sorry if you disagree with that.
For a rhythm game, I feel that the order of importance for the review should be gameplay, music, and finally plot.
Gameplay: The gameplay is basic and easy to follow. You hit the 6 designated buttons when prompted in alignment with the beat of the music. If you are good at both timing and memory, and enjoy them, I'd recommend this game. The game's first two stages will give you a lot of leeway to make mistakes to get yourself situated with the game. All stages have segments that enough misses will cause you to fail the level and you can start from either a checkpoint or from the beginning, it's up to you.
Music: I am no music connoisseur, but I really like the soundtrack. I think it's supposed to sound like pop, but I think that because Space Michael, a major character in the game, is voiced by Michael Jackson. It's really catchy, so I didn't have much trouble following the beat.
Plot: I won't give away spoilers, you can do it yourself by watching Youtube or similar video-sharing platforms if you wish. Going into a rhythm game or a Mario game for an interesting and deep story is like talking to a wall; You'll usually feel disappointment. The plot is easy to understand, quirky, random, not entirely logical, and pretty weird. I like it a lot.
Gameplay: 9/10
Music: 10/10
Plot: 8/10
Overall: 9/10

So I had just established my young but promising new colony, Ashton (a quite ironical name in the end ...). The basic needs were all covered, everyone had a nice place to sleep, decent clothing, enough to eat and time to relax. The people of Ashton were prosperous. They lived in harmony with nature and each other. Their wide fields provided them with plenty of food and they sold the surplus to the passing by caravans.
Now and then a few warriors of a near tribe, the Pig Face Men, attacked the settlement, but the people of Ashton were safe, relying on the strength of their automated defence systems. And so the colony grew and I thought: This is it, I finally have a colony which doesn't collapse after a few hours.
As if ...
Remember when I told you about the harmony between the people and with nature? I meant there were no rivalries between the colonists, most were friends and there even was a married couple, Tali and Waltz.
The harmony with nature also seems pretty coherent; the people relied mostly on their crops, eating only those animals which died by natural causes (e.g. old age or other animals), so the animal population in the near forests remained stable. So far so good. But taking those dead animals in meant of course someone had to leave the safe area of Ashton and wander through the wilds. Normally that wouldn't have been a problem, everyone was equipped with guns and armor of the Pig Face Men so they were quite ready to take on anything coming in their way.
Waltz left Ashton to get the still fresh corpse of a chinchilla which had been killed by some other animal. So Waltz has just grabbed it, when a tortoise nearby turned mad. I thought ok, those aren't that fast, Waltz will be able to safely carry the chinchilla inside and the turrets will take care of the tortoise.
I'm not quite sure what exactly happened, maybe this animal was on speed or something like thak. Anyway, when it saw Waltz it charged at him at a horrifying pace. Waltz had just lifted his weapon when this damn creature reached and hurt him badly. However, its hard shell was no match for Waltz' gun. And so he came back home, injured but happy, that now there was even more meat than expected. But the wraith of the tortoise was unforgiving. The bite wounds in his upper body infected themselves. The medical treatment didn't work and he got weaker and weaker. If the infection at least would've been in one of his limbs, that might had saved him, but you can't just amputate someones chest.
At last he couldn't fight any longer, the infection overwhelmed him. Tali, his wife, carved his story in the sides of his sarcophagus. The burial ceremony was heartbreaking. Everyone had come: Tali, his sister Julia, his friends Vas, Jones, Stephan, Boyd and Leia, Vas' tame wolf Nevile and Bacon 1 and Bacon 2. In the light of the evening sun they all waved a last goodbye to their fallen husband, brother and friend, before the people of Ashton went to bed. With Waltz dead or not, they had to cary on.
But apparently it was all too much for Tali, not very surprising if you think about it. There was only this one little problem: She was a pyromaniac. When the rest of the colony slept, she left her big and empty bed. Driven crazy by grief, she did the only thing able to ease her pain. She set the forest on fire. Finally, exhausted almost to unconciousness, she fell back into her bed again.
While she slept, the others, waken by the crackling fire, desperately tried to put out the flames which already started to spread over to the buildings. But they simply weren't enough, they could either try to save the buildings or the forest, not both. Of course they tended to the buildings, to the food storage to be exact. However it gave the fire the chance to spread through the forest, completely sorrounding the settlement.
In the end it was all too much.
Tali died in her own fire that she refused to extinguish, Jones and Boyd followed when they collapsed in the infernal heat. And then, when no hope was left, the gods, the ancestors, the Flying Spaghetti Monster or whatever thi people of Ashton believed in, heard their cries. Rain started falling down, putting out the fire. But it was too late. More than three quarters of the colony had been taken by the flames. Vas, Stephan and Leia were unconcious. Julia was the only one still able to stand. She did what she could, but with all the medicine burned she had no chance. Leia died first, Vas second. This caused his wolf Nevile, who had been laying loyal by his side, to turn mad like the damn tortoise and he ripped the still unconcious Stehpan into pieces before he went on attacking a herd of muffalos (some kind of marshmellow like buffalos) which was his end.
Traumatised Julia, who managed to flee when Stephan was killed, wandered through the burnt ruins of Ashton. Blackened stone walls and pieces of charcoal everywhere. All the food they stored for the winter was gone, the fields empty. With no medicine left and her own wounds hurting worse and worse, Julia found a last smokeleaf joint in one of the destroyed buildings. She leant against her brother's sarcophagus and lit it. So she didn't feel anything when the Pig Face Men attacked. With the solar panels a loss to the flames, the turrets didn't react when Ashton's last inhabitant finally exhaled her last breath.
12 / 10 - Creates more immersive storys than many RPGs; looking forward to my next colony (and possibly its desastrous destruction ...).

This is NOT, by any means, a Mario Kart clone. Saying that is like saying CoD is a Doom clone.
Choosing a character isn't as simple as just picking someone you like: each vehicle handles differently, and even then, each character has 3 of them: car, plane, and boat. And you WILL use all three on some races, as the tracks change mid-race (things like new paths opening, events off-track that affect the track itself, etc). Also, each vehicle can be customized to different playstyles (customizations available by leveling up characters or by unlocking them during Career mode), to aid in certain types of races. Besides the standard 10-car races, you have Boost Challenges, VS Races, Timed Events, and others.
The only issue I have with it is the difficulty. Playing on easy or normal is very forgiving: enemies rarely throw anything at you and just race normally. Go up to Hard, however, and suddenly they become much more aggressive, to the point where it becomes genuinely tough to win some races, frustrating even. And for those of you thinking you can just play on normal: you can't unlock all characters, customizations, and events on Career mode without doing some events on Hard. The different difficulty setting gives you different amounts of stars (1 for Easy, 2 for Normal, so on), and by the end game you will require several of them to unlock everything. Keep that in mind.

Sonic & All-Stars Racing: Transformed is a kart racer released in 2012, and is the sequel to Sonic & Sega All-Stars Racing. While the former entry was content being a simple Mario Kart clone (albeit with much better track designs), the latter is not. Playing this game and writing this article were strange and eye-opening experiences, partially because the game makes me feel like I’m betraying my Nintendo roots, playing a Sega game with a PS3 controller on a game I got on Steam…and having more fun than I’ve had in any Mario Kart game.
There is a wide array of selectable characters, many of which need to be unlocked. Several current and older Sega series are represented, like the Sonic franchise, Golden Axe, Shinobi, Nights, Alex Kidd, Skies of Arcadia, Super Monkey Ball, Samba de Amigo, Jet Set Radio, and Space Channel 5. There are also a few third-party characters (more if you’re playing the PC version), which is why they dropped “Sega” from the title of this game. These include (but are not limited to) Wreck-It Ralph, a Shogun and Willemus (representing two different games in the Total War series), and strangest of all – Danica Patrick. I normally would resent a choice like this, but the South Park episode where Cartman wanted to be a Nascar driver makes racing against her a lot of fun. Each character has five different stats: speed, acceleration, handling, boost, and all-star. These are each represented by a power level of 1-5 for each stat. You can also level your character up, although the only benefit to this is that it gives you different mods for your racer, changing your stats (the Speed mod raises your speed, as an obvious example).
The track designs are amazing, and really evoke the feeling of the games they’re based on. Like with the characters, a large variety of Sega games are represented, including After Burner, Panzer Dragoon, The House of the Dead, Burning Rangers, and Billy Hatcher and the Giant Egg, as well as the ones mentioned in the characters segment. There are 21 tracks in total, 4 of them returning from the previous game. This is where the game really shines.
QUICK MARIO KART RANT: Mario Kart tracks are somewhat based on the Mario franchise. Yoshi Circuit is neat, it’s a Yoshi-shaped track, but aside from that it’s not really “Mario-esque”. They’ve been getting somewhat better about making more than just the Ghost House track and Bowser Castle track feel like Mario levels, but then I think about one of my favorite tracks, Waluigi’s Pinball, and despite how as awesome of a level it is, there’s nothing about it at all that screams “this is based on the Super Mario series”.
The first All-Star racing game got the track design right the first time, and this time they knocked it out of the park. The deciding factor is the “Transformed” mechanic. If you like Diddy Kong Racing because of the multiple types of selectable vehicles, you’ll probably get a kick out of this, as you turn into different forms throughout the race. For example, the After Burner track has you racing along an aircraft carrier, then flying across an ocean battle zone, with ships firing at each other and aircraft flying overhead. You make your way to another aircraft carrier, turning back into a car, and keep racing like that along the carrier. After leaving that one, you transform into a boat as you race back to the first aircraft carrier, then back into a plane halfway along the ocean…and that happens in each lap. In a lot of the races, they’re designed so that crazy things happen in the second or third lap, completely re-shaping where you can go. This is also an added incentive to be in first place, to be able to see how the tracks are being changed. In the track based on Skies of Arcadia, you’ll be driving along a bridge in the first and second lap, only to see it destroyed in the third lap, transforming you into a plane and making you go in a different direction. And for those of you who weren’t a fan of Mario Kart 7′s underwater and hang gliding segments, know that the car is the slowest vehicle of the three in Sonic Transformed, and finding hidden opportunities to change into a plane or boat can really change the outcome of a race.
The last thing I’d like to mention is about the different modes, or really one mode in particular. They give you the standard Grand Prix, Single Race, Battle games, and Time Attack modes, but there’s also a World Tour mode. World Tour is set up similar to Diddy Kong Racing in that you have to win races to get stars to unlock more races/characters/mods, but the visual set up is akin to Super Mario Galaxy 2. You go along the map and select whichever races are available, and there are also a large assortment of race types in this mode. There are normal races, but also Sprint (essentially a Time Attack race against a ghost), Boost Challenges and Drift Challenges (getting boosts/doing drifts momentarily stops the countdown timer), Ring Races (flying through a series of rings), Versus (racing one on one against a series of opponents), Boost Races (no powerups, but there are a lot more boost pads on the track), Battle Races (defeating all opponents and/or getting first place without getting killed), Traffic Attack (weaving through waves of traffic), and Pursuit (chasing after a tank to blow it up with missiles). These help to make the World Tour mode a lot more fun, and some of them change the location of the track itself. I was a little surprised doing the Ring Race on the After Burner track, as it has you flying through one of the aircraft carriers at one point, something that isn’t possible during a normal race.
Overall, this game is fantastic. Boasting a wide variety of selectable characters with modifiable vehicles, excellent track designs, and a huge amount of game types, Sonic & All-Stars Racing: Transformed is recommended to all kart racing gamers, and may make you reconsider your excitement for Mario Kart 8.
DISCLAIMER: Racing games are a genre that keep getting noticeably better as technology improves. Mario Kart 8 could in fact be really awesome, and I’m not attempting to tell you not to get it. However, as someone who has been a loyal Nintendo fan since 1986 and has played every Mario Kart game in the series (as well as tons of others, like Diddy Kong Racing, Crash Team Racing, LittleBigPlanetKarting, Pac-Man Rally, Konami Krazy Racers, and Lego Racers), I’m simply asking you not to dismiss Sonic Transformed as I feel it has set the bar higher than any Mario Kart game has for a long time. Double Dash was great, but I’d argue that the series hasn’t brought much to the table since then that didn’t just feel like the same game with a cheap new gimmick attached.
DOUBLE DISCLAIMER: I’m apparently the only person in the world who thought (and still thinks) that Mario Kart 64 was an awful game.

It takes a lot for something to win over someone who has already set their mind against it. It's tough to even understand sometimes how such a thing even happens with someone who tries to keep a relatively open mind.
Something about Divekick rubbed me the wrong way from the outset. It was a silly little thing then, based on a (not at all funny) joke. But it was still that; just a joke. I didn't care for it at all, but I also didn't have to pay attention to it. A story here and there cropped up from time to time, but I could easily scroll past it.
But then, something happened. The guy behind it, Adam "Keits" Heart, decided to make a Kickstarter to make it a real thing. Now I'd been following Keits' writings for a while, and I respect the man, I really do. But I didn't have any interest in his project at all. However, the more I tried to avoid it, the more it was being thrown in my face. It plastered front page several times a week on every video game site I'd visited for months, every one of my fighting game fan friends kept asking me about it over and over (somehow, they all have less memory retention than I do), and every time the game was even mentioned online, in came hundred-page comments about how "gdlk" it was. It was like one giant hive-mind circle-jerk joke that would not leave me alone. Even once it released, the joke spilled over into reviews on every reputable site (and some that weren't) known to man, with short reviews about how perfect the game is, whilst using only fighting game memes and lingo in ways that didn't actually tell you why it was supposed to be so good.
A couple of months had passed, and the fervor died down, except for certain websites. I saw it on Steam sale for less than $3, and I figured "What the hell, the best I could do is give it a fair shot."
Worst two-something I've ever spent.
To be fair, it does have much more depth than I had anticipated. In every other regard, however, it falls short of even my already ground level expectations, and even the depth feels wrong.
Right from the get-go, you're visually assaulted by the graphical quality. The character and background drawings are decent enough, but they're godawful as sprites and have some utterly horrendous animation. It takes a lot of work to screw up animation for a game where 90% of the actions are rising into the air and dropping back down, but dammit, they managed.
The characters are mostly appalling, with half of the cast being parodies of real Fighting Game Community "personalities". It's this half of the roster that I absolutely loathe, with the remaining half being a mix of somewhat tolerable and "pretty okay." Look, video game memes can be hit or miss, but most of them are amusing for a while. Who didn't slip "All your base are belong to us" or "The cake is a lie" into conversation from time to time at some point? But video game community jokes and memes are pretty much never entertaining, between the tournaments and the talking heads and the bulldung Youtube Let's Players. Look, I GET the references, they are just stupid. There's literally only one character in the game that I genuinely like, and that's Stream.
So okay, the game could look like horse manure and still be great, and the characters are mostly a superficial thing anyway, so when it boils down to it, what is it that matters most? Gameplay. Strike three, Divekick. The game, as it is so often boasted, consists of literally just two buttons to control: Dive, and Kick - one to jump into the air, the other to come back down and attempt to plant down in the opponent's face. Simple enough, and just the fact that there is no way to maneuver your character outside of these acts does require a bit of strategical thinking. And then there's the gem system, which does about as much as it did in Street Fighter X Tekken (i.e. their effects are mostly barely noticeable), and that's how it all started. But then they started cramming in all the different other things - the air and ground specials, the character-specific eccentrics, and so on. It took what could have been a simple, quick one-on-one game, and made it into something much more complicated. It seems to detract from the game's original intended spirit, such as it was.
Compounding all of these annoyances, is the fact that despite the game being developed by the sort of guys that would masturbate over tier lists, it's got absolute♥♥♥♥♥♥for balance. There are a select few characters that head and shoulders above the rest, and a few that are absolute flounders, and the rest are stuck somewhere in the middle, grasping for a chance to rise or fall to either of the other sides. The CPU makes good use of this fact; the characters that are absolute trash in the hands of a player, also are the easiest to beat. The tougher characters, however, dominate nearly every time. The Baz in particular was the biggest source of frustration, even more so than the boss, because when the computer plays him, every single round has him firing himself in the direction your character is, faster than possible to react 90% of the time.
I guess probably the best part is that online is mostly functional, such as it is, or at least it was during the brief time that I monkeyed with it. They definitely have made sure they weren't one of those companies that believes that automatically slapping GGPO onto a game without customizing it to fit the game makes online "good", but then again there is a lot less to worry about in something that doesn't have command moves, 360s, proper combos, and the like.
I've been one of the biggest advocates for change, or at least trying something new, in fighting games, for the better part of the decade. As much as I love the genre, every game pretty much hits the same set of checkboxes and plays it safe, and that's what causes things to grow stale. However, I do not feel that Divekick is anywhere close to what is needed for a competently put-together fighting game that shuns the norm - it's all at once too much, and not enough. In fact, to be perfectly honest, despite its roots, I hesitate to consider it a fighting game at all. It's really more of a... PVP falling simulator.

This game has aged like milk.
I don't like to write negative reviews. I tend to look on the bright side for a lot of games. I like to crank up the difficulty, because sometimes, the developers intended for a game to be played on the higher difficulty settings. Unfortunately, most of the time, that winds up being "Let's boost the health pools of the enemies so that they are no longer fun to fight".
While people like to sing this game's praises when it comes to first person melee combat, in my experience it tends to be janky and unreliable. Not so much the main character's moves, which feel weighty and responsive, but the enemies', which tend to hurt you at random. Because someone awkwardly flailed their arm at you, you now take a third of your healthbar out. Whoops, now you're dead, because apparently that was a combo.
The kick is the best tool in the game and the devs clearly wanted to you to use it. There are a lot of fires and spike traps around, and it never gets old to kick people off of ledges. The spells are creative in how they're designed. I love that ice makes enemies slip and ragdoll across the ground. It's consistently hilarious.
I love throwing random garbage at my foes. It makes me feel scrappy, like I'm an underdog. At its best, the game makes you improvise, forces you to consider what's in your environment and just throw whatever's available.
But all this said? It feels like the fun parts of the game were accidental.
The game is full of really bizarre design decisions. Aside from how the enemies are apparently made of adamantium (and you can claim that armor makes people harder to kill, but this is a video game. There's an element of artifice to them. There has to be in order to make them, you know, FUN). Poison is cancerous, and the limited number of antidotes makes it just less bearable. Why do I have to stare at this idiot's sword-pull animation? It makes swapping between spells and magic completely unbearable. Even DARK SOULS, a game that loves its slow swinging animations, has instant weapon swapping. This isn't skillful, it's just tedious.
The scripted sequences are by far the worst part. They're all over the place and none of them are all that entertaining. I'm sure they were really impressive in 2006, but they have aged so, so poorly.
The strongest piece of evidence for this is how demon mode works. In that it sucks. It's terrible. Demon mode is awful. There's no contest. It's absolutely dreadful. It does piddly damage on the higher difficulties, the tail is trash, and worst of all, it removes the kick. In the section where you're forced to use it, you are best off just going in unarmed and kicking people.
It makes it all the funnier when they try making it a moral dilemma.
"B-But you get this rad demon mode if you go evi-"
"lol no contest give me this super sword that kills undead. which the final level is FULL OF."
Oh, right, that leads me to the story. It's trash, throw it in the recycle bin.
Like I tried loving this game. But after running into a spell that instakills the player (Like, it doesn't do damage. It just makes you dead. It looks EXACTLY like the normal fireball, and there's no way to dodge it. This is awful design), I decided to stop playing and uninstall it.
And what adds insult to injury is Ubisoft's insulting stupid decision to stop mod support. Like, all this? All this could be forgiven if you were allowed to mod the game and change how it's designed. Except they stopped it for what look like incredibly dumb reasons.
Basically, Ubisoft was trash a decade ago. So nothing's really changed.
It feels like a great game trapped inside of a terrible one. I hope Arkane develops better things down the...wait, they did. Nevermind.

I cannot begin to describe how utterly disappointed I am in this game.  I was and still am a huge fan of Crimes and Punishments, so I was thrilled to hear another chapter in the series was due to release.  The core mechanic I fell in love with from the previous game, the deduction mechanic, is still intact but that's about the only good thing I can say about this game.  There are these bizzare action sequences in the middle of the game that end up just being headaches due to the games horribly clunky controls and really just have no place whatsoever in the middle of the investigation.  The "puzzle" sections are just as bad since the most puzzling thing about them is trying to figure out who the hell thought any of these were a remotely good idea.  They suffer from the horrible controls as well along with the fact that absolutely none of them are remotely challenging.  The answer is literally spelled out for you on a couple of them, while the rest are just obvious.  The absolute worst thing of it all though?  The fact that the final conclusion to the case is just so unsatisfactory.  In Crimes & Punishments I felt like I had achieved something whenever I completed a case.  I had outsmarted the killer, had managed to uncover the truth but here in this game I get the same sense of accomplisment as I do when I walk down a hallway.  Except this hallway has a bunch of siderooms and diversions that really don't need to be there and are horrificly designed and are an utter bore to have to pass through.
TLDR; if you're a huge fan of the previous game Crimes & Punishment, then hold out for a really good steam sale.  Otherwise just avoid this game altogether.

Dark Messiah's biggest strengths are also it's biggest drawbacks. The kicking in this game is legendary- seriously, kicking enemies off cliffs and into spike traps is surprisingly rewarding. That said, a lot of the other physics can be difficult to maneuver or are simply a bit buggy. The combat can be tactical and varied, but later enemies like ghouls encourage spamming and all the bosses rely on mechanics that were done to death even back in 2006 (this is to say nothing about recycled boss fights.) The story has one interesting turn, but doesn't run with it. The music is forgetable. Character models are great for the time, but environments and textures are pretty bland (I hope you like underground dungeons.) Did I enjoy it? Yes, mostly. Am I itching to start a new playthrough? Well, no. The biggest fault with Dark Messiah is that it tried to do so much, and it was way before it's time. Unfortunately this doesn't change the fact that first person RPG players today will have already seen everything that made this game unique back in 2006.

The Logical Journey of the Zoombinis is an all-time PC classic. It shows us that educational games don't need to be boring, and can even be fun for adults. "Zoombinis" is a beautiful remaster of Logical Journey, and gives it a modern coat of paint while keeping the fun gameplay of the original in tact. The game has you leading the Zoombinis on a journey to escape the oppression of the bloats, and during this journey there are lots of perils. You will face many crazy challenges such as preparing food for a cranky pizza troll, trying to find a safe path over a sneezing cliff, or even riding on the backs of frogs.

Overall, it's a fun game filled with lots of unique puzzles. It being family friendly doesn't stop it from posing a formidable challenge. I just hope that they consider remaking the other games in the Zoombinis series in a similar manner.

Every world has a story, this is mine.
....in my colony, the two best soldiers happen to be brothers. They rescued a beautiful hardworking lady(that had ethical issues about prosthetics) that was on the run from a group of pirates. Locke and Daniel (Dan) ambushed the small band of raiders and the two surviving pirates fled unharmed. Locke sustained a bullet wound in the chest. It wasn’t too serious but the colony lacked a decent clinic and the current healthcare provider was a known smokeleaf addict that often made mistakes. The risk of infection was more serious than his wound. Dan carried Locke to get treated and was relieved when Jen the beautiful lady they had just rescued was a medic. She treated his wounds and in no time Locke was on his feet. She became the new Doc in town, which Larry didn’t mind because he had a burning passion for cooking and could now devote his free time to cloud watching. Jen was immediately drawn to Locke for his positive attitude and his compassion for animals. They became lovers, and built a small house next to the clinic.
They owned a shoddy bed that they decorated with pink hearts. They would lie in bed and discuss future plans for the colony. Less than a year later those plans would involve a wedding. Jen asked Locke to marry her and he accepted. The colony had grown considerably by then and the couple contemplated where they would choose to mark the occasion. They believed the clinic where they first met would be symbolic. The clinic was now much larger with sterile floors and improved bedding. The original bed had long since been scraped but they commissioned to have one created for ceremonial reasons only.
A few days later an announcement came that the colony was under attack. It was the same pirate group that had tried to harm Jen. He wondered if the two members that escaped were among them. He wouldn’t even recognize them now even if they were.  There was little time to prepare and the pirate’s raid was larger than expected. Fortunately the colony was well equipped and boasted its own modest defense force. They quickly mobilized the fighters and rushed towards a choke point they had once agreed on defending should such a situation occur. As expected the pirate funneled in and was met with a barrage of bullets. The pirates were suffering a few losses but they noticed another group of pirates had split off and was nearing the colony. The pirates had already killed the cat and were determined to raze the colony to the ground. Jen and a small group of colonist that claimed they were incapable of committing violence, watched helplessly as the pirates own commitment to violence progressed towards them. Locke and the other colonists broke off from the attack to intercept the other group. They had hoped to slow them down long enough for Dan and his group to finish up and reinforce them later.
Locke intercepted two pirates tearing up the colonies solar panels.  The group opened fire killing them. As they approached another group a shot rang out and Locke dropped. The bullet struck Locke in the head destroying his brain. The other colonists were shocked and the mood of the colony quickly sank. The shot came from a 27 y/o sniper named Goki. He wasn’t known for his skill but today he would be known for his luck, Or so he thought. The call for retreat was called soon after as Dan had caused significant casualties at the chokepoint. Goki and the rest of his crew fled but Dan cut their escape off. Goki and two others were downed and many of their group were dead. The colony was safe but at the cost of a terrible price. I tried it for free at first then bought it, and I played it a few hours, so I feel able to review it without getting (too) wrong. I'll show you pros, cons and 50/50, as a non-veteran, in order to letting you know if this is a game for you (wich it is for sure).
Pros : - communication is not just part of the game, IT IS the game. If you go alone and don't play the objective like a CoD player, you will either lose or die. The squad leader give orders, the squad follow them, and each squad have to be coordonate to win
- weapons feel like what they are, aka big pieces of metal made for death and destruction (and pretty much uncontrollable if you shoot in full auto)
- sound, because you'll♥♥♥♥♥♥in your pant every time a bullet will crack next to you. Footsteps, explosions, firing, hiting a target, motors, everything makes you feel like you're in a real war, and you feel the fear of dying at every engagement
- vehicules are here, from motorbike to armoured anti-infantry APC (and don't forget the islamist truck with a multiple rocket launcher mounted on it)
- community is awesome and will help you everytime you need it, as a newbie if you have a question, as a teamate if you're in trouble. It's like a family, without the anoying side of it
- it's about 40vs40 players on really big maps, and the dev said it'll be 50vs50 soon. Large-scale war at another level in video games
Cons : - learning curve is a bit tough, you'll need some hours and games to understand how the game itself works, because it's not just about killing everyone but mainly taking/destroying objectives (it will require specific actions to work, like throwing the incendiary of the squad leader on it) (and entering a vehicule is not easy at first if you don't know what's going on)
- not much choice of weapons/class and even less attachements. A squad leader, 2 medics, other are infantry 1st class (you get an AK with iron sights, one guy in your squad will get it with an optic, another will get a sniper, and that's all). Plus no customization at all (actually. The Workshop will be included in the current year)
- you'll lose yourself across the map, even more in town where your map is useless
50/50 : - each game is very long. Half a hour or more.You'll feel tired, but you'll get the true satisfaction of a hard victory (even more when it's by 10 tickets or less
- it's punitive AF, show your head out and boom, no more head for you, and you won't see from where. Same for your opponent though
- there's lag, but the lag issues are due to the number of player. I'm mean come on, it's 40vs40, on a giant map yes, but when everyone is attacking/defending the same objective, it may be hard for any PC to stay at 60fps (remember it is Early Access in Alpha)
- graphics are good in low/mid, but not astonishing in high/ultra (again it's Alpha so you won't see reality-like graphics. They're way more than just ok at this moment though, so it's fine)
- ATH is poor. Awesome to feel the intensity of each fights and for realism, but not knowing how many bullets you got in your clip can cause your death if you don't pay attention at it
So, here you are. If you want a realistic FPS, with modern combat features, vehicules, large-scale operation, teamplay-based gameplay, but not Battlefield because it's too arcade, and not ArmA because it's too difficult/complex for you, then run straigh to Squad and you'll not regret anything

Sonic & All-Stars Racing: Transformed is a kart racer released in 2012, and is the sequel to Sonic & Sega All-Stars Racing. While the former entry was content being a simple Mario Kart clone (albeit with much better track designs), the latter is not. Playing this game and writing this article were strange and eye-opening experiences, partially because the game makes me feel like I’m betraying my Nintendo roots, playing a Sega game with a PS3 controller on a game I got on Steam…and having more fun than I’ve had in any Mario Kart game.
There is a wide array of selectable characters, many of which need to be unlocked. Several current and older Sega series are represented, like the Sonic franchise, Golden Axe, Shinobi, Nights, Alex Kidd, Skies of Arcadia, Super Monkey Ball, Samba de Amigo, Jet Set Radio, and Space Channel 5. There are also a few third-party characters (more if you’re playing the PC version), which is why they dropped “Sega” from the title of this game. These include (but are not limited to) Wreck-It Ralph, a Shogun and Willemus (representing two different games in the Total War series), and strangest of all – Danica Patrick. I normally would resent a choice like this, but the South Park episode where Cartman wanted to be a Nascar driver makes racing against her a lot of fun. Each character has five different stats: speed, acceleration, handling, boost, and all-star. These are each represented by a power level of 1-5 for each stat. You can also level your character up, although the only benefit to this is that it gives you different mods for your racer, changing your stats (the Speed mod raises your speed, as an obvious example).
The track designs are amazing, and really evoke the feeling of the games they’re based on. Like with the characters, a large variety of Sega games are represented, including After Burner, Panzer Dragoon, The House of the Dead, Burning Rangers, and Billy Hatcher and the Giant Egg, as well as the ones mentioned in the characters segment. There are 21 tracks in total, 4 of them returning from the previous game. This is where the game really shines.
QUICK MARIO KART RANT: Mario Kart tracks are somewhat based on the Mario franchise. Yoshi Circuit is neat, it’s a Yoshi-shaped track, but aside from that it’s not really “Mario-esque”. They’ve been getting somewhat better about making more than just the Ghost House track and Bowser Castle track feel like Mario levels, but then I think about one of my favorite tracks, Waluigi’s Pinball, and despite how as awesome of a level it is, there’s nothing about it at all that screams “this is based on the Super Mario series”.
The first All-Star racing game got the track design right the first time, and this time they knocked it out of the park. The deciding factor is the “Transformed” mechanic. If you like Diddy Kong Racing because of the multiple types of selectable vehicles, you’ll probably get a kick out of this, as you turn into different forms throughout the race. For example, the After Burner track has you racing along an aircraft carrier, then flying across an ocean battle zone, with ships firing at each other and aircraft flying overhead. You make your way to another aircraft carrier, turning back into a car, and keep racing like that along the carrier. After leaving that one, you transform into a boat as you race back to the first aircraft carrier, then back into a plane halfway along the ocean…and that happens in each lap. In a lot of the races, they’re designed so that crazy things happen in the second or third lap, completely re-shaping where you can go. This is also an added incentive to be in first place, to be able to see how the tracks are being changed. In the track based on Skies of Arcadia, you’ll be driving along a bridge in the first and second lap, only to see it destroyed in the third lap, transforming you into a plane and making you go in a different direction. And for those of you who weren’t a fan of Mario Kart 7′s underwater and hang gliding segments, know that the car is the slowest vehicle of the three in Sonic Transformed, and finding hidden opportunities to change into a plane or boat can really change the outcome of a race.
The last thing I’d like to mention is about the different modes, or really one mode in particular. They give you the standard Grand Prix, Single Race, Battle games, and Time Attack modes, but there’s also a World Tour mode. World Tour is set up similar to Diddy Kong Racing in that you have to win races to get stars to unlock more races/characters/mods, but the visual set up is akin to Super Mario Galaxy 2. You go along the map and select whichever races are available, and there are also a large assortment of race types in this mode. There are normal races, but also Sprint (essentially a Time Attack race against a ghost), Boost Challenges and Drift Challenges (getting boosts/doing drifts momentarily stops the countdown timer), Ring Races (flying through a series of rings), Versus (racing one on one against a series of opponents), Boost Races (no powerups, but there are a lot more boost pads on the track), Battle Races (defeating all opponents and/or getting first place without getting killed), Traffic Attack (weaving through waves of traffic), and Pursuit (chasing after a tank to blow it up with missiles). These help to make the World Tour mode a lot more fun, and some of them change the location of the track itself. I was a little surprised doing the Ring Race on the After Burner track, as it has you flying through one of the aircraft carriers at one point, something that isn’t possible during a normal race.
Overall, this game is fantastic. Boasting a wide variety of selectable characters with modifiable vehicles, excellent track designs, and a huge amount of game types, Sonic & All-Stars Racing: Transformed is recommended to all kart racing gamers, and may make you reconsider your excitement for Mario Kart 8.
DISCLAIMER: Racing games are a genre that keep getting noticeably better as technology improves. Mario Kart 8 could in fact be really awesome, and I’m not attempting to tell you not to get it. However, as someone who has been a loyal Nintendo fan since 1986 and has played every Mario Kart game in the series (as well as tons of others, like Diddy Kong Racing, Crash Team Racing, LittleBigPlanetKarting, Pac-Man Rally, Konami Krazy Racers, and Lego Racers), I’m simply asking you not to dismiss Sonic Transformed as I feel it has set the bar higher than any Mario Kart game has for a long time. Double Dash was great, but I’d argue that the series hasn’t brought much to the table since then that didn’t just feel like the same game with a cheap new gimmick attached.
DOUBLE DISCLAIMER: I’m apparently the only person in the world who thought (and still thinks) that Mario Kart 64 was an awful game.

Crimes and Punishments is one of the best detective games of all time and a modern classic of the adventure game genre. So its follow-up, Devil's Daughter, was guaranteed to be good right?
Sadly no. Devil's Daughter is grossly inferior to C&P in almost every way. The game just screams getting rushed out the door and Frogwares having little confidence in the standard C&P set. The writing is much worse and utterly nonsensical at times, the mysteries are so rushed with barely any explanation of motives and real conclusive evidence that you pretty much have to guess who the culprit is. The game is bogged down with terrible puzzles and minigames that take away from what made C&P so great. The game looks nice and its neat how bigger some of the areas are, but it ultimately feels that it was a wasted effort that could have been used to tighten up what really mattered.
I'm at the end of the second case but I'm really tempted just to cut my losses, because I'm losing interest in it fast. Devil's Daughter is a huge disappointment and a super mediocre game. If you're new to the series just buy C&P, it’s the only truly great game in the series. For fans, just pick this up when its a super deep discount, because while not outright bad this game just isn't that good, especially when there is so many better adventure games to choose from nowadays.

Sherlock Holmes Crimes and Punishments was my favorite of the Frogware Holmes games and one of my favorite adventure games of recent years. After growing so much as a developer through Jack the Ripper, Testament and C&P it is a shame to see the huge step back Devil's Daughter is. Where C&P hit the perfect balance of detective work, story and puzzles this game has put action puzzles to the forefront and the game suffers for it.
I still recommend Devil's Daughter as much of what was great about C&P is here. The investigation parts of the game are still very enjoyable and overall I have liked the stories involved with the different cases. There are also some very funny moments during the third case including a Holmes actor and a cute exorcism scene.
The bad for this game though is very bad. The change of character models and voice actors was a huge step backwards. I honestly don't know what the developer intended, but it's a bit late to try and channel the Holmes movies that everyone has forgotten. This game had a unique style that has been derailed by changing just those two characters while leaving the rest of the game the same as C&P.
I can't finish without talking about the action puzzles. The lowest point I ever had in a Frogware game was the almost unplayable stealth puzzle in The Silver Ring. It essentially ended the game for me as it was so poorly designed that it killed any interest I had in trying to slog through it. This game has several puzzles that match that level. I didn't find any of the puzzles unbeatable, but they involve so much trial and error and in many cases keep coming back to back where you seriously start to lose interest in continuing. Thankfully you can just skip these if you want, but I got through them anyway and many of them felt more like a way to pad out a short game instead of a developer trying to challenge the gamer. The grind of getting through the pyramid in the second case was bad not just because most of the puzzles were trial and error and you have to restart each every time you failed, but also because they just stacked irritating puzzle after irritating puzzle back to back with no break. The game is just not well thought out or paced in many sections.
Edit: After beating the game and dealing with the stealth section and the QTE of the ending it is clear to me that they were padding out the game's length. No developer in this day and age would make you start at the beginning of a long stealth section or long dialog QTE segment unless they were counting on that to extend the game length. I also want to note I played through all 11.6 hours on my Alienware Alpha with its mobile 860 video card and had no technical issues on high settings so that was one positive to the game.
However, if you can be patient the puzzles in the game are all beatable (or just skippable if you would prefer) and you will eventually get back to solving the cases. The investigations are not up to the level of C&P, but I still found them enjoyable and I still make the game a recommendation even though it is one of the weaker of the series. If you haven't played Sherlock Holmes before then definitely play C&P, Testament and Jack the Ripper first. Save this one for a Steam sale.

It's easy to see why this game was so highly-rated by critics. Picturesque backgrounds, an interesting premise, and decent voice-acting work all contribute to a surface appearance of a quality game experience.
Sadly, the final product is yet another example of an interesting premise ruined by a shoddy delivery.
What could be a potentially-interesting sci-fi/paranormal mystery is hampered by uninteresting and unlikeable characters, and a slipshod plot filled with contrivances and held back from any explorations of the mystery theme to instead indulge in melodramatic teen angst. There's no plot to explore beyond "go to island, spoopy things happen", and none of the side characters are really explored in any depth. Instead everyone is shallow and one-note, a flat cutout for the player to interact with (or ignore, thankfully) that has no real bearing on the overall story beyond the now-prerequisite "Were you nice or mean?" checkboxes needed to decide which of the endings you get. That alone might be worth something if the player were given any reason to actually care about the side characters, but sadly, this just isn't the case. The player is never given a chance to really know any of the other characters in-depth, even if they choose to make the effort. Rather, they exist only in how they relate to the main character, who herself treads some pretty run-of-the-mill territory as far as protagonists go.
On that note, the player has a tiny bit of leeway to influence the main character's development, but even that is bungled since the option to choose numerous dialog options at various points means her personality can end up being completely uneven; you can be horrible jerk to everyone and still be randomly kind for no reason, or vice-versa, and the game can't really anticipate or react to that in any meanfully way beyond "well you were still a jerk 90% of the time, so I guess you get the jerk ending".
The problem, then, is player investment. If you care about teen angst and are willing to get drawn into a YA novella about unlikeable kids arguing with each other, then maybe you'll get something more out of the "plot" experience. But even if that's the case, there's still no real enjoyable game experience to be had. There are no real puzzles to solve beyond "go here, do X, go here, do Y". There are two spots in the game where you're given a "quiz", but failing them has zero effect on the plot so there's no reason to bother even trying. There are collectibles to find, but they all revolve around the player's radio item, which amounts to popping it open and scrolling until you get the right frequency—not a lot of brainpower involved there. All of this is made into even more of a chore given that the main character moves at an agonizingly-slow pace, only running seemingly at random. This is made even worse when you require a follower NPC, as they often have a tendency to lag behind or get stuck in the environment, forcing you to wait for them before you can transition to the next area or use whatever object you're looking at. This only exacerbates the game's already plodding pace into any absolute slog. I've heard tell the game can be finished in roughly 3 hours if you don't bother with collectibles, and I'd hazard a guess that at least 80% of that is just watching Alex slowly shuffle her way across the screen while one of her inane companions yammers on incessantly about nothing of relevance to the plot.
If you're willing to essentially turn off your brain and just let the game's developers pitch their ersatz-Stranger Things screenplay idea at you for a few hours, maybe you'll get something out of the hackneyed plot and shallow characters and faux-80s style. But for me personally, I've seen it all before, and there's just nothing here to grip me or invest me in the game beyond looking at the seams and realizing how easily it all comes apart,
tl;dr: The plot is a mess of annoying characters, and the game itself has no challenge or difficulty or thought to it. There's just not a lot to like here. But I mean, I guess the backgrounds are pretty? And the voice actors really did the best with the material they had? And it's got some of that faux-80s soundtrack going that's all the rage these days thanks to Stranger Things? So I guess that's an B+ right there, 8/10, 4 out of 5 stars, yadda yadda yadda.
It's not a terrible game, but I can't recommend it to anyone that enjoys a remote amount of depth. Go play Night in the Woods instead. It's more charming, the plot has better build-up and payoff, and there's some actual gameplay in there to boot.

I had a hard time getting into this game. The world is almost too open; it's hard to get a sense of where you should go next (and when you're done with an area), and I don't feel invested in any particular area when I can walk across practically the entire world map uninterrupted. If I can just walk into whatever dungeon I want, it doesn't feel like there's much separating the different areas from one another. The map looks big, but there's actually relatively few explorable areas. (The desert, while hardly the only example, is illustrative here: there are basically just three areas in the entire desert, despite it taking up quite a few tiles on the map. There are no enemies to fight and no challenges to encounter between the desert town and the desert ruins, which makes me question why the desert is there at all. Pretty much every area in the game is like this to a greater or lesser degree.)
The game is mostly pretty easy, though there are a couple rooms with a challenge level that's way out of scope compared to everything around them. There's no combat; there are enemies who can kill you, but you can't affect them in any way, so they're really just mobile obstacles rather than true enemies. This isn't necessarily the worst thing ever (I can respect a game with no fighting), but the fact that there aren't really very many of these enemies just intensifies the lack of feeling of challenge or opposition. There really isn't much standing in the way of anything you want to do; there are mobility upgrades you need before you can explore everywhere, but since you can just walk from one area to the next with basically nothing in your way, there's no struggle to get back to an area once you've picked up the relevant item. The entire game just seemed to lay itself at my feet, which made me question why I was bothering in the first place.
To give credit where it is due, I found the control scheme to be intuitive and reliable. The game's simple enough that it would be downright embarrassing for it to not have a simple control scheme, but I still felt like the controls were responsive, and I never really felt the need to blame the controls for any screw-ups I may have made. I played with an Xbox 360 controller, and it worked perfectly from the get-go.
The game's most unique feature is the graphical CRT simulation. The game does a good job of making itself look like you're playing it on an old TV, right down to a little reflection visible at the edge of the screen. Whether this is actually a good thing is debatable; I admit that it pushed a nostalgia button or two, but in general, I don't find myself pining for the days of old unreliable CRTs. The CRT simulation is cute, but it's ultimately nothing more than a gimmick, and I wouldn't count it as a selling point for the game.
The music is forgettable and fairly annoying. I respect chiptunes when they've got strong melodies, but that isn't the case with this game. It's tinny and artificial for the sake of being tinny and artificial, and the melodies aren't interesting enough to make up for the low technical quality. (Several areas also have songs that really don't seem to have anything to do with the mood of the area in question, which doesn't do the game any favors.)
Overall, I just never felt challenged playing this game. Without challenge, there's no real sense of accomplishment, so the whole thing was ultimately disappointing. I admit that I just beat the game without getting 100% of the gems, but I wasn't sufficiently invested in the game to really want to spend the time getting 100% completion. There's no real feeling of progression, even as you travel from area to area and pick up upgrade after upgrade. I understand that the game isn't asking for a lot of money, but you really aren't getting a lot of game in return for your investment.

My god this game gives me all sorts of happy feelings.  It reminds me so much of Zelda II from back in the day, which is a game I loved despite its flaws.
This game takes out all the frustrating aspects of Zelda II while maintaining a lot of the aesthetic and the tone.  But more than that, there's a lot of other legitimate retro references in here.  This feels less like a homage and more like a lost game from that era -- a good one.
I can't recommend it enough.  There are frequent checkpoints, and so the parts that would otherwise be frustrating are things that you can practice to your heart's content.  It thus has a great amount of challenge in parts without being annoying about it at any time.
The items and unlocks are good, and the feeling of exploration is tangible.  There are several methods of fast travel that you can make use of as you progress, and that makes backtracking not a thing anymore.
My sole complaint, and really this is just a matter of what the game is, is that there isn't any direct combat.   This is all about platforming, pure and simple.  There are enemies, sure, but you just avoid them.  To be honest, that works just fine and the game is great even so.  GET THIS GAME.  But what I'd love to see is a sequel that takes all the great stuff from this game, then adds in Zelda II or Castlevania style combat.  That would just be absolutely killer and take this over the top from being something I really really like to being something I desperately love.

Super Win the Game is Zelda 2 to the neck, with Metroid at the head. You are going to be exploring a large top-down overworld, you are going to scour side-scrolling dungeons, you are going to consult a myriad of townspeople, and you are going to find pieces of heart (not for you, however-- they're for the King).
I always found Zelda 2's combat to be somewhat frustrating, so for Super Win the Game to NOT feature combat was, honestly, a sigh of relief. That makes it purely about exploration, about finding secrets in the overworld map, about trying to jump to impossible places, and all of the fun that Metroidvanias (and Zelda games) inspire.
The visuals are a little plain but the CRT shaders are awesome, pretty perfectly implemented. You can turn them off but I just don't think it's the same experience if you do that.
Every region has its own Metroid mini-map which is great, although I wish the mini-map had more indicators than just gems (checkpoint and keys on the map would have been nice as you discovered them). I like that you can buy a skeleton key if you don't feel like hunting down all the keys (which is probably hard to say because that is a pretty important part of the exploration). Fast travel probably could have been a bit better but it's servicable.
Ultimately the important thing is the price: It's just 8 bucks, and very cheap at sales time. This is a good cheap Metroidvania that does honor to the NES classics and evokes some of those old feelings in an organic and genuine way.

I tried it for free at first then bought it, and I played it a few hours, so I feel able to review it without getting (too) wrong. I'll show you pros, cons and 50/50, as a non-veteran, in order to letting you know if this is a game for you (wich it is for sure).
Pros : - communication is not just part of the game, IT IS the game. If you go alone and don't play the objective like a CoD player, you will either lose or die. The squad leader give orders, the squad follow them, and each squad have to be coordonate to win
- weapons feel like what they are, aka big pieces of metal made for death and destruction (and pretty much uncontrollable if you shoot in full auto)
- sound, because you'll♥♥♥♥♥♥in your pant every time a bullet will crack next to you. Footsteps, explosions, firing, hiting a target, motors, everything makes you feel like you're in a real war, and you feel the fear of dying at every engagement
- vehicules are here, from motorbike to armoured anti-infantry APC (and don't forget the islamist truck with a multiple rocket launcher mounted on it)
- community is awesome and will help you everytime you need it, as a newbie if you have a question, as a teamate if you're in trouble. It's like a family, without the anoying side of it
- it's about 40vs40 players on really big maps, and the dev said it'll be 50vs50 soon. Large-scale war at another level in video games
Cons : - learning curve is a bit tough, you'll need some hours and games to understand how the game itself works, because it's not just about killing everyone but mainly taking/destroying objectives (it will require specific actions to work, like throwing the incendiary of the squad leader on it) (and entering a vehicule is not easy at first if you don't know what's going on)
- not much choice of weapons/class and even less attachements. A squad leader, 2 medics, other are infantry 1st class (you get an AK with iron sights, one guy in your squad will get it with an optic, another will get a sniper, and that's all). Plus no customization at all (actually. The Workshop will be included in the current year)
- you'll lose yourself across the map, even more in town where your map is useless
50/50 : - each game is very long. Half a hour or more.You'll feel tired, but you'll get the true satisfaction of a hard victory (even more when it's by 10 tickets or less
- it's punitive AF, show your head out and boom, no more head for you, and you won't see from where. Same for your opponent though
- there's lag, but the lag issues are due to the number of player. I'm mean come on, it's 40vs40, on a giant map yes, but when everyone is attacking/defending the same objective, it may be hard for any PC to stay at 60fps (remember it is Early Access in Alpha)
- graphics are good in low/mid, but not astonishing in high/ultra (again it's Alpha so you won't see reality-like graphics. They're way more than just ok at this moment though, so it's fine)
- ATH is poor. Awesome to feel the intensity of each fights and for realism, but not knowing how many bullets you got in your clip can cause your death if you don't pay attention at it
So, here you are. If you want a realistic FPS, with modern combat features, vehicules, large-scale operation, teamplay-based gameplay, but not Battlefield because it's too arcade, and not ArmA because it's too difficult/complex for you, then run straigh to Squad and you'll not regret anything

2. Your decisions are quicktime based and matter.
3. The graphics are about the same as Borderlands 1.
Look, I like first person shooters and even first person looters, however, these game genres are very difficult to marry to a decision based story where each decision matters.
