I don't get all the hate this game has been getting recently; I've scrolled through the reviews and saw about 10 negative reviews in a row as the most popular reviews. "They got rid of tiers!" they say. "It's too hard to make money!" they say. I uses to play this game back in 2014 and 2015, not even on the Steam client, RP was used for cash and those star things for the upgrade tree. I played the game a ton, but a crap load of grinding was needed to progress to every new tier ones you got past 4 or 5. I got up to tier 7, and every game I played got me enough to buy one single new block for the current tier of robot I was working on (and that’s if I won the game). I played the game so much that I eventually burned out, and got sick of grinding simply to get blocks that are exactly the same as the blocks I already had been using, but with a tiny bit more health and a different color scheme. Now after coming back after a few years, I am enjoying the game far more then I used to, rather than get the same boring money used in the Block Depot; I realized that we are now awarded with a crate of a certain tier depending on how well we played every single round. The crates for some reason are extremely satisfying to crack open (they remind me of the crates from TF2), and will always contain 3-4 items (6-8 if you are premium) with a chance of some of them being rarer items such as a machine gun or shotgun. You also have a chance to get robits from crates. Robots are the currency that replaces RP as of an update in 2015 (I think), it is uses in the forge to buy blocks, weapons, wheels, wings, and pretty much everything else in the game. Robits can also be obtained by recycling unwanted items for 1/6 of what the items can be purchases for, or 2/3 of what it was purchases for if you have premium. I'd have to say that robits seem to go way farther than RP ever went, and can be randomly found in amounts of a few hundred to the tens of thousands (depending on the rarity assigned to the pile of robits you receive), which can be rounded altogether for an average of I think way more than however much RP you used to receive for winning a match, considering all of the items given to you. People keep giving this game negative reviews because they liked it better in 2014 or 2015, I don't blame them, there are a lot of cool features that have been removed. I'll go through some of them.
*Boss battles no longer exist, these were a game mode where someone who was at tier 8 or so were pitted against many who were around tier 3.
*Upgrading system no longer exists, some may have found the upgrade tree to be tedious, some may have liked it, either way, it no longer exists.
*Tiers no longer exist, they were a way to categorizerobots, and this is how matches were sorted. I don't know how matches are decided now, but it seems to work out okay.
*RP has been replaced by robits.
Those are some of the bigger things that have been changed, but along with that, tons of new items have been added, so why all the negative reviews? If you look closely, you will see that almost every review is about how they want the old features to come back, and how it was so much better back then. People are angry because the game was changed so that it is basically a new game, and some people are happy for change (like me) and some people can simply not let the past go and keep whining about how they want alpha back. This is currently not at all a pay-to-play game and gives no fighting advantages to premium players versus non-premium, such as that two players who have both spent 10,000 hours in the game will be on an equal playing field, even if one of them has premium and the other does not. There are also some cosmetic paint colors that are premium only, all this is not a big deal to me, and am often 2nd or 1st in every game, even though I have not spent a dime. If you are new to Robocraft, I suggest not reading any of the negative reviews, as almost every single one will attempt to convince you that alpha was better. In my opinion, it was not.

Hero Siege PC –“If Diablo & Binding of Isaac made love, this would be the result”
By Joshua Alexander – R Alexis Wolfe
The first thing you will notice about Panic Art Studios Hero Siege is that it is saturated in tons of video game, pop culture, and movie references. The flies from Binding of Isaac, Various recreations of famous Diablo & Diablo 3 monsters just to name a few. Navigating the menu is simple either on keyboard and mouse or XBOX 360 controller. The options are limited as this is a “Retro” inspired game. You can change from full screen to windowed as well as tweak the graphics settings and resolution, and sound volumes. Upon pressing start you are asked to pick a character slot and choose a class. Each class has its plus and minuses, which a little play time, will have you figuring out your favorite fast.  Once you create and name your character you will be sent to the act/difficulty selection screen. Normal of course will be the only choice for starting followed by later difficulties being unlocked upon completion of the game.  For anyone expecting a AAA 3D APRG you will be disappointed. The sprites are all lovingly hand created, as well as the sound FX and Music. I found myself really enjoying the music as I battled endless waves of rats, undead minions and angry mages, only to run headfirst into the first randomly picked boss a floating eyeball. Bosses act like your typical raid boss as in they have special abilities and phases and a large life pool. With proper dodging and attacking you can win. Killing the final wave boss rewards you with a ton of gold and a new relic, which players of Binding of Isaac will be familiar with. Levels seem to be randomly generated from a pool of available layouts and the game is great for a quick pick up and play, Long time enjoyment is not a problem either but I can see this getting stale if you try to marathon it to completion. Simply put this is a game you pick up to kill a bunch of monsters spill a bunch of blood and feel better about yourself. And oh there is blood TONS of it. In fact so much blood is in this game that even the boxes bleed and explode into bloody chunks. I did find myself wondering why the hell the boxes bled but I laughed it off as this game is meant to be humorous anyways. With free copies available on the google and apple stores, as well as a currently discounted PC port on steam you can’t go wrong with picking this up. For those playing it on steam it comes with the favorite achievements and trading cards. No excuse to get this and support indie developers. If you are afraid of this becoming another early access DayZ issue you will be okay as the Developer regularly works on this and patches it.  So that brings us to the last part Bugs/issues. From my gameplay time I only noticed a couple non game breaking bugs, the first being that sometimes the character will refuse to attack and just run around doing no damage. This was solved by logging out of the game and restarting it. The second was not a bug but more of a design flaw in my opinion. The UI scales very well on larger screens but the HUD takes up a large portion of the playing field and led to several deaths for me. Maybe implementation of a Scaling option for the UI in the options menu could solve this? All in all I give this an 8.5/10 with most likely the upcoming DLC bringing it to a full 9! So I had just established my young but promising new colony, Ashton (a quite ironical name in the end ...). The basic needs were all covered, everyone had a nice place to sleep, decent clothing, enough to eat and time to relax. The people of Ashton were prosperous. They lived in harmony with nature and each other. Their wide fields provided them with plenty of food and they sold the surplus to the passing by caravans.
Now and then a few warriors of a near tribe, the Pig Face Men, attacked the settlement, but the people of Ashton were safe, relying on the strength of their automated defence systems. And so the colony grew and I thought: This is it, I finally have a colony which doesn't collapse after a few hours.
As if ...
Remember when I told you about the harmony between the people and with nature? I meant there were no rivalries between the colonists, most were friends and there even was a married couple, Tali and Waltz.
The harmony with nature also seems pretty coherent; the people relied mostly on their crops, eating only those animals which died by natural causes (e.g. old age or other animals), so the animal population in the near forests remained stable. So far so good. But taking those dead animals in meant of course someone had to leave the safe area of Ashton and wander through the wilds. Normally that wouldn't have been a problem, everyone was equipped with guns and armor of the Pig Face Men so they were quite ready to take on anything coming in their way.
Waltz left Ashton to get the still fresh corpse of a chinchilla which had been killed by some other animal. So Waltz has just grabbed it, when a tortoise nearby turned mad. I thought ok, those aren't that fast, Waltz will be able to safely carry the chinchilla inside and the turrets will take care of the tortoise.
I'm not quite sure what exactly happened, maybe this animal was on speed or something like thak. Anyway, when it saw Waltz it charged at him at a horrifying pace. Waltz had just lifted his weapon when this damn creature reached and hurt him badly. However, its hard shell was no match for Waltz' gun. And so he came back home, injured but happy, that now there was even more meat than expected. But the wraith of the tortoise was unforgiving. The bite wounds in his upper body infected themselves. The medical treatment didn't work and he got weaker and weaker. If the infection at least would've been in one of his limbs, that might had saved him, but you can't just amputate someones chest.
At last he couldn't fight any longer, the infection overwhelmed him. Tali, his wife, carved his story in the sides of his sarcophagus. The burial ceremony was heartbreaking. Everyone had come: Tali, his sister Julia, his friends Vas, Jones, Stephan, Boyd and Leia, Vas' tame wolf Nevile and Bacon 1 and Bacon 2. In the light of the evening sun they all waved a last goodbye to their fallen husband, brother and friend, before the people of Ashton went to bed. With Waltz dead or not, they had to cary on.
But apparently it was all too much for Tali, not very surprising if you think about it. There was only this one little problem: She was a pyromaniac. When the rest of the colony slept, she left her big and empty bed. Driven crazy by grief, she did the only thing able to ease her pain. She set the forest on fire. Finally, exhausted almost to unconciousness, she fell back into her bed again.
While she slept, the others, waken by the crackling fire, desperately tried to put out the flames which already started to spread over to the buildings. But they simply weren't enough, they could either try to save the buildings or the forest, not both. Of course they tended to the buildings, to the food storage to be exact. However it gave the fire the chance to spread through the forest, completely sorrounding the settlement.
In the end it was all too much.
Tali died in her own fire that she refused to extinguish, Jones and Boyd followed when they collapsed in the infernal heat. And then, when no hope was left, the gods, the ancestors, the Flying Spaghetti Monster or whatever thi people of Ashton believed in, heard their cries. Rain started falling down, putting out the fire. But it was too late. More than three quarters of the colony had been taken by the flames. Vas, Stephan and Leia were unconcious. Julia was the only one still able to stand. She did what she could, but with all the medicine burned she had no chance. Leia died first, Vas second. This caused his wolf Nevile, who had been laying loyal by his side, to turn mad like the damn tortoise and he ripped the still unconcious Stehpan into pieces before he went on attacking a herd of muffalos (some kind of marshmellow like buffalos) which was his end.
Traumatised Julia, who managed to flee when Stephan was killed, wandered through the burnt ruins of Ashton. Blackened stone walls and pieces of charcoal everywhere. All the food they stored for the winter was gone, the fields empty. With no medicine left and her own wounds hurting worse and worse, Julia found a last smokeleaf joint in one of the destroyed buildings. She leant against her brother's sarcophagus and lit it. So she didn't feel anything when the Pig Face Men attacked. With the solar panels a loss to the flames, the turrets didn't react when Ashton's last inhabitant finally exhaled her last breath.
12 / 10 - Creates more immersive storys than many RPGs; looking forward to my next colony (and possibly its desastrous destruction ...).

This game is really hard to talk about since I'm only 2 hours into the game as of this review. This will just be a first impressions review so don't take my word as complete gospel.
I started playing these games with the previous entry, Crimes and Punishments. I really loved that game. It took what I loved about mystery games and took it to the next level. Though there wasn't a big overarching story I felt that the focus on each individual case more than made up for it. I think my only real gripe with the game was the decision making. Although there were some cases where it could be fun to pick out the conclusion, there were also some cases that I felt were a bit too open-ended despite having a clear cut true ending.
That's where The Devil's Daughter comes in. I pre ordered this game for about 25 bucks off of a key website and I think that so far it's definately worth the price. I've just started the second case but the game has already improved on the already stellar sequences from Crimes and Punishments. The first case had a clear cut ending and I really loved the suspense I felt as the mystery of the case unraveled. Almost all of the deduction sequences have been made a bit easier to identify the true culprits and I like the addition of deductions during character profiling. I can safely say that investigations were definately improved in this game. There also seems to be a more overarching plot this time around which, for story spoiler reasons, I won't go into.
I think my only gripe so far is with the incredibly forced and lackluster action sequences. During the first case there were at least 3 or 4 action sequences and I can only really say that I enjoyed 1 MAYBE 2 of these sections if I'm being generous. The worst sequence comes at the end of the case and I felt that it showcased everything that was wrong with these scenarios. First, the animations were a little jerky and kind of glitchy. Second, the variety level during these portions were extremely small which leads into my next point. Personally I felt like most of these sections were way too long and felt pretty boring as a whole. I breezed past these sections but as soon as I saw one coming I literally faced walled since I felt that it kind of destroyed the pacing of the game.
TL;DR Yes this game is very good if you happen to be into mystery novels/ games, however some of the quick time and overly-long action sequences kind of hold up the pace that the game was otherwise doing a great job of keeping up.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Update:
So after beating this game I can safely say that this game was definately good but was clearly an experimental game in the Sherlock Holmes Frogwares series of games. While I found every single case to be very intriguing and fun to play, I felt as though the teams eyes were bigger than their stomachs when it came to writing this game. Without too many spoilers the last chapter of the game, while good, felt like there was supposed to be much more. I found the twist at the end to be shocking, but the game didn't really have much to offer after that and the game ends rather abrubtly as a result. It kind of feels like the team had a lot more planned for the end of this game but had to cut corners due to time constraints.
Other than that, my opinions still havent changed on the various quick time events. They are still too long and sometimes frustrating and could have done with more development as a whole. These were especially annoying as they took up almost the whole last case. I kind of wish there were more pure investigation scenes in this game as there were in Crimes and Punishments.
Overall I found that The Devil's Daughter was a really nice entry into the Sherlock Holmes fanchise. A lot of fans have made it clear that they aren't happy with the new character designs and approach to story telling and to that I say: to each their own. But I just want to make something clear, while I happened to really enjoy this entry it didn't mean that I didn't find problems overall with it. I feel that Frogwares still has a ways to go before they can truly nail this kind of story telling and gameplay experience. I did, however, notice the effort that the team put into making this game feel different. Can you really be angry at that? So many games now are focused on a one trick pony mindset where they change nothing and keep selling you the same experience everytime. I feel that a developer like Frogwares should at least be commended for trying something different instead of simply rehashing the same story over and over.
TL;DR I know my review isn't generally found helpful, meaning there are those out there who clearly don't agree with me liking this game. But for those who actually read this, I genuinly recommend trying this game if you can get for around 20 dollars like I did. Just know what you're getting yourself into.

If you have not played the Frogwares SH series before, do NOT start with this title. Instead:
If you want something more "modern"/"accessible", start with Crimes and Punishments (the previous game).
If you are more of a traditionalist and are looking for a purer experience, start with Testament (the game before C&P).
That should then give you an idea of whether you then want to continue with the rest of the series, in pretty much any order - there are some cross-title references that'll be lost on you if played out of order, but it's not a big deal.
While I still enjoyed Devil's Daughter (being an avid and not overly picky SH fan), I found it relatively disappointing compared to the previous titles.
It feels like they pushed the action movie gameplay concept introduced in preceding C&P too far and with inconsistent results. Some sequences do feel cinematic if you don't fail and understand what you're expected to do, but many simply feel unnecessarily long and/or frustrating. Although there is a variety of timed mechanics here besides just quicktime events, which is good, they don't all feel very fun. All of these are skippable, however, but at the expense of certain achievements.
The writing is generally not as good as previous cases, although there are some clever parts. Some aspects of the writing here are downright bewildering - in not a good way. While my recollection of previous plotlines is not great, I feel that this has the most questionable plotting in the whole series.
Similarly, this is the least genuine representation of SH in the series so far. Often the character behaves in a way I can't imagine SH ever would - part of that is the writing, and part of it is the voice actor's delivery.
The wildly varying length and complexity of the cases is odd. Perhaps the studio ran out of budget/time. The result feels strangely inconsistent - a relatively simple first case, a rather long and complex second case, followed by another average case, then a shorter one with limited travel. The final "case" isn't a true case, is short, with oddly direct scene cuts - but perhaps that was an intentional decision to maintain a fast, suspenseful pace.
Graphically, the environments are beautiful, continuing the positive trend in this area and the accompanying sound and music is up to par. Somehow SH and Watson look again younger and, uh, continuing that trend as well. But if you are hung up on how different the character looks from whichever your particular reference is (especially if it's not Paget), then you are missing the point (also there are several costume options).
For a bit more info about the type of gameplay here, see my C&P review, as this is a direct evolution of that and is very similar apart from the aforementioned increase in cinematic action elements.
Despite the criticisms above, there are still no other modern games quite like this series, and few that could even be called similar (that I know of). If you are looking for detective mystery that actually feels like one, this is it.

Overall, this plays like Crimes and Punishments.  It expands upon that formula by adding stealth and chase scenes.  While I appreciate the attempt to stop the game from feeling too much like Crimes and Punishments, most of these scenes go on for far too long.  The game would have benefited from them being less drawn out; even the best of them went from exciting to tedious in short order.  Fortunately, there is the option to skip these scenes (this may be a downside for completionists, as most of them are tied to achievements).
The graphics are beautiful; I love being able to make out fabric textures, skin blemeshes, and all the other little details.  The character redesigns are a bit odd at first, especially since this appears to take place late in the series (although it is hard to tell, given certain anachronisms and divergences from the Sherlock Holmes canon), but I personally found them easy enough to get used to.
Being able to wander around Baker Street is pretty cool.  Despite at first seeming like fairly useless eyecandy, there are several areas to pratice minigames (balance, shooting, boxing, armwrestling) that show up throughout the game.
In order to fully appreciate the story, I would recommend playing The Testament of Sherlock Holmes and Crimes and Punishments (and possibly The Awakened) before starting The Devil's Daughter, as they contain the diverngences from the original stories, and show events that are important to the overarching storyline and final case.

From the trailer, you may have assumed a few things about The Devil's Daughter. You may have assumed that it's a prequel to the rest of the series, explaining how young Sherlock and Watson look, and that it's a more supernatural game in line with The Awakened. Neither of these are true, unfortunately - this game actually seems to take place the latest in the series, and Sherlock and Watson have de-aged by about 20 years for no explainable reason while all the other returning characters look the same. The majority of the content that actually revolves around the titular Devil's Daughter storyline is restricted to the last 30 minutes of the game and has basically nothing to do with the rest of the cases, and it's a massively underwhelming twist that rivals the Testament of Sherlock Holmes twist in its stupidity.
In the 4 real cases that the game has, it's still a pretty solid mystery game. It follows up Crimes & Punishments in its open-endedness, and the cases are pretty challenging (though I played on the harder difficulties, so I don't know how much that affects). It took me around 12 hours or so to complete the game, though the cases do seem to get progressively shorter as the game goes on. The problem is that there's a significant amount of padding, in the form of fairly stupid action sequences. At any moment you may find yourself in a stealth segment, or running from cover to cover to avoid being shot, or any number of other things ranging from sensical to climbing a chimney while sweeping it while doing a stealth following mission. They're all skippable if you don't want to torture yourself, but it's baffling why they were ever included to begin with and seem to only exist to hide the fact that the game has less actual mystery content than Crimes & Punishments. There are a lot of fight scenes that were presumably inspired by the semi-recent films, and some of them are essentially just trial-and-error, like a bar fight where you basically just pick something and see if it kills you and then retry with the other option.
Overall I would recommend getting The Devil's Daughter, but not at its current price. If you can ignore the fact that it's supposed to be a Sherlock Holmes game there's still 4 pretty great mysteries for you to solve, but it's just not really worth $50.

This game is far from elementary, Dear Watsons of the gaming world.
I love the mental challenge this game brings, along with random moments of intensity to keep you drawn into an always evergoing mentally stimulating crime investigation. Plots that are so well written and articulated through the game dialouge that you cant help but sit and listen to many of the cutscenes they throw in; half of which you can interact with as Holmes. Therin lies what I love about this game; as Holmes, using his advanced abilities to see what others cannot in a "crime scene" scenario, you can interact with the environment to find clues that further your investigation, analyze them back at the fun old classic Sherlock Holmes home (that sounds strange if you say it 3x fast), and the best part of the home is, Toby is there! The dog isn't dead yet in this reality so.. yay!
The game forces you to use your brain as a tool half as much as Holmes within the game does; you have to sniff out every possible loose end.
My favorite thing in the game so far is the deep charecter analyzation you do as Holmes when he first encounters someone of suspect or relative to the plot. It reminds me of the Holmes short stories I always read as a kid; one was about where a lovely lady enters the room to seek their help, and after shaking her hand he tells her 10 things about her life such as that she rode a train to get there, that she had been crying, that she was married (or was a widow, which in this case, she was) etc etc. You get to pull off that exact same kind of analayzation in this game and I really appreciate how thrilling all of this can be. In a review this may sound dull.. but don't hate it till youve tried it. This is one of my first major crime games ever played, and not far in, I can say it is easily the best. No it isn't a perfect game, but I got what I paid for.

Let me begin by warning the completionists out there like me: PixelJunk Eden will frustrate you and waste hours of your time if you let it. Don't be tempted to go for the "Open All Seeds" achievements on any but the first few gardens (levels). The game gives you no tools to find any seeds that you've missed and most of the gardens later in the game are huge with at least a couple seeds in really obscure locations. To top it off there is a finite amount of life rejuvenating crystals in each map so there is a very real cap to how long you can spend searching before you can't sustain yourself anymore, die and have to start all over. I likely would have given this game a higher rating had I stopped playing at 10 hours instead of 20.
And what a pleasant first 10 hours it was. The experience included eye-catching visuals, a unique and fitting soundtrack, simple yet challenging enough gameplay and some good level design with plenty of variety. It had a relaxing feel to it. In the early to mid levels health crystals were plentiful enough that I hardly paid attention to the life bar. I'll admit that the soundtrack didn't appeal to my tastes but there seems to be a lot of praise out there for it. There were a couple tracks I liked and the rest at least weren't grating.
In my mind the life system that is constantly ticking down and needing to be refilled was a very poor design choice for this type of game. In a game all about exploration, collecting things and taking in the sights and sounds, why impose an unnecessary time constraint? It would have been better to let players set their own pace and have a more standard health bar so that the enemies still have teeth.
Despite my gripes I’d still recommend this game if you treat it casually. Bring too much hardcore gamer mindset to it and it’s likely to go sour on you.

was a highly authentic throwback to pre-console computer games, nailing down the graphics and the design philosophy of that era well beyond expectations. The sequel,
, goes a step further and boldly explores two new frontiers: the NES era, and a
. Is it worth the full price? Perhaps not, but you should still consider buying it anyway to show the developer your support for his labor of love. And that's not something I say very often!
First of all, the CRT screen simulator.
. It's so perfect, I honestly feel like half of the price tag was for the CRT simuation alone. It's got everything: the tri-color pixels, the motion blur, the scan lines, the bulbous shape... and you can adjust the sharpness, tint, color saturation, overscan, and more, and basically tweak it to look like any old CRT monitor you might remember seeing in real life. The CRT screen in
was nothing in comparison. It's amazing and I seriously want to see this implemented in more retro-styled games.
As for the gameplay, the biggest addition is the Zelda II overworld which links levels together. Unfortunately, unlike Zelda II, are no random encounters, EXP grinding, or secret powerups to hunt for, so the whole world seems a bit empty to trudge through at times. However, the overworld does manage to thoughtfully explore some old ideas like challenge caves, secret caches and surprise interconnected areas. But in the end, it does end up feeling like the world is just a bit too small and devoid of content. I wish there was a moment like in Zelda II where you sail to East Hyrule and discover that the map is twice as big as you thought.
The music is all your standard flat NES chiptunes, and there's nothing too special about the soundtrack save for two or three showstopper tunes. The best music in the game, "The Razor's Edge," is in the trailer. It might not sound like much there, but it takes on a completely different meaning when it plays in the hardest levels in the game, and it's been stuck in my head all week.
The story was probably the only real negative for me. In this game, the great king of the land was possessed by an evil wizard and you have to restore him to the throne by collecting pieces of his heart, while a mysterious race of creatures from another world keep watch and guide you. But for some strange reason, instead of filling the game with fascinating spoilers that tell a compelling narrative (like who the Arcadians are, who you are, what was up with the world from the first game, etc...) the designer instead opted to fill it with angsty, incoherent livejournal posts. I'm getting real tired of this trend of indie developers who fill the story with stuff that's so deeply personal that nobody else is expected to understand it, and then they don't tie it in to the game's story or give the player the means to find the answers on their own through gameplay. At best, it's mildly thought-provoking, but at worst, it's really annoying that there are just no clear answers to be found.
But these complaints were all easy enough for me to ignore. There's something great about the game in the way the music, the sprites, the interconnected level design, and the CRT screen all come together and really make you feel like you're back in your childhood living room playing Nintendo on a Saturday morning. For me it even managed to conjure some vibes of mystery and curiosity that even Shovel Knight couldn't. This game gets nostalgia, and I'm happy to support it.
(Achievement hunters: It's an easy 100% in less than 10 hours, though you might need a walkthrough to find the last few gems)

I have noticed a lot of confusion amongst new players, especially if they attempt to become Squad Leaders. I hope that this will inform any new players how to play as Squadleader, and why they'll enjoy doing it.
>Join a game with a low ping
>Make an awesomely-named Squad, such as "Anti-Commie Squad"
>Spend most of the intermission attempting to get two out of nine Squad members to go medic
>Spawn in
>Take a transport truck, and drive off of the nearest cliff to go off-roading (Hold Shift while doing this)
>Make it to the first or second objective
>Turn your soldiers into laborors as you wave an M9 at them, telling them to build a spawn bunker and other defenses
>Watch as your now-irrelavent town becomes a wonderful military base
>Declare yourself dictator, and tell other Squads that they'll have to pay a fee to pass
>Fight off one rambo squad, and brag about how great your base did while the combat is happening four objectives away
>Realize that all but one of your Squad members are running off to help in the combat
>Take your last loyal Squad member and load up into a Stryker
>Run down and slaughter the deserters in the name of Military-Base-landia
>Get kicked for teamkilling
>11/10 would become a hysterical dictator again
------------------------------------
Now, onto the serious review!
Community - 9/10, credited to how friendly and helpful most of the people are.
Combat - 8/10, due to it being fluid, manageable, and fun. Also, the guns sound amazing. However, the only reason it does not get a higher score is due to a lack of customization in terms of weapons. (For all the newbies out there, please. Learn how to use your grenades and smokes!)
Customization - 6/10, because as of right now, the only customization you get is choosing a loadout, and deciding if your Squad will use vehicles or not. However, I believe that there will be more of a choice to the players in future updates.
Maps - 8/10, as the maps that are provided are decent in size and compexity, without being overly-confusing.
Vehicles - 7/10, because the vehicles are easy to handle and are useful. They also look and sound great. I believe that a greater diversity of vehicles (possibly air, once we get larger maps) will come from future updates.

I played the game years ago in the 90's during the Dreamcast era.
I've always loved the original games and I thought I'd give the PC version a shot and compare the original to the PC port.
In every sense of the word, UGA's Space Channel 5: Pt. 2 is a traditional sequel; it fixes everything about the first Dreamcast game and adds new content to enhance the dance madness.
Visually, the port has several things straightened out from its original Dreamcast release.
The shimmering and aliasing have mostly vanished. The ungodly long load times have been made nearly seamless, and then there is all of the choreography,
There are modifications to some outfits, items, new characters, New game Plus and more.
This is sure to keep you busy if you are a completionist.
Luckily, the grind for "Perfect ranks" are not so bad as players can soft save from midway through a level.
The game also crashes and freezes less on PC than the older Dreamcast equivalent.
(However, this may be due to hardware limitations of early to late 90's hardware.)
The level design on a visual scale is classic. If the settings seemed unrealistic and weird before, the at times odd designs of space stations, rivers, schools and arboretums has a unique look in Space Channel 5: Pt. 2.
The environments are more colorful, offer more polygons and are more interactive. And they're filled with cheap but likeable puns and jokes.
At one point in the story, a giant plant who's captured the Space President manages to capture Ulala....
During this scene, the main villain Peace / Purge, uses the plants slimy tentacle like vines to grab Ulala. When she is grabbed in the Japanese and English dub, she says: "Oooooohhh, not there!" however this does not last long  as she naturally frees herself unprodded.  Though the entire scene is very odd, it is done in such a manner that it still makes me laugh!
UGA and SEGA have done an amazing job of porting both dubs for the pc market as it is almost the exact same dub as my original Dreamcast version (with a few things censored).
With regard to the gameplay, the tweaks and additions make Space Channel 5: Pt. 2 a far superior game to the first game in the series and more importantly, the original Dreamcast version.
Ulala's animations are more responsive, the animations are so quick that they never overlap with the upcoming beat.
Overall, Space Channel 5: Part 2 is a great port.
There are a few blemishes on Ulala's PC record such as the invisible models and sound issues, but it makes little impact to the experience.

Walking back into an old game series always has me on edge. Hoping the game could at least do something right that might match my potentially rose stinted expectations. This game was , err strange, but I ended up enjoying it for it. I enjoyed playing this game a great deal and I will come back to it again at some point, but it wasn't a on the stop full package. It has it's share of odd choices and setbacks.
I have to get this out of the way first. if you are looking for a shooter game that handles well, gives a great sense of bang when you pull the trigger, action and crazyness of older shooters, then look no further. This will be right up your alley. Most of my complaints are NOT related to the actual shooting portion of the game. That part the game does extremely well and why I had so much fun. Guns feel absolutely great. Assault rifle, shotgun, all of them not only handle well and have a great sense of power, but they went one step further and said "why the hell not double it". So you can just grab two shotguns, two assault rifles and so forth. Blazkowitcz just ends up death on two legs when you start plowing♥♥♥♥♥♥with double rocket launchers, double shotguns and so forth. It gives you that sense that you are a force of nature (if you ever played brutal doom, or better project brutality you should know exactly what I mean). Guns handle well, sound good and have great visual feedback as you send nazis to hell. Honestly if you want a SP game with this as its primary quality, just pick this up and go on.
Anyway, the more questionable choices are in some other mechanics and the narrative. One oddball choice was the perk system. You have numerous perks which give passive benefits such as slightly increased magazine size or reload speed or so forth. You get them by accomplishing challanges like 'shot x number of enemies from cover with x weapon'. Stuff like that. Personally I found this completely unecessary. Shooting was good without this, and this didn't add anything significant than me trying to kill enemies in certain ways to get minor passive boosts. It felt more like "we need to have a progression system in the game" because that is what games do these days. It isn't really a setback, since the stat boosts are minor at best, so you can just plain ignore it.
The Stealth also felt just tacked on. I would shoot  a guy in the head with suppressed pistol few meters away from his buddy, who would watch him crumble, then just turn around and go about his way. Didn't really matter, since you could just run in guns blazing not giving a single ♥♥♥♥. But like the perk design choice it was irrelavent. If I wanna play a more stealth oriented game where I feel powerful I'll play Dishonored. Here it's all about shotgun diplomacy.
Narrative wise I expected perhaps a slightly more involved story, especially how the game starts. More serious dire note. Forget that, it just turns into exactly what you would expect it to be. Blazkowitcz is a rage filled unstopable killing machine. To the point of hilarity . Stab wounds, grenades, shrapnel to the head? He just walks it off, though the last one took him nearly 15 years and somehow he didn't lose muscle mass or any of his impresive motor abilites.  He is just a one man army hell bent on killing every Nazi. There is no deeper moral story. Nazi are evil, period. They are guided by an evil genius cliche stereotype (honestly deathead could easily be put in the dictionary for that trope). If this game tried to pull off any serious emotion out of the player it didn't work for me, except laughter. The sex scenes especially had me laughing good. I never got a sense of 'big picture' with the resistance, it just seemed random, stupid, or actually mostly insane directions they decided go. Whole world ruled by Nazi, they need to break out a prisoner out of a nasty jail.♥♥♥♥♥♥just send good ole Blazko with no gear, or anything. He will murder the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of them and save the day. And that he does, remember the whole unstopable thing. That definately does go in line with how old school shooters were, but those games never took themselves seriously, or tried to show this 'emotional' narrative or  whatever. It was always tongue in cheek sort of approach, or just detachment from much story at all and just put you on the level to shoot♥♥♥♥♥♥ It isn't a big deal, just don't go in there expecting a meaningful story or involved characters. There will be some gags and some great lines ("Don't screw this up you magnificant♥♥♥♥♥♥quot;), just no sense of moral dilema, intricate storytelling, just cheap hollywood attempt at 'deep characters'.
The length of the game is about 10h. Or at least that is what took me to complete it. There is incentive to go through it again due fork in the beginning of the game where you are asked to chose. Pacing is slowed or broken by few segments where you have to go around the base and do stupid fetch quests and whatnot, but it is usually only for 10m or so and then you are back to killing nazis. Take it as you will. I personally didn't care. I rather have a game I have fun for 10h in a great deal, than have a game two or three times that length and can't stand most of it.
Overall definately positive impression. I had a lot of fun shooting stuff in this game. All the weapons were great, from bullet ones to laser ones. Burning officers to a crisp or stabbing them in the neck. Didn't matter good ole Blazko just kills everything in his way without thinking much about it. This isn't exactly 'old school' shooter. I don't know if many games even qualify that label these days, but it was great fun. At least it had me smiling when I was plowing through dozens of insane sci fi weird fantazy nazi nutfests.

Let me tell you the short story of Sactuary Colony:
Ten colonist set up a lovely little community, they have a thriving farm, two of them hunt animals for food and make clothing out of the leather, another man spends his days making swords to trade with the local tribes people. They even had a couple of pet giant sloths for company and security.
This all changed when one of the team, a wanderer who joins the colonists had a mental breakdown due to drug withdrawal and went on a rampage, causing him to be arrested and locked up in the colonists jail. Shortly afterwards a heatwave hospitalised 7 of the remaining colonists. This left two healthy colonists to tend to the ill and look after the crops. Our pet sloth then went into a bloodlust, killing the two healthy colonists while the rest died of heatstroke in their beds. Our crazy prisoner then died of starvation in his cell.
A fun game with a great challenge and interesting stories for each colonists, just don't get too attached to them. Would definitely recommend.

If you are a fan of the original Space Channel 5 or love rythm games than you may like this game. It is a fun game as long as you can get past some of the dificulties the game has in it. Unfortunately, as much as I love the game, I cannot fully recommend the game unless you are a fan.
First off, this review was after the major patch Sega made that increased resolution and made several other changes to the game.
The controls to the game are simple. The villians do their part and all you have to do is repeat what they did including the deliberate pauses. You have the up, down, left, right, and two other buttons for a total of 6 possible moves. If your timing is good and you can get 100% the level rewards you with a new costume.
This is where I cannot recommend the game. A few patches has worked to syncing the game to the keyboard/controller but there are several areas where you will know that you pushed the button correctly and it did not register at the right moment, the sequence starts a split second after the villians even though they had a longer starting pause, or your part of the song is off sync with the music because of what your side says compared to the villians. At this point, it becomes more memorization than anticipation. Since this is the main focus of the game, I cannot fully recommend the game.
Graphics wise, this is a port of a dreamcast game so you should not be expecting HD graphics. In fact, the original versions looked pretty much just like this. The fact that there is upscaling and V-sync is a bonus. One of the really interesting things is on some of the boss scenes the background moves in the same direction as the boss so you definitely know which move they did.
The music is a variety of upbeat songs some of which are from the original game. They do not stand out but are not overbearing. When playing through the game you will notice that same of the villians say "left" when they should be saying "right". This happens several times and with different villians. Also there is the character Pudding. During part of the game she is refered to as Padding (text and voice). While she is on stage the sign always says "Pudding".
There are several minor issues with the game. If you can figure out the sync issue in the game than it is a fun game. For $8 I cannot shoot it down to much.
Also, if you want to watch a perfect run Hold RB+LB+RT+LT while hitting B Y X, when it is your turn and the game will take over. You will hear Ulala's voice when you hit it correctly.

There isn't any specific glaring bad thing I can pull out, but a combination of frustrations that took away from the experience for me.
While I enjoyed the atmosphere of a Post WW2 where Germany stole super technology from magic super genious Jews, and the game does a great job of creating environments that have all sorts of cool and interesting Nazi flair, there is too much flawed with the gameplay for me to truely recommend it.
Sadly, Wolfenstein approaches the idea of difficulty in the worst way possible. It could have been entertaining of it maybe threw more enemies at you, but it takes the approach of enemies becoming bullet sponges while you turn into a moving piece of glass. This forces you as a player to rely heavily on the not so exciting stealth mechanics and when things have to go loud you are limitted to using the cover system. With enemies soaking up damage and your health pool limited, all the cool outragous stuff the game gives you, like dual weilding combat shotguns, becomes the least effective option.
You know something is wrong when I can throw a knife at someone's ankle for a 1HK but the same guy needs 3 shotgun pumps to the chest to go down! While the issue isn't apparent early in the game, it becomes more frustrating in the last 6 chapter when you are forced into full on combat scenarios
Furthering the frustrating difficulty, the checkpoint system is very unforgiving. I've often gone through 20 minute battles of attrition involving lots of hiding in cover and scouring for ammunition mid fight, you are taken out and are brought back to the beginning of the fight.
Now, I could probably lower the difficulty, but the game does a really good job of letting you know you are a lesser person for doing so. While I understand it's in good humour, better design would want me to play the higher difficulty for an enjoytable challenge, not a frustrating one. At this point I am sticking with it as i have three chapters to go and I can be a sucker for achievements.
Now, as an SP focused game, how is the story? Lackluster. There is no sense of consequence. BJ Blajkovitz (sp?) is so ♥♥♥♥ing badass he can be tortured to death, put in a Nazi furnace and jump out at the last minute and kill 30 nazis with his bare hands. Even the side characters get thrown in situations where they are mauled, shot to bits, and tortured and the next cutscene they are bandaged and fighting the good fight. None of the characters are particularly enjoyable, they're all bitter and pissy that nazis rule the world and instead of doing anything about it they'll turn to you and send you in a lone. And then you'll come back from a successful nazi slaughtering mission and some of them will have the nerve to be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at you because you only saved 5 jews and not 6.
Now you could skip the cutscenes but the game likes to put these prolonged "base" missions that involve you fetching cups of coffee for fellow resistance members and trying to find welders people have misplaced. These simple tasks turn into elongated sewer levels as you find out said cup of coffee was dropped off the side of a cliff and you have to go retrieve it and then find that 6 nazi robots live in said area of the sewers. Nobody seems to care that you nearly died trying to retrieve that welder and the guy who lost in the first place continues to be a pain.
The game tries to teeter-totter on the fringe of both being serious and ridiculous and in doing so it muddles itself down in an awkward middle zone. In one breath you are embracing the horror of a concentration camp and in the next the game is stuffing audio clips down your throat reciting what is effectively Nazi murdering fetish porn. Sometimes the game will give you a "oh look Nazis are people too" and then the next minute they're emotionless and personalityless generic bad guys that all beg to be stabbed in the neck.
Technologically the game is alright. It's 3 years old at this point and looks decent. My biggest disappointment is the depth of field that constantly blurs things in the background, probably to hide horrible draw distances and to run on lousier systems. The fact this isn't togglable is a major killer.
All said, I may have enjoyed myself a little more if the game didn't coerce me into the harder difficulty, but generally I have fun in similar titles at the same tier. If you like this sort of thing it can be worth your time, especially on sale, but personally I have better entertainment in other titles of the same genre

Whoa, easily the best Twin Stick Shooter I've ever played.  If you got a passing interest in Twin Stick Shooters, play it. I've only played with a controller though, not sure how keyboard is.
It doesn't do the "get hit 3 times and it's game over" thing either. You start out with 100 Energy(health), and lose health with each hit(duh). There are Energy(health) Pick-Ups though. There are Multiplier Pick-Ups that increase the score you get per hit, and Weapon Pick-Ups that increase the amount of bullets shot at a time. There are also a bunch game mode variations to the classic Geometry Wars type formula. And finally "Trials" which is the in-game non-steam achievements. There are 200 Trials, and while some require you to play in certain game modes, they can be done on any difficulty(easy, normal, hard, insane), but each difficulty awards a different percentage to the 100%, and only the highest difficulty counts, so to get 100% you need to do all on Insane Difficulty.
If you like Twin Stick Shooter and/or Bullet Hell type games like Geometry Wars, then download this free game, which is easily worth $5-$10 in my opinion. I definitely recommend.

This game remains in my top five all-time favorites even today, despite it being nearly 11 years old at the time of this review. The visuals hold up well, the audio is still good (though I still wish for more variety in vocal responses), and the overall quality of everything else is high. Sure, the game still crashes on exit every time, but that's a minor irritation; always has been, pretty much since day one.
Where it really shines, truly outdoing so many other games, is its bloody awesome mechanics. This game offers three different skill trees, and I don't think there's a useless skill in any of them. Seriously, I've played as a pure warrior, a pure mage, a pure assassin, and I can't even name all the blends along the way. Every single approach is viable, and the sheer variety of approaches to any given situation is amazing.
In the last decade-plus I've completed the game at least six times, and I've played through most of the missions far more than that. The way it lets the player seamlessly switch between sneaking up behind an enemy to pull off an assassin kill, throwing ice on the floor to make onrushing enemies slip, or just flat out slice and dice with a warrior's sword and shield, is fantastic. I never get tired of playing it.
Here I am today, playing through it yet again, because I happened to remember it fondly while playing another game. And I'll be damned if the opening mission didn't suck me right into it again. All these years later, some glitches still remain, but it's still a fantastic experience that should
be missed. Seriously, if you like RPG/action/melee games at all, you owe it to yourself to spring for its paltry price and give it a look.
I've played a lot more games since, but I don't know that I've ever played better.

The Space Channel 5 series is sort of an acquired taste. To put it simply, Space Channel 5 (both games) is very Japanese. Wild visuals, bright colors and it doesn't make a lot of sense. There's so much going on visually when it's really just a memory game. But it's not enough to memorize the patterns - you have to remember the rhythms too. And when the dance movements don't sync up with the voices and sounds, it's a lot more challenging than appearances imply.
This is, in all honesty, the first game series I've ever encountered where it is literally easier to play it with your eyes closed. When you don't have delayed dance moves throwing off your rhythm, you actually do better. Plus, you get to rescue Michael Jackson! Walking back into an old game series always has me on edge. Hoping the game could at least do something right that might match my potentially rose stinted expectations. This game was , err strange, but I ended up enjoying it for it. I enjoyed playing this game a great deal and I will come back to it again at some point, but it wasn't a on the stop full package. It has it's share of odd choices and setbacks.
I have to get this out of the way first. if you are looking for a shooter game that handles well, gives a great sense of bang when you pull the trigger, action and crazyness of older shooters, then look no further. This will be right up your alley. Most of my complaints are NOT related to the actual shooting portion of the game. That part the game does extremely well and why I had so much fun. Guns feel absolutely great. Assault rifle, shotgun, all of them not only handle well and have a great sense of power, but they went one step further and said "why the hell not double it". So you can just grab two shotguns, two assault rifles and so forth. Blazkowitcz just ends up death on two legs when you start plowing♥♥♥♥♥♥with double rocket launchers, double shotguns and so forth. It gives you that sense that you are a force of nature (if you ever played brutal doom, or better project brutality you should know exactly what I mean). Guns handle well, sound good and have great visual feedback as you send nazis to hell. Honestly if you want a SP game with this as its primary quality, just pick this up and go on.
Anyway, the more questionable choices are in some other mechanics and the narrative. One oddball choice was the perk system. You have numerous perks which give passive benefits such as slightly increased magazine size or reload speed or so forth. You get them by accomplishing challanges like 'shot x number of enemies from cover with x weapon'. Stuff like that. Personally I found this completely unecessary. Shooting was good without this, and this didn't add anything significant than me trying to kill enemies in certain ways to get minor passive boosts. It felt more like "we need to have a progression system in the game" because that is what games do these days. It isn't really a setback, since the stat boosts are minor at best, so you can just plain ignore it.
The Stealth also felt just tacked on. I would shoot  a guy in the head with suppressed pistol few meters away from his buddy, who would watch him crumble, then just turn around and go about his way. Didn't really matter, since you could just run in guns blazing not giving a single ♥♥♥♥. But like the perk design choice it was irrelavent. If I wanna play a more stealth oriented game where I feel powerful I'll play Dishonored. Here it's all about shotgun diplomacy.
Narrative wise I expected perhaps a slightly more involved story, especially how the game starts. More serious dire note. Forget that, it just turns into exactly what you would expect it to be. Blazkowitcz is a rage filled unstopable killing machine. To the point of hilarity . Stab wounds, grenades, shrapnel to the head? He just walks it off, though the last one took him nearly 15 years and somehow he didn't lose muscle mass or any of his impresive motor abilites.  He is just a one man army hell bent on killing every Nazi. There is no deeper moral story. Nazi are evil, period. They are guided by an evil genius cliche stereotype (honestly deathead could easily be put in the dictionary for that trope). If this game tried to pull off any serious emotion out of the player it didn't work for me, except laughter. The sex scenes especially had me laughing good. I never got a sense of 'big picture' with the resistance, it just seemed random, stupid, or actually mostly insane directions they decided go. Whole world ruled by Nazi, they need to break out a prisoner out of a nasty jail.♥♥♥♥♥♥just send good ole Blazko with no gear, or anything. He will murder the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of them and save the day. And that he does, remember the whole unstopable thing. That definately does go in line with how old school shooters were, but those games never took themselves seriously, or tried to show this 'emotional' narrative or  whatever. It was always tongue in cheek sort of approach, or just detachment from much story at all and just put you on the level to shoot♥♥♥♥♥♥ It isn't a big deal, just don't go in there expecting a meaningful story or involved characters. There will be some gags and some great lines ("Don't screw this up you magnificant♥♥♥♥♥♥quot;), just no sense of moral dilema, intricate storytelling, just cheap hollywood attempt at 'deep characters'.
The length of the game is about 10h. Or at least that is what took me to complete it. There is incentive to go through it again due fork in the beginning of the game where you are asked to chose. Pacing is slowed or broken by few segments where you have to go around the base and do stupid fetch quests and whatnot, but it is usually only for 10m or so and then you are back to killing nazis. Take it as you will. I personally didn't care. I rather have a game I have fun for 10h in a great deal, than have a game two or three times that length and can't stand most of it.
Overall definately positive impression. I had a lot of fun shooting stuff in this game. All the weapons were great, from bullet ones to laser ones. Burning officers to a crisp or stabbing them in the neck. Didn't matter good ole Blazko just kills everything in his way without thinking much about it. This isn't exactly 'old school' shooter. I don't know if many games even qualify that label these days, but it was great fun. At least it had me smiling when I was plowing through dozens of insane sci fi weird fantazy nazi nutfests.

I originally gave this game a thumbs down review, but there was a recent major patch that shifted my opinion of the game. The addition of an metroid-esque automapping feature and a price drop makes a middling, over-priced game actually pretty good.
There are still issues: the gameplay is kind of shallow and simple. Everything you see in this game is something you've seen before, probably executed with a great deal more complexity. But for what it is, it's a totally solid exploration-platformer.
The reason why the automapping feature is such a big deal to me is that this is fundamentally an _exploration_ platformer. The platforming is trivial, there's nothing that will have you stuck for more than a minute or two. Most of the fun comes from exploring the non-linear environments and finding the secrets within. The problem is, without a map, this can be very frustrating to play. I personally got stuck in one area for an absurd amount of time, because I simply couldn't figure out where to go. Once the automap feature got added, I was able to work out where I'd already been, and figure out how to go forward.
If you really like 2D platformers and exploration, this is a pretty decent, if simple, game. You also might want to try the free game You Have To Win The Game first, as it will give you a very good idea as to how this game plays.

There isn't any specific glaring bad thing I can pull out, but a combination of frustrations that took away from the experience for me.
While I enjoyed the atmosphere of a Post WW2 where Germany stole super technology from magic super genious Jews, and the game does a great job of creating environments that have all sorts of cool and interesting Nazi flair, there is too much flawed with the gameplay for me to truely recommend it.
Sadly, Wolfenstein approaches the idea of difficulty in the worst way possible. It could have been entertaining of it maybe threw more enemies at you, but it takes the approach of enemies becoming bullet sponges while you turn into a moving piece of glass. This forces you as a player to rely heavily on the not so exciting stealth mechanics and when things have to go loud you are limitted to using the cover system. With enemies soaking up damage and your health pool limited, all the cool outragous stuff the game gives you, like dual weilding combat shotguns, becomes the least effective option.
You know something is wrong when I can throw a knife at someone's ankle for a 1HK but the same guy needs 3 shotgun pumps to the chest to go down! While the issue isn't apparent early in the game, it becomes more frustrating in the last 6 chapter when you are forced into full on combat scenarios
Furthering the frustrating difficulty, the checkpoint system is very unforgiving. I've often gone through 20 minute battles of attrition involving lots of hiding in cover and scouring for ammunition mid fight, you are taken out and are brought back to the beginning of the fight.
Now, I could probably lower the difficulty, but the game does a really good job of letting you know you are a lesser person for doing so. While I understand it's in good humour, better design would want me to play the higher difficulty for an enjoytable challenge, not a frustrating one. At this point I am sticking with it as i have three chapters to go and I can be a sucker for achievements.
Now, as an SP focused game, how is the story? Lackluster. There is no sense of consequence. BJ Blajkovitz (sp?) is so ♥♥♥♥ing badass he can be tortured to death, put in a Nazi furnace and jump out at the last minute and kill 30 nazis with his bare hands. Even the side characters get thrown in situations where they are mauled, shot to bits, and tortured and the next cutscene they are bandaged and fighting the good fight. None of the characters are particularly enjoyable, they're all bitter and pissy that nazis rule the world and instead of doing anything about it they'll turn to you and send you in a lone. And then you'll come back from a successful nazi slaughtering mission and some of them will have the nerve to be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at you because you only saved 5 jews and not 6.
Now you could skip the cutscenes but the game likes to put these prolonged "base" missions that involve you fetching cups of coffee for fellow resistance members and trying to find welders people have misplaced. These simple tasks turn into elongated sewer levels as you find out said cup of coffee was dropped off the side of a cliff and you have to go retrieve it and then find that 6 nazi robots live in said area of the sewers. Nobody seems to care that you nearly died trying to retrieve that welder and the guy who lost in the first place continues to be a pain.
The game tries to teeter-totter on the fringe of both being serious and ridiculous and in doing so it muddles itself down in an awkward middle zone. In one breath you are embracing the horror of a concentration camp and in the next the game is stuffing audio clips down your throat reciting what is effectively Nazi murdering fetish porn. Sometimes the game will give you a "oh look Nazis are people too" and then the next minute they're emotionless and personalityless generic bad guys that all beg to be stabbed in the neck.
Technologically the game is alright. It's 3 years old at this point and looks decent. My biggest disappointment is the depth of field that constantly blurs things in the background, probably to hide horrible draw distances and to run on lousier systems. The fact this isn't togglable is a major killer.
All said, I may have enjoyed myself a little more if the game didn't coerce me into the harder difficulty, but generally I have fun in similar titles at the same tier. If you like this sort of thing it can be worth your time, especially on sale, but personally I have better entertainment in other titles of the same genre

Every world has a story, this is mine.
....in my colony, the two best soldiers happen to be brothers. They rescued a beautiful hardworking lady(that had ethical issues about prosthetics) that was on the run from a group of pirates. Locke and Daniel (Dan) ambushed the small band of raiders and the two surviving pirates fled unharmed. Locke sustained a bullet wound in the chest. It wasn’t too serious but the colony lacked a decent clinic and the current healthcare provider was a known smokeleaf addict that often made mistakes. The risk of infection was more serious than his wound. Dan carried Locke to get treated and was relieved when Jen the beautiful lady they had just rescued was a medic. She treated his wounds and in no time Locke was on his feet. She became the new Doc in town, which Larry didn’t mind because he had a burning passion for cooking and could now devote his free time to cloud watching. Jen was immediately drawn to Locke for his positive attitude and his compassion for animals. They became lovers, and built a small house next to the clinic.
They owned a shoddy bed that they decorated with pink hearts. They would lie in bed and discuss future plans for the colony. Less than a year later those plans would involve a wedding. Jen asked Locke to marry her and he accepted. The colony had grown considerably by then and the couple contemplated where they would choose to mark the occasion. They believed the clinic where they first met would be symbolic. The clinic was now much larger with sterile floors and improved bedding. The original bed had long since been scraped but they commissioned to have one created for ceremonial reasons only.
A few days later an announcement came that the colony was under attack. It was the same pirate group that had tried to harm Jen. He wondered if the two members that escaped were among them. He wouldn’t even recognize them now even if they were.  There was little time to prepare and the pirate’s raid was larger than expected. Fortunately the colony was well equipped and boasted its own modest defense force. They quickly mobilized the fighters and rushed towards a choke point they had once agreed on defending should such a situation occur. As expected the pirate funneled in and was met with a barrage of bullets. The pirates were suffering a few losses but they noticed another group of pirates had split off and was nearing the colony. The pirates had already killed the cat and were determined to raze the colony to the ground. Jen and a small group of colonist that claimed they were incapable of committing violence, watched helplessly as the pirates own commitment to violence progressed towards them. Locke and the other colonists broke off from the attack to intercept the other group. They had hoped to slow them down long enough for Dan and his group to finish up and reinforce them later.
Locke intercepted two pirates tearing up the colonies solar panels.  The group opened fire killing them. As they approached another group a shot rang out and Locke dropped. The bullet struck Locke in the head destroying his brain. The other colonists were shocked and the mood of the colony quickly sank. The shot came from a 27 y/o sniper named Goki. He wasn’t known for his skill but today he would be known for his luck, Or so he thought. The call for retreat was called soon after as Dan had caused significant casualties at the chokepoint. Goki and the rest of his crew fled but Dan cut their escape off. Goki and two others were downed and many of their group were dead. The colony was safe but at the cost of a terrible price. Locke lie dead, and Anna, a farmer, had multiple injuries and lost her leg. She died before she could be rescued. The colonist looked at Jen with empathy as she willingly treated the man who killed her fiancé. They found it odd that she worked so hard to keep this man alive. I am not a fighting game player.
That being said Divekick is the best fighting game I have ever played. Sure I really liked stuff like Street Fighter, Mortal Kombat, and the like... But Divekick is the first time I ever felt like I could compete legitimately.
The Lang Zone is in full effect here with a brilliantly minimalist design. All characters have a million health and every attack does four million damage. There are two buttons. You jump, and then you kick. The brilliance of this design is that it is so simple yet there is depth in the way each character jumps, how each one kicks, and how their supers behave. Even the super moves are brilliantly simple, being activated simply by hitting both buttons at once and changing depending on whether you are on the ground or in the air.
I watched this game developed from the ground up thanks to the beautiful romance between Dave Lang and the GB crew and I'm so happy I saw it all the way through. I might not play it nearly as much as I should but if you want a fun, fast, popcorn-like fighting game nothing does it better than Divekick.

Wow. This is the funnest hack-n-slash game I've ever played. Now, that being said, I haven't played too many games like this, but this really is gold, believe me. The gameplay is incredibly fast and fun. There is no story; you select a character (Viking, Pyromancer, Marksman, Redneck, Necromancer, Nomad, or, coming soon, Samurai), name it, and begin. Nothin' to it. You play in a large, square-shaped arena, terrain depending on what level you've selected (you'll have to beat levels, before you can progress to or select new ones; there are four in total); forest, desert, arctic, or underground, stone-ish landscapes are all available. Plus, every now and then, a crypt or dungeon will appear, and if you survive the current wave, it will open, allowing you to venture inside, requiring you to make your way through either a sh*tton of monsters or a confusing puzzle. Or both, if your luck isn't all there. But it's worth it; if you make it through, as well as picking up lots of gold to buy potions from killing monsters and breaking open crates and opening chests, you'll recieve a relic, which essentially is a boost for your character. We'll get into that later. Completing a dungeon or crypt also serves as a full wave, so when you return to the main level, it will have progressed twice since your last wave.
Relics. Rare to find, but there are a couple spots they'll always be; at the end of a crypt or dungeon, and the end of a boss fight (every 6 waves). There are hundreds of these relics, all of which give your character some sort of new perk to aid in slaughtering beasts. Anything from a staff which rains down meteors, to a spinning scythe that you can launch, to a demon sheep that circles your character and damages monsters with contact, to a zeppelin that follows you and fires homing rockets at your enemies. You can have multiple relics in use, as well; one exception would be relics that provide a new, cooldown-type ability for your character, such as the staff; only one of these can be equipped. Mind you, these items don't have health; they only expire when you die. And when you die, it's punishing. Although you don't lose your character or the leveling points you've obtained and used, you do lose all the relics you collected in that life, and you must start over from the last level you unlocked, or start from the beginning. Which is usually easier in the long run, because if you begin at the most recent level, you won't have the opportuity to obtain as many relics as you would if you simply restart. I enjoy this in a game, despite it being a real pain. It really gives players that desire to
.
There have been some interesting bugs, if you can call them that (EX. the Marksman class was
OP at one point, murdering everything in its path), but the developers are very diligent and dedicated to improving this overall marvelous piece of gaming material, and since I purchased it, it has changed a whole lot, for the better. Graphics are pleasing and not too attached to the pixelated theme, so it's easy to discern what's what, and not melt your corneas trying to watch all the epilepsy-seizure-inducing flashes and moving entities. It's extremely satisfying, especially when you kill 10+ monsters in a couple seconds and watch all the 8-bit blood and gore bounce around in a sick-cartoon fashion. The leveling system is a tad slow, but satisfying when you upgrade one of your many abilities and perks available for each character to annihilate yet more horrid creatures. Plus, there are quite a few hats which you can buy for your characters using crystals, another currency within the game specifically for that purpose. For 6 bucks, I'd definitely say this game is worth its' price.

Divekick is a really interesting concept that almost lives up to it's full potential. The biggest problem with fighting games tends to be the time investment it takes to learn a character, from their moveset to their matchups to actial execution of combos. Divekick removes most of that, mapping everything to two buttons. This moves most of the focus to the mindgame portion of fighting games, which is really what makes them interesting. My biggest problem with Divekick is that the characters are just varied enough that it serves to undermine the premise. You could stick with playing Dive or Kick, who are pretty simple, but what if you didn't know that Jefailey charges his dropkick? This makes the investment needed to truly enjoy this game clash a bit with the underlying simplicity. All in all, Divekick still executes really well what it set out to do, with some minor issues.

The game begins with considerable interest, and when you move a little more on it, you just want to go further. Visually the game is pretty good, feel antique or odd sometimes and not astonishing (but this is not an AAA game) the environments are fantastic, the characters modeling is not that brilliant but not bad. There's many details in the world of the game and the city feels really well. The game is an logical evolution from its predecessor, this one feels more like a game properly said, there's action, you do more things not only explore and search for clues. There is many "action" moments and minigames. The control is just fine for the kind of game it is, a little tough sometimes but not a big deal, just like the other games (ok, when you control the dog feels very awful and odd). You can explore streets and buildings freely. It's a solid experience, without bugs or weird things.
The typical things to do, and the ways you can search clues and reach your conclussions just like in the previous games are here, but there's more things to do and new mechanics. There's a level of difficulty only for expert without any help, a very good thing if you like that kind of challenge. Like always you can mess up the case if you designate as guilty the wrong person and all that, things are not always what they seem... The rhytm of the game feels more dynamic, in fact, all the game is more dynamic, and this is a great addition, is more varied in general.
Some things are not so good, the storylines feel rushed, little exposition or explanation of characters' motives, not many dialogues (it's a pitty 'cause the histories are awesome).  The gap between cases feel very big, like far in time. After finishing a case there is a simply change of scene and you find yourself in another, without a proper explanation, your character not even speak with the person who gave you the case. That's feels rushed and unnatural.
About the new Sherlock, feels great, is obiously a more young version that in previous games, a more contemporary and, at least, for me that's the best thing here, probably feels more in the way of Robert Downey Jr. and the new Holmes films, a more action focus, more versatile and crazier. That's great, something more close to this era.
So, if you are a fan of Sherlock Holmes or the previous games you will love this one for sure. And if you are not a fan, but you like the kind of game where you need to explore and search for clues, where you can change the history and stuff like that you need to try this too.

PixelJunk Eden plays as much like a high-flying physics momentum game as it does a platformer.  If you enjoy physics puzzles and collectathon games this is probably a must have game.  I really enjoyed how the mechanics in this game lend themselves to varying levels of difficulty.  If you break up multiple enemies in one jump, it allows you to progress faster so learning how to find those opportunities is critical to efficient runs.  The only annoying part of this to me was having to worry about energy management; it didn't seem to add much difficulty but would just generally get in the way of the fun parts of the game.  Even after you've beaten the game there's plenty to go back and do if you're up for mastering each level.
