I followed Rimworld since before it was accepted in to the Early Access on Steam and it has come leaps and bounds since those earlier versions I saw uploaded on
. The game is like Dwarf Fortress and Minecraft had a child and that child became an astronaut. When I say it's like Dwarf Fortress, I specifically mean the colony management parts. Minecraft shares the survival themes and it's the closest game I could think of that matched in that aspect.
In Rimworld, the three base scenarios are a group of 3 crash survivors, a group of 5 tribesman who have fled their land and a rich explorer. There are now tons of other scenarios (I haven't played any since most of my colonies die out early) and there's a lot of different ways to play Rimworld. After choosing the scenario you go on to choose from 9 different levels of difficulty. There are 3 AIs (in the base game, not in the other ones from Workshop), one that gives you a gradual progression in events, one that sends whatever the heck it wants at you whenever and one that's intended for playes that want a calmer experience. After choosing an AI you get to choose one of 6 overall game difficulties and if you want to include permadeath. There's peaceful if you just want to build a nice large colony that lives peacefully and then there's extreme where the game will try to ♥♥♥♥ing end you.
After all those tedious settings, and creating your colonists you enter the game ready to challenge nature and other AI-driven enemies on a Rimworld.
The game's great but if your attention span isn't very long you may have issues playing longer saves. It can be a little tedious just like all colony management games.

A functional top-down-view twin-stick "shooter" but lacks the hook to keep the player interested. In addition, the attacks are done only in four directions. For now, I've played the game only with two characters (viking and marksman) and cleared the normal difficulty with the marksman. After this, there are two more difficulty levels (and the hardcore mode, whatever that is.)
In a way, Hero Siege is like Gauntlet, except there's no running at the enemies to attack them but treading backwards, just keeping out of their range, if you picked a character with only melee attacks. The visual style is reminiscent of what would've been right at home on 16-bit home computers. The music is pretty repetitive and will become annoying, unless you turn it off.
The levels are procedurally generated, but this means little else than tossing traps and small obstacles with little rhyme or reason. All tiles the player can walk on are on the same level, so the randomness does not greatly vary the arena-like stages. In addition some traps may be hidden behind trees, which is a fault with the generator. Early on when the player is still pretty weak, guiding enemies to die at the traps is a good tactic, but a world or two later, you're probably enough of a tank to keep on rolling as long as you avoid the traps yourself.
There's a fair amount of enemy variety, but a lot of it comes from palette-swapping and enlarging the sprites.
Although the player characters lose the passive buffs ("relics") they've found during the game once they die, the experience levels they earn stay with them, as well as the their upgraded character statistics (attack strength, speed, points allocated to special attacks and so on). The points put into special attacks are what matters, since at the endgame you may have about 40 pts in each trait "basic" and some 250 extra as one-game buffs.
To mix up the game a bit, an entrance to a dungeon appears. These may contain minor puzzles, very tough boss enemies and some additional relics. Like on the "real" map, dying here means an instant Game Over. There also aren't all that many dungeon alternatives, maybe a dozen or so.
To lessen the impact of the random loot, the player can also shop for stat upgrades that last for the rest of the game.

However, by the time you get to the mid-game, with an abundance of physics-resistant enemies, or slog through the endgame, which is definitely a level or so too long, you'll note that the combat system (while more involved than even some modern RPG's) is fairly simplistic, the magic system (with a few exceptions) doesn't really take advantage of physics, and the stealth is just terrible.
Which isn't to say that any of the above makes the basic "invest in warrior skills, kick people, rush through the bad parts" experience any worse.

TL:DR:
An awesome FPS in a fantasy genre. Lots of great combat, physics puzzles, and Thief-like stealth with rope-arrows.
AMAZING GAME!
The best description I can give this game is a fantasy version of Half-Life II mixed with a generous helping of Thief. Physics puzzles, arrow ropes, fully interactive/destructible environment, climbing, jumping, running, swimming, swinging, crouching, setting stuff on fire, throwing stuff into the fire, setting people on fire, shocking people with lightning when they are standing in water, making people slip on ice and fall off a cliff, kicking someone into spikes, kicking tables over, kicking canopic jars into pieces, kicking people, kicking monster, kicking kicking kicking.
Honestly, the sheer amount of puzzles and battles in this game and the fact that you are allowed to tackle them in multiple ways (sometimes dozens of dofferent ways) is refreshing. The use of skillpoints instead of classes allows you to tailor-make your character and play the game how YOU want to. Add to this the variety of gear, weapons, potions, scrolls etc in the game, and the breadth of freedom really makes for a hard game to put down.
The voice acting and animations have really held up very well over the years. The lighting is still respectable. The textures are all still realistic and fun to look at. The monsters and NPCs all have conversations with one another. Some of the discussions monsters have when they aren't aware that you are there are really funny; especially the goblins. All of the wonderful graphics and sounds are coupled with the lively and detailed world to give you a believable and addictive experience. I actually cared about the characters I met in the game.
Finally, the combat is very well done. It makes Skyrim and even a lot of popular FPS's look amateur in comparison. There are tons of different attacks based on what direction you are moving, how hard you are swinging, what weapon you are using, and if you are running/jumping or not. You can kick enemies to interrupt them or send them sprawling into a moaning heap. You can bash with your shield to batter and daze. You can even crouch down or aim downward and chop people's legs off. Oh, you can chop arms and head off too or just completely disembowel somebody if you wish. There are no restrictions......see a villager looking down a well? Kick them in the♥♥♥♥♥♥and send them tumbling down. Good times!
I seriously could not put this game down and you probably won't be able to either.

I'm so hooked on this little game, But my reason for posting today is to clarify something that most people dont know about, and i have seen people complaining that they cannot play this game, the timing is of ect ect.
There is a little something out glorious HD tv's suffer from when it comes to games that is kinda transparent if you dont pay attention. Have you ever wondered why <insert character here>  jumps, shoots, or simply starts walking, say, half a second late? This is called input lag. Our tv's do a little post processing to the signal that comes in and there for what you see in the screen is a little late to what actually is going on in the system or in out case, the computer. This post processing is absolutly FABULOUS for movies, but DETRIMENTAL to games such as space chanel five. most tv's now days have a "game mode" which disable most if not all the filtering and almost compleatly remove input lag. some TV's don't eliminate input lag very well at all, so be warned. If you dont see game mode, try disabling motion filters, noise filters and all dynamic this and that. to test take a game, lets say a mario something, <yes it happens with consoles like I said.> smack the shoot botton...no really smack it! make it sound of that TAP! if the tap sound sync to the shoot sound, your good! if it doesn't, you have contracted a deadly condition called input lag!

I was able to try this game out thanks to GamesMatter on Twitter.
Super Win the Game is a retro platformer that really nails the 8-bit era Zelda II visual style with a bit of a different spin introducing a world map and non-linearity.
Pros
- Captures the NES Zelda II style perfectly. You really feel like you are playing a ROM from that era.
- Platforming is done well and sufficiently challenging.
- Overworld map let's you choose where you want to go in a non-linear fashion.
- Plenty of save points so you never have to backtrack very far.
- CRT filter is configurable and able to be turned off.
Cons
- There's really no game play beyond the platforming. I felt like it could have used a bit more to do and variety like combat and puzzles and so forth.
- Although the overworld is open and you can do it any order there are many areas are blocked off until you get a certain items resulting in a lot of backtracking.
- The $12.99 asking price is (subjectively) a bit high for what you're getting.
If you really love retro platformers Super Win the Game does it well with its own unique twists of overworld map and non-linearity. Just don't expect more than straight up platforming. While it may look visually like a near clone of Zelda II the dungeon portions actually play more like Super Mario Brothers.

Disclaimer: I got this game in a giveaway.
The first thing you notice is the CRT filter. While other games and emulators have attempted such filters before, I've never seen one this elaborate. Unfortunately, the filter gets to be a bit of a headstrain after a while, so I turned it off (although there are LOTS of options for customizing it) Without the filter, you get the typical NES style graphics.
The game is fairly basic. You collect items that allows you to pass further through the game (for example revealing platforms or allowing you to breath underwater). Through the game you can collect both keys and gems. Keys allow you to open locked doors, but if you're missing one you have the options to either buy one with gems or loan one from the key lenders. I never had to loan a key so I can't say if it makes a difference in the end.
Storywise, the king has been kidnapped by a wizard, who took his heart and divided it in six pieces across the land. Finding them allows entrance to the castle, where the wizard holds the king, and where you will restore his heart and win the game.
If the player gets lost and don't know where to go next they can visit the fortune teller, who will direct the player to their next objective. Retrieving some of the hearts required for entry to the final level can be rather frustrating, while an NPC points you in the general direction, finding them can involve a lot of trial and error.
Overall, would I recommend the game? Definitively.

Sections of the game may be skipped through skillful techniques, but most everyone should be able to see the end with enough fortitude and prowess.
Super Win the Game is a sequel to You Have to Win the Game. While it shares the same protagonist and general gameplay, the differences are immediately apparent upon starting. Not only is there a more in-depth tutorial, but the game has music. Along with that, more power-ups are placed in the world that grant access to different areas based on certain themes (lava, water, double-jump, etc).
The original game was a very simple idea. If one practiced enough, they could finish the game in under 10 minutes. Super Win the Game feels exactly like Super Metroid did to it's predecessor. Everything is bigger, more colorful and full of more detail. The level design is large, but not overly so. Progression is not limited to a linear path, even if the game will subtlely guide you to the correct area should you get lost.
That feature is easily the best part about Super Win the Game's accessibility. Older puzzle platformers would often leave the player high and dry. In a time of desperation, you would just quit the game or end up buying a strategy guide. Super Win the Game allows you to interact with a scant few NPCs, but each provides a hint that will further progression through the game world.
The level design also quickly allows you to figure out whether or not you are capable of getting past any specific sections. If you are lacking the red aura, you cannot enter lava. Instead of getting 4 screens into the next section, the game immediately throws a lava room at you to warn about the lack of upgrade.
Every item you acquire is automatic. The one options at your disposal are jump and talk. You press Up to enter doors, but the game keeps everything simple. You will never run into a section that has you firing off rounds or stomping on enemies to finish a section.
Enemies are pretty much obstacles. While they shoot out projectiles and obscure paths, you never need to kill any of them. You actually can't kill any of them, which makes this platformer unique. Now everything is based around avoidance and how quick you can react to a changing situation.
It makes Super Win the Game have tense moments in what would otherwise be a rather empty world. Sadly, not all that glitters is gold. Since the enemies are basically window dressing, it can be quite hard to truly call them stand out. The level design is also basically the same through-out the adventure.
Each area is made of very similar tiles, just with swapped color palettes. The very final level is wholly it's own, but getting lost is an easy feat in Super Win the Game. I know this was made with the mindset of a classic SNES adventure, but even just a bit more variety would be welcome.
I also feel like the dream sequences break the flow of the game. They do not last long, but they aren't really necessary to the experience. Conquering the final "boss" doesn't have a meaningful conclusion and the game mostly throws out psuedo-psychological questions. I am all for exploring deeper themes in games, but only if those themes end up being fleshed out or relevant.
Even with those flaws, Super Win the Game is a great little indie title. Developed by two people, this game is leagues ahead of most of it's contemporaries. That is evokes a charm of the "golden era" of platformers is just icing on the cake. I'd say get this if you have a longing for yesteryear or just want a solid platformer to play.

recommend Oxenfree to anyone interested in a good story, but more importantly, to anyone interested in playing a game more than once. I've played through...four times in its totality, and each time was different. Each time got me a different ending.

you.

There is very little depth to the characters or universe, and the core gameplay mechanics are pretty shallow too - once you know them, the whole thing becomes quite cut and paste - kick guy, power strike, kick guy, power strike, kick guy onto fire, heal and flee. The encounters rarely vary all that much. Linear would also be a good descriptor, so don't expect a huge expansive play area or a sprawling story.
I did my first playthrough with just a sword and a few spells. I put my skill points all over the place because whatever, still beat the game easily. There are a few weapon types with different movesets to use, and you can also use shields, but the reality is that there's just not enough variation in the enemies to warrant having some of these armaments in game. I used a shield effectively maybe three times before realising that kicking guards in the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and watching them tumble into a nearby campfire was more effective.
There's a few boss-fight type things that enable you to use the environment to defeat them; I had more difficulty fighting groups of regular mobs. The game is pretty short overall and there's not a huge deal of challenge to be had. I thought the movement and vertical controls of the game were fine, but the user interface for selecting spells is curmudgeonly and in no way facilitates switching between melee, magic and archery on the fly - although I still made more use of my bow than any damage spells.
Nonetheless, this is the best couple of quid I've spent in a long time. Where Dark Messiah succeeds, it really knocks it out of the park. Using your environment to deal with multiple enemies - whether you're throwing barrels at a bunch of guards on the stairs or setting up oil and fire traps - is satisfying and seriously fun. Even moreso when you get spotted by a guard as you try to sneak up on his friend; Dark Messiah is great at making you feel like an idiot sometimes, but gives you all the tools you need to wriggle out of an encounter with your braincase intact.
Overall, Dark Messiah is a middling sort of game, but it had enough really fun moments to make me enjoy pretty much every minute of it. I personally found the universe to be beautiful, age notwithstanding.

Probably the first thing to note when starting up the game is how beautiful the game looks. Once you reach the larger, more open areas, you'll be placed in an extremely expansive & scenic land as Croteam seems to be obsessed with beautiful but pointless open lands you can walk on. Using the new Serious Engine 4–possibly as a test for Serious Sam 4–the game looks fantastic when the graphics are turned up to the max.
In addition to that, the music further accentuates the theme of the location you're currently on, often making them feel larger than they already are. They have this "you've stepped in a holy land that stretches for miles" atmosphere to it, and on its own it can be relaxing to listen to.
The gameplay is really nothing more than just solving puzzles in a massive, 3D environment to collect giant tetrominoes to use for more puzzles that involve them in order to unlock more puzzles – the game's really just filled with these left & right. Sometimes, the puzzles are longer than they actually are just because the field you're currently on is far too large.
Each puzzle's difficulty is categorized by color: green, yellow, and red, going from easy to hard. Eventually, the easier difficulties will diminish as you progress. There's a large variety of puzzle types and the items & obstacle types used are just as varied. The red rooms make for great challenges as they get more creative with their solutions than the lower difficulty rooms. It takes an eventual understanding of the game's mechanics to come up with an answer, and some of them aren't at least tied down to just one.
The maps are categorized by worlds and room numbers. They give a sense of non-linearity to them thanks to the hub-like appearance and their ease of accessibility, but in truth you'll have to go through everything in an order anyway to unlock the next set of puzzles. Throughout the entire game you have to run up to everything. With the game already being as massively open as it is, it may feel like a chore to keep running from area to area, even if you modify the character speed in the options.
There are hidden "star" items throughout the entire game; they're often their own puzzles but most of them are so well hidden, you'll need extreme patience & observance to find & solve them unless you use a guide to help you even take the first step.
A plot exists in the game, but it's actually pretty small until you dig for the backstory in the terminals that pop up as you play. The terminals hold a lot of the game's lore, extremely cryptic notes, and philosophy. You can go about the game without reading anything or even caring about the story, though it'd be unwise to not at least check it out as that's one of the game's hidden strong points. There are 3 endings, 6 if you slightly alter one of them through a few various ways; the extra 3 are hardly different from one another. I didn't find any of them to be truly "morally good" or "bad" ends even if they're presented as all "good".
There's almost nowhere in the game that doesn't have a puzzle, as even reaching most hidden items and easter eggs require their own somewhat convoluted ways of getting to them. The increasingly complex puzzles make for a great challenge for anyone into this genre and it's fittingly atmospheric to boot. $40 base price may be too much for the game.

Unlike "traditional" rhythm games, like DDR, the notes you have to hit aren't displayed on screen as they normally are. An "enemy" on screen says the command and performs the action, so if they're poiting up you have to correctly remember how long after their turn started to press up. They're there to assist you, but aren't all you need.
This adds to the original by varying up the gameplay a bit in a very natural and satisfying way. It's also chock full of secrets and extras. Highly recommend if you're a fan of rhythm games. (I have no idea how this game holds up as a port as I have not played this game on console.)

Having played the first one and considering it the best hidden gem i've found, I was excited to hear there was a sequel in the works. While I must admit that I was dissapointed that it wasn't free like the first one was, I am happy to say that it was well worth the money. The controls feel spot on, and make most of the deaths feel like your fault (sometimes you respawn in such a way to fall right onto passing enemies, but it's far and few in between when it does happen). Respawning is very quick and the music keeps right on playing, which by the way is very good in it's own right. I'd buy the sound track if it had one.
As far as difficulty goes, it's not insanely hard to beat, which is good. There are several power ups to find along the way and 6 hearts to find to unlock the final dungeon, which are a bit cryptic to find, but luckily there's an npc in one of the first towns that can lead you to them. It has several fake walls that are about 50/50 in terms of secrecy. Some you can kinda tell are fake or can be passed through, but others catch you off guard. It has some invisible blocks, but none placed in such a way to prevent you from jumping over chasms.
I didn't 100% the game, cause going gem hunting isn't my cup of tea but if it's yours then there's a secret world map full of challenge courses for you to test your skill in.
All in all, a very good game. No real complaints to be had with it. Well worth its full price.

I played You Have to Win The Game and enjoyed it immensely, partially because of the atmospheric CGA graphics, partially because I just thought it was good. I'm going to start off with the review of this game and then talk about the pros and cons.
Oxenfree is a side scrolling game with 5 main characters. Three girls, Alex (our main character), Clarissa and Nona. Then we have the boys Ren and Jonas. They all meet on Edwards Island to the yearly beach party. Normally this is a rocking event, but this particular year it's a dud and only the 5 show up. After a short game of Truth and Slap, Ren convinces Alex and her new step-brother Jonas to check out the caves. He wants to show them something weird and cool that happens if you tune a small hand held radio near a pile of rocks. What happens after this is pretty awesome. Now I'm not going to go into any spoilers here, although if you've seen walkthroughs you might already know. Onwards toward my pros and cons.
Pros- The graphics are super cute. I love the color scheme the paper cut out feel of the graphics and the characters in general. I also love that you can decide exactly what the characters say and how they interact. This is what got me interested in purchasing the game. It's like a choose your own ending storyline. Which I found intriguing. Lastly, I loved all the creepiness this game has. The time-loops which you'll see once you play are eerie and super satisfying. I said lastly, but I forgot one other pro. If you play this game again, Alex will remember bits of it and ask what is going on. You also get new items in the game which was super fun to see.
Cons- This game took me about 4 hours to play that is including collecting all of Maggie's letters and tuning into all the anamolies. Although you can play this game again and again 4 hours is not alot of game time. Which segues into my next con, this game is $19.99 U.S. dollars. For 4 hours of game play that is pretty steep. Again, yes I realize you can play the game over and over, but it had a diablo feel to me. You basically do the same thing over and over collect the same things over and over. Nothing really changes besides the dialogue and maybe the extra goodies that show up randomly during talking parts. Now if you want to go into the fact that this is an indie game and that's why it's so expensive, I get that. I would have preferred the mobile phone price of $4.99 on my PC. Last con, is just me being nit picky, the movement speed is so slow. You only use the W,A,S,D keys on you keyboard which is standard for computer games, but the speed at which you walk through the trails and climb the rocks makes going around the island super tedious. Maybe that is the point. If you could walk faster the game play would be even less than 4 hours.
Overall I enjoyed playing the game, so much so I immediately played it again straight through to see if I could have a better outcome of events. I liked how it turned out the second time around. If this game ever comes out with a sequel I will probably try it out. I'm hoping more people play this game and the price will go down so that future gamers can love this game too.

Tales from the Borderlands é mais uma ótima obra da Telltale Games , o jogo se passa no Universo da franquia Borderlands , com a aparição já no primeiro capítulo do meu pensonagem favorito da franquia , o Zer0 , não permitida a gameplay com ele , afinal a história é contada aos olhos de Rhys e Fiona... Mais uma Vez a Telltale Games conseguiu mostrar o seu poder no mercado de games...Eu nunca havia jogado um jogo da empresa , mais vários amigos me falaram da Telltale e resolvi testar..Fiquei em Dúvida entre o The Walking Dead (Acompanho a série de TV e o game recebeu vários premios)...Mais como passei já várias horas no universo de Borderlands resolvi optar por Tales from the Borderlands. E ai vai uma análise minha do Primeiro Capítulo do game: ''Zer0 Sum''
Enredo: 10/10 (Lembrando que esse é o primeiro capítulo de cinco lançados, então só vou poder dar uma nota final a história depois de jogar os cinco, Atualizarei essa nota e de outras após o lançamento de todos os capítulos).
Tempo de Campanha: Uma média de 2 Horas por Capítulo (Esse tempo pode variar para mais ou menos, Depende do Jogador).
Trilha Sonora: 9.0/10 (As musicas que tocam de fundo se prendem bem aos cenários e eventos que são contados na história (Sofrerá atualizações com o lançamento de próximos Capítulos) ).
Efeitos Sonoros: 9.5/10 (Som das armas e de objetos da franquia Borderlands foram retratados fielmente, Me senti jogando Borderlands 2 ao escutar os Sons (Sofrerá atualizações com o lançamento de próximos Capítulos) ).
Gráficos: 10/10 (Os Gráficos já conhecidos da Telltale, os Famosos Cartoons, foram melhorados doque vi no primeiro game do The Walking Dead , mais na maior parte o jogo está lindo (Lembrando... Comparando com os gráficos que a empresa trabalha)... algumas texturas são mal rederizadas ou de resolução baixa , mais é uma minoria).
Gameplay: 9.5/10 (O mesmo sistema de Gameplay de todos os jogos da empresa, você escolhe uma fala para enteragir com o diálogo ou interage com algum objeto do cenário (Lembrando que como todos os jogos da Telltale áudio e lendas são Full inglês , então se vc não tem um conhecimento mínimo da língua terá dificuldades em entender o enredo).
Então Tales from the Borderlands é um ótimo game, Sem dúvida um dos melhores que já joguei, ele tem problemas?, Claro! Tudo tem, mais nada irá influenciar na sua Gameplay, esse game me apresentou o universo da Talltale e sem dúvida jogarei outros games da empresa :).
Minha Nota Final Para: Tales from the Borderlands: 9.5/10

I just watched a colonist bury his brother and the love of his life on the same day. His brother, the 17 year old doctor who successfully amputated the leg of a prisoner to stop the spread of infection, had died of a heatstroke. Update 6.Nov.17: Since I wrote my review new informations occurred, and some discussions took place, both make me think some alterations and extensions of my original review are necessary. You find the original review in the comments; hope you still agree, it's helpful.
Still not even worth a cent for nostalgic reasons. At least here.
It has it's charm and it's fun to play, if it could be played. Several of the 12 puzzles have bugs known since release. Some of them make the game simply not enjoyable, like graphical issues, or the infamous mirror machine bug, up to unplayable, when the game f.e. generates an unsovable puzzles in Bubble Wonder Abyss, or doesn’t alter the reflections properly in the mirror machine.
Furthermore, occasionally players reported their game simply won't start at all, none of whom ever stated if the the issue could be resolved or not though. In the case of corrupted save files, which also still happen, and making the game unplayable, the community manager at least posted a workaround solution. [1] It's no proper fix, but as the save game is written into the registry, it may help getting the game running again.
By now chances of a fix for any bugs are zero. While there are some very dim signs of some people actually still work on the game, it seems likely, that the Steam version was abandoned, right after the Amazon Kindle version, afaik. The only update for the Steam version released in March 2016, while the Windows Store version [2], the itunes version [3] and the Android version received more updates, the latter even until January 2017 [4, 8].
Other requests wont get any reply as well, like adding the sound effects for movement from the original. The "foot sounds", as someone informed me, apparently even were in the game at some point during development and taken out because „in scenes where multiple Zoombinis were moving it resulted in a cacophony“ [5]. They opted to remove them, instead of polishing the game before release; this sums up the overall impression of the game.
Or adding the other languages, in which the original game – French and German - was available. Contrary to what I wrote a few month ago, the game in it’s current state could only easily support several languages on written only level. For the audio files the game would currently indeed need different branches, which would come with different Unity assets archives, in which the files with voice lines would match the choosen language. Now it may be like that the game can't support multiple languages itself, but the effort it would take to create those other .assets-files is basically swapping out about 150 .wav-files [6]. Not much work at all, as some more knowledgeable gamers informed me. While my assumption of a support of multiple languages in game was incorrect, its falsiness gets undermined by the little effort it would take to give us French and German voices - so a bit given, a bit taken.
To sum it up, the devs and the publisher of this game currently... well, follow the sales and their work. The Steam version didn’t really sold great so far. [7] And furthermore, the Android and iOs versions seem to be the ones, they used for their research project, which includes the Zoombini game. [8] Without great earnings, and no way to utilize Steam for their work as well, it's no wonder why they ditched the support of this version so quickly.
If you going to buy it, don't do it here. Here it probably will stay buggy till eternity.

I first played this game on my Android tablet and was immediately struck by how good the game could be if it was controlled by (not incidentally) a controller. A week later I found it on Steam and was not disappointed with my earlier judgement call. While able to be played via keyboard, I recommend using a controller if you have one.
The game consists of a mixture of rogue-like and dungeon crawler elements that combine well enough to have you running in fear if you're foolish enough, with all your many years of gaming experience, to go unprepared for the next wave. I like to think of it as Diablo 2 with instant gratification. The game is, at its core, not difficult to play - you just have to be quick, and know your surroundings. Your character - chosen from a pool of classes - utilises his own abilities while simultaneously trying to use the environment to his advantage, guiding oncoming monsters in to the paths of traps scattered throughout the level. Move slightly too far to the left and you're the liquified victim of your own trap attempts; move slightly too slowly and you'll be pummelled to death by something hideous and disgusting.
The level-up system is simple, and familiar to any who have played Diablo 2. Each level you gain a couple of points toward attributes and one point toward a talent. The enemies, of course, scale with your level - and the challenges only get more extreme as you attempt to shoot, smash or spell your way through what can only be described as 16-bit mayhem. Power-ups exist as a 2-slot quick inventory, and range from potions to a ludicrously powerful rainbow cannon. In addition, you have four skill slots that you should absolutely use as often as possible, because they're the only thing saving you from a sticky death at the hands of a giant rat.
The graphics are quite good, even at 1080p resolution. While lacking the artistic polish of a AAA title like the Diablo series, the game makes up for it with well-detailed sprites and clever use of environment space. Almost every square inch of your screen has something destructible in it, and therein lies one of the charms of this game: the crates. There's nothing like seeing a crate erupt in blood to satisfy the urge for some creatively over-the-top hilarity in the midst of all the bloodshed you'll commit.
There is a decent variety of classes to play and each had their own wonderful little quirks. Each class feels very different, and that's incredibly imporatnt for a cheap indie game like this because the replay value is so high as a consequence. Gameplay is fast and brutal, often unforgiving of even the most casual mistake.
Although there is a lot to like about this game and some surprising depth to the tactics within it, a lot of the game simply comes down to how well you can kite enemies in to traps (which are seemingly everywhere). This is less true at higher levels, but unless you put in the time and effort to get to those lofty heights of monster slaying then you're going to find that, at best, this game will fulfill a desire for a quick, casual game that can probably be played in between your next League of Legends match.

Rating: 9/10
Have you ever replayed one of your treasured childhood 8-bit games, only to be disappointed? It felt so different in your memory... Well, Super Win The Game feels the exact opposite of that. In fact, SWTG is what old childhood games should have been in the first place. Don't know what I am talking about? Try its freeware prequel "You Have To Win The Game", that is, if you grew up playing games on an old CGA-monitor. Put it simply, it is PURE AWESOMENESS.
Pros
Level Design: this is probably what most reviewers will overlook, since the best level designs are the ones you don't even notice. The levels are just so complex and fun to explore, with its different themes and multiple secrets. And speaking of secrets, oh my, you will be served. I literally discover one every single time I load the game.
Mechanics / Physics: Also an overlooked aspect for the same reason mentioned above. It just feels good to play. And the more items you collect, the freer you become. Again, try YHTWTG if you want to know how it feels beforehand, it's the same home-made self-developed pro-level NERD engine.
Television Emulation: This one just completes the whole retro experience. It also has more options to experiment with than its predecessor. Although I recommend the default settings, which are the best in my opinion. Oh, if only we could apply it to other retro games on Steam...
Cons
The music: It can become really annoying and repetitive. Especially for the fact that more than half of the tracks just don't fit the area you are in. The best example would be the ice area. In most old games, the area is expressed musically by a certain mystery and some high-pitched "icy" notes. Think SMB3's ice level map or even Zeliard for PC gamers. On the other hand, the main tune (let's call it the "black and white" track) is really good and fits the mystery and loneliness of the whole game. The waterways, lair and lava area tunes also fit adequately. The rest just soon gets on your nerves. So it's up to you to keep the music on or not.
Length: I guess a speed-run could be done in less than two hour, though the first time you play, you will go back and forth, get lost, try to figure out what to do next, etc. I guess it took me about 7 hours of "normal" gameplay to beat. Then you can go back and look for all the secrets you missed the first time. Still, the downside of having an amazing game like this is that you will always want more of it.
Other observations
Weird messages/poems (black and white sequences): This one, well, I'm not sure what to think of it. Perhaps they are some kind of riddles I haven't figured out yet. The other possibility is that they are just the author's personal poetic thoughts, which add even more artistic value and mystery to the game.
Interaction: By this one, I mean that I feel there could have been more interactions with non-playable characters populating the cities and such. I guess the author wanted the player to feel a certain loneliness, but some Zelda-like sub-quests for example would have been fun.
Secrets: As I mentioned in the pros, there are secrets everywhere. The thing is, if you are a bit of a perfectionist and want to collect all the gems and items, you will end up wasting a lot of your time scrutinizing each screen (i.e. stick to walls and jump like an idiot) in hope of finding new invisible secret passages.
As you can probably see by the length of this review, I have just had A BLAST playing this game. I am now just wishing for some DLC of sort that could add quests, items, heck even an entire new level with some good chiptune music. A retro boxed version would be awesome too. Anyway, It is a MUST-BUY for all you nostalgic gamers, especially of the 8-bit generation.
p.s. There is now a DRM-free version that include a Steam key on the author's website for those who feel somewhat uncomfortable with the "Steam-way".

-DISCLAIMER-
I'm going to talk about this game assuming you've played the original version and I won't be going over the gameplay that much.
At it's heart, this game is the original "Logical Journey of the Zoombinis" with new and/or smoothed out graphics. Given how fantastic an edu-tainment game the original was, you'd think that all that and more would make this game the superior version. In my opinion...
...it's not...
...or at least it isn't yet.
Probably the most noticable change to people who played the original game is the redesign of the Zoombinis themselves, as well as that of the backgrounds. All of the backgrounds have been redrawn, and overall, they look really cool! As for the Zoombinis have more of a horizontal oval shape as opposed to the original egg shape, and their features have been redrawn to look either better, or completely different. I think they look pretty cute this way, and it would be a great change if they blended in with everyone else! Although the Zoombinis have been redesigned, every other character in the game has been ripped from the original and they had their pixels smoothed out. Even though the nostalgia factor from this is nice, they feel very out of place when viewed next to the Zoombinis, especially considering that they didn't even bother to give the characters any new frames of animation to make them look smoother. In fact, in some cases, it appears the animation has gotten worse! In the original game's puzzle with the frogs, the frogs had very neat authentic looking hopping animations. In this version, their animations have been dumbed down so that they just kinda move to each lilypad.
I'll spare you the other aesthetic errors I've found as they are relatively minor. honestly, my biggest complaint is that this version is actually very glitchy. I've run into puzzles where I'd let go of the mouse and my Zoombini would just hang in the air, forcing me to leave it behind and ruining my perfect runs. As far as I can tell, the game is just a port of the original with new graphics. How did they manage to screw that up? To be fair, it's been a long time since I've played the original, so it could have been just as glitchy as this game is, butit doesn't make it any less frustrating. if the original did have the glitches, then this would have been a great opprotunity to fix them.
However, at the end of the day, I really didn't regret getting this version of the game that much. Again, at it's heart, it's the original game with really good new/revamped graphics. All of the puzzles are the same as before and all of the great voice acting from the narrator to the pizza trolls is still there. If you haven't played the original and wanna give it a shot, this is probably a good way to do it! I give the game an 8/10.
In conclusion...

As someone who grew up in the early age of the SNES, NES and earlier platformers, this game is top grade nostalgia. In the day and age where literally every "pixel indie game" is generic, boring and uninspiring, it's a shocker to see a game that actually feels like it's something that would have been released a few decades ago. Super Win the Game is the sequel to You Have to Win the Game as stated, and boy does it deliver. The game takes a lot of inspiration from age old classics such as Super Mario Bros 2, Zelda 2, and much more. What really delivers in this game is a lot of backtracking, which was a key essential in adventure games back in the day. Some paths are inaccesible until you find certain powerups or items to advance or get jewels. The game overall would be quite short without the backtracking, but it's this exact key concept that retro games back then used to expand playtime on cartridges with rather small storage space, which is why the game feels exactly like an NES game. But of course, it's not just that. The additional options and features of having the old "CRT TV Monitor" with adjustable visual settings, along with the optional "reverb" for the chiptune styled music completes the experience and makes you feel like this game was actually made ages ago and not in 2014.
TL;DR Nostalgia and NES freaks, this one is for you!

Let me start by mentioning that I'm not very fond of platform games. Never have been. They usually feel way to linear and restricted to me, and hardly ever offer exciting game mechanics.
While PixelJunk Eden technically is a platform game, this label wouldn't do much justice to it, as it truly is so much more! The game mechanics are simple yet innovative and the gameplay is very fluent. The player can move around freely over the entire map, explore every corner and in the meanwhile develop the map as it grows with you (by seeding plants).
No need to use the keyboard; the mouse does it all for you. This however doesn't mean it's a simple point-and-click game. Different combinations of mouse buttons make you jump in different ways and it all feels very natural.
The artwork is amazing and the 15 maps all offer something new. The minimal house music compliments the game very well.
Is there nothing negative to mention about the game? Of course, there always is. While the gameplay has the potential to be very relaxing, the timer that decreases your health can be stressful. You have to pick up crystals to recharge it, but these are not always around in the later stages of the map and it can be a little frustrating to die just before reaching your goal. In my opinion your health shouldn't be affected by time that much, but rather more by the enemies you have to defeat. These do some occasional damage, but more often interfere with your jumps.
Overall a very nice game with high replay value. You can play for just 10 minutes or for several hours, which makes it a game you can easily come back to. Even the main menu is fun to play around with.

A love story set between mysteriously ubiquitous spike racks, and a man's foot.
Remember Ubisoft? The wonderful studio that birthed the wretched abomination that is uplay? Well, nowadays, when they aren't milking the Farcry franchise or making the latest iteration of Just Dance 20XX, they're shoveling garbage like they're on fire. And why wouldn't they? That garbage is literally made of money! Do you know how much money Watch Dogs made these guys? More than what us dirty peasants will ever see, that's for sure.
Well, let me take you back to a simpler time; 2006. Rayman Raving Rabbids explodes onto the gaming scene. Fans and critics alike are crying in the streets. It is the end of an era. But just before, in October, Ubisoft pushed out this odd little thing. What appears to be the Elder Scrolls Oblivion's estranged cousin. Except, here's the catch: this is a game set in the Might and Magic universe. Novel concept, right? A series primarily known for strategy games is thrown a brief, but interesting first person action RPG party. And I gotta say, all in all, I'm pretty satisfied with the results.
The first thing anyone should know about this game is that this is a world dominated by spike racks. Practically every area in this game has at least a few, if not more. They're leaned up against walls, like its natural run-of-the-mill decor for any cave or urban setting. Perfect for hanging implements after a hard days work, or for dispatching your enemies in an effective and satisfying way. And not only that, but some areas of the game are downright brutal without these nifty death traps. Seriously, some of the enemies you encounter aren't very forgiving, so using your environment to your advantage is a must. Personally, by the end of the game, I was subconsciously springing traps and kicking dudes off cliffs; not only because its fun, but because these baddies are no joke.
You play as Severus Snape, the wizard warrior thief, on a quest to have larping sessions with various local peoples. Meanwhile, there's some artifacts, and the fate of the world wedged in there somewhere. Honestly I wasn't paying any attention to that. The story is the weakest part of this game hands down. Can't say I cared for anything in the plot, really, especially since all of the characters, including the main boy himself, felt about as compelling as overcooked spaghetti. However, the main guy is voiced, and does occasionally say things; so I'll give the game some points for that. As for everyone else, I'd prefer that they did not say things, on account of the voice acting being forgettable and wooden. Even the best voice acting in the game is merely passable, with other line reads being hilarious for the wrong reasons.
Bottom line: what pushed me to make my choices in this game was not my moral compass, but rather who's voice acting I liked better. And here's a hint, of the two female leads, one of them has the aforementioned "passable" talent in this area. Also, did I mention there's choices to be made in this game? AND they affect the ending you get? Whahhhaoha, slow down there. Hey, speaking of passable, the graphics are pretty that. They're serviceable, and I more or less breezed by without being impressed nor disappointed. I'm sure for 2006, this is above average, but it might be that I'm spoiled by this point. Either way, the game makes a very solid effort to build atmosphere and convince you that the places you visit are actual places and not cardboard cutout set pieces you're supposed to walk through.
The gameplay is what carries this game. The combat is superb, especially by the end of the game, where the sense of progression leads you up to feeling like a death machine. In contrast, the beginning of the game feels like a struggle against forces that are far more powerful than you. By the end, I was cutting through piles of enemies without any care at all. That is one thing this game does that I'm absolutely in love with. There's strategy in combat, and managing your resources is just as potent as using the environment. Eventually you out scale your enemies; either by leveling up important abilities, or getting powerful gear to make you nigh unstoppable. Its a joy, and it is by far the best experience this game has to offer.
Of the 20 some hours I played this game, there was one major bug I encountered involving a broken shield staying in my inventory. Aside from that, this game is reasonably rigid, and rarely unfair. Some of the enemies hit really hard, but that shouldn't be a problem if you're maximizing your advantages. I'd honestly recommend this game for the feeling of kicking orcs off cliffs alone. It's stellar. And despite this game's flaws, I regard this as an admirable first person RPG that isn't made by Bethesda. It has it's problems, but for what it is, this game is a fun ride through and through. And as an added bonus, you don't need to install uplay to enjoy the game that you purchased, so hey, that's always nice.

Pros:
- Really fun gameplay generally. The combat is creative and more like a puzzle than a test of your characters strenght, and although you'll be doing most of the combat with your right foot, the melee, archery and spell systems are all solid.
- Levels are athmospheric, interesting, sprawling and allows for creative navigation thanks to the implementation of the thief staples: Ledge grabbing and rope arrows. Memorable locations and scenes. Many secrets to find (again, in the style of thief).
- Soundtrack is minimalistic, but perfectly accentuates what is going on in the game. I like that.
- Good lenght if you disregard the time lost due to bugs. Took me 13 hours on hardcore difficulty.
Neutral:
- While the controls offer plenty of maneuverbility, they are clunky at times (can't look straight down, can't run backwards, tripping over a tiny physics object will undo your defensive stance, which you have to re-click to button to slowly activate)
- Supplies seemed a bit too common. I was almost always fully stocked on potions for the first 2/3 of the game despite playing on hardcore for my first ever playthrough.
Cons:
- Quite a few enemies just plain ♥♥♥♥ing suck. The Kao Pai is an abomination of game design (think a dragon flying around dealing instakills with a HITSCAN attack. It will kill you instantly if you stand still, but it will never hit you if you are moving sideways), every cyclops in the game can be killed with the good ol' skyrim cheese (shooting at it from a place it can't reach), necromancers shoot homing missiles, meaning you have to take cover from them and wait for them to come to you rather than being able to dodge while moving up to them, those flying spaghetti thingies, and finally, the levels where you get assaulted by waves of ghouls also sucked (when there are so many enemies, you can't fight them head on without getting instakilled. Instead of are forced to dance around the nearest environmental hazard with your guard up as you wait for your stamina to recharge to a point where you can kick another beast to its death).
- Game is prone to crashing.
- Can't skip cutscenes.
- Many bugs
- Cheesy story
- Forgetable characters. Xana was the only one to have any semblance of character.
Overall: This game blends an impressive amount of systems just right and allows for some really creative and fun gameplay. Unfortunately, the flow of the game is often ground to a halt by crashes, major bugs, frustrating combat scenarios featuring dull bosses or unfair numbers of ♥♥♥♥♥♥ enemies. A game with great potential, which could easily have become a classic of the immersive sim genre, along with titles such as thief and deus ex, if just the developers had spent another year polishing the undeniably coarse edges of the game.
Verdict: 7/10

So I guess it is time, I am back in that depressive mood where all I can feel is that I really want to do some intensive typing to some equally intensive music, this Topsy-turvy feeling brings on the mood to review a game! And today my scrutinising eye has befallen Sonic and all-stars Racing Transformed. This game was a questionable buy when I first bought it, with my first opinions being: Mario clone. This game is not anything like Mariokart. I can say that for a start, it is a nice peer into the possiblities of racing games, this game has pretty much every character you could think to belong in an internet meme regarding childhood! Even after my first race I was drawn in to the difficult racing style, it is a hard one to get used to at first, but learning the tricks such as how to do tricks effectively to eventually get enough speed to pass that speedy blue dude.
As Wreck-It-Ralph is my favourite movie of all time currently It was a very nice pleaseure to play as him, and his boat, and his Helicopter, Ok so this game makes no vehicular sense, but still! Mario fought for at least 10 years against a Turtle then went racing with him. Point proven?
Anyhow, back to the game. It is an adventure to say the least, the progression is nice and the necessities such as going out of your way to get coins seem a bit out of place as all you can do with them are gamble them away, I never really had enough to do so as I was always in first, so never really bothered! Another thing is the map design, it is superb! Whilst the Mario kart map design was mainly Road, Road, Road, GIANT MONSTER, Road, Road. But the difference is smart in this game, Due to the fact that the maps feature compulsory bits where you Fly and Sail around the map and dodge giant monsters and scenery, it adds some finesse, it means that the maps are always chaning from Laps 1-3 the map changes with every rotation which is very fun to play around with.
This game is by far one of my favourite Racing games of this year not much considering the fact it is one of the only ones. Consider this one, the only downside is the slightly wasted features and learning curve, once climbed make this a rewarding and exciting racing game which peered into my Childhood in terms of characters.

I bought this game because I am a childhood fan of the spin-off "Heroes and Might and magic", but with the newer games all being♥♥♥♥♥♥and the older games having aged like♥♥♥♥♥♥I decided to still my hunger for more in one of the core might and magic games, and by chance came along this game!
First off all, I kinda bought this because it's made with Valve's source engine and I wanted to play an RPG game where killing someone doesn't just mean clicking them until you win, but instead it means using your surroundings and tactical advantage to kill, and as it turns out Dark Messiah of Might & Magic handles that♥♥♥♥♥♥pretty well! So yeah if you're also interested in how half-life would look if it had orcs and magic, this is essentially it.
However, like many older games, Dark Messiah is a rage inducing piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥ and you may have to retry a passage multiple times because the game isn't clearly pointing to where you have to go and what you have to do, or because you make a jump trying to unveil secret areas only to realize that there's ♥♥♥♥ing nothing there after you've died 50 times trying to get there. But that's also part of the fun I'd say, not knowing what will happen next is a beautifully refreshing experience in the modern gaming world.
On the other hand this game is also packed with the beforementioned secrets and as I said the mechanic of killing enemies trough manipulating the envoirment works greeaat, I've never seen this concept executed this well, in no game. Also this game is quite atmospheric for such an old title, the love to detail and former disregard to how much money this and that is going to make gives it a nice touch, and you truly feel invested in the story. I actually wanted to find out how the story goes on, and the odd destiny of my character was legit interesting to me, I wanted to find out who I am truly playing as. And the characters of this game where neato.
If you're asking about choices, they do (at least feel like they) matter, and they're also based on how you wanna play, not like in other games like fallout where choices are only a matter of how much tedious work you're willing to do in order to unlock more story dialogue. In Dark Messiah the story has many hidden aspects which you can discover by accident while just following your own pace and playstyle, and that's beautiful.
Additionally to the great physics-based combat system, this game has neat weapons like a string-bow, explosive weapons, ice weapons and so much more which all can be used in even more ways, even sometimes in conjunction with the envoirment to kill enemies, progress the story or reach cast off areas, it feels great to play around with what you can do and how you yourself can interact with the scene around you.
In conclusion:
This game is actually made with effort and a solid engine, the creators apparently didn't give a flying ♥♥♥♥ about casual gamers and or making money and although thanks to tech limits this game can have some frustrating areas it still is worth it's entire asking price.

Disclaimer: I purchased the game when it was on sale and it was worth every penny.
So let me preface this review with the fact that this is game is probably not for everyone. If logic puzzles are not your thing, this game is probably not for you. If you don't like philosophy, this game is probably not for you. If you've never asked youself 'Why?' this game is probably not for you.
If you would however decribe yourself as curious, intellectual, and entertained by logical challenges (be in in puzzle AND philosophy) this might be just the game that can change your perception of the world.
While solving over 120 puzzles (with about 20 teaching you the basics... so not really hard) you get to break you brain trying to solve them all, wreck it even harder for the star challenges, read philosophical documents, wander through inviting and ancient worlds, talk to a programm which makes you rethink everything, all while examining the meaning of your existence as well as the struggle of humans to find its answer.
Of course it's not perfect. The philosophical answers you can give sometimes felt too limitating, the tetris puzzles felt unnecessary and when it comes to puzzle solving (especially when collecting the stars in the DLC) there is some miscommunication on how far or high you can jump. In the end these fault are mildly annoying at best and are not outweighing the intellectual stimulation the game can offer.
It really is a shame more games like this don't exist.

There's not much I can say about this game that has not already been said, except to highlight the extreme attention to detail the dev has put into it. Of course there is the very comprehensive crt effects, sounds etc., that have been used to make one of the most faithful retro gaming experiences out there, but to me it shows most in the level/world design. If judging this game by the screenshots and gameplay videos, one could be excused for thinking it's just a series of bland, linear dungeons scattered about an overworld, but nothing could be further from the truth. Words that spring to mind when describing the level design are "interwoven", "deep", "deliberate" and "meticulous". Everything in this game is interconnected, everything has a purpose, and not a tile is out of place. Exploration in this game is an absolute pleasure, and while the overworld seems at times a little bit small, the various intersecting layers underneath it make up for it. The lack of combat is also refreshing, provided you can appreciate a game for what it is, not by what it is not.
That being said, I think the world map is again let down a little for its complete lack of action - without combat, there is no real reason for random encounters, and besides randomness goes very much against the precision grain of this game anyway. Something feels missing in the world map to make it a little more engaging, but I don't know what it is...
Overall though, if you enjoy hardcore platforming and extremely tight level design, or just love retro aesthetics this is the game for you. 8.5/10

It's a platformer. There's no combat. Some enemies are tricky to dodge, and the "boss" rooms have bullet hell obsticles. But mostly it's platforming and exploring. The exploring feels like a mix of Zelda II and a Metroidvania, but without combat.
You probably want to know if it's worth the full price. If you like achievements and go for 100%, there's a good amount of stuff. There are optional areas with challenging jumps. There are 128 gems hidden throughout the world. Just "looking out for them" will get you around 100. Getting the full 128 takes a lot of exploring, and probably took me 10 hours of actual play. I stretched it to ~16 by doing replays for the "big" achievements, but I was stretching on purpose because I like replays. You can 100% in one playthrough.
Without achievements, just playing to finish once, is probably 4-6 hours. It's lovely, has a variety of art and music, and a cool story. The themes (dreams, sense of self, etc.) are done beautifully, and avoided being pretentious. It probably helps that the game is written by a single dev, and is heartfelt. Whether to pay full price just to play through once would be very subjective. It's a better deal than a movie, or a pizza. But perhaps not compared to other games.
Oh, the aesthetic. The CRT is great. It goes far beyond simple scanline effects seen in NES emulators and SweetFX. There's blurring, and little types of fuzziness and flickering that I don't know the right words for. They should seriously license this out to other pixel games. There's nothing else like it.
edit: Btw, my playtime on this game looks crazy high because I was experimenting pulling map data out of it, to make guides. And once it was open, I tended to leave it open for the music. I like it, but 60+ hours is not something you should expect to get out of it, heh.

I really did not know what to expect but the price was right and I'm glad I bought this game.  It is a unique take on a platformer but with several twists.  The basic premise is you are looking for "Spectra" of which each garden contains a total of five.  You are a "Grimp" which has the ability to jump and cling to plants as well as collect pollen which is used to boost your score and to pollenate plant seeds.  When you jump into the pollenated seeds they sprout plants which give you access to more of the level or perhaps a handy platform/cannon in case you make a mistake jumping.
Throughout the course of the first several gardens you will gain a few upgrades and you unlock more gardens by collecting more "Spectra".  The art style and music are outstanding and make this game worth a try just to experience that.  The controls are pretty solid especially if played with a mouse as you get precision aiming for your jumps.
There's something very calming about flying around the levels collecting pollen and taking out enemies.  It's as casual or hardcore as you want it to be as when a garden is beaten (all five "Spectra" collected) you can revisit the garden to try and get all five at once (can be challenging and some "Spectra" are quite challenging to collect in their own right).  Note that you cannot fly around forever as you must collect "Crystals" to keep your oscillator in tune or you will fail the level and take a decent hit on your score.  Thankfully "Crystals" are liberally spread out throughout the garden and some can be spawned by jumping into pollentated seeds or by getting combos.
Overall I recommend this game and I bought it purely on impulse not really knowing what to expect.  I hope you enjoy it!

Oxenfree is a supernatural adventure in which you play as Alex, a teen girl who is on her way to spend the weekend with some friends on a local island. This is all I will say about the actual storyline because the less you know about it the better, as this is really the main appeal to this very underrated game. The story is really amazingly done, and kept me on the edge of my seat wanting to know what would happen next and how it would all end. It is very spooky at times, and there were a few points that I found to be intensely creepy. If you're like me and are a huge fan of all things supernatural I highly recommend this game, as it really does a great justice to this genre.
The gameplay itself is very minimal. There is no combat and you spend most of the game walking around interacting with things, listening to dialogue, and choosing what to say. Unlike many other games, your choices do actually matter, and there are multiple ways the game can end depending on what kind of person you decide to be. As I mentioned, the main drive behind this game is the storyline, which is truly rich and captivating. Obviously this kind of game does not appeal to everyone, so if you want more involved gameplay it might be best to avoid this. However, if you are someone who can appreciate a more story-based game I highly recommend you give this a chance. Games such as this can be hit or miss for me, but never once did I find myself getting bored. In fact, quite the opposite, as the mystery and intrigue pushed me onwards.
The dialogue is very well-written, as are the characters who actually seem like real people rather than one-dimensional cutouts. I found myself emotionally invested in them and their personal struggles, and really wanting to see what would become of them. It is also worth mentioning that the voice acting is great, and provided by some big name voice actors (such as Erin Yvette, of "Firewatch", Telltale's "Walking Dead" and "Wolf Among Us"). I also very much enjoyed the art style, which is simple but very beautiful while still managing to wonderfully convey some of the more scary moments. The soundtrack is very well done as well, and really was nicely paired with the game.
Overall this game is truly an underrated gem and I really am surprised that I never hear people talking about it, because it really deserves far more praise and attention. I first got it on a whim, not even having heard about it before and having no idea what it would be like, and it really was one of the most pleasant surprises I've had in gaming. Although it took me a while to get around to writing this review (first played it in December of last year), this was one of the best gaming experiences of 2016 for me and I really do hope to see more games such as this in the future.

There was a thing...probably still a thing, called 'trip toys' back in the day.  Stoners, acid heads, etc. would get toked up, find something flashy that would keep them transfixed for hours.  PixelJunk Eden is a digitized trip toy that will keep you transfixed, much like a cat hopped on catnip and a laser pointer!
The setup's simple.  You have a little dude, you right click to jump, left click to swing on a bit of silk.  Jump, climb, explode pollen, grow seeds.  Explore, find a seed, repeat.  Sounds simple?  Because it is simple.  But it's captivating in that simplicity, which let's face it...is a great quality in a trip toy!
The gameplay's not all.  The music is absolutely fantastic.  Trance-like as it starts, the music is atmospheric and driving.  As you climb higher, grow your garden deeper, the beat picks up and the strains open up even more.
So yes, I made a lot of weed jokes there because...they go really well together.  But hey, I'm not condoning nothing here, right?  Besides, PixelJunk Eden is just as catchy and engrossing without all that other stuff and you should be playing it.  It's going to keep you entertained for a few hours, guaranteed.

Another nice thing is the items which are only there to spice the game up rather than giving sucky players an unfair advantage. The game looks amazing when running at max settings though I've noticed some significant issues with fps even when at minimal settings(Though this may just be my computer.  The game does have it's flaws, characters aren't varried that much especially since all star moves are so much more bland compared to the first game, and the leveling up system is dull and tedious beyond words.  Also I highly reccomend you play this using a controller only as playing with the mouse and keyboard sucks so much its not even worth trying.  But this is the definitive version of All stars transformed as it has additional characters with more promised while the console ports are left in the dust. I played "The Talos Principle" with such a joy. This is an incredible game, and it has been a long while since a game can entertain me so much that I can play it for 3 or more hours straight. The puzzles are not really that difficult. They are not easy, don't get me wrong here, but they're not too hard either. The game has a lot of replayability due to the bonus items and extra story you can get not to mention the easter eggs. These bonus items are a lot harder to find, but their difficulty is still very manageable.
I would definitely recommend everyone to get the main game. If you like puzzle games, this is going to be one hell of a great game for you.
However, I started to play the expansion Road To Gehenna. My friends recommended me to play it too, and although I already got it, it was next on my to-do list.
Well, I have completed all puzzles in 1 and 2, and half of 3, and I'm now at the point where I'm stopping the game. The bonus items are too hard to get. I have not gotten a single one of them, and to make things even worse, I have not even a clue how to get even one of them. Okay, I have a clue how to get one of them, but the work involved just is not fun. So I decided that I would continue without getting those and just complete the game first. The massive story line through the terminals in this game is something I just try to skip as much as I can, but its a lot of the game. In the first game Its not that much so I could easily skip it there. Here its a different story.
Then the puzzles themselves, They are much bigger and more complex. Complex enough that I do get to solve them, but it just eats so much of my energy to do that, its no fun for me. They're on the limit of what I can do. I like small puzzles, and the first game had many of those. Brilliant! This one has fewer but larger puzzles. One puzzle, I could simply not solve, but it was poorly designed, I could use the scenery to jump over the fence that blocked me and still got it.
I do definitely not recommend playing the DLC "Road to Gehenna" unless you want to be challenged.

I just watched a colonist bury his brother and the love of his life on the same day. His brother, the 17 year old doctor who successfully amputated the leg of a prisoner to stop the spread of infection, had died of a heatstroke. His lover, a 17 year old girl who was blunt on all points and helped hold up a constantly crumbling village, also died of a heatstroke. Us mere tribals did not have the technology to even come close to saving them. The colonist lost himself in grief, and attacked the others in a fit of rage. He is currently in a hospital bed recovering from a gunshot wound and the severe beating my village had to give him to stop his rampage. His pain both mentally and physically is indescribable, but we are down to only four settlers. As broken as he is, we need him. To describe what this game is, it is a game where you construct a settlement, care for its people, and try your hardest to keep them surviving. The world is constantly trying to kill your people through disease, nature, and the violence of man. The settlers interact, form relationships, and survive as one or fall apart alone by themselves. I have to recommend this game. It's frustrating. It's heartbreaking. It's art. It's fun to build up the colony and challengeing to keep everyone from dying. I love this game.

RimWorld is a special game.  Few games can equal the dynamic storytelling RimWorld offers.  Especially on the higher difficulties, this game is a very large, intricate design puzzle.  A wrong move can cost you dearly; but if you play your cards right, you can wind up with a nearly impenetrable, self-sustaining fortress.  The game feels close to done as it is, though with this sort of framework the possibilities are limitless.  Espcially with the latest update, in which you can send caravans out to trade and conquer, suddenly the world map has become important.  Playing multiple colonies simultaneously is fun, but can be very challenging, so I tend to keep it to one major base and then a trading outpost or two.  It helps to have spots for caravans to get more food.
The best thing about this game is you can play it however you want.  Wanna be a gang of drug addict cyborg cannibal slavers?  Absolutely nothing stopping you.  One time, a tribe kept attacking me, so I skinned them, made armchairs from their skin, and placed them in the jail cells of their captured tribesmen.  In my current game, I have a large portion of my base devoted to drug mass manufacturing.  I have 3 colonists that basically do nothing but grow and manufacture narcotics.  Build a planet-spanning drug empire!
Or you could kill pirates and sell your artwork, but I really don't understand why you would want to play the game that way.

I pre-ordered Dungeon Land, I gave into the hype that it was generating, only now after it was too late do I realize that most of that hype was from two things; being an indie game and being from a developer in Brazil.
Dungeon Land is mostly a poorly planned "Gauntlet" clone, placed in the theme of a Theme Park. Sounds like a good idea right? It should have been an amazing game and the developers messed up badly.
To begin with, although Dungeon Land is set in a Theme Park setting, you wouldn't realize it. The special events that happen are very few and far between, there's a complete lack of mini games and character customization is the equivalent of dressing dolls.
Theme Parks are notorious for over priced food, hard games of "skill", rides, actors in suits and expensive vendors. Dungeon Land has almost none of that. Each stage usually has a single ride "event" that boils down to a mini boss before you eventually make your way to the end boss and most of these events are poorly thought out.
You collect gold in the game, but only to buy skill upgrades or new costumes. Costumes do nothing but change how your character looks. I thought part of the appeal of a dungeon crawl was finding all sorts of loot. I mean, wouldn't it have been awesome if they had random venords in stages selling different kinds of gear and stuff? Well, forget that. You don't get that.
The character AI is awful, if you can't find enough people to play with, the character AI is going to be the reason why you die. Me and my friends have literally watched in horror as the last surviving player, a NPC, runs into a wall and does nothing else while being murderd by hordes of enemies. It's awful.
To add further insult to injury, the game is now Free-to-Play, everyone who bought the game gets a kick in the butt and that's about it. But don't worry, there's more "content" for you to buy now if you want.
In all honesty I think this was the plan from the beginning, get as much cash flow from paying members as possible, then after all intrest is lost in their crappy, shoddy, ill thought out game, they make it free to play to bring in even more money. I'll never trust this developer again.

One of my all time favorites, this game delivers hours of fun!
Dark Messiah of Might and Magic is a fantasy action adventure with one of the best melee combat systems ever made.
Sure, the kick is overpowered but the swordplay is simply a blast!
The story, while nothing amazing, is told in a very engaging way and the characters are interesting enough but what really carries the atmosphere of this game is the visual storytelling communicated to you through the levels.
This game runs on the source engine and came out in 2006. However, the indoor levels hold up extremely well, only the exteriors really show their age. It also makes fantastic use of the whole phsyics engine shenanigans you usually find in source engine games. Kick enemies through wooden structures, let barrels crush your enemies, incinerate boxes and toss them on your hostiles... all can be done too. There is a spell that allows you to shrink your enemies and step on them.
If you are , like me, a fan of the thief series you can also use stealth in this game. There even is a homage to Thief in this game as you can find a lookalike of Garrets armor.
This game is a linear action game and can be beaten in around 10 hours. You can update the stats of your character and unlock new abilities too but thats as far as the RPG influence goes.
Recommended to friends of fantasy games and first person shooters alike.

So 35 hours into the game, I guess it is time for a review.
The game is addictive as a whole, playing against the AI is challenging itself, more challenging than playing against other players, single player is therefore very competitive and fun to play. Taking the AI on higher difficulty head on is a suicide mission and will result in your army dying out. It requires strategy and quick thinking.
Eg: The Persians were attacking my front base and taking them head on was not an option, I stationed my archers at the walls and directed infantry and cavalry to a forest where I used an Onager to clear a path, of course I walled it up later. I sent my troops through that path and flanked the enemy only then was I able to repel the attackers.
As you can see, the game at times will make you try out unconventional strategies and methods and these are the moments that you will enjoy.
The single player campaigns are fun to play aswell and are very informative and historically accurate to a certain extent. (The Scotts lost the Battle of Falkirk) Campaigns are worth playing.
Multiplayer is fun but the community is quite toxic and not very welcoming to new comers. So it is advised that you learn your stuff before going into multiplayer cause you will be pressed down hard.
Though I do experience a funny thing in multiplayer. While I may be lagging in AOE 2, at the same time when I quit AOE 2 and launch AOE 3 multiplayer, I don't experience any; I suspect it is ESO at play.
The modding community and official updates of the game are alive and regular so that is not an issue.
Even at full price the game is worth it and you get a whole bunch of content to play around with.
I recommend this game highly and a must add for your library.
