A mostly unexciting, poorly written videogame. Despite what everyone seems to be saying, the combat is extremely basic - there's no point in having four directions to power attack from when the enemies react pretty much the same to all of the four strikes.
Interaction with the environment in combat is limited to dropping things on people, kicking them into hazards, off pits, or swinging things into them. Definitely neat for the time, but with how stale the combat already is, it certainly doesn't hold up, and it most definitely isn't a "deep" combat system.
I figured the game would have a decent amount of variety with it's weapons, but a quick play around with console commands revealed they were mostly just one of the four weapon types with fancy effects and more damage. Not very exciting. That said, letting us fire a bow with a climbeable rope attached to it is a simple, effective, rather ingenious way of letting the player explore the otherwise well-designed levels, which is very important.
Stealth is functional, if only that. As long as you level up at least once in stealth and don't walk directly in front of your enemy, sticking to the shadows, you won't have much of a hard time staying undetected.
While I can certainly see the charm of this game - the fast, albiet easy combat that makes you feel like a swashbuckling hero as you kick one foe down a pit and smash someone behind you over the head with a crate you just found on the ground, it doesn't make up for the game's overall lack of excitement. Indeed, it's combat and RPG mechanics feel like they'd be much, much more at home in an open-world RPG, and it shows.

Super Win the Game is basically a metroidvania with the visual style of Zelda 2 from the NES.  It is not a terribly long game, clocking in at around 4 hours for me which includes time trying to find some of the hidden stuff in the game.   A 100% playthrough would take a little longer, but I could also see the game being speedran in under an hour if you knew exactly what to do.
Gameplay is pretty good, controls are simple and solid.  One button for jump, one button for interacting with stuff and you are good to go.  You have fairly good control over your character, so the platforming never feels cheap or unfair.   There is no attack button of any kind in this game, so don't expect any real boss fights.
Game contains the type of power ups you'd expect from a metroidvania.  Double jump, wall jump, swimming, lava proof upgrades.  You basically need to explore the world to find 6 pieces of the King's Heart.   They are not hidden in obvious places, you may accidentally find them, but if you get stuck there is a fortune teller NPC at town who can guide you to where to look or go next at any point in the game.  There are no heart containers or HP, one hit and you are dead, but checkpoints are very frequent to the point where death never really hurts.
Overall I enjoyed the game, but given it's length you may want to consider if it's priced in a place to justify about 4 hours for a playthrough (I was gifted it for free by a friend).  If you are an achievement ♥♥♥♥♥, you will probably get a fair amount more time out of it as there is a lot of hidden stuff and fake walls hiding secrets etc.

PixelJunk Eden is a game full of visual art and magnificent music, which pair greatly together. You play as a small seed/bug/something which has the ability to stick to the plants and rocks. There are 15 "gardens", AKA levels, in which you can find these things called spectas. There are 5 in each garden. Every garden has a very unique color, atmosphere, and music that makes discovery all the more interesting. As well, each garden introduces a new feature, be it an ability or environmental challenge. It's hard to put this game into a category. It isn't really a casual relaxing game, as you have a meter that you must refill constantly, as well as enemies that can really screw you over when they make you fall. It is equally frustrating as amazing. Overall, Eden is really a beautiful game that I'm glad I bought.

To be fair this is one of the least buggy games I have encountered in the under 10 dollar indie section. The only real bug is the occasional enemy flying straight up into nothingness. It runs fine and the partial controller support may as well be listed as full controller support since everything functions well as far as I know of.
That said, this game just doesn't really have anything of interest to me. The shooting is meh, your enemies are just a bunch of cubes that zerg you while you shoot them down.  The "puzzles" are more along the lines of either get through timed obstacles to reach things to unlock doors or go across a bunch of timed platforms that lead in different paths until you find the right path.
It all feels very lackluster, even falling to your death is just a slow fall down and then the music does a mini fade out and resets. I mean, at least give me some kind of sound when I fall off.
I was expecting something more musical or rhythmic like beat hazard or crypt of the necrodancer but honestly the background sounds pretty awful half the time and beside some obstacles that move and make a sound when they move there isn't really much rhythm required. "Player generated procedural music" hasn't really seemed to be a thing yet, especially if you consider that the maps are all predesigned levels and you can't input music I'm not entirely sure how "player generated procedural music" would even be possible beside the sound of you shooting enemies.
The game description on steam talks describes the setting as a place where "the most peculiar and unfortunate of events have occurred." But beside the plot actually written in the steam description there isn't much to find. In the game itself all I could find were these nodes in game which would open an image with some pictures and some stuff that's supposed to be alien language or something.
All in all, couldn't keep my attention in any way, so not recommended.

Spending $5 (sale) on this wasn't a terrible decision, but it could've been put to better use.
Pros:
Easy to pick up
You can level up and get new skills that do things like stun or summon minions
Bosses are good and reasonable, their AoE attacks are flashy but fair. Surprisingly, ones with ranged immunity are also reasonable, even if you're playing a purely-ranged class due to how common traps are.
Cons:
Simple and repetitive gameplay - Walk away from hordes of monsters while attacking them with sword/bow/magic/whatever, while also using skills whenever their cooldowns run out. This gets mixed up at times due to enemies with unique attacks ('maggot' enemies can poison a small area so it damages you if you walk on it), and the fact that melee classes involve a bit more skill since you have to be close to enemies, but it's not enough.
Some skills are bugged or awkward to use - My Viking has a Stun skill that you have to stop walking away from an enemy to hit them with instead of walk-away-while-hitting which melee classes should be doing and a 'charge' skill that makes him run in a seemingly random direction (usually towards an enemy at least).
You will die in one hit to an arbitrarily high-damage projectile or trap while enemies normally only do about a tenth of your health in damage. It will be unexpected and stupid.
Getting the right beneficial potions, which randomly drop, will make you win too easily
A few potions will suddenly KILL YOU INSTANTLY when you have half health. Especially annoying because I've also wasted tons of full-healing potions because I don't want to die to a negative one.
Devil Statues. Another terrible mechanic. They don't give you some kind of upside-and-drawback like 'evil' themed mechanics should, they can just PERMANENTLY lower one of your stats by 2, basically making you a level-5 character that levels up as slowly as a level-6 character, and so on for the rest of the game. Might as well just abandon that character to quickly level a different one up to 5.

These days it's difficult to appreciate a good free game. Back (old man alert!) when I was a kid, I didn't get more than 2 or 3 games a year, the rest had to be rentals. Nowadays, we have access to hundreds of thousands of games. Once you take into account the indie bundles, the incredible discounts, the F2P MMOs, the freeware, all the "free" games made possible via emulators, you get several times more bang for your buck than ever before.
Echoes+ is a free game, no strings attached either. You're not obligated to pay for the full game, there aren't any microtransactions, and it isn't free because nobody in their right mind would play it let alone pay for it. Echoes+ is simply free, and pretty dang good.
The best description I can come up with this game is that it's a twin-stick-not-quite-asteroids shooter. Yes, I'm well aware that it's not the catchiest term but whatever. Basically the goal is to survive as long as possible and get the high-score. You survive by dodging rocks, and you score high by shooting everything and collecting multiplier bonuses. There are multiple difficulties for ever-increasing rock intensity and a variety of modes. Limited leaderboards (top 10 only) and non-Steam achievements round out the package. There's even a more traditional Asteroids clone.
Unlike most twin-stick shooters, you actually get a health meter in this game. This tends to result in longer attempts than most 1-3 life games. However, as you progress there are about 300 rocks for every health pick-up you'll find, and whenever you take damage you lose a number of weapon power-ups. Well actually they get scattered, so while you can pick them up again, it just adds to the chaos. In short, you can get hit, but you shouldn't get hit. That sounds sensible enough doesn't it? After a certain point it becomes seemingly impossible to not take damage. This is about where the "git gud wall" makes its appearance. You can't have a classic arcade game, without an invisible wall that forces you to step your game up to the next level.
I'm not sure where I'd rank Echoes+ in the great pantheon of free videogames, but it is good enough to check out. It's challenging enough, has the right hooks and incentives to keep you playing, and is competently designed and executed. I've certainly paid for worse games.

Okay I'm going to write a short review quick and to the point.
FIrst off, the game is fun. For $5 (bought it on a sale) it is defintely worth picking up for the price.
The game plays like what you might expect Diablo 2 on SNES to play mixed with a bit of rogue flavoring. I like a lot of the gameplay itself, the mindless ARPG hack and slash. One critique I will say though is that you can only attack/shoot in 4 directions which is sort of annoying. Even Realm of the Mad God which has arguably worse graphics and gameplay mechanics here can do 8 directional movement and firing. One other critique I will make is that you often find yourself dying in very cheap ways. You will be going along for 20 monster waves and then BAM some mob has an explosion on death mechanic that I can't evade and I'm dead. Huge turnoff for Hardcore mode (if you play this mode, it's extra hardcore in this game because death can be unavoidable). Another critique I have is the traps seem ridiculously overpowered. You can cheese any mob with a trap which most will 1 or 2 shot you on any map.
All in all though I really appreciate the gameplay and vision this game has and think that with some solid polish the score could be higher. Given the amount of games I've played which aren't worth coming back to, saying this game has a lot of potential and is worth keeping an eye on is high praise around here.

Pros:
- The retro CRT TV filter is great. It may be a little overmuch at first, but the effect is totally cusomizable, or you can just turn it off entirely.
- The story (although rather buried) is interesting. Not groundbreaking or absolutely stunning, but interesting...which is more than I can say for a lot of recent games.
- There are a lot of "borrowed assests" in this game. While I'd normally take umbrage to swiping sprites from older, better games, they're here as homage, and are used with minor changes that make them more than xerox copies.
- Secrets. False walls, floors, and hidden areas on the world map are fun to find, accidentally or not. The NPCs will point you in the direction of a lot of them, but hopefully you'll find some on your own, too.
Cons:
- The music is short loops that restart every time you enter a new area (which is frequently). I love chiptunes, but I had to turn it down to keep my head from exploding.
- There's nothing to it. I'm now just shy of 2 hours into the game. I have seen the entire world map, cleared all the major dungeons, and have collected 3 of the 5 pieces of the King's Heart (i.e. "The Big End Item"). I'm already tired of backtracking...
- It's not "open world". Although you're immediately free to roam anywhere on the world map, you can't do anything (save talk to a few cryptic NPCs) until you get some items. The items must be acquired in a specific order, too. It's a bummer walking to the ends of the Earth just to have to walk all the way back because you can't double jump yet.
- No fighting allowed. This game is strictly a platformer. You walk, you jump, you listen to villagers. You don't fight, you don't cast magic, and you dodge anything that looks like it might bite you. Not very fun.
- It's expensive. Even with the 10% discount, this game just doesn't have that meaty cash-to-fun ratio I love as a PC gamer. Twelve bucks got me maybe 3-4 hours of game, and that's just not a very good value.
All in all, if I had to compare this game to something, it'd be a piece of Fruit Stripe gum. A blast from the past that isn't bad but doesn't quite taste right, and gets stale far too soon.

Strife is the first MOBA that's clicked with me.
I tried League, Dota, and a few others (I'm looking at you, Infinite Crisis), but I just couldn't get into them. Learning how to play so many characters, memorize so many items, and deal with toxic communities that aren't welcoming to new players turned me off to the genre. Thankfully, Strife is different.
The traditional MOBA gameplay is there, but it's much easier to grasp, learn, and enjoy than any of the other MOBA's I've tried. While some of the other games in the genre might have more depth, Strife is a much better entry for newcomers to the genre. It teaches you the rules in a fun and interesting way, the characters are easier to play and wield effectively, and it has a slight sense of humor that I haven't seen in other MOBA's.
The only real downside I've found in my nearly 10 hours with the game? The community seems to be practically non-existent. I've been primarily playing matches against the computer, which is still fun, but I wish there were more active players so that I could really get into this community.
The game is free (which is always nice), so you really have nothing to lose by downloading it and giving it a shot.

Not quite a diamond in the rough, but rather an unpolished gem, Dark Messiah was initially developed as Arx Fatalis 2, which might have been a far superior game if it came together, but as a Ubisoft-published game it turned into a generic and linear fantasy action-adventure with soft RPG elements on top. From the very start it's very obvious that they pushed for an extremely dumbed-down tutorial style full of reminders and handholding, as Ubisoft has a long history in assuming the players are too stupid to figure things out for themselves.
When it comes to the gameplay itself, the Arkane signature becomes apparent: they wanted to make an immersive sim RPG where you can light arrows on fire before shooting them (but you can't shoot arrows through prison bars, which is disappointing); where the combat is responsive and satisfyingly physical; where you can use the environment against your opponents in different ways; where you can even use a spell to freeze the ground and watch the opponents slip and collapse. Unfortunately, Arkane's higher creative instincts were kept on a tight leash by Ubisoft, who tried to get them to make some kind of fantasy Half-Life 2 clone on the Source engine. And it has great moments as such, but most of the time it plays like a very constraining and linear first-person action game with no distinct identity because Arkane didn't have enough creative freedom to make the game they wanted to make.
As mentioned before, the story is a somewhat generic fantasy set in the Ubisoft Might & Magic universe, which is quite lacking in depth. If you played Heroes of Might & Magic back in the 90s and then tried the recycled sequels Ubisoft keeps churning out, you'll know what I mean by generic fantasy. Arkane tried to give it a special tone and included some limited choices in the ending, but it fell flat with very few redeeming qualities. In fact, the fantasy universe is so poor that it has almost no lore apart from a handful of books here and there with no flavour in the writing. And it's all never quite dark enough as the title might suggest; it never plunges beneath the surface to flesh out the universe or the characters, especially the female characters, which are both busty lasses who just tease and titillate the player.
What it does very well is the atmosphere. If you play it with a headset you'll have a great experience in the dungeon-crawling parts, especially the final levels. The level design is also pretty good, and parts of it are reminiscent of Dishonored, with some variety of pathways. The stealth gameplay was probably the basis for Dishonored: the backstabbing animation and the serviceable AI with their taunts... it's all very similar to Dishonored.
Performance is patchy: it crashes just about as much as Oblivion (I mean as another 2006 fantasy game), which is very odd for a Source game. Running it on Windows 10 I've had over 20 crashes in my 19 hours of playtime, not a good rate at all. But it's playable, it just takes some patience to get through it.
I would like to recommend this game, but apart from everything else it has no replay value whatsoever. The endings are very short and the reactivity to the choices is just not interesting at all. If I'd played it back in 2006 I might have liked it, but age hardly makes a difference in the quality of a game: Ultima Underworld, System Shock, Fallout, Half-Life are some excellent old games that I have come to enjoy much more the older I get. Arx Fatalis remains Arkane's greater achievement from their early years.

I'm honestly surprised the ratings are so good for this game. It's a fairly basic first person fantasy game and if that's what you're looking for, it does scratch that itch. But it hasn't aged well, and Skyrim came along a few years later and did almost everything better than this game.
The combat is a mixed bag. The actual sword fighting isn't overly intuitive and the hitboxes behave in a strange way. The kicking is a lot of fun, even if it doesn't make sense that everyone has walls of spikes for some reason. That being said, most fights are at their easiest when you just block and awkwardly try to get the enemies to stupidly put themselves between you and a fire right after you kick five of their friends into it.
The game has a good sense of progression. While the skill system is very slow and could use a re-work, the weapons are where the game shines. Mostly I was just upgrading skills to meet the requirements for weapons. There's some great moments where you have to fight spiders in the early game and they're a pain to deal with, followed by a few hours later where you have a fire sword and you can just murder the crap out of them. It also happens in the late game with the fast zombies, and it feels really rewarding. Though there are also really odd difficulty spikes. I breezed through a lot of the bosses, but the moment I found a swarm of fast enemies I got completely messed up. The hardest boss in the game is the Orc chief, a fight that's somewhere in the middle of the game. I used up so many damn health potions on that guy and every boss after that felt super easy by comparison.
The game's weakest element is it's story. It's a generic chosen one narrative, the characters are laughably shallow. The only two women of note in the game fall in love with you the instant they see you, and they both call you "my love" like the writers couldn't think of a second pet name. They sort of try to work in a moral choice thing, where you can be a demon lord or save the world, but it's fairly sloppy and requires the protagonist to seemingly change his whole personality near the end, and then suddenly change back. It's dumb. The game is dumb.
If you're craving a game like this and you've already poured through better entries in the genre, then it's worth a look on sale. I did end up putting almost twelve hours into the game, so it's not garbage, but there's nothing all that notable about it either.

PIxelJunk Eden is the type of game you casually play and have fun. If you liked gameplay such as "World of Goo" or have nice sounds like "Dust: Elysian Tale" you would want to try this game out.
You are basically a creature that eats spore-like stuff jump around pretty much the whole game where you acquire and unlock "Gardens" which are considered areas/stages in the game.  Upon unlocking other gardens you unlock other abilities such as rope swinging on a plant, defying time and whatever, making a dive attack and so on. It is a game you would play on your spare time.
So here is my short review and here are my scores:
Before I procede, I am basing this review on Indie games so don't compare this scores to actual big games out there.
Story: 4/10 (Not Considered in Final Score)
For this type of game i won't consider the story for the total score since yeah this game is more of a casual game than a full length rpg/adventure/other-things-that-needs-story-game. You would rather be curious and actually interested on how the developers thought of a concept of a creature unlocking gardens and defeating or collecting spores. Really i don't even know what to call these things.
Graphics: 7/10
It has a really good 2D vibrant visuals but the movement around the plants, spores, guardians what not are too slow and would make you even drowsy if you aren't playing with any sounds
Sounds: 8/10
"Funky Club Music"
Contrasting to the mild and calming visuals the funky club music actually matches it. Making the game a bit more exciting and you could probably even bop your head while you play. The background music in this game is just that good.
Gameplay: 7/10
For an indie game going with the casual type of gameplay is always a good choice. It's basically kind of an arcade game where you jump and hop around collecting stuff, no not like mario but more of that "LocoRoco" game (Search it up). Imo it has one of the best gameplay for a casual indie game
Total Score: 7.33 / 10
Verdict: Would definitely recommend this game if you are into that casual games. It's on sale in steam right now at 75% (Holiday 2013) you might aswell get it but there are other games that might be better for your $2.50 (I got mine on 90% $0.99 so i took the advantage and bought it ;D). Oh and one more thing the game also has "Steam Trading Cards" for you to collect. If it's not on sale for at least 50%, i won't recommend you to buy it.

As a kid in the 90s, the original "Logical Journey of the Zoombinis" was a game I played regularly.  As an adult, I still love the logic puzzles it presents to the player; it's still a challenge no matter how old you are.  When I heard about the Kickstarter campaign to bring this game to the modern era, I immediately got on board, and I'm glad I did.
The goal of the game is to bring groups of creatures called Zoombinis to their new homeland by navigating through mutiple puzzle levels.  They all involve different types of logical thinking, though they never stray too far from the basic "trial and error" approach.  Some involve set theory, multi-dimensional thinking, or recognizing patterns as examples.  They start out simple (and if you're an older player, you may find the first couple difficulty levels tedious because of that), but as you successfully bring groups home, sections will increase in difficulty, and that's when the challenge really kicks in.
If you've played the original and want to know the differences between that and the remake, the main difference is graphics.  The original 16-bit artwork was great in the DOS era, but that was locked at 320x240 resolution (maybe 640x480, but regardless, it looks really tiny on today's monitors).  The new version is made for bigger screens and the artwork has been totally redone, and it looks gorgeous.  The Zoombini sprites have been updated, though many other in-game sprites are unchanged.  The sound clips are all the same, though some have been shuffled around a bit and others are absent in places I would normally expect to hear them.  It's a bit weird, but if you've never played the original it won't matter to you anyway.
Overall, I highly recommend picking this up.  It's great for kids as well as adults.
UPDATE: I nominated this game for the 2017 Steam Awards for a category related to games that make you suspend disbelief.  This game has plenty of that, since the premise and imagery are all very wacky.
Take a chance on this game.

When people started saying that this is the future of dialogue in games, I was quite skeptical. After having played this game though, out of the 500+ games I have played, this game probably has the best dialogue system, and it clearly focuses on it.
You can talk whenever it seems natural and you can almost always pick what you say. Usually the choices actually make a difference too and give different responses. Honestly when someone explains the system, it doesn't sound that innovative, but it's just that it's so seamless with gameplay and so similar to real interaction that it drags you in to the world of the game. Not to say I didn't experience a couple of immersion-breaking bugs, but both times it was just an NPC climb animation getting stuck and ignoring it fixed the problem.
I don't recommend playing with subtitles on, but I tried it just to see how the game handles it, and even there you can see just how much effort they put into the dialogue system. Even when the game itself knows that your long monologue will be interrupted, it still types out the full expected subtitles, so you can never really predict when it happens. It's just little details like this that differentiate this dialogue system from all the other ones. It also feels much more realistic to be actively talking to people WHILE you're exploring, instead of stopping dead, staring in the faces of your party members and picking between different long blocks of text while numbers tick down.
The story isn't much to write home about. It's neat spooky mystery stuff, but it's nothing amazing. However, it has a nice theme to it which blends with the overall style quite well. Combined with the dialogue system I would absolutely recommend this game to anyone looking for an interesting sci-fi mystery story that just drags you in for four to six hours. The price is a tad high, so I'm glad I got it on  a sale, but I'm a bit of a cheapskate in general.

I've wanted my son to get into games and had him dabble with the likes of Mario since he was 3. He liked them, but none really took to the point he wanted to play alone. A couple years later enter Castle Crashers. I didn't realize it until we started playing more, but it really is the perfect gateway game for kids to learn gaming concepts. I realized we're starting from scratch here, so even the concept of health was new. In the few weeks we played he's learned the following from Castle Crashers:
-Menu Navigation (understanding that certain buttons or text will get you where you want to be and start the game, choosing a character, etc.)
-Movement (basic navigation of the levels, getting to and facing enemies to attack them or avoid their attacks, jumping)
Combat (understanding X is light attack, Y is heavy attack, RTrigger activates magic in combination with other buttons for different effects, LTrigger to block and knowing when blocking is needed)
-Health (both losing it and dying or using potions or eating food to restore it)
-Magic (being aware of your mana bar and when you run out you can't cast till it regens)
-Leveling (becoming stronger, increasing stats, reaching a level to be able to wield certain weapons)
-Currency (earning gold and affording new weapons and items)
-Items (understanding you have a variety of items and cycling through them with the shoulder buttons. Using the bow and arrow on a boss or using items at appropriate times, like beefing up your character with a sandwich to tear down an otherwise impassable wall. Which leads to..)
-Gating (understanding you need certain items to unlock gated areas which stop you from progressing. like the 3 items needed to use the boat and get across the ocean. understanding where those items are or what boss on what level possesses them.)
-Companions (pets and their passive abilities)
-Unlocking Characters (understanding you have to beat the game with one character to unlock another)
He'll now be able to reference everything he learned in this game as a foundation to pickup other games. On top of all of that, the art style is fun and very slick. The animations are smooth and the controls are responsive. The story is pretty basic (save the princess, kill the bad guys) and it's easy for them to understand the motive. It's also very repeatable. The icing on the cake is you can coop with them to enjoy it together or help them through it. So if you're looking for a game to play with your kids and you don't mind a bit of cartoon violence Castle Crashers is an excellent choice. If anyone has a similar experience with this or another game with their kids, please share.

I think most shooter enthusiasts are familiar with how far back the Wolfenstein series goes and if not, I'll just tell you: the very beginning of shooters as a genre. Wolfenstein: The New Order has pretty big boots to fill with a pedigree like that, but I think it does so admirably.
First and foremost, the game lives up to the id Software legacy. The controls are wonderfully smooth, and combat is frenetic with plenty of ways to kill Nazis. Headshots are satisfying, stealth kills even more so, and there's a good amount of collectibles in each level to find. One thing of particular note is the Enigma meta-game. Throughout the campaign you'll find little red folders, each unlocking a code segment to be solved. Hints on how to actually solve it are written on chalkboards throughout the game, and finally cracking the code on your own to unlock the bonus game modes is far more fun than it has any right to be.
The story is suprisingly good. Certainly, the alternate universe where the Nazis won is a setting we've seen before, but the details behind the Germans suddenly becoming so powerful and how our protagonist and his allies go about destroying the Nazi war machine are intriguing. To me, though, the characters are what really sell it. Blaskowicz himself is more human in this portrayal than he's ever been, quietly reflecting during the both the calm and poignant moments during the story. It really feels as if what he's seen has hurt him, despite his best attempts to conceal it, and his fellows all have similar stories of grief to tell. The player is free to explore those stories through the dossier.
Overall, this is a solid choice of game and a well-crafted shooter. You can't go wrong with this in your library.

Originally released late January of 2013, Dungeonland is a class-based cooperative isometric dungeon crawler. Seemingly borrowing elements from numerous other games- such as Diablo and Left 4 Dead's AI Director- Dungeonland seems like one of those games that really just wants to be adored. And it CAN be quite likable, so long as you have enough friends to bring along for the ride.
Dungeonland's attractions are divided into two similar modes: Adventure and DM Mode. In both modes, teams of 3 heroes of either the warrior, rogue, or mage classes must make their way through one of 4 environments and reach the final boss before the Dungeon Maestro- of either the Human or AI variety- overwhelms them (Or just last as long as you can in the case of the 4th environment: The Infinite Dungeon).
With a full house of human players, Dungeonland has the all-out potential to be a treat with how it can make the heroes work together through both the abilities and customization mechanics. The basic starting form of each of the three hero classes have definite roles they are meant for; Mages for support and light crowd control, Rogues for single-target damage, and Warriors for defense and crowd control. However, each class has at least some potential to fill out just about any role through the game's equipment options. Rogues and even to a lesser extent warriors have the potential to act as support instead of a mage for instance (Warriors can have an ability that can immediately resurrects downed allies!). Of course, none of these classes can fill every role at once- which helps to mandate Dungeonland's teamwork. That and the matter of enemies being numerous, hitting quite hard, and coming from almost any direction if the DM wills it.
Speaking of the DM, be prepared for a zany experience if a human is the one behind the controls. The various DM abilities are what really steal the show in Dungeonland, further enhancing the experience for both sides. DM powers range from mere annoyances such as directional fans and basic monster spawns, to catastrophic events such as elite monster spawns, sheep transformations, and teleportations of various descriptions that can affect either the monsters or the heroes.
The one slight pity with DM Mode is that a LOT of the DM's abilities have to be unlocked via in-game currency. This isn't quite as bad as it sounds, as in-game currency comes in very high quantities to players successful in both the Adventure and DM Modes. So if you want some in-game currency very quickly: Just do some offline DM Mode games against the bots for some quick wins. This same in-game currency is also used to unlock cosmetic items and new abilities/traits for the heroes.
With all of its elements working in conjunction Dungeonland is an absolute blast, but this only holds true when you have a full house of human players. When Dungeonland's bots start getting more and more involved in the proceedings, things quickly start to turn sour- regardless of what the AI is controlling. The problem is that the AI for both sides does not have access to all of the mechanics of the game. AI Heroes cannot use any abilities beyond their most basic equipment-based ability, and they only know how to use one equipment option per class. If that's not enough to render the Hero AI a complete liability, then its their suicidal tendencies and reliability for getting stuck between a wall and a monster horde perpetually dodging instead of fighting back.
Then there's the AI DM which only has access to monster-spawning actions; and absolutely none of the Human DM's abilties. Adventure mode PARTIALLY makes up for the AI DM's deficits through set-pieces that never appear in DM Mode (Such as an arena with a sheep cannon... Or an arena where you periodically have to avoid a giant worm that will insta-kill you... Or an arena where you have the option to throw explosive frogs, virtually guaranteeing friendly fire will be your doom.), but these lose their novelty pretty quickly- especially since some of them are more annoying than fun.
With everything considered, Dungeonland is a recommendable game- but only for a specific subset of consumers. If you have enough friends to bring along for the ride, you will most likely have a blast. But if you have to get even just one AI involved- the quality of the game starts to downturn very quickly. Since the game is now partially free to play, there's plenty of opportunity to see if you can convince a few others to download it and try out the one full level the free-mode offers.

This game. I've always loved it, but have never had the friends willing to play it with me. At least not for very long.
Allow me to explain why that's relevant, and why I don't recommend this game, even though I love it. The one worthwhile mode is the GM mode, where one player is the GM, controlling tricks, traps, and monsters to beat three other players struggling to the goal. For people who believe themselves cunning (regardless of if they are in reality) and enjoy pulling the strings to create a challenge and experience for other players, this is a real great game for you. I'm one of those types, and I sincerely enjoyed splitting my friends apart and trying to pick them off, sowing discord and trying (with varying results) to surprise them at every turn.
However, for those who come to this game with the intent of playing as a hack and slash hero, which is advertised and is forced upon three of the four players every round, you will get bored of this fairly quickly. All the fun of the GM mode is for the GM to have, the players essentially running a gauntlet to the end. Some players get stressed or bored with how little they can actually do, and it in essence becomes a forced march to the end. The GM is given all sorts of ways to express his cunning and strategy, but the players? Kill what's in front of you and progress. Hardly exciting.
This loops me back to my first comment. I enjoyed playing GM, so I like this game. My friends did not as much, or got sick of playing adventurer when I was GM, and eventually lost interest. I feel like this is less a story about me and my friends than it is a story pointing out a major flaw with the design of this game.
In summary, while GM mode is fun, it seems to only be fun for the GM. You can take turns being GM with your friends, but in the end, it sacrifices the role of three other players for the experience of one, and that just doesn't last long.

This is one of my first computer games growing up, and I'm grateful that the developers were able to port it to modern systems. However, if you're able to find the original version of Zoombinis, I would advise you to play that version instead. My gripes with this version are not the game's puzzles (as frustrating as they are), but with the bugs and inconsistencies left in.
I recommend playing this version for its speed and accessibility, though. Except for the intro cutscene starting the game up for the first time, every other scene as well as each level transition can be skipped. The game length is also shorter; it requires only 400 Zoombinis (25 trips total, assuming no lost Zoombinis) instead of the original 625 (about 40 trips, assuming no lost Zoombinis). The sprites have been updated as well as all twelve puzzles and four difficulties.
What's problematic (in an annoying way, not game-breaking way) are the technical problems still present. Most of the breaking bugs have been fixed (listed in the forums), but problems like inconsistent hitboxes still exist, such that clicking on one Zoombini ends up on clicking on another; little details omitted due to technical restraints, such as the walking sound effects no longer in-sync and/or present.
Perhaps the worst feature is not only no Cloud Saves (for a Steam game), but trying to back up your save is a chore itself. There are more details in the forums, but it's not as simple as a single file, but something to do with the Registry files. So say your hard drive or such breaks (like mine) and you invested plenty of hours, there's (a lot of) frustration when you find out about this afterwards and then have to start over.
Conclusion: The puzzles are still great; even better is the option to practice any level at any difficulty. (I do not recall the original allowing for that.) You need a lot of patience (and time) to play, so it's better in short sessions.

When people started saying that this is the future of dialogue in games, I was quite skeptical. After having played this game though, out of the 500+ games I have played, this game probably has the best dialogue system, and it clearly focuses on it.
You can talk whenever it seems natural and you can almost always pick what you say. Usually the choices actually make a difference too and give different responses. Honestly when someone explains the system, it doesn't sound that innovative, but it's just that it's so seamless with gameplay and so similar to real interaction that it drags you in to the world of the game. Not to say I didn't experience a couple of immersion-breaking bugs, but both times it was just an NPC climb animation getting stuck and ignoring it fixed the problem.
I don't recommend playing with subtitles on, but I tried it just to see how the game handles it, and even there you can see just how much effort they put into the dialogue system. Even when the game itself knows that your long monologue will be interrupted, it still types out the full expected subtitles, so you can never really predict when it happens. It's just little details like this that differentiate this dialogue system from all the other ones. It also feels much more realistic to be actively talking to people WHILE you're exploring, instead of stopping dead, staring in the faces of your party members and picking between different long blocks of text while numbers tick down.
The story isn't much to write home about. It's neat spooky mystery stuff, but it's nothing amazing. However, it has a nice theme to it which blends with the overall style quite well. Combined with the dialogue system I would absolutely recommend this game to anyone looking for an interesting sci-fi mystery story that just drags you in for four to six hours. The price is a tad high, so I'm glad I got it on  a sale, but I'm a bit of a cheapskate in general.

The Logical Journey of the Zoombinis was one of my very first computer games ever - I must have been three years old when I first saw it. I was very happy seeing a remake for modern devices. Finally I can play this game without the trouble of setting up a windows 98 virtual machine... Or can I. While in terms of gameplay I adore the puzzles and couldn't praise the game enough, this remake fails in many areas. If you can't play the original, then try this one when you can. If you still have the old one running, don't bother.
I'll be blunt: I played the original game a lot and while it's nice to see other people will now get to play it, this remake is quite the letdown.
The Logical Journey of the Zoombinis was beautiful. With carefully drawn animations on top of quality painted backgrounds (in glorious 256 colors), a great soundtrack (of midi files) and lines voiced in multiple languages, the game was a piece of art. The Zoombinis reboot is quite disapointing in comparison. The cartoonish look is charming but animations are terribly choppy, the sound effects glitch and often get cutoff or are simply missing, the backgrounds have much less interactive details and the overall look and feel is a lot less polished. Even if I wasn't comparing it to the original, this games feels unpolished.
Then comes the gameplay. While the original game had ruber-band difficulty where the game would become much harder very quickly for players which never failed, the reboot drags on forever before making things interesting. The ability to create twins has been removed, which caused many issues and balancing concerns in the original. The practice also gets its own button instead of being hidden behind a keyboard shortcut. Good thing they kept it in.
I've faced a couple gameplay bugs so far, but I was playing on Linux with wine back then (which isn't supported by the creators) so I can't blame the developpers for that - but I can blame them for not porting the game to Ubuntu - especially considering the game was released on mobile. That's a bit lazy of them. I've had a few complete crashes thought, and seeing how many people are complaining about bugs, it seems they're having trouble maintaining it on just a few platforms. Another one that suffers from the patch-era.

Talos principle to me at least is the best of the philosophical puzzle games.

It is not annoying.
It is not stuck up.
It is just a legit fun and well crafted puzzle game with tons of eye opening and mind expanding ideas thrown in.
Be it disscussing the nature of the soul on pc moniters or trying to prove you even exist between levels or coming into another set of quality puzzles that blow your mind in that those old tools you had can do whole new things.
There is a lot to do here, maybe a bad thing for some, but it consistantly gives you new tools, rules and twists on old stuff that helps remove a lot of boring side to repetition. Plus, there is a great modding side with tons of extra fun bits to try. The story alone keeps you so involved that you want to play more and more and more just to know what in the hell is going on.
I can not recommend this game enough if you like to think and puzzle.

I am bad at puzzle games.  For some reason I just don't think in the way these kinds of games require of you.  And so, even though this game has some glowing reviews, I expected to try it, suck at it, and never play it again.  Instead, I got hooked on it and finished it in only a few days.
I won't lie, the puzzles in the last world were extraordinarily difficult for me to figure out sometimes, and there were a few times when I almost rage quit. I doubt I'll ever beat the DLCs without guides if they're more difficult than the main game.  Even so, I only needed a walk though for three of the puzzles in the entire game.  If you don't include the twisting block puzzles (which I needed guides for about half the time).
Those Tetris-esque twisting block puzzles are stupid.  I don't like them, I don't think they're fun, and I think they definitely make this game worse than if they wouldn't have been in it at all.  I don't know if they just require a different way of thinking, but to me they don't seem to rely on skill or your problem solving ability (as all the other puzzles do), but only on sheer luck.  Sometimes you can guess where a few of the blocks go to make your life easier, but very often you'll end up with a space that would definitely fit one type of block, but it's not the one you have left.  It's annoying, it's frustrating, and I wish the devs had just stuck to logic puzzles with lasers and stuff all of the time instead of using these stupid things.
Also, the game doesn't feel like something a triple A developer would make.  Sure, it's pretty enough, and the controls aren't bad, but some parts of it just aren't quite polished enough.  For instance, if you use the recording device and then watch your character move and interact with things, it looks janky as hell.  Really, all of the animation is just... kind of off.  It doesn't look fluid, and it breaks your immersion when you have to watch one of the NPCs or your own recorded character moving around.  Thankfully there aren't too many places where you have to see these issues, since you're on your own for most of the game.
Besides the animation... maybe I would have just gotten frustrated more often if there were more puzzle elements, but it felt like for as long as the game was that it could have used a few more different ways to challenge it's players.  It kind of felt like I stopped gaining new abilities half way though the game and everything was the same after that.  Also not a huge problem though, as at least the settings of the puzzles were interesting.
For all that though, the game was fascinating enough to keep me putting up with it.  Between the god figure and the chat bot constantly fighting for your attention to the questioning of my validity as an actual person, this game is just too cool.  It actually kind of reminds me of Soma, in a way; I'm not much good with survival horror either, but the interesting game world and plot kept me pushing on.  Plus that game left me questioning the definition of consciousness and life as well, just like this one.
I've only played it though once, and I don't know if I'll ever fully finish it a second time, but all-in-all I really like this game.  I could go on for a while longer, too, but I think I'll end it here.  It's a great game with some glaring issues; I'd probably give it an 8/10.  9.5 if the issues I mentioned were addressed.

My most resent set up of Rim World was my best and my worst. I started out great. Got electricity. I had plenty of food. I had two cash crops “corn that became simple meals and herbal meds” that I was selling to the traders. Even got up to 7 people Everything was going great.
Till one day. It was like every other day. Just a normal day. I just got through the hard summer and now in the fall with no heat injuries, which was a first. Everything was looking up. Then a Raid came. I have already been through a bunch. So, I knew the drill. I had sandbags already lined up in a defensive positon. I posted up all my people. All in the right spots. They all had great weapons for that point in the game. Snipers, and LMG. What made this raid different was something I did not see till it was too late. I normally check the enemy’s weapons to know what I a dealing with. But I missed one enemy, and guess what that mother f**Ker had. “FRAG GERANDES”. We starting firing. I got two of the three down. I had this in the bag till that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ threw that grenade and killed two of my colonist. It was now a bad day. One was a best friend and a fiancé. The other was a best friend to the whole group. I was also upset. I lost a great builder that day and a great craft’s man.
I had to re-group the rest of the team to prepare for the big mood drops. I had to hold them together. After the hard winter and three colonists going bezerk. The winter was finally over. We hit the spring with the colonist were almost done with their mood drops. I was getting happy that we made it through with no more people dying. Plus, we even had a new couple get married.
But what I learn is that Rim World is not for happy endings. The first heat wave was setting in. the problem is that this one was the worst. I had two coolers for the colonists, but it was not enough. They were going down with heat strokes. I was getting worried. But I kept my drive. I quickly threw in that new cooler, but it was not fast enough.  With only one to two more days left on that mood drop. The heat wave took out 3 of my last 5. My last two were pushing, but then the worst came. One of my last two ran out to mine something. She went down. I made my last guy go save her. I was lucky too. He knew some medical skill. I thought I could first save my doc then the rest. But then that red flashy box drops down. “MAD F**KING AMIANL.” I was like RUUUNNNNNN!!!!!, but that animal caught up to him. It bit him and he went down. All my colonist was unable to walk. I watched in shock for 10secs before I turned off my computer. I was hurt that my best colony ended up with the worst ending.
The moral of the story is to f**king check every enemy, because those freaking FRAG GRENADES ARE NO JOKE. :’’(

After the abomination that is the mobile version, I'm glad the PC version does away with microtransactions. As for the game itself, it's 100% worth any price you pay for it. The gameplay is a breath of fresh air and games are dead simple to pick up and play for 20 minutes before stopping. Item variety leaves little to be desired, too. Difficulty is the biggest letdown, as if you get one or two high-tier items before the end of Act 1, you can pretty much sail through the rest of the game's 4 acts. Barring that, it's an overall solid game.

Sure, the combat is loose and floaty. You can't really tell when any particular piece of steel of your own or that your enemy's is going to make contact. But that's not your primary ammunition -- it's your leg.
They picked the right physics engine, because while the ornate traps they tried to create may have fallen flat, watching an orc's rag doll physics model tumble down a flight of stairs or off a cliff, is enough to forgive any faults in the game.
And I've never kicked an orc down a flight of stairs in such beautiful, lush environments -- the graphics have aged well and still convey a sense of mystery and wonder.
Conversely, the entirety of the story and its artifically branched endings feel bland and tacked on (particularly so for an RPG-ish title). But as I kick another orc off a mountain, I realize.. I just can't say mad.

this game helped me develop the logical thinking processes i still use today as an engineer. i had wondered if maybe age and feelings of nostalgia were clouding my memory of how good this game is, but after playing through all the puzzles on easy, i think i can safely say that it is every bit as good as i remembered it being. this isnt like a lot of the learning games aimed at kids today, it doesnt have a focus on elementary school subjects like math or writing, and it doesnt hold your hand or coddle you either. its a pure logic game that is universally applicable, even for adults. the game is not overly easy, and starts out with a heavy focus on logical process of elimination, with increasing need for logical analysis as the difficulty increases. these are skills that are no longer taught in most primary schools and are seriously lacking in much of modern society. this is definitely a game aimed at kids, up into the pre-teen years (which is when i mainly played it), but even adults looking to hone their logic skills (and i highly recommend that they do) will certainly find a healthy challenge here.
*One final note. the game is not lacking in instructions, you are in fact expected to figure out how most of these puzzles work through a process of elimination during the easy phase. though there are some (sometimes vague) hints provided by the narrator during the (skippable) loading scenes.

My wifi is usually unstable, and I often get disconnected from games and receive a huge AFK timer. What I'd like in replacement would either be: adding a thing where you can reconnect to a game in progress that you disconnected from, a phase where your computer attempts to reconnect before sending you back to the garage (just like League) or, although not very realistic, implement a system that can identify the reason of disconnecting. If it's like an AFK or *exit game*, it would still issue a timer penalty, whereas if it's because the wifi experiences interruptions, it lets you go. People might start unplugging their routers in order to disconnect, but people with terrible wifi can at least be able to play.

A truly fantastic game with a compelling story, unique gameplay and wondrous execution.
Taking place before the game Suguri, a war tearing the planet apart threatens to cause the extinction of mankind, by the hands of their own creations: r e p l o i d s.
In all seriousness, I went in this expecting a shallow game with good gameplay that would challenge me, but still be manageable. What I got was a game with a unique, interesting story that made me geniunely feel emotions unseen outside of a special few films and books, with unique characters that had real personality, a real motive behind all of it, and a fair amount of vague description and intrigue to keep me wondering about the details even after I had beaten the game. Furthermore, the gameplay was unlike anything I'd ever seen before, and even more soul-crushing than I expected, offering more challenge than any game I've ever played before (and I've played Touhou.) For fans of bullet hell games who want something to mix the old formula up a bit, this game is perfect, and for entry-level bullet hell/shmup players, it's a great game to come into the genre with.

Oxenfree is another interactive movie game with little in the way of gameplay but a lot in the way of story and, bonus, a few of your choices actually matter in terms of the game's outcome.  Unfortunately, the emotional rollercoaster leaves you with about as much time to react to dialogue choices as a regular rollercoaster leaves you time to get accustomed to the feeling of falling.  That is to say, choices flash by way too damn fast some of the time, and you're often left with the choice of interrupting all of your friends mid-sentence or never getting a word in edgewise.  Worse, on PC you need to manually click the dialogue choices (which, again, often disappear way too quickly), and sometimes when you're reloading from your last checkpoint the camera takes too long to zoom in to your character for you to actually, you know, DO that.  Apparently the game is meant to be played with a controller where all of these things are button presses, which makes you wonder why you can't just, you know, map the corresponding buttons to keyboard inputs like a normal game.
Anyway, despite my frustration with that, it was still an overwhelmingly positive experience.  I felt attached to the characters pretty quickly and I cared about what was going on in their lives.  I just wish it was easier to see your "reputation" with them, because I was totally being good buds with Jonas for like 90% of interactions, yet the game apparently decided that I was "distant" because I missed like one critical dialogue at the beginning of the game which honestly, after everything, should not have mattered as much as the rest of the night.  Ugh!  Not that I'm bitter.  I think this game brought back all that teenage angst from over a decade ago.  Seriously though, it's great and you'll love it.

This game is another excellent installment in the adventures of William "BJ" Blazkowicz.  Considered a reboot of the series, the game starts out in the middle of a combat mission to take down Wilhelm "Deathshead" Strasse, the German scientist behind the Nazis' almost supernatural technology.  It goes horribly wrong, and BJ is left in a coma for 14 years while the world moves on.  When he wakes up from his vegetative state, he finds that the Nazi's have conquered the world and rule it with a cruel, totalitarian regime.  BJ, of course, will have none of this.
You waste no time getting your hands bloody and locating what's left of the resistance.  From there, you undertake several missions to cripple the Nazis and increase the strength of the resistance as you move closer to a final confrontation with Deathshead.  This includes a trip the Nazi Lunar Base, because of course it would.
Combat is pretty straight forward - you can carry at least one of every weapon in the game - from trusty knives, to shotguns, to assault rifles, all the way up to laser rifles.  Many of the weapons have an alternate fire such as a silencers, RPGs, scopes, or different types of ammo.  Many can also be dual wielded, and you can select either or both to use their alternate fire when doing this.  Cover mechanics are present - you can lean around or over cover, but you'll find that most cover deteriorates under heavy fire before too long.  A neat addition is the slide, where you start off sprinting and then can slide in a straight line by crouching.  You can aim and fire normally while doing this.  Weapons have an "aim down the sight" fire mode when you aren't dual wielding.  Ammo isn't excessive - ~250 bullets for an assault rifle, 60 for the shotgun, and so on.
Stealth is somewhat of an option - the silenced handgun or knives can one-shot enemies if you take the time to get a headshot or get close enough for a knife takedown, and the game often provides an alternate path to some fights such as the option to go in guns blazing through the door, or to sneak through a crawlspace and flank the enemy.  If you have more than one knife, you can throw them while sneaking around for a stealth takedown, too. There is a passive perk tree that allows you to unlock various improvements by completing certain tasks such as dual-wielding kills, kills with explosives, using cover, and so on.  Each perk is listed along with the requirements to unlock it.  Note: progress towards unlocking perks is maintained for the entire game including across restarts at the last checkpoint after dying.  So you can replay a section and gain additional progress towards the next perk.
There are plenty of collectibles to find, from records and letters, to golden treasures and character art and bios.  Finding the numerous enigma codes allows you to unlock new game modes such as ironman, or unlimited ammo.
Health only regenerates to a bare minimum, so you'll need to find medkits and armor lying around if you want to stay alive.  Enemies drop some ammo and a little armor usually.
If you're going through the game without doing much exploring, you'll probably get 15-20 hours of good gameplay in the  campaign.  As I said, I ended up around 25 with some collectible and perk hunting.  I don't see a lot of potential for replay value - there is technically two paths you can progress in the story based on a choice you have to make at the beginning, but really it's just a cosmetic difference with the main difference being the type of upgrades (health or armor) you can find throughout the game.  If the perk progress carried over, I'd probably do another run through to get the associated achievements for unlocking those perks, but since it doesn't I'll call it a good game and move on.
The voice acting is excellent, and there's a diverse set of characters you'll interact with.  The graphics have held up well considering it's been out for 3 years, though some of the cutscenes look a little off when they are animating the characters through actions.

Well, after 11 hours of gameplay and making trough the Normal stages, I have to say that Sora is an awesome game.
I like a lot the art style, more than Suguri's , and the mechanics... I LOVED them.
The game seems pretty hard, and, it is. But once you start having more control of the Dash, knowing how and when to use the weapons, and start to know the bosses patterns, it becomes more easy.
You have a lot of weapons, which can make levels more or less easy. A lot of the time you will only use the basic weapons or change one or two, but I think that all of them makes a lot of situations and have a lot of possibilities to use.
The principal thing you need to master is the Dash. I loved a lot the Dash, because, it doesn't feel bad to use it in a keyboard, so you don't need to buy a Gamepad (and I think it would even be harder to use in a Gamepad). It's confortable and simple, so you only have to put it in a good key to reach and GG. My keybinding was: Z: 1st Weapon , X: 2nd weapon , A: 3rd weapon , Space: Ults , Left Ctrl: Dash , and I recommend it.
The bosses are pretty unique. Every one have a reason to fight, even if it's a bit hidden (like Alte's husband. You can say that she was an explosive girl).
All the stages give you a little sub-boss which probably will annoy you a bit, but practice is all you need.
The soundtrack is magnificent, and some helps you to empathize with Sora in some stages.
To summarize, I think that Sora is a very good game, with a good design, bosses, stages, and good (in my opinion) controls, and an OST I'll hear ALL the day, and I higly reccomend it if you like bullet hell games.

When this game first came out ten years ago, I needed to have it. I begged my mum to get if for me when I saw it in a Scholastic catalogue. I couldnt stop playing until I got stuck at the contraption/puzzle you have to solve in order for the shop owner at Zeke's to sneeze and aid as a distraction for Bess to sneak in back to look for an important clue (not gonna say too much in case it spoils the game).
Playing it again, I thought it was a bit boring after a couple hours. You're stuck in this one house, with a garden and cemetary and the lack of characters doesn't make it hard to figure out who did it early on in the game. It's also pretty challenging, I played as Senior and if I hadn't of googled a lot of things I wouldn't have finished the game. Walked back and forth between all the same locations, gathering clues, going back again etc got really irritating after a while. The story itself is good: but I think it could've been a lot better if there were more characters and locations to explore, and if the whole walking to and from taking up half of the game. The game took me 9 hours to complete and I'm sure most if the nine hours was getting to and from places.
On a positive note, the graphics are surprisingly good for a game thats been out for so long! The creepy and somewhat gothic atmosphere was definitely cool, fitting in with the storyline nicely. Plus, I couldn't stop playing even though it infuritated me more than anything.
Overall, feelings of nostalgia aside, I probably wouldn't rush to play this game. As much as I love Nancy Drew, it didn't please me much. Although I am incredibly fussy when it comes to games, and games have improved a lot since 2007. Maybe it's me being too harsh but I won't recommend this one. But hey, if you want to play it go straight ahead! One persons opinon to another are all completely different and for the most part people enjoyed this game, I'm just with the minority of people who didn't.

This game is incredible, and although it is pretty pricey, it's worth every penny. I currently have over 150 hours played on this game, and I don't plan on stopping. Its so satisfying building a functioning colony and whatching it grow, and also entertaining when it inevitably gets torn down by some curve ball the game throws that you somehow forgot to plan for. The way I see it, there are two ways to play this game ( or I suppose 3). #1: Get emotionally attached to characters, get into each of their stories, and craft a nice colony, playing without permadeath so that you can go back to saves when something goes wrong. #2: Enable permadeath, play on a hard difficulty, don't get attached to your colonists, watch them come and go without getting very upset, and making every descion based on the good of the colony in the long-run. And I guess #3 would be play on permadeath with emotional attachment, but then your just asking for emotional trama :)
But in all seriousness, this is an amazing game, and if you like top down base builders, or just whacky stories( and I mean really weird stories, for a good hour before I bought the game, I read the stories of colonies people built and then wrote in their reviews) Then you should really get this game, trust me, its worth it.

This game had everything I was looking for in a mystery game. A mansion, a secret room, a dusty journal,  a graveyard, plenty of personal belongings to rifle through, and a nearly perfect combination of gothic creepiness and quirky fun.
Unlike some of the other Nancy Drew games you don't get bogged down by minigames or tasks that feel unrelated to the plot. Everythign you do from solving riddles to exploring the environment to interrogating the suspects feels like it's driving the storyforward but the game still lets you set the pace and come up with solutions on your own. The puzzles are challenging but not frustrating, the story is complelling, and the characters - while there aren't too many of them - are all interesting. On top of that you have a great atmosphere, detailed settings, and teamwork between Bess and Nancy.
In fact it's difficult to find flaws with this game. My only gripe is that it was over too soon.

There is a way to make the game harder, so I would say that if you could probably do pattern matching really well. 12 puzzles isn't a lot since some of them repeat but it's for kids so whatever.

You can click on the backgrounds for animations. E.g. Clicking on the fire causes 2 sticks to jump out and start a fire.

If you bring Zoombinis to the end, a town is constructed depending on the number of Zoombinis that made it, how you got there and how hard the difficulty was.

Oxenfree is another interactive movie game with little in the way of gameplay but a lot in the way of story and, bonus, a few of your choices actually matter in terms of the game's outcome.  Unfortunately, the emotional rollercoaster leaves you with about as much time to react to dialogue choices as a regular rollercoaster leaves you time to get accustomed to the feeling of falling.  That is to say, choices flash by way too damn fast some of the time, and you're often left with the choice of interrupting all of your friends mid-sentence or never getting a word in edgewise.  Worse, on PC you need to manually click the dialogue choices (which, again, often disappear way too quickly), and sometimes when you're reloading from your last checkpoint the camera takes too long to zoom in to your character for you to actually, you know, DO that.  Apparently the game is meant to be played with a controller where all of these things are button presses, which makes you wonder why you can't just, you know, map the corresponding buttons to keyboard inputs like a normal game.
Anyway, despite my frustration with that, it was still an overwhelmingly positive experience.  I felt attached to the characters pretty quickly and I cared about what was going on in their lives.  I just wish it was easier to see your "reputation" with them, because I was totally being good buds with Jonas for like 90% of interactions, yet the game apparently decided that I was "distant" because I missed like one critical dialogue at the beginning of the game which honestly, after everything, should not have mattered as much as the rest of the night.  Ugh!  Not that I'm bitter.  I think this game brought back all that teenage angst from over a decade ago.  Seriously though, it's great and you'll love it.

TL DR: Dark Messiah is a really great action game with solid gameplay which sometimes gets ridiculous with its use of physics, but it does force you out of stealth and into combat later on. Still, there's just an insane number of hilarious ways to kill things.
Dark Messiah of Might & Magic is a first-person action game with some RPG elements developed by Arkane Studios and Floodgate Entertainment.
In the game, you play as Sareth, the underling of a mage, in a quest to find a powerful item. The plot is pretty bad, with the only remotely funny thing about it being that there are two women constantly stroking your ego on proportions that the Half-Life 2 devs wish they had achieved. It's so much that I actually found it funny unlike Half-Life 2 which was plain annoying.
Anyway, there are 10 levels, all mostly linear, though with some wide open spaces throughout. The game provides you with an extensive assortment of tools with which to murder you enemies (ghosting is also possible but not in the entirety of the game, as there are too many well-lit areas where you can't hide.) There's physics, weapons and magic. "Wait, physics?" Yes. Dark Messiah uses and abuses the Source Engine with weakly-supported structures whose weak supports can usually be brought down by sword, arrow or fireball. You also have a mighty kick which can be used against high drops and spikes to instantly kill enemies. Most objects are also grabbable and therefore throwable. You have a freeze spell and bow which when used on the ground can create a surface where enemies will slip and maybe fall to their deaths.
By now some people already realized the amount of insanely entertaining♥♥♥♥♥♥you can do in this game and are playing it. Have fun!
Apart from that, there's a great melee combat system. The direction of your movement affects the type of attack you can power up, and upgrading the Close Combat skill allows for charges, jump attacks and whirlwinds, bringing your number of attacks per weapon to seven. There's also an adrenaline meter which when full will mean your next attack is slow-mo and instantly kills and dismembers/beheads the enemy. The adrenaline meter also has special effects on each spell. You've also got bows, which can usually instantly kill with a well-placed headshot out of hiding (though the hitboxes are somewhat clunky), and even sometimes nail and enemy to the wall, which is pretty fun. There's also a rope bow like in the first two Thief games, which makes vertical exploration pretty fun. Weapons beyond the basic usually have skill requirements whch restrict you from equipping them.
The aforementioned skill system is divided into Combat, Magic and Misc skills. You get skill points for completing objectives, which means you don't have to kill everyone for an optimal character. The amount of skill points lets you max out a skill tree and then more, though it's cooler to make a jack-of-all-trades kind of character. I started with a sneaky assassin (Archery and Stealth), and then started building more into open combat (Close Combat and Strength.) I managed to get through some areas undetected with wall-nailing headshots out of darkness, which was pretty cool. As for stealth, there is a meter indicating how well you are hidden but the parameters for being seen are never explained and sometimes it seems you're invisible in pretty light spots, which is strange.
As fun as the game is, by chapter 9 I was already done with all the fun. I did finish the game but the repetitiveness of it was pretty evident, and the fact that chapter 9 does throw a lot of the same enemy at you at once, making it pretty hard to get through it without anything but straight close combat doesn't help. There's also not a huge variety of enemies in game, and by about half of the game you've seen all of them, even though that's compensated by the variety in killing methods that you have.
Overall Dark Messiah is a pretty fun and silly game, and prefectly replayable if you don't feel you got enough on the first run.

I'd bought this game on sale some time ago and decided it was finally time to play it. I notice coincidentally it is on sale again at the time of writing so if you are in doubt: get it, it's easily worth a 10 euros pricetag.
In short, what's good about this game is that it's beautiful, atmospheric, fun, subtly story-driven, and finally made me feel like I was any good at Tetris.
The game starts as you, a robot, wake up in a garden, and the voice of your creator, EL0HIM, speaks to you, informing you that the purpose of your existence is to enjoy the world he has created for you and prove your worth by collecting Sigils (objects shaped like Tetris blocks) to prove you are worthy of Eternity. Sigils are collected by solving the puzzles within the subsections of the gardens, tasks which start out very simple, but gain in complexity towards the end.
Additionally there are "Stars" to collect with a bit more creative thinking which unlock bonus levels and an alternate ending. While the Sigil puzzles are generally straightforward and have logical solutions, collecting the Stars requires a bit more exploration. Solving the puzzles was a good bit of fun but trying to find the location of some of the Stars involved a lot of running around and trial and error, which was a small point of frustration that could've been done a bit better. While the world is beautiful, it is also repetitive and involves a lot of empty space so running around until I coincidentally found the location at which I had to apply logic was the least enjoyable part of the game for me.
The reason for this was that both the underlying story and the puzzles quickly had their hooks in me. Towards the end the puzzles did get a bit repetitive, there are only 6 tools used to solve puzzles and there's only so many ways you can combine these into a challenge. Most puzzles could be solved by simply collecting tools, applying tools to unlock more tools, repeat until Sigil is unlocked. The reason for this is that what "you, Robot" can do, is very limited, for example you do not even have the ability to climb a ladder with an object in hand. You can barely jump anywhere, unless the game has predetermined that you can jump this distance. Screw running around, get on with the story!
It is the story, ultimately, where the Talos Principle shines. There is a reason for *everything*, from the world you are in, to EL0HIM, to why you are collecting Sigils, and the obnoxious Milton Library Assistant that you engage with through the terminals in the game. Through various documents found on these terminals, QR codes found in the world, and the amazing voice recordings of a female scientist, you get a glimpse of why you are, and possibly what you are.
Through these bits of information the game reveals its central question of what it means to be a person, a denomination typically reserved for humans. If you are only in it for the puzzles, you'll probably have a good time with the Talos Principle but it'll be a brief and shallow experience. If you take the time to collect information and figure out what's going on, you will be provided with many answers, many perspectives, and it is ultimately up to you to consider; what it means to be human, to be a person, or to even be conscious.

The town started as soon as our spaceship crashed. Three of us, Leeta, my wife, trevor, my uncle, and I were the only survivors. We began to build, I was the miner and builder, Leeta was the gardener and cook, and trevor was the doctor and inventor. Soon, our little home was blessed with a new survivor, I don't remember his name, but I always called him steve the failure. Steve was an assassin that could only shoot. and when he did, he fired all the bullets. Whatever. We made him our hunter, and he went about killing every animal he saw. And he was good. Then winter came. The Crops that were still in the ground died, and the animals turned mean. Then the raiders came, and stole trevor away. We never saw him again, I still have the necklace that belonged to my mother her gamve to me. I blamed steve for our loss, he didn't care, he could never care. He just seemed incapable of it.
In the spring, I found out that Leeta was with child. I was the happiest i have ever been. Our love had culminated in a child. Then, one day, while she was in the fields, she was attacked by a pack of manhunting elephants. I held her in my arms as she died. Tears fell down my face as I buried my wife in a ditch that steve had the gall to call a grave.
I took my anger our on steve. It was just us now, I couldn't hurt him, I couldn't hurt anyone, not the elephants that came to kill my wife and unborn child, not the raiders that took my uncle, and not the man that I despised. I lost control, my eyes went red, and I attacked steve, until he had beaten me unconscience. He totally destroyed my nose and ears, and I gave him a bruise on his right tibia. Serves him right.
That night, as I lay in my bed, I hear the raiders come, their drums pound in the night, I hear the crack of the hunting rifle from steve, but since he fires so fast he just didn't aim. I hear his rifle fire abruptly stop, I hear new sounds of fire. I don't like fire, not since that accident when I was a kid. I'll just lay here for a little while longer. They are in the house, I see them, one punch and i'm on the ground, helpless, they put a sack over my head, hoist me over their raider's leader's shoulder, I just hope that they opened up that wall that I suspect was the house of an ancient danger...
