Fantastic. A must-have classic for music gamers.
What impressed me most is their idea that, a whole plot can be added to a very simple kind of gameplay. You "chu" and "hey" all the way with Ulala, saving the Space President and breaking the evil plan. You meet accidents. You fight, and then ally with the police. You rush for a save, only to run into an ambush. You die and get revived. You defeat an enemy who used to be your friend. And of course there's the final showdown.
And the music is just awesome. In every part the music gives a different feeling that perfectly fits the corresponding scenario, yet the same theme keeps appearing once in a while. The voice actors also do well. Not fully satisfying, but well (personal opinion: the Japanese voiceover sounds better than the English one). As for graphics, well, just don't expect too much from a 2002 game. A recent update added support for big resolutions and FXAA, so things should look at least okay. The dancing is pretty sexy though.
You play the game simply by repeating whatever command is chanted to you, such as "up, down, up, down, chu, chu, chu". It sounds easy, and yes, it is easy. What's hard is the hidden command. You have to press keys at specific moments during cutscenes. This is not QTE: there aren't any obvious hints for these, so you have to research and remember when to do this. Only by hitting all the hidden commands can you get a full score. I suppose the purpose of adding this is to add difficulty and replayability, but sometimes these commands get way too hard to hit. And since the stages are really long, it takes too much time to try again after a failed attempt.
Conclusion: overall, this game is fabulous. Classical. So classical that Michael Jackson himself came to play a role. There are certain aspects that people may not like, but they don't ruin the game as a whole. Recommended to any music game player, and other players looking for a never-before-seen genre of gaming.
P.S. Sega really gave us a big surprise by making an update TWELVE years after the original game shipped. This update fixed almost all existing problems with the previous version, such as you had to tweak system registry to make the configuration tool work, as well as added support for achievements, high resolutions, V-sync and FXAA. However I still encountered two problems after this update:
1. Occasionally the game goes out of sync with the music. I met this problem without V-sync, so I turned it on, and now all characters have disappeared. WTF?
2. Though the new configuration tool makes English voiceover the default option, my game still uses the Japanese one. Fixed by changing the option to Japanese, and then back to English again. Just a one-time problem.

I almost recommend Sora. Almost. The story's great, I love the characters (if not a bit too much), and there's options for which weapons you want to use to bring variety to the game. However...
It's not very fun to play.
It
fun at first; I accepted how challenging it was. But then, as the game progressed, it just got worse and worse; rather than feeling like a battle of self-improvement to conquer the game, it felt like a constant battle of attrition to just get by. It's very rare for a game to stay in that perfect balance between "Very difficult" and "enjoyable to play". However, it is entirely possible for a game to be extremely difficult yet still feel like an enjoyable experience throughout the entire game; titles like Furi, Risk of Rain, Crypt of the Necrodancer and Hotline Miami did it for me, for example. When playing other "hard" games, it feels like I can always improve upon something, learn from the previous attempt, or at least have some motivation to continue. Sora starts out with those qualities, but loses them as you progress through the game. Whether or not I manage to make it just a bit farther in each level feels like luck more than skill after a while.
Ironically enough, the weapons the game starts you out with are the most viable, and the 'meta' way of playing is to abuse the dash mechanic to maximize DPS while keeping your heat maxed out at 300% (meaning you'll die super fast if you make any mistakes). However, the dash is difficult to control (especially if playing with a controller) and the game's fast-paced enough as-is. Also, ironically, the tutorial hints towards avoiding this kind of play. I think if the game was slowed down just a bit (at least on easy mode), it'd be a lot more enjoyable as you could actually react to the things on screen; that's part of what makes bullet hell games manageable to play.
I did manage to beat the game, but I don't feel very accomplished about it. It wasn't quite a waste of time, but there are far better titles that you can invest your time in to "git gud" at. I'd only recommend this game if you're a masochist, play regular bullet hell games at 1.5x speed, want the 100% Orange Juice DLC character, or a combination thereof.

I love rhythm games. From Dance Dance Revolution to Just Dance and everything in between, if it's got a good soundtrack and good controls I am there playing (or failing) to my heart's content. I have a history with space channel 5, since I played it on the PlayStation2 as a package ( the original and part 2) and although the game was a hard as hell simon says rhythm game with no prompts other than “memorize these moves or kiss your ratings goodbye” I welcomed the challenge. Nothing made me happier than beating both games the first time as a kid and I was the rhythm queen!
So when my friends gifted me space channel 5 part 2 on steam I was so excited to revisit Ulala and save space Michael Jackson all over again. When I played the first stage a number of concerns ran through my mind as the intro started playing. The first one being:
1. Why is this not in HD?
The game starts and I quickly figure out the commands for CHU and HEY are S and D. Not really the best setup when on a keyboard which led to my next concern.
2. I can't customize my input style? Oh man I'm gonna ruin my S and D keys by the time this is over with.

Despite getting used to the keyboard controls it was overall enjoyable...and then came the second stage: the space park...aquarium..garden place and oh god was it painful. Most people that play this know about stage 2 because the guitar battle with Pudding this was my favorite part of the stage. I say was because I quickly found out about the keyboard's unresponsive commands in the worst way possible. The part I could easily do on console with flair turned into frustration and borderline rage. Pudding wiped the floor with me when before I could do it perfectly. My hands were tired so I took a break, and closed the game, knowing that the game auto saves once you clear a stage. Only to come back to it days later to realize NONE of my progress was saved. NONE OF MY PROGRESS WAS SAVED.
This raised huge a red flag for me. Despite me only losing stage 1 progress I know how difficult and long the later stages get. And yes, its possible to do this whole game in one setting but I don't recommend it. The people you save, the costumes you unlock the secrets you find will not save at all. Meaning you could play this game perfectly get to the end and then never be able to play a new game with a different outfit unless you just leave the game running.
No, that's unforgivable. Ulala, get your act together. This is not how a famous space reporter should represent themselves on steam. There have been updates that help with a few of these problems but the game is still not smooth enough for me to recommend it with a clear conscious. Sorry Ulala, I'm canceling your show.

I've played some strange MS-DOS games in my lifetime, and Zoombinis was always one of those obcure oddities that will always have a soft spot in my heart. I remember playing this game on the computers in my third grade classroom whenever it was recess on a rainy day. Zoombinis a puzzle strategy game where you must guide a heard of blue innocent creatures called Zoombinis to a safe haven called Zoombiniville (great name). Each puzzle is a point-and-click as you spend the game thinking about how to apporach each puzzle without putting any of your Zoombinis in harms way. Think of it as a kiddie watered-down version of Lemmings without the stress of keeping track of every single member in your heard. Each puzzle gets more complex as your progress and after carrying one heard all the way to their safe haven you must direct the next group down that same path. To avoid repetition and boredom the game has branching paths  where you can choose the sets of puzzles you want to complete and this makes solving these puzzles more worthwhile. The game is also nice enough to increase the difficulty by the time you've done at least one or two runs of a certain path. There's even a practice mode to help train you on the puzzles that give you some trouble. The game's graphics have also been enhanced from the original game's format. I like how some of backdrops looks like paintbrush strokes. This game can help anyone improve their critical thinking skills if they spend enough time learning the ropes. $15 isn't a bad price, but if possible, wait until the Steam sales for a price cut. The game provides enough otherworldly, but relaxing atmosphere that makes brings out that springtime joy. If you haven't played this game before, try it out! You might like it.

A pleasant palate cleanser of a game, well worth the price of admission if you’re after something a little different from the usual platforming tropes.
At it's heart Eden is a simple platformer, each level or “garden” has five items to collect, with a cumulative total of these items unlocking additional levels. To traverse these levels you have a jump and grip/swing mechanic, the physics involved in which are slightly “floaty” therefore offering a good degree of mid-air readjustment. Reaching the higher areas of a level requires the player to pollinate plants, a process achieved by picking up nearby items, or destroying enemies in the vicinity, with larger pollen rewards generated for destroying multiple enemies in a single jump. Players are required to accomplish all of this against the clock, though that clock can be topped up by acquiring some items dotted around the gardens.
There are no great bold innovations to be seen here, the pleasure of the game is derived from the fact that the design of the game mechanics, the visuals and the sound all come together to make a very pleasant gaming experience. In an odd juxtaposition of perception and content, the easy going almost Zen-like meditative vibe of Eden in the early stages is tempered with some really rather infuriating moments in the later in the game, but that’s alright, because you can simply drop back a few levels and do a run through an earlier level for no other reason than the fact the world of Eden is a very pleasant one to visit.
Finally it should be noted this is the definitive version of the game, controls redesigned for mouse and keyboard, several annoyances ironed out from the original PSN version (Thankfully you no longer have to collect all 5 items in one run to clear a level), all of the Encore content included, and the addition of a nifty “warp” function which allows for the rapid repair of any mistimed jump.

Pixeljunk Eden is an indie game developed by Q-Game. The music for the game was composed by a man who is referred to in game as Baiyon. Indie games are projects involving smaller teams with stricter budgets and often showcase a much needed level of creativity in the gaming industry today.
The game involves a tadpole like creature soaring seamlessly through lush environments and vibrant flora in order to collect a special type of object called Spectra.
The levels are referred to as gardens and the player takes an active role in their creation. Various floating pollen clouds are scattered through the gardens and touching them causes the closest un-blossomed flower to begin to bloom.
As the plants grow the garden bursts into life and new visual imagery and heights can be reached. As the player continues through the gardens the flowers blooming become increasingly larger and more detailed.
The music in the game is what sets it apart from a lot of other games in the gaming industry. Entirely composed by Baiyon, the soundtrack showcases amazing techno and sublime trance that adds to the immersive experience of the game.
Pixeljunk Eden is a captivating and innovative game idea that offers players of all ages a visually spectacular and musically rich experience.

Educational games are often some of the worst games out there. The main reason being that they either A: Hold the players hand through the whole thing, resulting in the player not learning anything. B: Are boring to the point where just playing the game is tedious. Or C: Don't keep a player invested enough to get the most out of the game.
Zoombinis however avoids each of these issues. For the first problem I listed, most games feel the need to make the puzzles they provide insultingly easy or outright give the answer to the player, Zommbinis however will only give the player what they need to complete the puzzle and nothing more. Leaving the player to figure things out for themselves.
As for the second problem, most educational games feature bland enviroments, characters, and very bland music. Zoombinis avoids this by delivering beutiful enviroments that feel alive, characters that have actual personalities, and music that you will remember for years. (I know I did)
As for the final problem, most educational games don't offer much in terms of variety, often times players are met with the same puzzle over and over again. Zoombinis however avoids this by having each puzzle be different, and even in some puzzles that feel similar to each other like the Allergic Cliffs and the Stone Cold Caves, have something that sets them apart from each other. Not only that but due to the games steady difficulty curve the game stays fresh for far longer than most.
However while I will continue to praise this game for being such a masterpiece among educational games, it does have its flaws much like every game.
For one, the game does become boring after you've saved a couple dozen zoombinis, and some puzzles on the higher difficulties can prove very difficult, even for some adults. However apart from those flaws, everything else is just nit picking.
All in all, I strongly believe that Zoombinis is one of the finest games for any child and adult. The game is fun and beneficial to children but can provide a welcoming challenge for adults. Personally, I give zoombinis a full 10/10.

The game takes place in Edward's Island, in the late hours of the night. The player takes control of Alexandra, one of the five teenagers that go to the island presumably to have a good time, but their adventure takes a quick turn as Alex uses her pocket radio to tune into some strange signals in a cave.
One of the coolest aspects of the game is the pocket radio Alex carries around. The pocket radio can be used to tune into signals, find anomalies (there are about 12 of them), open certain locks and interact with objects when there's a red light glowing from them. At some point in the game, you get your hands on an enhanced pocket radio, which has about 100 different frequencies and opens up over 10 new collectibles to be found throughout the island.
In some cases, if you tune into some very specific frequencies you can hear music as well as people speaking.
The game offers a great thrilling experience with an extremely spooky atmosphere as Alex and her friends try to stop the ghostly menace. All the areas in the island are well thought out and can be explored if one would like to dive deeper into the story.
This game requires at least 3 different playthroughs to 100%, taking about 15 hours to do so.

Negative reviews says the game gets repetitive. False.
If you hesitate to get the game, buy it when it's on sale. It's a steal.

Sora is a bullet hell shmup developed by Orange Juice and localized by Fruitbat Factory. The player controls Sora, a girl with extraordinary powers fighting during the time of war, following her desire to protect innocents and once again see the clear sky.
Graphically, the game is... well okay. The backgrounds are generally mostly static and one-color, occassionally giving some actual land to look at, with most of the characters portrayed as sprites, small and sufficient. Portraits during cutscenes do a good job of showing off details and conveying emotions of each character, but that's not much to make up for the rest. The bullets are bright and colorful, just like in most bullet hell shmups, except for live ammo types for obvious reasons.
Sound-design, it's mostly just techno that doesn't stand out. Basic sound effects do what they're supposed to, I guess.
Gameplay-wise, that's where this becomes interesting. The stages have the usual layout of going through a gauntlet of enemies with a midboss in the middle before the end-stage boss. Unlike most standard bullet hell shmups, you get a lot of freedom of movement - Sora possesses a dash ability that lets her jet around and graze beam weapons taking no damage. However it increases her Heat level, which increases damage taken should she get hit before it falls down. Also, besides beam weapons there is live ammo which is slower, but more powerful and ungrazeable via dash. Controlling Sora while she's dashing can be difficult, and it's often easy to, in the heat of battle, just bump into live ammo and suffer a solid amount of damage.
You get to bring three weapons with yourself, two normal ones which can be either beam or live ammo (former being faster, latter being stronger) and one special - a melee weapon of choice, dealing a lot of damage but having short range. Using any of them forces you to stand still for a moment, which leaves you vulnerable to fire. Choosing your time to attack is key to survival.
As much as I'd like to talk about the story, which after the rather amazing intro I feel would be deep and touching, I can't get very far into the game.
This is a major issue with the game, which unfortunately kills the whole experience for me.
This game is hard.
Now I don't have anything against hard games or bullet hell shmups, in fact I've been enjoying
games for years now, experience with those does not help much in trying to play through Sora. The gameplay is just too different. Still, I see that beating the game on Easy would certainly be possible.
Except it's hard for the
reasons.
No health pickups. No extra lives. No continues.
If you die during a stage, you are kicked back to stage select screen, and you get nothing to your name. Even on Easy, by the time I reach the boss I'm all beat up due to taking damage all throughout and having basically no way to recover it, and I don't get much time to practice the boss' patterns before I inevitably die in a couple hits and have to start over. This is a textbook example of Check Point Starvation aspect of Fake Difficulty right there - the only real way to "save" your progress and refill your health is to beat a stage, and for someone who's just starting out, those stages, especially when you get no health pickups or extra lives whatsoever, are marathons in the war of attrition. Your only real hope of progressing further is to play this game like you're walking on a tightrope, until via sheer trial and error you inevitably get good enough to somehow go through the stage, and then repeat the same process with the next one. This isn't what I would consider fun, especially if a simple addition of health pickups and / or extra lives would eliminate this issue completely.
Can I reccommend this game? Unfortunately no. As much as I wanna see the rest of this story and the game is fun enough, having to play it like a test where less than perfect result means going back to the start of the current stage is too frustrating. Don't bother unless you're alright with repeating the same stage over and over until you finally master it and be able to progress further.

There’s something about the atmosphere in this one.
It’s hard to pin down, and so, so many factors contribute to it, but it’s got this hauntingly beautiful, relaxing yet slightly spooky vibe that only a small sliver of games are able to achieve. An intoxicating mixture of isolation, voyeurism (you are privy to all sorts of mundane, personal, and ethical insights into the lives of the scientists via the audio logs), communication with AI, wonderful restrained ambient music, breathtaking vistas, and really, really good puzzles jam-packed with deadly obstacles. And despite the often melancholy feeling and deep philosophical topics, The Talos Principle isn’t afraid to lighten up with moments of very welcome, very funny comedy, which helps set it apart from the likes of Myst, The Witness, and other more serious puzzle based adventures.
I enjoyed every moment of this game, including the equally excellent Road to Gehenna expansion. I still find it remarkable that the team behind the long-running Serious Sam franchise had this in them, and I’m stoked that they’ll continue this venture with a sequel. For puzzle fans and adventure gamers, I give this my highest recommendation.

Sora is a great bullet hell game,
anyone who plays bullet hell games or especially ones from Fruitbat (or Orange Juice) know they can be quite brutal for difficulty, Sora however is a perfect balance.
After endless struggles with Suguri, i tried sora, not only does the game feel possible but it still stays a challenge, i have only done easy through (bullet hell is the only game i play easy mode, i swear) and it was really tough but possible, a few retries, learning how bosses fight and a hard battle with Hime/Suguri later and i got to see the end game.
For a bullet hell the game it is great, most bullet hell don't have much of a story but Sora does actually, Sora (the ultimate weapon) is fighting alone to put an end to the war, unfortunately not many share her wish, you fight through the bosses to get your wish. The story has some sad moments, especially is you are able sympathise with characters, keeping it spoiler free i will just say i was sad at both my meeting with Sham and the end battle with Star breaker (the ending is great though!)
The soundtrack is brilliant, i never really buy the ost for games as whilst some are good i feel i will never actually get my money worth but in this case i just kind of wanted the ost, from the great electro background musics to the even vocalled track, i just wanted it. It really is great for creating a setting, the bgm for the stages is commonly quite catchy and works well considering your struggle against the mobs whilst the vocals for the bosses are really mood setting.
If you enjoy bullet hell games i strongly suggest trying Sora, i enjoyed Suguri and QP shooting dangerous and now can say this takes my favourite of them.
Additionally, if you play 100% Orange juice, you get a free extra character (Sora Military), i brought the game a while back mainly for the character extra (i did plan to play it eventually), but now i know i got a great game and the character extra was a awesome bonus.
Seriously, it is worth a try if this is your style game. If you aren't into the bullet hell shooters, you might not enjoy this as much as others.

Want a cheap way to keep yourself entertained for hours on end? This game.
The Review in Short:
Pros -
Classes feel different
Random level components feel nice (for the most part)
You can sit down and only play a single level (but you'll find that hard once you get started)
The bosses are interesting
The graphics fit the game
Cons -
Sometimes the random elements in a level will be placed over pits and places where they shouldn't be
The voices in the game are bad (I mean bad)
The chapters stick around for too many levels
Item attributes aren't explained properly (unless I am missing something)
Wall of text and explainatons:
So this is a good game and it is incredibly addicting. I've played through most of the game with two classes now, the redneck and the pyromancer. The creators have done a great job at making each class feel different even with the limited number of skills they have. The arenas feel very different for the most part, but I feel that the chapters stick around for far too long. After about 3 bosses the chapter gets old and it feels like the pacing needs to be a little quicker for this type of game. Along with the bosses come the items (or relics as they're called in game) and these have some very interesting attributes. The bad thing is that if they do something other than stat boosting then you really have to guess at their effects and this is easy for your first few items, but if you have 25 items on all at the same time it is hard to tell what the new item is doing. I think that this could be fixed by having tooltips from hovering items in the pause screen or by having an ingame encyclopedia of some sort that lets you go back after encountering an item to see what it does. Another negative is that sometimes things like chests, bushes, and other destructible things can be placed 'out of bounds' on like pits or bodies of water that you can't get to without certain items.
All in all I absolutely love this game. It is very fun and incredibly addicting. I can't tell you to buy it enough, because it is worth the money. You will get your money's worth of entertainment.

I can't really recommend this game.  It's nothing at all like the original Borderlands games.
This game is like watching a story on TV, with the exception that once in a while you have a few seconds to quickly press a button to force the character to move in a given direction (or else you die and have to start over at a previous checkpoint and watch the dialog leading up to the action all over again).  Alternately, you might have just a few seconds to select one of three different dialog choices, and depending on which you chose it may alter the flow of the story somewhat.
It felt like playing "Space Ace" or "Dragon's Lair" (early 1980's laser video disc games), in that you didn't really interact with the game very much.  For most of the game you are a spectator watching TV.  That's not what I had in mind when I bought the game.  Sigh.
I will admit that the story line is a bit intriguing, but it doesn't really tie in with the other three Borderlands games, so it was hard to really care about the story like I did for Borderlands.  Yeah, it's in the same basic universe, but you have different characters, different motivations, and a different setting to boot.  So why do I care about these people again?  I really had a hard time getting into it.
The other downfall is that the entire game only lasts about 2 hours - maybe a bit less even.  Sure, once you've finished you can re-start and select different dialog to see how the story changes, but honestly the outcome is going to be nearly the same no matter what.
They say there will be more content coming soon, but even if there are more stories, it's still boring to watch.  Not my kind of game I guess.

PixelJunk Eden is a tough game to describe. I am not really sure what the developers' intent was with this game... on the surface, it looks like a sort of casual interactive art piece showcasing a synergy of music and colors. But once you get deeper into it, there are increasing levels of challenge (and frustration), which go against the laid-back casual vibe. But what is it, exactly? I'm not really sure... I guess my best simple summary would be to say it's sort of like an unholy union of the artistic games "Flow" and "Flower" on the PS3 (if you've played/heard of those). Anyways, you play as some sort of little bug thing that can jump around and stick to plants. By jumping into floating spores, you release pollen that fills in seeds, which when filled, sprout new plants that allow you to reach new areas. You just keep exploring in this way until you find a special glowy thing called a "spectra", which ends the level. There are 15 levels (or "gardens", as they are called), each of which contains 5 spectra. So there is plenty of content to play through. While no major mechanics are introduced after the first few levels, the game mostly stays interesting throughout, due mostly to the diversity in the look and music. Each garden has a unique vibe, due to the music and color palette/design. As each spectra is collected, the levels evolve slightly to introduce more visual elements. It's a pretty neat effect. As I mentioned earlier, while the game is fairly simple at its core, some frustration creeps in during the latter portion of the game due to the introduction of really annoying enemies and some slightly more challenging platforming bits (the sometimes wonky controls don't help, either). It's nice for the challenge, but it also sort of goes against the enjoyable casual feel of the early parts of the game. It felt somewhat like the game had an identity crisis to me... but I dunno, maybe it's just me. That said, it is still a super enjoyable experience if you go into it not expecting some sort of blockbuster. It's a great experimental art piece that is perfect for those times when you just want to turn your mind off and get lost in a spaced out state of sights and sounds... and yes, that means it's definitely the perfect game for you if your favorite time of day is 4:20. But even if not, it's still an enjoyable experience and worth checking out.

So, deleted my previous review and writing a new one as I have just recently finished "sora".
Trying my best to keep it spoiler-free.
==
==
The game's a bullet hell, a rather unique one. It's challenging and fun. Some may say it's unfair, but once you get the hang of it, everything becomes a breeze.
You have three weapons at your disposal, the main gun, a secondary and a melee, each weapon does a unique attack whenever you attack after a dash.
There's two unique mechanic that are called Heat Gauge and Dash, the first basically serves as a balance to punish you from getting ahead of yourself with dashing by taking more damage as more heat rises, heat gauge increases from taking damage, dashing and from some certain bosses' attacks.
Dashing is self-explanatory, it's your main ability to dodge and go through enemy's projectiles (That are hopefully not live shells as those will still hit you), however the long you dash the faster your heat gauge rises, controlling this is hard and takes time to get the hang of it's manuevers.
Now, there's two kinds of enemy attacks, a projectile and live shell, the first one you can dash through, the second one you cannot, the former doesn't block your secondary attacks, but the latter can block your secondary and melee attacks. Keep that in mind.
And finally there's this special attacks called Hyper, you have a gauge over on the left side of it, and can hold up to 3 charges, it gets fueled by dashing through enemy attacks and or attacking the enemy themselves. It is very helpful and crucial at times, as it gives you a few second shield that negates any kind of damage. Each weapons has different Hyper attacks, so test them all out to know what to use at the right time.
==
==
Now, the gameplay aspects aside. The setting, story, characters and music are pretty well-done.
Sora may come off as your generic "wants to save the world"-protagonist, but this is because she doesn't know her purpose but to fight. And as you go through the game she develops more character to reflect on the things she've done and the things she've seen.
The music is trance-melody-ish, a few scores have songs in them which are nice and gives an emotional feeling to it while you listen, it suits and fits the setting of the game and the gameplay of "sora". I'd say it's one of the best underrated soundtracks I've heard in games in my opinion.
==
==
It's a pretty small game, around 500mb download and you can experience good trance bullet hell, it's a 2D side-bullet hell shooter so it shouldn't need that much in terms of system, a laptop can even run it. Just beware that on higher difficulties, means more particles to handle however.
The controls are comfortable, arrow keys for movement, Z for the main gun/confirmation, X for the secondary/cancel, C for Hyper, V for dashing, A for the melee, and S to lock on or disable lock-on/fast forward dialogues. And if you want, you can play it with a controller too!
==
==
A nifty underrated gem of a game, "sora" is a must to play even if you are not a fan of bullet hell shooters, the gameplay is fun and challenging, and the story is pretty good. It is the prequel of Suguri
which means you can play this before playing Suguri, or vice versa.
Now go on and save the world!
That's all! Thank you for reading!

Sora is an amazing, fast paced, challenging, shoot 'em up where you play as a girl named Sora (Japanese for "Sky") who was born as the ultimate weapon to fight in a war.
Let me just skip to the end here and say: Sora is a great game and despite everything I say about it, it is most certainly worth your time, so check it out!
Plot:
******
Gameplay:
************
Sora is a fast paced bullet hell, shoot 'em up and at times can be quite challenging. Sometimes the screen is so filled with projectiles it can be hard to tell where you actually are and where enemies are (especially on higher difficulties). The weapon system is quite good: Beam weapons can be passed through by dashing to charge the hyper gauge and recover health, while "Live-Ammo" projectiles cannot be dashed through, but tend to move slower and do more damage. The dash is also worked into gameplay quite well, allowing quick maneuvers to deal damage without taking to much yourself.
Pros vs. Cons:
****************
Pros:
- Very fun, but still challenging gameplay.
- Amazing story and characters (They will stay with you long after you finish the game).
- Huge variety of weapons and weapon combinations.
- Incredible Soundtrack.
- Different playable modes such as arcade mode (All levels back to back) and match mode (Boss Rush).
- Record you best runs and watch the replays.
- Anime art style.
Cons:
- Story is a little too short and although very good, could have been developed further.
- Some weapons have very limited applications and are never used.
- Replays don't record certain parts of some levels (such as Credits and Cutscenes) meaning you have to replay levels to see them again.
- The game can be brutally difficult at times.
- Voice acting is absent from almost the entire game, except the end of the second-to-last level and the last level making it feel weird and out of place. (
)
Final Words:
**************
As I said at the beginning of this review, Sora is a great game, and is most certainly worth your time. I have had more fun playing Sora than I have in a long time with most other games, and I game alot. If there is one thing to take away from this review make sure it's this: There are far worse uses of your time than Sora!

Repetitive and frustratingly unrewarding. As a mathematician and game programmer, I tried for hours to understand how this game's maths work. This was all in vain: 100% chance to throw sand, yet does nothing more than half the time; 40 dmg somehow becomes 300 damage (with no crit). The value of attack speed is never explained and makes no sense (it's not attacks per second, nor attacks per 1/10th of second). Considering that levelling and talenting your character tends to make little difference in the game due to artifacts being so powerful in comparison, this makes it very hard to enjoy the game or customize/optimize characters to your liking.
There's also a large amount of easy-to-fix bugs which make the game even more frustrating, such as dungeons or crypts spawning at the same time a boss does, leaving you no way of accessing it (not exactly pleasing when it happens twice and you have gotten no crypts or dungeons for the past 30 mins or so), particles getting stuck on the map, arrow indicator pointing to non-existent mobs, boss spawning with entire waves, and the worst of all, save files getting corrupt.
The game also only gives you 6 character slots, meaning you can't even get all of the achievements without deleting at least 4 characters (5 classes + optional hardcore mode = 10 characters).
Glad I got this off a cheap bundle. Really not worth the price on Steam.

This game is incredible, and although it is pretty pricey, it's worth every penny. I currently have over 150 hours played on this game, and I don't plan on stopping. Its so satisfying building a functioning colony and whatching it grow, and also entertaining when it inevitably gets torn down by some curve ball the game throws that you somehow forgot to plan for. The way I see it, there are two ways to play this game ( or I suppose 3). #1: Get emotionally attached to characters, get into each of their stories, and craft a nice colony, playing without permadeath so that you can go back to saves when something goes wrong. #2: Enable permadeath, play on a hard difficulty, don't get attached to your colonists, watch them come and go without getting very upset, and making every descion based on the good of the colony in the long-run. And I guess #3 would be play on permadeath with emotional attachment, but then your just asking for emotional trama :)
But in all seriousness, this is an amazing game, and if you like top down base builders, or just whacky stories( and I mean really weird stories, for a good hour before I bought the game, I read the stories of colonies people built and then wrote in their reviews) Then you should really get this game, trust me, its worth it.

I played this game before, like a year and a half ago, but then I bought Overwatch and forgot about Dirty Bomb. Nowadays, I was looking for something that would keep me away from OW so I installed DB again.
Was not disappointed. Game is alot of fun. Requires some serious skill when you're infront of somebody who knows the game through and throughout so you actually have to "git gud" at aiming, moving, remembering the map overlay, staying together with teammmates and play appropriate merc to fill in the medic or shielder spot in your team.
Back in the day, Splash Damage developed a game called Wolfenstein Enemy Territory. It was totally free of charge and I remember it was a huge deal to release a full, free, multiplayer game only. ET was actually the only one of it's kind if I remember correctly. No additional ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, no microtransactions, stupid limitations, adverts mid-game or ingame currency. All classes unlocked, all modes unlocked, no limits, just start the game, connect to a server and it was just you with your skill.
Today it's a different time we live in. Today, when there's a ton of "free" to "play" games on Steam, pretty much every single one of these is pumped up with microtransactions and in-game currency. Dirty Bomb is no different I'm affraid. Biggest complain I have is paying for the mercs to unlock and use them in game. I mean I get it - the game is free at it's core and developers have to make some money out of it if they want to develop more games, but come on. Most credits I got for a win so far was 250 credits. The cheapest merc costs around 30K credits if I'm not mistaken, which is around 5€ if you wanna pay with real money upfront. All up to 40K and 50K credits for a playable characted in the game that only has 3 mercs unlocked out of 10+. So to unlock every single merc, you gotta pay the full premium price for the game or grind extensively for months, until you get measly 40K credits for a merc that was in free rotation and you want to play with. That's not exactly a definition of a free game but more like pay2win and players who bought the whole game have enormous advantage over newbies. Thankfully, matchmaking seems to be good enough to not pair you with higher level players with every single merc unlocked and you actually get paired with people who have roughly the same composition as you do, which is good enough. So paying for game seems to be optional, but it still doesn't have to be here. Paying for loadout cards, that's fair enough. But paying for mercs is not such a good idea to me. Especially when I can't really recommend this game to any of my friends, because they're all like: "U wot m8, u only have 3 classes unlocked from the start and u have to grind4rest? No thanks bruh, Imma go play Destiny some more!". Apart from that, game is alot of fun and reminds me of old days when there was only Wolfenstein ET around.
So yeah, first complain goes to paying for additional content, the second complain is about performance. I'm playing it on extremely low-end laptop (Intel Core i3, 8GB of RAM, Intel HD 4400 integrated GPU) and I've been able to run Overwatch on this same setup just fine on low graphics, among few other games from 3 or 4 years ago. Dirty Bomb is giving me headaches. Main menu is lagging so bad it's almost unplayable. I tried lowering graphic setting all the way down to 800x600 resolution, with every single option set to "Low" but it still doesn't matter. When I'm in main menu and selecting a game mode, it runs at appr. 10 FPS. When I'm in the actual game it runs just fine, ocassionally it drops down to 15 FPS which is annoying as hell, but it doesn't last long, couple of seconds usually but it's still a pain in the butt. Once I'm done with the round, I'm lucky if I get back to main menu, because it lags so freaking bad. I've searched for a solution, nothing useful came along. Users were reporting menu lag as far back as 2014 and 2015 and they didn't found no solution for it. I found a guy saying that you need to put some command line in launch options of the game on Steam, but it still doesn't work. It takes like 3 minutes for the game to start up and I have to pray that it won't lag out in the first 5 minutes of playing.
So no, I cannot really recommend this game, but I'm speaking strictly from my point of view. Had this lagging issue been fixed, I'd play it hellova lot more and probably recommend it here on store page, but I cannot do that, unfortunately. Please, fix this issue with lagging, cuz I cannot be the only one with this problem. I can't really recommend this game.  It's nothing at all like the original Borderlands games.
This game is like watching a story on TV, with the exception that once in a while you have a few seconds to quickly press a button to force the character to move in a given direction (or else you die and have to start over at a previous checkpoint and watch the dialog leading up to the action all over again).  Alternately, you might have just a few seconds to select one of three different dialog choices, and depending on which you chose it may alter the flow of the story somewhat.
It felt like playing "Space Ace" or "Dragon's Lair" (early 1980's laser video disc games), in that you didn't really interact with the game very much.  For most of the game you are a spectator watching TV.  That's not what I had in mind when I bought the game.  Sigh.
I will admit that the story line is a bit intriguing, but it doesn't really tie in with the other three Borderlands games, so it was hard to really care about the story like I did for Borderlands.  Yeah, it's in the same basic universe, but you have different characters, different motivations, and a different setting to boot.  So why do I care about these people again?  I really had a hard time getting into it.
The other downfall is that the entire game only lasts about 2 hours - maybe a bit less even.  Sure, once you've finished you can re-start and select different dialog to see how the story changes, but honestly the outcome is going to be nearly the same no matter what.
They say there will be more content coming soon, but even if there are more stories, it's still boring to watch.  Not my kind of game I guess.

Dark Messiah is a first person RPG, set in the universe of "Might & Magic". From what I can tell Arkane studios really seems to have  a patern in there games, which is they always manage to miss some thing, which in this game ironically, was its story line. Its not so much as its bad, its just really cliche and not very origanal. The detail in this game is amazing, as is the combat system(hasnt been topped in 11 years), very good voice acting, despite its poor story, and some really neat scenes you wont forget. I will never forget fighting my first Orc in this game, I slashed at him he deflected my blow, i blocked his, I hit with two quick strokes and then, he picked me up and threw me into a wall. Needless to say the combat in this game is the reason its so big. Any ways this isnʻt gonna be a broad way reveiw so ill get on with the pros and cons.
Pros:
+Good combat(you can kick people of cliffs, ITS AWESOME)
+Good voice acting
+"Classses"(point system, you wont be able too unlock every thing, but you dont need to specailize in any certain skill tree.)
+Secrets(not mentioning the game has alot of replay ability alone)
+Bad♥♥♥♥♥weopons
+Sick magical attacks (telekinesis is amazing)
+Fatalities
+Multiple endings
-/+ The stealth system if fullly decked is very exploitable but it doesnt remove any thing from the experience over all, its just kinda cheap.
Cons:
-Not a very "grabbing" story line, which is kinda odd considering these are the same guys that made the Dishonoed Games WHICH are known for being really story Rich
-Glitches, but forgiveable as none of them are game breaking.
-The necroplis is a little insane and not very balanced, I mean yes I beat the game on the hardest difficulty, but IT took a lot of time to do so.
-Ending boss battle isnt bad, its pretty fun, but I would have expected it to be a bit more epic, but over all still fun.
Over all iʻd highly suggest this game to any one whos a fan of "Might & Magic" or some one who REALLY likes sword play, cause belive me after playing this game i cant play other sword fighting games with out not feeling "as satisfyed, like when I play this one. This game is certainly worthy of  a sequal.

*LE GASP* How could I have reviewed Suguri but not Sora!? Blasphemy!?
Anyways... Sora, like Suguri, is a bullet hell style shoot 'em up with unique mechanics. We follow our protagonist Sora, a war machine created solely to end said war, fighting back against those who choose to disturb the peace and continue fighting, meeting some familiar faces along the way. The game consists of 7 regular stages and a bonus stage, which may seem small but more than makes up for it in both the difficulty and replayability value.
Sora is in no way as hard as Suguri, however there were some fairly major tweaks in the gameplay to stop the more cheesy strats, such as adding heat penalties for constantly dashing to turn sharply and cancelling delays after shooting. This said, however, the game can be very challenging to those who seek such a challenge with the hard and special difficulties, as well as having a moderate challenge for those like myself who were apparently just never given those bullet hell genes.
The game in general runs smoothly with fairly little lag even on awful laptops such as mine, and the animations are very fluid. The game looks beautiful when we get half a second to look at it, and each little area seems unique, from a snowy alpine region to a barren desert to a gloomy city, never seeming bland or unimaginative to me in the least. The character designs are also very interesting to me, genuinely making me want to get to know these characters more and what caused them to do the things they did.
The game also has it's own little way of teaching you the game mechanics without really teaching you at all. The bosses seem to serve as tutorials, forcing you to get to grips with a certain mechanic and punishing hard if you fail to do so. For example in the first boss battle, the boss uses many fast energy based attacks to force you to learn dashing, whilst the second teaches you how to deal with projectiles that cannot be dashed through and melee attacks. I always find it charming when games like this don't just pop up a little text box, and instead teach you the mechanics through many many tears fighting that one boss over and over until you finally get it... Gotta love it...
The gameplay itself is extremely intuitive, as someone who didn't own a controller for a while, I managed to beat the whole game with keyboard. There aren't a whole lot of buttons to have to learn, there's no having to press 15 buttons at the same time to pull off a super secret special mega ultra attack, just a select few, and that's really all the game needs. The game forces you to make quick decisions but instead of forcing you to fit in a tiny gap between bullets, there are several ways to dodge attacks or beat a boss. The starting weapons are actually pretty good in my opinion, the game doesn't force you to grind in order to get better weapons, instead encourages you to try with what you have, and if that doesn't work, well tough, you just need to get better. By the end of the game, you'll probably have unlocked the majority if not all of the weapons, so it's nice to just go back, play through the stages again and wonder 'what if I used this', or 'what if I did this differently', making the game very enjoyable to play through again.
And if, after playing the game through once, you're thinking 'IF I HAVE TO FIGHT THAT STUPID STAGE 3 MINIBOSS ONE MORE TIME TABLES WILL BE FLIPPED', well you're in luck. The boss battle mode makes for a nice, stressful time, especially on special difficulty, but it's definitely nice to not have to do the whole stage again just to practice the end boss if you're trying on a higher difficulty.
But I mean one good thing in playing the stages over and over and dying over and over is being able to experience the amazing soundtrack Sora has to offer. Honestly in my first playthrough I was too stressed to pay attention, it took a friend pointing out certain tracks for me to realise how wonderful they were, and oh my are they wonderful. After buying the soundtrack I honestly can't name a single track I dislike, even the main menu theme... And that's saying something after you've finished one of the two songs with lyrincs in them, both of which are a nice touch, and not grating as I understand lyrical tracks can be sometimes in games. Honestly I'd buy this game just to listen to the soundtrack, it's just that wonderful.
In conclusion, Sora is a wonderful addition to the bullet hell genre, subverting the norm of 'just shoot and try to fit yourself into these tiny gaps' and improving very much over the original, Suguri, which is also a great game in it's own right. With a great atmosphere, great graphics and a much greater soundtrack, Sora has probably become my favourite bullet hell I've ever played, having probably the 3rd or 4th spot in my favourite OSTs list. I'd recommend buying this dut to all these reasons, and it being fairly cheap certainly helps.

My most resent set up of Rim World was my best and my worst. I started out great. Got electricity. I had plenty of food. I had two cash crops “corn that became simple meals and herbal meds” that I was selling to the traders. Even got up to 7 people Everything was going great.
Till one day. It was like every other day. Just a normal day. I just got through the hard summer and now in the fall with no heat injuries, which was a first. Everything was looking up. Then a Raid came. I have already been through a bunch. So, I knew the drill. I had sandbags already lined up in a defensive positon. I posted up all my people. All in the right spots. They all had great weapons for that point in the game. Snipers, and LMG. What made this raid different was something I did not see till it was too late. I normally check the enemy’s weapons to know what I a dealing with. But I missed one enemy, and guess what that mother f**Ker had. “FRAG GERANDES”. We starting firing. I got two of the three down. I had this in the bag till that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ threw that grenade and killed two of my colonist. It was now a bad day. One was a best friend and a fiancé. The other was a best friend to the whole group. But what I learn is that Rim World is not for happy endings. The first heat wave was setting in. the problem is that this one was the worst. I had two coolers for the colonists, but it was not enough. They were going down with heat strokes. I was getting worried. But I kept my drive. I quickly threw in that new cooler, but it was not fast enough.  With only one to two more days left on that mood drop. The heat wave took out 3 of my last 5. My last two were pushing, but then the worst came. One of my last two ran out to mine something. She went down. I made my last guy go save her. I was lucky too. He knew some medical skill. I thought I could first save my doc then the rest. But then that red flashy box drops down. “MAD F**KING AMIANL.” I was like RUUUNNNNNN!!!!!, but that animal caught up to him. It bit him and he went down. All my colonist was unable to walk. I watched in shock for 10secs before I turned off my computer. I was hurt that my best colony ended up with the worst ending.
The moral of the story is to f**king check every enemy, because those freaking FRAG GRENADES ARE NO JOKE. :’’(

Divekick is probably the most accurate title for any game ever. The idea of the game being only two buttons (dive and kick) is a fresh breath from the world of competitive fighters where 6 or 7 button strings are not uncommon. Yet there's a subtle complexity to a game with only two buttons. The spacing of the characters and mindgames that go on with such a short round period make for a very deep sense of strategy, despite a shallow control scheme.
The characters are diverse in playstyle and feel very different from one another. The story mode for each character is pretty short and the cutscenes could stand to be better, but story is never a big part of fighting games anyway. It can be a little iritaing using the two button control scheme to navigate menus, but you get used to it.
The online mode is as barren as you would imagine with a fighting game, but joining a reliable steam group can fix that. The "Casual Divekick Tournament Group" that I'm subscribed to here on steam meets almost every Friday at 10pm EST for maybe an hour to set up a round robin style tournament. Without them, I think this game would be tragically left as a competitive curiosity for LAN parties.
*Edit as of 11/24/2015: Divekick is now $5 for a non-sale price. I feel like this is a very solid price point for this game and hope that the couple new characters that have been added since release help to foster more players online. A great buy at this price now.

Tales from the Borderlands is an outstanding game (which I would definitely recommend) that is made by Telltale Games that canonically comes after Borderlands 2.

For example, the choice you make at the end of Episode 2 makes a HUGE impact on what happens throughout Episode 3.

You don't even to know a single thing about Borderlands to play this game to understand it. The only difference is that you won't remember some of the returning characters and details that return from the previous games. I honestly have only played Borderlands 2 and that helped with that, but as mentioned before it is not necessary. You can tell that Telltale has made sure that this game led up to the hype.

Borderlands is a simple game: go here, shoot some stuff, collect a whole bunch of loot, and repeat ad infinitum. There is an outline of a story that keeps things moving along, but it's mostly about the shooting and collecting. Given its core simplicity, it makes for a surprisingly compelling experience. The design is good, and makes for a concincing universe, although the colour pallete consists of various shars of grey and brown, which gets a bit drab after a while. The game provides good value for money: I got 28 hours out of a complete playthorugh (completing the main story and most of the side missions), but the experience gets a bit grindy towards the end, so the game could have benefited from being about 20% shorter. Overall, I enjoyed this game, and would recommend it. I'm looking forward to playing Borderlands 2 next, since this is widely held to be the better experience. Since there is not much story to the first game, one could play the sequal first without missing out on a great deal.

Deceptively difficult puzzles that require a great deal of planning and ingenuity. The game is pretty long, but is paced very will with gradual step ups in difficulty that require different types of problem solving to be employed.
The game is littered with extremely well hidden secrets, satisfying puzzles and easter eggs. It rewards thorough completion and exploration.
My favorite aspect of the game is how much it rewards your ability to think outside the box. For example, I was able to solve 3 of the final 4 puzzles on the final level by effectively cheating the system. I macgyver'd the final level, puzzles I was staring at for an hour to solve the way the game wanted me to, only to solve 3 of them in a matter of 5 minutes by using a trick that the devs didn't plan. But I wasn't punished for it...it worked using mechanics the game used before, and it felt very rewarding to not be told "Nope" just because it wasn't the proper way.
If you like difficult puzzlers, you're doing yourself a great disservice by not playing this.
Pro's
-Story does just enough to keep you interested in what is essentially just a room-to-room puzzle solver
-The back and forth with the library AI is hilarious, especially when you find out what triggers it
-Looks fantastic, the controls are very fluid and fast
-The intricacy and level of detail in not just the puzzles themselves, but the way secrets are hidden is far beyond what most developers are capable of
-Lots of content in the base game, doesn't feel like it starts to drag and is very satisfying if you complete 100% of the puzzles
Con's
-My only real complaint of the game is that sometimes the game does a poor job of explaining how some things work. There is a level on the B world that I'm sure you'll see what I'm talking about...but it's not a huge deal. Once you figure it out, you'll realize you just need to toy with things more often
This was fun, outside of the box... worth the price!

Space Channel 5: Part 2 is the greatest rhythm game ever made.
Whereas literally every other rhythm game ever is merely about watching symbols and icons falling into their place, perfectly playable with the music muted simply just by watching the screen, requiering no actual sense of rhythm, Space Channel 5: Part 2 features ABSOLUTELY NO VISUAL INDICATION of when you are supposed to press the buttons! Space bad guys bust a move in perfect synch to the (awsome, nigh-infinitely varied) background music, and you need to use the arrow keys or the D-Pad to bust those move right back at 'em! If you have no sense of rhythm, if you can't feel the beat of the music, if you can't use it to instantly determine when is the right moment to press buttons, you will fail, and fail hard. Simple as that.
The game, as far as video games have come as of yet, is the medium's ultimate example of merging a game's music in perfect synchronicity with the player's actions. Playing the game is essentially palying an interactive dance flick with occasional musical numbers. A Broadway production in which YOU are the star.
Did I mention that this game looks like whath the future would look like if the sixties never ended? Did I mention that this game ACTUALLY TELLS A STORY? WIth CONFLICT and stuff?
Oh, and did I mention that this game has MICHAEL JACKSON?
There is so much, oh so so so much more to be said about this game, but alas the Steam review section could simply never accomodate for it. Suffice it to say, to this day, there has yet to be a a rhythm game developed that is superior to Space Channel 5: Part 2.
(Some audio had to be cut from the first level of the english language PC and Xbox 360 releases of the game, as the game was originally localized exclusively for the Playstation 2, so the phrases "use the X button to shoot the robots, "when you hear "hey", press the Circle button" and "press the X button when you hear "chu"" would make no sense to players using a keyboard or an Xbox 360 controller, but the fact that Sega provides players with the original japanese voice track upon purchase of the PC version more than makes up for the lack of any newly-recorded audio.)
(Also, the Steam release of the PC version (there is also a boxed retail version of the game available in the "Dreamcast Collection") may have problems writing registry values in Windows so it's possible that the game won't recognize the settings you configure, such as resolution, language etc.. Check the game's community hub for the existing solution to this problem should it occour.)

I am a FPS gamer and mainly stick to the tactical and competative shooter genre. I've never liked or played MOBAs, RPGs,  RTSs, simulators and survival crafting games just wear out after a few hours of playtime. However, Rimworld could be considered an RTS, RPG survival, crafting, game all-in-one and I have dumped 66 hours into it after owning it for 5 days. The most similar game I can compare this to is Dwarf Fortress, but Rimworld is modernized and has a slick coat of paint. This game is very complex and has many different layers and facets to it. It has an active developer who is awesome and each uppdate adds another layer of gameplay. I should also mention that this game has two setting. The "have a laugh and a good time" difficulty settings and the "will kick your♥♥♥♥♥through the roof" difficulty settings. Literally anything, and I mean anything can destroy your colony and ruin your day. This game is also really good at getting you attached to the low-res cartoon Russian nesting dolls that are your colonists. My first successful colony (my third try) lasted four in-game years and then everyone was killed by an insect hive that spawned in my storage room. I almost cried because so much effort had gone into the colony and I wanted to keep on playing with those characters. The bottom line is that this game should go down as one of the greatest indie games ever. BUY IT RIGHT NOW

Wolfenstein is a pretty fun shooter game, with historical fiction elements and a "macho man" protagonist.
I have played it off and on for months now, and still haven't quite finished the main storyline. This is mainly because, while the game is really fun and has some hard choices to make, there are also some parts of the game that even on regular/hard difficulty take forever to work through. I've never died so much in a shooter as I have in Wolfenstein, mainly because its unclear how to beat "super" enemies, and also where to progress. So I ended up trying different weapons and strategies on big enemies and dying dozens of times before finally making it past certain checkpoints. This got very frustrating and is why I have quit playing it for so long.
Nevertheless, this game is still a good one. It has a decent storyline, a pretty exciting beginning, fun guns to shoot, and a really cool "what if" historical situation where the Nazi's have won World War 2. The story and setting are definitely my favorite part about Wolfensteien: TNO even if the gameplay isn't what I like the most. Perhaps others will have better luck with the parts of the games I struggle with.
Overall, this is a good game to try especially on sale. If you're younger I'd strongly suggest waiting as there are straight-up sex scenes in there. Either way be warned. Not a big deal for me.

While this is amusing for the purpose of playing around, it's plagued with bugs, poor coding decisions, and is a right mess. Command keys such as Delete will just stop working randomly, wall placement and movement will randomly decide whether it wants to move the wall, move the wall and everything attached to it, move the wall but angle everything attached to it, et cetera, and object scaling will randomly decide whether to scale only the side you move, or to scale both sides at once. There doesn't appear to be a way to manually enter the scale of objects, and speaking of scale, EVERYTHING in the menus for objects is dead wrong, in terms of scale. Cabinets do not fit standard scale for pretty much anything, every fridge is exactly the size fridges aren't, the doors are all wrong, the stairs are a waking nightmare, and I've yet to see a couch that isn't a bad joke. Wall height can only be adjusted in certain places, and there's no way to cap reduced-height walls, there's no shelf-fill, there's no ceiling option, and "rooms" properly "Fill" the floor and ceiling themselves only about 50% of the time, ultimately filling a floor that cannot be split, so if your "room" initializes improperly across multiple spaces, or a wall is put in after the fact, the wall you attach it to will split, but the floor will not.
Ultimately I think this utility could be interesting. Maybe with a LOT more work, and perhaps a team to go over this sort of thing to ensure proper scaling, and proper fitting of pretty much everything involved(Including fixing the default wall thickness, as only masonry walls typically hit the 8 inch mark). But as it stands right now? It's a cesspit in dire need of a floor-to-ceiling rework.
Assuming the ceiling even fills in properly.

If you haven't heard of the Windows 95 series, "Zoombinis", it's an edutainment game that was suggested for 7 and up. But seriously, an 8 year old would never figure out some of the puzzles on the harder difficulties! It's the kind of things little kids can play, but won't really be able to figure out (i.e. a Rubik's Cube). It might seem like a kids game, and it is directed towards young children, but I feel its better for peple around 13 and up.
Back in the early 2000's, I used to play the original "Zoombinis: A Logical Journey" and I am happy to see a 2015 remake. Heck, when I downloaded this game I didn't even know it was a reboot! It really captures the fun of the original, and I hope to see remakes of other games in the Zoombinis series.
Zoombinis is a problem-solving game in which the end goal is to get all 400 Zoombinis to Zoombiniville. But you can only have up to 16 Zoombinis get there at a time. To get there, you have to complete a series of puzzles that get increasingly harder as you play them over again. They introduce new concepts to each challenge as they get harder.
Overall, buy the game! It's only $4.99, and it's a game you'll spend hours playing! If you are into puzzles and problem-solving, you'll DEFINITELY enjoy this title!

This is the sort of game that you either stomp into oblivion, or struggle vainly against. Having played for a few hours, the skill factor of this game seems nonexistent; there are simply so many enemies on screen that it's impossible to dodge everything, and often enemies spawn from underground beneath you. Now while that may seem like an allure, every death I've experienced has been an instant kill on one hit, making the Stamina stat completely worthless unless you devote an excess of points to leveling it, or get the right items. Doing that won't be an option, however, as you deal out so little damage to enemies that without dumping points into pure attack or swiftness for ranged characters that even though you survive longer, you'll find it impossible to defeat most basic enemies at higher waves.
Here's the paradox, though. Depending on the items you pick up, you'll either become so massively overpowered that the game is trivialized as soon as the first wave of the game, or you'll die before you get your first item. The first item I received was a blood wave which deals so much damage that I haven't seen a single boss on screen for more than about five seconds, which is because of the death animation. I'm on my 90th wave total, and thanks to items, it's now completely implausible that my character will ever be killed by anything other than an intentional effort on my part, and with that, any sense of tension or challenge is gone, and Hero Siege becomes a slog to the end driven by curiosity about what broken item I'll get next.
For the record, if you do buy the game, just play as the archer. From what I've seen, he has the best skills.

A very good and very underrated game in my opinion! I bought Dark Messiah because it is a game related to one of my favorite strategy game franchises; Heroes of Might and Magic. The game itself does not much in common with the strategy ones, apart from the storyline, but the gameplay in general was really satisfying.
The engine allows for some really neat mechanics and physics to be used (and even exploited in some situations) during combat, which is, for me, the best part of the game. The difficulty is trickier than some other first person RPGs I've played - in most situations you can't just click a button and slash through enemy lines, you have to utilize different strategies versus different enemy types. You have to take note of the environment and use it to your advantage!
The story is mediocre, but an easy one to follow. There are a few choices you'd have to make and pick sides as the story progresses which I thought was a neat twist, but again it does not affect the game in a major aspect. I love this game, definitely recommending it!

If you're looking for great singleplayer or expansive online play, look elsewhere.
If you are, instead, looking for something to play with a group of friends, or at parties, it's great for some laughs. The rounds are short enough to cycle losers out, and new challengers in, which keeps everyone involved in a two-player game pretty nicely.
The mechanics of the game are as simple as they can get: You dive (jump) and you kick. There are also two specials (One in the air, one on the ground) which can be activated by hitting both buttons at once. If you get hit, you lose. OHKO. But there is a surprising amount of depth to the play: One character teleports before every move, making him close to unreadable. Another one can go invisible, and a third can kick you through a tear in reality. And on top of this, every character has different jump heights, kick angles, and some can change these numbers in-game. It certainly helps to know your opponent, just as in any standard fighting game.
But again, this is definitely best if you have friends close by that you can play with: It shines in local multiplayer.

(My last review seems to have disappeared, so here we go again...)
I got this game from backing the Kickstarter to revive this game since I loved Zoombinis in my childhood. In fact, I still have the old CD but unfortunately, it doesn't work on my current laptop. I recommend this game overall because the essence of it and the puzzles are still pretty much the same, and that's what really matters. That is not to say that I don't have a few complaints about this game.
My most practical complaint is that you now have to click and hold/drag in order to move the Zoombinis around, which is a pain compared to the old version where you could just click to pick up a Zoombini, move it around without holding any buttons, and click again to set the Zoombini down.
Additionally, the windowed version doesn't fit my screen properly, with the bottom slightly cut off.
I had trouble clicking some of the Zoombinis in the Crystal Caverns in both the windowed and non-windowed versions. It seems to be random at what time and which Zoombinis are hard to pick up. (Also on that level, some of the crystals you can chose from aren't well integrated graphically either. For example, the sneakers stick out. If a crystal is partially behind another crystal, the Zoombini on the back crystal will still show up completely in front of the front crystal, which I guess makes sense since you would want to be able to see the whole Zoombini, but there are far better fixes to that like spacing the crystals apart so they don't overlap in the first place.)
The new background graphics are absolutely gorgeous (I love the little transition drawings, too, nice touch), and the difference between the style of art for the background and the characters doesn't really bother me. What does bother me is that they aren't integrated well in many spots. For example, in the Stone Cold Caves, the Zoombinis don't follow the path exactly-- like for the top left one, the Zoombinis go halfway off the path for upper part. Even worse, there are some parts where the Zoombinis stick out of the background when they aren't supposed to, like when entering doors in Hotel Dimensia or, more noticeably, when traveling through the Crystal Caverns and not going behind any of the support beams. I'm disappointed that with all the effort put into making the game look nicer, mistakes like this would slip through. Also, the Zoombinis look simply shrunken down for the Titanic Tattoooed Toads in an awkwardly pixellated fashion. The font for the Zoombiniville sign looks rather slapped on and not well integrated either.
Most of the sounds are essentially recycled from the first game since the sounds were fortunately high-quality enough to be used again-- which is great because I loved the sounds for the first game. However, they aren't really improved from the first game; there are still awkward overlaps of some audio clips-- like the first time I visited Hotel Dimensia in this remake, the squirrel talked over herself at one point in her introduction. Even worse, some of the sounds that I loved have been taken out. For example, in Mudball Wall, the sound of the mud being sucked up is gone-- and not even neatly taken out, just awkwardly clipped out to my ears-- as are the sounds of the Zoombinis crash-landing and making cute "oof" noises. I would really like all those sounds to be added back in; it's just strange and even discontinuous for only some parts of the mudball making and firing process to make noise but others not to. Additionally, the Mudball Wall sounds now kind of awkwardly overlap when a mudball is being made at the same time that the Zoombinis are being fired over. The only sound I appreciate being gone is the annoying jangling that comes from a spring-footed Zoombini carrying a pizza. (I can't believe pineapples got put in as a topping...)
It's sad that while Mudball Wall's efficiency was awkwardly increased, nothing was done, as far as I could tell, about Bubblewonder Abyss-- it's still as much of a drag to wait for the Zoombinis to drift across as it was before.
Anyway, the game is still fun overall; if you're new to it, you likely won't even find what I complained about to be a problem since a bunch of them are differences between the original and this version. Zoombinis is still something I'd recommend to people young and not-as-young, haha~

On the surface, Divekick is not much of anything - It's a fighting game built on the fundimental premise of jumping and kicking, mixed with humor that really only works on the fighting game community. However, this isn't a game to buy for what it is on the surface.
Underneath the simplistic and honestly lackluster facade is the biggest crash course in fighting game fundimentals you'll ever experience. If you just mash buttons and divekick randomly, you are going to get absoultely murdered. Spacing and mindgames are everything. You need to trick your opponent into making a mistake, and you need to make sure you maintain control of the situation.
Overall, Divekick isn't a good game because of what it is, but because of what it does. It teaches you to play mind games with opponents. It teaches you the importance of making your attacks safe, and above all else, it teaches you the fundimentals of fighting games.
Now, it's time for the breakdown... Oh dear...
Graphics: Love the resolution and the framerate. Hate the jerky animations.
Sound: Nothing to mention.
Story: Fighting games don't lend themselves to storywriting and Divekick is no exception.
Gameplay: Overly simple but at the same time extremely deep.
Recommended for: People who are serious about fighting games.
Not recommended for: People who aren't serious about fighting games.
Bottom line: A fighting game that strips the whole concept of fighting games to their bare minimum, removing the flash and showyness but keeping the fundimentals intact.

So this is kind of like a much less polished version of Piloteer, but with procedurally generated stages. The basic concept is challenging and enjoyable.
Yet this might be the most critical I'll ever be toward a game that I still really like and would recommend.
1. The main criticism is that there's no real sense of progression. The game does keep track of how many levels you've completed, and after a certain number, new concepts are introduced (like the grey areas in which your boosters don't work anymore), but every level is procedurally generated, so you never feel like you've completed a task to be checked off. You just move on to another procedurally-generated level. It kind of leaves you empty. There's also no time-trials or anything either.
[UPDATE (12/23): After completing 100+ levels, I'm not really bothered anymore by the things I mentioned in the previous paragraph. There's some thrill in never knowing what you're going to get next, and I enjoy seeing the number of completed stages keep going up and up (presumably infinitely, lol).]
2. The procedural generation often doesn't make a lot of sense. I regularly experienced stages where it was a straight shot from platform to platform, and the "obstacles" were nowhere near being in my way.
[UPDATE (12/23): This is still true, but I also periodically get stages that truly do feel impossible at first. I even start to wonder if the game accidentally created an unbeatable stage. And it's satisfying when I figure out a way to beat them after all.]
3. The sound is pretty bad. The only sound you hear is the jet-boosting of the ship, which literally sounds like television static.
But other than these things, great little game! :)
